Fare estimation, final fare and surge

The upfront estimate comes from the routing provider's predicted distance and duration, the city's pricing rule set, and the surge multiplier for the pickup cell, all frozen into quote_snapshot. The final fare is computed at completion from what actually happened:

// pricing/fare-calculator.service.ts
export function computeFare(trip: CompletedTrip, rules: PricingRules): FareBreakdown {
  const distanceFare = (trip.distanceM / 1000) * rules.perKm;
  const timeFare     = (trip.durationS / 60) * rules.perMinute;
  const waitingFare  = Math.max(0, trip.waitingS - rules.freeWaitS) / 60 * rules.perWaitMinute;

  // Surge applies to the variable portion only, never to tolls or taxes, and uses the
  // multiplier locked at quote time so the rider is never charged more than they agreed.
  const variable = (rules.baseFare + distanceFare + timeFare + waitingFare) * trip.surgeLocked;
  const beforeMin = Math.max(variable, rules.minimumFare);
  const afterPromo = Math.max(0, beforeMin - trip.promotionAmount);

  const tax        = round2(afterPromo * rules.taxRate);
  const total      = round2(afterPromo + trip.tolls + tax + trip.tip);
  const commission = round2(afterPromo * rules.commissionRate);
  const driver     = round2(afterPromo - commission + trip.tolls + trip.tip);
  return { distanceFare, timeFare, waitingFare, surge: trip.surgeLocked, tax, total, commission, driver,
           pricingVersion: rules.version };
}

pricing_version is stored on the fare row so a rule change never makes an old fare unreproducible. Recomputing a three-month-old fare with today's rules is the ride-booking equivalent of recomputing an old order total, and it is equally wrong.

Surge is computed per H3 cell every 60 seconds from open requests versus available drivers, then damped and smoothed exactly as in the food delivery design, with three additional guards specific to this domain: a hard cap set per city by regulation, a floor of 1.0, and a minimum dwell time of 5 minutes at any level. Without dwell time, surge oscillates: the multiplier rises, riders stop requesting, demand collapses, the multiplier drops, riders return, it spikes again. Riders experience that as the app playing games with them, and it is one of the most reputationally damaging bugs in the product. Surge is also always shown before commitment and locked into the quote, so an oscillation can never change the price of a trip already agreed.

Payments and the ledger

Money moves in three steps. At match, the rider's payment method is authorized for the upper bound of the estimate. At completion, the actual fare is captured (a partial capture of the authorization). Afterwards, the fare is posted to the ledger as a set of double-entry transfers.

// ledger/ledger.service.ts
async postTripFare(fare: Fare, tripId: string): Promise<void> {
  const transferId = uuidv5(tripId, TRIP_FARE_NAMESPACE);   // deterministic: retries post once
  const rows = [
    { account: acc('rider', fare.riderId),      dir: 'DR', amount: fare.totalAmount },
    { account: acc('driver', fare.driverId),    dir: 'CR', amount: fare.driverEarnings },
    { account: acc('platform', fare.cityId),    dir: 'CR', amount: fare.commissionAmount },
    { account: acc('tax', fare.jurisdiction),   dir: 'CR', amount: fare.taxAmount },
  ];
  const debits  = sum(rows.filter((r) => r.dir === 'DR'));
  const credits = sum(rows.filter((r) => r.dir === 'CR'));
  if (debits !== credits) throw new Error(`unbalanced transfer ${transferId}: ${debits} vs ${credits}`);

  await this.ds.transaction(async (m) => {
    for (const r of rows) {
      await m.query(
        `INSERT INTO ledger_entries (transfer_id, account_id, direction, amount, currency, ref_type, ref_id)
         VALUES ($1,$2,$3,$4,$5,'trip',$6)
         ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`,                            // idempotent under retry
        [transferId, r.account, r.dir, r.amount, fare.currency, tripId]);
    }
  });
}

The rules that make a ledger trustworthy: entries are never updated or deleted (corrections are new balancing transfers), every transfer balances and the code refuses to write one that does not, a balance is always sum(CR) - sum(DR) over the account (materialised into a snapshot row per account per day so the sum is bounded), and posting is idempotent through a deterministic transfer_id. Payouts are a separate transfer type: a weekly job computes each driver's balance, creates a payout transfer that debits the driver account and credits a payout-clearing account, and only then calls the bank. If the bank call fails, the transfer is reversed with an explicit compensating transfer, never by deleting rows.

Cash markets invert the flow: the driver collects the fare directly, so the ledger debits the driver's account for the platform's commission, and the driver's balance goes negative until they settle. That is the same machinery with different signs, which is exactly why a real ledger beats a driver_balance column.

Ratings and safety

Ratings are collected from both sides after completion, stored per trip, and aggregated into a rolling average over the last 100 trips (so a driver can recover from a bad month). Ratings below a threshold trigger a review, never an automatic ban, because a single hostile rider can otherwise end someone's livelihood.

Safety features are engineered as a separate path with independent capacity:

  • SOS posts to a dedicated endpoint that writes to its own small database and pages the safety team within seconds, and it works even when the main trip service is degraded, because it depends on nothing except the location cache and its own store.
  • Trip sharing produces a signed, expiring URL that renders live position and ETA to anyone with the link, with no authentication and no PII beyond a first name and vehicle plate.
  • Ride check watches every in-progress trip for anomalies: a long unexpected stop, a large route deviation, a trip that has not moved for 10 minutes, or a sudden end far from the destination. It sends an in-app check-in to both parties and escalates to the safety team on no response.
  • Retention for safety is longer than for anything else: trip breadcrumbs and audio recordings (where enabled and consented) are retained for the legally mandated period in a separately-encrypted store with break-glass access that is logged and reviewed.

40.11.10 Database design

The database is sharded by city from day one, because 9.1 billion trip rows a year cannot live in one cluster and because cities are naturally independent. Cities are grouped so each shard carries a similar load, and the mapping lives in a small configuration table replicated to every service; a city can be moved between shards during a maintenance window by a copy-and-cutover procedure.

Within a shard, trips, trip_events, driver_locations and ledger_entries are all range-partitioned by time: trips monthly (retain 24 months, then S3 Parquet), trip_events monthly (retain 3 months hot), driver_locations daily (retain 3 days), ledger_entries monthly (retained for the legal period, typically 7 to 10 years, because financial records do not get archived away as casually as telemetry).

The ledger lives in its own cluster, not a shard of the trip database. Reasons: different retention, different access control (finance and auditors, not engineers), different consistency posture (no eventual anything), and different growth profile. Cross-referencing a trip to its ledger entries is a ref_id lookup, not a join, and that is fine because it happens in support tooling, not on a hot path.

The query that decides whether the driver app feels fast:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, state, rider_id, pickup, requested_at
FROM trips
WHERE driver_id = $1
  AND state IN ('MATCHED','ARRIVING','ARRIVED','IN_PROGRESS')
  AND requested_at > now() - interval '12 hours';
Append  (cost=0.56..16.62 rows=1 width=96) (actual time=0.048..0.071 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using trips_2026_09_driver_idx on trips_2026_09
        (cost=0.56..16.61 rows=1 width=96) (actual time=0.047..0.049 rows=1 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((driver_id = 'd41c...'::uuid) AND (requested_at > (now() - '12:00:00'::interval)))
        Filter: (state = ANY ('{MATCHED,ARRIVING,ARRIVED,IN_PROGRESS}'::trip_state[]))
        Buffers: shared hit=5
Planning Time: 0.331 ms
Execution Time: 0.104 ms

Five buffer hits and a tenth of a millisecond, because the partition pruning from requested_at and the leading driver_id column do all the work. The same query without the time bound would touch 24 partitions and cost 30x more planning time for an identical result, which is why every hot query in this system is written with a time bound whether it strictly needs one or not.

One more decision worth stating: trips is not partitioned by city_id inside a shard. City is already the shard key, so partitioning by it again just multiplies partition count. Time is the dimension that determines what is hot, so time is the partition key.

40.11.11 Caching

What Where TTL Invalidation Notes
Driver current state and position Redis hash drv:{city}:{driverId} 60 s sliding Overwritten every 2 to 4 s Live state, not a cache; the TTL is the liveness check
Cell membership sets Redis set cell:{city}:{h3} none, maintained by moves SREM on move, offline or match The supply index
Surge per cell Redis surge:{city}:{h3} 90 s Recomputed every 60 s Missing means 1.0
Route ETA between cell pairs Redis, keyed by origin cell, destination cell and 15-minute bucket 10 min Time Cuts routing-provider spend by about 80 percent
Active trip snapshot Redis JSON trip:{id}:live life of the trip plus 10 min Updated on every transition Serves socket reconnects with no database read
Rider and driver profile summary Redis, 15 min 15 min Deleted on profile or rating update Read on every offer and every trip screen
Pricing rules per city In-process map, refreshed every 60 s 60 s Pub/sub on change Read on every quote and every fare computation
Driver account balance snapshot Ledger database materialised daily, plus Redis for the current day 5 min On every posting Avoids summing a partitioned ledger on every app open

The trip snapshot cache deserves a note. Mobile clients on poor networks reconnect constantly, and each reconnect wants the full current state. Without a cache, 1.46 million sockets reconnecting during a network blip would produce a million database reads in a few seconds. With trip:{id}:live maintained on every transition, a reconnect is a single Redis GET.

40.11.12 Messaging

Topic Key Partitions Events Consumers
driver.locations cityCode (sharded for large cities) 400 Location pings Tracking gateways, location writer, spoof detector, supply analytics
trip.events trip_id 120 TripRequested, TripMatched, DriverArrived, TripStarted, TripCompleted, TripCancelled Matching, payments, notifications, safety, analytics
match.events trip_id 60 OfferSent, OfferAccepted, OfferDeclined, OfferExpired, RoundExhausted Matching metrics, driver scoring, ops
payment.events trip_id 60 Authorized, AuthFailed, Captured, CaptureFailed, Refunded Trip service, ledger, collections
ledger.events account_id 60 TransferPosted, PayoutInitiated, PayoutSettled, PayoutFailed Driver app, finance warehouse
safety.events trip_id 12 SosRaised, RideCheckTriggered, AnomalyDetected Safety console, paging
*.dlq Poison messages On-call

driver.locations uses acks=1, no compression on the produce path (the payloads are already protobuf and tiny; compression costs more CPU than it saves bandwidth at this message size), and a short linger.ms of 5 to batch without adding perceptible latency. Everything financial uses acks=all, the transactional outbox, and consumers that are idempotent by a deterministic key.

safety.events gets its own small topic with a dedicated consumer group and its own alerting, so a consumer lag incident on the 400-partition location topic cannot delay an SOS. Separating the critical low-volume path from the high-volume path is a pattern worth copying anywhere a life-safety or money-safety signal shares infrastructure with telemetry.

40.11.13 Scaling

At 1x (833 trips per second, 175,000 location updates per second, 1.46M sockets). 200 API pods, 82 tracking gateway pods, 40 location gateway pods, 6 PostgreSQL city-shard clusters plus 1 ledger cluster, an 8-shard Redis Cluster per region, Kafka with 400 location partitions. Matching runs as a per-city consumer group.

At 10x (8,300 trips per second, 1.75 million location updates per second, 14 million sockets). This is planetary scale and the changes are structural:

  • Location ingest moves entirely to a persistent binary protocol (gRPC bidirectional streams or MQTT) terminated at regional edges, with adaptive ping intervals (2 s on trip, 4 s idle and moving, 20 s idle and stationary). Stationary detection alone removes about 35 percent of the volume, since a large fraction of idle drivers are parked.
  • Matching becomes a stateful in-memory service, one owner per city, holding the entire supply index in process and rebuilding from Kafka on failover. A scoring pass over 40,000 drivers takes under 15 ms in memory versus 20 ms of Redis round trips plus deserialisation, and it makes batch matching (below) feasible.
  • Redis stops being the query path and becomes the recovery and cross-pod-visibility path.
  • City shards multiply to 40 or more clusters, and the shard map becomes a real control-plane service with online migration.
  • Tracking gateways partition by city so each pod consumes only relevant Kafka partitions, and the fan-out uses a shared-nothing routing layer rather than every pod seeing every message.
flowchart TB
    subgraph Region
      EDGE["Edge ingest: gRPC streams"] --> KL["Kafka driver.locations 400 parts"]
      KL --> MP["Matching pod per city, in-memory H3 index"]
      KL --> TG["Tracking gateways per city"]
      MP --> SH1[("City shard 1")]
      MP --> SH2[("City shard 2")]
      API["Trip APIs"] --> SH1
      API --> SH2
    end
    SH1 --> CDC["CDC stream"]
    SH2 --> CDC
    CDC --> LED[("Global ledger cluster")]
    CDC --> DW["Warehouse and ML feature store"]
    GLB["Global control plane: shard map, pricing policy, fraud models"] --> MP
    GLB --> API

At 100x. The interesting constraint stops being throughput and becomes blast radius and locality. Each region is fully self-sufficient: its own Kafka, its own Redis, its own shards, its own matching, its own tracking. Nothing is globally synchronous except the shard map and the identity system, both of which are read-mostly and cached everywhere. The ledger federates by currency and jurisdiction because data residency laws require it anyway. And the biggest engineering investment moves from serving traffic to matching quality: at that scale, a one percent improvement in matching efficiency is worth more than the entire infrastructure budget, which is why mature platforms replace greedy matching with batch optimisation over 3 to 5 second windows.

40.11.14 Security

  • Location privacy. A driver's live position is visible to a matched rider and to ops, and to nobody else. Idle-driver positions are never exposed through any public API, including the "cars near you" animation, which shows synthetic markers derived from aggregate supply rather than real driver positions. Historic tracks require a case id and are access-logged.
  • Rider address exposure. The driver sees the pickup on match and the dropoff only at trip start. Phone numbers are proxied through masked calling. Home and work labels are never sent to the driver app.
  • GPS spoofing. Detection combines implausible speed between consecutive points, teleportation beyond what elapsed time allows, mock-location flags from the OS, accuracy values that are too perfect, inconsistency between GPS and cell-tower or Wi-Fi positioning, and a fingerprint of the reporting cadence (spoofers tend to be metronomic where real GPS jitters). Response is graduated: shadow-suppress from matching, require a selfie identity check, then human review. Instant bans are avoided because tunnels, urban canyons and cheap GPS chips produce the same signals.
  • Account takeover. Driver accounts are targets because they hold a payout balance. Payout destination changes require re-authentication, a cooling-off period, and a notification to the previous contact details.
  • Fake trips and collusion. A driver and a colluding rider can run trips that never happened to farm incentives. Controls: telemetry must be consistent with the claimed route, repeated pairs are flagged, incentive payouts are held for review above a threshold, and payment method reuse across accounts is a strong signal.
  • Idempotency and replay. Every state-changing endpoint validates the trip's state and the caller's role; a driver cannot complete a trip they are not on, and a replayed complete call is a no-op rather than a second fare.
  • Ledger access control. Only the ledger service may write postings, the database role has no UPDATE or DELETE grant on ledger_entries, and all reads by humans go through an audited tool.
  • Data residency. Trips and locations stay in the region where they occur; cross-region access is through aggregated, de-identified extracts.
  • SOS integrity. The SOS endpoint cannot be rate limited into uselessness, but it also cannot be a denial-of-service vector, so it is rate limited per account at a generous level (one per 60 seconds) and its capacity is reserved separately from the main API.

40.11.15 Failure scenarios

Can it time out, fail, slow down, duplicate, return something wrong, or partially succeed? Every row below is a real incident class.

Failure Detection Impact Mitigation What the user sees
Driver app goes offline mid-trip No location for 60 s while IN_PROGRESS; status hash TTL expires Rider's map freezes; trip cannot be completed by the driver The trip stays IN_PROGRESS (never auto-cancelled); the rider's app shows "connection lost, last seen 90 s ago" honestly; the driver app buffers events locally and replays them on reconnect with original timestamps; if the driver never returns, ops completes the trip from the last known position and the fare is computed from the breadcrumbs already received An honest stale indicator, then a fare computed from real data
Double match (two drivers accept one trip) Normal race, counted per city Two drivers drive to one pickup; one is unpaid and furious Redis Lua claims trip and driver atomically; PostgreSQL WHERE driver_id IS NULL is the independent second gate; the loser is told in under 500 ms and stays in the pool The losing driver sees "taken" before they start driving
One driver accepts two trips Same Lua script, driver key Driver double-booked, one rider stranded The script claims the driver key as well as the trip key; the second claim fails Second offer shows "no longer available"
GPS spoofing Speed, teleportation, mock-location flag, sensor inconsistency, cadence fingerprint Fake supply, farmed incentives, fraudulent trips Graduated response: shadow-suppress from matching, identity re-check, human review; incentive payouts held pending review Genuine drivers occasionally get an identity check; spoofers stop receiving offers
Surge oscillation Variance of the multiplier per cell over 15 minutes Prices flicker; riders feel manipulated; demand becomes unstable Exponential smoothing, a maximum change of 0.2 per minute, a 5-minute minimum dwell, a per-city regulatory cap, and the multiplier locked into the quote A stable price that changes slowly and never after they agreed
Payment fails after the trip completed Capture failure event Service delivered, money not collected; the driver must still be paid The trip completes regardless (never hold a rider in the car for a payment problem); the fare is posted to the ledger, the driver is credited, and the rider's account carries an outstanding balance; retry the capture with backoff over 7 days, then try a backup payment method, then collections; the rider cannot request a new trip until it is settled "There was a problem with your payment", a retry prompt, and a blocked next request until fixed
Payment authorization fails at match Auth decline Trip should not start Authorization happens at match, before the driver drives; on decline the trip is cancelled with no fee and the rider is asked for another method "Payment method declined" within seconds, before a driver is dispatched
No driver accepts after 4 rounds RoundExhausted events Rider waits and gives up Widen the search rings, raise the driver incentive automatically, and after 120 s cancel with CANCELLED_NO_DRIVER, apologise and offer a scheduled ride "No drivers available right now", with alternatives, rather than an endless spinner
Redis Cluster shard failover Topology change, error rate The supply index for those cities is empty Drivers re-register their cell on the next ping, so the index rebuilds in 2 to 4 seconds; matching retries with backoff and, if still empty, falls back to a PostGIS query over driver_locations breadcrumbs Match takes a few seconds longer
Location gateway saturation at peak Event-loop lag, ingest p99 Stale positions, degraded matching, frozen maps Aggressive HPA, adaptive ping intervals, and load shedding that drops stationary idle drivers first and never drops on-trip pings Nothing for riders on a trip
Kafka lag on driver.locations Consumer lag Tracking maps behind reality Tracking consumers seek to the latest offset and skip the backlog: freshness beats completeness for a live map; the writer catches up independently The map jumps to the current position
Duplicate complete call from a retrying driver app Same trip, already COMPLETED Would double-charge and double-post the ledger The state machine makes a same-state transition a no-op; the ledger posting uses a deterministic transfer_id with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING Nothing
Ops or a bug moves a trip to an illegal state illegal_transition counter Trip stuck or wrongly completed The transition table rejects it; ops overrides require a reason and are audited; a repair tool replays trip_events to rebuild state Nothing, or a short support-assisted fix
City shard primary failover Write errors Requests fail in that city for 30 to 90 s Multi-AZ, PgBouncer reconnect, 503 with Retry-After; in-progress trips continue because the driver app buffers events locally and replays them New requests fail briefly; ongoing trips are unaffected
Routing provider outage or rate limit Error rate, quota alarm No ETAs, no upfront fares Fall back to straight-line distance times a learned city road factor and a learned speed for this hour; mark quotes as estimates with a wider band Slightly less precise ETAs and a wider fare range
Clock skew between a phone and the server Timestamps in the future or far past Wrong durations, wrong speeds, wrong fares Server timestamps are authoritative for fare-affecting events; client timestamps are only used for ordering within a batch and are clamped to a sane window Nothing
Ledger posting unbalanced due to a code bug The service refuses to write, error metric Fare not posted, driver not credited The balance assertion throws before any write; the event goes to a DLQ; a replay tool reposts after the fix; drivers see the amount as pending, not lost "Pending" earnings that settle after the fix

40.11.16 Observability

  1. match_time_to_match_seconds histogram per city and vehicle class. p95 above 20 s is a page; it is the number the whole business is judged on.
  2. match_rounds_per_trip and trips_unmatched_total. Rising values mean a supply problem, which is answered with incentives, not a rollback.
  3. offer_acceptance_rate per city and driver cohort. A sudden drop is usually a driver-app release or a fee change.
  4. double_match_total. Any non-zero value pages immediately.
  5. location_ingest_rate, location_gateway_event_loop_lag_seconds, supply_index_size per city. A falling index size with a flat online-driver count means the index is losing entries.
  6. tracking_push_latency_seconds (Kafka timestamp to socket write) and tracking_ws_connections.
  7. trip_state_stuck_total by state with per-state thresholds; ARRIVED for over 15 minutes and IN_PROGRESS for over 3 hours are the two that matter most.
  8. fare_dispute_rate and fare_recompute_mismatch_total (a job that recomputes a sample of yesterday's fares from stored inputs and compares). Any mismatch is a P1.
  9. ledger_unbalanced_total (must be zero), ledger_posting_lag_seconds, payout_failed_total.
  10. payment_capture_failure_rate and outstanding_balance_total per city.
  11. surge_multiplier gauge and surge_change_rate per cell, plus a "cells at cap" count.
  12. sos_to_ack_seconds. This has the tightest alert threshold in the system.

Traces cover a trip end to end with tripId and cityCode as span attributes, and sampling is tail-based on outcome: 100 percent of trips that end in CANCELLED_NO_DRIVER, a dispute, a payment failure or an SOS, and 0.1 percent of the rest. A 20-minute trace with 200 spans is expensive to keep for 25 million trips a day and invaluable for the few thousand that go wrong.

The ops console is again the most useful tool: a live per-city map with supply, demand, surge cells, unmatched requests and stuck trips, plus a "trip inspector" that replays trip_events and breadcrumbs side by side. Most support and safety work happens there, and the quality of that tool determines how fast a city team can respond to anything.

40.11.17 Deployment

Workload Kind Replicas Notes
trip-api Deployment 60 to 200 Per region; blocked from deploying during local peak hours
pricing-api Deployment 20 to 60 Stateless, cache-heavy
location-gateway Deployment 40 to 120 Persistent connections; terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 90; scales on event-loop lag
tracking-gateway Deployment 82 to 200 WebSocket; staggered reconnect on preStop; 15 percent surge cap on rollouts
matching StatefulSet 1 owner plus 1 standby per city City lease in Redis with a 5 s TTL; standby rebuilds from Kafka in under 10 s
offer-expiry-worker Deployment 4 SKIP LOCKED over match_offers
location-writer Deployment 12 Polylines to S3, downsampled breadcrumbs to daily partitions
payments Deployment 10 Authorize, capture, retry with exponential backoff
ledger Deployment 6 Own database, own on-call rotation shared with finance
payout-worker CronJob weekly per country 1 Balances, transfers, bank files
surge-calculator Deployment with a 60 s tick 1 per region Writes Redis keys with TTL
safety-consumer Deployment 4 Dedicated group, dedicated alerting
partition-maker CronJob daily 1 per shard 14 days of driver_locations, 60 days of monthly partitions

Two deployment rules earn their keep. First, in-progress trips must survive every deploy: the driver app buffers state changes locally and replays them with original timestamps, so a 40-second gap in API availability produces no lost trips and no lost fares. This is tested in staging with a chaos job that kills every trip-api pod during synthetic trips. Second, deploys are blocked during local peak hours per region, enforced in the pipeline, and the matching StatefulSet is deployed one city at a time with an automatic pause if match_time_to_match_seconds regresses.

Migrations use expand-migrate-contract, run per shard, and are validated on the smallest city shard first. A migration that takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on trips is never acceptable; every DDL is checked for lock level in review, and SET lock_timeout = '3s' is set for all migration sessions so a blocked migration fails fast instead of queueing every query behind it.

40.11.18 Cost considerations

Item Sizing Monthly (USD, approximate)
PostgreSQL city shards 6 clusters, db.r6g.8xlarge Multi-AZ plus readers 26,000
Ledger cluster db.r6g.4xlarge Multi-AZ plus reader, long retention 3,000
Storage and backups 40 TB gp3 across shards plus PITR 6,000
Redis Cluster 3 regions x 8 shards cache.r6g.2xlarge with replicas 9,500
Kafka (MSK) 3 regions x 9 brokers kafka.m5.2xlarge, 60 TB 18,000
EKS compute about 1,800 vCPU average 42,000
Network egress and cross-AZ 320,000 tracking messages per second plus replication 12,000
S3 for polylines and archives 38 GB per day growing, lifecycle to Glacier 900
Maps, routing and traffic provider about 3 calls per trip x 25M trips x 0.003 USD 67,500
Payment processing 2.4 percent of gross bookings far larger than everything above
Total infrastructure about 185,000

The same lesson as the delivery design, only louder: the routing provider costs more than any individual infrastructure line, and payment processing dwarfs the entire technology budget. The highest-leverage engineering projects at this scale are therefore an in-house routing engine on OpenStreetMap data (which typically pays back within a year at this volume), smarter payment routing per country, and reducing failed captures, because each of those moves a number that is measured in millions rather than thousands. It is worth internalising early: a senior engineer reads the cloud bill and the vendor invoices before deciding what to optimise.

40.11.19 Tradeoffs

  • H3 cells in Redis rather than PostGIS for supply. Sub-millisecond candidate queries at 175,000 writes per second, at the cost of a second geospatial system, a discretisation error at cell boundaries (mitigated by searching a ring), and a supply index that is rebuilt rather than durable.
  • Offer to three drivers with a 15-second timeout. Faster matching and higher acceptance, at the cost of two drivers being told "taken", which erodes trust if the count is too high; tuned per city by acceptance rate.
  • Redis arbitration with a PostgreSQL gate. Fast plus provably correct, at the cost of two systems that can disagree and code that must resolve the disagreement in favour of the database.
  • Upfront fare locked at quote time. Riders get certainty and surge cannot bite them mid-trip; the platform absorbs the risk when a trip takes far longer than estimated, which is a real cost paid deliberately for trust.
  • Trip completes even when payment fails. Nobody is held in a car over a declined card; the platform carries collection risk and a small fraction becomes bad debt.
  • A real double-entry ledger instead of balance columns. More tables, more code, an extra service and a finance-owned schema, in exchange for money that always adds up, corrections that are auditable, and disputes that can be answered.
  • Raw locations never in PostgreSQL. 500 GB a day of write load avoided, at the cost of forensic replay depending on S3 and downsampled breadcrumbs rather than every point.
  • City sharding from day one. Cross-city queries move to the warehouse and a shard map must be operated, in exchange for a blast radius of one city group and linear scaling.

40.11.20 Alternative architectures

Batch matching over a short window instead of greedy per-request matching. Collect all open requests and all available drivers for 3 to 5 seconds, then solve a global assignment problem (min-cost bipartite matching, or a min-cost flow when pooling is involved). In dense conditions this reduces total pickup distance by 10 to 20 percent, raises driver utilisation, and makes shared rides genuinely tractable, because pooling is an optimisation problem that greedy matching cannot express. It wins at high density and at peak, where dozens of requests and hundreds of drivers are in play at once. It loses in thin markets, where waiting 4 seconds to batch a single request just adds 4 seconds to a rider standing in the rain, and it is much harder to build, tune, explain and debug: "why did I not get the ride 100 metres away" has no simple answer when the answer is a global optimum. The mature approach is adaptive: greedy below a density threshold, batch above it, decided per cell per minute.

A stateless matching service using only Redis, versus a stateful in-memory matcher per city. The design above starts stateless because it is far easier to operate: pods are interchangeable, a crash costs nothing, and scaling is an HPA setting. The stateful alternative holds the full city supply index in process, which removes tens of milliseconds of Redis round trips per round, makes complex scoring and batch matching cheap, and is where every large platform eventually arrives. It costs leader election, lease management, state rebuild from Kafka, careful memory budgeting and a much higher operational bar. Move to it when profiling shows the geospatial query path dominates match latency, not because the diagram looks more sophisticated.

Buy the marketplace: a white-label ride-hailing platform, or run on a managed geospatial and matching stack. Several vendors sell the whole stack, and managed services (a geospatial database with built-in indexing, a managed matching engine, a payments platform with driver payouts and tax handling built in) can replace large chunks of this design. It wins decisively for a startup entering one or two cities: time to market drops from a year to weeks, regulatory and payout complexity comes bundled, and the engineering team can be five people instead of fifty. It loses when matching quality becomes the competitive advantage, when per-trip vendor fees start scaling with success (they always do), when local regulation demands custom behaviour the vendor will not build, and when the data needed to improve the product lives in someone else's system. The pattern that repeats across this industry is: buy to launch, then rebuild the matching engine first (because it drives unit economics), the pricing engine second, and the ledger third, leaving payments and mapping as vendor relationships for far longer.

40.12 Social Media Feed

40.12.1 Requirements

A social media feed is the screen a user opens first: a list of recent posts from the accounts they follow, newest or most interesting first, refreshed every time they pull down. Behind that simple list is one of the most instructive problems in backend engineering, because the naive implementation ("select posts from people I follow, order by time, limit 20") is correct, obvious, and completely unusable at scale.

The users are two groups with opposite needs. Readers want the feed to open in under 200 ms, always, on a phone with three bars of signal. Writers want their post to appear for their followers within seconds. Between them sits a fan-out problem: one write from a writer must become visible in millions of readers' feeds, and one read from a reader must merge content from hundreds of writers.

Imagine a newspaper delivery service in a city. Option one: every morning the printing press prints a personalised paper for every subscriber and a van delivers it to their door. Reading is instant (the paper is already on the doormat), but printing is enormous work, and when a very popular columnist writes something, the press must print fifty million copies of that column. Option two: nobody delivers anything. When you want to read, you walk to every columnist's office and collect their latest pages yourself. Writing is free, but reading takes an hour. Every real feed system is a mix: deliver the papers for ordinary columnists, and let readers pick up the famous ones on the way in. That mix is the hybrid fan-out, and the rest of this design is the machinery that makes it work.

40.12.2 Functional requirements

  1. A user can follow and unfollow another user; follows may require approval for private accounts.
  2. A user can create a post with text up to 2,000 characters and up to four images or one video, and can delete it.
  3. A user's home feed shows posts from the accounts they follow, newest first, with cursor-based pagination.
  4. A user's profile timeline shows only their own posts, newest first.
  5. A user can like and unlike a post, and comment on a post. Both show counts.
  6. Counts (likes, comments, reposts) are shown on every post in the feed.
  7. Blocked users' content never appears; private accounts' posts appear only to approved followers.
  8. Deleting a post removes it from every feed, including feeds already materialised.
  9. Media is uploaded directly to object storage and served from a CDN.
  10. The feed supports two ranking modes: strictly chronological, and a scored "For you" ranking.

40.12.3 Non-functional requirements

Property Target Why
Feed read latency p50 under 80 ms, p99 under 250 ms server-side The first screen decides whether the app feels alive
Post visibility lag p95 under 5 s for ordinary accounts, under 60 s for accounts with millions of followers Users refresh right after posting and expect to see it
Availability of reads 99.99 percent A feed that does not load is an outage in the news
Availability of writes 99.9 percent A failed post is annoying but recoverable by retry
Consistency of the feed Eventual, seconds Nobody can tell whether a post arrived 2 s or 5 s ago
Consistency of privacy Strong. A blocked or private post must never leak This is a trust and legal boundary, not a cache concern
Counter accuracy Approximate above 1,000, exact below "12.4K likes" is fine; "3 likes" must be right
Durability of posts No post ever lost once acknowledged PostgreSQL is the source of truth, feeds are derived

40.12.4 Constraints

  • Existing stack: NestJS on Kubernetes, PostgreSQL (Aurora), Redis Cluster (ElastiCache), Kafka (MSK), S3 plus CloudFront.
  • Team of twelve; no capacity to run a custom storage engine. Everything must be managed AWS or a well-known open-source component.
  • Mobile clients on flaky networks, so every read must be retry-safe and every write must accept a client-supplied idempotency key.
  • Regulatory: deletion must be honoured within 30 days across all derived stores, including feeds and analytics.
  • Budget target under 60,000 USD per month at the modelled scale.

That last row is the whole argument. Fan-out on write for the top accounts does not merely cost money; it makes the cluster unable to keep up with itself, and while it is busy the ordinary users' posts queue behind it. So the top accounts must be pulled at read time.

148,000 small reads per second across 20 shards is 7,400 per shard: nothing. The hybrid moves 1.4 billion daily writes into 148,000 cheap, highly cacheable reads per second.

CDN egress is the largest single line in the bill, which is why thumbnails are aggressively sized and why the feed returns image URLs rather than bytes.

POST /v1/blocks { targetUserId } 201 Yes User token

Two API decisions deserve a note. Likes use PUT and DELETE rather than POST /like and POST /unlike because a like is a state, not an event: a client that retries PUT three times on a bad network must end with exactly one like, and PUT says that in the protocol. And the feed uses a cursor, never an offset. The cursor is an opaque base64 of (score, postId); the server decodes it into WHERE (score, post_id) < ($1, $2) or a Redis ZREVRANGEBYSCORE upper bound. Offsets break in a feed because rows are inserted at the head constantly: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40 on a moving list shows the reader duplicates and skips items.

CREATE TABLE users (
  id             uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  handle         citext NOT NULL,
  display_name   text NOT NULL,
  is_private     boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  follower_count integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,   -- denormalised; drives the push/pull decision
  created_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_handle_uidx ON users (handle);         -- serves login and @mention lookup

CREATE TABLE follows (
  follower_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  followee_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  state       text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active' CHECK (state IN ('active','pending')),
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id)                          -- serves "do I follow X" and "who do I follow"
);
CREATE INDEX follows_followee_idx ON follows (followee_id, follower_id)
  WHERE state = 'active';                                         -- serves fan-out: "who follows the author"

CREATE TABLE posts (
  id          bigint PRIMARY KEY,               -- Snowflake id: time-ordered, so id sorts like created_at
  author_id   uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  body        text NOT NULL CHECK (length(body) <= 2000),
  visibility  text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'public' CHECK (visibility IN ('public','followers')),
  reply_to_id bigint,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  deleted_at  timestamptz
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);
CREATE INDEX posts_author_idx ON posts (author_id, id DESC) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
  -- serves the profile timeline and the pull half of the hybrid feed

CREATE TABLE likes (
  post_id    bigint NOT NULL,
  user_id    uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (post_id, user_id)                                   -- makes a double-like a no-op, not a duplicate
) PARTITION BY HASH (post_id);

CREATE TABLE post_counters (
  post_id  bigint NOT NULL,
  shard    smallint NOT NULL CHECK (shard BETWEEN 0 AND 15),
  likes    bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  comments bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  PRIMARY KEY (post_id, shard)                                     -- 16 rows per post spread lock contention
);

feed_entries exists in PostgreSQL as a durable backup of the materialised feed, but it is written only for a sampled subset of users and for accounts whose feed we want to rebuild cheaply. The live feed lives in Redis.

CREATE TABLE feed_entries (
  user_id   uuid NOT NULL,
  post_id   bigint NOT NULL,
  author_id uuid NOT NULL,
  score     bigint NOT NULL,                    -- snowflake id for chrono, ranking score for 'for you'
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, score DESC, post_id)    -- serves keyset pagination on rebuild
) PARTITION BY HASH (user_id);

Posts are partitioned by month, which makes retention a DETACH PARTITION instead of a 3-billion-row DELETE, and keeps each index small enough to stay in memory. Likes and feed entries are partitioned by hash because there is no time-based access pattern for them, only per-key lookups, and hash partitioning spreads the write load evenly across 32 partitions instead of hammering the tail of one index.

Post ids are Snowflake-style 64-bit integers: 41 bits of millisecond timestamp, 10 bits of worker id, 12 bits of sequence. This matters more than it looks. A time-ordered integer id means the feed's sort key, the pagination cursor and the primary key are the same value, so ORDER BY id DESC needs no extra index, cursors are 8 bytes, and Redis sorted-set scores can hold the id directly.

The read path and the write path touch almost nothing in common, which is deliberate. A write goes to PostgreSQL, then to Kafka, and returns. A read goes to Redis, and only touches PostgreSQL when Redis has nothing. The two paths can be scaled, deployed and broken independently.

The heart of the design is one decision made per post: push or pull.

// fanout/fanout.worker.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { FollowerPageService } from './follower-page.service';
import { FeedStoreService } from '../feed/feed-store.service';

const PUSH_THRESHOLD = 10_000;   // above this follower count we do not fan out on write
const PAGE = 2_000;              // follower ids per batch, one Redis pipeline per batch

@Injectable()
export class FanoutWorker {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(FanoutWorker.name);
  constructor(private readonly followers: FollowerPageService, private readonly feeds: FeedStoreService) {}

  // Called for every post.created message. Kafka key = authorId so one author is ordered.
  async handle(msg: { postId: string; authorId: string; followerCount: number; createdAt: number }) {
    // Every post always lands in the author's own timeline list: this is the pull side.
    await this.feeds.pushToAuthorTimeline(msg.authorId, msg.postId);

    if (msg.followerCount > PUSH_THRESHOLD) {
      this.logger.log(`post ${msg.postId} is pull-only, author has ${msg.followerCount} followers`);
      return;                                     // celebrity: readers will merge it at read time
    }

    let cursor: string | null = null;
    let written = 0;
    do {
      const page = await this.followers.page(msg.authorId, cursor, PAGE);   // keyset over follows
      if (page.ids.length > 0) {
        // ZADD score=postId member=postId into each follower's feed, then trim, in one pipeline
        await this.feeds.fanoutBatch(page.ids, msg.postId, msg.authorId);
        written += page.ids.length;
      }
      cursor = page.nextCursor;
    } while (cursor);

    this.logger.debug(`post ${msg.postId} fanned out to ${written} feeds`);
  }
}

The feed store owns every Redis key shape, so nothing else in the codebase knows what a feed looks like.

// feed/feed-store.service.ts
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Cluster } from 'ioredis';
import { REDIS_CLIENT } from '../redis/redis.module';

const FEED_CAP = 200;             // entries kept per user feed
const AUTHOR_CAP = 100;           // entries kept per author timeline
const FEED_TTL = 7 * 24 * 3600;   // idle feeds expire; rebuild on demand

@Injectable()
export class FeedStoreService {
  constructor(@Inject(REDIS_CLIENT) private readonly redis: Cluster) {}

  feedKey(userId: string) { return `feed:{${userId}}`; }
  authorKey(authorId: string) { return `tl:{${authorId}}`; }

  async fanoutBatch(followerIds: string[], postId: string, authorId: string): Promise<void> {
    const pipe = this.redis.pipeline();
    for (const uid of followerIds) {
      const k = this.feedKey(uid);
      pipe.zadd(k, postId, `${postId}:${authorId}`);       // score is the snowflake id: time ordering for free
      pipe.zremrangebyrank(k, 0, -(FEED_CAP + 1));         // keep only the newest FEED_CAP entries
      pipe.expire(k, FEED_TTL);
    }
    await pipe.exec();
  }

  async pushToAuthorTimeline(authorId: string, postId: string): Promise<void> {
    const k = this.authorKey(authorId);
    await this.redis.multi().zadd(k, postId, postId).zremrangebyrank(k, 0, -(AUTHOR_CAP + 1)).exec();
  }

  async readFeed(userId: string, beforeScore: string, limit: number) {
    return this.redis.zrevrangebyscore(this.feedKey(userId), `(${beforeScore}`, '-inf', 'LIMIT', 0, limit);
  }

  async readAuthorTimeline(authorId: string, beforeScore: string, limit: number) {
    return this.redis.zrevrangebyscore(this.authorKey(authorId), `(${beforeScore}`, '-inf', 'LIMIT', 0, limit);
  }
}

Two details in fanoutBatch carry the whole memory budget. ZREMRANGEBYRANK after every insert is what caps a feed at 200 entries, so memory is bounded by active users rather than by post volume. And EXPIRE is what limits materialised feeds to users who actually come back; a user who has not opened the app in a week costs nothing until they return, at which point the rebuilder fills their feed from PostgreSQL in about 40 ms.

The read side merges the two halves.

// feed/feed.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { FeedStoreService } from './feed-store.service';
import { HydrationService } from './hydration.service';
import { VisibilityFilter } from './visibility.filter';
import { FollowsService } from '../social/follows.service';
import { FeedRebuilderService } from './rebuild/feed-rebuilder.service';

const MAX_SNOWFLAKE = '9223372036854775807';

@Injectable()
export class FeedService {
  constructor(
    private readonly store: FeedStoreService,
    private readonly hydration: HydrationService,
    private readonly visibility: VisibilityFilter,
    private readonly follows: FollowsService,
    private readonly rebuilder: FeedRebuilderService,
  ) {}

  async getFeed(userId: string, cursor: string | null, limit = 20) {
    const before = cursor ?? MAX_SNOWFLAKE;

    // 1. Push half: the materialised feed. Over-fetch because filtering removes some.
    let pushed = await this.store.readFeed(userId, before, limit * 2);
    if (pushed.length === 0 && !(await this.store.exists(userId))) {
      pushed = await this.rebuilder.rebuild(userId, before, limit * 2);   // cold or evicted feed
    }

    // 2. Pull half: recent posts from the few big accounts this user follows.
    const bigOnes = await this.follows.celebrityFollowees(userId);        // cached list, usually under 20 ids
    const pulled = await Promise.all(
      bigOnes.map((a) => this.store.readAuthorTimeline(a, before, limit)),
    );

    // 3. Merge by snowflake id descending, de-duplicate, cut to the page size after filtering.
    const ids = [...new Set([...pushed.map(stripAuthor), ...pulled.flat()])]
      .sort((a, b) => (BigInt(b) > BigInt(a) ? 1 : -1));

    const visible = await this.visibility.filter(userId, ids);
    const page = visible.slice(0, limit);
    const items = await this.hydration.hydrate(userId, page);
    return { items, nextCursor: page.length === limit ? page[page.length - 1] : null };
  }
}

function stripAuthor(entry: string) { return entry.split(':')[0]; }
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant A as FeedAPI
    participant R as Redis
    participant P as Postgres
    C->>A: GET /v1/feed cursor=null
    A->>R: ZREVRANGEBYSCORE feed:user42
    R-->>A: 40 post ids from ordinary accounts
    A->>R: MGET celebrity followees list
    A->>R: ZREVRANGEBYSCORE tl:celebA and 7 more
    R-->>A: 8 lists of recent ids
    A->>A: merge by snowflake, de-duplicate
    A->>R: MGET post:<id> hydration cache
    R-->>A: 34 hits, 6 misses
    A->>P: SELECT posts WHERE id = ANY for the 6 misses
    P-->>A: rows
    A->>R: SETEX the 6 into the hydration cache
    A-->>C: 20 posts with counts and viewer state

40.12.10 Database design

PostgreSQL is the source of truth for posts, follows, likes and comments; nothing in Redis is authoritative. The write path uses the transactional outbox so that a post and its Kafka event cannot diverge: the insert into posts and the insert into outbox happen in one transaction, and a relay process reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka. Without it, a crash between COMMIT and producer.send gives you a post that exists but never fans out, which the user experiences as "my post disappeared".

// posts/posts.service.ts (excerpt)
async create(authorId: string, dto: CreatePostDto, idempotencyKey: string) {
  return this.dataSource.transaction(async (m) => {
    const existing = await m.findOne(IdempotencyRecord, { where: { key: idempotencyKey } });
    if (existing) return existing.response;                       // retry-safe

    const id = this.snowflake.next();
    await m.insert(Post, { id, authorId, body: dto.text, visibility: dto.visibility });
    await m.insert(Outbox, {
      topic: 'post.created',
      key: authorId,                                              // per-author ordering in Kafka
      payload: { postId: id, authorId, followerCount: dto.followerCount, createdAt: Date.now() },
    });
    await m.insert(IdempotencyRecord, { key: idempotencyKey, response: { id } });
    return { id };
  });
}

Reads are split across replicas: the feed hydration misses and the profile timeline go to a read replica, while anything read inside a write transaction (a follow check before creating a private post reply) goes to the writer, because replica lag of 20 to 200 ms is enough to produce a wrong authorisation answer. The rule the team follows is blunt and easy to review: if the result of the read decides whether a write is allowed, it reads from the primary.

Retention: post partitions older than five years move to cheaper storage; feed_entries partitions are dropped after 30 days because they are pure derived data. Vacuum settings on likes are tuned aggressively (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02) because unlike-then-like churn creates dead tuples faster than the default threshold reacts.

40.12.11 Caching

What Where Structure TTL Invalidation
Home feed Redis Cluster Sorted set feed:{userId}, capped at 200 7 days idle Rebuilt from PostgreSQL on miss
Author timeline Redis Cluster Sorted set tl:{authorId}, capped at 100 30 days Post delete removes the member
Post hydration Redis String post:{id} with a packed JSON body 6 hours Delete or edit publishes an invalidation
Counters Redis Hash cnt:{postId} with likes, comments 60 s for hot posts Refreshed by the counter worker
Viewer state Redis Bitmap-free set liked:{userId}:{bucket} of liked post ids 24 h Written on like and unlike
Celebrity followee list Redis Set cel:{userId} 10 min Follow and unfollow rewrite it
Blocks and mutes Redis Set blk:{userId} 1 h Block writes invalidate immediately

The hydration cache is the one that carries the traffic. A feed page needs 20 posts; a popular post appears in millions of feeds within minutes, so the hit ratio on post:{id} sits above 97 percent and PostgreSQL sees only the tail. Stampede protection matters here: when a very popular post's cache entry expires, thousands of concurrent requests would all query PostgreSQL for it. The hydration service uses a short per-key lock (SET post:lock:{id} NX PX 200); the winner queries and refills, the losers serve the slightly stale value they already have or wait up to 50 ms.

Blocks are cached but never only cached. The visibility filter reads the Redis block set, and the post-detail endpoint additionally re-checks in PostgreSQL, because a leak through a stale cache is a trust failure, not a performance issue.

40.12.12 Messaging

Topic Key Partitions Events Consumers
post.created authorId 64 new post with author follower count Fan-out workers, search indexer, ranking feature builder
post.deleted authorId 64 post id, author id Feed cleaner, search indexer, media reaper
social.engagement postId 32 like, unlike, comment Counter aggregator, ranking signals
follow.changed followerId 32 follow, unfollow, approve Celebrity-list cache, backfill worker
post.created.dlq 8 poison messages On-call inspection

Keying post.created by authorId guarantees per-author ordering, so a create followed 200 ms later by a delete cannot be processed out of order for the same author. Keying social.engagement by postId means all likes for one post land in one partition, which lets the counter aggregator batch them: it accumulates deltas in memory for two seconds, then issues one UPDATE post_counters SET likes = likes + $delta WHERE post_id = $1 AND shard = $2. Fifty thousand likes per second on one viral post become 30 database writes per minute instead of 3 million.

Consumers are idempotent by construction. The fan-out worker's operation is ZADD with a fixed member, which is naturally idempotent: processing the same message twice produces the same sorted set. The counter aggregator is not naturally idempotent (adding a delta twice double-counts), so it commits the Kafka offset in the same PostgreSQL transaction as the counter update, using a consumer_offsets table. That turns at-least-once delivery into effectively-once accounting.

Retries use a tiered backoff: three in-process retries at 100 ms, 500 ms, 2 s, then a re-publish to post.created.retry with a 30-second delay, then the DLQ after five attempts. Anything in the DLQ pages the on-call during business hours and creates a ticket otherwise, because a post that never fanned out is invisible to its followers forever unless someone replays it.

40.12.13 Scaling

At 1x (50 million daily actives, 18,500 feed reads per second peak). Sixty API pods, twenty fan-out worker pods, a 20-shard Redis Cluster with replicas holding about 530 GB, an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with a writer and four readers, 64 Kafka partitions on post.created. The push threshold is 10,000 followers. Nothing exotic; the design as described.

At 10x (500 million daily actives). Three things break in order.

First, Redis memory: 4.2 TB of feeds. The fix is not more RAM but a smaller working set. The feed cap drops from 200 to 120 entries (nobody scrolls past 120 without triggering a rebuild anyway), the materialisation window shrinks from 7 days of inactivity to 2 days, and the entry becomes a bare 8-byte snowflake instead of postId:authorId, cutting per-entry cost by 30 percent. Combined, memory lands near 1.8 TB, which is 40 shards.

Second, fan-out throughput: 280,000 ordinary fan-out writes per second at peak. The push threshold drops from 10,000 to 2,000 followers, moving more accounts to the pull side, and fan-out workers are sharded by author-id hash so that consumer rebalances do not shuffle work. Follower pages grow from 2,000 to 5,000 ids per pipeline to cut round trips.

Third, PostgreSQL write volume on likes and follows. The cluster is split by domain: a graph database cluster for follows and blocks, a content cluster for posts and comments, and an engagement cluster for likes and counters. Each is independently sharded by hash of the leading key using Citus or application-level routing.

flowchart TB
    subgraph OneX
        A1["1 Redis cluster 20 shards"]
        B1["1 PG cluster"]
        C1["push threshold 10k"]
    end
    subgraph TenX
        A2["40 shards, feed cap 120, 2-day window"]
        B2["3 PG clusters by domain"]
        C2["push threshold 2k"]
    end
    subgraph HundredX
        A3["Regional feed clusters, per-region fan-out"]
        B3["Sharded PG plus a purpose-built feed store"]
        C3["Ranking service in the read path"]
    end
    OneX --> TenX --> HundredX

At 100x (5 billion daily actives, which is beyond any real product but useful as an exercise). The feed stops being a cache and becomes a service with its own storage engine, because Redis's memory cost per feed entry is no longer acceptable: a log-structured store on NVMe with an in-memory index for the hot head of each feed halves the cost. Fan-out becomes regional: a post fans out only within the author's region synchronously, and cross-region followers pull. Ranking moves into the read path as a separate service that scores a candidate set of about 500 posts per request with a model, which changes the feed from "merge two sorted lists" to "retrieve candidates, score, sort", and adds a 30 ms budget the current design does not have.

40.12.14 Security

  • Authorisation on read, not only on write. A post's visibility is checked at read time against the current follow and block state, because a user can be blocked after a post was already fanned out into their feed. The filter runs on every feed page; being in someone's materialised feed is never proof of permission.
  • Private accounts. When a public account switches to private, a background job removes its posts from the feeds of non-approved followers. Until that job finishes, the read-time filter is what protects the content, which is the reason the filter exists at all.
  • Enumeration. Snowflake ids are time-ordered and therefore guessable. The post-detail endpoint enforces visibility on every fetch, and unauthenticated access to /v1/posts/{id} is rate limited per IP to stop scraping the whole corpus by walking ids.
  • Media. Upload URLs are presigned S3 POST policies scoped to one key, one content type and a byte range, valid for 5 minutes. Uploaded files are scanned and re-encoded before being served, which strips EXIF GPS data and defuses polyglot files that pretend to be images.
  • Abuse and spam. Post creation is rate limited per user and per IP (see 40.3), new accounts have a lower limit, and follow actions are limited to stop follow-churn bots. A report endpoint feeds a moderation queue.
  • Blocked-user leakage through counters. A blocked user's like still increments a counter the blocker can see. That is accepted; hiding it would leak the block. What must not leak is identity, so the "liked by" list is filtered.
  • Deletion. DELETE /v1/posts/{id} sets deleted_at, publishes post.deleted, and the hydration cache entry is removed immediately, which makes the post vanish from every feed within the next hydration even before the feed cleaner runs.

40.12.15 Failure scenarios

Failure Detection Impact Mitigation What the user sees
Celebrity post storm: ten large accounts post in the same minute and fan-out lag spikes Kafka consumer lag on post.created, fan-out duration histogram Ordinary users' posts are delayed behind celebrity work Push threshold makes large accounts pull-only, so the storm never enters the fan-out path; a runtime-tunable threshold can be lowered during an incident Nothing
Redis eviction or node loss wipes a set of feeds feed_miss_total spike, Redis evicted_keys Affected users' feeds are empty FeedRebuilder detects the missing key and rebuilds from posts joined to follows with a keyset query, capped at 200 entries, in about 40 ms; the rebuild is protected by a per-user lock so a thundering herd of retries rebuilds once A slightly slower first load
Duplicate fan-out after a consumer rebalance Duplicate detection counter on ZADD returning 0 Same post appears twice in a feed ZADD with a deterministic member makes duplicates a no-op; the merge step also de-duplicates by post id Nothing
Stale counters: the aggregator lags and likes appear frozen Aggregator lag metric, counter age gauge Counts under-report for minutes Redis holds an optimistic delta applied on top of the last aggregated value; the client's own like is always reflected immediately from viewer state Count may jump when it catches up
Fan-out worker crashes mid-post, having written 300,000 of 900,000 feeds Consumer restart, offset not committed Partial fan-out The message is redelivered from the last committed offset; because ZADD is idempotent the first 300,000 are rewritten harmlessly and the rest complete A short delay for some followers
PostgreSQL writer failover Connection errors, Aurora event Posting fails for 20 to 40 s Retries with jittered backoff in the client, feed reads unaffected because they are served from Redis "Could not post, tap to retry"
Kafka partition unavailable Producer errors, outbox backlog grows Posts persist but do not fan out The outbox relay retries; posts are already durable, so nothing is lost, only delayed Post visible on own profile but not in followers' feeds for a while
Deleted post still visible in materialised feeds Reports, deleted_hydration_total A removed post is displayed Hydration returns a tombstone for deleted_at IS NOT NULL and the client drops it; the feed cleaner removes members asynchronously Post disappears on next refresh
Hot post: one item gets 200,000 likes per minute Per-key Redis CPU, counter shard contention Counter row contention, cache stampede on hydration Sharded counters spread writes over 16 rows; the hydration entry gets a longer TTL and a lock-protected refill Nothing
Feed rebuild storm after a full Redis cluster restart 30 million missing feeds at once PostgreSQL overwhelmed by rebuild queries Rebuild is admission-controlled by a semaphore of 500 concurrent rebuilds per pod; over the limit the API serves a pull-only feed built from the user's followees, which is slower but works Slower feeds for a few minutes
Follow-graph read on a lagging replica Replica lag metric A just-followed account's posts do not appear Follow writes also push the new followee into the user's Redis followee cache synchronously Nothing
Clock skew produces out-of-order snowflake ids Monitoring on id generator clock Feed ordering slightly wrong The generator refuses to emit ids if the clock moves backwards and waits; ordering errors are bounded by milliseconds Nothing

40.12.16 Observability

Metrics that matter: feed_read_duration_seconds split by push-only, hybrid and rebuild paths; feed_entries_returned histogram (a drop means the visibility filter is removing too much); fanout_lag_seconds measured as the difference between post.created timestamp and the moment the last follower's feed was written, at p50 and p99; fanout_followers_written_total; feed_rebuild_total and its duration; hydration_cache_hit_ratio; counter_lag_seconds; Kafka consumer lag per topic; Redis memory, evictions and per-shard key count.

The single most valuable alert is on fanout_lag_seconds p99 above 60 seconds, because it is the number that describes the product promise ("your post reaches your followers"). The second is on feed_entries_returned p10 falling below five, which catches a broken visibility filter faster than any error rate, since a filter bug returns 200 OK with an empty feed.

Traces cover the read path with spans for feed.readPush, feed.readPull, feed.filter and feed.hydrate, which makes it obvious in one flame graph whether a slow feed is Redis, PostgreSQL or the merge. Logs record every rebuild with the user id and the reason, sampled at 1 percent for successes and 100 percent for failures.

40.12.17 Deployment

Workload Kind Replicas Notes
feed-api Deployment 60, HPA on p95 latency and CPU Read path only; scaled by request volume
posts-api Deployment 20 Write path; PDB keeps two available during rollouts
fanout-worker Deployment 20, KEDA scaled on Kafka lag The lag-driven autoscaler is what absorbs evening peaks
counter-aggregator Deployment 6 Consumer group on social.engagement
outbox-relay Deployment 3 Leader-elected via advisory lock, only one active
feed-cleaner CronJob every 5 min 1 Removes deleted posts from materialised feeds
media-transcoder Deployment 10 S3 event driven

Migrations are expand-and-contract: add nullable columns, deploy code that writes both, backfill in batches of 10,000 rows with a sleep, deploy code that reads the new column, drop the old one a release later. Partition creation for posts runs a month ahead via a scheduled job, because a missing partition turns every insert into an error at midnight on the first of the month.

Rollout is canary at 5 percent for 30 minutes with automatic rollback if feed_read_duration_seconds p99 or the empty-feed ratio regresses. Feature flags gate the push threshold, the feed cap and the ranking mode, so an incident can be mitigated by changing a number rather than by deploying.

40.12.18 Cost considerations

Item Sizing Monthly (USD, approximate)
CloudFront egress for media 640 TB per day at negotiated rates 28,000
S3 storage and requests 1.2 PB growing, Intelligent-Tiering 9,000
ElastiCache Redis Cluster 20 shards of cache.r6g.4xlarge with replicas 12,500
Aurora PostgreSQL 1 writer plus 4 readers, r6g.8xlarge, 6 TB 9,000
EKS compute for API and workers about 120 pods across 30 nodes 6,000
MSK Kafka 6 brokers, 64 plus partitions, 3-day retention 2,500
OpenSearch for search 6 data nodes 2,000
Media transcoding 3.2 TB per day of images and short video 3,500
Observability metrics, logs, traces 2,500
Total about 75,000

The dominant cost is CDN egress, not compute or storage, and it scales with reads, not with posts. That single fact drives more engineering than anything else: aggressive thumbnail sizing (a 200 KB feed thumbnail instead of a 900 KB original saves about 18,000 USD per month), modern formats (AVIF over JPEG saves another 30 percent), long cache lifetimes on immutable media URLs, and lazy loading below the fold. Redis is the second driver, which is why the feed cap and the inactivity TTL are treated as budget levers, not implementation details.

40.12.19 Tradeoffs

  • Hybrid fan-out instead of pure push or pure pull. Two code paths, a merge step and a threshold to tune, in exchange for bounded write amplification and a read path that stays under 100 ms. Pure push is simpler until one account has ten million followers; pure pull is simpler until a user follows a thousand accounts.
  • Capped feeds. A user who scrolls past 200 items pays a rebuild. The alternative, unbounded feeds, multiplies Redis memory by ten for a behaviour under 1 percent of sessions exhibits.
  • Redis as the feed store with PostgreSQL as the source of truth. Losing Redis loses no data, only speed. The price is the rebuild path, which must be written, tested and load-tested even though it runs rarely, because when it does run it runs for everyone at once.
  • Approximate counters above 1,000. Users cannot tell 12,412 from 12,438, and the exact version costs a synchronous write per like on a hot row. Below 1,000 the number is exact, because "3 likes" being wrong is noticeable.
  • Visibility filtering at read time. Every feed page pays a set-membership check against blocks and follows. Filtering at write time would be cheaper but wrong, because permissions change after fan-out.
  • Snowflake ids instead of UUIDs. Time-ordered ids give free sort order, 8-byte cursors and clustered inserts, at the cost of leaking creation time and needing a worker-id allocation scheme.
  • Chronological by default, scored behind a flag. Chronological is explainable, debuggable and cheap. Scoring needs a feature store, a model service and a 30 ms budget, and it makes "why did I see this?" a support question.

40.12.20 Alternative architectures

Pure fan-out on read with a materialised view per author. Keep no per-user feeds at all. On every feed request, fetch the user's followee list and merge the newest N posts from each author's cached timeline. This is dramatically simpler: no fan-out workers, no Kafka topic, no rebuild path, no duplicate handling, and posting is instant for everyone including celebrities. It wins when the average user follows few accounts (under about 50) or when the product is a professional network where feeds are read a few times a day rather than continuously. It loses when users follow hundreds of accounts, because a merge across 500 timelines costs 500 Redis reads per page, or 9 million reads per second at our peak, and the tail latency becomes the number of followees rather than a constant.

A purpose-built feed store instead of Redis. Replace the sorted sets with a partitioned log-structured store (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, or a custom NVMe-backed service) keyed by (user_id, bucket) with the newest posts in a wide row. Storage cost per feed entry drops by roughly 10x compared to RAM, feeds can be much longer, and durability comes for free so the rebuild path becomes an optimisation rather than a necessity. It wins above a few hundred million active feeds where Redis memory becomes the dominant bill. It loses on latency (1 to 5 ms instead of 0.3 ms), on operational complexity (you now run a distributed database), and on the sheer convenience of ZADD plus ZREMRANGEBYRANK being one atomic capped insert.

Ranking-first architecture with a candidate generator. Drop the idea of a stored feed entirely. On each request, a retrieval service produces a few thousand candidate posts from several sources (followed accounts, topical interest, trending, friends-of-friends), a model scores them, and the top 20 are returned. This is what large recommendation-driven feeds actually do. It wins on engagement and on cold-start users who follow nobody, and it makes the "one celebrity, fifty million followers" problem disappear because nothing is materialised. It loses on cost (a scoring pass per request instead of a sorted-set read), on latency budget, on explainability, and on the enormous machine-learning platform investment it presumes: a feature store, training pipelines, online model serving and an experimentation framework are all prerequisites, not details.

40.13 Video Streaming Platform

40.13.1 Requirements

A video streaming platform takes a file from a creator's laptop and turns it into something that plays instantly, at the right quality, on a phone on a train, a laptop on hotel Wi-Fi and a television on fibre. The interesting engineering is not the player. It is everything between "upload finished" and "playable", and everything between "playable" and "the bill did not bankrupt us".

The users are creators, who upload and want to know when their video is live and how it is doing, and viewers, who want playback to start in under two seconds and never buffer. There is a third stakeholder nobody puts on the diagram: finance, because a streaming platform's cost curve is dominated by bytes leaving the CDN, and a design that ignores that fact is not a design.

Imagine a bakery that must serve bread to customers all over the country. You do not bake on demand at each shop; you bake once at a central bakery (transcoding), cut the loaf into slices of different thickness for different customers (the bitrate ladder), put a printed list of available slice sizes on the counter (the manifest), and ship pallets to local shops overnight so customers get bread from around the corner instead of from the central bakery (the CDN). When a shop runs out, it calls the bakery, which is the cache miss. If every shop calls at once because a new loaf just became famous, the bakery melts. That is the cache-miss storm, and preventing it is a large part of this design.

40.13.2 Functional requirements

  1. A creator uploads a video file up to 20 GB, resumably, and sees progress and status.
  2. The platform transcodes each upload into an adaptive bitrate ladder and packages it as HLS and DASH.
  3. Playback starts within 2 seconds and adapts quality to the viewer's bandwidth without stalling.
  4. Thumbnails are generated automatically (a grid of sprites for scrubbing plus a poster frame), and a creator can pick or upload a custom one.
  5. Videos have visibility: public, unlisted, private, or restricted to a subscription tier.
  6. Views are counted, with a definition of what counts as a view, and watch progress is remembered per user per video so playback resumes where it stopped.
  7. Viewers can comment on a video and reply to comments.
  8. The catalogue is searchable and a recommendation service can be plugged into the home and watch-next surfaces.
  9. Creators see analytics: views, watch time, retention curve, quality of experience.
  10. Live streaming is supported for a subset of creators, with the same player and CDN.

40.13.3 Non-functional requirements

Property Target Why
Startup time (join to first frame) p50 under 1.2 s, p95 under 2.5 s Every extra second of startup loses viewers measurably
Rebuffer ratio Under 0.4 percent of watch time The only quality metric viewers actually feel
Upload to playable p50 under 8 minutes for a 10-minute 1080p video, p95 under 30 minutes Creators watch the status page
Playback availability 99.99 percent Streaming is the product
Catalogue API availability 99.95 percent Degrades to cached pages
Durability of masters 11 nines (S3) A lost master cannot be re-encoded
Consistency of metadata Read-your-writes for the creator, eventual (under 30 s) for viewers A creator editing a title must see the change
View count accuracy Within 1 percent, converging within 10 minutes It drives payouts, so it must be auditable

40.13.4 Constraints

  • AWS: S3, CloudFront, MSK, Aurora PostgreSQL, ElastiCache Redis, EKS. Transcoding either on EKS with FFmpeg or on AWS MediaConvert; the design supports both behind one interface.
  • No custom CDN. Egress is billed per gigabyte and is the largest line item.
  • Mobile clients on cellular networks; the manifest and the segment size must tolerate 300 ms round trips and abrupt bandwidth changes.
  • Content licensing for a premium tier requires DRM (Widevine, FairPlay, PlayReady), which forces packaging decisions early.
  • A team of twenty, so the pipeline must be operable, restartable and observable by people who did not write it.

Two conclusions fall out of the arithmetic and drive the whole design. Egress dominates: it is more than half the bill and it scales with viewing, not with the catalogue, so every percent shaved off delivered bitrate is worth thousands of dollars a month. And storing every rung for every video is waste: 80 percent of watch time goes to 5 percent of videos, so the tail should be stored as a mezzanine plus a small ladder and re-packaged on demand.

40.13.6 API design

Method Path Request Response Status codes Idempotent Auth
POST /v1/videos { title, description, visibility } { videoId, uploadId, partUrls[], expiresAt } 201, 400, 401 No Creator token
PUT S3 presigned part URL binary part ETag 200, 403 Yes Presigned
POST /v1/videos/{id}/upload/complete { uploadId, parts:[{n, etag}] } { status: 'processing' } 202, 400, 409 Yes Creator token
GET /v1/videos/{id}/status { state, progressPct, renditions[], error? } 200, 404 Yes Creator token
GET /v1/videos/{id} metadata plus poster and duration 200, 403, 404 Yes Optional
POST /v1/videos/{id}/playback { deviceProfile } { manifestUrl, cookies?, drm? } 200, 402, 403, 404 Yes Optional or subscriber
PATCH /v1/videos/{id} { title?, description?, visibility?, thumbnailId? } video 200, 403 Yes Owner
DELETE /v1/videos/{id} 204, 403 Yes Owner
POST /v1/videos/{id}/heartbeat { positionSec, sessionId, playedSec, quality, rebufferMs } 204 Yes, keyed by session and position Optional
GET /v1/videos/{id}/progress { positionSec, updatedAt } 200, 404 Yes User token
POST /v1/videos/{id}/comments { text, parentId? } plus Idempotency-Key comment 201, 403 Yes, via key User token
GET /v1/videos/{id}/comments ?cursor=&sort=top { items[], nextCursor } 200 Yes Optional
GET /v1/search ?q=&cursor= results 200 Yes Optional
GET /v1/recommendations ?context=watch_next&videoId= list 200 Yes Optional

The POST /v1/videos/{id}/playback endpoint is the security boundary of the whole system. It checks entitlement (is this video public, is this user a subscriber, is this region allowed), then mints either a signed CloudFront cookie scoped to the video's path prefix or a set of signed segment URLs, plus a DRM licence token when the video is protected. Manifests and segments themselves are static files on the CDN; the API never proxies video bytes, because proxying 780 Gbps through NestJS pods is not a plan.

The heartbeat endpoint is the highest-volume write in the system. At 312,000 concurrent streams with a heartbeat every 10 seconds it is 31,200 requests per second, which is more than the entire catalogue API. It returns 204 with no body, does no database work, and drops its payload straight onto Kafka.
