Discovery cost Calculation Result
Discovery tick interval 1 s
Ticks per day 86,400
Rows returned per tick, average 1M / 86,400 11.6
Rows returned at the midnight tick without jitter 200,000
Index used (next_run_at) WHERE enabled Index-only range scan
Cost per tick, normal Index scan of a few rows under 1 ms

Two numbers dominate every decision below. The average of 11.6 runs per second is trivially small, so this is not a throughput problem. The 200,000-runs-at-midnight spike is 17,000 times the average, so it is entirely a burst problem, and the design is shaped around spreading and absorbing that burst rather than around raw capacity.

40.15.6 API design

Method Path Request Response Status codes Idempotent Auth
POST /v1/jobs { name, handler, timeoutSec, retryPolicy, maxConcurrency, tenantId? } job 201, 409 Yes, by name Service token
PUT /v1/jobs/{name} full definition job 200, 404 Yes Owner team
POST /v1/jobs/{name}/schedules { cron, timezone, catchUpPolicy, enabled } schedule 201, 400 Yes, by (job,cron,tz) Owner team
PUT /v1/schedules/{id} { cron?, timezone?, enabled? } schedule 200, 404 Yes Owner team
POST /v1/schedules/{id}/pause 204 Yes Owner team
POST /v1/jobs/{name}/runs { payload, runAt?, priority?, dedupeKey? } { runId, state } 201, 202, 409 Yes, by dedupeKey Service token
GET /v1/runs/{id} run with attempts and logs 200, 404 Yes Owner or admin
GET /v1/jobs/{name}/runs ?from=&to=&state=&cursor= list 200 Yes Owner
POST /v1/runs/{id}/cancel { reason } run 200, 409 Yes Owner
POST /v1/runs/{id}/retry new run 201, 409 Yes, by (runId,attempt) Owner
POST /v1/jobs/{name}/backfill { from, to, maxParallel } { backfillId, plannedRuns } 202, 400 Yes, by (job,from,to) Owner
GET /v1/dlq ?job=&cursor= failed runs 200 Yes Owner
POST /v1/dlq/{runId}/requeue run 201 Yes Owner

Worker-facing endpoints are deliberately absent. Workers do not poll an HTTP API; they claim rows directly from PostgreSQL with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, which removes an entire tier from the hot path and makes the claim atomic with the state transition. The HTTP API is for humans and for services that enqueue jobs.

dedupeKey on one-off enqueue is the caller-side idempotency key. POST /v1/jobs/send-invoice/runs with dedupeKey: "invoice-2026-09-payer-77" returns the existing run on a second call rather than creating a duplicate, which is what makes it safe for an upstream service to retry a network timeout.

40.15.7 Data model

erDiagram
    JOBS ||--o{ JOB_SCHEDULES : scheduled_by
    JOBS ||--o{ JOB_RUNS : produces
    JOBS ||--o{ JOB_DEPENDENCIES : depends
    JOB_RUNS ||--o{ RUN_ATTEMPTS : attempted_as
    TENANTS ||--o{ JOBS : owns
    JOBS {
        text name PK
        uuid tenant_id
        text handler
        int timeout_sec
        int max_attempts
        int max_concurrency
        smallint priority
        boolean enabled
    }
    JOB_SCHEDULES {
        uuid id PK
        text job_name FK
        text cron_expr
        text timezone
        text catch_up_policy
        timestamptz next_run_at
        timestamptz last_scheduled_for
        boolean enabled
    }
    JOB_RUNS {
        uuid id PK
        text job_name FK
        timestamptz scheduled_for
        text state
        smallint attempt
        timestamptz lease_until
        text worker_id
        jsonb payload
    }
    JOB_DEPENDENCIES {
        text job_name PK
        text depends_on PK
        text mode
    }
    RUN_ATTEMPTS {
        uuid run_id FK
        smallint attempt
        timestamptz started_at
        text outcome
        text error
    }
CREATE TABLE jobs (
  name            text PRIMARY KEY,                    -- 'billing.daily-invoice'
  tenant_id       uuid,                                -- NULL means a platform job
  handler         text NOT NULL,                       -- routing key to the owning service
  region          text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'eu-west-1',   -- data residency
  timeout_sec     integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 300 CHECK (timeout_sec BETWEEN 1 AND 21600),
  max_attempts    smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 5,
  backoff_base_ms integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 2000,
  max_concurrency smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 10,        -- per job name
  priority        smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 5 CHECK (priority BETWEEN 1 AND 9),
  enabled         boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true
);

CREATE TABLE job_schedules (
  id                  uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  job_name            text NOT NULL REFERENCES jobs(name) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  cron_expr           text NOT NULL,                   -- '0 7 * * *'
  timezone            text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'UTC',     -- IANA name, e.g. 'Europe/Berlin'
  catch_up_policy     text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'skip'
                        CHECK (catch_up_policy IN ('skip','run_once','run_all')),
  next_run_at         timestamptz NOT NULL,            -- always stored in UTC
  last_scheduled_for  timestamptz,
  enabled             boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
  UNIQUE (job_name, cron_expr, timezone)               -- registering the same schedule twice is a no-op
);
CREATE INDEX schedules_due_idx ON job_schedules (next_run_at)
  WHERE enabled;                                        -- serves the due-schedule scan: the hottest query

CREATE TABLE job_runs (
  id            uuid NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  job_name      text NOT NULL,
  tenant_id     uuid,
  scheduled_for timestamptz NOT NULL,                   -- the logical time, not the actual time
  state         text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'
                  CHECK (state IN ('pending','claimed','running','succeeded','failed','dead','cancelled','skipped')),
  attempt       smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  priority      smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 5,
  run_after     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),     -- backoff target for retries
  lease_until   timestamptz,
  worker_id     text,
  payload       jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,
  dedupe_key    text,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

-- The execution key. One row per (job, logical time) makes a duplicate schedule tick a no-op.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX job_runs_exec_key_uidx ON job_runs (job_name, scheduled_for);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX job_runs_dedupe_uidx ON job_runs (job_name, dedupe_key) WHERE dedupe_key IS NOT NULL;

-- The claim query's index: only rows a worker could take, ordered the way it takes them.
CREATE INDEX job_runs_claim_idx ON job_runs (priority, run_after, id)
  WHERE state = 'pending';
-- The takeover query's index: running rows whose lease has expired.
CREATE INDEX job_runs_lease_idx ON job_runs (lease_until)
  WHERE state IN ('claimed','running');
-- History lookups: "did job X run for date D".
CREATE INDEX job_runs_history_idx ON job_runs (job_name, scheduled_for DESC);

CREATE TABLE job_dependencies (
  job_name   text NOT NULL REFERENCES jobs(name) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  depends_on text NOT NULL REFERENCES jobs(name) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  mode       text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'success' CHECK (mode IN ('success','completion')),
  PRIMARY KEY (job_name, depends_on),
  CHECK (job_name <> depends_on)
);

UNIQUE (job_name, scheduled_for) is the single most important line in this design. It is the idempotent execution key. The scheduler does not need to be perfect; it needs to be allowed to try twice. Two scheduler instances that both believe they are the leader will both compute scheduled_for = 2026-09-09 00:00:00+00 for the same job and both try to insert; the database accepts one and rejects the other with a unique-violation, which the scheduler swallows as "already scheduled". Split-brain becomes a metric instead of an incident.

scheduled_for is a logical time, not the moment the run actually started. That distinction is what makes backfills, dependencies and re-runs coherent: a run for 2026-09-08 means the same thing whether it executed on time, six hours late, or during a backfill three weeks later.

40.15.8 High-level architecture

flowchart LR
    API["Scheduler API, NestJS"] --> PG["PostgreSQL: jobs, schedules, runs"]
    L["Scheduler leader, 3 replicas"] -->|"advisory lock"| PG
    L --> DISC["Discovery tick every 1s"]
    DISC --> PG
    PG --> W1["Worker pod A"]
    PG --> W2["Worker pod B"]
    PG --> W3["Worker pod N"]
    W1 --> H["Handler services over Kafka or HTTP"]
    W1 --> PG
    RD["Redis: concurrency tokens, fairness counters"] --- W1
    RD --- W2
    PG --> DLQ["DLQ view"]
    PG --> OBS["Metrics: lag, stuck, DLQ depth"]

There are exactly two moving parts. The scheduler leader turns schedules into job_runs rows. The workers turn job_runs rows into executed work. They communicate only through PostgreSQL, which means there is no queue to lose, no broker to partition, and the entire state of the system is one table you can query.

Why not Kafka between them? Because the claim, the lease and the state transition must be atomic with each other, and because cancellation of a queued item is a UPDATE ... WHERE state='pending' in PostgreSQL versus an unsolvable problem in a log-based broker. At a million runs a day PostgreSQL is not the bottleneck; at a hundred million it would be, and 40.15.13 covers that.

40.15.9 Component design

Component Responsibility
LeaderElection Holds a PostgreSQL session advisory lock; only the holder ticks
DiscoveryService Every second, finds schedules whose next_run_at has passed, creates runs, computes the next occurrence
CronParser Turns a cron expression plus an IANA timezone into the next UTC instant, DST-aware
WorkerService Claims runs with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, heartbeats leases, dispatches, records outcomes
ConcurrencyGate Redis token buckets for per-job and per-tenant concurrency
DependencyResolver Checks whether all upstream jobs succeeded for the same scheduled_for
ReaperService Reclaims runs whose lease expired, applies backoff, moves exhausted runs to dead
BackfillService Materialises a range of scheduled_for values with bounded parallelism
HistoryService Queries, partition rotation, archival

    leader-election.service.ts
    discovery.service.ts
    cron-parser.service.ts
    reaper.service.ts
  worker/
    worker.module.ts
    worker.service.ts

    jobs.controller.ts
    runs.controller.ts
    backfill.controller.ts

Leader election uses a PostgreSQL session-level advisory lock. It is not a general-purpose consensus system, and that is the point: it is fifteen lines, it needs no new infrastructure, and its failure mode is well understood.

// scheduler/leader-election.service.ts
@Injectable()
export class LeaderElectionService implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly LOCK_KEY = 0x5CHED01;          // any stable 64-bit integer
  private client?: PoolClient;
  private leader = false;

  async onModuleInit() { this.timer = setInterval(() => this.tryAcquire(), 5_000); }

  private async tryAcquire(): Promise<void> {
    if (this.leader) return;
    // A dedicated connection: session advisory locks live as long as the session, and are released
    // automatically if the pod dies or the TCP connection drops. That is the failover mechanism.
    this.client = await this.pool.connect();
    const { rows } = await this.client.query('SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock($1) AS ok', [this.LOCK_KEY]);
    if (rows[0].ok) {
      this.leader = true;
      this.metrics.gauge('scheduler_is_leader', 1);
      this.logger.log('acquired scheduler leadership');
    } else {
      this.client.release();
      this.client = undefined;
    }
  }

  isLeader() { return this.leader; }

  async onModuleDestroy() {
    // Release explicitly on graceful shutdown so failover takes milliseconds, not the TCP timeout.
    if (this.client) { await this.client.query('SELECT pg_advisory_unlock($1)', [this.LOCK_KEY]); this.client.release(); }
  }
}

The honest caveat: a pod that is alive but network-partitioned from PostgreSQL loses the lock (the server drops the session) while still believing it is the leader for a few seconds. That is genuine split-brain, and the unique execution key is what makes it harmless. Belt and braces: the discovery loop re-checks pg_advisory_lock ownership before every tick, and a run whose insert fails on conflict is counted in scheduler_duplicate_schedule_total, which should be near zero and is an early warning when it is not.

Discovery turns time into rows.

// scheduler/discovery.service.ts
@Interval(1000)
async tick(): Promise<void> {
  if (!this.election.isLeader()) return;
  const now = new Date();

  const due = await this.schedules.query(
    `SELECT id, job_name, cron_expr, timezone, next_run_at, last_scheduled_for, catch_up_policy
       FROM job_schedules
      WHERE enabled AND next_run_at <= $1
      ORDER BY next_run_at
      LIMIT 5000
      FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, [now]);     // bounded batch: a midnight spike cannot block a tick

  for (const s of due) {
    const occurrences = this.plan(s, now);            // catch-up policy decides how many
    for (const scheduledFor of occurrences) {
      try {
        await this.runs.insert({
          jobName: s.job_name, scheduledFor,
          runAfter: this.jitter(scheduledFor, s.job_name),   // spread the midnight herd
          state: 'pending', priority: await this.jobs.priorityOf(s.job_name),
        });
      } catch (e) {
        if (isUniqueViolation(e)) { this.metrics.inc('scheduler_duplicate_schedule_total'); continue; }
        throw e;
      }
    }
    const next = this.cron.nextAfter(s.cron_expr, s.timezone, occurrences.at(-1) ?? s.next_run_at);
    await this.schedules.update(s.id, { nextRunAt: next, lastScheduledFor: occurrences.at(-1) });
  }
}

// Deterministic jitter: the same job always gets the same offset, so ordering stays stable across restarts.
private jitter(scheduledFor: Date, jobName: string): Date {
  const spreadSec = 180;
  const offset = hash32(jobName) % spreadSec;
  return new Date(scheduledFor.getTime() + offset * 1000);
}

The jitter is what turns 200,000 midnight runs into 1,100 per second over three minutes. It is deterministic on the job name so a job always fires at the same offset, which keeps behaviour reproducible and keeps dependent jobs in a sensible order. Jobs that genuinely must fire at exactly 00:00:00 set spread_sec = 0 explicitly and are counted; there are eleven of them, and every one had to justify itself.

Timezones and DST are where correctness quietly dies. All storage is UTC (timestamptz). The cron parser takes the expression and the IANA timezone and computes the next instant using a real timezone database, then converts to UTC. Two rules handle the transitions:

  • Spring forward (02:30 does not exist on the transition day): the run is scheduled at the first valid instant after the gap, so 0 30 2 * * * in Europe/Berlin fires at 03:00 local on that day. It fires once.
  • Autumn back (02:30 happens twice): the run fires on the first occurrence only. The parser computes the next occurrence strictly greater than last_scheduled_for in UTC, and because the two local 02:30s are different UTC instants, the second one would produce the same scheduled_for only if the parser worked in local time. It does not, so the second occurrence yields a UTC instant one hour later, which would be a genuine second run. The guard is the unique key on (job_name, scheduled_for) combined with computing scheduled_for as the local wall-clock time labelled with the date, so both 02:30s map to the same logical 2026-10-25T02:30 key and the second insert is rejected.

Claiming is the worker's hot path.

// worker/claim.repository.ts
async claimBatch(workerId: string, batch: number, region: string): Promise<JobRun[]> {
  return this.dataSource.query(
    `UPDATE job_runs r
        SET state = 'claimed', attempt = r.attempt + 1, worker_id = $1,
            lease_until = now() + make_interval(secs => j.timeout_sec + 30)
       FROM jobs j
      WHERE r.id IN (
        SELECT r2.id
          FROM job_runs r2
          JOIN jobs j2 ON j2.name = r2.job_name
         WHERE r2.state = 'pending'
           AND r2.run_after <= now()
           AND j2.enabled AND j2.region = $3
         ORDER BY r2.priority ASC, r2.run_after ASC
         LIMIT $2
         FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)          -- the whole concurrency story in one clause
        AND j.name = r.job_name
      RETURNING r.*, j.handler, j.timeout_sec, j.max_attempts, j.backoff_base_ms`,
    [workerId, batch, region]);
}

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is what allows 330 worker pods to poll the same table without blocking each other: each transaction locks the rows it selects and skips rows another transaction already holds. Without SKIP LOCKED, 330 workers would queue behind one another on the same hot rows and throughput would collapse to one claim at a time.

The run loop then heartbeats the lease and records the outcome.

// worker/worker.service.ts (execution of one claimed run)
private async execute(run: ClaimedRun): Promise<void> {
  const gate = await this.concurrency.acquire(run.jobName, run.tenantId);   // Redis token, or requeue
  if (!gate) { await this.runs.release(run.id, /* run_after */ addMs(now(), 250)); return; }

  const hb = setInterval(() => this.runs.extendLease(run.id, run.timeoutSec), (run.timeoutSec * 1000) / 3);
  const started = Date.now();
  try {
    await this.runs.setState(run.id, 'running');
    // The execution key travels to the handler so the handler can be idempotent too.
    await this.dispatcher.dispatch(run.handler, {
      runId: run.id, jobName: run.jobName, scheduledFor: run.scheduledFor,
      idempotencyKey: `${run.jobName}:${run.scheduledFor.toISOString()}`,
      payload: run.payload, attempt: run.attempt,
    }, run.timeoutSec * 1000);
    await this.runs.succeed(run.id, Date.now() - started);
  } catch (err) {
    const permanent = err instanceof NonRetryableError;
    const exhausted = run.attempt >= run.maxAttempts;
    if (permanent || exhausted) await this.runs.markDead(run.id, String(err));
    else await this.runs.scheduleRetry(run.id, backoffWithJitter(run.attempt, run.backoffBaseMs), String(err));
  } finally {
    clearInterval(hb);
    await this.concurrency.release(run.jobName, run.tenantId);
  }
}

Fairness and concurrency. Two Redis counters guard execution: conc:job:{name} capped at jobs.max_concurrency and conc:tenant:{tenantId} capped at the tenant's plan limit. A worker that cannot acquire a token releases the run back to pending with a 250 ms delay rather than holding it, so a saturated job does not occupy worker slots. On top of that, the claim query's ORDER BY priority, run_after gives strict priority, which alone would let a high-priority tenant starve others; the fix is a fairness pass that caps how many consecutive claims one tenant can win, implemented as a per-tenant claim counter in Redis with a sliding window. When a tenant exceeds its share, the worker adds AND tenant_id <> $starved to the next claim.

DAG dependencies are resolved at claim time, not at schedule time, so an upstream job that is late delays its downstream rather than skipping it.

flowchart LR
    E["extract 02:00"] --> T1["transform-orders"]
    E --> T2["transform-users"]
    T1 --> L["load-warehouse"]
    T2 --> L
    L --> R["rebuild-search-index"]
    L --> RPT["daily-report"]

Before a run for load-warehouse with scheduled_for = D can be claimed, the resolver checks that runs for transform-orders and transform-users with the same scheduled_for are in state succeeded. If any upstream is still pending or running, the run's run_after is pushed forward by 30 seconds and it goes back to pending. If an upstream reached dead, the downstream run is marked skipped with the reason, and skipping propagates transitively. Cycles are rejected when a dependency is created, by running a topological sort over the dependency graph and refusing an edge that closes a loop.

Backfills materialise the same rows the scheduler would have created, with the same execution key, which is why a backfill for a date that already ran is automatically a no-op:

INSERT INTO job_runs (job_name, scheduled_for, state, priority, run_after, payload)
SELECT 'reports.daily', gs, 'pending', 8, now(), '{"backfill":true}'::jsonb
  FROM generate_series($1::timestamptz, $2::timestamptz, interval '1 day') AS gs
ON CONFLICT (job_name, scheduled_for) DO NOTHING;

Backfill runs get a low priority (8 of 9) so they never compete with live traffic, and maxParallel is enforced by a dedicated concurrency token so a 400-day backfill trickles rather than floods.

Catch-up policy decides what happens to occurrences missed while the scheduler was down.

Policy Behaviour after a 6-hour outage on a 15-minute job Use for
skip Run once at the next due time; the 24 missed occurrences are recorded as skipped Cache warmers, health pings, anything where only "now" matters
run_once Run once immediately for the most recent missed occurrence, then resume Reports, digests: you want the latest, not twenty-four of them
run_all Create all 24 missed runs, in order, at low priority Anything that processes a window of data, where every window matters

Default is skip, because the failure mode of run_all on a per-minute job after a long outage is a self-inflicted denial of service. Choosing run_all requires setting a maxCatchUp bound.

40.15.10 Database design

The scheduler is one of the few systems where PostgreSQL is the queue, and that works only with attention to three things.

Bloat. A million runs a day with several state transitions each produces millions of dead tuples. job_runs gets autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01 and autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = 2000, and a fillfactor = 85 so HOT updates keep state transitions off the indexes where possible. Without this, the claim index bloats within days and the claim query goes from 2 ms to 200 ms.

Partitioning. job_runs is range-partitioned by created_at, one partition per week. Retention is DETACH PARTITION plus an archive to S3 in Parquet, never a DELETE. Partitioning also keeps the claim index small: only the current partition contains pending rows, so the index the workers hammer holds thousands of entries, not ninety million.

Connections. 330 worker pods claiming every 200 ms would be 1,650 queries per second and 330 connections. PgBouncer in transaction mode fronts them, and workers claim in batches of 10 to 50 rather than one at a time, cutting query rate by an order of magnitude. Workers also back off adaptively: an empty claim doubles the poll interval up to 2 seconds, so an idle cluster costs almost nothing.

The claim query's plan is worth checking on every schema change:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) claim query at midnight
 Update on job_runs r  (cost=... rows=50) (actual time=3.911..3.913 rows=50 loops=1)
   ->  Nested Loop  (cost=... rows=50) (actual time=0.512..3.104 rows=50 loops=1)
         ->  LockRows  (actual time=0.498..1.882 rows=50 loops=1)
               ->  Index Scan using job_runs_claim_idx on job_runs r2
                     (actual time=0.031..0.402 rows=50 loops=1)
                     Index Cond: (run_after <= now())
                     Filter: (state = 'pending')
                     Rows Removed by Filter: 0
         ->  Index Scan using jobs_pkey on jobs j  (actual time=0.010..0.011 rows=1 loops=50)
   Buffers: shared hit=612 read=4
 Planning Time: 0.412 ms
 Execution Time: 4.021 ms

Four milliseconds for a batch of 50 at the worst moment of the day is the number that makes "PostgreSQL as a queue" defensible.

40.15.11 Caching

What Where TTL Why
Job definitions In-process Map per worker 30 s refresh plus pub/sub invalidation Read on every claim; a database lookup per run would triple query load
Concurrency tokens Redis counters conc:job:*, conc:tenant:* Lease-bound, auto-expiring Must be shared across pods; PostgreSQL would serialise on hot rows
Fairness counters Redis sliding window per tenant 60 s Cheap, approximate by design
Dependency results Redis dep:{job}:{scheduledFor} 10 min Avoids re-querying upstream state on every retry of a blocked run
Cron next-occurrence In-process memo keyed by expression plus timezone plus anchor until process restart Parsing 58,000 expressions per tick would dominate the tick budget
Leader identity In-process The lock itself is the truth

Nothing in Redis is authoritative. If Redis is unavailable, the concurrency gate fails closed for jobs with a concurrency limit (they wait) and open for jobs without one (they run), because a limit that silently stops applying is how a job with max_concurrency = 2 opens 300 database connections and takes down a downstream service.

40.15.12 Messaging

The scheduler uses PostgreSQL for the queue and Kafka for dispatch and observability.

Topic Key Events Consumers
jobs.dispatch.{handler} jobName the run envelope with idempotencyKey The owning team's service
jobs.result runId success, failure, error class, duration Worker service to close the run
jobs.lifecycle jobName scheduled, started, succeeded, failed, dead, cancelled, skipped Metrics, audit, team notifications
jobs.dlq jobName runs that exhausted attempts On-call tooling

Dispatch is either a direct in-process handler (for jobs owned by the scheduler itself), an HTTP call with a timeout (for simple handlers), or a Kafka message (for heavy handlers owned by other teams). The Kafka path is asynchronous, so the worker keeps the lease alive until it receives a matching jobs.result or the lease expires. The idempotencyKey of {jobName}:{scheduledFor} travels with every dispatch, and handler teams are contractually required to use it: exactly-once effect is a property of the handler, and the scheduler's job is to give it a stable key and a bounded number of attempts.

Notifications on jobs.lifecycle are what make the system usable by other teams: a job that reaches dead posts to the owning team's Slack channel with the run id, the error and a one-click requeue link.

40.15.13 Scaling

At 1x (1 million runs per day). Three scheduler replicas with one leader, 40 worker pods scaling to 120 at midnight, one PostgreSQL cluster, one Redis. The bottleneck is the midnight burst, handled by deterministic jitter over 180 seconds and KEDA scaling on pending row count.

At 10x (10 million runs per day, 2 million at midnight). Three changes. First, the single leader becomes a sharded leader: sixteen advisory locks, each covering hash(job_name) % 16, so discovery parallelises across replicas and one slow shard does not delay the rest. Second, the claim path moves to per-shard partitions of job_runs (PARTITION BY HASH (job_name) under the weekly range partitions) so claim indexes stay small and workers can be pinned to shards, eliminating cross-worker contention. Third, history moves out: runs older than 7 days go to ClickHouse for querying, and job_runs keeps only the live window.

At 100x (100 million runs per day). PostgreSQL stops being the right queue. The durable state (schedules, execution keys, history) stays in PostgreSQL, but the ready-to-run queue moves to a dedicated broker with per-key ordering and delayed delivery, and the claim becomes a broker operation with the database used only for the idempotent execution key check. At this point the honest recommendation is to stop building and adopt Temporal, which has already solved this and adds durable execution semantics this design does not have.

flowchart TB
    S1["1x: one leader, one PG, jitter"] --> S2["10x: 16 lock shards, hash-partitioned runs, ClickHouse history"]
    S2 --> S3["100x: PG for keys and history, dedicated broker for the ready queue"]
    S3 --> S4["Beyond: adopt Temporal or an equivalent durable execution engine"]

40.15.14 Security

  • Multi-tenant isolation. Every job carries a tenant_id; the API enforces that a tenant's token can only register, list, cancel and backfill its own jobs. Handlers receive a scoped token derived from the job's tenant, so a job cannot read another tenant's data even if its payload is tampered with.
  • Payload integrity. Payloads are validated against the job's registered JSON schema at enqueue time, not at execution time, so a malformed payload fails fast and visibly instead of at 03:00.
  • Handler authentication. Dispatch over HTTP is signed with a short-lived token containing the run id and job name; a handler that receives an unsigned request rejects it. This prevents anyone who can reach the handler's URL from triggering arbitrary jobs.
  • Cron as an attack surface. A user-supplied cron expression of * * * * * on an expensive job is a resource exhaustion attack. Minimum intervals are enforced per plan (free tier: no more often than every 15 minutes), and the parser rejects expressions producing more than N occurrences per day.
  • Backfill blast radius. A backfill of two years on a per-minute job is a million runs. The API caps planned runs per backfill, requires an explicit confirmation above a threshold, and always assigns the lowest priority.
  • Cancellation authorisation and auditing. Cancelling or pausing a platform job requires an elevated role, and every mutation writes an audit row with actor, before and after.
  • Secrets. Job payloads must not contain credentials; handlers fetch secrets from the secret manager using the job's identity. Payloads are stored in job_runs for 90 days and would otherwise leak into history, logs and backups.
  • Denial of service by poison job. A job that reliably crashes its worker is a per-tenant availability problem; the concurrency gate and the attempt cap contain it, and repeated deaths auto-disable the schedule with a notification.

40.15.15 Failure scenarios

Failure Detection Impact Mitigation What the user sees
Scheduler split-brain: two replicas both believe they are leader after a network partition scheduler_is_leader gauge summing above 1; scheduler_duplicate_schedule_total rising Both create runs for the same occurrence UNIQUE (job_name, scheduled_for) rejects the second insert; the loser counts a metric and continues; the lock is re-verified before every tick Nothing
Clock skew: a scheduler pod's clock is 90 seconds ahead Comparison of pod clock with now() from PostgreSQL, alert above 2 s Runs created early or late Discovery uses now() from the database, never the pod clock; the scheduled_for value comes from the cron parser anchored to database time; NTP is enforced by the node image Runs are on time
Worker dies mid-run (OOMKilled, spot reclaim) Lease expiry; runs_leases_expired_total The run is stuck in running The reaper reclaims runs whose lease_until < now(), increments the attempt and returns them to pending with backoff; a preStop hook releases the lease immediately on graceful shutdown The job runs slightly later
Duplicate run: a reclaimed run executes while the original worker was actually alive and slow Two run_attempts rows with overlapping times The handler runs twice The idempotencyKey of {jobName}:{scheduledFor} is passed to the handler, which must be idempotent; the lease is timeout + 30 s so a healthy worker always renews before expiry; long jobs must set a realistic timeout_sec Nothing, if the handler honours the key
Thundering herd at midnight: 200,000 runs due at 00:00:00 Claim latency spike, pending backlog, PostgreSQL CPU Claims slow, scheduling lag climbs to minutes Deterministic per-job jitter over 180 s; bounded discovery batches of 5,000; KEDA pre-scales workers at 23:55; claim batches of 50 Runs start within 3 minutes instead of all at once
DST double-fire: a job scheduled at 02:30 local on the autumn transition day scheduler_duplicate_schedule_total on that date The job would run twice scheduled_for is the local wall-clock label, so both instants map to the same execution key and the second insert is rejected; spring-forward gaps schedule at the next valid instant The job runs exactly once
Poison job: a payload that crashes the worker process every time Repeated attempts with the same error, job_deaths_total per job A worker slot cycles; a tenant's other jobs are delayed Attempt cap moves it to dead and the DLQ; three consecutive deaths auto-disable the schedule; per-tenant concurrency stops it from consuming the whole fleet "Job disabled after repeated failures" with the error
PostgreSQL failover Connection errors on both scheduler and workers Scheduling and claiming pause for 20 to 40 s The advisory lock is released with the session, so a new leader is elected on the new primary within seconds; workers retry claims with jitter; leases were sized to survive the gap A short delay; catch-up policy handles anything missed
Redis unavailable Gate errors Concurrency limits cannot be enforced Jobs with a limit fail closed and wait; jobs without one proceed; alert fires immediately Limited jobs are delayed
Reaper stops running Gauge of runs in running past their lease Dead runs never recovered The reaper is itself a scheduled job with a liveness metric and a separate alert on stuck_runs above zero for 5 minutes Some jobs never complete until the alert is handled
Handler is up but slow, exceeding timeout_sec Timeout counter per job Run marked failed, retried, handler now runs twice concurrently The dispatcher sends a cancellation signal on timeout; handlers are required to be idempotent; max_concurrency prevents an unbounded pile-up Longer completion, no duplicate effect
Long outage then catch-up storm pending backlog after recovery Thousands of missed runs flood the fleet Catch-up policy defaults to skip; run_all is bounded by maxCatchUp and runs at low priority Historical runs trickle through
Dependency deadlock: someone creates a cycle A -> B -> A Rejected at creation Nothing runs Topological check on every dependency insert refuses the edge An error when saving the dependency

40.15.16 Observability

The two metrics that define this system are scheduling lag and stuck runs.

scheduler_lag_seconds is claimed_at - scheduled_for, reported as a histogram per job and per priority. It answers "is the scheduler keeping up" in one number. The alert is p95 above 60 seconds for 5 minutes, and it fires for leader failure, worker starvation, database slowness and a midnight herd alike.

scheduler_stuck_runs counts rows in claimed or running whose lease_until has passed. It should always be zero within one reaper interval. Any sustained non-zero value means the reaper is broken or leases are being set too short, both of which are silent failures otherwise.

Other metrics: job_runs_created_total and job_runs_completed_total by outcome and job; job_duration_seconds histogram per job with an alert when p95 exceeds twice the 7-day baseline; job_attempts_total by attempt number (a rising second-attempt rate is the earliest signal of a flaky downstream); dlq_depth per job; scheduler_is_leader summed across replicas (must equal 1); scheduler_duplicate_schedule_total; pending_backlog by priority; concurrency_gate_rejections_total by job and tenant; per-tenant claim share for fairness.

Every run carries a trace id propagated into the handler, so a slow nightly job shows its full downstream call tree. run_attempts stores the error class and a truncated stack per attempt, which is what makes "why did this fail three weeks ago" answerable. A single dashboard per team lists their jobs with last run, next run, success rate over 7 days, p95 duration and DLQ depth, and it is the page the on-call opens first.

40.15.17 Deployment

Workload Kind Replicas Notes
scheduler-leader Deployment 3 Only one holds the advisory lock; the others are warm standbys
scheduler-api Deployment 3 CRUD, backfills, DLQ
job-worker Deployment 40 to 330, KEDA on pending backlog terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120, preStop releases leases
reaper Deployment 2 with leader election Reclaims expired leases every 10 s
history-archiver CronJob daily 1 Detaches old partitions, exports to S3
partition-manager CronJob weekly 1 Creates next week's partitions three weeks ahead

Worker pods are the only ones that scale, and they scale on backlog rather than CPU, because a worker waiting on a slow downstream uses no CPU while the backlog grows. KEDA is configured with a scheduled pre-scale at 23:50 so the midnight burst meets a warm fleet rather than a cold autoscaler.

Graceful shutdown matters more here than in most services. On SIGTERM a worker stops claiming, finishes in-flight runs up to the grace period, and releases the leases of anything it cannot finish so the reaper does not have to wait for expiry. Without that, every rolling deploy adds a lease-timeout-sized delay to a handful of jobs.

The partition-manager running three weeks ahead is not paranoia. A missing partition turns every INSERT into an error, which means the scheduler stops creating runs entirely, which means nothing runs, which is the worst possible failure of this system and one that a calendar boundary can cause at midnight when nobody is awake.

Migrations follow expand-and-contract, and there is one extra rule: never change the meaning of scheduled_for or the uniqueness of the execution key in a rolling deploy, because old and new pods computing different keys for the same occurrence would produce exactly the duplicate the key exists to prevent.

40.15.18 Cost considerations

Item Sizing Monthly (USD, approximate)
PostgreSQL (Aurora) writer r6g.2xlarge plus 1 reader, 200 GB 1,800
Worker compute 40 pods baseline, bursting to 330 for 10 minutes a day 1,400
Scheduler and API pods 6 small pods 250
Redis 1 small cluster 300
Kafka share dispatch and lifecycle topics 400
ClickHouse or S3 archive for history 2 years of Parquet 200
Observability 1M runs a day of metrics and traces, sampled 900
Total about 5,250

This is a cheap system, and that is the point of comparing it with the alternatives in 40.15.20. The real cost is not infrastructure; it is the engineering time to build and operate correctness features that Temporal or Airflow already ship. Roughly six engineer-months to build this properly and about 10 percent of one engineer's time to run it. If your workload is 1 million runs a day of simple jobs, that trade can be worth it; if your workload is complex multi-step workflows with human approvals and long timers, it never is.

40.15.19 Tradeoffs

  • PostgreSQL as the queue. Atomic claim plus state transition, trivially queryable state, cancellation as an UPDATE, and no extra infrastructure. The price is vacuum discipline, index care, connection management and a ceiling somewhere around ten million runs a day.
  • Advisory lock leader election instead of etcd or ZooKeeper. Fifteen lines and no new operational surface, at the cost of a genuine split-brain window on a network partition, made harmless by the idempotent execution key rather than by consensus.
  • Exactly-once effect, not exactly-once delivery. The scheduler guarantees a stable key and a bounded number of attempts; the handler guarantees the effect. This is the only honest contract in a distributed system, and pretending otherwise is how systems ship double invoices.
  • Deterministic jitter. Spreads the midnight herd over three minutes and makes lag predictable, at the cost of jobs not firing at the exact second, which eleven jobs opted out of.
  • Dependencies resolved at claim time. A late upstream delays the downstream rather than skipping it, which is almost always what teams want; the price is polling and a run_after push instead of an event-driven trigger.
  • Catch-up defaults to skip. Prevents a self-inflicted flood after an outage, at the cost of silently not running things; every skipped run is recorded and visible, so the choice is auditable.
  • Leases sized as timeout + 30 s. Fast recovery from worker death, but a job whose real duration exceeds its configured timeout will be duplicated. Configuring timeout_sec honestly is a requirement, not a suggestion.
  • Building this at all. The largest tradeoff. See below.

40.15.20 Alternative architectures

BullMQ (Redis-backed queues, with @nestjs/bullmq). Job queues with delayed jobs, repeatable jobs (cron), retries with backoff, priorities, rate limiting and a good dashboard, all in a library you add in an afternoon. It wins for a single team, for hundreds of thousands of jobs a day, and when the jobs are "do this thing soon" rather than "run this pipeline for this logical date". It loses on durability semantics (Redis persistence is weaker than PostgreSQL WAL, and a failover can lose recently added jobs), on history (there is no queryable multi-month execution record without exporting it yourself), on DAG dependencies and backfills, and on multi-tenant fairness. If BullMQ meets your needs, use BullMQ; most teams that build the system in this section should have used it.

Temporal (or Cadence). A durable execution engine: your workflow is ordinary code whose state is persisted at every step, so a process crash resumes exactly where it stopped, timers survive restarts for months, retries and compensation are first-class, and every execution has a complete replayable history. It wins whenever the unit of work is a multi-step workflow rather than a single job: order sagas, onboarding flows, anything with human approvals or long waits. It also subsumes cron (ScheduleClient). It loses on operational weight (a Temporal cluster is a real system to run, or a per-action bill on Temporal Cloud), on the determinism constraints workflow code must obey, and on the learning curve for a team that only needs "run this every hour".

Apache Airflow (or Dagster, Prefect). Purpose-built for DAGs on logical dates. It has exactly the concepts this design reinvented: execution_date as a logical time, backfills, catch-up policies, sensors, pools for concurrency, and a UI where a data engineer can see the grid of runs and clear one cell to re-run it. It wins overwhelmingly for data pipelines and ETL. It loses for low-latency operational jobs (its scheduler loop and task startup overhead make sub-minute scheduling awkward), for high job counts (tens of thousands of small runs a day strain it), and for multi-tenant SaaS use, where its permission model and Python-centric operators are a poor fit.

Quartz (JVM) or a database-backed cron in the application. Quartz is the mature JVM answer: clustered scheduling with database locking, misfire policies (its name for catch-up policies) and calendars. It wins in a JVM shop that already runs it. In a Node stack the equivalent is @nestjs/schedule plus a distributed lock, which is fine for a handful of platform jobs and becomes the mess described in the opening paragraph the moment there are fifty of them across ten services.

The decision table:

Situation Choose
A few dozen jobs in one service @nestjs/schedule plus a Redis or advisory lock
Hundreds of thousands of "do this soon" jobs, one team BullMQ
Data pipelines on logical dates, backfills, a data team Airflow or Dagster
Multi-step business workflows, long timers, compensation Temporal
Multi-tenant SaaS scheduling as a product feature, with per-tenant limits, regions and an audit trail Build it, roughly as described here

40.16 Cross-cutting lessons from the fifteen designs

Fifteen systems, fifteen different problem statements, fifteen different bills. And yet if you read the deep-dive sections back to back, the same nine or ten mechanisms keep appearing, wearing different clothes. That repetition is the real content of this part. The designs are worked examples; the patterns are the transferable skill.

Here is what actually repeated, why it repeated, and how to recognise the moment you need each one.

40.16.1 Idempotency is not a feature, it is the default posture

Every single design in this part has an idempotency mechanism, and in most of them it is the mechanism that makes correctness possible at all.

The URL shortener deduplicates by content hash. The authentication system rotates refresh tokens with a replay-detection window. The rate limiter accepts that a client retry consumes tokens and says so explicitly. The notification system deduplicates by (user, template, dedupe_key). The upload system makes complete idempotent by checksum. The payment system carries an idempotency key into the provider so a retry returns the original intent instead of charging twice. The order and inventory designs make reservation a conditional update. The e-commerce checkout enforces UNIQUE (idempotency_key) on orders. The feed's fan-out is ZADD with a deterministic member, which is idempotent by the nature of the data structure. The transcoder's task rows are unique on (job_id, step, rendition) and write to deterministic S3 keys. The scheduler's UNIQUE (job_name, scheduled_for) turns split-brain into a metric.

The reason is the same in all fifteen cases and it is worth stating as a law: in a distributed system, "did it happen?" is not always answerable, so every operation must be safe to attempt again. A timeout is not a failure; it is an unknown. The client cannot tell the difference between a request that never arrived, one that succeeded but whose response was lost, and one that is still running. So the client retries, and it is right to retry.

There are only three ways to be idempotent, and every design in this part uses one of them:

  1. A natural key with a uniqueness constraint. UNIQUE (job_name, scheduled_for), PRIMARY KEY (post_id, user_id) on likes, PRIMARY KEY (promotion_id, customer_id) on redemptions. The database refuses the duplicate. This is the strongest form because it does not depend on anyone remembering to check.
  2. A client-supplied key stored with the result. Idempotency-Key on checkout and on post creation, dedupe_key on scheduled runs. The second request returns the first request's stored response. This is the right form for anything a client initiates over an unreliable network.
  3. An operation that is naturally repeatable. SET instead of INCR, ZADD with a fixed member, PUT for a like, writing to a deterministic object key. Cheapest of all, when the domain permits it.

What does not work, and appears in every incident review, is "check whether it exists, then insert". Under concurrency that is a race, and the window is exactly as wide as your network latency.

40.16.2 The outbox: the only honest way to write to two places

Six designs write to a database and publish an event, and all six use the transactional outbox: notifications, chat, payments, orders, the feed, e-commerce.

The problem is always identical. You need COMMIT and producer.send() to happen together, and they cannot, because they are different systems with no shared transaction. If you publish first and the commit fails, consumers act on something that never happened. If you commit first and the publish fails, the world never learns about something that did.

The outbox resolves it by making the intent to publish part of the same transaction as the data change: insert the row, insert the outbox row, commit. A relay reads unsent outbox rows and publishes them, marking each sent afterwards. Delivery becomes at-least-once, never zero-times, and consumers handle duplicates because of 40.16.1.

flowchart LR
    TX["One transaction"] --> D["INSERT order"]
    TX --> O["INSERT outbox row"]
    TX --> C["COMMIT"]
    C --> R["Relay polls unsent rows"]
    R --> K["Kafka"]
    K --> CO["Idempotent consumers"]
    R --> M["Mark sent"]

The cost is one extra table, a relay process with leader election, and a small publish delay (typically under a second with LISTEN/NOTIFY or a 200 ms poll). The alternative, sometimes called "just publish after commit and hope", works fine until the pod is OOMKilled in the gap, and then it produces the class of bug that takes three days to find because the database and the message log disagree about reality.

40.16.3 Keyset pagination, never offsets

The feed, chat history, order history, notification inbox, comment threads, run history and search results all paginate, and none of them uses OFFSET.

Two reasons, and the second is the one people forget. First, cost: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000 makes PostgreSQL find and discard 100,000 rows, so page 5,000 is 5,000 times more expensive than page one. Second, correctness: on a list where rows are inserted at the head, offsets shift under the reader. A user scrolling a feed while new posts arrive sees duplicates and misses items, and no amount of database tuning fixes it because the bug is in the addressing scheme.

The keyset form is always the same shape: order by a stable, unique, monotonic key and ask for rows strictly beyond the last one you saw.

SELECT * FROM orders
 WHERE customer_id = $1 AND (created_at, id) < ($2, $3)
 ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
 LIMIT 20;

The tuple comparison matters: created_at alone is not unique, so ties would be skipped or repeated. The index must match the order exactly ((customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)), and then every page costs the same as the first. Encode the cursor as an opaque base64 string so clients cannot construct one and you can change the internals later. This is why the feed uses Snowflake ids: a single 8-byte, time-ordered, unique value that serves as primary key, sort key and cursor at once.

40.16.4 Redis plus PostgreSQL, and knowing which one is the truth

Every design uses both, and the discipline that keeps them sane is a single question asked of every piece of state: if this store is wiped right now, what have we lost?

If the answer is "nothing but speed", Redis can hold it. Feeds, product read models, hydration caches, session lookups, watch progress, availability badges, policy caches: all rebuildable from PostgreSQL, all in Redis, all with a rebuild path that is written and tested before it is needed.

If the answer is "money, an audit trail, or something a customer will call about", PostgreSQL holds it. Orders, payments, inventory ledgers, job definitions and execution keys, posts, follows, users.

The interesting middle is state that lives in Redis for performance but must not be lost: the rate limiter's token buckets (losing them means a brief over-allowance, accepted), the cart (losing it costs a sale, so it is backed up asynchronously to PostgreSQL), the flash-sale stock counter (losing it is contained because the real constraint is a CHECK in the database). In each case the design names the consequence of loss and then chooses deliberately. That naming is the whole discipline. "We put it in Redis because it is fast" is not a design decision; "we put it in Redis, and if Redis dies we lose at most five seconds of cart edits, which we accept" is.

Two rules fall out of this that appear in almost every design. Redis is never the only place a limit is enforced when the limit protects money or stock; the database has the authoritative constraint. And every cache has a documented rebuild path, because the day the cache is empty for everyone at once is the day you find out whether one exists.

40.16.5 Per-key ordering is the only ordering you get

Kafka, SQS FIFO and every partitioned log give ordering within a partition, never globally. Six designs depend on this, and all six choose their partition key to make the ordering they need line up with the key they have.

post.created is keyed by author id, so a create and a delete for the same author cannot be processed out of order. order.lifecycle is keyed by order id, so paid cannot overtake confirmed and the notification worker cannot send "shipped" before "confirmed". social.engagement is keyed by post id, which lets the aggregator batch all likes for one post in one consumer. transcode.task is keyed by job id, so the orchestrator sees ordered completions per video. Chat messages are keyed by conversation id, because ordering within a conversation is the product and ordering across conversations is meaningless.

The tradeoff is always the same and it is worth naming: the key that gives you the ordering you need is also the key that creates your hot partition. A viral post, a celebrity author, a huge tenant, a single hot video: all of them concentrate on one partition. The standard escape is a composite key (postId:bucket) applied only to keys detected as hot, with the consumer summing the buckets. You give up strict ordering for that key in exchange for throughput, which is acceptable for counters and unacceptable for state transitions.

If you need global ordering, you do not need a distributed system; you need one writer. Say so early.

40.16.6 Read models: pre-compute what is read a thousand times more often than it is written

The product page, the order history page, the feed entry, the chat conversation list, the video watch page and the notification inbox are all read models: denormalised documents assembled by a worker consuming events, stored as a single blob, fetched with one key lookup.

The arithmetic that justifies them is always a ratio. The e-commerce product page is read 83,500 times a second at peak and changes a few times a day. Rendering it from normalised tables costs a join across products, variants, inventory, reviews and promotions; rendering it from a Redis GET costs 0.3 ms. When the read-to-write ratio is above roughly a hundred to one, pre-computing wins, and above a thousand to one it is not really a choice.

The three things that make read models work in production, all of which appear in these designs:

  • The projector is idempotent and replayable. You will need to rebuild a projection because of a bug, and you must be able to do it without stopping writes.
  • Projection lag is a monitored metric with an alert. A read model is a promise about staleness; unmonitored, it becomes a promise about nothing.
  • Anything that must be correct is re-verified at the decision point. The e-commerce checkout re-reads the price from the source of truth even though the page came from a read model, because a stale page must never produce a wrong charge. Search indexes match and rank; they never decide.

40.16.7 Partitioning by time or by tenant

Large tables in these designs are partitioned exactly two ways, and the choice follows the access pattern mechanically.

By time when data has a natural lifetime and queries are recent-biased: posts, orders, order events, job runs, notification logs, chat messages, video stats. The benefits are retention as DETACH PARTITION instead of a multi-hour DELETE, indexes small enough to stay in memory for the hot partition, and vacuum that only ever touches the current partition. The cost is partition management, which must run ahead of time — the scheduler creates partitions three weeks in advance precisely because a missing partition turns every insert into an error at a calendar boundary, at midnight, when nobody is awake.

By hash of a key when there is no time dimension, only point lookups, and the goal is spreading write load: likes by post id, feed entries by user id, watch progress by user id, order events by order id. This avoids the tail-of-the-index hotspot that a monotonic key creates.

By tenant when isolation matters more than balance: a large tenant gets its own partition or its own schema so its volume, its vacuum behaviour and its slow queries do not affect anyone else. The scheduler, the rate limiter and the e-commerce platform all carry a tenant dimension for exactly this reason, even before it is strictly needed, because retrofitting a tenant column into a hundred queries is a year of work.

40.16.8 State machines with append-only event tables

Orders, payments, transcode jobs, scheduled runs, chat message delivery, upload sessions and checkout sagas are all state machines, and all of them keep two things: a state column for querying, and an append-only event table for truth.

The state column answers "show me all pending orders over 500 EUR" with a WHERE clause. The event table answers "what actually happened, in order, and when" — which is the first question in every payment dispute, every "my job did not run" ticket and every post-incident review. Keeping both is a deliberate middle path between a bare status field (fast, unauditable) and full event sourcing (auditable, and a much larger commitment).

Three properties make this pattern pay off:

  • Transitions are validated, not assigned. order.transitionTo('paid') checks that the current state permits it and throws otherwise. A state machine implemented as scattered UPDATE ... SET state = ... statements is not a state machine; it is a set of race conditions with a naming convention.
  • The event row is written in the same transaction as the state change, usually alongside the outbox row. Otherwise the history lies.
  • Illegal transitions are a metric. Their count should be zero, and when it is not, it points at the bug faster than any log search.

40.16.9 The hybrid fan-out

The last pattern is the most specific and the most instructive, because it is the one where arithmetic, not taste, produces the answer.

Whenever one write must reach many readers, there are exactly three strategies: push at write time into every reader's materialised list, pull at read time and merge, or split the population and do both. The feed uses it for celebrities. The notification system uses it for broadcast campaigns versus personal alerts. The chat system uses it for large group conversations versus one-to-one. The inventory and pricing designs use it for cache invalidation of very popular SKUs.

The decision is a single comparison. Push costs followers x posts writes. Pull costs followees x reads reads. With 50 million daily actives, ordinary accounts make push cheap (200 followers, 10 million posts a day, 2 billion writes spread over 24 hours) and celebrity accounts make it impossible (one account with 50 million followers occupies the entire Redis cluster for 12.5 seconds per post). So you set a threshold, push below it, pull above it, and merge at read time. The threshold is a runtime-tunable number, not a constant in code, because during an incident lowering it is the fastest available mitigation.

Recognise this pattern by its shape rather than its domain: a heavy-tailed distribution where the mean is harmless and the tail is fatal. The general answer is never "pick one strategy"; it is "pick a threshold, handle each side with the strategy that suits it, and make the threshold adjustable at runtime".

40.16.10 Each design, its hardest problem, and the pattern that solved it

# Design The single hardest problem The pattern that solved it
40.1 URL Shortener 10,000 redirects per second that must never hit disk, with unique short codes generated concurrently Redis-first read path with PostgreSQL as truth, plus pre-allocated id ranges and a content hash for idempotent creation
40.2 Authentication System A stolen refresh token is indistinguishable from a legitimate one Refresh-token rotation with reuse detection: an append-only token family where replaying a rotated token revokes the whole family
40.3 Rate Limiter One shared counter across sixty pods, decided in under 2 ms An atomic Lua token bucket on the Redis server clock, plus local hybrid buckets for hot subjects
40.4 Notification System The same event must not notify a user twice across three channels and many retries Deduplication keys plus the outbox, with per-user ordering from the partition key
40.5 File Upload System The client, S3 and the database must agree that an upload finished Presigned multipart upload with an idempotent, checksum-verified complete step and a state machine over the session
40.6 Chat System Ordering and delivery guarantees across devices that are offline half the time Per-conversation sequence numbers with per-key ordering in the log, and an append-only message table read by keyset
40.7 Payment System Money that has moved in a system you do not control Idempotency keys passed to the provider, authorise-then-capture, signed deduplicated webhooks, and a reconciliation job as the safety net
40.8 Order Management System Many partial failures across many downstream systems An orchestrated saga over an explicit state machine with an append-only order_events table and compensations
40.9 Inventory System Two customers buying the last unit at the same millisecond A conditional UPDATE ... WHERE on_hand - reserved >= qty plus a CHECK constraint, so the database refuses to oversell
40.10 Food Delivery System Assigning couriers on live, constantly changing geospatial state Redis geospatial indexes as the hot read model with PostgreSQL as truth, and per-order state machines for the handoffs
40.11 Ride Booking System Matching supply and demand in real time without double-assigning a driver A short-lived distributed lock or conditional claim per driver, with per-driver ordering and an expiring offer state machine
40.12 Social Media Feed One post from an account with fifty million followers Hybrid fan-out: push below a follower threshold, pull above it, merged at read time over capped Redis sorted sets
40.13 Video Streaming Platform Egress cost, and a multi-step pipeline that must survive crashes at any step Unique (job, step, rendition) task rows with deterministic output keys and leases, plus immutable versioned CDN paths
40.14 E-commerce Platform Payment captured but the order not created Ordered saga with the irreversible step last, a UNIQUE (idempotency_key) on orders, and a provider reconciler that sweeps the gap
40.15 Distributed Job Scheduler Two schedulers, one clock, and a job that must run exactly once UNIQUE (job_name, scheduled_for) as an idempotent execution key, with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED claims and heartbeat leases

Read that table twice. Nine of the fifteen hardest problems are some form of "this might happen twice", and every one of them is solved by a uniqueness constraint or a stable key rather than by coordination. That is the single most useful thing to carry out of Part 40.

40.16.11 What senior engineers refused to do

The absences are as consistent as the patterns.

No design used a distributed transaction or two-phase commit. Where atomicity across systems was needed, a saga with explicit compensation and a state machine did the job, because 2PC turns two systems' availability into their product and blocks on a coordinator failure.

No design put a synchronous third-party call inside a database transaction. Payment providers, carriers, tax services and transcoders are all called outside the transaction, with the state machine recording the intent before and the result after.

No design used floating point for money. Integer cents, everywhere, with the currency stored next to the amount.

No design trusted a client-supplied price, total, limit or identity. Everything that decides an outcome is recomputed server-side.

No design started with microservices. The e-commerce platform is explicit about it: a modular monolith with named seams and an extraction order, because a thirty-person team's bottleneck is coordination cost, not machine capacity, and a distributed system you did not need is a permanent tax.

And no design left a cache without a documented rebuild path, a queue without a dead-letter queue, a retry without a maximum attempt count, or a failure table with fewer than eight rows. Those four omissions are what turn a working system into a 3 a.m. page.

Senior Checklist — Part 40

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can take a one-sentence problem statement and produce requirements, non-functional targets and constraints before drawing anything
  • I can do capacity arithmetic out loud: users, DAU, RPS average and peak, read/write ratio, bytes per record, storage per year, bandwidth, cache size, connection count
  • I can write an API table with method, path, request, response, status codes, idempotency and auth for any system in this part
  • I can write PostgreSQL DDL with real types and constraints, and justify every index by the query it serves
  • I can choose between fan-out on write, fan-out on read and a hybrid, and show the arithmetic that decides it
  • I can make any write endpoint idempotent by one of the three mechanisms, and say which one I chose and why
  • I can explain the transactional outbox and why publishing after commit is not equivalent
  • I can write keyset pagination with a tuple comparison and the matching index, and explain why OFFSET breaks on a moving list
  • I can decide what belongs in Redis and what belongs in PostgreSQL by naming the consequence of losing each store
  • I can design a saga with explicit compensations and place the irreversible step last
  • I can prevent oversell with a conditional update and a CHECK constraint rather than a read-then-write
  • I can claim work from a table with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, hold it with a heartbeat lease, and recover it when the worker dies
  • I can choose a Kafka partition key that gives the ordering the domain needs, and handle the hot partition it creates
  • I can partition a large table by time or by hash and explain which retention and vacuum problems that solves
  • I can produce a failure table with at least eight modes, each with detection, impact, mitigation and what the user sees
  • I can give a 1x, 10x and 100x scaling ladder that says what concretely changes at each step
  • I can estimate a monthly bill and name the dominant cost driver, and I know that in a media system it is egress
  • I can name at least two alternative architectures for any design and the conditions under which each wins
  • I know when not to build: BullMQ instead of a scheduler, a commerce platform instead of a checkout, a managed pipeline instead of a transcoder

Part 40 — Key Takeaways

  • Design is a method, not a memory: clarify, estimate, define APIs, model data, draw, deep-dive the hot path, cover the cross-cutting concerns, state tradeoffs, offer alternatives. The fifteen case studies are that method applied fifteen times.
  • Numbers decide architectures. The hybrid fan-out, the queue-based flash-sale checkout, the lazy bitrate ladder and the midnight jitter were all forced by arithmetic, not by preference. Do the arithmetic before you draw the boxes.
  • Assume every request will be retried. Idempotency by a uniqueness constraint, a stored client key, or a naturally repeatable operation is what separates a system that survives retries from one that double-charges.
  • Never write to two systems and hope. The transactional outbox is the standard answer, and at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers is the standard contract.
  • Redis holds what you can afford to rebuild; PostgreSQL holds what a customer will call about. Write the rebuild path before you need it, and name the loss you are accepting.
  • The database's constraints are your best concurrency control. CHECK (reserved <= on_hand), UNIQUE (job_name, scheduled_for) and UNIQUE (promotion_id, customer_id) prevent bugs that no amount of application-level checking can.
  • Pre-compute what is read far more often than it is written, monitor its lag, and re-verify anything that decides money or permissions at the decision point.
  • Ordering is per key or it does not exist. Choose the partition key for the ordering the domain needs, then plan for the hot partition that choice creates.
  • Every long-running thing needs a lease, a heartbeat and a reaper: transcode tasks, scheduled runs, reservations, upload sessions and saga steps all die mid-flight eventually.
  • The cost model is part of the design. In a streaming platform egress dominates; in e-commerce payment fees dwarf infrastructure; in a feed the CDN and Redis memory are the levers. Optimising the wrong layer is the most expensive kind of busy work.
  • Failure tables and 1x/10x/100x ladders are where seniority shows. Anyone can draw the happy path; the job is knowing what breaks, how you find out, and what the user sees while you fix it.
  • The best architecture is the simplest one that meets the requirement. Start with a modular monolith and named seams, extract a service when a specific pain justifies it, and know which battles to skip entirely by buying BullMQ, Temporal, a commerce platform or a managed pipeline instead of building one.

Part 41 — Capacity Estimation and Back-of-the-Envelope Math

Capacity estimation is the skill that separates an engineer who has opinions from an engineer who has numbers. It is not forecasting and it is not budgeting. It is the ten minutes of arithmetic you do before you choose an architecture, so that the architecture you choose is the one the traffic actually needs.

The whole discipline rests on one idea: an estimate that is right to within a factor of three, computed from assumptions you stated out loud, is worth more than a precise number computed from an assumption nobody checked. A factor of three is the difference between "one PostgreSQL instance" and "one PostgreSQL instance with a bigger disk". A wrong assumption is the difference between "one PostgreSQL instance" and "you need Kafka and a columnar store".

This part teaches the skill by doing it. Every section is worked, with the arithmetic in tables, because reading someone else's conclusion teaches nothing. Copy the tables. Change the inputs. That is the exercise.

41.1 The numbers every backend engineer should know

You cannot estimate anything without a handful of memorized magnitudes. You do not need precision; you need to know which numbers are a thousand times bigger than which other numbers, because that is where design decisions live.

41.1.1 Latency: how long one thing takes

Operation Typical time Human scale (if 1 ns = 1 second) What it means for design
L1 cache reference 1 ns 1 second Free. Never think about it.
Branch mispredict 3 ns 3 seconds Free at backend scale.
L2 cache reference 4 ns 4 seconds Free.
Mutex lock and unlock (uncontended) 17 ns 17 seconds Free until contended.
Main memory reference 100 ns 1.5 minutes 100x slower than L1. Cache locality matters in hot loops.
Compress 1 KB (snappy/lz4) 2 us 33 minutes Cheap. Compress before you send over a network.
Read 1 MB sequentially from RAM 50 us 14 hours Building a 10 MB JSON array in memory is not free.
NVMe SSD random read (4 KB) 50–150 us 14–40 hours A PostgreSQL page miss to local NVMe.
Network-attached SSD random read (EBS gp3) 250–600 us 3–7 days 4x worse than local NVMe. This is what your RDS actually has.
Round trip, same availability zone 0.25–0.5 ms 3–6 days The floor for any network call in your cluster.
Redis GET, same AZ, small value 0.2–0.6 ms 3–7 days Dominated by the round trip, not by Redis.
Indexed PostgreSQL lookup, page in cache 0.3–1 ms server-side 4–12 days The pg_stat_statements mean_exec_time of a healthy PK lookup.
Same lookup, seen from the NestJS service 0.8–2 ms 10–24 days Adds pool acquire, round trip, driver parse, row hydration.
Indexed PostgreSQL lookup, page from disk 5–20 ms 2–8 months 10–20x worse. This is why shared_buffers and cache hit ratio matter.
Kafka produce, acks=all, same region 2–10 ms 1–4 months Includes replication to two followers and an fsync policy.
Round trip, cross-AZ same region 0.5–2 ms 6–24 days Cheap enough to ignore; not free at 100k calls per request-second.
Round trip, cross-region (Mumbai to Frankfurt) 110–140 ms 3–4 years Never put a synchronous cross-region hop on a user path.
Round trip, cross-region (Virginia to Ireland) 70–90 ms 2–3 years Same rule.
Round trip, mobile client to your edge 50–250 ms 2–8 years The user's latency budget is mostly not yours.
Read 1 MB sequentially from network storage 5–15 ms 2–5 months Large SELECT * results are an I/O decision, not a code style decision.
Third-party HTTPS API call 80–800 ms 3–25 years Always has a timeout. Always.
bcrypt hash, cost factor 12 250–350 ms 8–11 years About 3 logins per second per CPU core. Size for it.

Two rules fall straight out of this table. First, anything that crosses a network is at least a thousand times more expensive than anything that does not, so the number of network round trips per request is the single most important architectural number you control. Second, a cache miss that becomes a disk read costs 10–20x a cache hit, which is why a cache hit ratio is not a nice-to-have metric, it is a capacity metric.

41.1.2 Throughput: how many things per second

Component Sustained throughput Conditions
One PostgreSQL instance, 8 vCPU / 64 GB, simple indexed reads 20,000–40,000 queries/s Working set fits in shared_buffers + page cache; short transactions; connections pooled
Same instance, complex joins over 3–5 tables 1,000–5,000 queries/s Depends entirely on rows touched
Same instance, small write transactions (INSERT + index maintenance) 3,000–10,000 tx/s synchronous_commit=on, fast WAL disk; 2–3x more with COPY or multi-row INSERT
Same instance, bulk load with COPY 100,000–500,000 rows/s Indexes dropped or few; one session
One Redis instance (single-threaded core) 80,000–150,000 ops/s Small values, no pipelining. 500k+/s with pipelining
One Kafka broker 100–300 MB/s Batched producers, acks=all, replication factor 3
One Kafka partition 10–30 MB/s, or 10k–50k small messages/s This is the parallelism unit. Consumers cannot exceed partitions
PgBouncer (transaction pooling) 20,000–50,000 tx/s per process Single-threaded; run several with SO_REUSEPORT
One NestJS pod (1 vCPU, 1 GB), trivial JSON endpoint 1,500–4,000 RPS No I/O, small response, no class-transformer
One NestJS pod, one indexed query + DTO validation 400–900 RPS Realistic "read one entity" endpoint
One NestJS pod, 3–5 queries + serialization of 50 rows 120–350 RPS The realistic "list endpoint" number
One NestJS pod, heavy class-transformer + 200 KB response 40–120 RPS Serialization becomes the bottleneck

The loudest caveat in this part: these are starting points, not facts about your system. A pod's RPS depends on your CPU limit, your Node version, your middleware stack, your logging volume, your payload size and your query plans. The correct workflow is to start from the table, design with it, then replace every number with a measured one from your own load test (Part 24 — Performance and Optimization covers how to run that test). An estimate built on a measured constant is engineering; an estimate built on a remembered constant is a guess with a table around it.

41.1.3 Time and size shortcuts

A day is 86,400 seconds. Round it to 10^5. That single approximation removes almost all of the arithmetic pain, and it errs on the safe side by 16 percent: it makes your computed RPS slightly higher than reality, which is the direction you want to be wrong in.

Rate Per day Per month (30 d) Per year
1 per second 86,400 (~10^5) 2.6 million 31.5 million
10 per second 864,000 26 million 315 million
100 per second 8.6 million 260 million 3.2 billion
1,000 per second 86 million 2.6 billion 32 billion
12 per second 1 million 31 million 380 million
11,600 per second 1 billion 30 billion 365 billion

Read it in both directions. "One million a day" is 12 per second, which is nothing. "One billion a day" is 11,600 per second, which is a real system. "One million a month" is 0.4 per second, which is a cron job.

For bytes, memorize one anchor: 1 KB at 1,000 per second is 1 MB/s, which is 86 GB/day and 2.6 TB/month.

Payload At 100/s At 1,000/s At 10,000/s
1 KB 0.1 MB/s = 8.6 GB/day 1 MB/s = 86 GB/day 10 MB/s = 864 GB/day
10 KB 1 MB/s = 86 GB/day 10 MB/s = 864 GB/day 100 MB/s = 8.6 TB/day
100 KB 10 MB/s = 864 GB/day 100 MB/s = 8.6 TB/day 1 GB/s = 86 TB/day

The last cell is why nobody serves 100 KB responses at 10,000 RPS from an origin server. That is a CDN's job, and the arithmetic tells you so in five seconds.

41.2 The method

The method is five moves plus one discipline. It takes ten minutes and it works for every system you will ever be asked to size.

41.2.1 The five moves

1. State the assumptions out loud. Write them as a list with numbers and units. "20 million monthly actives", "10 percent of them are active on a given day", "each active user makes 25 API calls". Every one of these is a guess; the point of writing them down is that a reviewer can attack the guess instead of attacking the conclusion. In a design review, the assumption list is the most valuable part of the document, because it is the part that will be wrong.

2. Write the formula before you compute. average_rps = dau * actions_per_user / 86400. Writing the formula separates a modelling error from an arithmetic error, and it lets you change one input later without redoing the whole thing. It also makes the estimate reusable: next quarter the DAU changes and the formula still holds.

3. Compute, rounding to one significant figure. 2,847 becomes 3,000. 41,900 becomes 40,000. Rounding is not laziness; it is a statement about the precision of your inputs. If your DAU assumption is plus or minus 40 percent, reporting 2,847 RPS is a lie about how much you know. Round in the direction of safety: up for load, up for storage, down for the throughput a component can deliver.

4. Sanity-check against something you already know. This is the move that catches the catastrophic errors, and it is the move juniors skip. "3,000 RPS peak" — is that a lot? Compare it to a component: one PostgreSQL instance does 20,000 simple reads per second, so 3,000 RPS with a 95:5 read ratio is comfortable for one primary. Compare it to a system you have run: "our current service does 800 RPS on 8 pods, so this is 4x that, so about 30 pods". Compare it to physics: "500 GB per day of writes on a gp3 volume is 6 MB/s sustained, which is well under the 125 MB/s baseline, fine". If a number fails every comparison you can think of, you made a modelling error, not a rounding error.

5. Add headroom, explicitly and by name. Never present a peak number as the capacity target. Systems queue badly above roughly 70–80 percent utilization (Part 24 covers the queueing curve), autoscaling takes 60–180 seconds to react, and one availability zone can disappear. So:

Headroom type Multiplier Why
Utilization target 1.5x (run at ~65%) The knee of the latency curve is near 80%
Autoscaling reaction time included above A burst must be absorbed before pods arrive
AZ loss (N+1 across 3 AZs) 1.5x Losing 1 of 3 zones means the other 2 carry everything
Growth to next planning cycle 1.3–2x Six to twelve months of growth
Total, typical 2.5–4x the average Applied to peak, not to average

Say which multipliers you used. "Peak 3,000 RPS, target 65 percent utilization, N+1 across three zones, so provision for 3,000 / 0.65 * 1.5 = 6,900 RPS of capacity" is a sentence a reviewer can argue with productively.

41.2.2 The discipline: precision is not accuracy

Here is the failure that this discipline prevents. Two engineers estimate storage for an order history table.

Engineer A Engineer B
Row size "312.4 bytes, computed from pg_column_size on a sample" "about 300 bytes"
Rows per day "60,000 orders" (took last Tuesday's number) "60,000 orders, but Black Friday is 20x and December runs 3x, so call it 90,000 average"
Retention not mentioned "3 years hot, then archive"
Indexes not mentioned "PK plus 3 indexes, roughly 1x the table"
Replicas and backups not mentioned "primary + 2 replicas + 14 daily backups"
Result 6.8 GB per year ~40 GB per year of table+index, ~120 GB of provisioned storage across copies

Engineer A's number has four significant figures and is wrong by a factor of 17. Engineer B's number is rounded to one significant figure and is right to within a factor of two. Engineer A will discover the error when the volume fills at 2 a.m.
