A factor-of-three error in an estimate is normal and survivable. You provision one instance class larger, or you scale out. A factor-of-thirty error is an architecture mistake, and factor-of-thirty errors come from missing terms, not from imprecise ones. So the checklist matters more than the calculator: did you count indexes, replicas, backups, WAL, peak vs average, and retention? Every one of those is a multiplier that a careless estimate silently sets to 1.

flowchart TB
  A["State assumptions with units"] --> B["Write the formula"]
  B --> C["Compute, round to 1 significant figure"]
  C --> D["Sanity check against a known system"]
  D --> E{"Plausible?"}
  E -->|"No, off by 10x or more"| F["Find the missing term or wrong assumption"]
  F --> A
  E -->|"Yes"| G["Add named headroom: utilization, AZ loss, growth"]
  G --> H["Map to concrete settings: pods, pool, instance class, partitions"]
  H --> I["Load test and measure"]
  I --> J{"Model within 3x of reality?"}
  J -->|"No"| K["Correct the constant, not the method"]
  K --> A
  J -->|"Yes"| L["Record the model next to the runbook"]

The last box matters more than it looks. An estimate that lives in a Slack thread is lost by the next quarter. An estimate written next to the runbook, with its assumptions, becomes the thing you update when traffic doubles, and the thing that tells the next on-call engineer what "normal" is supposed to be.

41.3 Requests per second

Almost every capacity conversation starts here, and almost every one starts from a marketing number: monthly active users. The job is to walk that number down to a peak second.

41.3.1 From monthly actives to average RPS

The chain is: MAU -> DAU -> sessions per day -> actions per session -> requests per action -> requests per day -> average RPS.

The step everyone gets wrong is "requests per action". A user tapping "place order" is one action and eight API calls: cart fetch, address list, shipping options, payment methods, order creation, payment intent, order confirmation poll, and an analytics beacon. Count the API calls, not the user's intentions.

Worked example, an e-commerce app:

Step Formula Value Assumption behind it
Monthly active users given 20,000,000 From the product team
Daily active users MAU * DAU/MAU ratio 20M * 0.10 = 2,000,000 10% is typical for retail apps; 25–35% for social, 60%+ for a work tool
Sessions per DAU per day given 1.4 Analytics
API calls per session given 18 Counted from a real session trace, not guessed
API calls per day 2M * 1.4 * 18 50,400,000
Round 50,000,000/day One significant figure
Average RPS 50M / 86,400 578
Round 600 RPS average

Sanity check: 600 RPS on a service that does 250 RPS per pod is about 3 pods of raw capacity, which is small. That feels right for 2 million daily users doing light browsing, and it should make you suspicious of any design that starts with "we will need Kafka for the API traffic".

The DAU/MAU ratio is worth its own table, because it is the assumption most likely to be off by 3x:

Product type Typical DAU/MAU Note
Messaging / social feed 50–70% People open it many times a day
Ride hailing / food delivery 8–20% Bursty and habitual but not daily
E-commerce marketplace 5–15% Purchase intent is rare; browsing is not daily
B2B SaaS used at work 40–70% on weekdays, 5% weekends The weekday/weekend split is a real capacity factor
Banking / utility app 10–25% Spikes on salary day and bill due dates

41.3.2 Peak-to-average ratio

Average RPS is a fiction. Nobody experiences the average. You size for the peak.

Traffic pattern Peak / average Example
Global consumer app, users spread over many time zones 1.5–2.5x The curves overlap and flatten each other
Single-country consumer app 3–5x One evening peak
B2B tool in one country 5–8x Nothing overnight, nothing on weekends, everything at 10 a.m.
Food delivery 6–10x Two sharp meal peaks, near-zero at 4 a.m.
Payroll / billing / statements 20–50x on one day Month-end, salary day, invoice day
Flash sale, ticket drop, result announcement 30–100x for 60–300 seconds A step function, not a ramp

For our e-commerce example, a single-country app with an evening peak: 600 * 5 = 3,000 RPS peak. During a flash sale on a specific SKU: 600 * 50 = 30,000 RPS, but concentrated on two endpoints (product detail and checkout) rather than spread across eighteen.

That distinction is the whole design conversation. A 5x diurnal peak is an autoscaling problem. A 50x flash-sale peak is an architecture problem: a CDN in front of the product page, a queue or a waiting room in front of checkout, precomputed stock counters in Redis, and a rate limiter that sheds rather than melts. You do not scale your way through a 50x spike; you change the shape of the work.

41.3.3 The diurnal curve

A rough single-country curve, expressed as a percentage of daily volume per hour:

% of daily traffic per hour (single-country consumer app)

12 |                                          ####
10 |                                       ####  ####
 8 |                                    ####        ##
 6 |                      ####       ####             ##
 4 |                 ######    #######                  ##
 2 |          #######                                     ####
 0 |##########                                                ####
   +----------------------------------------------------------------
    00  02  04  06  08  10  12  14  16  18  20  22
                                        ^ peak hour: 20:00-21:00

If traffic were flat, each hour would hold 4.17 percent of the day. In this shape the peak hour holds about 10–12 percent. That single fact gives you the first half of the peak factor:

Quantity Formula Value
Requests per day given 50,000,000
Share of traffic in the peak hour from the curve 11%
Requests in the peak hour 50M * 0.11 5,500,000
Peak-hour average RPS 5.5M / 3,600 1,530 RPS
Ratio to daily average 1,530 / 578 2.6x

41.3.4 The peak second is not the peak hour

Inside the peak hour, traffic is not smooth either. Arrivals cluster: a push notification goes out, a TV ad airs, a train arrives and four hundred people unlock their phones. Empirically, the busiest second within the busiest hour runs 1.5–3x the peak hour's average for organic traffic, and far more when something triggers a synchronized arrival.

Quantity Formula Value Sizes what
Daily average RPS 50M / 86,400 580 Cost, storage growth, monthly bills
Peak-hour RPS 50M * 0.11 / 3,600 1,530 Autoscaling target, replica count, steady-state capacity
Peak-second RPS 1,530 * 2 3,000 Pod count, connection pool, rate limits, queue depth
Provisioned capacity 3,000 / 0.65 * 1.5 (AZ loss) 6,900 What you must be able to serve

Use the right one for the right decision. Sizing storage from the peak second wastes a fortune. Sizing the connection pool from the daily average causes an incident. A useful shorthand: averages buy hardware, peaks prevent outages, and the peak second is the one that pages you.

One more distinction that costs people real money: a burst of 3,000 RPS for 5 seconds is absorbed by queueing if your pods have any spare capacity and your clients have any patience. A sustained 3,000 RPS for 20 minutes is not; it must actually be served. Ask "for how long?" before you size for a spike. Buffers absorb bursts; only capacity absorbs load.

41.4 Reads and writes

Total RPS is not a workload. A thousand reads per second and a thousand writes per second are completely different machines. Split the number early.

41.4.1 Read/write ratios by system type

System Read:write Consequence
Product catalog / content site 100:1 to 1000:1 Cache and read replicas solve almost everything
Social feed 50:1 to 200:1 Read-heavy, but fan-out on write inverts the cost
E-commerce (browse + buy) 20:1 to 100:1 Reads cache well; writes are the transactional core
Order management / back office 5:1 to 20:1 Cache helps less; writes need real transaction throughput
Chat / messaging 1:1 to 3:1 Writes dominate; caching barely helps
Financial ledger 5:1 to 15:1 Writes must be durable and serialized; no cheating
IoT / telemetry ingestion 1:50 to 1:1000 Write-dominated. A relational primary is the wrong tool
Analytics event pipeline 1:1000 Append-only; columnar store or object storage

Establish the ratio from your own logs or from pg_stat_statements (calls grouped by statement kind), not from the table. The table is for the case where the system does not exist yet.

For the running e-commerce example at 3,000 RPS peak with a 95:5 split:

Class Share Peak RPS
Reads 95% 2,850
Writes 5% 150

41.4.2 Where each read goes

Not every read is equal. Route them by staleness tolerance, which is a product decision, not a technical one. Ask the product owner: "if this number is 30 seconds old, does anything bad happen?"

Read type Staleness tolerance Destination Peak RPS (example)
Product detail, category listing minutes Redis, then CDN for anonymous traffic 1,400
Search results seconds to minutes Search index (OpenSearch), cached 400
User profile, addresses seconds Redis with 5 min TTL 300
Order history list seconds Read replica 350
Cart contents none (user just changed it) Primary, or Redis as system of record 250
Stock availability at checkout none Primary only 100
Payment status none Primary only 50

The rule: a read must hit the primary only if a user action in the last few seconds must be visible in it. Everything else is a cache or a replica question. In practice 70–90 percent of reads in a typical product tolerate seconds of staleness, and that is what makes read-heavy systems cheap to scale.

flowchart LR
  C["Client: 2850 reads per second"] --> CDN["CDN: anonymous catalog"]
  CDN -->|"about 900 rps offloaded"| C
  CDN --> API["NestJS API: 1950 rps"]
  API --> R["Redis: hot keys"]
  R -->|"hit, about 1330 rps"| API
  R -->|"miss, about 70 rps"| PG1
  API --> RR["Read replicas: tolerant reads, 350 rps"]
  API --> PG1["Primary: strict reads 200 rps plus writes 150 rps"]
  RR --> PG2["Replica 1"]
  RR --> PG3["Replica 2"]

41.4.3 The arithmetic of a cache hit ratio

This is the highest-leverage calculation in capacity estimation, and it is one line:

database_read_rps = cacheable_read_rps * (1 - hit_ratio) + uncacheable_read_rps

Take 1,400 RPS of cacheable catalog reads and vary the hit ratio:

Hit ratio Misses reaching PostgreSQL Change vs 95% Effect
0% (no cache) 1,400 rps 20x worse Needs several replicas just for the catalog
50% 700 rps 10x worse Cache is not earning its operational cost
80% 280 rps 4x worse One replica, comfortable
90% 140 rps 2x worse Comfortable
95% 70 rps baseline Catalog reads are effectively free
99% 14 rps 5x better Diminishing returns on capacity, big win on p99 latency

Two conclusions that every senior engineer carries around:

A cache is a multiplier, and multipliers are fragile. Going from 95 to 90 percent doubles database load. Going from 95 to 50 percent puts 10x the load on the database instantly. That is exactly what happens when a deploy changes a cache key format, when Redis restarts with an empty keyspace, when maxmemory is reached and eviction starts, or when a bot walks the long tail of your catalog and pollutes the working set. Your database must be able to survive a cold cache, or your cache is a single point of failure wearing a performance costume. The honest way to size this is to write down two numbers: steady-state database load (70 rps) and cold-cache database load (1,400 rps), then decide explicitly which one you provision for and what protects you in between (request coalescing, stale-while-revalidate, a staged warm-up, load shedding).

Above 95 percent, extra hit ratio buys latency, not capacity. Going from 95 to 99 percent saves 56 rps of database load, which is nothing, but it removes a 5 ms tail from 4 percent of requests, which shows up directly in p99. Know which of the two you are optimizing.

Writes have their own multiplier that estimates routinely forget: each write usually costs more than one database operation. One order creation is an INSERT into orders, three into order_items, an UPDATE on products.available, an INSERT into the outbox table, plus index maintenance on all of them. So:

Write Logical rate Database operations each Actual database write rate
Order created 4 rps peak 6 24
Cart updated 90 rps 2 180
Session touched 40 rps 1 (send it to Redis instead) 0
Analytics event 400 rps 1 (send it to Kafka instead) 0
Everything else 16 rps 2 32
Total to PostgreSQL ~240 write ops/s

240 write operations per second against a primary that does 3,000–10,000 is comfortable, and the two rows that were moved out (sessions to Redis, analytics to Kafka) are exactly the decisions the arithmetic is supposed to produce. That is the point of this whole exercise: the table is not the deliverable, the two moves are.

41.5 Storage

Storage estimates are where the missing-multiplier failure does the most damage, because the answer is not "the service is slow", it is "the volume is full at 03:40 on a Sunday and PostgreSQL has stopped accepting writes". Work bottom-up: bytes per row, rows per day, then every multiplier.

41.5.1 Estimating a row from its column types

PostgreSQL stores each row (a tuple) with a 23-byte header, padded to 24 bytes, plus a null bitmap when the table has nullable columns, plus 4 bytes for the line pointer in the page. Then the columns themselves, each aligned to its natural boundary.

PostgreSQL type Bytes on disk Notes
boolean 1
smallint 2
integer 4
bigint, double precision, timestamptz, timestamp, time 8 timestamptz is 8 bytes, not more; it stores UTC
date 4
uuid 16 Fixed. Not 36. The 36 characters are only the text rendering
numeric(12,2) 8–12 Variable length: ~8 bytes overhead + 2 bytes per group of 4 digits
real 4
char(3) 4 1-byte length header + 3 characters
varchar(n) / text 1 + length (short) or 4 + length (over 126 bytes) Store the average length, not n
jsonb 4 + encoded size, usually 1.1–1.3x the JSON text Keys are stored per row, so short keys matter
bytea 4 + length
Enum type 4 Much cheaper than varchar for status columns
Array 20 + elements
Tuple header + alignment 24 Once per row
Line pointer in page 4 Once per row

Worked example, an orders table:

Column Type Bytes Reasoning
id uuid 16
user_id uuid 16
status order_status enum 4 Was varchar(20); the enum saves 8 bytes per row
total_amount numeric(12,2) 10 Values around 4–7 digits
currency char(3) 4
payment_intent_id varchar(64) 32 Average length 31 + 1 header
shipping_address jsonb 210 Measured with pg_column_size on 1,000 real rows
placed_at timestamptz 8
updated_at timestamptz 8
created_at timestamptz 8
Column subtotal 316
Alignment padding 4 Columns are 8-byte aligned where required
Tuple header 24
Line pointer 4
Total per row ~348 Round to 350 bytes

Verify it rather than trusting the arithmetic, because jsonb and text averages are the terms most likely to be wrong:

-- Average on-disk size of one row, measured on real data
SELECT pg_size_pretty(avg(pg_column_size(o.*))::numeric) AS avg_row,
       pg_size_pretty(avg(pg_column_size(o.shipping_address))::numeric) AS avg_address
FROM orders o TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (1);

-- Actual bytes per row including page overhead and bloat
SELECT pg_total_relation_size('orders') AS total_bytes,
       (SELECT reltuples::bigint FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'orders') AS approx_rows,
       pg_total_relation_size('orders') / NULLIF((SELECT reltuples FROM pg_class WHERE relname='orders'),0) AS bytes_per_row;

Page overhead: a page is 8,192 bytes with a 24-byte page header and a 16-byte special area reservation, so about 8,150 usable. At 350 bytes plus a 4-byte line pointer, a page holds 8150 / 354 = 23 rows, giving an effective 354 bytes per row including page overhead. With the default fillfactor of 100 for a table that is mostly appended, that is realistic. For a heavily-updated table set fillfactor to 80–90 so HOT updates can stay on the page, and multiply your storage estimate by 1.1–1.25 accordingly.

41.5.2 Index size

A B-tree index entry is roughly key_bytes + 8 bytes of index tuple header + 4 bytes of line pointer, aligned to 8, plus internal pages (about 1 percent) and the default fillfactor of 90 which leaves 10 percent free. A workable rule:

index_bytes ≈ rows * (key_bytes + 12) * 1.3
Index Key columns Key bytes Formula Size at 22M rows
orders_pkey uuid 16 22M * 28 * 1.3 800 MB
idx_orders_user_placed uuid, timestamptz 24 22M * 36 * 1.3 1.0 GB
idx_orders_status_placed enum, timestamptz 12 22M * 24 * 1.3 690 MB
idx_orders_payment_intent varchar(64) 32 22M * 44 * 1.3 1.3 GB
Table itself 22M * 354 7.8 GB
Indexes as a fraction of the table 3.8 GB / 7.8 GB ~0.5x

Two lessons. Indexes are not free storage-wise, and they are not free write-wise either: every INSERT writes to the table plus all four indexes, and that write amplification is the reason your WAL volume is bigger than you expect. And a uuid primary key is expensive: random v4 UUIDs also cause index page splits and poor locality. If you are still choosing, bigint identity keys or UUIDv7 (time-ordered) cut both the size and the write amplification. A partial index (WHERE status = 'pending' on a table where 0.5 percent of rows are pending) can be 200x smaller than the full index and is often the right answer for status columns.

Typical whole-database rule of thumb: indexes total 0.5x to 2x the table data. If a table's indexes exceed 2x its data, someone has been adding indexes without deleting any; check pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0 for indexes nobody uses.

41.5.3 TOAST

When a row would exceed about 2 KB, PostgreSQL compresses the largest variable-length columns and, if still too big, moves them out of line into a side table called the TOAST table, in roughly 2,000-byte chunks with their own index.

This changes estimates in three ways:

  1. The main table stays small. A product_description text column averaging 12 KB does not make your products table 12 KB per row; the main table holds an 18-byte pointer and the bytes live in pg_toast.pg_toast_<oid>. pg_relation_size('products') will look reassuringly small and be misleading; always use pg_total_relation_size, which includes TOAST and indexes.
  2. Compression is real. TOAST applies LZ compression by default (pglz, or lz4 if the column's STORAGE/compression says so). Text and JSON commonly compress 3–5x, so a 12 KB description may occupy 3 KB. Estimate the compressed size for TOASTed columns and the raw size for inline ones.
  3. Reads get more expensive. SELECT * on a TOASTed row costs extra index lookups and page reads per row. This is a latency estimate, not a storage estimate, but it is the same decision: do not select large columns in list endpoints.
-- How much of a table is actually TOAST?
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('products')) AS main,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('products') - pg_relation_size('products')
                      - pg_indexes_size('products')) AS toast,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size('products')) AS indexes,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('products')) AS total;

41.5.4 Growth per year and retention

Growth is rows per day times bytes per row times 365, and then a retention policy decides whether that number keeps compounding.

Table Rows/day Bytes/row (incl. page) GB/year (table) Indexes GB/year (total)
orders 60,000 354 7.8 0.5x 11.7
order_items 180,000 120 7.9 0.6x 12.6
order_status_history 300,000 90 9.9 0.4x 13.9
payment_events (raw webhooks, jsonb) 130,000 1,400 66.4 0.2x 79.7
audit_log 900,000 300 98.5 0.5x 147.8
Total ~266 GB/year

Now apply retention, which is a product and legal decision you must go and get:

Table Retention Steady-state size Mechanism
orders, order_items 7 years (tax law) 82 GB, 88 GB Monthly partitions; partitions older than 24 months moved to cheaper storage or archived to S3 as Parquet
order_status_history 18 months 21 GB Monthly partitions, DROP PARTITION
payment_events 90 days hot, archive after 20 GB Daily partitions, dropped after 90 days
audit_log 13 months 160 GB Monthly partitions, dropped
Hot total ~370 GB Instead of unbounded growth of 266 GB every year

DROP TABLE on a partition is instantaneous and returns the space. DELETE FROM ... WHERE created_at < ... is hours of work, generates as much WAL as the data it deletes, leaves the indexes bloated, and returns nothing to the operating system without a VACUUM FULL that takes an exclusive lock. If a table has a retention policy, it should be partitioned from day one. That decision is made at estimation time, not when the volume is 90 percent full.

41.5.5 The multipliers everyone forgets

Multiplier Factor What it is
Indexes 1.5x Already counted above, but frequently forgotten entirely
Bloat and free space map 1.1–1.3x Dead tuples between vacuums; fillfactor below 100
Replicas x(1 + N) 2 read replicas means you pay for 3 full copies of everything
Backups 0.3x per retained full backup, compressed 7 daily + 4 weekly + 12 monthly = 23 copies at ~0.3x = 7x the data size if they are full backups. Incremental or pgBackRest differential backups cut this to 1–2x
WAL write volume x 2–4 per day, retained until archived Full-page writes after each checkpoint inflate WAL far above the logical write volume
Temp files (sorts, hashes, index builds) +10–20% peak headroom A CREATE INDEX on a 100 GB table needs temp space
Free headroom never above 75% utilization Autovacuum, VACUUM FULL, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY and pg_upgrade all need room

Worked total for the 370 GB hot dataset:

Item Formula Size
Tables + indexes given 370 GB
Bloat allowance 370 * 1.2 444 GB
Temp / maintenance headroom +15% 511 GB
Provisioned volume at 70% utilization 511 / 0.70 730 GB, round to 800 GB
Primary + 2 replicas 800 * 3 2.4 TB of provisioned block storage
WAL per day ~40 GB/day of writes * 2.5 100 GB/day, retained 3 days locally
WAL archive to object storage 100 GB/day * 35 days retention 3.5 TB in S3
Backups (pgBackRest, weekly full + daily incremental, 35 days) ~2x logical 900 GB in S3

The headline changes from "we need 370 GB" to "we need 2.4 TB of block storage and about 4.4 TB of object storage". That is a factor of 12, and it is entirely made of multipliers that a careless estimate sets to 1. When someone tells you a database is "about 400 GB", ask which of those twelve numbers they meant.

41.6 Bandwidth and memory

41.6.1 Bandwidth in and out

bytes_per_second = rps * average_payload_bytes

Do it separately for ingress and egress, because they are wildly asymmetric and only one of them has a price tag.

Direction RPS (peak) Average payload Throughput Per day (at average RPS 580)
Requests in 3,000 1.5 KB (headers + small JSON body) 4.5 MB/s 75 GB/day
Responses out 3,000 15 KB (JSON, gzip already applied) 45 MB/s = 360 Mbps 750 GB/day
Product images (before CDN) 8,000 90 KB 720 MB/s 12 TB/day

Egress is billed; ingress usually is not. At a typical cloud rate of USD 0.09 per GB for internet egress:

Path Monthly volume Monthly egress cost
API JSON straight from origin 22 TB ~USD 2,000
Images straight from origin 360 TB ~USD 32,000
Images via CDN at 92% offload, CDN rate ~USD 0.02–0.085/GB 29 TB origin + 331 TB CDN USD 2,600 origin-to-CDN + ~USD 8,000 CDN = **USD 10,600**
Cross-AZ chatter (often forgotten) depends USD 0.01–0.02 per GB each way

Three decisions fall out immediately. Put a CDN in front of anything static or anonymous-cacheable; the arithmetic above pays for the CDN twenty times over. Compress JSON responses (gzip or brotli at the edge): 15 KB of JSON compresses to 2–4 KB, cutting egress 4–5x, though it costs CPU on the compressing machine, which is why the edge is the right place to do it. Count cross-AZ traffic: a chatty microservice mesh that sends 200 MB/s across zones costs more per month than the instances running it, and nobody notices because it does not appear on a single service's dashboard.

41.6.2 Cache working set

The question is not "how much data do we have" but "how much of it is hot enough to be worth keeping in RAM".

redis_bytes ≈ hot_keys * (key_string_bytes + value_bytes + per_key_overhead)

Redis overhead per key is roughly 60–100 bytes for a simple string key: the dictEntry, the robj header, the SDS header on both key and value, the expiry entry in the expires dict, and allocator rounding. For hashes, sets and sorted sets it is higher and depends on whether the small-object encodings (listpack) apply.

Cache Hot keys Key string Value Overhead Bytes each Total
Product detail JSON 500,000 24 B (product:v3:<uuid>) 3,000 B 90 B 3,114 B 1.56 GB
Category listing pages 20,000 40 B 18,000 B 90 B 18,130 B 0.36 GB
User sessions 2,000,000 40 B 350 B 90 B 480 B 0.96 GB
Carts 250,000 32 B 1,800 B 90 B 1,922 B 0.48 GB
Rate limiter counters 400,000 48 B 30 B 90 B 168 B 0.07 GB
Logical subtotal 3.4 GB
Allocator fragmentation (mem_fragmentation_ratio 1.2–1.5) x1.3 4.4 GB
Replication backlog + client output buffers + COW headroom during BGSAVE +30% 5.8 GB
maxmemory set to 70% of instance RAM 5.8 / 0.7 8.3 GB
Instance choice cache.r6g.large (13.07 GB) primary + replica

Two traps. First, BGSAVE and replica sync can double memory transiently through copy-on-write, which is why maxmemory must sit well below the instance size; a Redis that is at 95 percent of instance RAM will be killed the first time it forks. Second, check the working set assumption. If 500,000 products are hot but your catalog has 8 million and a crawler walks all of them, your eviction rate goes to the moon and your hit ratio collapses. Measure it: INFO keyspace for key counts, INFO stats for keyspace_hits / keyspace_misses / evicted_keys, and redis-cli --bigkeys for the one key that is 400 MB and nobody knew about.

41.6.3 PostgreSQL memory

PostgreSQL uses a process per connection, and each has costs your estimate must include.

Item Size Notes
Backend process baseline 3–10 MB RSS Catalog caches grow with the number of tables and partitions touched
work_mem per sort/hash node, per parallel worker The dangerous one. work_mem = 64MB with a query using 3 hash nodes and 4 parallel workers can allocate 768 MB for one query
maintenance_work_mem per autovacuum worker and per CREATE INDEX 3 autovacuum workers at 1 GB = 3 GB
shared_buffers 25% of RAM, typically Shared, not per connection
OS page cache the rest PostgreSQL relies on it heavily

Worked sizing for a db.r6g.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 64 GB):

Item Formula Value
shared_buffers 25% of 64 GB 16 GB
maintenance_work_mem * autovacuum_max_workers 512 MB * 3 1.5 GB
Connection baseline 300 connections * 7 MB 2.1 GB
work_mem exposure 300 * 4 MB * 2 nodes avg 2.4 GB (worst case far higher)
Reserved for OS and page cache remainder ~42 GB

The trap is setting work_mem globally high "because sorts spill to disk". Set it low globally (4–16 MB) and raise it per session or per role for the reporting queries that need it: SET LOCAL work_mem = '256MB'; inside the transaction that runs the big aggregate.

41.6.4 Node heap per pod

Node's default old-space limit is derived from available memory, and in a container it may read the host's memory rather than the cgroup limit, depending on version and runtime. Do not rely on the default. Set it.

Container memory limit --max-old-space-size Reasoning
512 MiB 350 Heap plus RSS overhead must fit
1 GiB 700 ~70% of the limit
2 GiB 1400
4 GiB 2800 Above this, GC pauses grow; prefer more pods

RSS is always larger than the JS heap: add the Node binary and code (~40 MB), native buffers (Buffer allocations live outside the heap), the ICU data, thread pool stacks, and the pg/Redis driver buffers. A rough rule: RSS ≈ old-space limit + 150–250 MB. Setting --max-old-space-size equal to or above the container limit is the classic OOMKill: V8 believes it has room, delays a major GC, and the kernel kills the process before V8 ever tries to collect (Part 42 walks through exactly this incident).

For a memory-per-pod estimate, count what your code actually retains: in-flight request contexts (concurrency * bytes per request), any in-memory cache (bounded, please), and the largest single response you build in memory.

Item Formula Value
In-flight requests 150 concurrent * 400 KB (parsed body + entities + response) 60 MB
Bounded LRU of pricing rules 5,000 * 8 KB 40 MB
Baseline heap after warm-up measured 180 MB
GC headroom (heap should peak below ~75% of limit) (60+40+180) / 0.75 373 MB heap
--max-old-space-size round up 512
Container limit 512 / 0.7 768 MiB, round to 1 GiB

41.7 Connections and queues

41.7.1 The connection arithmetic

Every PostgreSQL connection is a process on the database server. max_connections is a hard wall: when you hit it, new connections get FATAL: sorry, too many clients already and your entire fleet starts failing at once, including the connection your on-call engineer needs to diagnose it. (PostgreSQL reserves a few slots via superuser_reserved_connections, which is the only reason you can still get in.)

peak_connections = SUM over deployments of (replicas * pool_max) * surge_factor
                   + workers + cron + migrations + monitoring + human sessions
Consumer Replicas Pool max Connections
orders-api 20 10 200
catalog-api 12 8 96
notification-worker 8 5 40
settlement-cron 2 5 10
Migration job (during deploy) 1 2 2
Metrics exporter, backups, admin humans 12
Subtotal 360
Rolling deploy surge (old pods still draining while new pods start) x1.5 typical, x2 worst case 540–720
max_connections on the instance 500

That table is an incident with a date on it. Everything is fine until the third deploy of the day, when a slow-terminating pod holds its connections a little longer than usual and the surge peak crosses 500. The surge factor is the term everyone forgets, and it is why connection exhaustion incidents almost always coincide with a deploy.

Two fixes, and you generally want both:

Size the pool from Little's law, not from a feeling. concurrency = throughput * latency. If a pod serves 150 RPS and the average time a connection is held is 4 ms, it needs 150 * 0.004 = 0.6 concurrent connections. A pool of 10 is 16x oversized. Pool max should be roughly p99_hold_time * peak_rps_per_pod, with a small floor (say 4) so a slow query does not serialize everything. Most NestJS services run pools that are 3–10x larger than they need, purely from copying a default.

Put PgBouncer in transaction mode between them. PgBouncer holds thousands of client connections and multiplexes them onto a small server pool, assigning a server connection only for the duration of a transaction.

flowchart LR
  subgraph Pods
    P1["orders-api x20, pool 10"]
    P2["catalog-api x12, pool 8"]
    P3["workers x8, pool 5"]
  end
  P1 --> B["PgBouncer, transaction pooling"]
  P2 --> B
  P3 --> B
  B -->|"default_pool_size 40"| PG["PostgreSQL primary, max_connections 200"]
  B -->|"reserve_pool_size 10"| PG
  P1 -.->|"336 client connections"| B
  B -.->|"40 server connections"| PG

Sizing the PgBouncer server pool is Little's law again: server_connections = query_rate * average_transaction_duration. At 3,000 transactions per second and 3 ms average duration, that is 9 concurrent server connections; set default_pool_size = 25 for burst and reserve_pool_size = 10. You have turned 360 client connections into 35 server connections, and max_connections can now be 200 instead of 700, which also frees several gigabytes of database RAM.

The cost of transaction pooling: session-level features break. No session-scoped SET, no LISTEN/NOTIFY, no advisory locks that outlive a transaction, and prepared statements need care (max_prepared_statements in PgBouncer 1.21+, or disable statement caching in your driver). Know these before you deploy it, not during the incident.

41.7.2 Queue sizing and drain time

A queue's capacity question is not "how many messages fit". Brokers hold enormous backlogs. The real questions are how big does the backlog get during an incident and how long does it take to drain afterwards.

backlog = producer_rate * outage_duration
drain_time = backlog / (consumer_rate - producer_rate)

The second formula only has a solution when consumer_rate > producer_rate. If your consumers can only just keep up in steady state, you never recover from an outage; the lag grows forever until you add capacity. That is why consumer capacity should be provisioned at 2–3x the producer rate, not at 1.2x.

Worked example. A notification pipeline:

Quantity Value Source
Producer rate (peak) 1,200 messages/s From the RPS estimate
Per-consumer throughput 250 messages/s Measured: 4 ms per message, dominated by the provider HTTP call
Consumer pods 8
Total consumer rate 8 * 250 = 2,000/s
Headroom ratio 2,000 / 1,200 = 1.67x Adequate but not generous

Now the incident: the push provider is down for 40 minutes and the consumers cannot make progress.

Step Formula Value
Outage duration given 2,400 s
Backlog at recovery 1,200 * 2,400 2,880,000 messages
Drain rate 2,000 - 1,200 800/s
Drain time 2,880,000 / 800 3,600 s = 60 minutes
Total user-visible delay for the last message 40 + 60 100 minutes

Is 100 minutes acceptable? For a marketing push, yes. For a one-time password, catastrophically no. If the SLO is "drained within 15 minutes", solve for the consumer rate you need:

Step Formula Value
Required drain rate 2,880,000 / 900 s 3,200/s
Required consumer rate 3,200 + 1,200 4,400/s
Pods needed 4,400 / 250 18 pods
Partitions needed at least 18, round up 24 partitions

And there is the decision the whole exercise existed to produce: the partition count of the topic is a capacity decision made before the topic is created, because a Kafka consumer group cannot have more active consumers than partitions. Increasing partitions later is possible but it rehashes key-to-partition assignment and breaks per-key ordering for in-flight keys. Estimate the recovery consumer count, not the steady-state one, and set partitions from that.

flowchart TB
  A["Steady state: produce 1200 per second, consume 2000 per second, lag 0"] --> B["Provider outage at 09:00"]
  B --> C["Consumers stall, producers continue"]
  C --> D["Backlog grows 1200 per second"]
  D --> E["09:40 recovery, backlog 2.88 million"]
  E --> F["Drain at 2000 minus 1200 equals 800 per second"]
  F --> G["10:40 lag back to zero"]
  E --> H["Alternative: scale to 18 pods, drain at 3200 per second"]
  H --> I["09:55 lag back to zero"]

Also size the storage the backlog needs, because a broker with a full disk is a much worse incident than a lagging consumer:

Quantity Formula Value
Message size measured, including headers 1.5 KB
Backlog bytes 2.88M * 1.5 KB 4.3 GB
Replication factor 3 13 GB
Retention (7 days at peak rate, the real sizing driver) 1,200/s * 86,400 * 7 * 1.5 KB * 3 3.3 TB across the cluster
Per broker, 6 brokers 3.3 TB / 6 * 1.3 headroom ~700 GB each

For a BullMQ or RabbitMQ queue the arithmetic is identical, but the storage lives in Redis memory or in the RabbitMQ node's disk and RAM, and both are far less comfortable holding 3 million messages than Kafka is. A backlog that Kafka shrugs at will OOM a Redis-backed queue, so if your mitigation plan is "let it queue", check what "it" is made of. For BullMQ specifically: 2.88 million jobs at roughly 1.5 KB of Redis memory each (job data, options, and the several sorted sets and hashes that back a job) is around 5–7 GB of Redis, which is more than most teams provision for their queue.

41.8 Five worked estimations

Each of these follows the same method: assumptions, formulas, tables, sanity check, then a conclusion that names instance sizes and replica counts. Read them as templates.

41.8.1 An e-commerce API at 2 million daily actives

Assumptions

Path Peak RPS Destination

Cacheable reads, misses 85 Primary

That last row is the one that matters: the design survives a Redis restart, which means Redis is a latency optimization and not a single point of failure.

Application tier

Quantity Formula Value
Measured RPS per pod (1 vCPU, mixed endpoints) load test 250
Pods at 100% 3,000 / 250 12
At 65% utilization 12 / 0.65 19

Deployment HPA min 12, max 40, target CPU 60%, steady 20

Component Sizing

PostgreSQL primary db.r6g.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 64 GB), 800 GB gp3 with 6,000 provisioned IOPS
Read replicas 2 x db.r6g.xlarge
PgBouncer 2 pods, transaction pooling
Redis cache.r6g.large primary + replica, Multi-AZ
Kafka Shared cluster; order.events 12 partitions
CDN Images and anonymous catalog pages, ~92% offload

The whole system is one medium database. Say that out loud in the design review, because the instinct to shard at 2 million daily actives is strong and the arithmetic says it would be a self-inflicted wound.

41.8.2 A notification system sending 50 million pushes a day

Assumptions: 50M notification events/day; average 1.4 devices per user, so 70M device sends/day; a marketing campaign can target 5 million users and is expected to be delivered within 10 minutes; provider call takes 80 ms at p50, 400 ms at p99; message payload 600 bytes.

Quantity Formula Value
Device sends/day 50M * 1.4 70,000,000
Average sends/s 70M / 86,400 810
Transactional peak (diurnal 4x) 810 * 4 3,240
Campaign burst 5M * 1.4 / 600 s 11,700/s
Design target max of the two, +20% 14,000/s

Worker sizing

Quantity Formula Value
Provider call latency (p50) measured 80 ms
Concurrency per pod (async HTTP, bounded) chosen 60
Throughput per pod 60 / 0.080 750/s
Reality factor (p99 tail, retries, JSON work) x0.7 525/s
Pods at 100% 14,000 / 525 27
At 65% 27 / 0.65 42 pods
Kafka partitions >= 42, rounded 64

Kafka

Quantity Formula Value
Throughput 14,000/s * 600 B 8.4 MB/s
With replication factor 3 8.4 * 3 25 MB/s of broker write
Retention 3 days at average rate 810 * 86,400 * 3 * 600 B * 3 378 GB
Brokers 3 (throughput is trivial; 3 is the availability floor) 3 x kafka.m5.large, 500 GB each

Storage

Table Rows/day Bytes/row Per day Retention Steady state
notification_log 70,000,000 220 15.4 GB 30 days, daily partitions 460 GB
Indexes on it 0.6x 276 GB
device_tokens 60M rows total 260 forever, with a pruning job 16 GB
Total ~750 GB provisioned

70 million rows a day is 810 inserts/s average and 14,000/s during a campaign. A single primary cannot absorb 14,000 individual INSERT statements per second, but it absorbs them easily when the worker batches: 14,000/s in batches of 500 is 28 multi-row inserts per second. Batching is what makes this fit on one database, and it is the design decision the estimate produces.

Deduplication: 70M idempotency keys per day with a 24-hour TTL. At 110 bytes each (key + value + overhead) that is 7.7 GB, fragmentation x1.3 = 10 GB, at 70% maxmemory = 14 GB. Two shards of cache.r6g.xlarge (26 GB each) gives room and halves the ops rate.

Conclusion

Component Sizing
API (accepts notification requests) 6 pods; it only writes to Kafka
Sender workers 42 pods (1 vCPU, 1 GiB), KEDA-scaled on consumer lag, min 8 max 80
Kafka 3 brokers, topic notifications.send with 64 partitions, RF 3, 3-day retention
PostgreSQL db.r6g.xlarge primary + 1 replica, 1 TB, daily partitions on notification_log
Redis (dedupe) 2 shards x cache.r6g.xlarge
Rate limiting per provider Token bucket at the provider's documented quota, shared across all 42 pods

The scaling constraint is not your capacity, it is the provider's. FCM, APNs and every SMS gateway have per-project quotas. Estimate against their limit, not against your workers, or you will build 42 pods that spend their lives receiving 429s.

41.8.3 A chat system with 5 million concurrent connections

Assumptions: 5,000,000 concurrent WebSocket connections at peak; each connection sends 4 messages per hour; average group size 8 recipients; heartbeat every 30 seconds; message payload 250 bytes.

Quantity Formula Value
Messages sent/s 5M * 4 / 3,600 5,600/s
Deliveries/s (fan-out) 5,600 * 8 44,800/s
Heartbeats/s 5M / 30 167,000/s
Total socket events/s 44,800 + 167,000 + 5,600 ~217,000/s

Stop and look at that. The heartbeat is 77 percent of the workload. This is the single most valuable output of the estimate, and it is invisible without doing the arithmetic. It immediately produces two decisions: heartbeats must be the cheapest possible code path (no logging, no database, no Redis write, just a counter and a timestamp in the connection object), and the heartbeat interval is a capacity knob (moving from 30 s to 60 s halves 77 percent of your load, at the cost of detecting dead connections twice as slowly).

Gateway pods

Quantity Formula Value
Memory per connection (JS objects + socket buffers, measured) 45 KB
Connections per pod, memory-limited 3.5 GB usable / 45 KB 78,000
Connections per pod, event-loop-limited (measured under load) 50,000
Pods at 100% 5M / 50,000 100
At 65% (a pod dying must not tip the rest) 100 / 0.65 154, round to 160
Reconnect storm check if 1 pod dies, 50,000 clients reconnect within the backoff window must be spread by jittered backoff, or 160 pods receive 312 new connections/s each: fine

The reconnect-storm line is the one that separates a working chat system from an outage loop. If all 5 million clients reconnect at once (a load balancer restart), that is 5 million TLS handshakes; at 2,000 handshakes/s per pod that is 15 seconds of pure CPU on every pod, during which nothing else happens. Jittered exponential backoff on the client is a capacity requirement, not a nicety.

Fan-out: 44,800 deliveries/s must be routed to whichever pod holds each recipient's socket. Options: Redis Pub/Sub (every message goes to every pod, so 5,600 publishes/s become 5,600 * 160 = 896,000 deliveries across the fabric: wasteful but workable), or a routing table (user_id -> pod_id in Redis, 5M keys at 80 B = 400 MB) with direct pod-to-pod delivery. At this size, use Redis Cluster sharded Pub/Sub keyed by conversation, or a routing table.

Presence: 5M keys with a TTL refreshed by the heartbeat is 167,000 Redis writes/s, which exceeds a single node. Shard 4 ways (42,000/s each) or, better, keep presence in the gateway pod's memory and publish a compact delta every 5 seconds: 160 pods * 1 message/5 s is nothing.

Storage

Quantity Formula Value
Messages/day 5,600 * 86,400 484,000,000
Bytes/row (250 B body + ids + timestamps + overhead) 420
Per day 484M * 420 203 GB/day
90-day hot retention 203 * 90 18 TB
Indexes 0.5x 9 TB

18 TB of hot data at half a billion rows a day is past the comfortable range of a single PostgreSQL primary. This is where the estimate legitimately produces "you need a different database": either PostgreSQL partitioned by month and sharded by conversation id across 8 primaries, or a wide-column store (Cassandra/ScyllaDB/DynamoDB) whose data model is exactly "rows sorted by time within a partition key". Archive to Parquet on S3 after 90 days.

Conclusion: 160 gateway pods (2 vCPU, 6 GiB) behind an NLB; 24 fan-out worker pods; Redis Cluster of 6 shards (cache.r6g.xlarge) for routing and presence; 8 sharded PostgreSQL primaries (db.r6g.4xlarge, 4 TB each) with monthly partitions, or ScyllaDB with 12 nodes; Kafka with 48 partitions for the delivery-receipt stream.

41.8.4 Event ingestion at 100,000 events per second

Assumptions: 100,000 events/s sustained, 250,000/s peak; average event 800 bytes JSON; clients batch 500 events per HTTP request with gzip; retention 3 days in Kafka, 90 days in the analytics store.

Quantity Formula Value
Bytes/s in (raw) 100,000 * 800 B 80 MB/s
Compressed on the wire (gzip ~6x on JSON) 80 / 6 13 MB/s
HTTP requests/s 100,000 / 500 200 RPS
Events/day 100,000 * 86,400 8.64 billion
Raw bytes/day 8.64B * 800 B 6.9 TB/day

200 RPS. That is the payoff of batching, and it is why an ingestion endpoint is a small service and not a heroic one. Without batching this would be 100,000 RPS and a completely different (and far more expensive) architecture.

Ingest tier

Quantity Formula Value
CPU per batch (gunzip 130 KB + parse + validate 500 events + produce) measured 22 ms
Batches/s per vCPU 1,000 / 22 45
vCPU at peak (250,000/s = 500 batches/s) 500 / 45 11
At 60% utilization 11 / 0.6 19
Pods (1 vCPU each) 20, HPA 8–40

Kafka

Quantity Formula Value
Producer throughput (snappy-compressed, ~4x) 80 MB/s / 4 20 MB/s
With RF 3 60 MB/s of broker write
Storage, 3-day retention 20 MB/s * 86,400 * 3 * 3 15.5 TB
Brokers at 70% of 4 TB each 15.5 / (4 * 0.7) 6 brokers
Partitions: throughput floor 20 MB/s / 10 MB/s per partition 2
Partitions: consumer parallelism consumer does 6,000 events/s; 250,000 / 6,000 = 42 consumers 48
Partitions max of the two, with headroom 96

Note how the partition count is driven entirely by consumer parallelism, never by throughput. That is almost always true, and it is why "how many partitions?" is answered by "how fast is one consumer, and what recovery time do you need?"

Analytics store

Quantity Formula Value
Raw/day 6.9 TB
Columnar compression (ClickHouse / Parquet, 8–12x on event data) 6.9 / 10 690 GB/day
90-day retention 690 GB * 90 62 TB
ClickHouse nodes at 70% of 20 TB 62 / 14 5 nodes, use 6 for replication

Conclusion: 20 ingest pods (1 vCPU, 512 MiB) behind an ALB; Kafka 6 brokers (kafka.m5.2xlarge, 4 TB gp3), topic events.raw with 96 partitions and RF 3; 45 consumer pods writing batched inserts to ClickHouse; ClickHouse 6 nodes (16 vCPU, 64 GB, 20 TB); S3 for archive beyond 90 days at roughly USD 0.023/GB. PostgreSQL appears nowhere in this design, which is the correct answer for append-only analytical data at this rate and the thing the arithmetic proves in thirty seconds.

41.8.5 Ride-hailing location updates from 500,000 drivers every three seconds

Assumptions: 500,000 drivers online at peak; one location update every 3 seconds; payload 120 bytes; 200,000 ride requests/day; matching searches a 3 km radius.

Quantity Formula Value
Updates/s 500,000 / 3 166,700/s
Bytes/s 166,700 * 120 B 20 MB/s
Updates/day 166,700 * 86,400 14.4 billion
Ride requests peak/s 200,000 / 86,400 * 6 14/s

The single most important line of this estimate: 166,700 writes per second is 20–50x what one PostgreSQL primary can do. Location updates never touch the relational database. If someone proposes UPDATE drivers SET lat = $1, lng = $2 WHERE id = $3, the arithmetic ends the conversation in one line.

Ingest tier: persistent connections (WebSocket or MQTT), 500,000 of them.

Quantity Formula Value
Connections per pod measured 50,000
Pods for connections 500,000 / 50,000 / 0.65 16
CPU per update (parse, validate, geohash, pipeline to Redis) measured 55 us
vCPU for 166,700/s 166,700 * 0.000055 9.2
At 60% 9.2 / 0.6 15
Pods max of the two 16 pods (1 vCPU, 4 GiB)

Redis geospatial index

Quantity Formula Value
Ops/s (GEOADD) 166,700 Exceeds one node (~120,000/s comfortable)
Shards, by city or geohash prefix 166,700 / 25,000 target per shard 8 shards
Memory: 500,000 drivers in a sorted set 500,000 * ~90 B + per-city set overhead ~50 MB total
GEOSEARCH rate 14/s, returning ~40 drivers each Trivial

The memory is nothing; the operation rate is what forces sharding. That is a common shape: geospatial state is small and hot. Batch with pipelining (each pod pipelines 200 updates per round trip, turning 166,700 commands/s into 830 round trips/s) and the shard count could drop, but keep the shards for failure isolation by city.

The trail question. Storing every point is 14.4 billion rows/day; at 40 bytes packed that is 576 GB/day and 52 TB over 90 days. Ask the product question: who reads a driver's location from last Tuesday? The answers are trip replay for disputes, and analytics.

Policy Rows/day Bytes/day 90 days
Every point, every driver, always 14.4B 576 GB 52 TB
Only during an active trip (100k concurrent trips, avg 18 min) 2.9B 116 GB 10.4 TB
Active trips, downsampled to 1 point per 15 s 576M 23 GB 2.1 TB
Plus full resolution kept 7 days for dispute windows +116 GB * 7 +0.8 TB

A 25x reduction from two product questions. Write the trail as Parquet on S3 partitioned by date and city, not into PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL holds the small, transactional part: drivers, trips, fares, payments, at roughly 200,000 trips/day and a few hundred writes per second, which is comfortable on one db.r6g.2xlarge.

Conclusion: 16 ingest pods; Redis Cluster of 8 shards (cache.r6g.large) for live positions and presence; Kafka with 32 partitions for the raw location stream feeding the archiver; 6 archiver pods writing Parquet to S3; PostgreSQL db.r6g.2xlarge primary + 1 replica for the transactional core; matching service 8 pods.

41.9 Turning estimates into decisions and validating them

An estimate that does not change a configuration value is a maths exercise. Every number should land on a setting.

Estimate Setting it determines Example from 41.8.1
Peak RPS / measured RPS per pod Pod count, HPA minReplicas / maxReplicas 3,000 / 250 / 0.65 = 20 pods, HPA 12–40
Measured knee of the latency curve HPA target utilization Knee at 80% CPU, so target 60%
p99 connection hold time * peak RPS per pod Pool max 8 ms * 150 = 1.2, floor to 8
Pods * pool * surge max_connections, PgBouncer default_pool_size 315 peak, so PgBouncer with pool 30, max_connections 200
Reads after cache, split by staleness tolerance Read replica count 800 rps tolerant / 400 per replica = 2 replicas
Rows per day * retention Partition strategy and interval 60k orders/day, 7 years: monthly RANGE partitions
Working set * (value + overhead) / 0.7 Redis instance class and maxmemory 8.3 GB, cache.r6g.large, maxmemory 9gb, allkeys-lru
Recovery consumer count Kafka partition count 18 pods to drain in 15 min, so 24 partitions
Peak bytes/s out CDN decision, egress budget, response size limits 45 MB/s: CDN for images, brotli for JSON
Heap peak / 0.75 --max-old-space-size and container limit 373 MB, so 512 MB heap in a 1 GiB container
Backlog during the longest tolerable outage Broker disk, queue memory, DLQ policy 4.3 GB * RF 3

41.9.1 Validate with a load test, then correct the model

Estimates are hypotheses. The load test is the experiment. Do it in this order: write the predictions down first, then run the test, then compute the ratio. Writing them afterwards is not validation, it is rationalization.

Quantity Predicted Measured at 3,000 RPS Ratio What it taught
RPS per pod 250 165 0.66 class-transformer on the order DTO costs 2.1 ms per response; the constant was optimistic
p95 latency 180 ms 240 ms 1.33 Acceptable; driven by the same serialization
Primary ops/s 665 1,180 1.77 Cache hit ratio was 88%, not 95%: the long tail of the catalog is hotter than assumed
Redis memory 8.3 GB 6.1 GB 0.73 Values compress better than assumed; maxmemory can stay
Connections at peak 315 298 0.95 Model was good
Egress 45 MB/s 31 MB/s 0.69 Brotli at the edge did better than the gzip assumption

Every ratio outside 0.5–2.0 is a lesson, not a failure. Correct the constant, not the method: the pod count becomes 3,000 / 165 / 0.65 = 28, and the cache assumption becomes 88 percent, which raises the primary's steady load to 1,180 and still leaves it at 6 percent utilization. Then record the corrected constants in the runbook so the next estimate starts from measured numbers. After two or three cycles your constants are your own, and your estimates land inside 30 percent routinely.

Re-run the validation when anything material changes: a new instance class, a Node major version, a serialization change, a 2x growth in data volume, or a new region.

41.9.2 The formulas, in one table

What Formula
Seconds per day 86,400, round to 10^5
Average RPS dau * actions_per_user / 86400
Peak-hour RPS daily_requests * peak_hour_share / 3600 (share ~0.10–0.12)
Peak-second RPS peak_hour_rps * 1.5 to 3
Provisioned capacity peak_rps / utilization_target * az_loss_factor
Database read load cacheable_rps * (1 - hit_ratio) + uncacheable_rps
Row bytes sum(column_bytes) + 24 (tuple header) + 4 (line pointer) + alignment
Rows per page 8150 / (row_bytes + 4)
Index bytes rows * (key_bytes + 12) * 1.3
Table growth rows_per_day * row_bytes * retention_days
Provisioned storage (tables + indexes) * bloat * (1 + replicas) / 0.7
Bandwidth rps * payload_bytes; 1 KB at 1,000/s = 1 MB/s = 86 GB/day = 2.6 TB/month
Redis memory keys * (key_bytes + value_bytes + 90) * 1.3 / 0.7
Node RSS max_old_space_size + 150 to 250 MB
Concurrency (Little's law) throughput * latency
Pool size p99_hold_seconds * peak_rps_per_pod, floor ~4
Peak connections sum(replicas * pool_max) * surge + workers + cron + humans
PgBouncer server pool tx_per_second * avg_tx_seconds, then round up for burst
Consumers needed required_rate / measured_rate_per_consumer
Partitions >= max(recovery_consumers, throughput / 10 MB per second)
Backlog producer_rate * outage_seconds
Drain time backlog / (consumer_rate - producer_rate)
Connections per gateway pod min(usable_memory / bytes_per_conn, measured_event_loop_limit)

41.9.3 Interview questions

  1. We have 20 million monthly actives on a shopping app. How many API pods do we need? Expected: walk the chain out loud — DAU/MAU ratio, calls per user, average RPS, peak factor, measured RPS per pod, utilization target, zone loss. The interviewer is checking whether you state assumptions before computing, and whether you ask for the measured per-pod number instead of inventing one.
  2. Your cache hit ratio is 95 percent. Redis restarts empty. What happens? Expected: database read load jumps 20x instantly; name the protections (request coalescing so one miss per key rebuilds it, stale-while-revalidate, staged warm-up, load shedding) and say whether the database was provisioned for the cold number. Follow-up: what does your dashboard show in the first 30 seconds?
  3. How do you decide the number of partitions for a Kafka topic? Expected: from the consumer count needed to drain a backlog within the recovery SLO, not from throughput; mention that consumers cannot exceed partitions and that raising the count later breaks per-key ordering.
  4. A table has 50 million rows and the "database is 20 GB". What is missing from that number? Expected: indexes, bloat and fillfactor, TOAST, replicas, backups, WAL and archive, temp space, and 30 percent free headroom.
  5. We need to store every GPS point from 500,000 drivers. How much storage? Expected: compute it (576 GB/day), then push back with product questions about who reads it, and show the 25x reduction from downsampling and trip-scoping. The interviewer wants to see that you treat the requirement as negotiable.
  6. Why is 80 percent CPU utilization a bad target? Expected: the queueing curve — latency rises hyperbolically as utilization approaches 1; autoscaling needs 60–180 seconds to react; losing one of three zones instantly adds 50 percent load.

41.9.4 Practical exercise

Take a service you already run. Without opening a dashboard, estimate: peak RPS, RPS per pod, primary database operations per second, the size of the largest table including indexes, the peak connection count during a rolling deploy, and monthly egress. Write the assumptions and formulas first. Then open the dashboards and fill in a measured column.

Acceptance criteria: every predicted value has a stated formula and assumption; you compute the ratio measured/predicted for each; you identify at least one ratio outside 0.5–2.0 and explain which assumption was wrong; and you commit the corrected constants into the service's runbook next to a sentence naming which resource saturates first.

41.10 Edge cases and failure modes

  • Planning for the average instead of the peak. The most common and most expensive error. A service sized for 580 RPS falls over every evening at 20:00 and nobody can explain why the dashboards "look fine" (they show 24-hour averages). Always compute three numbers: daily average, peak hour, peak second, and label which decision each one drives.
  • Forgetting indexes, replicas and backups in the storage number. A 370 GB dataset becomes 2.4 TB of block storage and 4.4 TB of object storage once you count indexes, bloat, headroom, two replicas, WAL archive and backups. Present the provisioned number, not the logical one, or the finance conversation and the volume-full incident both arrive as surprises.
  • Ignoring payload growth over time. The order response was 4 KB at launch. Two years later it embeds the loyalty summary, three promotion objects, a recommendation block and full address history: 22 KB. Egress went up 5.5x, serialization CPU went up 5x, and nobody made a decision. Track average response size as a metric with an alert on a 30-day trend, and put a hard size budget in the API design review.
  • Unbounded retention. "We might need it later" is how a table gets to 4 billion rows with no partitioning, at which point every maintenance operation is a project. Every table gets a retention answer at creation time, even if the answer is "forever, and here is why". Tables with a finite retention are partitioned from day one.
  • Hot partitions make the average meaningless. 8 Redis shards at 21,000 ops/s each is fine on paper; if one city produces 40 percent of the traffic, that shard is at 67,000 ops/s and it is the only one that matters. The same applies to Kafka partitions keyed by tenant_id when one tenant is 60 percent of the volume, and to database partitions when today's partition takes every write. Always ask "what is the distribution?" after computing an average, and estimate the hottest unit, not the mean one.
  • Assuming linear scaling. Doubling pods does not double throughput once the shared resource behind them saturates. 20 pods at 250 RPS each is 5,000 RPS only if the database, the cache, the connection pool and the downstream provider all have room. Every capacity estimate should name which resource saturates first and at what number; that is the real capacity of the system.
  • Ignoring the CPU limit on a Node pod. Node is single-threaded for JavaScript. A pod with limits.cpu: 2 does not run your handler twice as fast; the second core helps GC, libuv threads and native crypto, and that is all. Worse, CPU limits are enforced by CFS quota over a 100 ms period: a pod that briefly needs more than its quota gets throttled, adding tens of milliseconds of latency while kubectl top cheerfully reports 55 percent usage. Watch container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total, and prefer more small pods to fewer large ones.
  • Connection arithmetic that quietly exceeds max_connections on the third deploy of the day. Steady state is 360 connections against a limit of 500 and everything is green. Each rolling deploy briefly runs old and new pods together; usually the surge peaks at 480. On the third deploy, one pod drains slowly because a long query is still running, the surge reaches 505, and every service in the fleet starts throwing sorry, too many clients already simultaneously. Compute the surge peak explicitly, put PgBouncer in the path, and alert at 70 percent of max_connections.
  • Estimating throughput but not recovery. Consumers sized at 1.2x the producer rate keep up perfectly and can never catch up. The drain-time formula has no solution near 1.0x. Size consumers from the recovery requirement.
  • Cache hit ratio treated as a constant. It is a variable that drops to zero on a Redis restart, on a key-format change, on a cold deploy and during a crawler run. Provision the database for the cold-cache load, or add explicit protection (request coalescing, stale-while-revalidate, staged warm-up) and say which one you chose.
  • Estimating with the wrong unit of work. "100,000 events per second" sounds like 100,000 requests per second until you notice the client batches 500 per call and it is actually 200 RPS. Conversely "1,000 orders per second" is 6,000 database operations per second. Always convert to the unit the constrained component actually counts.
  • Forgetting the cost of the estimate being right. A design that needs 160 gateway pods, 8 Redis shards and a sharded database is correct arithmetic and possibly wrong engineering. Compute the monthly bill next to the capacity, and ask whether a product change (a longer heartbeat, a smaller payload, a shorter retention, a batched client) removes an order of magnitude. The best capacity work usually deletes work rather than provisioning for it.

Senior Checklist — Part 41

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I know the latency ladder from L1 cache to cross-region round trip by order of magnitude
  • I use 86,400 s/day (~10^5) and can convert between per-second, per-day and per-month rates in my head
  • I state assumptions with units before computing, and round to one significant figure
  • I sanity-check every estimate against a component limit or a system I have run
  • I compute daily average, peak hour and peak second, and I know which decision each one drives
  • I split total RPS into reads and writes, and route reads by staleness tolerance
  • I can compute database load from a cache hit ratio, and I size the database for a cold cache
  • I can estimate a PostgreSQL row from its column types, including the 24-byte tuple header
  • I never present a storage number without indexes, bloat, replicas, backups, WAL and headroom
  • I size connection pools with Little's law and compute the rolling-deploy surge against max_connections
  • I can compute queue drain time and derive the partition count from the recovery requirement
  • I map every estimate to a concrete setting, then validate it with a load test and correct my constants

Part 41 — Key Takeaways

  • An estimate right to within 3x from stated assumptions beats a precise number from an unexamined one; the fatal errors are missing terms, not imprecise ones.
  • Memorize the latency ladder and the throughput table, then replace every constant with a measured one from your own system.
  • A day is 86,400 seconds; call it 10^5 and the arithmetic becomes mental.
  • State assumptions, write the formula, compute to one significant figure, sanity-check, then add named headroom for utilization, zone loss and growth.
  • Nobody experiences the average: size storage from the daily average, autoscaling from the peak hour, and pods, pools and rate limits from the peak second.
  • Split reads from writes, route reads by staleness tolerance, and remember one logical write is usually 2–6 database operations.
  • Cache hit ratio is a multiplier on database load and it is fragile; provision for the cold-cache number or protect it explicitly.
  • Storage estimates need indexes, bloat, replicas, backups, WAL and 30 percent free headroom; a 370 GB dataset is a 2.4 TB bill.
  • Partition any table with a retention policy from day one; DROP PARTITION is instant, DELETE is an outage.
  • Connection count is pods * pool * surge, and the surge during a rolling deploy is the term that causes the incident.
  • Queue capacity is a recovery question: drain_time = backlog / (consumer_rate - producer_rate), and partition count comes from the consumers you need to recover, not the ones you need in steady state.
  • Every estimate must land on a setting: pod count, pool size, partition count, maxmemory, instance class, HPA threshold. Then load test, compare, and correct the constant.

Part 42 — Production Debugging: Ten Real Scenarios

42.0 The senior debugging process

Part 24 — Performance and Optimization gave you a runbook for one symptom: the API suddenly got slow. This part goes wider and deeper. Ten incidents, each traced from the first alert to the prevention item, with the commands, the output, the wrong turns and the reasoning. The wrong turns matter as much as the fix, because in a real incident you do not know which theory is correct, and the skill being taught is how to eliminate theories cheaply.

Stay calm. This is not a personality trait, it is a technique. Panic makes you skip steps, and skipped steps are how a 20-minute incident becomes a 3-hour one. The physical version: sit down, open a scratch document, write the current time and the symptom in one sentence. That sentence takes fifteen seconds and it forces you to state what you actually know versus what you assume. If your hands are shaking, type the timeline anyway; the writing calms you down and you will need it for the post-mortem.

Mitigate before you diagnose. Users do not care why. The first question is never "what is the cause" but "what is the fastest safe action that reduces harm". Roll back, scale out, flip the kill switch, shed the noisy tenant, kill the blocking query, fail over the replica. Root cause analysis is much easier when nobody is paging you, and a mitigated incident gives you the luxury of thinking. The trap is the opposite instinct, which every engineer has: "I almost have it, give me five more minutes." You never almost have it.

Establish a timeline. Write down: when did it start (the exact minute from the graph, not "around 2 o'clock"), what changed near that minute, when did the alert fire, when did each of your actions happen and what did each one do. Nearly every incident is caused by a change, and the timeline is the cheapest way to find it. It is also the artifact that turns an incident into organizational learning instead of a story.

Form hypotheses from metrics, not from hunches. The difference between a mid-level and a senior engineer is visible here. The mid-level says "I bet it's the cache" and spends forty minutes in Redis. The senior says "p50 moved as well as p99, so everything is slower, which means a shared resource, so let me look at the four saturation graphs before I have an opinion." A hypothesis is worth holding only if you can name the observation that would kill it. Write both down: "Theory: the deploy. Killer observation: rolling back does not help."

Bisect the system. A request passes through client, CDN, load balancer, pod, cache, database, broker, downstream service. Do not walk it end to end; cut it in half. Is the latency inside the pod or outside it? A trace answers that in one look. Is the database slow, or is the pod waiting for a connection? pg_stat_statements mean time versus your pool wait metric answers that. Each bisection halves the search space, and three good bisections take you from eight suspects to one.

Change one thing at a time. Under pressure the urge is to restart the pods and bump the pool and clear the cache. If the symptom goes away you have learned nothing, you cannot revert safely, and you may have introduced the next incident. One change, announced, then observe for at least one full metric scrape interval before the next one.

Write everything down as you go. Commands, output, times, theories killed. Two reasons beyond the post-mortem: you will forget what you tried by minute forty, and the person who takes over at handover needs it. A shared incident channel where you narrate is better than a private terminal.

Communicate on a schedule. Every 20 to 30 minutes, even when there is nothing new: what is broken, who is affected, what you have done, what you are trying next, when the next update comes. Silence makes stakeholders invent their own theories and start "helping". A fixed cadence buys you uninterrupted thinking time, which is the scarcest resource in an incident.

42.0.1 The ladder

Symptom -> Metrics -> Logs -> Traces -> Application -> Database -> Infrastructure -> Root Cause -> Fix -> Prevention

Work down it. Each rung narrows the search. You may jump a rung when a rung above gives you a certain answer, but never start in the middle because you have a hunch. The ten scenarios below all use this exact order, so that reading them trains the habit.

flowchart TB
  S["Symptom: what the user or alert says"] --> M["Metrics: which routes, since when, p50 vs p99, errors, saturation"]
  M --> L["Logs: exact error text, correlation ids, first occurrence"]
  L --> T["Traces: which span grew, serial or parallel, gaps"]
  T --> A["Application: the code path, the config, the recent diff"]
  A --> D["Database: plans, locks, waits, stats, connections"]
  D --> I["Infrastructure: pods, nodes, throttling, DNS, network, broker"]
  I --> R["Root cause: the mechanism, stated in one sentence"]
  R --> F["Fix: the smallest change that removes the mechanism"]
  F --> P["Prevention: alert, test, constraint, runbook"]
  M -.->|"mitigate at any point"| MIT["Roll back, scale, shed, kill, fail over"]

42.0.2 The tool belt

Tool Question it answers Typical command or query
Grafana + PromQL Which routes, since when, how bad, which resource is saturated histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le,route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))
Log query (Loki, CloudWatch, ELK) What is the exact error, and when was the first one {app="orders-api"} |= "QueryFailedError" | json | line_format "{{.correlationId}} {{.msg}}"
Jaeger / Tempo Which span grew; is the work serial Filter by route and duration > 1s, sort by duration, open five
kubectl Restarts, events, exit codes, previous logs, node pressure kubectl describe pod, kubectl logs --previous, kubectl top pod
pg_stat_activity What is running or waiting right now SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type, now()-query_start FROM pg_stat_activity
pg_stat_statements Which query burns the most total time ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10
pg_locks + pg_blocking_pids() Who blocks whom SELECT pg_blocking_pids(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE wait_event_type='Lock'
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) Why one query is slow; estimate versus actual rows Run it against the real parameters
Redis INFO, SLOWLOG GET 25, --bigkeys Memory, evictions, replication lag, slow commands, oversized keys redis-cli INFO stats, redis-cli --bigkeys
Kafka consumer group tools Lag per partition, member assignment, rebalances kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group notifications
Node heap snapshot + clinic Where memory or CPU is going inside the process v8.writeHeapSnapshot(), clinic doctor -- node dist/main.js

42.1 API latency increased from 100 ms to 2 seconds

Symptom

14:02 — PagerDuty: orders-api p95 latency > 1s for 5m. The customer support channel has three messages about the app "spinning" on the orders page. GET /orders p95 is 2.1 s, up from 105 ms. p50 is 890 ms, up from 42 ms. Error rate is 0.3 percent, essentially unchanged. Request rate is 640 RPS, flat.

The first sentence in the incident doc, written at 14:03: "Since ~13:55, GET /orders p50 and p95 are both up ~20x. Errors flat, traffic flat."

p50 moving is the important detail. When only p99 moves, a subset of requests is slow: a lock, a GC pause, one tenant, one shard. When p50 moves too, everything is slower, which points at a shared resource: the database, the pool, the node, the network.

First five minutes (mitigation)

The deploy dashboard shows orders-api v2024.9.41 went out at 13:41, twenty minutes before the latency started. That is close enough to be the prime suspect, and the rule is roll back first, investigate second.

kubectl rollout undo deployment/orders-api -n prod
kubectl rollout status deployment/orders-api -n prod   # completed 14:09

14:12 — p95 is still 2.0 s. The rollback did not help.

This is a genuinely valuable five minutes, not a wasted one. It killed the most attractive theory with one cheap action, and it did it before anybody spent an hour reading the diff. The deploy at 13:41 is the red herring of this incident: it was a copy change to an email template, it touched nothing on this path, and its proximity in time was a coincidence. Coincidences happen several times a day in a team that deploys twenty times a day.

Second mitigation attempt at 14:14: scale out.

kubectl scale deployment/orders-api --replicas=24 -n prod   # from 12

14:18 — p95 unchanged at 2.0 s. Also informative: if adding 100 percent more application capacity does nothing, the bottleneck is not in the application tier. Two theories dead in sixteen minutes.

Metrics

Now, with no more cheap mitigations, look properly.

# p95 by route, last hour
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{app="orders-api"}[5m])))

Only two routes moved: GET /orders and GET /orders/:id/summary. Everything else is normal. That already narrows it: a shared resource that is only used by those routes, or one specific query.

The saturation panel:

Signal Before 13:55 Now Verdict
Pod CPU 38% 22% Down. Pods are waiting, not working
Event loop lag p99 8 ms 11 ms Fine. Not CPU-bound in Node
pg_pool_waiting (custom metric) 0 9.4 average Red. Requests queue for connections
pg_pool_borrow_time_ms p95 0.4 1,180 Red
RDS CPU 31% 94% Red
RDS blks_read rate 900/s 41,000/s Red. 45x more disk reads
RDS buffer cache hit ratio 99.4% 88.1% Red
Replica lag 200 ms 340 ms Fine

Pod CPU going down while latency goes up is the signature of waiting. The database is reading 45x more blocks from disk. Something is scanning.

Logs

kubectl logs -l app=orders-api -n prod --since=40m | grep -c "slow query"
# 4,812

And the PostgreSQL log, with log_min_duration_statement = 500:

2026-03-11 13:54:38.221 UTC [21847] LOG:  duration: 1841.203 ms  execute <unnamed>:
        SELECT o.id, o.status, o.total_amount, o.placed_at FROM orders o
        WHERE o.user_id = $1 AND o.status = ANY($2) ORDER BY o.placed_at DESC LIMIT 20
2026-03-11 13:54:38.904 UTC [21851] LOG:  duration: 1903.771 ms  execute <unnamed>: ...

The first occurrence of that line is 13:53:19. Nothing before it. The onset is sharp, not gradual, which is a strong signal: gradual degradation is growth, a sharp step is a change of state.

Traces

Jaeger, filter service=orders-api operation=GET /orders duration>1s, open five traces. All five have the same shape:

GET /orders                                  2,041 ms
├── auth.verify                                   3 ms
├── pool.acquire                                181 ms   <-- queueing
├── db.query orders.findByUser               1,839 ms   <-- the whole thing
├── db.query order_items.findByOrderIds          6 ms
└── serialize                                   11 ms

One span is 90 percent of the request. Everything else is noise. The bisection is finished: the problem is one query in the database.

Application

The code has not changed in six weeks:

// src/orders/orders.repository.ts
async findRecentForUser(userId: string, statuses: OrderStatus[]): Promise<Order[]> {
  return this.repo.createQueryBuilder('o')
    .where('o.user_id = :userId', { userId })
    .andWhere('o.status IN (:...statuses)', { statuses })
    .orderBy('o.placed_at', 'DESC')
    .limit(20)
    .getMany();
}

Nothing wrong with it. The query is the same query it has always been. So what changed is not the query; it is what the database decides to do with it.

Database

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT o.id, o.status, o.total_amount, o.placed_at FROM orders o
WHERE o.user_id = '7c1f...'::uuid AND o.status = ANY('{pending,paid,shipped}')
ORDER BY o.placed_at DESC LIMIT 20;
Limit  (cost=1284410.22..1284410.27 rows=20 width=52) (actual time=1836.401..1836.410 rows=7 loops=1)
  ->  Sort  (cost=1284410.22..1284412.55 rows=931 width=52) (actual time=1836.399..1836.404 rows=7 loops=1)
        Sort Key: placed_at DESC
        Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 26kB
        ->  Seq Scan on orders o  (cost=0.00..1284385.44 rows=931 width=52)
                                  (actual time=402.118..1836.301 rows=7 loops=1)
              Filter: ((status = ANY ('{pending,paid,shipped}')) AND (user_id = '7c1f...'::uuid))
              Rows Removed by Filter: 24118773
              Buffers: shared hit=18422 read=1043117
Planning Time: 0.211 ms
Execution Time: 1836.462 ms

There it is. A sequential scan over 24 million rows to return 7, reading a million pages from disk. The index exists:

\d orders
-- "idx_orders_user_placed" btree (user_id, placed_at DESC)

So why is the planner ignoring it? Because it thinks the scan is cheap enough, and it thinks that because its statistics are wrong:

SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_mod_since_analyze, last_analyze, last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'orders';
 relname | n_live_tup | n_mod_since_analyze |     last_analyze      |   last_autoanalyze
---------+------------+---------------------+-----------------------+-----------------------
 orders  |   24118780 |            14209455 | 2026-01-04 02:11:09   | 2026-03-05 03:22:41

Six days since the last autoanalyze, and 14.2 million rows modified since. The default autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor is 0.1, so analyze triggers at 10 percent of the table plus 50 rows. But the table had been growing: a data migration backfilled historical orders from an acquired platform over the previous ten days, taking orders from 9.4 million rows to 24.1 million. The planner's row estimate for the user_id predicate was computed when the table was small and the distribution was different. Its estimate of 931 rows for the filter was off by a factor of 26,000 in the wrong direction: it believed the scan would return so few rows so quickly that the index was not worth it.

14:31 — mitigation that works:

ANALYZE orders;

Eleven seconds. p95 back to 118 ms by 14:33.

Infrastructure

Checked and cleared: node CPU 40 percent, no container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total growth, no evictions, RDS storage 62 percent used, no burst credit exhaustion on the volume (gp3 with provisioned IOPS, so no credits to exhaust). The infrastructure rung had nothing, which the metrics had already implied.

Root cause

A bulk backfill grew orders from 9.4 M to 24.1 M rows. Autoanalyze did not run often enough to keep column statistics current, so the planner's selectivity estimate for user_id was stale by four orders of magnitude and it flipped from an index scan to a sequential scan. Each GET /orders then held a pooled connection for 1.8 s instead of 3 ms, and pool saturation turned a slow query into a slow service.

The compounding is worth its own arithmetic, because it explains why p50 on unrelated routes also crept up. Little's law says required concurrency equals throughput times latency:

Before After
GET /orders rate 190 RPS 190 RPS
Connection hold time 3 ms 1,839 ms
Required concurrent connections 190 * 0.003 = 0.6 190 * 1.839 = 349
Pool size (12 pods x 8) 96 96
Result plenty of room 3.6x oversubscribed; everything queues 
flowchart TB
  BF["Backfill: orders grows 9.4M to 24.1M rows"] --> ST["Column statistics go stale, autoanalyze threshold not reached"]
  ST --> PE["Planner estimates 931 rows for the user_id filter, actual 7 of 24M"]
  PE --> FLIP["Plan flips from index scan to sequential scan"]
  FLIP --> SLOW["Query time 3 ms becomes 1839 ms"]
  SLOW --> HOLD["Each request holds a pooled connection 600x longer"]
  HOLD --> SAT["Pool saturated, requests queue for a connection"]
  SAT --> ALL["p50 rises on every route that touches the pool"]
  SLOW --> IO["Disk reads 900 per second become 41000 per second"]
  IO --> CPU["Database CPU 31 percent becomes 94 percent"]

Fix

  1. ANALYZE orders; — immediate, done at 14:31.
  2. Make analyze aggressive on this table, because a 24-million-row table should not wait for 2.4 million modifications:
ALTER TABLE orders SET (autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.02,
                        autovacuum_analyze_threshold = 5000,
                        autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.05);
  1. Give the planner better statistics on the skewed column:
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN user_id SET STATISTICS 500;
ANALYZE orders (user_id);
  1. Make the index unmistakably cheaper than a scan for this exact query, so a small estimate error cannot flip the plan again:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user_status_placed
  ON orders (user_id, status, placed_at DESC)
  INCLUDE (total_amount);
