  1. Put a ceiling on the damage any single query can do:
// src/database/database.module.ts — TypeORM DataSource options
extra: {
  statement_timeout: 3000,          // no query may run longer than 3 s
  idle_in_transaction_session_timeout: 30000,
  application_name: `orders-api@${process.env.HOSTNAME}`,
},

Prevention

  • ANALYZE at the end of every backfill migration. Add it to the migration template so nobody has to remember. This one line would have prevented the whole incident.
  • Turn on auto_explain (auto_explain.log_min_duration = 500, log_analyze = on, log_buffers = on) so that when a plan flips you have the before and after plans in the log instead of having to guess.
  • Alert on plan-level symptoms, not just latency: rate(pg_stat_database_blks_read[5m]) jumping 10x, buffer cache hit ratio below 95 percent, and pg_stat_user_tables.n_mod_since_analyze exceeding 20 percent of n_live_tup.
  • Alert on pg_pool_waiting > 0 sustained for 2 minutes. Pool saturation shows up as latency, never as errors, so an error-rate alert can stay green through the entire incident (see Part 24).
  • A weekly job that dumps the plan of the ten hottest queries and diffs against last week. Plan flips are invisible until they are an incident.

Junior versus senior

Junior Senior
First move Reads the deploy diff for 40 minutes Rolls back in 4 minutes to test the theory, then discards it
Reaction to "p50 moved too" Does not notice Immediately narrows to shared resources
Scaling pods Sees no improvement, adds more pods Sees no improvement, concludes the bottleneck is downstream
The query "The query is fine, it has an index" "The query is fine; the plan is not. Show me EXPLAIN ANALYZE with real parameters"
Fix ANALYZE, closes the ticket ANALYZE, then per-table autovacuum settings, statistics target, a covering index, statement_timeout, and an alert that would have paged at the right layer
Timeline In their head In the incident doc, minute by minute

42.2 PostgreSQL CPU is at 100 percent

Symptom

02:41 — RDS CPUUtilization > 90% for 15m on orders-primary. API p99 has doubled from 220 ms to 480 ms but nothing is failing. The alert has fired at roughly the same time on each of the last three nights, and each time the previous on-call acknowledged it and it cleared by 05:00. Tonight the on-call is annoyed enough to actually look.

First five minutes (mitigation)

Nothing is broken for users yet, so the mitigation bar is low and the diagnostic value of watching it live is high. The on-call does one cheap protective thing:

SET statement_timeout = '60s';  -- for their own session only

and starts observing rather than acting. That is a defensible senior choice: mitigating a recurring, non-user-impacting event before understanding it guarantees a fourth night.

Metrics

Signal Value Note
RDS CPU 97% Pinned since 02:05
RDS blks_read 88,000/s Massive sequential I/O
Buffer cache hit ratio 76% Normally 99.3%
DatabaseConnections 71 Normal
Write IOPS 4,100 Elevated but not extreme
API RPS 40 It is 02:41; almost no user traffic

Forty requests per second and 97 percent CPU. Whatever is burning the database is not user traffic.

Logs

02:00:04 [batch] INFO  promotions.expiry job started, correlationId=b41c2f19
02:00:04 [batch] INFO  found 3184 promotions to expire
02:41:52 [batch] INFO  processed 940 / 3184

Forty-two minutes to process 940 rows: 2.7 seconds per row. The job deletes expired promotions and their eligibility rows.

Traces

The batch job is instrumented. One iteration:

promotions.expiry.iteration                    2,684 ms
├── db.query promotions.findOne                     2 ms
├── db.query promotion_rules.delete                 4 ms
└── db.query promotions.delete                  2,671 ms   <-- a single-row DELETE by primary key

A DELETE of one row by primary key taking 2.7 seconds is the kind of observation that should stop you cold. A primary key delete is microseconds. Something is happening because of the delete, not in it.

Application

// src/promotions/promotion-expiry.job.ts
@Cron('0 0 2 * * *')
async expirePromotions(): Promise<void> {
  const expired = await this.promotions.find({ where: { endsAt: LessThan(new Date()) } });
  this.logger.log(`found ${expired.length} promotions to expire`);
  for (const p of expired) {
    await this.rules.delete({ promotionId: p.id });
    await this.promotions.delete(p.id);   // 2.7 s each
  }
}

Loop-per-row is not efficient, but it is not the problem either; 3,184 fast deletes would take seconds.

Database

SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS age, state, wait_event_type, wait_event, left(query, 90)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle' AND backend_type = 'client backend'
ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 10;
  pid  |      age       | state  | wait_event_type | wait_event |                      left
-------+----------------+--------+-----------------+------------+-------------------------------------------
 30412 | 00:00:02.41    | active | IO              | DataFileRead | DELETE FROM promotions WHERE id = $1
 30418 | 00:00:00.19    | active |                 |            | SELECT o.id, o.status FROM orders o WHERE
 29901 | 00:04:11.02    | active | IO              | DataFileRead | autovacuum: VACUUM public.orders
 29903 | 00:02:55.71    | active | IO              | DataFileRead | autovacuum: VACUUM public.promotion_rules

The red herring appears here. Two autovacuum workers are visible, both doing heavy I/O, and it is tempting to conclude that autovacuum is eating the database. Several teams "fix" this by disabling autovacuum, which converts a nightly slowdown into a permanent catastrophe three weeks later.

The senior test: is autovacuum a cause or a consequence? Check the order of events. Autovacuum on orders started at 02:29, twenty-four minutes after the CPU went to 97 percent at 02:05. It is also vacuuming promotion_rules, the very table the batch job has been deleting from. Autovacuum is downstream of the batch job, not upstream. It is the cleanup crew, not the vandal. Theory discarded at 02:52.

Now the real question: why is a primary key DELETE slow? pg_stat_statements:

SELECT calls, round(total_exec_time::numeric) AS total_ms, round(mean_exec_time::numeric,1) AS mean_ms,
       left(query, 120) AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 5;
 calls | total_ms  | mean_ms |                                      query
-------+-----------+---------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------
   940 | 2510440   |  2670.7 | SELECT 1 FROM ONLY "public"."orders" x WHERE $1 OPERATOR(pg_catalog.=)
       |           |         | "promotion_id" FOR KEY SHARE OF x
   940 |    3760   |     4.0 | DELETE FROM promotion_rules WHERE promotion_id = $1
  8821 |    1102   |     0.1 | SELECT o.id, o.status, o.total_amount FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = $1

That first query is not written by anyone. It is the referential integrity trigger PostgreSQL runs internally to enforce a foreign key: before deleting a promotions row, it must verify that no orders row references it. And it is doing so with a sequential scan of 24 million rows, 940 times.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT 1 FROM ONLY public.orders x WHERE '9f2a...'::uuid = promotion_id FOR KEY SHARE OF x;
LockRows  (cost=0.00..1301882.00 rows=1 width=38) (actual time=2664.9..2664.9 rows=0 loops=1)
  ->  Seq Scan on orders x  (cost=0.00..1301872.00 rows=1 width=38) (actual time=2664.9..2664.9 rows=0 loops=1)
        Filter: ('9f2a...'::uuid = promotion_id)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 24118780
        Buffers: shared hit=2104 read=1041013
Execution Time: 2664.98 ms

Confirmed. Find every foreign key in the database with no supporting index:

SELECT c.conrelid::regclass AS child_table,
       a.attname            AS fk_column,
       c.confrelid::regclass AS parent_table
FROM pg_constraint c
JOIN unnest(c.conkey) WITH ORDINALITY AS k(attnum, ord) ON true
JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = c.conrelid AND a.attnum = k.attnum
WHERE c.contype = 'f'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM pg_index i
    WHERE i.indrelid = c.conrelid
      AND (i.indkey::smallint[])[0] = k.attnum   -- FK column is the leading index column
  )
ORDER BY 1;
 child_table |    fk_column    | parent_table
-------------+-----------------+--------------
 orders      | promotion_id    | promotions
 order_items | gift_wrap_id    | gift_wraps

Two of them. The promotion_id column was added by a migration eleven days earlier with ADD CONSTRAINT ... FOREIGN KEY and no index.

Infrastructure

Nothing. Instance class unchanged, storage 63 percent, no throttling, no failover. Confirmed in two minutes and dismissed.

Root cause

A foreign key orders.promotion_id -> promotions.id was created without an index on the child column. PostgreSQL creates an index automatically for a primary key and for a unique constraint, but never for a foreign key's referencing column. Every DELETE or key UPDATE on the parent therefore triggers a full sequential scan of the 24-million-row child table. The nightly expiry job performs 3,184 such deletes, so the job costs 3,184 sequential scans of orders, which is roughly 3.3 billion row examinations and a saturated CPU for three hours. Autovacuum on the churned tables was a consequence.

flowchart TB
  MIG["Migration adds FK orders.promotion_id with no index"] --> JOB["Nightly job deletes 3184 promotions"]
  JOB --> RI["Each DELETE fires the RI check: SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE promotion_id = $1"]
  RI --> SEQ["No index on promotion_id, so each check is a seq scan of 24M rows"]
  SEQ --> CPU["3184 seq scans, 88000 blocks read per second, CPU 97 percent"]
  SEQ --> DEAD["Deletes create dead tuples in promotion_rules and orders"]
  DEAD --> AV["Autovacuum wakes up and adds more I/O"]
  AV --> HERRING["Looks like the cause, is actually the consequence"]
  CPU --> LAT["Buffer cache hit ratio 99 percent falls to 76 percent, API p99 doubles"]

Fix

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_promotion_id ON orders (promotion_id)
  WHERE promotion_id IS NOT NULL;   -- partial: only 4% of orders have a promotion
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_order_items_gift_wrap_id ON order_items (gift_wrap_id)
  WHERE gift_wrap_id IS NOT NULL;

Built in 90 seconds; the partial index is 38 MB instead of 800 MB. The next night's job finished in 41 seconds with database CPU peaking at 34 percent.

Also fix the job so it does set-based work rather than a loop:

await this.dataSource.transaction(async (m) => {
  const ids = await m.query(
    `SELECT id FROM promotions WHERE ends_at < now() ORDER BY id LIMIT 500 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`);
  if (ids.length === 0) return;
  const list = ids.map((r: { id: string }) => r.id);
  await m.query(`DELETE FROM promotion_rules WHERE promotion_id = ANY($1)`, [list]);
  await m.query(`DELETE FROM promotions WHERE id = ANY($1)`, [list]);
});
// called in a loop until it returns nothing: batches of 500, each its own transaction

Batching in chunks of 500 with a transaction per chunk keeps lock durations short and lets autovacuum keep up, which is exactly what a long single transaction prevents.

Prevention

  • A CI check that fails any migration adding a foreign key without an index on the referencing column. Run the pg_constraint query above against the migrated schema in the pipeline and fail the build on any row. This is the single highest-value prevention item in this scenario, because the mistake is invisible in review and expensive in production.
  • Alert on database CPU above 80 percent for 10 minutes, regardless of time of day. The alert existed; what was missing was the expectation that somebody investigate rather than acknowledge. Add a runbook link to the alert.
  • Batch jobs get their own application_name and their own statement_timeout. A job that would take 2.7 s per statement should fail loudly, not run for three hours.
  • Schedule batch jobs against the traffic curve, and give them a lower-priority connection budget so they cannot starve interactive traffic.
  • Track the "unindexed foreign keys" query as a weekly report, because constraints get added by many hands.

Junior versus senior

Junior Senior
Sees autovacuum in pg_stat_activity "Autovacuum is killing us" and considers disabling it Checks the start time of autovacuum against the start of the CPU spike; concludes consequence, not cause
Reads pg_stat_statements Skips the query they did not write Recognises the RI trigger text as PostgreSQL's own foreign key check
Fix Bigger instance class An index, a partial one, plus the CI check that stops the class of bug
Recurring alert Acknowledges it three nights running Treats the third occurrence as a design problem, not an ops problem

42.3 Redis is returning stale data

Symptom

10:18 — the merchandising manager messages the team channel: "I dropped the price on the winter jacket to 2,499 forty minutes ago. The app still shows 3,999. The admin panel shows 2,499." Support has four tickets from customers whose cart total does not match the listing price.

Reproducing it is maddening: refreshing the product page shows 3,999, then 2,499, then 3,999 again. Roughly 40 percent of requests return the old price.

Intermittent wrong data with a stable error rate is the signature of a cache coherence problem, and the "sometimes correct" pattern specifically points at some copies being updated and others not.

First five minutes (mitigation)

Wrong prices are a commercial and legal problem, so mitigate immediately and diagnose after. The safe blunt instrument:

# Flush only the product namespace, never FLUSHALL on a shared Redis
redis-cli --scan --pattern 'product:*' | xargs -L 500 redis-cli DEL

10:26 — prices are correct everywhere. Database load spikes from 90 to 1,400 reads/s for about four minutes as the cache refills, which the primary absorbs (this is precisely the cold-cache headroom that Part 41 told you to provision for).

The incident is mitigated but not resolved: the next price change will do the same thing. And the on-call now writes the crucial line in the doc: "Deleting the keys fixed it, so the cache held a value that invalidation failed to remove. Question: which key was not deleted?"

Metrics

Signal Value Note
Redis keyspace_hits / misses 96.2% hit ratio Healthy, so the cache is being used
evicted_keys 0 Not eviction. Nothing was pushed out
expired_keys 3,200/min Normal TTL churn
used_memory 4.1 GB of 9 GB maxmemory Room to spare
master_repl_offset vs replica offset Equal No replication lag
cache.invalidation.deletes (app metric) 41/min Invalidations are happening
Total keys 1,240,110 Up 38% week over week

That last row is quietly interesting: the key count grew 38 percent in a week without a corresponding catalog change.

Logs

The invalidation path logs every delete:

10:02:11 [catalog-admin] INFO price updated productId=8f31a2c4 old=3999 new=2499 correlationId=c8a1
10:02:11 [catalog-admin] INFO cache invalidated key=product:v2:8f31a2c4 deleted=1 correlationId=c8a1
10:02:11 [catalog-admin] INFO cache invalidated key=product:v2:8f31a2c4:price deleted=1 correlationId=c8a1

deleted=1 on both. The invalidation ran, found the keys, and removed them. So how is the old price still being served?

Traces

Two traces of GET /products/8f31a2c4, taken a second apart, differ:

Trace A (returns 2499)                       Trace B (returns 3999)
GET /products/:id              14 ms          GET /products/:id              11 ms
├── redis.get product:v2:8f31a2c4  0.4 ms     ├── redis.get catalog:product:8f31a2c4  0.3 ms
│     result: MISS                            │     result: HIT
├── db.query products.findOne     6 ms        └── serialize                    2 ms
└── redis.setex product:v2:...    0.5 ms

Two different key names. That is the whole incident, visible in one screen. Some requests read product:v2:<id>, others read catalog:product:<id>.

The red herring dies here as well. The initial theory in the channel had been replication lag: reads are served by two Redis replicas, so "the replicas must be behind". It was plausible, it was worth checking, and it was checked three ways: INFO replication showed master_repl_offset identical to both slave_repl_offset values; master_last_io_seconds_ago was 0; and pinning reads to the primary with a temporary config flag still produced stale responses at the same rate. Replication lag ruled out at 10:34. A theory that survives only because you have not tested it is not a theory, it is a preference.

Application

Find both key formats in the codebase:

grep -rn "product:" src/ --include=*.ts | grep -v spec
src/common/cache/cache-keys.ts:14:  static product(id: string) { return `product:v2:${id}`; }
src/common/cache/cache-keys.ts:15:  static productPrice(id: string) { return `product:v2:${id}:price`; }
src/catalog/catalog-read.service.ts:38:    const key = `catalog:product:${id}`;
src/catalog/catalog-read.service.ts:52:    await this.redis.setex(key, 86400, JSON.stringify(dto));

The offending code, shipped nine days earlier as part of a "catalog read path v3" refactor behind a 40 percent traffic flag:

// src/catalog/catalog-read.service.ts  (the bug)
async getProduct(id: string): Promise<ProductDto> {
  const key = `catalog:product:${id}`;              // hand-rolled key, not CacheKeys.product(id)
  const cached = await this.redis.get(key);
  if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached) as ProductDto;
  const dto = await this.buildProductDto(id);
  await this.redis.setex(key, 86400, JSON.stringify(dto));   // 24-hour TTL
  return dto;
}

And the invalidation, which was never told about the new format:

// src/catalog/catalog-admin.service.ts  (unchanged for two years)
async onPriceChanged(productId: string): Promise<void> {
  await this.redis.del(CacheKeys.product(productId));        // product:v2:<id>
  await this.redis.del(CacheKeys.productPrice(productId));   // product:v2:<id>:price
}

Both halves are individually correct. Together they are a silent data-corruption engine. And the failure is invisible: the invalidation logs deleted=1 and looks successful, because it did delete the key it knew about.

The 40 percent flag explains the 40 percent stale rate, and the 38 percent key growth was the new namespace accumulating alongside the old one, doubling memory for products behind the flag.

Database

Checked and clean: SELECT price FROM products WHERE id = '8f31a2c4' returns 2499, updated_at is 10:02:11. The source of truth was always right. Worth doing explicitly and early: if the database had been wrong, everything above would have been the wrong investigation.

Infrastructure

Redis cluster healthy, no failover events, no CLUSTER slot migration, no OOM, no restart in 34 days. The instance is not the problem; the protocol between two pieces of application code is.

Root cause

A new read path introduced a second cache key format (catalog:product:<id>) for data that an existing invalidation path removes under the old format (product:v2:<id>). Invalidation silently missed the new keys, and with a 24-hour TTL the stale value persisted for up to a day. The traffic flag at 40 percent meant 40 percent of reads hit the stale namespace, producing intermittent wrongness that looked like a replication or eventual-consistency problem.

flowchart TB
  ADM["Admin changes price to 2499"] --> DB["UPDATE products, source of truth correct"]
  DB --> INV["Invalidation: DEL product:v2:id"]
  INV --> OK["Old namespace cleared, deleted=1 logged"]
  ADM -.->|"never told about it"| NEW["catalog:product:id still holds 3999, TTL 24h"]
  R1["60 percent of reads: old path"] --> OK
  OK --> FRESH["Cache miss, rebuild from DB, returns 2499"]
  R2["40 percent of reads: flagged new path"] --> NEW
  NEW --> STALE["Cache hit, returns 3999 for up to 24 hours"]

Fix

Immediate (done at 10:26): delete the product:* namespace, then also catalog:product:*.

Structural: cache keys become a single typed module that both the read path and the invalidation path must use, and building a key by string interpolation anywhere else is a review failure.

// src/common/cache/cache-keys.ts
export const CACHE_VERSION = 'v3';   // bump to invalidate an entire namespace on deploy

export class CacheKeys {
  static product(id: string): string { return `product:${CACHE_VERSION}:${id}`; }
  static productPrice(id: string): string { return `product:${CACHE_VERSION}:${id}:price`; }

  /** Every key that must die when a product changes. Read paths and invalidation share this list. */
  static productInvalidationSet(id: string): string[] {
    return [CacheKeys.product(id), CacheKeys.productPrice(id), CacheKeys.productCard(id)];
  }
  static productCard(id: string): string { return `product:${CACHE_VERSION}:${id}:card`; }
}
// src/catalog/catalog-admin.service.ts
async onProductChanged(productId: string): Promise<void> {
  const keys = CacheKeys.productInvalidationSet(productId);
  const deleted = await this.redis.del(...keys);
  this.metrics.increment('cache.invalidation.keys_deleted', deleted);
  this.metrics.increment('cache.invalidation.keys_requested', keys.length);
  if (deleted === 0) {
    // Either nothing was cached, or we are deleting the wrong key names. Make it visible.
    this.logger.warn({ productId, keys }, 'invalidation deleted nothing');
  }
}

Three defences in that snippet. The invalidation set is derived from the same module the readers use, so a new cached view cannot be added without appearing here. The version constant lets a deploy retire an entire namespace at once. And the deleted === 0 warning turns a silent miss into a log line, which is the difference between finding this in staging and finding it in a customer's cart.

TTL as a backstop: price-bearing values move from 24 hours to 300 seconds.

await this.redis.setex(CacheKeys.product(id), 300, JSON.stringify(dto));

A short TTL does not fix incorrect invalidation, it bounds the blast radius. The design question is "how long may this be wrong if invalidation fails?" For prices the honest answer is minutes. For a product description it is hours. Never cache without a TTL; a key with no expiry that invalidation misses is wrong forever.

Prevention

  • A test that asserts the read key and the invalidation key are the same. Cheap, and it would have caught this in the pull request:
it('invalidates every key the read paths write', async () => {
  const id = 'p-1';
  await catalogRead.getProduct(id);              // populates whatever key it uses
  await catalogAdmin.onProductChanged(id);
  const leftovers = await redis.keys(`*${id}*`); // real Redis via Testcontainers
  expect(leftovers).toEqual([]);                 // nothing survives invalidation
});
  • A metric on keys_deleted / keys_requested with an alert when the ratio collapses, plus hit ratio broken down by key prefix so a new namespace appearing is visible on a dashboard.
  • A lint rule (or a review checklist item) banning template-literal cache keys outside cache-keys.ts.
  • Include cache-key changes in the deploy risk checklist. A key format change is a cache flush in disguise: it drops the hit ratio to zero for that namespace and moves the full read load to the database. Warm the new keys, or ship it during a low-traffic window with the database watched.
  • When a value must never be stale, do not cache it. Stock at checkout and payment status are read from the primary. Deciding this per field, at design time, is cheaper than deciding it during an incident.

Junior versus senior

Junior Senior
First theory "Redis is eventually consistent" Redis is strongly consistent for a single key on the primary; the question is which key
Replication lag Assumes it, mentions it in the post-mortem as the cause Tests it three ways in five minutes and writes down that it was ruled out
Evidence Reads code and reasons about it Compares two traces of the same endpoint and sees two different key names
Fix Adds a redis.del for the new key Makes it structurally impossible to have two key formats, adds the test, shortens the TTL, adds the metric
Cache flush FLUSHALL Namespace-scoped delete, with the database's cold-cache capacity checked first

42.4 Kafka consumer lag keeps increasing

Symptom

16:40 — alert: kafka_consumergroup_lag{group="notifications"} > 100000. By 17:20 the lag is 1.4 million and climbing at roughly 900 messages per second. Order confirmation emails are arriving 35 minutes after checkout. Nothing is throwing errors; the consumer pods are Running with zero restarts; CPU on them is 12 percent.

Lag that grows with idle consumers is the interesting case. If consumers were saturated you would see CPU at 95 percent and the answer would be "add pods". Twelve percent CPU and growing lag means the consumers are not consuming, and that is a very different problem.

First five minutes (mitigation)

The instinctive mitigation, and the one somebody suggests in the channel within ninety seconds, is "add partitions and more consumers".

# NOT run. Written in the incident doc as a rejected option, with the reason.
kafka-topics.sh --alter --topic order.events --partitions 48

Rejected for three reasons, and understanding them is most of this scenario. First, the consumer group currently has 12 members for 12 partitions and each member is using 12 percent of a CPU: the existing consumers are not the constraint, so more of them cannot help. Second, changing the partition count triggers a rebalance, and a rebalance is exactly what appears to be going wrong. Third, repartitioning changes the key-to-partition mapping, so events for the same order_id can land in a different partition than earlier events for that order, breaking per-key ordering permanently for in-flight work. Adding partitions is a capacity decision made at design time (see Part 41), not an incident mitigation. This is the scenario's red herring, and it is attractive enough that many teams run it and make the incident worse.

The actual mitigation at 16:52, after one look at the metrics below, is to shrink the amount of work each poll must do:

# Helm values, rolled out at 16:52
env:
  - name: KAFKA_MAX_POLL_RECORDS
    value: "50"          # was 500
  - name: KAFKA_MAX_POLL_INTERVAL_MS
    value: "600000"      # was 300000, temporary breathing room
  - name: PROFILE_SERVICE_TIMEOUT_MS
    value: "800"         # was 10000

16:58 — commit rate goes from 0 to 780/s. Lag peaks at 1.51 million and begins falling.

Metrics

The panel that ends the investigation in one look:

Metric Value Meaning
kafka_consumergroup_lag 1,400,000 and rising The symptom
kafka_consumer_records_consumed_rate 5,900/s Records are being fetched
kafka_consumer_commit_rate 0.0/s Nothing is ever committed
kafka_consumer_rebalance_rate_per_hour 244 A rebalance every 15 seconds
kafka_consumer_join_time_avg 3,100 ms Every rebalance costs 3 s of stopped work
Consumer pod CPU 12% Idle
Downstream POST /profiles/batch p99 3,480 ms Was 42 ms this morning

Records consumed but never committed is the entire diagnosis. The consumers fetch messages, start processing, get kicked out of the group before they finish, and their offsets are never advanced. The next generation of the group re-fetches the same messages and repeats. The system is doing work at full speed and making zero progress, forever. This is a rebalance loop, sometimes called a livelock.

Logs

kubectl logs -l app=notification-consumer -n prod --since=30m | grep -i "rebalanc\|poll\|leave" | head
17:02:11 WARN  [Consumer clientId=consumer-notifications-3, groupId=notifications]
   Member consumer-notifications-3-9f2a1 sending LeaveGroup request to coordinator
   b-2.kafka.internal:9092 due to consumer poll timeout expired. This means the time
   between subsequent calls to poll() was longer than the configured max.poll.interval.ms,
   which typically implies that the poll loop is spending too much time processing messages.
   You can address this either by increasing max.poll.interval.ms or by reducing the
   maximum size of batches returned in poll() with max.poll.records.
17:02:14 INFO  [Consumer ... ] Request joining group due to: rebalance failed due to
   MemberIdRequiredException
17:02:17 INFO  [Consumer ... ] Successfully joined group with generation Generation{generationId=8814}
17:02:17 INFO  [Consumer ... ] Notifying assignor about the new Assignment(partitions=[order.events-4])
17:02:31 WARN  [Consumer clientId=consumer-notifications-7 ...] sending LeaveGroup request ...

Generation 8814. A healthy consumer group's generation increments a handful of times a day. Eight thousand generations means the group has been re-forming continuously, and the Kafka client library has told you the answer in plain English in the log message. It is worth pausing on that: the client wrote the diagnosis and the two fixes into the log, and the incident still took forty minutes because nobody read the warning-level logs until they were forced to.

Traces

One message's processing trace, before the mitigation:

notification.process (order.shipped)                3,612 ms
├── db.query notification_prefs.findByUser              4 ms
├── http POST /profiles/batch                       3,480 ms   <-- was 42 ms
├── template.render                                     9 ms
└── http POST fcm.googleapis.com/v1/.../send           110 ms

And the arithmetic that turns that into the incident:

Quantity Before During incident
max.poll.records 500 500
Time per record 165 ms 3,612 ms
Time to process one poll batch 500 * 0.165 = 82 s 500 * 3.612 = 1,806 s (30 min)
max.poll.interval.ms 300,000 (5 min) 300,000
Verdict 82 s < 300 s: fine 1,806 s > 300 s: evicted every time

The margin was always thin. The service ran at 82 seconds against a 300-second limit, a 3.7x buffer that nobody had ever computed. A 22x slowdown in one downstream call consumed it instantly.

Application

// src/notifications/notification.consumer.ts  (the shape of the bug)
@Controller()
export class NotificationConsumer {
  @EventPattern('order.events')
  async handle(@Payload() message: OrderEvent): Promise<void> {
    const prefs = await this.prefs.findByUser(message.userId);
    // one HTTP call per message, no timeout, no circuit breaker
    const profile = await this.profiles.fetch(message.userId);
    const rendered = this.templates.render(message.type, profile, prefs);
    await this.push.send(profile.deviceTokens, rendered);
  }
}

Three design faults, each individually survivable, jointly fatal:

  1. A synchronous downstream call inside the poll loop. Every millisecond the profile service adds is multiplied by max.poll.records.
  2. No timeout. this.profiles.fetch used the client's default, which was 10 seconds. A call that should take 40 ms was allowed to take 250x that.
  3. No relationship between max.poll.records and the worst-case per-record time. Nobody had ever written max.poll.records * p99_processing_time < max.poll.interval.ms on a whiteboard, so nobody knew how close to the edge the service ran.

Database

Checked and cleared in three minutes: pg_stat_activity shows nothing long-running, notification_prefs.findByUser averages 4 ms in pg_stat_statements, and connection count is normal. Ruling the database out early matters because "the consumer is slow" instinctively points at the database, and it was innocent here.

Infrastructure

Why did POST /profiles/batch slow from 42 ms to 3,480 ms? The profile service's own dashboard shows CPU at 62 percent, which looks fine, and container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total climbing steeply, which is not. A configuration change at 15:55 had reduced the profile service's CPU limit from 2 to 1 while leaving its request at 1. The pods were being CFS-throttled: usage looks moderate because throttled time is not counted as usage, while every request pays tens of milliseconds of forced sleep per 100 ms period.

This is the real chain: an unrelated resource-limit change in a different service manifested as unbounded lag in the notification pipeline three hours later.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Joining
  Joining --> Assigned: partitions assigned, generation N
  Assigned --> Processing: poll returns 500 records
  Processing --> Evicted: 30 minutes elapse, max.poll.interval.ms exceeded
  Evicted --> Joining: LeaveGroup, generation N+1
  Processing --> Committed: would commit offsets here
  Committed --> Assigned: progress
  note right of Evicted
    Offsets never committed
    Same 500 records fetched again
    by the next generation
  end note

Root cause

A downstream service was CPU-throttled by a limit change, raising its p99 from 42 ms to 3.5 s. The notification consumer called it synchronously once per record with no timeout, so processing one max.poll.records=500 batch went from 82 seconds to 30 minutes, exceeding max.poll.interval.ms=300000. Kafka evicted each member as unresponsive, triggering a rebalance before any offsets were committed. The group re-formed, re-fetched the same records, and repeated: full CPU-free throughput, zero progress, lag growing at the producer rate.

Fix

Immediate (16:52): max.poll.records 500 -> 50 (worst case 180 s, under the 300 s limit), a temporary max.poll.interval.ms of 600,000, and an 800 ms timeout on the profile call. Lag drained from 1.51 M to zero in 47 minutes at a net 800 messages/s (drain_time = backlog / (consumer_rate - producer_rate) from Part 41 predicted 44 minutes; close enough).

Durable, in order of importance:

// 1. A hard timeout and a circuit breaker on every downstream call
const profile = await firstValueFrom(
  this.http.post<Profile[]>('/profiles/batch', { userIds }).pipe(
    timeout({ each: 800 }),
    retry({ count: 1, delay: 200 }),
    catchError(() => of({ data: [] as Profile[] })),   // degrade, do not block the poll loop
  ),
);
// 2. Batch the downstream call: one request per poll batch, not one per record
@EventPattern('order.events')
async handleBatch(@Payload() messages: OrderEvent[]): Promise<void> {
  const userIds = [...new Set(messages.map((m) => m.userId))];
  const profiles = await this.profiles.fetchMany(userIds);   // 1 call instead of 50
  const byId = new Map(profiles.map((p) => [p.userId, p]));
  await Promise.all(messages.map((m) => this.deliver(m, byId.get(m.userId))));
}

One batched call turns 50 x 3.5 s into 1 x 3.5 s, a 50x reduction in worst-case poll time, and it is the fix that would have made the incident impossible rather than merely survivable.

// 3. Heartbeat and commit incrementally within a long batch (KafkaJS eachBatch)
await consumer.run({
  eachBatch: async ({ batch, resolveOffset, heartbeat, isRunning, isStale }) => {
    for (const message of batch.messages) {
      if (!isRunning() || isStale()) break;
      await this.process(message);
      resolveOffset(message.offset);   // progress is committed even if we are evicted later
      await heartbeat();               // tell the coordinator we are alive
    }
  },
});

resolveOffset plus heartbeat is the structural answer: work already done is never redone, and a slow batch does not look like a dead member.

4. Write the budget down as a constant next to the config, so the relationship is a reviewable fact rather than tribal knowledge:

// max.poll.records * p99_processing_ms must stay under 50% of max.poll.interval.ms
// 50 records * 800 ms budget = 40 s, versus 300 s limit. Margin 7.5x.

5. Restore the profile service's CPU limit and set requests == limits so it gets a Guaranteed QoS class and predictable scheduling.

Prevention

  • Alert on commit_rate == 0 while records_consumed_rate > 0. This single alert detects every rebalance loop, and it fires within a minute rather than after an hour of accumulating lag. Lag alerts tell you something is wrong; this one tells you what.
  • Alert on rebalance rate above 6 per hour. A healthy group barely rebalances.
  • Alert on container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total for every service, not just CPU utilization. Throttling is invisible in the usage graph and it is a leading cause of mysterious downstream slowness.
  • A timeout on every network call, enforced by a shared HTTP client factory so a service cannot make an untimed call by accident.
  • Autoscale consumers on lag (KEDA) with maxReplicaCount <= partitions, and size partitions from the recovery requirement, as Part 41 sets out.
  • A load test with an artificially slowed downstream in the pipeline: inject 3 s latency into the profile client and assert the consumer still commits. This exact test would have caught it.

Junior versus senior

Junior Senior
First action Adds partitions and pods Notices consumers are at 12 percent CPU, so capacity is not the constraint
Metric read Watches lag Watches lag and commit rate; zero commits with nonzero consumption is the whole answer
Logs Filters to ERROR Reads WARN, where the Kafka client had written the diagnosis and both fixes
Downstream "The profile service is slow, tell that team" Fixes their own resilience (timeout, batching, degrade) and then tells that team
Fix Raises max.poll.interval.ms to 30 minutes Reduces the work per poll, batches the call, commits incrementally, and writes down the budget inequality

42.5 Users are receiving duplicate notifications

Symptom

09:31 — support escalates 12,400 tickets received in 20 minutes: "Your order has shipped" push notifications arriving 3 to 7 times. Twitter has screenshots. Some users received the same email eleven times. The window of affected notifications is narrow: everything sent between 09:12 and 09:18.

First five minutes (mitigation)

Duplicate sends are a reputational problem that gets worse every second, so stop the sending first and understand it after.

kubectl scale deployment/notification-consumer --replicas=0 -n prod   # 09:34

Sending stops. Kafka retains the events, so nothing is lost; the queue simply grows (at 800/s, a 30-minute investigation builds a 1.4 M backlog that will take about 30 minutes to drain afterwards, which the on-call announces in the channel so nobody is surprised).

Then a blast-radius limiter is deployed before consumers are turned back on: a per-user cap of 5 notifications per hour, enforced in Redis. It does not fix the bug, but it converts "eleven identical emails" into "five", which is the difference between an apology and a churn event.

Metrics

Metric Normal 09:12–09:18
notifications_sent_total 800/s 3,900/s
order.shipped events produced 780/s 790/s
Ratio sent / produced 1.02 4.9
Consumer pod restarts 0 3
kafka_consumergroup_lag ~200 spiked to 61,000 then drained

Producers produced the normal number of events. Consumers sent five times as many notifications. The duplication is on the consuming side, which eliminates half the possible causes immediately.

Logs

kubectl logs -l app=notification-consumer -n prod --previous --since-time=2026-04-02T09:10:00Z | head -40
09:12:41 INFO  processing orderId=a91f topic=order.events partition=3 offset=88410231
09:12:41 INFO  push sent orderId=a91f userId=u-77 providerMessageId=fcm-8e21aa
09:12:41 INFO  processing orderId=b02c partition=3 offset=88410232
09:12:42 INFO  push sent orderId=b02c userId=u-91 providerMessageId=fcm-8e21ab
...
09:12:53 FATAL JavaScript heap out of memory

and from the replacement pod:

09:13:09 INFO  [Consumer] Successfully joined group with generation 4471
09:13:09 INFO  [Consumer] Assignment(partitions=[order.events-3])
09:13:10 INFO  processing orderId=a91f topic=order.events partition=3 offset=88410231   <-- again
09:13:10 INFO  push sent orderId=a91f userId=u-77 providerMessageId=fcm-8e21bd           <-- new provider id

Offset 88410231 is processed twice, six hundred milliseconds of wall-clock apart in different pods, and each processing produced a different providerMessageId.

That last detail is the one that kills the red herring. The prevailing theory in the channel for the first fifteen minutes was that the push provider was retrying deliveries on its side. It is a comfortable theory because it makes the problem someone else's. The evidence against it is decisive and takes two minutes to gather: if the provider were retrying, there would be one providerMessageId delivered several times. Instead there are five distinct provider message ids for one order_id, each with its own accepted timestamp in the provider's dashboard. The provider did exactly what it was told, five times. "We sent it five times" went into the incident doc at 09:47, and the investigation turned inward.

Traces

The trace of a single duplicated notification is unremarkable and that is the point: each of the five sends is a complete, correct, successful trace. There is no error anywhere. Duplicates are not a failure of any single operation; they are a failure of the protocol between operations.

Application

// src/notifications/notification.consumer.ts  (the bug)
@EventPattern('order.events')
async handle(@Payload() event: OrderEvent): Promise<void> {
  if (event.type !== 'order.shipped') return;
  const user = await this.users.findOne(event.userId);
  await this.push.send(user.deviceTokens, this.templates.shipped(event));  // side effect
  await this.log.record(event.orderId, 'push', 'sent');
  // offsets are committed by the framework, after the handler returns
}

The consumer config:

// src/main.ts
{
  transport: Transport.KAFKA,
  options: {
    client: { brokers: [...] },
    consumer: { groupId: 'notifications', sessionTimeout: 30000 },
    run: { autoCommit: true, autoCommitInterval: 5000 },   // commits every 5 s
  },
}

Two facts combine. Every message broker worth using is at-least-once: it guarantees a message is delivered at least once, never exactly once, because "exactly once" across a broker and an external HTTP call is not something any broker can promise. And autoCommitInterval: 5000 means up to five seconds of successful sends may be uncommitted at any moment. A pod that dies in that window has performed the side effect but not recorded that it did.

The pod died because of the memory leak described in section 42.6, which is why these two scenarios often arrive on the same day.

sequenceDiagram
  participant K as Kafka
  participant C1 as ConsumerPodA
  participant F as PushProvider
  participant C2 as ConsumerPodB
  K->>C1: records offsets 88410231 to 88410260
  C1->>F: send push for order a91f
  F-->>C1: accepted fcm-8e21aa
  C1->>F: send push for order b02c
  F-->>C1: accepted fcm-8e21ab
  Note over C1: OOMKilled before autoCommit fires
  K->>C2: rebalance, same records from last committed offset
  C2->>F: send push for order a91f again
  F-->>C2: accepted fcm-8e21bd
  C2->>F: send push for order b02c again
  F-->>C2: accepted fcm-8e21be

Three crashes, each re-delivering up to five seconds of already-sent messages, and one user who happened to be in three of those windows received the notification four times.

Database

notification_log confirms it in one query, and this query is also the tool for measuring the blast radius:

SELECT order_id, channel, count(*) AS sends,
       min(sent_at) AS first_send, max(sent_at) AS last_send
FROM notification_log
WHERE sent_at BETWEEN '2026-04-02 09:10' AND '2026-04-02 09:20'
GROUP BY order_id, channel HAVING count(*) > 1
ORDER BY sends DESC LIMIT 10;
 order_id | channel | sends |     first_send      |      last_send
----------+---------+-------+---------------------+---------------------
 a91f...  | push    |     5 | 2026-04-02 09:12:41 | 2026-04-02 09:17:52
 b02c...  | email   |     4 | 2026-04-02 09:12:42 | 2026-04-02 09:16:03

The table recorded every duplicate faithfully. It was a log, not a guard: nothing ever read it before sending.

Infrastructure

Confirmed: three OOMKilled events on notification-consumer pods between 09:12 and 09:18, exit code 137, memory limit 1 Gi, --max-old-space-size unset. That is section 42.7's failure mode, and it is the trigger; the duplicates are the consequence of a non-idempotent consumer meeting an ordinary crash.

Root cause

The consumer performed an external, irreversible side effect (a push and an email) and then relied on an offset commit that happened up to five seconds later. When the pod was OOMKilled between the side effect and the commit, Kafka's at-least-once delivery correctly redelivered those messages to the new pod, which performed the side effect again because nothing made the send idempotent.

The crash is not the bug. Pods die: OOM, node drain, spot reclamation, rolling deploy, a bad kubectl delete. A consumer that produces duplicates when a pod dies is broken by design, and it will produce duplicates eventually no matter how stable your pods are.

Fix

Make the send idempotent with a deterministic key and a uniqueness constraint the database enforces.

ALTER TABLE notification_log
  ADD COLUMN idempotency_key text,
  ADD COLUMN state text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'sent';
UPDATE notification_log SET idempotency_key = encode(sha256((order_id || ':' || channel || ':' || event_version)::bytea),'hex')
  WHERE idempotency_key IS NULL;
ALTER TABLE notification_log ALTER COLUMN idempotency_key SET NOT NULL;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY uq_notification_idempotency
  ON notification_log (idempotency_key);
// src/notifications/notification.consumer.ts  (fixed)
@EventPattern('order.events')
async handle(@Payload() event: OrderEvent): Promise<void> {
  if (event.type !== 'order.shipped') return;

  const key = createHash('sha256')
    .update(`${event.orderId}:push:${event.version}`)   // deterministic: same event, same key, always
    .digest('hex');

  // Claim the send. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING makes this an atomic test-and-set.
  const claimed = await this.dataSource.query(
    `INSERT INTO notification_log (idempotency_key, order_id, channel, state, claimed_at)
     VALUES ($1, $2, 'push', 'sending', now())
     ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING
     RETURNING id`,
    [key, event.orderId],
  );
  if (claimed.length === 0) {
    this.metrics.increment('notifications.duplicate_suppressed');
    return;                       // someone already sent, or is sending, this exact notification
  }

  const user = await this.users.findOne(event.userId);
  const providerMessageId = await this.push.send(user.deviceTokens, this.templates.shipped(event));

  await this.dataSource.query(
    `UPDATE notification_log SET state = 'sent', provider_message_id = $2, sent_at = now()
     WHERE idempotency_key = $1`, [key, providerMessageId],
  );
}

Be honest about what this does and does not guarantee. The claim is atomic, so two consumers can never both send. But if the pod dies after the INSERT and before the provider accepts the push, the row is stuck in sending and the notification is never delivered. That is the at-least-once/at-most-once trade made explicit, and you must choose per notification type:

Notification Choice Mechanism
Marketing push At most once. A missed one costs nothing Leave stuck sending rows alone; a report counts them
Order shipped At least once, deduplicated on the client where possible A sweeper re-queues rows stuck in sending for over 10 minutes
One-time password At least once, always Sweeper at 60 seconds; a duplicate OTP is far better than a missing one 
-- The sweeper, run every minute
UPDATE notification_log SET state = 'retry', claimed_at = now()
WHERE state = 'sending' AND claimed_at < now() - interval '10 minutes'
RETURNING id, order_id, channel;

Add a Redis fast path in front of the insert (SET key 1 NX EX 86400) to keep the common case off the database, but keep PostgreSQL as the source of truth: Redis can lose a key, and a lost dedupe key means a duplicate.

Prevention

  • A chaos test in CI that kills the consumer mid-batch and asserts that replaying the same offsets produces exactly one send. Run it against real Kafka and PostgreSQL containers.
  • notifications.duplicate_suppressed as a metric. After the fix it should be small but nonzero, and a spike in it is an early warning that pods are crashing.
  • Set autoCommit: false and commit explicitly after the side effect and its record, which narrows the window from five seconds to one message.
  • The per-user rate cap stays permanently. A blast-radius limiter is worth keeping even when the specific bug is fixed, because the next bug is unknown.
  • A design rule stated in the team's coding standard: every consumer of a message broker is at-least-once, so every side effect it performs needs an idempotency key derived from the event, not from the wall clock or a random id.

Junior versus senior

Junior Senior
First theory The provider is retrying Checks provider message ids; five distinct ids means we sent five times
Framing "How do we stop the pod crashing?" "Pods will always crash. Why does a crash cause duplicates?"
Fix Adds a sentAt check with a SELECT before the send Uses a unique constraint with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, because a SELECT-then-INSERT is the same race one layer up
Guarantees "We fixed the duplicates" Names the remaining window explicitly and chooses at-least-once or at-most-once per notification type
Testing Manual retest A test that kills the consumer between the side effect and the commit

42.6 Memory usage keeps increasing

Symptom

Ongoing, noticed 11:20 on a Tuesday. The orders-api memory graph over seven days is a sawtooth on a rising slope: each pod starts at about 380 MB of RSS, climbs to roughly 1.4 GB over 40 hours, gets OOMKilled, restarts at 380 MB, and repeats. Nobody had noticed because the restarts happen at different times on different pods and the service never becomes unavailable. It surfaced only because the duplicate-notification incident in section 42.5 traced back to a consumer OOM, and someone finally looked at the memory graphs for the whole fleet.

A sawtooth with a flat baseline is healthy garbage collection. A sawtooth with a rising baseline is a leak. The distinction is the entire diagnosis, and it is visible in one graph.

First five minutes (mitigation)

There is no user impact right now, so the mitigation is minimal and reversible: raise the memory limit from 1 Gi to 2 Gi, which converts a 40-hour restart cycle into an 80-hour one and buys time to investigate properly.

Say clearly in the channel that this is not a fix. Raising a memory limit to stop OOMKills is the production equivalent of turning up the radio to hide the engine noise, and teams that do it three times in a row end up with 8 GB pods that still leak.

Metrics

Metric Behaviour What it rules in or out
container_memory_working_set_bytes Rises 25 MB/hour, sawtooth on a rising baseline The leak is real
nodejs_heap_size_used_bytes Rises in step with RSS, from 210 MB to 1.15 GB The leak is in the JS heap, not in native memory
nodejs_external_memory_bytes Flat at 22 MB Not Buffers, not a native addon
nodejs_gc_duration_seconds (major) 40 ms rising to 310 ms GC is working harder over the same live set: classic retention
nodejs_active_handles_total Flat at 34 Not leaked sockets or timers
Event loop lag p99 9 ms rising to 60 ms The GC pauses are starting to hurt latency
RPS Flat Not traffic growth

Heap and RSS rising together, external flat, handles flat. That combination says: JavaScript objects are being retained. If RSS had risen while the heap stayed flat, the hunt would be entirely different (native buffers, a leaking pg result cache, an addon, or fragmentation).

Logs

Nothing useful, which is itself informative. There is one exception, found by grepping the startup logs:

11:02:03 WARN  MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected.
               11 order.created listeners added to [EventEmitter2]. Use emitter.setMaxListeners()
               to increase limit

That warning appeared once, four months ago in the deploy logs, and stopped appearing after a commit whose message was "silence noisy listener warning". Node was telling the truth and someone turned off the alarm. Keep this in mind; it becomes the second leak.

Traces

Traces show nothing: every request is normal, the slow ones are slow because of GC pauses that appear as unexplained gaps with no child span. This is expected. Tracing finds slow requests; it does not find leaks. Knowing which tool cannot answer your question is half of debugging.

Application

Time for a heap snapshot. You cannot attach Chrome DevTools to a production pod, so expose an admin endpoint on the internal port, and take the snapshot from a pod removed from the load balancer, because writeHeapSnapshot blocks the event loop for seconds on a large heap and briefly doubles memory.

// src/ops/heap.controller.ts  (internal port, admin guard, rate limited)
import { Controller, Post, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { writeHeapSnapshot } from 'node:v8';

@Controller('internal/heap')
@UseGuards(InternalAdminGuard)
export class HeapController {
  @Post('snapshot')
  snapshot(): { file: string } {
    const file = `/tmp/heap-${process.pid}-${Date.now()}.heapsnapshot`;
    writeHeapSnapshot(file);   // blocks; take it off the load balancer first
    return { file };
  }
}
POD=orders-api-7d9f4c8b6-x2k9q
# 1. Take the pod out of rotation so the snapshot pause hurts nobody
kubectl label pod $POD -n prod app-                     # removes it from the Service selector
kubectl exec -n prod $POD -- curl -s -XPOST localhost:9100/internal/heap/snapshot
kubectl cp prod/$POD:/tmp/heap-1-1743500000000.heapsnapshot ./t0.heapsnapshot
# 2. Put it back, let it serve traffic for four hours, repeat
kubectl label pod $POD -n prod app=orders-api
# ... four hours later ...
kubectl cp prod/$POD:/tmp/heap-1-1743514400000.heapsnapshot ./t4.heapsnapshot

Open Chrome DevTools, Memory panel, load both snapshots, select the second, and switch the view to Comparison against the first, sorted by Size Delta. One snapshot tells you what is in memory; two snapshots tell you what is accumulating, and only the second question matters.

Constructor                  # New    # Deleted   # Delta   Size Delta
(object)                    1,284,110    9,412  +1,274,698   +412 MB
Map                                 3        0         +3    +398 MB
(string)                      642,004    8,110    +633,894   +181 MB
PricingContext                318,441       12   +318,429     +98 MB
(closure)                     319,006    1,004   +318,002     +64 MB
Array                          12,884      440    +12,444     +51 MB
OrderEntity                     4,110    3,980       +130      +2 MB

Three Maps holding 398 MB, 318,429 PricingContext objects, and 318,002 closures. Select the Map row, expand an instance, and read the Retainers pane bottom-up:

Map @1284110
  in cache            @982110  PricingCacheService
    in _providers     @441002  Map (Nest DI container)
      in container    @12      NestApplicationContext

The retainer path names the culprit: a Map field on a singleton NestJS provider, held by the DI container, held by the application. Nothing will ever collect it.

Here is the red herring, and it consumed a full day before the snapshots were taken. The initial theory was "a leak in a dependency", supported by a GitHub issue on the HTTP client library describing a leak under keep-alive. The team upgraded axios, then pg, then bumped Node from 20.11 to 20.14, deploying each on its own and waiting eight hours to observe. The slope did not change. Three days and four deploys spent on a theory that a four-hour heap comparison disproved in ten minutes, because the comparison pointed at application constructors (PricingContext) rather than at library internals. The lesson is not "dependencies never leak" but "measure before you upgrade": an upgrade is a change with its own risk, and using it as a diagnostic is expensive.

The code:

// src/pricing/pricing-cache.service.ts  (leak 1)
@Injectable()
export class PricingCacheService {
  private readonly cache = new Map<string, PricingContext>();   // unbounded, singleton scope

  get(key: string, build: () => PricingContext): PricingContext {
    let ctx = this.cache.get(key);
    if (!ctx) { ctx = build(); this.cache.set(key, ctx); }       // nothing ever deletes
    return ctx;
  }
}

The key is ${userId}:${cartHash}:${currency}, which is effectively unique per request. Every request inserts a new entry and nothing is ever removed. At 640 RPS with an object graph of roughly 1.3 KB, this is about 3 GB a day of pure retention.

The second leak explains the (closure) growth and the old MaxListenersExceededWarning:

// src/orders/order-events.interceptor.ts  (leak 2)
@Injectable()
export class OrderEventsInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  constructor(private readonly events: EventEmitter2) {
    this.events.setMaxListeners(0);   // "silence noisy listener warning": removed the alarm
  }

  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request>();
    // A new listener on a long-lived singleton emitter, for every request. Never removed.
    this.events.on('order.created', (e: OrderCreatedEvent) => this.audit(req.correlationId, e));
    return next.handle();
  }
}

Each listener closure captures req, which captures headers, the parsed body and the response object. That is why the (string) and (object) counts grow alongside the closures: the leak is not the function, it is everything the function keeps alive.

Verify it live without a snapshot:

setInterval(() => {
  logger.log({ listeners: this.events.listenerCount('order.created') }, 'listener count');
}, 60_000);
// 1204 ... 2417 ... 3630 ... rising monotonically with request count
flowchart TB
  REQ["Each request"] --> M["PricingCacheService.cache.set with a per-request key"]
  REQ --> L["events.on('order.created', closure capturing req)"]
  M --> SING["Map lives on a singleton provider held by the Nest DI container"]
  L --> EM["Listener array lives on a singleton EventEmitter2"]
  SING --> GC["GC roots reach every entry, so nothing is collectable"]
  EM --> GC
  GC --> HEAP["Heap baseline rises 25 MB per hour"]
  HEAP --> PAUSE["Major GC pauses grow from 40 ms to 310 ms"]
  HEAP --> OOM["RSS crosses the 1 Gi container limit, OOMKilled, exit 137"]

Database

Ruled out in two minutes and worth doing: pg_stat_activity shows no growth in connection count, no idle in transaction accumulation, and the pool metrics are flat. A leaked connection or an accumulating result set would have shown here.

Infrastructure

kubectl describe pod on a restarted pod confirms Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137. Node memory is fine; no other pod on the node is affected. The infrastructure is correctly enforcing a limit the application is violating.

Root cause

Two independent retention bugs on singleton-scoped objects. An unbounded Map cache keyed by a per-request value on a singleton provider, and an event listener registered per request on a singleton EventEmitter2 and never removed, whose closure retained the entire request object. Both are reachable from the NestJS DI container, which is a GC root for the process lifetime, so nothing was ever collectable.

Fix

// Fix 1: bound the cache by size and time
import { LRUCache } from 'lru-cache';

@Injectable()
export class PricingCacheService {
  private readonly cache = new LRUCache<string, PricingContext>({
    max: 10_000,               // hard object ceiling
    ttl: 5 * 60_000,           // and a time ceiling
    maxSize: 64 * 1024 * 1024, // and a byte ceiling
    sizeCalculation: (v) => v.approximateBytes,
  });
  // ... get() unchanged
}

Three ceilings, because any one of them can be defeated by an unexpected object shape. An unbounded cache is not a cache, it is a leak with a hit ratio.

// Fix 2: do not subscribe per request. Subscribe once, at module init.
@Injectable()
export class OrderEventsListener implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private readonly handler = (e: OrderCreatedEvent) => this.audit(e);

  onModuleInit(): void { this.events.on('order.created', this.handler); }
  onModuleDestroy(): void { this.events.off('order.created', this.handler); }  // symmetric
}

The correlation id that the interceptor was trying to capture comes from AsyncLocalStorage instead, which is what request context is for (see section 42.12). Also revert setMaxListeners(0): the warning is a leak detector, and disabling it is disabling the detector.

Set the heap limit relative to the container limit so V8 collects aggressively before the kernel intervenes:

env:
  - name: NODE_OPTIONS
    value: "--max-old-space-size=1400"   # ~70% of the 2 Gi limit
resources:
  requests: { memory: "2Gi", cpu: "1" }
  limits:   { memory: "2Gi", cpu: "2" }

After the fix: RSS settles at 410 MB with a flat baseline over six days, major GC pauses back to 35 ms, and the memory limit is returned to 1 Gi.

Prevention

  • Alert on the slope, not the level: deriv(nodejs_heap_size_used_bytes[6h]) > 5e6 sustained for two hours. Level alerts fire when it is already too late; a slope alert fires on day one.
  • A soak test in CI: 60 percent of peak load for four hours in staging, failing the build if the heap baseline (measured after a forced GC) rises more than 10 percent. This is the test that catches leaks before users do.
  • Review rules with teeth: no Map, Set or array as a mutable field on a singleton provider without a documented bound; every .on() has a matching .off() in onModuleDestroy; never call setMaxListeners(0).
  • A documented heap-snapshot runbook so the next engineer does not spend three days upgrading dependencies. The procedure above (label off, snapshot, label on, wait, snapshot, compare) should take twenty minutes.
  • --max-old-space-size set from the container limit in a shared base image or Helm template, so no service can get it wrong individually.

Junior versus senior

Junior Senior
First move Raises the memory limit and closes the ticket Raises the limit to buy time, states loudly that it is not a fix
Theory "It's a leak in a dependency" Compares heap snapshots before touching a single dependency version
Snapshot use Takes one snapshot and stares at the biggest object Takes two, four hours apart, and sorts by delta
Reading the result Sees a big Map, guesses which one Reads the retainer path bottom-up to the exact field on the exact provider
Fix Clears the Map on an interval Bounds it three ways, fixes the listener symmetry, and sets the heap limit from the container limit
Prevention None Slope alert, soak test in CI, review rules, runbook

42.7 NestJS pods keep restarting

Symptom

08:05 — kubectl get pods during a routine morning check:

NAME                            READY   STATUS             RESTARTS       AGE
orders-api-6c8f9d7b5-2xnpq      1/1     Running            47 (3m ago)    3h12m
orders-api-6c8f9d7b5-4tk8v      0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   51 (18s ago)   3h12m
orders-api-6c8f9d7b5-9wzlm      1/1     Running            44 (7m ago)    3h12m

Forty-seven restarts in three hours. Users see intermittent 502s (roughly 0.4 percent of requests) when a pod is killed mid-request, and p99 is spiky because a fraction of traffic keeps landing on pods that are still warming up.

First five minutes (mitigation)

Two immediate actions. Increase the replica count so that pods restarting is a smaller fraction of capacity, and stop the bleeding on the readiness side so traffic is not sent to pods that are not ready:

kubectl scale deployment/orders-api --replicas=18 -n prod   # from 12

Then, before changing anything else, capture the evidence, because a restart destroys it.

Metrics

Metric Value
kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total Rising steadily since 04:55
container_memory_working_set_bytes Reaching exactly 2,147,483,648 before each restart on some pods
probe_duration_seconds{probe="liveness"} 1.0 s (the timeout) on the failing pods
Startup duration (first request served after start) 44 s
Event loop lag during startup 3,800 ms peak

Two different numbers stand out, and that is the clue that there are two different problems. Some pods die at exactly the memory limit; others die while their liveness probe times out during startup. It is tempting to look for one explanation. Resist it: the restart counts tell you a pod can die for more than one reason.

Logs

kubectl describe pod orders-api-6c8f9d7b5-4tk8v -n prod
Containers:
  api:
    State:          Waiting
      Reason:       CrashLoopBackOff
    Last State:     Terminated
      Reason:       OOMKilled
      Exit Code:    137
      Started:      Wed, 15 Apr 2026 08:01:12 +0000
      Finished:     Wed, 15 Apr 2026 08:03:58 +0000
    Restart Count:  51
    Limits:         memory: 2Gi        cpu: 2
    Requests:       memory: 512Mi      cpu: 500m
Events:
  Type     Reason     Age                    From     Message
  ----     ------     ----                   ----     -------
  Warning  Unhealthy  14m (x38 over 3h4m)    kubelet  Liveness probe failed: Get
             "http://10.44.2.19:3000/health": context deadline exceeded
             (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
  Normal   Killing    14m (x19 over 3h4m)    kubelet  Container api failed liveness probe,
             will be restarted
  Warning  BackOff    2m (x214 over 2h51m)   kubelet  Back-off restarting failed container

Exit codes are worth committing to memory, because they classify the death in one glance:

Exit code Meaning Typical cause
0 Clean exit Process returned from main; usually a bug in a server
1 Uncaught exception Unhandled rejection, config validation failure at boot
137 128 + 9 = SIGKILL OOMKilled by the kernel, or a liveness kill after the grace period
143 128 + 15 = SIGTERM Graceful shutdown requested (deploy, scale-down, eviction)

And the previous container's logs, which are the only place the truth survives a restart:

kubectl logs orders-api-6c8f9d7b5-4tk8v -n prod --previous
08:01:12  [Nest] LOG [NestFactory] Starting Nest application...
08:01:14  [Nest] LOG [InstanceLoader] TypeOrmModule dependencies initialized
08:01:15  [Nest] LOG [CatalogWarmupService] loading product catalog into memory...
08:01:52  [Nest] LOG [CatalogWarmupService] loaded 1,240,000 products (37,412 ms)
08:01:52  [Nest] LOG [NestApplication] Nest application successfully started
08:01:52  [Nest] LOG server listening on :3000

Thirty-seven seconds inside CatalogWarmupService, and the probe configuration:

livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health, port: 3000 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 10
  timeoutSeconds: 1
  failureThreshold: 3

Ten seconds of grace plus three failures at ten-second periods is forty seconds before the kubelet kills the container. Startup takes forty-four. The pod is killed four seconds before it would have become healthy, every single time, in a perfect loop.

Traces

The catalog warm-up shows as one 37-second synchronous span with no children. It is a for loop over a million rows building nested objects, entirely synchronous, so the event loop never yields. Even after the HTTP server binds the port, an in-progress synchronous block means the probe's connection is accepted by the kernel but never answered by JavaScript. The process is alive and the probe still times out, which is precisely the failure mode liveness probes are worst at distinguishing.

Application

// src/catalog/catalog-warmup.service.ts
@Injectable()
export class CatalogWarmupService implements OnApplicationBootstrap {
  async onApplicationBootstrap(): Promise<void> {
    const rows = await this.repo.find();                  // 1.24 M rows into memory
    for (const row of rows) { this.index.set(row.sku, this.toDto(row)); }   // sync, 37 s
  }
}

onApplicationBootstrap runs before listen() completes in the sense that matters: the application does not begin serving until it returns. And the health endpoint itself:

@Get('health')
async health(): Promise<{ status: string }> {
  await this.dataSource.query('SELECT 1');       // a database call in a LIVENESS probe
  await this.redis.ping();
  return { status: 'ok' };
}

A liveness probe that depends on the database means that when the database has a hiccup, Kubernetes restarts every pod in the fleet simultaneously, converting a two-second database blip into a full outage. That is a latent second incident sitting in this manifest.

Database

Not the cause here, and confirmed quickly: SELECT 1 runs in 0.3 ms, connections are normal. But the investigation notes it as a serious latent risk because of the liveness dependency above, and the fix removes it.

Infrastructure

The second death mode. Some pods are OOMKilled at exactly 2 GiB with no probe failures. Their config:

env:
  - name: NODE_OPTIONS
    value: "--max-old-space-size=3072"     # 3 GiB heap
resources:
  limits:
    memory: 2Gi                            # 2 GiB container

V8 is told it may use a 3 GiB old space, so it happily grows past 2 GiB before deciding a major collection is worthwhile. The kernel's cgroup limit is 2 GiB and it does not negotiate. V8 never gets the chance to collect, because the process is killed while V8 still believes it has a gigabyte of headroom. Add the catalog's 1.24 million objects (about 900 MB) to normal request memory and the pods that survive startup die in the first hour.

The red herring: for the first thirty minutes the working theory was the cluster autoscaler evicting pods to consolidate nodes, which had been enabled the previous week. It is a good theory, it explains restarts, and it was checked and discarded in four minutes: kubectl get events --field-selector reason=Evicted returned nothing for this namespace, node count had been stable at 14 for three days, and evictions produce exit code 143 with a Killing event citing eviction, not 137 with OOMKilled. Exit codes discriminate between causes; use them before you theorize.

Root cause

Two independent faults arriving together. A liveness probe budget of 40 seconds against a 44-second startup, made worse by a synchronous 37-second catalog load that blocked the event loop so the probe could not be answered even after the port was bound. And --max-old-space-size=3072 set above a 2 GiB container limit, so V8 deferred major GC past the point where the kernel killed the process.

flowchart TB
  START["Pod starts"] --> WARM["onApplicationBootstrap loads 1.24M products, 37 s of synchronous work"]
  WARM --> BLOCK["Event loop blocked, /health cannot be answered"]
  BLOCK --> PROBE["Liveness: initialDelay 10 s plus 3 failures at 10 s equals 40 s budget"]
  PROBE --> KILL["Kubelet kills at 40 s, startup needed 44 s"]
  KILL --> START
  WARM --> MEM["900 MB retained by the in-memory index"]
  MEM --> V8["max-old-space-size 3072 above the 2 Gi container limit"]
  V8 --> LATE["V8 defers major GC, believing it has headroom"]
  LATE --> OOM["Kernel OOMKills at 2 Gi, exit code 137"]
  OOM --> START

Fix

# 1. A startupProbe owns the slow start; liveness only takes over once the pod is up.
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: 3000 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 30            # 150 s of startup budget, 3x the observed 44 s
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: 3000 }   # cheap: no I/O at all
  periodSeconds: 10
  timeoutSeconds: 3
  failureThreshold: 3
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: 3000 }  # checks dependencies, cached for 10 s
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 2
  failureThreshold: 2
// 2. Liveness answers "is this process healthy enough to keep", not "is the database up".
@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
  constructor(private readonly health: HealthCheckService, private readonly db: TypeOrmHealthIndicator) {}

  @Get('live')
  live(): { status: string } {
    return { status: 'ok' };   // no I/O. If the event loop can answer, the process is alive.
  }

  @Get('ready')
  @HealthCheck()
  ready() {
    // Readiness may depend on the database: a failing pod is removed from the Service,
    // it is not killed. This is the difference that matters.
    return this.health.check([() => this.db.pingCheck('database', { timeout: 1500 })]);
  }
}
// 3. Do not block the event loop during warm-up; yield, and serve traffic while it fills.
async onApplicationBootstrap(): Promise<void> {
  void this.warm();   // do not await: the app becomes ready immediately
}

private async warm(): Promise<void> {
  const stream = await this.repo.createQueryBuilder('p').stream();
  let n = 0;
  for await (const row of stream) {
    this.index.set(row.p_sku, this.toDto(row));
    if (++n % 5_000 === 0) await new Promise((r) => setImmediate(r));  // yield to the loop
  }
  this.warmed = true;
}

Better still, delete the warm-up: 1.24 million products in every pod's heap is 900 MB per pod times 18 pods of duplicated data that Redis already holds once. The reason it existed was a 6 ms Redis lookup that somebody wanted to be 0.05 ms. That trade cost 16 GB of cluster memory and this incident.

# 4. Heap limit below the container limit, and requests == limits for Guaranteed QoS.
env:
  - name: NODE_OPTIONS
    value: "--max-old-space-size=1400"
resources:
  requests: { memory: "2Gi", cpu: "1" }
  limits:   { memory: "2Gi", cpu: "1" }
// 5. Graceful shutdown, so a restart does not produce 502s.
app.enableShutdownHooks();
// terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 in the manifest, and readiness fails first so the
// Service stops sending traffic before the server stops accepting it.

Prevention

  • Alert on increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total[1h]) > 3. Restarts hide behind a healthy replica count; nothing else will tell you.
  • Alert specifically on OOMKill events, which are a distinct and always-actionable signal.
  • A CI check on the manifests: --max-old-space-size must be present and must be at most 75 percent of resources.limits.memory; startupProbe.failureThreshold * periodSeconds must exceed the measured p99 startup time by 3x.
  • Measure startup time as a metric and alert when it grows. Startup time creeps up quietly as modules are added, and it is invisible until it crosses a probe budget.
  • A standing rule: liveness probes never perform I/O. Readiness checks dependencies; liveness checks only that the process can answer.
  • A PodDisruptionBudget so voluntary disruptions cannot remove too many pods at once.

Junior versus senior

Junior Senior
First look kubectl logs pod (empty, the container just restarted) kubectl logs --previous and kubectl describe for the exit code and events
Restart cause Assumes one cause Notices two death modes in the metrics and treats them separately
Exit code 137 "It crashed" "SIGKILL: OOMKilled or a liveness kill; the describe output distinguishes them"
Probe design Health endpoint checks everything, used for both probes Liveness with no I/O, readiness with dependencies, startupProbe for slow boot
Heap flag Raises --max-old-space-size to stop OOMKills Sets it below the container limit, because above it guarantees the kill
Warm-up Optimizes the loop Asks whether 900 MB per pod of duplicated cache should exist at all

42.8 Database connections are exhausted

Symptom

17:44 — every service starts failing at once. The API returns 500s on 60 percent of requests. Two distinct errors dominate the logs:

QueryFailedError: sorry, too many clients already
TimeoutError: ResourceRequest timed out

The second is TypeORM's pool refusing to hand out a connection within connectionTimeoutMillis. The first is PostgreSQL refusing to accept a new one at all. The on-call cannot open psql either, until they remember that superuser_reserved_connections exists and connects as the admin role.

Simultaneous failure across every service is characteristic. When one service breaks, suspect that service. When everything breaks at the same second, suspect the thing they share: the database, the cache, DNS, or the network.

First five minutes (mitigation)

-- Connect as the reserved superuser
SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_type = 'client backend' GROUP BY state;
         state          | count
------------------------+-------
 idle                   |   210
 idle in transaction    |   118
 active                 |    61
 idle in transaction (aborted) |  9

398 of 400 slots used, and 127 of them are sitting inside an open transaction doing nothing. Those are pure waste and they hold locks. Reclaim them:

-- Kill sessions idle inside a transaction for more than 5 minutes. Safe: they are doing nothing,
-- and killing them rolls their transaction back.
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid), left(query, 60), now() - state_change AS idle_for
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state IN ('idle in transaction', 'idle in transaction (aborted)')
  AND state_change < now() - interval '5 minutes';

17:49 — 118 sessions terminated, error rate drops to 3 percent within thirty seconds. Then a guard so it cannot recur while the investigation runs:

ALTER SYSTEM SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';
SELECT pg_reload_conf();

17:52 — error rate at 0.1 percent. Mitigated in eight minutes without a single deploy or restart.

Metrics

Metric Normal At 17:44
pg_stat_activity total 210 398 of 400
idle in transaction count 2 127
Application pool waitingCount 0 84 per pod
Pool totalCount 8 per pod 10 per pod (at max)
Pod count (orders-api) 20 30, mid-deploy
RDS CPU 41% 22% (the database is barely working)

The database is at 22 percent CPU while everything fails. It is not overloaded; it is full. Distinguishing "slow" from "full" is the first fork in any connection incident, and the CPU graph answers it in a second.

idle in transaction climbing from 2 to 127 over the previous six hours (visible on the graph in hindsight) is the leak signature. Those sessions began a transaction and never ended it.

Logs

Attribute the connections. This works only because application_name was set per pod, which is why section 42.12 insists on it:

SELECT application_name, state, count(*)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 3 DESC LIMIT 10;
        application_name          |        state        | count
----------------------------------+---------------------+-------
 orders-api@orders-api-6c8f-2xnpq | idle in transaction |    31
 orders-api@orders-api-6c8f-9wzlm | idle in transaction |    29
 orders-api@orders-api-6c8f-4tk8v | idle in transaction |    28
 catalog-api@catalog-api-77d-h4x  | idle                |    18
 settlement-cron@settlement-2xk   | active              |     3

orders-api alone holds 88 idle-in-transaction sessions across three pods. Now find what they were last doing:

SELECT pid, application_name, now() - xact_start AS xact_age, left(query, 100) AS last_query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
ORDER BY xact_start LIMIT 5;
 pid   |    application_name    |   xact_age   |                     last_query
-------+------------------------+--------------+------------------------------------------------
 41102 | orders-api@...-2xnpq   | 05:41:22.114 | SELECT p.id, p.available FROM products p WHERE p.id = $1 FOR UPDATE
 41118 | orders-api@...-9wzlm   | 05:12:04.882 | SELECT p.id, p.available FROM products p WHERE p.id = $1 FOR UPDATE

A transaction open for five hours and forty-one minutes, holding a FOR UPDATE row lock on a product the whole time. The application log for that correlation id:

12:03:14 ERROR reserveStock failed correlationId=e41a orderId=91bc
        error=InsufficientStockError: only 0 of 2 available
        at StockService.reserve (/app/dist/inventory/stock.service.js:62:15)

An error path. Every leaked connection is preceded by an exception.

Traces

Traces of failing requests show pool.acquire spans of 9,800 ms ending in a timeout, with no database span after them. The requests never reached PostgreSQL. Traces of the original failures, hours earlier, show a complete db.transaction span that ends normally with an error status. The span closes; the connection does not.
