A trace shows you the logical operation finished; it cannot show you that a resource was not released. Know your tools' blind spots.

Application

// src/inventory/stock.service.ts  (the leak)
async reserve(productId: string, qty: number): Promise<void> {
  const queryRunner = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner();
  await queryRunner.connect();               // takes a connection from the pool
  await queryRunner.startTransaction();
  try {
    const product = await queryRunner.manager.findOne(Product, {
      where: { id: productId }, lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' },
    });
    if (!product || product.available < qty) {
      throw new InsufficientStockError(`only ${product?.available ?? 0} of ${qty} available`);
    }
    product.available -= qty;
    await queryRunner.manager.save(product);
    await queryRunner.commitTransaction();
    await queryRunner.release();             // released ONLY on the happy path
  } catch (err) {
    await queryRunner.rollbackTransaction();
    throw err;                               // no release. The connection is gone forever.
  }
}

The catch rolls back and rethrows. It never calls release(), so the connection is never returned to the pool. In TypeORM the QueryRunner holds a real pooled connection, and a QueryRunner that is not released is a permanently lost slot. Worse, the rollbackTransaction() on line one of the catch can itself throw (if the connection has already broken), in which case even the rollback is skipped and the session stays idle in transaction holding locks.

The leak rate matches the arithmetic: roughly 22 InsufficientStockErrors per hour on a popular SKU, times three pods, over six hours, equals about 120 leaked connections. Exactly what pg_stat_activity shows.

The red herring was investigated between 17:46 and 17:50. Somebody said "the analytics team must be running a huge report again", which had genuinely caused a similar-looking incident four months earlier. It is checked in one query and dismissed:

SELECT usename, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
--  orders_app | 312
--  catalog_app | 61
--  analytics_ro | 4        <-- four connections. Not them.

Four connections. The analytics role is also capped by ALTER ROLE analytics_ro CONNECTION LIMIT 10, which was the fix from that earlier incident and which worked. Ruling it out took forty seconds because the earlier incident had left behind both a limit and a habit.

Database

Even without the leak, the arithmetic was already unsafe. The deploy at 17:41 is what tipped it:

Consumer Replicas Pool max Connections
orders-api 20 10 200
catalog-api 12 8 96
notification-worker 8 5 40
settlement-cron 2 5 10
Exporters, backups, humans 14
Steady-state total 360 of 400
During a rolling deploy (old pods draining, new pods started, maxSurge: 25%) x1.25 to x1.5 450–540

Steady state used 90 percent of max_connections. A rolling deploy needed 112 to 135 percent. The system had been surviving deploys only because pods terminated quickly; on this deploy, three pods drained slowly (they were holding those five-hour transactions, which had to be rolled back), and the surge crossed the limit. This is Part 41's "third deploy of the day" failure, arriving on schedule.

Infrastructure

Nothing wrong at the infrastructure layer: the RDS instance was healthy, no failover, no network event. max_connections was 400 on a db.r6g.2xlarge because RDS's default formula sets it from instance memory, and nobody had ever computed whether 400 was the right number for this fleet.

flowchart TB
  ERR["InsufficientStockError on an error path"] --> NOREL["catch rolls back, never calls queryRunner.release()"]
  NOREL --> LEAK["One pooled connection lost per error, about 22 per hour per pod"]
  LEAK --> IIT["Sessions sit idle in transaction, holding row locks, for hours"]
  BASE["Steady state: 20 pods x pool 10 plus other services equals 360 of 400"] --> TIGHT["90 percent of max_connections in normal operation"]
  DEPLOY["17:41 rolling deploy: old and new pods overlap"] --> SURGE["Peak demand 450 to 540 connections"]
  IIT --> WALL
  TIGHT --> WALL
  SURGE --> WALL["max_connections 400 reached"]
  WALL --> FAIL["sorry, too many clients already, across every service at once"]

Root cause

A QueryRunner leaked on an error path in StockService.reserve, losing one pooled connection per InsufficientStockError and leaving the session idle in transaction holding a row lock. Independently, the fleet's steady-state connection demand was 90 percent of max_connections, so the surge of a normal rolling deploy exceeded the limit. Either fault alone would have caused an incident eventually; together they picked 17:44 on a Tuesday.

Fix

// Fix 1: use the managed transaction helper, which cannot leak.
async reserve(productId: string, qty: number): Promise<void> {
  await this.dataSource.transaction('READ COMMITTED', async (manager) => {
    const product = await manager.findOne(Product, {
      where: { id: productId }, lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' },
    });
    if (!product || product.available < qty) {
      throw new InsufficientStockError(`only ${product?.available ?? 0} of ${qty} available`);
    }
    product.available -= qty;
    await manager.save(product);
  });
  // Commit, rollback and release are all handled. Throwing from the callback rolls back.
}

If a raw QueryRunner is genuinely required (streaming, advisory locks, LISTEN), the finally block is not optional:

const queryRunner = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner();
try {
  await queryRunner.connect();
  await queryRunner.startTransaction();
  // ...
  await queryRunner.commitTransaction();
} catch (err) {
  if (queryRunner.isTransactionActive) await queryRunner.rollbackTransaction();
  throw err;
} finally {
  await queryRunner.release();          // ALWAYS. This line is the whole fix.
}

Fix 2, the arithmetic. Size pools from Little's law rather than from a copied default. Measured p99 connection hold time is 9 ms; peak per-pod rate is 32 RPS; required concurrency is 32 * 0.009 = 0.29. A pool of 4 is generous.

Consumer Replicas Old pool New pool New total
orders-api 20 10 4 80
catalog-api 12 8 4 48
notification-worker 8 5 3 24
settlement-cron 2 5 4 8
Exporters, humans 14
Steady state 360 174
With deploy surge x1.5 540 261 of 400

Fix 3: PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of the primary, so the fleet's client connections stop being the database's problem at all (default_pool_size 40, reserve_pool_size 10), sized as Part 41 shows.

Fix 4: make the settings enforce the invariants.

// TypeORM DataSource
extra: {
  max: Number(process.env.DB_POOL_MAX ?? 4),
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 2000,      // fail fast; a 30 s wait hides saturation as latency
  idleTimeoutMillis: 30000,
  statement_timeout: 5000,
  idle_in_transaction_session_timeout: 30000,   // the database kills leaks by itself
  application_name: `orders-api@${process.env.HOSTNAME}`,
},

idle_in_transaction_session_timeout is the single most valuable line. It turns "a leak that accumulates for six hours" into "a leak that self-heals in thirty seconds and shows up as an error in the logs".

Prevention

  • Export pool metrics and alert on them: pool.totalCount, pool.idleCount, pool.waitingCount. Alert when waitingCount > 0 for 2 minutes, and when totalCount stays at max while RPS is flat, which is the leak signature.
  • Alert at 70 percent of max_connections, computed from pg_stat_activity. This would have paged at about 11:00, six hours before users noticed.
  • An integration test that asserts the pool returns to baseline after an error path. Call reserve() with insufficient stock fifty times and assert pool.totalCount is unchanged. It is ten lines and it catches the entire bug class.
  • A lint or review rule: createQueryRunner() is only allowed inside a reviewed helper; everything else uses dataSource.transaction().
  • idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and statement_timeout set on every role, in the database, not only in application config, so a connection from anywhere is bounded.
  • application_name on every connection string. Without it, the attribution query above returns nothing useful and the investigation takes hours instead of minutes.

Junior versus senior

Junior Senior
First action Restarts all the pods Queries pg_stat_activity, sees the state breakdown, kills idle-in-transaction sessions
Reading the numbers "The database is overloaded" "Database CPU is 22 percent: it is full, not slow"
Fix Raises max_connections to 800 Fixes the leak, right-sizes pools from Little's law, adds PgBouncer, sets the timeouts
Attribution Guesses which service application_name per pod answers it in one query
Prevention Closes the ticket Adds the pool-return test, the 70 percent alert, and the database-side timeout

42.9 Payment succeeds but the order stays pending

Symptom

Reported at 14:20 by finance, not by monitoring, which is itself a finding. Over the preceding six hours, 47 customers were charged by the payment provider while their order sat at status = 'pending_payment'. The customers see "payment failed, please try again" in the app; several tried again and were charged twice. The provider dashboard shows all 47 payments as captured.

Money moved and the system does not know. This is the highest-severity class of bug in commerce backends, because it is silent, it compounds (customers retry), and it is invisible to every latency and error-rate dashboard you own.

First five minutes (mitigation)

Stop the harm to customers before understanding it. Two actions:

  1. Freeze the retry path. A feature flag disables the "Retry payment" button on the order screen, replacing it with "Payment is being confirmed, contact support". No new double charges after 14:26.
  2. Reconcile manually for the 47 known orders using the query below, so those customers get their goods today.

Metrics

Metric Value Note
payment_webhooks_received_total 18,400 today Normal
payment_webhooks_processed_total 18,353 47 short
payment_webhooks_rejected_total{reason="unknown_order"} 47 Exactly the missing ones
orders_stuck_pending_gt_15m (metric did not exist) The gap that let this run six hours
outbox_oldest_unprocessed_age_seconds 11,400 (3h10m) Red. Nobody was watching this either

The rejection counter existed and had the exact right value all day. Nobody alerted on it. A metric nobody alerts on is a metric that exists to make the post-mortem embarrassing.

Logs

One affected order, by correlation id:

11:03:41.220 [orders-api]  INFO  BEGIN order creation orderId=91bc userId=u-4412 corr=7f2a
11:03:41.238 [orders-api]  INFO  INSERT orders id=91bc status=pending_payment corr=7f2a
11:03:41.402 [orders-api]  INFO  INSERT order_items x3 corr=7f2a
11:03:41.455 [orders-api]  INFO  calling provider createPaymentIntent corr=7f2a
11:03:41.980 [orders-api]  INFO  provider returned intent pi_3Nq8 status=requires_capture corr=7f2a
11:03:42.104 [payments-api] INFO  webhook received event=payment.captured intent=pi_3Nq8 order=91bc
11:03:42.140 [payments-api] WARN  webhook: order 91bc not found, acknowledging corr=c19f
11:03:42.141 [payments-api] INFO  webhook response 200 body={"ignored":"unknown order"}
11:03:42.702 [orders-api]  INFO  COMMIT order creation orderId=91bc corr=7f2a

Read the timestamps. The webhook arrived at 11:03:42.104. The transaction that created the order committed at 11:03:42.702, six hundred milliseconds later. The webhook handler queried for an order that existed only inside another session's uncommitted transaction, and under READ COMMITTED it was correctly invisible.

Then the line that turned a transient race into a permanent loss: the handler returned 200 OK. The provider marked the event as successfully delivered and never retried it. A git log on that file finds the commit:

commit 8c41f2a  "webhook: stop retry storms from unknown orders"
-   return res.status(404).json({ error: 'unknown order' });
+   // Provider retries 404s for 3 days and floods our logs with test-mode events.
+   return res.status(200).json({ ignored: 'unknown order' });

The engineer solved a real annoyance (test-mode webhooks for orders that genuinely do not exist) by telling the provider "handled" for events that were not handled. It worked for eighteen months. It is the single most dangerous line in this scenario, because it converts a retryable race into permanent data loss.

Traces

The trace of order creation shows why the race window existed at all:

POST /orders                                  1,482 ms
└── db.transaction                            1,464 ms
    ├── db.query INSERT orders                    18 ms
    ├── db.query INSERT order_items x3            53 ms
    ├── http POST provider/payment_intents       525 ms   <-- external call INSIDE the transaction
    ├── db.query UPDATE orders SET intent_id       9 ms
    ├── db.query INSERT outbox                     7 ms
    └── commit                                   852 ms

An external HTTP call inside a database transaction. The transaction is held open for the entire 525 ms provider round trip plus a slow commit, and the provider can (and does) fire its webhook the instant it responds. Any external call inside a transaction creates a window in which the outside world knows something your database has not yet committed.

Application

// src/payments/payment-webhook.controller.ts  (the bug)
@Post('webhooks/provider')
async handle(@Body() event: ProviderEvent, @Headers('x-signature') sig: string) {
  this.verifySignature(event, sig);
  const order = await this.orders.findOne({ where: { id: event.metadata.orderId } });
  if (!order) {
    this.logger.warn(`webhook: order ${event.metadata.orderId} not found, acknowledging`);
    return { ignored: 'unknown order' };      // HTTP 200. The event is now lost forever.
  }
  await this.orders.markPaid(order.id, event.data.intentId);
  return { ok: true };
}

The red herring: the first theory, held for about twenty minutes, was clock skew. The webhook's created timestamp from the provider was slightly earlier than the application's own log line for the provider's response, which looked impossible and suggested the provider's clocks were wrong or that the application server's NTP had drifted. It was checked: chronyc tracking on the nodes showed 1.2 ms of offset, and the provider's timestamps are second-granularity, which fully explains the apparent inversion. Fifteen minutes spent, theory discarded at 14:52. It was a reasonable thing to check and the mistake would have been to keep believing it after the evidence came back clean.

Database

The compounding failure. There is a transactional outbox precisely so that a missed webhook does not matter: order state changes write to outbox, a relay polls it, and a reconciliation job re-queries the provider for any order pending more than fifteen minutes. None of it ran.

SELECT count(*), min(created_at), max(created_at), now() - min(created_at) AS oldest_age
FROM outbox WHERE processed_at IS NULL;
 count |         min         |         max         |  oldest_age
-------+---------------------+---------------------+--------------
 41208 | 2026-05-19 08:14:02 | 2026-05-19 14:19:51 | 06:05:49

Six hours of unprocessed outbox rows. The relay uses a PostgreSQL advisory lock for single-writer leader election:

SELECT pid, application_name, now() - state_change AS held_for, l.objid
FROM pg_locks l JOIN pg_stat_activity a USING (pid)
WHERE l.locktype = 'advisory';
  pid  |    application_name    |   held_for   |   objid
-------+------------------------+--------------+-----------
 38820 | outbox-relay@relay-9wz | 06:11:33     | 774451201

A session holding the advisory lock for six hours. The pod relay-9wz was OOMKilled at 08:14 (the leak from section 42.6 again), but its TCP connection was half-closed: the node died in a way that never sent a FIN, and with tcp_keepalives_idle unset PostgreSQL kept the backend alive indefinitely. The lock is held by a session belonging to a process that no longer exists. The replacement relay pod started, tried to take the lock, failed, logged relay: another instance holds the lock, sleeping every ten seconds for six hours, and nobody read it.

Infrastructure

Confirmed: relay-9wz OOMKilled at 08:14:02, exit 137. One dead pod, no alert, six hours of stalled reconciliation.

sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant O as OrdersAPI
  participant DB as PostgreSQL
  participant P as PaymentProvider
  participant W as WebhookAPI
  U->>O: POST /orders
  O->>DB: BEGIN, INSERT orders id=91bc
  O->>P: createPaymentIntent
  P-->>O: intent pi_3Nq8 captured
  P->>W: webhook payment.captured order=91bc
  W->>DB: SELECT orders WHERE id=91bc
  DB-->>W: 0 rows, the INSERT is uncommitted
  W-->>P: 200 OK ignored unknown order
  Note over P: event marked delivered, never retried
  O->>DB: COMMIT
  Note over DB: order exists, status pending_payment, forever

Root cause

The provider's webhook arrived 600 ms before the transaction that created the order committed, so the handler could not see the order. The handler returned 200, telling the provider the event was handled, which permanently discarded the only notification of a successful payment. The outbox relay, which would have caught the discrepancy through reconciliation, had been stalled for six hours because a dead pod's session still held its advisory lock. Two independent safety nets, both with holes, both unmonitored.

Fix

1. Never reject a webhook you cannot yet process. Store it, then process it.

@Post('webhooks/provider')
@HttpCode(200)
async handle(@Body() event: ProviderEvent, @Headers('x-signature') sig: string) {
  this.verifySignature(event, sig);      // verify BEFORE storing: never persist unverified input
  await this.dataSource.query(
    `INSERT INTO payment_events (provider_event_id, type, order_id, payload, received_at)
     VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, now())
     ON CONFLICT (provider_event_id) DO NOTHING`,   // idempotent: the provider retries
    [event.id, event.type, event.metadata.orderId, JSON.stringify(event)],
  );
  return { received: true };   // 200 means "durably stored", not "fully processed"
}

A separate worker processes payment_events, and because the row is durable it can retry for as long as it takes for the order to appear. 200 must mean "I have this", never "I looked and gave up". When a webhook genuinely cannot be stored, return 503 so the provider retries with backoff.

2. Move the external call out of the transaction. Create the order and commit; then call the provider; then update. The order row exists before the provider has any reason to call back, which closes the race at its source.

3. The reconciliation query, run every five minutes and also available for manual use during an incident:

-- Arm A: a captured payment event exists, but the order never advanced.
SELECT o.id AS order_id, o.status, o.created_at, o.total_amount,
       pe.provider_event_id, pe.received_at, pe.payload->'data'->>'intentId' AS intent_id
FROM orders o
JOIN payment_events pe ON pe.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'pending_payment'
  AND pe.type = 'payment.captured'
  AND o.created_at < now() - interval '15 minutes'
ORDER BY o.created_at;

-- Arm B: pending too long with no event at all. These must be checked against the
-- provider's API directly, because the webhook may never have arrived.
SELECT o.id, o.payment_intent_id, o.created_at, now() - o.created_at AS pending_for
FROM orders o
WHERE o.status = 'pending_payment'
  AND o.payment_intent_id IS NOT NULL
  AND o.created_at < now() - interval '30 minutes'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payment_events pe WHERE pe.order_id = o.id)
ORDER BY o.created_at
LIMIT 500;

Arm A catches the race in this incident. Arm B catches a webhook that was never delivered at all, which is a different failure with the same symptom, and the provider's GET /payment_intents/:id is the source of truth for it. Both arms feed a job that either advances the order or raises an operations task. Run reconciliation even when everything is healthy: it should find nothing, and the day it finds something is the day it pays for itself.

4. Fix the stalled relay. Set tcp_keepalives_idle = 60, tcp_keepalives_interval = 10, tcp_keepalives_count = 3 on the database so dead sessions are reaped in ninety seconds instead of never; and replace advisory-lock leader election with a lease row carrying an expiry:

UPDATE relay_lease SET owner = $1, expires_at = now() + interval '30 seconds'
WHERE name = 'outbox' AND (owner = $1 OR expires_at < now())
RETURNING owner;   -- 0 rows means someone else holds a live lease

A lease expires on its own. A lock held by a ghost does not.

Prevention

  • Alert on orders_stuck_pending_gt_15m > 0. This is a business-invariant alert, and business-invariant alerts catch the incidents that latency and error dashboards structurally cannot see.
  • Alert on outbox_oldest_unprocessed_age_seconds > 300. Queue and outbox age is the right signal; depth can look fine while nothing is moving.
  • Alert on payment_webhooks_rejected_total with any reason. It was already being counted correctly.
  • Ban 200-on-unhandled in code review. A 2xx to a webhook is a durability promise.
  • A chaos test: deliver a webhook for an order id that does not exist yet, then create the order, and assert the order reaches paid within the reconciliation interval.
  • A daily finance reconciliation comparing the provider's settlement report against orders totals, with a report that a human reads. Every payments team that has been through this incident has one.

Junior versus senior

Junior Senior
Framing "The webhook failed" "The webhook succeeded. Our handler discarded it."
Timestamps Reads the logs in order Reads the sub-second timestamps and spots a 600 ms ordering inversion
Webhook contract 200 means "I received the HTTP request" 200 means "I have durably stored this and take responsibility for it"
Fix Retries the 47 orders by hand Stores events first, moves the provider call out of the transaction, writes reconciliation for both arms, fixes the ghost lock
Monitoring Adds a log line Adds business-invariant alerts, because no infrastructure metric can see money that went missing

42.10 Two users purchase the last item at the same time

Symptom

20:07, during a flash sale. A support ticket: two customers received order confirmations for the last unit of a limited-edition sneaker. Warehouse has one. Then the query that turns one ticket into an incident:

SELECT id, sku, available FROM products WHERE available < 0;
                  id                  |      sku       | available
--------------------------------------+----------------+-----------
 3f19c2a1-...                         | SNK-LTD-42     |        -2
 a81be440-...                         | SNK-LTD-43     |        -1
 c02f1188-...                         | HOODIE-BLK-M   |        -1

Negative stock. A column that represents a count of physical objects holds a number that cannot exist. When a database contains an impossible value, the cause is almost always a race or a missing constraint, and usually both.

First five minutes (mitigation)

Stop the oversell, then reconcile. Two actions:

-- 1. Take the affected SKUs off sale immediately. Cheaper than being wrong twice more.
UPDATE products SET is_purchasable = false WHERE available <= 0;
  1. The three affected SKUs are handed to operations: contact the customers whose orders cannot be fulfilled, refund or offer an alternative, and hold the rest. Doing this within the first ten minutes is worth more than the root cause, because a customer who hears from you before they notice is a different customer from one who finds out when the parcel does not arrive.

Metrics

Metric Value Note
Checkout RPS on SNK-LTD-42 41/s at 20:04 Flash sale on one SKU
reserve_stock p99 38 ms Fast. No lock contention visible
InsufficientStockError rate 380/min Working normally for the majority
Oversells 4 across 3 SKUs 0.02% of reservations
Database CPU 48% Healthy

Nothing looks broken. The bug affects a handful of requests out of tens of thousands, only at high concurrency on a single row. This is the defining property of a race condition: it is invisible in aggregate metrics and it scales with concurrency, so it appears exactly when it hurts most.

Logs

Two orders, interleaved by microsecond:

20:04:11.402118 [orders-api-2xnpq] INFO reserveStock sku=SNK-LTD-42 qty=1 read available=1 corr=a1
20:04:11.402684 [orders-api-9wzlm] INFO reserveStock sku=SNK-LTD-42 qty=1 read available=1 corr=b7
20:04:11.409901 [orders-api-2xnpq] INFO reserveStock committed available=0 corr=a1
20:04:11.411330 [orders-api-9wzlm] INFO reserveStock committed available=0 corr=b7

Both read available = 1. Both wrote available = 0. Two units sold, one decrement recorded. This is a textbook lost update, and the log line read available=1 twice is the entire proof.

Traces

POST /checkout (corr=a1)                    62 ms      POST /checkout (corr=b7)          64 ms
├── db.query products.findOne     4 ms                 ├── db.query products.findOne     4 ms
├── pricing.calculate             9 ms                 ├── pricing.calculate            11 ms
├── db.query products.save        6 ms                 ├── db.query products.save        7 ms
└── db.query orders.insert       21 ms                 └── db.query orders.insert       22 ms

Note what is absent: no pessimistic_write lock, no wait time, no serialization. The two transactions never contended for anything, because nothing asked them to.

Application

// src/inventory/stock.service.ts  (the bug)
async reserveStock(sku: string, qty: number): Promise<void> {
  const product = await this.repo.findOne({ where: { sku } });        // READ
  if (!product || product.available < qty) {                          // CHECK
    throw new InsufficientStockError(sku);
  }
  product.available -= qty;                                           // ACT (in JavaScript)
  await this.repo.save(product);                                      // WRITE
}

Read, check, act, in three separate steps with the decision made in application memory. Under PostgreSQL's default READ COMMITTED isolation, two concurrent transactions both see available = 1 (neither has committed a change the other can see), both pass the check, both compute 1 - 1 = 0, and both write 0. The second write silently overwrites the first. No error, no lock, no warning. TypeORM's save() issues UPDATE products SET available = 0 WHERE id = $1: the new value is a constant computed in Node, and the UPDATE has no idea what the row contained when it was read.

The red herring occupied 25 minutes. The product page reads stock from a read replica, and replica lag was 340 ms during the sale. The theory: "the checkout read stale stock from a replica". It is plausible, it explains oversells, and it is wrong. It was killed with evidence rather than argument:

// Both transactions were logged with their connection target
logger.log({ sku, available: product.available, host: this.dataSource.options.host }, 'reserveStock read');
// -> host: orders-primary.internal   for BOTH corr=a1 and corr=b7

Both reads went to the primary. DataSource for the write path has no replication config; only the catalog DataSource uses replicas. And the decisive argument: a stale read would have shown available as some older, larger number, while both logs show exactly 1, which is the correct current value. Replica lag would have produced a different wrong answer than the one observed. Theory discarded at 20:41.

Reproducing it

A race you cannot reproduce is a race you cannot prove fixed. Force the interleaving with two real transactions and a barrier:

// test/inventory/reserve-stock.race.spec.ts
describe('reserveStock concurrency', () => {
  it('never sells more than the available quantity', async () => {
    await dataSource.query(`UPDATE products SET available = 1 WHERE sku = 'SNK-LTD-42'`);

    // 20 parallel attempts on a single unit of stock
    const attempts = Array.from({ length: 20 }, () =>
      stockService.reserveStock('SNK-LTD-42', 1)
        .then(() => 'ok' as const)
        .catch((e) => (e instanceof InsufficientStockError ? 'rejected' as const : Promise.reject(e))),
    );
    const results = await Promise.all(attempts);

    expect(results.filter((r) => r === 'ok')).toHaveLength(1);        // exactly one winner
    const [row] = await dataSource.query(
      `SELECT available FROM products WHERE sku = 'SNK-LTD-42'`);
    expect(Number(row.available)).toBe(0);                            // never negative
  });
});

Against the buggy code this fails immediately and dramatically: Expected length: 1, Received length: 14, with available = -13. Twenty parallel requests through a real pool against a real PostgreSQL reproduce it every time. Promise.all over a real connection pool is the cheapest concurrency test you will ever write, and it belongs in the suite for every contended write in the system.

Database

The fix is to make the check and the act a single atomic statement, so the database evaluates the condition against the row it is about to modify, under the row lock it takes to modify it:

UPDATE products
   SET available = available - $2,          -- relative, not absolute
       updated_at = now()
 WHERE sku = $1
   AND available >= $2                      -- the check, evaluated inside the write
RETURNING available;

Two properties make this correct. available - $2 is computed by PostgreSQL from the row's current value, so nothing read earlier can be stale. And under READ COMMITTED, when two transactions target the same row, the second blocks on the first's row lock, then re-evaluates its WHERE clause against the updated row once the first commits. The second sees available = 0, 0 >= 1 is false, the row does not match, and the statement affects zero rows. Zero rows is your out-of-stock signal.

sequenceDiagram
  participant A as RequestA
  participant B as RequestB
  participant PG as PostgreSQL
  Note over A,PG: Before, read-check-act
  A->>PG: SELECT available -> 1
  B->>PG: SELECT available -> 1
  A->>PG: UPDATE SET available = 0
  B->>PG: UPDATE SET available = 0
  Note over PG: two sold, one decremented, available = -1 after the next sale
  Note over A,PG: After, atomic conditional UPDATE
  A->>PG: UPDATE ... SET available = available - 1 WHERE available >= 1
  PG-->>A: 1 row, available = 0
  B->>PG: UPDATE ... SET available = available - 1 WHERE available >= 1
  Note over PG: B waits on A's row lock, then re-evaluates WHERE
  PG-->>B: 0 rows, out of stock

Infrastructure

Ruled out quickly and deliberately. Pod count, node health, clock synchronization (chronyc tracking showed 0.9 ms offset), and load balancer behaviour were all normal, and none of them could produce a negative integer in a database column anyway. The only infrastructure fact that mattered is the one that made the bug visible: 20 pods serving 41 checkouts per second on one SKU means two requests land inside the same 10 ms window many times per minute. Infrastructure did not cause this race; it supplied the concurrency that exposed it. The same code had been correct-looking for three years at 2 requests per second on any given SKU.

Root cause

reserveStock read the row, checked availability in application memory, decremented in JavaScript, and wrote an absolute value back. Under READ COMMITTED two concurrent transactions both observed available = 1, both passed the check, and both wrote available = 0, so the second write silently discarded the first. Nothing in the database prevented the resulting value from going negative, because there was no CHECK constraint. A lost update plus a missing invariant.

Fix

// src/inventory/stock.service.ts  (fixed)
async reserveStock(sku: string, qty: number): Promise<number> {
  const result = await this.repo
    .createQueryBuilder()
    .update(Product)
    .set({ available: () => 'available - :qty', updatedAt: () => 'now()' })
    .where('sku = :sku AND available >= :qty', { sku, qty })
    .returning('available')
    .execute();

  if (result.affected === 0) {
    throw new InsufficientStockError(sku);   // no row matched: sold out, atomically determined
  }
  return Number(result.raw[0].available);
}

The Sequelize equivalent, since the same bug is written the same way in both ORMs:

const [affected] = await Product.update(
  { available: sequelize.literal(`available - ${Number(qty)}`) },   // qty is validated as an integer
  { where: { sku, available: { [Op.gte]: qty } }, transaction: t },
);
if (affected === 0) throw new InsufficientStockError(sku);

The backstop constraint. The application fix is correct today; the constraint is correct forever, including against the next developer, the next ORM upgrade, a manual psql session, and a data migration:

-- Repair the impossible rows first: a constraint cannot be validated over invalid data.
UPDATE products SET available = 0 WHERE available < 0;   -- after operations reconciles physically

-- Add as NOT VALID: takes only a brief lock, does not scan the table, enforces on all new writes.
ALTER TABLE products
  ADD CONSTRAINT chk_available_non_negative CHECK (available >= 0) NOT VALID;

-- Then validate existing rows with a weaker lock that does not block reads or writes.
ALTER TABLE products VALIDATE CONSTRAINT chk_available_non_negative;

The two-step NOT VALID then VALIDATE pattern is how you add a check constraint to a large hot table without an outage (see Part 31 — Database Migrations). With the constraint in place, a future read-check-act bug fails loudly with 23514 check_violation and a rolled-back transaction instead of quietly selling stock that does not exist. A wrong number in a database is worse than a failed request, and a constraint is what enforces that preference.

Alternatives, and when each is right:

Approach How Wins when Costs
Atomic conditional UPDATE SET x = x - n WHERE x >= n The decision is one row and one arithmetic condition. Default choice Cannot express complex multi-row logic
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE Lock the row, then read-check-act Several rows or complex logic must be decided together Serializes all buyers of a hot SKU; throughput bounded by lock hold time
Optimistic locking (@VersionColumn) WHERE version = $n, retry on 0 rows Low contention, long think-time between read and write Retry storms under high contention
SERIALIZABLE isolation Let PostgreSQL detect the anomaly Complex invariants across many tables Serialization failures must be retried by the caller; throughput cost
Redis DECRBY reservation Decrement a counter in Redis, settle in PostgreSQL later Extreme contention: 30,000 checkouts/s on one SKU Two sources of truth; needs reconciliation and expiry of unclaimed reservations

For a flash sale, the honest answer is often the atomic UPDATE plus a Redis admission gate in front, so the database only ever sees as many checkout attempts as there is stock, plus a margin.

Prevention

  • Keep the parallel test permanently. It runs in 400 ms, it fails loudly on regression, and it documents the invariant better than a comment can.
  • A nightly invariant check across the schema, alerting on any row that violates a business rule: SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE available < 0, plus the equivalents for balances, quantities and totals. Invariant checks find the bugs that no error rate can.
  • A code-review rule: no read-modify-write on a contended row. If a value is decremented, incremented or conditionally changed, it happens in one statement or under an explicit lock.
  • Constraints for every business invariant that can be expressed as one: CHECK (available >= 0), CHECK (total_amount >= 0), unique indexes on natural keys, EXCLUDE constraints for overlapping bookings. The database is the last honest layer.
  • Load test the contended path specifically. A general load test spreads requests over 5,000 SKUs and will never reproduce this. Point 200 virtual users at one SKU with stock 50 and assert exactly 50 succeed.

Junior versus senior

Junior Senior
Reaction to negative stock Fixes the rows with an UPDATE Fixes the rows, then asks what allowed an impossible value to exist
Explanation "Race condition, hard to reproduce" Writes a 15-line parallel test that reproduces it every run
Fix Adds SELECT ... FOR UPDATE everywhere Uses the atomic conditional UPDATE, keeps FOR UPDATE for genuinely multi-row decisions
Isolation "We should use SERIALIZABLE" Knows READ COMMITTED re-evaluates the WHERE clause after a blocking write, which is exactly the needed semantics here
Backstop None CHECK (available >= 0) added NOT VALID then validated, plus a nightly invariant alert

42.11 Patterns across incidents

Ten incidents, and the same shapes keep recurring. This table is the compressed version: match the symptom class, check the three metrics, then work the usual suspects in order.

Symptom class First three metrics Usual suspects
Latency up, errors flat p50 vs p99 split; pool waitingCount; database CPU and blks_read Plan flip after stale statistics; pool saturation; a slow downstream with a generous timeout; GC pauses; lock waits
Latency up, 5xx up Error rate by route and status; downstream error rate; pod restarts Failing dependency; timeouts firing; pods being killed mid-request; connection exhaustion
Everything fails at the same second Shared-resource metrics: connections used, Redis memory, DNS failures max_connections reached; Redis eviction or failover; DNS or certificate expiry; a config rollout
Database CPU high pg_stat_statements top by total time; blks_read rate; buffer cache hit ratio Missing index (especially on a foreign key); plan flip; a batch job; an N+1 loop; autovacuum as a consequence
Memory growing nodejs_heap_size_used_bytes slope; external_memory; active_handles Unbounded cache on a singleton; listeners added per request; retained request objects; native buffers if the heap is flat
Pods restarting Restart count; exit code from describe; startup duration OOMKilled (heap limit above container limit); liveness probe budget under startup time; liveness doing I/O
Queue or consumer lag growing Lag; commit rate; rebalance rate Processing exceeding max.poll.interval.ms; slow downstream; a poison message; consumers fewer than partitions; a dead consumer
Stale or wrong data Cache hit ratio by prefix; invalidation counters; replication lag Two cache key formats; missed invalidation; no TTL; reading a replica when the write must be visible
Duplicates Sends vs events produced; consumer restarts; provider message ids At-least-once redelivery with a non-idempotent side effect; retries without an idempotency key; auto-commit windows
Missing or stuck records Business-invariant counts; outbox oldest age; webhook rejection counters A race between an external callback and a commit; a swallowed error; a stalled relay; a 2xx returned for unhandled work
Impossible values in the database Invariant query counts; contention on the hot row Read-check-act race; missing CHECK constraint; a manual UPDATE; a migration that skipped validation

Five meta-patterns run underneath all of it.

Most incidents are caused by a change, but the change is often not the obvious one and often not in your service. A CPU limit on the profile service caused a Kafka rebalance loop. A backfill migration caused an API latency spike. Correlate with change first, and cast a wide net.

The symptom is rarely the cause. Autovacuum burning CPU was the consequence of a missing index. Duplicate notifications were the consequence of an OOM. Pool exhaustion was the consequence of a plan flip. Always ask "what would have to be true upstream of this?"

Saturation shows up as latency long before it shows up as errors. A pool with a 30-second acquire timeout will make every request slow and none of them fail. Alert on saturation signals (pool waiting, event loop lag, replica lag, connection count, consumer lag, heap slope), not only on error rates.

Every "impossible" state is a race or a missing constraint. Negative stock, an order paid but pending, a notification sent five times: none of these are mysteries once you look for the window between two operations that are not atomic.

The third incident of a kind is a design problem, not an ops problem. An alert acknowledged three nights running is a signal that the team has normalized a defect. Escalate it into a design change rather than a better runbook.

42.12 Building a debugging-friendly system

Every incident above was solved faster or slower depending on what existed before it started. These are the investments, roughly in order of value per hour spent.

Correlation ids everywhere. One id, generated at the edge, propagated through every log line, every trace, every queue message and every downstream HTTP header. Without it, section 42.9's six-hundred-millisecond ordering inversion is invisible.

// src/common/correlation/correlation.middleware.ts
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';
export const als = new AsyncLocalStorage<{ correlationId: string }>();

@Injectable()
export class CorrelationMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {
  use(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction): void {
    const correlationId = (req.headers['x-correlation-id'] as string) ?? randomUUID();
    res.setHeader('x-correlation-id', correlationId);
    als.run({ correlationId }, () => next());   // available anywhere downstream, no plumbing
  }
}

Propagate it onto every outbound call and every message header, and make the id part of the event payload written to the outbox so an asynchronous chain remains traceable hours later.

Structured logs, with fields you can query. logger.log({ orderId, sku, available, host }, 'reserveStock read') is queryable; logger.log(\reserving ${sku}`)is not. Log atinfo` the facts a future investigator needs (ids, decisions, counts, which host, which key), never request bodies or personal data. Sample high-volume paths rather than turning them off, so a rare event is still represented.

application_name on every database connection, per pod. One line of config, and it converts "some service is holding 300 connections" into "these three pods of orders-api are". Section 42.8 was diagnosed in minutes because of it.

extra: { application_name: `${process.env.SERVICE_NAME}@${process.env.HOSTNAME}` }

Slow query logging on by default. log_min_duration_statement = 200ms and auto_explain with auto_explain.log_min_duration = 500, log_analyze = on, log_buffers = on. The cost is a small amount of logging; the benefit is that when a plan flips at 03:00 you have the plan, with real parameters, instead of a theory. Also log_lock_waits = on and log_temp_files = 0.

Dashboards built before the incident. Four per service, and they must exist while things are calm because nobody builds a good dashboard at 02:00: RED (rate, errors, duration by route), saturation (pod CPU and throttling, event loop lag, heap, pool waiting, connections used versus max_connections), dependencies (latency and error rate per downstream, per database, per cache, per topic), and business invariants (orders pending over 15 minutes, outbox oldest age, negative stock count, notifications sent versus events produced). The fourth is the one most teams do not have, and it is the one that catches money going missing.

Runbooks linked from alerts. Every alert carries a runbook_url annotation pointing at a page that says what the alert means, what to check first, what the safe mitigations are, and who owns it.

- alert: PgConnectionsHigh
  expr: sum(pg_stat_activity_count{state!="idle"}) / on() pg_settings_max_connections > 0.7
  for: 5m
  labels: { severity: page }
  annotations:
    summary: "PostgreSQL connections above 70 percent of max_connections"
    runbook_url: "https://wiki.internal/runbooks/pg-connections-high"

Feature kill switches. Every non-essential feature behind a flag that can be turned off in seconds without a deploy: recommendations, the retry button, a new read path, a chatty analytics beacon. In section 42.9 the flag that disabled the retry button stopped double charges four minutes into the incident. A kill switch is a mitigation you can use before you understand anything, which is exactly when you need one.

A rollback you have actually practised. Not "we can roll back", but "we rolled back last Thursday in a game day and it took 3 minutes 40 seconds". Practise reveals the parts that do not roll back: a migration that dropped a column, a cache format the old version cannot read, a Kafka message schema the old consumer rejects, a feature flag whose default changed. Expand-contract migrations (Part 31) and backward-compatible schemas (Part 32) are what make rollback real rather than aspirational.

Two smaller items that repay themselves quickly: timeouts and limits everywhere (statement_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, lock_timeout, HTTP connect/headers/body timeouts, connectionTimeoutMillis, body size limits), because every incident above got worse in proportion to how long something was allowed to take; and an admin diagnostics endpoint on an internal port, guarded, offering a CPU profile and a heap snapshot on demand, so the tooling in sections 42.6 and 24.12 is available at 02:00 instead of requiring a deploy.

Senior Checklist — Part 42

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I mitigate before I diagnose, and I announce every mitigation with a timestamp
  • I keep a written timeline during an incident and communicate on a fixed schedule
  • I form hypotheses from metrics and name the observation that would kill each one
  • I read p50 versus p99 to tell "everything is slower" from "some requests are slower"
  • I can read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and recognise a plan flip from stale statistics
  • I know that a foreign key never creates an index on the referencing column, and I can find every unindexed FK
  • I treat autovacuum activity as a possible consequence and check its start time against the symptom's
  • I diagnose cache staleness by comparing the read key with the invalidation key, and I never cache without a TTL
  • I know that zero commit rate with nonzero consumption means a rebalance loop, not a capacity problem
  • I make every consumer side effect idempotent with a key derived from the event
  • I can take and compare two heap snapshots and read a retainer path to the leaking field
  • I know exit code 137, use kubectl logs --previous, and set --max-old-space-size below the container limit
  • I use a startupProbe for slow boots, keep liveness free of I/O, and put dependency checks in readiness
  • I read the pg_stat_activity state breakdown, kill idle in transaction sessions, and set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
  • I never return 2xx to a webhook I did not durably store, and I keep a reconciliation query for both arms
  • I replace read-check-act with an atomic conditional UPDATE and back it with a CHECK constraint
  • I can reproduce a race with a parallel integration test before claiming it is fixed
  • My services carry correlation ids, structured logs, application_name, slow query logging, dashboards, runbook links and kill switches

Part 42 — Key Takeaways

  • Mitigate first, diagnose second; a rollback that does not help is four minutes well spent because it kills the most attractive theory.
  • Walk the ladder: symptom, metrics, logs, traces, application, database, infrastructure. Never start in the middle because of a hunch.
  • p50 moving with p99 means a shared resource; p99 alone means a subset (locks, GC, one tenant, one key).
  • A deploy near the start time is a suspect, not a verdict; coincidences are common in teams that deploy often.
  • Every scenario had a red herring that cost real minutes; kill theories with evidence, and write down that you did.
  • Plan flips come from stale statistics after bulk data changes; ANALYZE after every backfill and make autoanalyze aggressive on large tables.
  • PostgreSQL never indexes a foreign key's referencing column; every parent delete then becomes a full scan of the child table.
  • Cache correctness is a key-naming problem: one module owns key construction, invalidation is derived from it, and every entry has a TTL.
  • Growing lag with idle consumers and a zero commit rate is a rebalance loop; reduce work per poll, batch the downstream call, commit incrementally.
  • Brokers are at-least-once, so every side effect needs an idempotency key and a uniqueness constraint; pods will always crash mid-batch.
  • Leaks are found by comparing two heap snapshots and reading the retainer path, not by upgrading dependencies and hoping.
  • Set --max-old-space-size below the container limit; above it guarantees the kernel kills the process before V8 collects.
  • Liveness probes must never do I/O, slow startups need a startupProbe, and exit code 137 with --previous logs tells you which death you had.
  • Connections leak on error paths: use managed transactions, always release() in finally, size pools with Little's law, and let the database enforce idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
  • A 2xx to a webhook is a durability promise; store the event first, process it asynchronously, and reconcile on a schedule for both the "event without order" and "order without event" arms.
  • Read-check-act on a contended row is a lost update; use one atomic conditional UPDATE, prove it with a parallel test, and add the CHECK constraint as the backstop.
  • Alert on saturation and business invariants, not only on errors; the incidents that cost money are the ones no latency dashboard can see.
  • Build the debugging-friendly system before you need it: correlation ids, structured logs, application_name, slow query logs, four dashboards, runbook links, kill switches, and a rollback you have actually practised.

Part 43 — The Senior Engineering Mindset

At 09:40 on a Tuesday, two engineers read the same design document. It proposes a new notifications service that reads from a Kafka topic and writes to PostgreSQL.

The first engineer reads it and thinks: the code looks fine, the module structure is clean, I would rename one DTO. The second engineer reads the same page and thinks: what happens when the consumer crashes between the database write and the offset commit? Who else writes to this table? Is user_id indexed for the query on line 40? If Kafka is down for twenty minutes, does the checkout flow still work, or does it block? Who gets paged at 03:00 when this backs up?

Both engineers can write TypeScript. The difference is not knowledge of syntax. It is the set of questions that fire automatically when they look at a system.

This part is that question set. It is the closest thing to a transferable senior skill that exists: not a list of technologies, but a list of interrogations you run on every design, every pull request and every incident, until they become reflex. I have used the same questions on a two-person startup and on a platform doing 40,000 requests per second. The systems changed. The questions did not.

43.1 What "senior" actually means

Companies write career ladders full of words like "impact" and "scope". They are not wrong, but they are hard to act on. Here is a definition you can use tomorrow morning.

A senior engineer is someone the organisation can hand an ambiguous, important problem to, and then stop worrying about it.

Unpack that sentence and you get four things: ownership (you carry it to the end), judgment (you make good calls without being told what to do), communication (other people know what is happening and why), and multiplication (the people around you get better, so the organisation is not dependent on you personally).

flowchart TB
    P["Ambiguous problem"] --> O["Ownership: I carry it to production and after"]
    P --> J["Judgment: I choose well under incomplete information"]
    P --> C["Communication: others can act on what I know"]
    P --> M["Multiplication: the team can now do this without me"]
    O --> R["The organisation stops worrying"]
    J --> R
    C --> R
    M --> R

Concept

Seniority is measured in removed uncertainty, not in lines of code, not in years, and not in the number of frameworks on your CV. Every organisation has a queue of things nobody is sure how to do. A senior engineer takes items off that queue and returns them as things that are now certain: shipped, monitored, documented, and understood by more than one person.

Mental model

Imagine a hospital. A medical student can recite drug interactions. A junior doctor can run a standard treatment for a standard case. The consultant is the person you page when the case is not standard: when the symptoms conflict, when the textbook answer would hurt the patient, when someone has to decide with incomplete information and own the outcome. The consultant does not know more facts than the student who just crammed for exams. They have seen more failures, they know which signals matter, and they will still be responsible in the morning.

Backend engineering is the same. The senior is not the person who has memorised the most PostgreSQL configuration parameters. They are the person you want in the room when the payment flow is double-charging customers and nobody knows why.

43.1.1 Ownership

Ownership means the problem is yours until it is actually solved, not until your code is merged.

A concrete story. A mid-level engineer on my team shipped a feature that let customers export their order history as CSV. Code was clean, tests passed, PR merged, ticket closed. Three weeks later, support raised a ticket: exports were timing out for large customers. The engineer's reaction was, honestly, reasonable-sounding: "that's an infra problem, the gateway times out at 30 seconds."

The senior version of that same engineer would have known at design time that the export was unbounded: a customer with 400,000 orders will always break a synchronous endpoint, no matter how fast the query. They would have shipped it as a background job writing to S3 with a signed URL emailed to the customer, or at minimum they would have measured the p99 order count per customer before choosing. And after shipping, they would have checked the dashboard for that endpoint in week one rather than waiting for support to find it.

Ownership in practice:

  • You know how your feature behaves in production, because you looked, not because nobody complained.
  • You added the dashboard and the alert before you needed them.
  • When it breaks, you do not wait to be asked. You pick it up.
  • When it is someone else's component but your customer's problem, you still drive it to a resolution and hand it over cleanly.
  • You wrote down what future-you will need at 03:00.

Ownership is not heroism, and it is not working weekends. It is refusing to let a problem sit in the gap between two teams.

43.1.2 Judgment

Judgment is choosing well when the information is incomplete and the options all have costs. It is the hardest thing to teach and the most valuable thing you have.

Judgment shows up as restraint far more often than as cleverness. The junior instinct on hearing "we need to handle more traffic" is to reach for Kafka, or sharding, or a service split. The senior instinct is to ask what the traffic actually is, measure where the time goes, and discover that 80 percent of the load is one unindexed query on a 12-million-row orders table, fixable in an afternoon with a composite index and a LIMIT.

I once watched a team spend five months migrating to microservices because "the monolith does not scale". Their monolith was serving 90 requests per second on two 2-vCPU containers with a database at 4 percent CPU. It scaled fine. What did not scale was their deployment process, which took 50 minutes and required a manual database migration step. The right project was a two-week CI/CD fix. They spent five months and ended up with the same slow deploys spread across nine repositories.

Judgment is: what problem are we actually solving, and what is the cheapest thing that solves it?

43.1.3 Communication

If you understand the system perfectly and nobody else can act on that understanding, your value is capped at what you can personally type.

Communication for engineers is mostly writing, and mostly unglamorous: a design doc that a product manager can read, an ADR that explains why you rejected the obvious option, a Slack update during an incident that says what you know and what you do not, a commit message that explains why, a runbook with the exact command to run.

The test I use: could a competent engineer who joins in eighteen months, with no access to me, make a correct decision about this system from what I wrote down? If not, I have not finished.

43.1.4 Making the people around you better

The organisational value of a senior engineer is not their own throughput. A strong mid-level engineer might produce 1.3x the output of an average one. A senior who lifts eight people by 20 percent has produced 1.6 engineers of value without writing a line, and it compounds because those people teach the next cohort.

This is why code review, pairing, design review and writing are not "overhead" at senior level. They are the job. A review comment that teaches somebody why SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a long transaction will melt under load prevents a class of future incidents, not one.

43.1.5 Fifteen years, or one year fifteen times

The uncomfortable truth: time does not automatically produce seniority. I have interviewed engineers with fifteen years who had, functionally, one year of experience repeated fifteen times. They had built the same CRUD API on the same stack in the same way, and had never operated it under load, never had a bad night, never had to migrate a hot table, never had to argue for a decision in front of people who disagreed.

Experience compounds only when it includes feedback. Feedback comes from:

  • Running what you build in production, and watching the graphs.
  • Being on call for your own systems.
  • Being wrong publicly and writing down why.
  • Working on systems bigger than you can hold in your head, so you must reason rather than memorise.
  • Reading other people's code and postmortems, which is borrowed feedback at low cost.

The engineer who has shipped four systems and operated all four for a year each will be more senior than the one who has shipped twenty and operated none.

Common mistakes

  • Equating seniority with technology breadth. Knowing Kafka, Kubernetes, gRPC, Elasticsearch and Terraform by name is not judgment. It is vocabulary.
  • Equating seniority with speed. Shipping fast while leaving landmines is a debt transfer to your future team.
  • Refusing the unglamorous work. Someone has to fix the flaky test suite, write the runbook and upgrade Node. Seniors do it because the leverage is real.
  • Hoarding context. If the system only works because you are around, you are a single point of failure, not a senior engineer.

Practical exercise

Take the last three tickets you closed. For each, write down: (1) how you would know today if it is broken in production, (2) what happens at 10x the current volume, (3) who else could operate it if you were on holiday. If you cannot answer all three for all of them, you have found this quarter's growth plan.

43.2 Architecture questions

These are the five questions I ask in every design review. They take four minutes and they have saved more engineering-years than any framework I have used.

43.2.1 Is this the simplest thing that solves the problem?

Why the question matters

Every piece of architecture you add is a permanent tax: it must be deployed, monitored, secured, upgraded, understood by new hires, and debugged at 03:00 by somebody who did not build it. Complexity that is not paid for by a real requirement is pure loss, and it is almost impossible to remove later because removal has no visible business value.

How to actually answer it

Write down the requirement in one sentence with a number in it. Then design the crudest thing that satisfies it. Then ask what specifically breaks about the crude thing. Only add machinery in response to a break you can name.

A useful forcing function: describe the design to yourself as a list of moving parts, and put a cost next to each one. "Kafka" is not a line item, it is: a cluster to run or a managed bill, topic and partition decisions, consumer group monitoring, a schema registry or a compatibility convention, a dead-letter strategy, a rebalance failure mode, and one more thing that can be down when you are paged.

Worked example

Requirement: "When an order is placed, send a confirmation email. We do about 3,000 orders per day, peaking at 15 per minute."

The proposed design was: order service publishes OrderPlaced to Kafka, a notification service consumes it, writes to a notifications table, publishes to a second topic for the email sender, which calls SendGrid.

The simplest thing that solves it: the order service writes a row into an outbox table inside the same transaction as the order, and a BullMQ worker backed by Redis picks it up and calls SendGrid with retries. One extra table, one worker process, one Redis instance you already run for caching. It handles 15 per minute without noticing, it survives SendGrid being down, and it can be understood by a new hire in fifteen minutes.

At 3,000 orders per day, Kafka buys you nothing you need. At 3 million per day, with eleven consumer teams wanting the same event, Kafka buys you a lot. Ask which world you are in today, and whether the migration cost from simple to complex is high. If moving from a queue to Kafka later is a two-week project, and you are not sure you will need it, do not pay for it now.

The mistake people make

Designing for the company you hope to be in three years instead of the one you are in this quarter, and calling it "future proofing". The usual outcome is that the future does not arrive in the predicted shape, and you have paid the operational cost the whole time. The senior version of future proofing is keeping the option open cheaply: a clean module boundary, an interface, an event you already emit. Not a running cluster.

43.2.2 What happens at 10x traffic? At 100x?

Why the question matters

Systems do not degrade smoothly. They work, work, work, then hit a wall: the connection pool saturates, the table stops fitting in the buffer cache, the nightly job stops finishing before the next one starts. The wall is usually visible in advance if anyone does the arithmetic.

How to actually answer it

Do the arithmetic out loud. Take the current numbers, multiply by 10, and walk each resource:

  • Requests per second, and therefore concurrent requests in flight.
  • Database connections needed: pods times pool size. Compare against max_connections.
  • Rows written per day, and the table size in a year.
  • Redis memory and key count.
  • Queue arrival rate versus consumer drain rate.
  • Bytes per second out of the service and across the network.

Then say which resource hits its limit first, and at what multiple. You do not need precision. You need to know whether the wall is at 3x or 300x, because that tells you whether this is a design problem or a next-year problem. Part 41 — Capacity Estimation and Back-of-the-Envelope Math is the full method.

Worked example

A product search endpoint does 200 requests per second, each running one PostgreSQL query at 8 ms, on 6 pods with a pool of 10.

At 10x, 2,000 RPS: by Little's law we need roughly 2000 * 0.008 = 16 concurrent database queries on average, which is fine, but the peak-second burst and the p99 of 40 ms push it to 80 in flight. Six pods times ten connections is 60. We start queueing inside the pool, latency climbs non-linearly, and the p99 goes from 40 ms to 900 ms. The fix is not "more pods" (that multiplies connections towards max_connections); it is a cache in front of the query, since search results for the top 200 terms cover 70 percent of traffic.

At 100x, 20,000 RPS: PostgreSQL is the wrong tool for this access pattern regardless of pooling. This is where a search engine, a read replica pool, or a materialised result cache with a strict TTL earns its complexity. Now Elasticsearch is not resume-driven development, it is arithmetic.

The mistake people make

Answering "we'll scale horizontally" as if it were a plan. Horizontal scaling of stateless application pods is the easy half. The hard half is everything shared: the database, the cache, the queue, the third-party API with a 100 RPS rate limit, the single-writer table with a hot row. Name the shared resource that saturates first, or you have not answered the question.

43.2.3 What is the blast radius when it fails?

Why the question matters

Everything fails. The design decision is not whether it fails, but how much of the product goes down with it. Two designs with identical throughput can differ by a factor of fifty in how bad the worst day is.

How to actually answer it

For each dependency, ask: if this is completely unavailable for thirty minutes, what stops working? Then classify the answer:

Blast radius Meaning Example
Cosmetic A non-critical feature degrades, users may not notice Recommendation panel is empty
Contained One feature is unavailable, the rest of the product works Cannot download invoices
Revenue Customers cannot complete the core transaction Checkout returns 500
Correctness The system keeps working but produces wrong data Double-charged payments, lost orders
Existential Data loss, or a breach Backups unusable, customer data exposed

Correctness failures are worse than availability failures, and juniors systematically underrate them. An outage is embarrassing for an hour. Silently wrong money movement is a six-month cleanup, a finance reconciliation project and a trust problem.

Worked example

We put a Redis cache in front of the product catalogue. Design A calls Redis, and on a Redis error the request fails with 500. Design B calls Redis, and on error falls through to PostgreSQL with a per-request timeout of 100 ms and a circuit breaker.

Design A converts a cache outage into a full catalogue outage: blast radius revenue. Design B converts it into elevated database load and slower pages: blast radius cosmetic-to-contained, provided PostgreSQL can survive the cold-cache load, which is exactly the arithmetic from 43.2.2. If the database cannot take 100 percent of catalogue traffic, then Design B is a lie and you need either a bigger database, a stale-while-revalidate local cache, or a load-shedding rule that serves a reduced catalogue.

Notice what the question forced: it turned "add a cache" into three concrete decisions.

The mistake people make

Treating a cache, a search index or a message broker as infallible infrastructure because it has been up for a year. Anything that can be unreachable will be unreachable, usually during your busiest hour, usually because of a network change nobody told you about.

43.2.4 What are we optimising for?

Why the question matters

Time to market, cost, reliability and flexibility trade against each other. Teams argue for weeks because two people are optimising for different things and neither has said so. Naming the objective ends most architecture arguments in ten minutes.

How to actually answer it

Force a ranking, not a wish list. Everybody wants all four. Ask the product owner or the business stakeholder to order them for this project, and write the order into the design doc.

Optimising for You accept You choose Typical context
Time to market Tech debt, manual ops, lower ceiling Modular monolith, managed services, boring stack Pre-product-market-fit, a bet you may kill
Cost More engineering effort per feature, more ops Self-hosted, tighter instance sizing, aggressive caching Thin margins, high volume, mature product
Reliability Slower delivery, more redundancy spend Replication, multi-AZ, circuit breakers, canaries Payments, healthcare, anything regulated
Flexibility Upfront design cost, some indirection Clear boundaries, events, versioned contracts Platform used by many teams, unstable requirements

Worked example

A team was designing a promotions engine. Two proposals: a rules DSL with a configuration UI, six weeks; or hardcoded promotion types with a new deployment per type, one week.

The unspoken disagreement was the objective. The engineer proposing the DSL was optimising for flexibility, because marketing "will want to change rules constantly". The product manager was optimising for time to market, because the whole promotions bet might be cancelled in a quarter. When we said this out loud, the answer was obvious in five minutes: build three hardcoded promotion types now behind an interface, and if marketing requests a fourth type twice in one quarter, build the DSL then. They requested one more type in six months. The DSL was never built. That is a saved five weeks and a system nobody had to learn.

The mistake people make

Optimising for flexibility by default, because flexibility feels like good engineering. Flexibility has an ongoing cost paid by every reader of the code. Buy it when the variability is real and observed, not imagined.

43.2.5 How do we undo this if we are wrong? One-way and two-way doors

Why the question matters

Decisions are not all equally serious, and treating them as if they were is the single biggest source of slow teams. A choice you can reverse in an afternoon deserves an afternoon of thought. A choice that is effectively permanent deserves a week, a document and other people's eyes.

flowchart TB
    D["Decision to make"] --> Q{"Can we reverse it in under a week without data loss?"}
    Q -->|"Yes: two-way door"| F["Decide fast, one owner, note it in the PR"]
    Q -->|"No: one-way door"| S["Slow down: write an ADR, prototype, get reviewers"]
    F --> M["Measure in production, revert if wrong"]
    S --> P["Spike the risky part first"]
    P --> A["ADR with alternatives and consequences"]
    A --> C["Decide, then commit publicly"]

How to actually answer it

Ask three sub-questions: what would we have to do to undo this, how long would it take, and what data would we lose or have to migrate? Then place the decision on the scale.

Two-way doors (reversible, decide fast): the HTTP client library, the folder structure, the logging format, whether a service is one module or two inside the same deployable, the caching TTL, most library choices, the Jest config.

One-way doors (expensive or impossible to reverse): the primary datastore for a large table, the public API contract once external clients depend on it, splitting a monolith into separately deployed services with separate databases, an event schema that other teams have already consumed and stored, a data model that loses information (once you throw away the original event, you cannot reconstruct it), the choice of a cloud provider's proprietary service that has no equivalent elsewhere, and anything to do with customer identifiers.

Worked example

Two decisions from the same project, treated very differently, on purpose.

The first: which UUID version for order identifiers. We chose UUIDv7 for the time-ordering benefit on B-tree inserts. Is this reversible? Not really: identifiers appear in URLs customers bookmark, in exported CSVs, in third-party webhooks and in support tickets. Changing the format later means dual identifiers forever. So this was a one-way door, and it got half a day, a benchmark against bigint and uuidv4, and a written decision.

The second: whether the notification worker uses BullMQ or a plain setInterval poller over an outbox table. Reversible in about two days, since the job payloads are internal and the interface is one method. Two-way door, decided in a fifteen-minute conversation, and revisited nine months later when retry semantics started to matter. Nobody wrote a document. That was the correct amount of process.

The mistake people make

Two symmetrical errors. Juniors walk through one-way doors quickly, because the code change looks small: adding a field to a public API response is three lines and forever. Newly promoted seniors freeze in front of two-way doors, holding three-hour meetings about the folder layout, because they have learned that decisions matter and have not yet learned to grade them.

The senior habit is to say the classification out loud: "this is a two-way door, let's pick one and move on" or "careful, this is a one-way door, I want it written down before we build it."

Interview questions

  1. "Give me an example of a one-way door decision you made, and how you handled it differently from a normal decision." Expected: a concrete choice about data model, public contract or datastore; evidence of prototyping, written alternatives and reviewers. Follow-up: what would reversing it have cost?
  2. "A team wants to introduce Kafka for a feature doing 20 events per second. What do you say?" Expected: not a flat no. Ask what problem it solves, who else consumes, what the retention and replay requirements are, and what the operational owner situation is. Offer the cheaper option and the trigger that would change the answer.
  3. "Your service is at 500 RPS and the business projects 10x in a year. Walk me through what breaks first." Expected: resource-by-resource arithmetic, not "add pods".
  4. "How do you decide how much design process a decision deserves?" Expected: reversibility and blast radius as the two axes.

Practical exercise

Take the architecture of the service you work on. List every external dependency: database, cache, broker, third-party APIs, internal services. For each, write one line: "if this is down for 30 minutes, X stops working, blast radius Y". Then find the two entries where the blast radius is larger than the business would accept, and write a paragraph on the cheapest change that would shrink it. Acceptance criteria: at least one of those changes is small enough to ship in a week, and you can name the metric that would prove it worked.

43.3 Database questions

The database is where seniority becomes visible fastest, because the database is where mistakes become permanent. You can rewrite a bad service in a sprint. You cannot rewrite three years of badly modelled data in a sprint, and you cannot take back a query that has been locking a hot table for six months.

These six questions run on every schema change and every new query.

43.3.1 Does this query scale?

Why the question matters

Almost every "the API got slow" incident I have handled traces back to a query whose cost grows with the size of the table rather than the size of the result. It works perfectly in development with 2,000 rows and dies at 20 million. Nothing in the code changed. The data grew.

How to actually answer it

Ask: as the table grows by 100x, does this query do 100x more work, or the same work? Then prove it with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on production-shaped data.

The signals that a query does not scale:

  • Seq Scan on a large table inside a request path.
  • Rows Removed by Filter far larger than the returned row count: you are reading and discarding.
  • A Sort with external merge Disk in the plan: it did not fit in work_mem.
  • OFFSET with a large number: the database walks and discards every skipped row.
  • Any plan whose cost is a function of total rows rather than matched rows.

Worked example

Order history, page 500, 20 per page:

-- Does not scale: at offset 10000 PostgreSQL reads 10,020 rows to return 20.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, created_at, total_cents, status
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = '7c1f...'
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
OFFSET 10000 LIMIT 20;
Limit  (cost=18240.11..18276.59 rows=20 width=44) (actual time=126.884..126.901 rows=20 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=8123 read=2314
  ->  Index Scan Backward using idx_orders_customer_created on orders
        (cost=0.56..1824533.20 rows=1000210 width=44)
        (actual time=0.061..118.402 rows=10020 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (customer_id = '7c1f...'::uuid)
Planning Time: 0.183 ms
Execution Time: 126.939 ms

Ten thousand rows read to return twenty, and it gets worse on every page. The keyset version reads twenty:

-- Scales: the index seeks straight to the cursor position, page cost is constant.
SELECT id, created_at, total_cents, status
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = '7c1f...'
  AND (created_at, id) < ('2026-02-11 09:14:22+00', 'a41d...')
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
Limit  (cost=0.56..37.02 rows=20 width=44) (actual time=0.038..0.061 rows=20 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=7
Execution Time: 0.081 ms

126 ms to 0.08 ms, and the second one stays at 0.08 ms on page 5,000. Same index, same data, different question asked of it.

The mistake people make

Testing performance on a development database. A seeded 5,000-row orders table makes every plan look fine because everything fits in memory and a sequential scan of 5,000 rows costs nothing. Load a production-shaped copy, or at minimum generate the right order of magnitude with generate_series, before you claim a query is fast.

43.3.2 What happens when this table has a billion rows?

Why the question matters

Table size changes which operations are possible, not just how fast they are. At a billion rows, ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT behaviour, index creation time, VACUUM duration, backup and restore time, and even count(*) all move from "a moment" to "a maintenance window".

How to actually answer it

Estimate the growth rate first: rows per day times 365. If the answer is under a few million, most of this does not apply and you should not over-engineer. If the answer is hundreds of millions, decide these things now, while the table is small:

  • Is there a retention policy? If rows can be deleted or archived after N months, partition by range on the time column from day one. DROP TABLE orders_2024_01 is instant; DELETE FROM orders WHERE created_at < ... on 200 million rows is an outage, a replication lag spike and a bloat problem.
  • What is the natural access pattern? Almost always "recent rows for one tenant". That is the composite index, and it is also the partition key candidate.
  • Which columns are actually needed at read time? Wide rows with large JSONB blobs push data out to TOAST and make index-only scans impossible. Consider splitting cold columns into a side table.
  • Can index creation be done concurrently? CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY takes longer but does not block writes. On a billion rows it might take four hours. Plan for it.

Worked example

An events table for user activity, 40 million rows per month, kept for 13 months: 520 million rows steady state, growing.

Unpartitioned, the monthly cleanup DELETE touched 40 million rows, generated ~12 GB of WAL, pushed the replica 90 seconds behind, and left the table 30 percent bloated until autovacuum caught up two days later. Partitioned by month with PARTITION BY RANGE (occurred_at), the cleanup is:

-- Instant, no WAL for row deletions, no bloat, no replica lag.
ALTER TABLE events DETACH PARTITION events_2025_08 CONCURRENTLY;
DROP TABLE events_2025_08;

The cost of partitioning at design time was about two hours of work. The cost of adding it later, on a live 500-million-row table, was a two-week project with dual writes and a backfill.

The mistake people make
