Assuming you will "deal with it when we get there". You will get there on a Thursday during a product launch, and the fix will need a maintenance window you cannot get. Part 31 — Database Migrations and Zero-Downtime Schema Changes exists because of this mistake.

43.3.3 Which indexes does it need, and what do they cost on writes?

Why the question matters

Indexes are the highest-leverage tool for read performance and one of the most common causes of write amplification. Every index must be updated on every insert and on every update that touches its columns. Eight indexes on a hot table can triple your write cost and your WAL volume.

How to actually answer it

For reads: for each query in the request path, write the index that serves it. Column order is equality first, then range, then sort. Check whether the query can be index-only by including the few extra columns with INCLUDE.

For writes: count the indexes on the table and multiply. Ask what the insert rate is, what fraction of updates touch indexed columns, and whether any index is on a randomly distributed value like a UUIDv4 (random inserts scatter across the B-tree and destroy cache locality).

Then hunt for indexes nobody uses:

-- Unused indexes: pure write cost, zero read benefit. Check on a primary
-- that has been up long enough for the stats to be meaningful.
SELECT relname AS table_name,
       indexrelname AS index_name,
       idx_scan,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) AS size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE idx_scan < 50
  AND indexrelid NOT IN (SELECT conindid FROM pg_constraint WHERE contype IN ('p','u'))
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexrelid) DESC;

Worked example

A payments table taking 300 inserts per second at peak had nine indexes, added one at a time by five engineers over two years for one-off support queries. Three had idx_scan in the low hundreds after 60 days of uptime. Dropping those three cut WAL generation by 22 percent, cut the p99 insert latency from 11 ms to 7 ms, and shaved 40 GB off the backup. Nobody noticed a slow query afterwards, because the support tooling ran on the read replica where those queries could afford a sequential scan.

The senior move here was not "add an index". It was "audit the indexes and delete", which is invisible work that made everything faster.

The mistake people make

Adding an index in response to every slow query, without checking whether an existing index could be extended. Two indexes (customer_id) and (customer_id, created_at) are one index too many: the second serves both queries. Also: adding indexes on a table without knowing its write rate.

43.3.4 What happens under concurrency?

Why the question matters

Code that is correct when one request runs it is frequently wrong when fifty run it at once. Read-then-write patterns, uniqueness checks in application code and counter updates are the classic three, and they fail rarely enough in testing to reach production and often enough at scale to cost money.

How to actually answer it

For every write path, ask: if two requests execute this at exactly the same moment, what happens? Walk the interleaving explicitly. Then check which of the four tools you need:

Problem Tool Cost
Two writers overwriting each other's read SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or optimistic version column Row lock held for the transaction; contention on hot rows
Duplicate creation of a logical entity Unique constraint plus ON CONFLICT None at read time; must handle the conflict path
Lost counter increments UPDATE ... SET n = n + 1 in the database, not in application code Serialises on the row; consider sharded counters if hot
Two workers grabbing the same job FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED Small; the correct pattern for queue tables

Worked example

Inventory reservation, the code that every e-commerce system gets wrong once:

// WRONG: read-check-write across two statements. Two concurrent requests both
// read stock = 1, both pass the check, both decrement. Stock becomes -1.
const item = await this.repo.findOne({ where: { id: sku } });
if (item.stock < qty) throw new ConflictException('out_of_stock');
await this.repo.update({ id: sku }, { stock: item.stock - qty });
// RIGHT: the check and the write are one atomic statement, and the constraint
// is the final authority. affected === 0 means somebody else won the race.
const result = await this.dataSource
  .createQueryBuilder()
  .update(InventoryItem)
  .set({ stock: () => 'stock - :qty' })
  .where('id = :sku AND stock >= :qty', { sku, qty })
  .setParameter('qty', qty)
  .execute();

if (result.affected === 0) {
  throw new ConflictException('out_of_stock');
}

Plus the guard rail in the schema, so no future code path can break the invariant:

ALTER TABLE inventory_items ADD CONSTRAINT stock_non_negative CHECK (stock >= 0);

Two layers: the atomic statement makes the common path correct, the constraint makes the whole system incapable of being wrong. Part 13 — Database Transactions and Concurrency Control and Part 21 — Concurrency in Node.js and NestJS go deeper.

The mistake people make

Testing concurrency serially. A Jest test that calls the endpoint twice in sequence proves nothing. Run 50 in parallel with Promise.all against a real PostgreSQL in Docker and assert the invariant afterwards. That test finds real bugs.

43.3.5 Who owns this data, and who else reads it?

Why the question matters

A table with one writer and one reader can be changed on a Tuesday. A table with one writer and six readers, two of which are other teams' services and one of which is a BI dashboard, is a public API with no version number. Most "we cannot change our schema" paralysis comes from not knowing who reads it.

How to actually answer it

Write down, per table: the owning service, who writes, who reads, and how. "How" matters: an application reading through your API is coupled to your API. An analytics job reading your table directly is coupled to your column names.

Then set the rule: one service writes; everyone else reads through an interface you control — an API, an event, or a replicated view. If another team needs direct SQL, give them a versioned database view, not the base table. A view is a contract you can keep stable while the table underneath changes.

Worked example

We wanted to rename orders.total (in dollars, a numeric) to orders.total_cents (an integer), because the floating conversions were producing rounding complaints. The change looked like a ten-minute migration. Then we asked who reads it: the order service (ours), the invoicing service (another team), a Metabase dashboard used by finance, a nightly export to the data warehouse, and a customer-facing CSV export.

The actual plan was expand-contract over six weeks: add total_cents, dual-write, backfill in batches, create a view orders_v1 exposing the old total computed from total_cents for the external readers, migrate readers one at a time with the owning teams, then drop the column. Not glamorous, zero downtime, zero incidents.

The senior behaviour was not the migration technique. It was asking the ownership question before estimating the work.

The mistake people make

Letting other services connect directly to your database "just for reads, just this once". It happens in an afternoon and takes two years to undo. If you must, do it through an explicitly named, versioned view and a read-only role with GRANT SELECT limited to that view.

43.3.6 How will we migrate it later?

Why the question matters

Every schema you write will be wrong eventually. The question is whether the fix is a migration you can run online, or a project. Design choices made in five minutes determine which.

How to actually answer it

Before merging a schema, ask: to change this later, would we need to rewrite the whole table, take a long lock, or reconstruct information we did not keep?

Cheap-to-evolve choices: nullable new columns, additive enums stored as text with a check constraint rather than a PostgreSQL enum type, storing the raw event alongside the derived state, timestamps with time zone, surrogate keys.

Expensive-to-evolve choices: changing a column type on a large table, adding NOT NULL without a default on an old PostgreSQL version, natural primary keys made of business data that turns out to be mutable, a native enum type that requires ALTER TYPE coordination, and anything that discards information.

Worked example

We modelled a subscription's state as a single status column: active, paused, cancelled. Eighteen months later, finance asked "how many subscriptions were paused in March, and for how long?" The information did not exist. We had stored the current state and thrown away the transitions.

The cheap version of this choice, made at design time, would have been an append-only subscription_events table alongside the status column: two extra columns of work, and the ability to answer any historical question forever. That is what "designing for migration" actually means most of the time: keep the facts, derive the state.

Interview questions

  1. "You need to add a NOT NULL column with a default to a 400-million-row table with no downtime. Walk me through it." Expected: awareness that modern PostgreSQL handles the default without a rewrite for most types, but that the safe general recipe is add nullable, backfill in batches with a sleep between them, add a NOT VALID check constraint, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT. Follow-up: what is your lock_timeout and why?
  2. "An endpoint got 20x slower after a release with no query changes. Where do you look?" Expected: plan change from statistics drift, a new index missing after a restore, data growth crossing a threshold, parameter sniffing on a prepared statement, autovacuum falling behind, or a lock wait. Ask for EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and pg_stat_activity.
  3. "How do you decide between optimistic and pessimistic locking?" Expected: contention rate and the cost of a retry versus the cost of holding a lock.
  4. "Who is allowed to read your service's tables directly?" Expected: ideally nobody, and a clear story about views, APIs or events if someone does.

Practical exercise

Pick the busiest write table in your system. Produce: the row count and daily growth rate, every index with its idx_scan count and size, the top three queries against it from pg_stat_statements with their plans, and a one-page answer to all six questions in 43.3. Acceptance criteria: you can name at least one index to drop or one query to rewrite, with the measured before and after.

43.4 Distributed systems questions

The moment your system has two processes that talk over a network — and a NestJS app plus PostgreSQL is already two processes — you own a distributed system. You do not get to opt out. You only get to decide whether you thought about it.

These seven questions are the interrogation I run on every remote call. I ask them in this order, out loud, in design reviews.

flowchart TB
    R["Remote call to a dependency"] --> T{"Can it time out?"}
    T --> D{"Can it be duplicated?"}
    D --> L{"Can it arrive late?"}
    L --> O{"Can it arrive out of order?"}
    O --> P{"Can it partially succeed?"}
    P --> S{"What is the source of truth?"}
    S --> F{"What do we do when it is down?"}
    F --> A["Design has an explicit answer for all seven"]

43.4.1 Can this request time out?

Yes. Always yes. The interesting question is what happens next.

Why the question matters

A call without a timeout is a call that can hang forever, and in Node.js a hung call holds a connection from a pool, a request slot and memory. Fifty hung calls to a slow third party will take down an endpoint that has nothing to do with that third party, because they share the event loop and the pool. This is how one dependency's bad afternoon becomes your outage.

How to actually answer it

Every network call gets an explicit timeout, and the timeouts must form a budget that decreases as you go deeper. If the client gives up at 5 s, the gateway must give up before that, your handler before that, and the database query before that. Otherwise you do work nobody is waiting for.

// A timeout budget expressed in config, not scattered magic numbers.
// Client 5000ms > handler 3000ms > payment call 2000ms > db 800ms.
const res = await firstValueFrom(
  this.http.post('https://api.psp.example/charges', body, {
    timeout: 2000,                       // socket + response timeout
    headers: { 'Idempotency-Key': key }, // because a timeout means "unknown"
  }).pipe(timeout({ each: 2500 })),      // hard ceiling including retries
);

Worked example

At 14:20 our checkout p99 went from 240 ms to 9 s. The payment provider was healthy at 99.4 percent, but 0.6 percent of calls were hanging past 30 seconds. We had no timeout. Each hung request held one of 10 pool connections per pod. With 6 pods and a steady trickle of hangs, we exhausted the pools in eleven minutes and started failing product page requests, which never touch payments at all.

The fix was two lines: a 2-second timeout and a bulkhead limiting concurrent payment calls to 4 per pod. Blast radius went from "the whole site" to "some checkouts are slower".

The mistake people make

Believing that a timeout is a failure. A timeout is not a failure. A timeout is unknown. The payment may have succeeded. This is the single most important sentence in distributed systems, and it leads directly to the next question.

43.4.2 Can this be duplicated?

Why the question matters

Because timeouts mean unknown, every sane client retries. Every retry can duplicate. Kafka gives you at-least-once delivery. HTTP clients retry on 502. Users double-click. Mobile apps retry on network change. If your handler is not idempotent, duplication means double charges, double emails, double stock decrements.

How to actually answer it

Assume every operation will be executed twice, and make the second execution a no-op with the same response. The tools:

  • A natural unique constraint. UNIQUE (order_id) on payments makes a duplicate insert fail loudly and cheaply.
  • An idempotency key supplied by the client, stored with the response, and returned on replay.
  • A state machine with guarded transitions: UPDATE orders SET status='paid' WHERE id=$1 AND status='pending' returns zero affected rows on the second attempt.
-- The idempotency table: the key, the request fingerprint, and the stored response.
CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key            text PRIMARY KEY,
  request_hash   text NOT NULL,
  response_code  int,
  response_body  jsonb,
  created_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  completed_at   timestamptz
);
-- Insert first, do the work, then fill in the response. A concurrent duplicate
-- hits the primary key and waits or is told the request is in flight.

Worked example

A retail client double-charged 213 customers in one morning. Root cause: their mobile app retried on a 504 from the CDN, and the charge endpoint had no idempotency key. The provider had actually processed both charges — correctly, from its point of view, because it received two distinct requests. The refunds took three days and a public apology.

The fix was 40 lines: the client generates a UUID per checkout attempt and sends it as Idempotency-Key; the server stores it before calling the provider and passes it through to the provider, which is itself idempotent on that key. Two systems, one key, zero double charges since.

The mistake people make

Adding idempotency only at the outermost layer while the internals are not idempotent, so a retry after a partial failure re-sends the email but skips the charge. Idempotency has to be reasoned about per side effect. Part 19 — Distributed Transactions: Sagas, Outbox, Inbox and Idempotency is the full treatment.

43.4.3 Can it arrive late? Can it arrive out of order?

Why the question matters

Networks delay messages, brokers redeliver, consumers rebalance, and retries with backoff mean a message written first can be processed last. If your logic assumes ordering, it is wrong under exactly the conditions where being wrong matters.

How to actually answer it

Two defences. First, partition for the ordering you need: Kafka guarantees order only within a partition, so key by the entity whose order matters, usually order_id or user_id. Second, make handlers order-insensitive with a version or timestamp check, so a late message cannot overwrite newer state.

// Ignore stale updates. The event carries the version of the entity it describes.
const result = await this.repo
  .createQueryBuilder()
  .update(OrderProjection)
  .set({ status: event.status, version: event.version })
  .where('order_id = :id AND version < :v', { id: event.orderId, v: event.version })
  .execute();

if (result.affected === 0) {
  this.logger.debug({ orderId: event.orderId, v: event.version }, 'stale event ignored');
}

Worked example

An order status projection showed orders flipping back from shipped to paid for a few seconds. Cause: the paid event failed once, went to a retry queue with 30 seconds of backoff, and was reprocessed after the shipped event had already been applied. The consumer wrote whatever it was handed. Adding the version < guard above made the problem structurally impossible, and it is four words of SQL.

The mistake people make

Assuming a timestamp on the message is safe to compare across producers. Clocks on different machines disagree, sometimes by seconds. Use a monotonic per-entity version from the writer, or the broker's per-partition offset, not Date.now() from three services.

43.4.4 Can it partially succeed?

Why the question matters

The most dangerous outcome is not failure. It is half-success: the order row is committed, the payment is captured, but the inventory service call failed. The system is now internally inconsistent and no exception describes it.

How to actually answer it

Enumerate the steps, then mark the boundary of the local transaction. Everything inside the boundary is atomic. Everything outside it must be either idempotent-retryable or compensatable. If your handler writes to the database and calls two other services, you have three failure points and you need a plan for each.

The two workhorses: the transactional outbox (write your state and your intent-to-notify in one local transaction, publish asynchronously) and the saga (a sequence of local transactions with explicit compensating actions).

// One local transaction: state and outbox row commit together or not at all.
await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
  const order = await manager.save(Order, { customerId, totalCents, status: 'pending' });
  await manager.insert(OutboxMessage, {
    aggregateId: order.id,
    type: 'OrderPlaced',
    payload: { orderId: order.id, customerId, totalCents },
  });
});
// A separate relay publishes outbox rows to Kafka and marks them sent.
// If the relay crashes mid-publish, the message is re-sent: consumers are idempotent.

Worked example

A food delivery platform captured payment, then called the restaurant's POS integration to place the order. When the POS timed out, they rolled back nothing: the customer was charged, no food was cooked, and the order sat in pending forever. About 60 cases a week were caught by support, one at a time.

The redesign made payment_captured and order_dispatched separate states with a saga: if dispatch fails after N attempts, a compensating refund transaction runs automatically and the customer gets a notification. Support tickets went to near zero, and the cases that remained were visible on a dashboard within 90 seconds instead of a day.

The mistake people make

Wrapping HTTP calls inside a database transaction to "make it atomic". It does the opposite: it holds row locks for the duration of a network call, and it still cannot roll back the remote side effect. Never hold a transaction open across a network call you do not control.

43.4.5 What is the source of truth?

Why the question matters

When two systems disagree, somebody has to be right. If nobody has decided which one, every reconciliation bug becomes an argument, and the fix is guesswork.

How to actually answer it

For every important fact, name exactly one owner: "the payment provider is the source of truth for whether money moved; our payments table is a local record that must be reconciled against it." Then design the reconciliation: a nightly job, a webhook, or both. Caches, search indexes, read models and analytics copies are never sources of truth. They are derived and must be rebuildable from the source.

The test: if this store is wiped, can I rebuild it? If yes, it is a derivative. If no, it needs backups, and it is truth.

Worked example

Our search index and PostgreSQL disagreed about product prices during a promotion. Two engineers spent an hour arguing about which to fix. The answer, once we wrote it down, was trivially: PostgreSQL owns price, the index is derived, so the bug is in the indexing pipeline, and the immediate mitigation is a reindex of the affected category. Ninety minutes of the incident had been spent on a question that a one-line ownership statement in the design doc would have answered instantly.

The mistake people make

Letting a cache become truth by accident, usually because writes go to Redis and are flushed to PostgreSQL later. The first Redis restart takes your data with it.

43.4.6 What do we do when this dependency is down?

Why the question matters

The default behaviour — propagate the error to the user — is sometimes right and frequently terrible. Choosing deliberately per dependency is one of the clearest markers of senior design.

How to actually answer it

For each dependency, pick one strategy and write it down:

Strategy When to use Example
Fail fast The dependency is essential to correctness Payment provider during checkout
Fall back to a degraded answer The feature has a sensible default Recommendations return best sellers
Serve stale Data changes slowly and staleness is acceptable Cached catalogue with extended TTL
Queue and process later The user does not need the result now Email, webhooks, analytics events
Shed load Protecting the core matters more than this feature Disable CSV export during an incident

Then implement it with a circuit breaker so you stop hammering a dying dependency, and make sure the fallback path is exercised regularly, because an untested fallback is a second outage waiting.

Worked example

During a 40-minute Redis outage, our catalogue survived because reads fell through to PostgreSQL with a concurrency limiter. Our session store did not, because sessions lived only in Redis, so every user was logged out. The post-incident change was not "make Redis more reliable" — it was to move sessions to signed cookies with a short expiry plus a Redis-backed revocation list, so a Redis outage degrades revocation checks rather than logging out every customer.

Interview questions

  1. "Your service calls a third-party API that starts responding in 30 seconds instead of 200 ms. Walk me through what happens to your system and what you would have built to prevent it." Expected: pool and event-loop exhaustion, timeouts, bulkheads, circuit breaker, blast-radius reasoning.
  2. "What does an HTTP 504 from your payment provider mean?" Expected: unknown, not failure. Follow-up: how do you find out the truth, and what do you tell the customer meanwhile?
  3. "How do you make a Kafka consumer idempotent?" Expected: unique key on a processed-messages table or a guarded state transition, plus the observation that offset commits and database writes are not atomic together.
  4. "Two services disagree about an order's status. How do you decide who is right?" Expected: named source of truth, derived stores, reconciliation job.

Practical exercise

Draw the request path of your most important write endpoint, marking every network call. For each call, write the seven answers: timeout value, duplication defence, late/out-of-order handling, partial-failure plan, source of truth, and the behaviour when it is down. Acceptance criteria: no call has "no timeout" and no side effect lacks a duplication defence. Anything you cannot answer becomes a ticket.

43.5 Production questions

There is a moment in every engineer's career when they stop thinking of "done" as "merged" and start thinking of it as "running safely in production, observable, deployable, reversible, and operable by someone else". That shift is most of what separates mid from senior.

These six questions are the ones I ask before approving any design that will run in production. If a design cannot answer them, it is not finished, no matter how good the code is.

43.5.1 How do we know it is broken before a customer tells us?

Why the question matters

The worst way to learn about an outage is a customer email at 09:00 about something that broke at 22:40. It means you were blind for ten hours, you have no data about what happened, and the trust cost is far higher than the outage cost.

How to actually answer it

Name the signal and the threshold before you ship. A signal is a metric you already emit or will emit; a threshold is the number that means "a human should look now".

The default set for any HTTP service:

  • Error rate: 5xx as a fraction of requests, per route.
  • Latency: p95 and p99 per route, not the average.
  • Saturation: pool usage, event loop lag, memory versus limit, CPU throttling.
  • Traffic: requests per second, so you can tell "broken" from "nobody is using it".

Then the business-level signals, which are the ones that actually catch the subtle failures: orders per minute, payment success ratio, queue depth, consumer lag, jobs completed per minute. A deploy that breaks checkout for one payment method will not move your 5xx rate at all. It will drop payments_succeeded_total{method="upi"} to zero, and that is the alert that saves you.

Then decide which of them pages a human and which merely appears on a dashboard. My rule: page only for things that are both urgent and actionable. Everything else is a ticket.

Worked example

We shipped a change to the coupon service. Error rates stayed at 0.02 percent, latency was unchanged, CPU was flat. Every technical dashboard was green. What had broken was a validation rule that silently rejected every percentage-based coupon, returning a clean HTTP 200 with applied: false.

We found out 90 minutes later from a marketing manager. The alert we added afterwards was one line of PromQL on a business metric:

sum(rate(coupons_applied_total[10m])) < 0.5 * sum(rate(coupons_applied_total[10m] offset 1d))

"Coupons applied is less than half of the same time yesterday." It has fired three times since, twice for real problems, and both times we knew within four minutes.

The mistake people make

Alerting on causes instead of symptoms. "CPU above 80 percent" pages you at 03:00 for a batch job that is supposed to use CPU. "p99 latency above 1 s for 5 minutes on /checkout" pages you when customers are actually suffering. Alert on what the user feels; use the cause metrics for debugging once you are awake. See Part 25 — Observability and Part 37 — Site Reliability Engineering.

43.5.2 How do we deploy it?

Why the question matters

Deployment is where correct code meets reality: two versions running at once, connections draining, migrations half-applied, caches warm for one version and cold for another. Most "mystery" production bugs are deployment-window bugs.

How to actually answer it

Answer three sub-questions explicitly.

Can version N and version N+1 run at the same time? During a rolling deploy they will, for minutes. That means every change must be backwards compatible with the immediately previous version: no removing a response field the old client still reads, no renaming a queue, no schema change the old code cannot tolerate. This is the expand-contract discipline from Part 32 — Backward Compatibility.

What is the rollout shape? Rolling for most services, canary for risky ones, feature flag for anything user-visible where you want to decouple deploy from release. The flag is the cheapest safety mechanism ever invented: it turns a rollback from a 10-minute redeploy into a 5-second config change.

What happens to in-flight work? Graceful shutdown: stop accepting new requests, mark readiness false, finish in-flight ones with a deadline, close the pool, exit. If you skip this, every deploy drops a handful of requests and you will spend an afternoon chasing "random" 502s that only happen at release time.

Worked example

A team deployed a change that renamed a BullMQ job from send-email to notifications.send-email. Producers and consumers were in the same repository, so it looked atomic. During the 4-minute rolling deploy, old producers pushed send-email jobs that new consumers ignored, and new producers pushed notifications.send-email that old consumers ignored. About 1,900 emails vanished into a queue nobody was reading. They were only discovered because a customer asked where their password reset went.

The correct sequence is three deploys: consumers listen to both names; producers switch to the new name; consumers drop the old name once the old queue is empty. Boring, and nothing is lost.

The mistake people make

Coupling the database migration to the application deploy in one step. If the migration runs first and the old code cannot handle the new schema, you have broken production before the new code lands. If the new code lands first and the migration has not run, the same. Always make migrations independently deployable and backwards compatible.

43.5.3 How do we roll it back?

Why the question matters

Rollback is the fastest mitigation available, and teams routinely discover in the middle of an incident that they cannot use it. Every minute spent debugging a bad release while customers are affected is a minute you could have bought back with a rollback that takes 90 seconds.

How to actually answer it

Write the rollback procedure down before the deploy, and mark whether it is safe. A release is rollback-safe if the previous version can run against the current state of the world: the current schema, the current cache format, the current message formats.

Things that break rollback safety:

  • A migration that drops or renames a column the old code reads.
  • Writing a new field into Redis with a format the old code cannot parse.
  • Emitting an event version the old consumer rejects rather than ignores.
  • Any data written by the new version that the old version will misinterpret.

If a release is not rollback-safe, say so in the pull request, and put a "forward fix only" note in the runbook so nobody wastes ten minutes trying.

Worked example

At 01:12 an on-call engineer rolled back a release after error rates spiked. The rollback made things worse: the new version had started writing session data as MessagePack instead of JSON, and the old version threw on every session read. Every logged-in user got a 500. Total outage went from 6 minutes to 34.

The fix afterwards was a rule we still use: new format writes are gated behind a flag that stays off for one full release cycle. Ship the reader first, then enable the writer. Every format change becomes reversible.

The mistake people make

Testing the deploy but never testing the rollback. Practise it: roll back a real release in staging every month. The first time you try it during an incident should not be the first time.

43.5.4 How do we migrate the data?

Why the question matters

Application rollbacks are cheap. Data migrations are not: they take time proportional to the data, they hold locks, they generate WAL, they lag replicas, and half-finished ones leave you in a state neither version expects.

How to actually answer it

Every migration gets four answers: how long it runs, what it locks, whether it can be resumed, and how to undo it.

The safe pattern for anything on a big table:

-- Never let a migration wait forever on a lock. Fail fast and retry.
SET lock_timeout = '3s';
SET statement_timeout = '30s';

-- Additive and instant: no table rewrite, no long lock.
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN total_cents integer;
-- Backfill in bounded batches with a pause, so replication and autovacuum keep up.
-- Run from a script, not from a migration that must finish in one transaction.
UPDATE orders
SET total_cents = round(total * 100)
WHERE total_cents IS NULL
  AND id IN (
    SELECT id FROM orders WHERE total_cents IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000
  );

Then validate the constraint separately, which takes a weak lock:

ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT total_cents_not_null CHECK (total_cents IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT total_cents_not_null;

Worked example

A backfill on 90 million rows was written as a single UPDATE. It ran for 26 minutes, generated 38 GB of WAL, pushed the read replica 11 minutes behind, and caused a customer-visible incident on the reporting dashboards that read from that replica. Rewritten as 18,000 batches of 5,000 rows with a 150 ms pause, it took 70 minutes of wall clock, generated the same WAL spread over time, and nobody noticed. Longer is often safer.

The mistake people make

Running the backfill inside the schema migration, so a deployment blocks for half an hour and the deployment tool times out halfway through with no idea what has been applied. Schema changes are fast and transactional; backfills are slow, resumable and run separately.

43.5.5 How does someone debug this at three in the morning?

Why the question matters

The person paged will not be you. They will have been asleep 90 seconds ago, they will not know this service, and they will be looking at a dashboard on a phone. Design for that person.

How to actually answer it

Three deliverables per service:

  1. Structured logs with a correlation id that flows from the gateway through the service, into the queue message, and into the worker. Being able to type one id and see the whole story is worth more than any other observability investment.
  2. A runbook that is not prose. It is: what this alert means, the three most likely causes in order, the exact query or command for each, and the mitigation for each including the "just restart it" option and when that is safe.
  3. A dashboard with the golden signals for this service on one screen, plus its dependencies. Not forty panels. Eight.
// A log line built for 03:00: identifiers first, no string interpolation,
// and the fields you will actually filter on.
this.logger.warn(
  {
    correlationId: ctx.correlationId,
    orderId: order.id,
    customerId: order.customerId,
    provider: 'psp-primary',
    attempt,
    latencyMs: Date.now() - startedAt,
    outcome: 'timeout',
  },
  'payment capture timed out',
);

Worked example

Two services, same incident type. Service A logged Error: request failed with a stack trace and no identifiers. The on-call engineer spent 40 minutes correlating timestamps across three systems to work out which customer and which provider. Service B logged the structure above. The on-call engineer filtered by outcome=timeout, saw all of them were provider=psp-primary, flipped the provider failover flag, and went back to bed in 6 minutes. The code quality of the two services was similar. The operability was not.

The mistake people make

Logging for the developer writing the code instead of the engineer reading it under stress. console.log('here 3') in production, log messages with no ids, errors swallowed and re-thrown with less context than they had, and the classic catch (e) { this.logger.error(e.message) } that discards the stack and the cause chain.

43.5.6 Who is on call for it?

Why the question matters

A system nobody is responsible for at 03:00 is a system that will be broken for hours. And the answer shapes the design: if you are on call for it, you will build it differently.

How to actually answer it

Before launch: name the on-call rotation, confirm the alert routes to it, confirm the team knows the service exists, and hand over the runbook in a real conversation rather than a link. If the answer is "we don't have a rotation for that yet", the launch is not ready.

There is a deeper principle here: you build it, you run it. Teams that are paged by their own systems build systems that page less. It is the tightest feedback loop in software engineering, and it converts abstract quality arguments into personal sleep.

The mistake people make

Launching a service on a Friday, with alerts routed to an email address nobody reads, owned by a team that was not consulted. Two months later it fails, and the archaeology begins.

Practical exercise

Take a service you own and write its runbook page for its most likely alert. It must fit on one screen and contain: what the alert means in one sentence, the three most likely causes with the exact command or query for each, the mitigation for each, the escalation contact, and when a restart is safe. Acceptance criteria: an engineer from another team can follow it without asking you anything.

43.6 Security questions

Security is not a phase at the end. It is four questions asked at design time, and they cost about ten minutes each. Part 22 — Security has the mechanisms; this section is the habit.

43.6.1 Who is allowed to call this?

Why the question matters

The most common serious vulnerability in real backend systems is not exotic. It is a missing authorisation check: an endpoint that verifies who you are and forgets to verify whether this object is yours. OWASP calls it broken access control, and it is number one on their list because it is everywhere.

How to actually answer it

For every endpoint, state two things: the authentication requirement, and the object-level authorisation rule. The second one is where bugs live.

// Authentication says "you are user 42". Authorisation says "order 918 is yours".
// The scoping must be in the query, not in an if-statement after the fetch,
// so that no future code path can skip it.
async findOne(orderId: string, actor: Actor): Promise<Order> {
  const order = await this.repo.findOne({
    where: actor.role === 'admin'
      ? { id: orderId }
      : { id: orderId, customerId: actor.userId },   // scoped in SQL
  });
  if (!order) throw new NotFoundException();          // 404, not 403: do not leak existence
  return order;
}

Then encode the rule where it cannot be forgotten: a guard, a repository that requires a tenant id, or PostgreSQL row-level security for multi-tenant systems.

Worked example

An invoicing endpoint was GET /invoices/:id, protected by a JWT guard. Any authenticated customer could read any invoice by incrementing the id, because the ids were sequential integers and the query was findOne({ where: { id } }). It was found by a customer who mistyped their own invoice number and saw someone else's company name. That is an IDOR, it is a reportable data incident in most jurisdictions, and it was one where clause.

The fix was the scoped query above plus a repository method that made the unscoped version unavailable. UUIDs would have made it harder to find but would not have fixed it: obscurity is not authorisation.

The mistake people make

Believing that "the frontend only shows the user their own invoices" is a control. The frontend is not a security boundary. Anything reachable with a token can be called with curl.

43.6.2 What if the input is hostile?

Why the question matters

Every input is attacker-controlled: body, query parameters, headers, file names, webhook payloads, message bodies from a queue, and data from a third-party API. If your code assumes shapes, sizes or contents, someone will eventually violate the assumption, deliberately or by accident.

How to actually answer it

Validate at the boundary with an allowlist, and set limits on everything that has a size.

// Validation is a contract, not decoration. Whitelist unknown fields away,
// bound every string and number, and never trust a client-supplied enum.
export class CreateOrderDto {
  @IsUUID('4') productId!: string;
  @IsInt() @Min(1) @Max(100) quantity!: number;
  @IsIn(['standard', 'express']) shipping!: 'standard' | 'express';
  @IsOptional() @IsString() @MaxLength(280) note?: string;
}

// main.ts: forbidNonWhitelisted rejects extra fields instead of silently keeping them.
app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({
  whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true, transform: true,
}));

Then the boundaries beyond the DTO: request body size limits, upload size and MIME validation, pagination limit capped server-side, rate limits per identity and per IP, statement_timeout so a pathological query cannot run forever, and parameterised SQL everywhere so no string concatenation touches a query.

The "hostile input" checklist I run mentally: empty, absent, wrong type, enormous, negative, zero, unicode with combining characters and right-to-left marks, deeply nested JSON, a valid value belonging to another tenant, and the same request sent 10,000 times per second.

Worked example

A product search endpoint accepted ?limit=. Nobody capped it. A scraper sent limit=1000000, the query returned 400 MB of JSON, the Node process serialised it, heap went past the container limit, and the pod was OOMKilled. Three pods died in sequence as the scraper retried. The fix was Math.min(limit ?? 20, 100) and a rate limit, which is about as cheap as a fix gets.

The mistake people make

Validating only the fields the happy path reads. The attack is always in the field you did not think about: the sort parameter interpolated into an ORDER BY, the file name used to build a path, the webhook payload trusted because "it comes from Stripe" without verifying the signature.

43.6.3 What data does this expose?

Why the question matters

Data leaks more often through carelessness than through attacks: an entity serialised whole into a response, a debug log containing a full request body with a card token, an error message returning a stack trace with a connection string.

How to actually answer it

Classify the fields, then make exposure explicit. Return DTOs, never entities. Redact in the logger, not at each call site.

// Serialisation is an allowlist: the response contains what you listed, nothing more.
export class OrderResponseDto {
  @Expose() id!: string;
  @Expose() status!: string;
  @Expose() totalCents!: number;
  // internalNotes, costPrice, fraudScore and customerEmail are simply not here.
}

// One redaction config beats a hundred careful log calls.
pino({ redact: ['req.headers.authorization', 'req.body.password', '*.cardNumber', '*.token'] });

Also ask what the aggregate exposes. An endpoint returning one order is fine. The same endpoint with ?limit=1000 and no tenant scoping is a data export. Rate limits and pagination caps are privacy controls, not just performance controls.

Worked example

An internal admin API returned the full user entity, including the bcrypt password hash and a password reset token, because it did return user. The endpoint was internal-only, behind VPN, and low risk in theory. Then a frontend engineer cached the response in the browser to speed up a table, and the hashes ended up in local storage on every admin laptop. Nobody was malicious at any point. The response DTO would have made it impossible.

The mistake people make

Returning entities from controllers. It works, it is fast to write, and it means that every future column added to that table is automatically published to your API. Someone will add internal_risk_score in eight months and never think about the endpoint.

43.6.4 What happens if this token or key leaks?

Why the question matters

Credentials leak. They end up in Git history, in CI logs, in Slack messages, in a screenshot, in a browser extension, in a laptop that was stolen. The question is not prevention alone; it is containment and recovery.

How to actually answer it

For every credential, answer four things: what can it do, how long is it valid, how would we know it leaked, and how fast can we rotate it.

Credential Scope it should have Lifetime Rotation
User access token (JWT) One user, minimal claims 5–15 minutes Refresh token rotation, revocation list in Redis
Refresh token One user, one device Days, one-time use Rotate on every use; reuse detection revokes the family
Service-to-service credential One service, specific actions Short, issued by the platform Automated; no human ever holds it
Database password One role, least privilege Long-lived if unavoidable Secrets manager, rotation runbook tested twice a year
Third-party API key Restricted by IP or scope where the provider allows Long-lived Two keys supported at once so rotation is not an outage

The design rule that follows: short lifetimes and small scopes make leaks survivable. A 15-minute access token that leaks is a small incident. A never-expiring admin API key that leaks is a company incident.

Worked example

A junior engineer pasted a .env file into a public GitHub gist for a friend to help debug. The database credentials were in it. Automated scanners found it in under four minutes; we saw connection attempts from three countries within ten. What saved us was that the database was not publicly reachable, the credentials were for a role with SELECT only on two tables, and rotation was a documented 90-second procedure we had practised. It was a bad afternoon, not a catastrophe.

The lesson is not "train people not to paste secrets", though we did that too. It is that the blast radius of a leaked credential is a design decision you make months earlier.

The mistake people make

Treating rotation as theoretical. If you have never rotated a credential, you do not know that three services read it from a config file baked into an image at build time, and rotation will be a four-hour outage. Rotate something on a calm Tuesday and find out.

Interview questions

  1. "How would you prevent IDOR across an entire codebase, not one endpoint?" Expected: repository-level tenant scoping, a guard that requires an explicit policy per route, row-level security, and tests that assert cross-tenant access returns 404.
  2. "A customer's JWT leaks. Walk me through the impact and the response." Expected: token lifetime, what claims it carries, revocation mechanism, refresh token reuse detection, and how you would detect abuse.
  3. "Where does validation belong in a NestJS app, and why not in the service?" Expected: at the boundary via ValidationPipe and DTOs so unvalidated data never enters the domain; services still assert invariants that DTOs cannot express.

43.7 Business questions

Engineers who ask only technical questions get overruled by people who ask business ones. Engineers who ask both get to decide the architecture. These four questions are how you make a technical argument in a language that survives contact with a budget.

43.7.1 What does this complexity actually cost?

Why the question matters

"It's just one more service" is never just one more service. Naming the cost in units the business understands converts an aesthetic argument into a decision.

How to actually answer it

Cost has four columns, and you should be able to fill them in for any proposal:

Cost type How to estimate it Example for "add Kafka"
Engineer time to build Person-weeks, honestly 3 weeks for the first producer and consumer, done properly
Ongoing operations Hours per month plus who is on call ~4 h/month steady state, more during upgrades; a new alert class
Cloud spend Monthly bill, with the growth curve 3-broker managed cluster from ~$700/month, plus network
Onboarding Days added to a new hire's ramp-up +2 days per engineer, forever, plus a permanent skill dependency

Worked example

A team proposed splitting a well-functioning modular monolith into six services. The technical argument was "independent deployability". Writing out the costs gave: 14 person-weeks of migration, six pipelines, six sets of dashboards and alerts, distributed tracing that they did not have yet, a jump from one database to four, and an estimated $1,900 per month extra infrastructure. Against that, the benefit was that the two teams could deploy without coordinating, which was currently costing them roughly one hour per week of friction.

Fourteen weeks to save one hour per week pays back in 14 years of hours. Stated that way, the team themselves chose a smaller change: fix the 50-minute pipeline, split the deployment into two services along the one boundary that was genuinely painful, and stop. That took three weeks and captured most of the benefit.

The mistake people make

Comparing only build cost. The ongoing costs dominate over a system's lifetime, and they are the ones that quietly consume a team's capacity until it can no longer ship features.

43.7.2 Does the business actually need it?

Why the question matters

Engineers build for imagined requirements more often than they admit: multi-region for a company with customers in one country, a plugin architecture for an integration nobody has requested, 99.99 percent availability for an internal tool used by 30 people during office hours.

How to actually answer it

Ask for the requirement in numbers, and ask what happens if it is not met. "We need high availability" becomes "how many minutes of downtime per month is acceptable, and what does an hour of downtime cost us?" 99.9 percent is 43 minutes per month and is achievable with a well-run single-region setup. 99.99 percent is 4 minutes and typically means multi-region, which is a different engineering budget entirely, often 3-5x.

If nobody can answer what an outage costs, the requirement is a feeling, and you should design for the feeling cheaply.

The mistake people make

Accepting a non-functional requirement without a number, then spending six months delivering an expensive interpretation of it. Ask for the number. It is usually smaller than you feared, and occasionally much bigger, which is equally important to know.

43.7.3 What is the cost of being wrong versus the cost of being slow?

Why the question matters

This is the deepest business question in engineering, and it decides how much rigour a project deserves. Both errors are real: shipping something wrong costs money and trust; shipping late costs opportunity and sometimes the whole business.

How to actually answer it

Put the two costs next to each other:

  • Cost of being wrong: is it reversible? Does it corrupt data? Does it move money? Does it expose customer data? Is it visible to customers or to one internal team?
  • Cost of being slow: is there a deadline tied to revenue, a competitor, a contract, a regulatory date, or a seasonal peak? What is the cost of a month?

High wrong-cost plus low slow-cost means take the extra week: payments, auth, migrations, anything with customer data. Low wrong-cost plus high slow-cost means ship it behind a flag and learn: a new UI feature, an experiment, an internal tool.

Worked example

Two projects in the same quarter. A new recommendation widget: wrong-cost low (worst case, poor recommendations, revert the flag), slow-cost moderate (it was tied to a campaign). We shipped it in nine days with thin tests and a kill switch. A change to how refunds are calculated: wrong-cost very high (money, finance reconciliation, regulatory reporting), slow-cost low (no deadline). We spent three weeks, wrote a design doc, had finance review the rules, ran a shadow calculation against 90 days of historical refunds before switching, and found four edge cases in the process.

Same team, same quarter, deliberately different levels of rigour. Applying the recommendation-widget process to refunds would have been negligent. Applying the refund process to the widget would have wasted a fortnight.

The mistake people make

Having one speed. Some engineers are careful about everything and are seen as slow; some are fast about everything and are seen as risky. The senior skill is varying deliberately and being able to explain why.

43.7.4 What would we build if we had half the time?

Why the question matters

It is the fastest way to find the actual core of a project. Under a hard constraint, people stop defending nice-to-haves and reveal what they think really matters. It works on your own designs too.

How to actually answer it

Ask it literally, in the design review: "if this had to ship in three weeks instead of six, what would we cut?" Write the answer down. Then ask the harder follow-up: "why are we building those things at all in the six-week version?" Sometimes there is a good reason. Often the six-week version was padded with speculative flexibility.

Worked example

A returns-management project was scoped at eight weeks: a rules engine for return eligibility, an admin UI, automated refund processing, a customer self-service portal, and integration with three carriers. The half-time answer was: eligibility rules hardcoded for the two policies that cover 96 percent of returns, no admin UI (a support tool already existed), automated refunds only under a threshold, one carrier.

We shipped the four-week version. Six months later we had added a second carrier and raised the refund threshold. The rules engine, the admin UI and the portal were never built, because usage data showed they were not the bottleneck. Four weeks saved, and a smaller system to maintain forever.

The mistake people make

Treating the half-time version as a lesser thing to be ashamed of. Often it is the correct product, and the full version was a plan built on assumptions nobody had tested.

Practical exercise

Take a design you are currently working on. Write the four-column cost table for its most complex component, get the actual monthly cloud number from your provider's calculator, and write the half-time version in one paragraph. Acceptance criteria: you can present both to a product manager in five minutes, and you have a defensible recommendation rather than a preference.

43.8 How seniors make decisions

Junior engineers make decisions in their heads. Senior engineers make decisions on paper, because a decision that exists only in someone's head cannot be reviewed, cannot be revisited, and evaporates the moment that person changes team.

The mechanism is not bureaucracy. It is a small set of lightweight artefacts, each with a specific job.

43.8.1 The Architecture Decision Record

Concept

An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) is a short document — one page, ten minutes to write — that captures one decision: the context, the options, the choice, and the consequences. It is written at the time of the decision, stored in the repository next to the code, and never edited afterwards except to mark it superseded.

The value is almost entirely in the future. Eighteen months from now, someone will look at a strange design choice and think "this is stupid, let me fix it". The ADR tells them whether it was stupid or whether it was the least bad option given three constraints that no longer show in the code. Both answers are useful; the second one prevents a disaster.

Mental model

Imagine buying a house. The photographs show the house as it is. The ADR is the note explaining why you chose the smaller garden: the school catchment area, the commute, the budget on that specific week. Five years later the photos still make no sense without the note.

Template

# ADR-0017: <decision in a short sentence>

- **Status**: Proposed | Accepted | Superseded by ADR-00XX | Rejected
- **Date**: 2026-03-04
- **Deciders**: <names>
- **Reversibility**: two-way door | one-way door

## Context
What forces us to decide? Constraints, requirements, current numbers, deadlines.
Facts only. No solutions here.

## Options considered
1. Option A - one paragraph
2. Option B - one paragraph
3. Option C - one paragraph

## Trade-offs
| Criterion | Option A | Option B | Option C |
|---|---|---|---|

## Decision
We choose X, because ...

## Consequences
- Positive: ...
- Negative / what we accept: ...
- What we will monitor: ...
- What would make us revisit this: <a concrete trigger, with a number>

The two fields people skip are the two that matter most: reversibility (it tells the reader how much this decision was allowed to cost) and the trigger to revisit (it turns a permanent-feeling choice into one with an expiry condition).

ADR lifecycle

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Proposed
    Proposed --> Accepted: reviewers agree or lead decides
    Proposed --> Rejected: a cheaper option wins
    Accepted --> Superseded: trigger fires or context changes
    Rejected --> [*]
    Superseded --> [*]
    Accepted --> Accepted: still true at review time

43.8.2 Worked ADR 1 — modular monolith instead of microservices

# ADR-0004: Build v1 as a modular monolith, not microservices

- **Status**: Accepted
- **Date**: 2025-06-11
- **Deciders**: Backend team (4 engineers), Head of Product
- **Reversibility**: two-way door for the first 12 months; becomes harder once
  a module owns data another module writes to.

## Context
We are building an e-commerce backend for launch in 5 months. Expected launch
traffic: 40 RPS average, 200 RPS peak on campaign days, 3,000 orders/day.
Team: 4 backend engineers, none with production Kubernetes experience.
We have one on-call rotation, no dedicated platform engineer, no distributed
tracing yet. The product scope is still moving: two of the six domains
(promotions, returns) have unstable requirements.

## Options considered
1. **Microservices from day one.** Six services: catalogue, orders, payments,
   inventory, notifications, promotions. Separate databases, Kafka between them,
   six pipelines, six deployments.
2. **Modular monolith.** One NestJS deployable, one PostgreSQL database, one
   pipeline. Strict module boundaries: each module owns its tables, other modules
   call it only through its service interface, no cross-module joins in SQL.
   Domain events published through an in-process event bus with the same payload
   shape we would use on Kafka.
3. **Two services.** A single application plus a separate worker deployable for
   background jobs and consumers, sharing the database.

## Trade-offs
| Criterion | Microservices | Modular monolith | Two services |
|---|---|---|---|
| Time to launch | +8 to 10 weeks | Baseline | +1 week |
| Operational surface | 6 deployments, 6 DBs, broker | 1 deployment, 1 DB | 2 deployments, 1 DB |
| Debugging a request | Needs tracing we do not have | Single stack trace | Mostly single stack trace |
| Independent deploys | Yes | No | Partially |
| Boundary mistakes | Expensive to fix (network + data) | Cheap to fix (move a folder) | Cheap |
| Failure blast radius | Smaller, if done well | Whole app | Web survives worker crash |
| Cost at launch | ~$1,400/month | ~$380/month | ~$430/month |
| Team capability fit | Poor today | Good | Good |

## Decision
We build option 3: a modular monolith deployed as two processes (API and worker)
against one PostgreSQL database. Modules: catalogue, orders, payments, inventory,
notifications, promotions. Rules we enforce in review and with an import-boundary
lint rule:
- A module may only import another module's public `*.service.ts` interface.
- No SQL join across module table boundaries; cross-module reads go through the
  owning service.
- Every cross-module side effect is published as a domain event with the same
  payload we would publish to Kafka, so extraction later is a transport change.

## Consequences
- Positive: we launch on time with a team that can operate what it built. One
  stack trace per request. One database to back up, tune and migrate. Refactoring
  a wrong boundary is a folder move, not a data migration.
- Negative / accepted: all modules deploy together, so one bad release affects
  everything; we mitigate with feature flags and canary deploys. Nothing stops a
  determined engineer from writing a cross-module join except review and lint.
  Scaling is coarse: we scale the whole API even if only catalogue is hot.
- Monitor: p99 per module route group, deploy frequency, and the number of times
  a release is blocked because two teams need different release timing.
- Revisit when any of these is true: (a) more than 8 backend engineers across
  more than 2 teams working in this repository, (b) one module needs a resource
  profile the others do not, for example a memory-heavy search module, or
  (c) release coordination blocks a team more than twice a month.

That ADR is 500 words, took twenty minutes, and did three things: it stopped the recurring "should we do microservices" conversation, it gave the reviewers concrete rules to enforce, and it set the numeric trigger that would eventually justify a split. Fourteen months later, trigger (a) fired. The team split off two services, and the extraction took three weeks instead of three months because the module boundaries had been enforced the whole time.

43.8.3 Worked ADR 2 — keyset pagination for order history

# ADR-0021: Use keyset pagination for customer order history

- **Status**: Accepted
- **Date**: 2026-01-22
- **Deciders**: Backend team, Mobile lead
- **Reversibility**: one-way door for the public API shape once the mobile app
  ships; two-way door internally.

## Context
`GET /customers/{id}/orders` uses `OFFSET`/`LIMIT`. The `orders` table has
1.4 billion rows overall; the top 1 percent of B2B customers have between
80,000 and 400,000 orders each. Measured p99 for page 1 is 12 ms; for page 500 it
is 310 ms, and support reports timeouts for two customers who script exports by
walking pages. Traffic is 60 RPS on this endpoint, rising. The mobile app ships
in 6 weeks and will use this endpoint for an infinite-scroll list.

We also have a correctness bug: with `ORDER BY created_at DESC OFFSET n`, new
orders inserted while a customer pages cause rows to shift, so items are
duplicated or skipped between pages.

## Options considered
1. **Keep OFFSET, cap max page.** Cap at page 100 and tell heavy users to use the
   export API. Zero engineering cost, breaks two existing customers.
2. **Keyset (cursor) pagination.** `WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY
   created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT n`, opaque base64 cursor in the response.
   Requires a composite index and a client change.
3. **Materialised page cache in Redis.** Precompute page boundaries per customer.
   Adds a cache invalidation problem for every new order.

## Trade-offs
| Criterion | Capped OFFSET | Keyset | Redis page cache |
|---|---|---|---|
| p99 on deep pages | 310 ms and rising | ~1 ms, constant | ~1 ms, if warm |
| Stable under concurrent inserts | No | Yes | No |
| Random page access ("jump to page 400") | Yes | No | Yes |
| Total row count available | Yes, at a cost | Not cheaply | Yes |
| Client change required | No | Yes | No |
| New infrastructure | None | None | Redis keys, invalidation |
| Engineering cost | 1 day | 4 days including clients | 8 days plus ongoing bugs |

## Decision
Option 2, keyset pagination, with an explicit contract:
- Response envelope: `{ data: [...], nextCursor: string | null }`.
- Cursor is opaque base64 of `{ createdAt, id }`; clients must not parse it.
- Index: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer_created_id
  ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC);`
- The UI drops "jump to page N" for order history and uses infinite scroll plus
  date filters, which analytics show covers 98.6 percent of observed usage.
- Total counts are not returned; where a count is genuinely needed we return an
  approximate count from statistics, clearly labelled.
- The old `page`/`offset` parameters keep working for 2 releases, marked
  deprecated in the response headers, then are removed.

## Consequences
- Positive: deep pages become constant time; the duplicate/skip bug disappears;
  the index also serves the customer dashboard's "recent orders" query.
- Negative / accepted: no arbitrary page jumps; no exact total; the cursor is a
  contract we must keep stable, so changing the sort order later is a breaking
  change requiring a new cursor version field. We add `v` inside the cursor now
  so that future change is possible.
- Monitor: p99 of the endpoint by page depth, and the count of requests still
  using the deprecated `offset` parameter, which gates the removal.
- Revisit if product requires exact totals or arbitrary page access, or if the
  sort key must change.

Notice what the second ADR does that a code comment could not: it records that "jump to page 400" was consciously traded away with a usage number behind it, and it puts a version field inside the cursor because the author thought one step ahead about the next one-way door.

43.8.4 Design docs and RFCs

An ADR captures one decision. A design doc describes one system before it is built. Use a design doc when the work is bigger than a sprint, crosses teams, or touches money, auth or customer data.

A structure that works, in the order that gets read:

  1. Problem — what is broken or missing, with numbers. If you cannot state the problem without naming a solution, you are not ready.
  2. Goals and non-goals — the non-goals section prevents 80 percent of review scope creep.
  3. Constraints — deadline, team size, existing systems, compliance.
  4. Proposed design — diagrams, data model, API contract, failure behaviour.
  5. Alternatives considered — with the reason each was rejected.
  6. Migration and rollout — how we get from here to there, including rollback.
  7. Operational impact — new alerts, dashboards, runbooks, on-call load, cost.
  8. Risks and open questions — the honest list.

Two habits make design docs work. First, share the doc when it is 70 percent done, not when it is polished, because feedback on a finished document is expensive to act on and people can feel that. Second, timebox review: "comments by Thursday, I will decide Friday". Documents without a decision date collect comments forever.

An RFC is the same artefact with a wider audience and a formal comment period. Use it when the decision affects other teams: a shared library, an event schema everyone consumes, a change to the deployment platform.

43.8.5 Trade-off tables

The single most effective communication tool in engineering, and it takes five minutes. A trade-off table forces you to name the criteria before you compare, which is where honesty lives. If you invent the criteria after you have picked the winner, everyone can tell.

Rules that keep them honest:

  • Criteria first, options second. Write the rows before you fill the columns.
  • Include the criteria that make your preferred option look bad. Reviewers trust a table with a visible weakness far more than one where your favourite wins every row.
  • Use numbers where numbers exist: milliseconds, dollars per month, person-weeks, RPS. "Good/bad" ratings are opinions in a grid.
  • No more than four options and eight criteria. Beyond that, nobody reads it.

43.8.6 Spikes

A spike is a timeboxed experiment that answers one question. It is what you do instead of arguing, and instead of committing.

The discipline is in the framing: write the question and the timebox before you start. "Can PostgreSQL full-text search handle our catalogue query at acceptable latency, or do we need OpenSearch? Two days. Success means p95 under 80 ms on a copy of production data with our top 500 real queries."

Two rules. Spike code is throwaway; if you find yourself making it production quality, you are no longer spiking. And a spike must produce a written answer, even if the answer is "we could not determine this in two days, here is what we learned and what it would take". A spike that ends in a shrug in someone's head was two days spent for nothing.

43.8.7 Deciding under uncertainty

You will never have enough information. Here is the ladder I use, cheapest first:

  1. Can we not decide yet? Deferring is free if the cost of delay is low and the decision is not blocking anything. Deliberate deferral is a decision, and you should say so out loud rather than letting it drift.
  2. Can we make it a two-way door? Sometimes an interface, a feature flag or a strangler pattern converts a scary permanent decision into a reversible one. This is the highest-leverage move in the list.
  3. Can we buy information cheaply? A spike, a load test, a query against production data, a conversation with the team that already did this.
  4. Can we hedge? Ship the simple version behind an abstraction thin enough that swapping it later is a week, not a quarter. Be careful: abstractions built for imagined futures usually fit the actual future badly. Hedge only where the uncertainty is real and the abstraction is small.
  5. Decide and set a trigger. Choose the option that is best under the most likely scenario, write down the number that would prove you wrong, and put a review date in the calendar.

What you must not do is stall. An unmade decision blocks people, and the cost is invisible so nobody bills you for it. In my experience, on genuinely close calls, the cost of choosing the slightly worse option is almost always smaller than the cost of three more weeks of deliberation.

43.8.8 Disagree and commit

Sometimes the team, or the person with the decision rights, chooses the option you argued against. What happens next is a defining senior behaviour.

Do this: state your disagreement once, clearly, in writing, with your reasoning and what you predict will go wrong. Ask that it be recorded in the ADR under "options considered". Then commit fully. Build the chosen option as well as you would have built your own. Do not litigate it in Slack for the next month, do not quietly build a shadow version, and do not say "I told you so" when a predicted problem appears; instead, point at the recorded prediction calmly and propose the fix.

The reason this matters is that teams move at the speed of their unresolved arguments. A team where every decision can be reopened by anyone at any time cannot ship. And the recorded prediction is what makes it safe: your position is preserved, so committing does not mean pretending you agreed.

I have been overruled on plenty of decisions and been proved right on some of them. The times it improved anything were the times the disagreement was written down calmly in advance, so that when the trigger fired we could change course in a day without anybody having to lose face.

43.9 How seniors review code

A senior code review is not a search for style violations. It is a risk audit. The reviewer is asking one question in seven different ways: what will this do at 03:00 on the worst day of the quarter?

43.9.1 What they actually look for

Correctness under concurrency. Any read-then-write, any counter, any uniqueness check in application code, any "check if exists then insert". I mentally run two copies of the code at once. This is the number one source of real bugs that pass review.

// Review comment: "Two concurrent requests can both pass this check.
// Use ON CONFLICT with the unique index on (user_id, product_id) instead."
const existing = await this.repo.findOne({ where: { userId, productId } });
if (existing) throw new ConflictException('already in wishlist');
await this.repo.insert({ userId, productId });

Failure handling. Every await on a network call is a place the code can stop. Does it have a timeout? What does the caller see when it throws? Is the error swallowed? Is a retry safe here, or will it duplicate a side effect? Is there a transaction open across this call?

Data and migrations. Does the migration lock a big table? Is it rollback-safe? Is the new query covered by an index? Does this add an unbounded query with no LIMIT? Does the entity now serialise a field it should not?

Observability. If this code path misbehaves in production, what would I see? Is there a log line with identifiers at the failure branch, a metric for the outcome, and a span if it is a remote call? Silent catch blocks are a blocking comment every time.

Security. Is the query scoped to the tenant or user? Is input validated at the boundary? Is anything interpolated into SQL or a shell command? Does the response include fields the caller should not see? Is the new endpoint covered by a guard, and did the author think about who may call it?

Tests that would fail if the code were wrong. This is subtler than coverage. A test that mocks the repository and asserts the mock was called proves the code calls the mock. Does any test assert the actual invariant: that stock never goes negative, that a duplicate request produces one charge, that a 500 from the provider leaves the order in a recoverable state? I look for at least one test per pull request that would genuinely catch a real regression.

43.9.2 How to give feedback that lands

Review comments are read by a person who has just spent two days on this code, often at the end of their day. Tone is not politeness theatre; it determines whether the fix happens well or resentfully.

What works:

  • Ask instead of assert when you might be wrong. "What happens if two requests hit this at once?" invites thought. "This is a race condition" invites defensiveness, and is embarrassing when there is a unique constraint you did not see.
  • Explain the consequence, not just the rule. "No timeout here means a slow provider will exhaust the connection pool and take down the product pages too" teaches. "Add a timeout" does not.
  • Give the fix when it is short. A two-line suggestion saves a round trip.
  • Praise specifically and rarely. "The idempotency key handling here is exactly right, including the in-flight case" is worth a hundred "LGTM"s.
  • Take the big stuff off the pull request. If a comment would require redesigning the approach, that is a five-minute call, not a thread of eleven comments. Then summarise the outcome back on the PR so the record exists.
  • Review promptly. A perfect review two days late is worse for the team than a good review in two hours.

What does not work: sarcasm, a wall of thirty comments with no priority, relitigating a decision that already has an ADR, and reviewing the person rather than the code.

43.9.3 Blocking versus preference

The most common failure in code review is ambiguity about how serious a comment is. Fix it with explicit labels, which cost nothing and change everything:

Label Meaning Examples
blocking I will not approve until this changes Race condition, missing authorisation check, unbounded query, migration that locks a hot table, secret in code, swallowed error on a money path
question I do not understand; the answer may resolve it "Why is the transaction opened before the HTTP call?"
suggestion I think this is better; author decides Extract this into a method, use Promise.all here
nit Cosmetic; never blocks Naming, ordering, a comment typo
praise This is good, and I want it repeated Anything you want to see more of

Rules of thumb: if you have more than three blocking comments, the design was wrong and you should have a conversation instead. If you have zero blocking comments and eleven nits, you probably should have approved with comments. And never block on something you cannot explain the consequence of.

43.9.4 A review checklist

  • Do I understand what problem this solves? If not, ask before reviewing lines.
  • Concurrency: is any read-then-write, uniqueness check or counter safe with 50 parallel callers?
  • Transactions: are boundaries explicit, short, and free of network calls?
  • Failure: does every remote call have a timeout, and is the error path sensible?
  • Retries: is every side effect idempotent, or explicitly documented as not retryable?
  • Queries: is each new query served by an index, bounded by a LIMIT, and free of OFFSET on large tables?
  • Migrations: additive, rollback-safe, no long locks, backfill separated?
  • Authorisation: is the query scoped to the actor? Would a different tenant's id return data?
  • Input: validated at the boundary, sizes capped, nothing interpolated into SQL?
  • Output: DTO not entity, no sensitive fields, errors do not leak internals?
  • Observability: identifiers in logs, a metric for the outcome, no silent catch?
  • Tests: is there at least one test that fails if the core behaviour breaks?
  • Config: no hardcoded URLs, timeouts or secrets; new settings documented?
  • Deletion: did this leave dead code, an unused index or a stale flag behind?
  • Blast radius: if this throws in production, what breaks and how loudly?

Practical exercise

Take your last five approved pull requests from your team's repository and re-review them against the checklist above. Count how many issues you find that were missed. Then pick the single most common category and make it a shared checklist item for the team. Acceptance criteria: a written list of findings, and one process change agreed with the team.

43.10 How seniors handle incidents and pressure

An incident is the only time engineering is watched by everyone at once, and it is where seniority is most visible. Not because seniors debug faster — sometimes they do not — but because they impose structure on a situation that is trying to become chaos.

flowchart TB
    A["Alert fires or a report arrives"] --> B["Declare: severity, incident channel, one commander"]
    B --> C["Mitigate: restore service, do not diagnose yet"]
    C --> D{"Is the customer impact stopped?"}
    D -->|"No"| E["Next mitigation: rollback, flag off, failover, shed load, scale"]
    E --> D
    D -->|"Yes"| F["Diagnose with the pressure off"]
    F --> G["Fix forward, verify, monitor"]
    G --> H["Timeline, blameless postmortem, dated action items"]
    B --> I["Communicate on a fixed schedule"]
    I --> I

43.10.1 Mitigate first

The instinct under pressure is to find the root cause. Resist it. Stopping the bleeding and understanding the wound are different jobs, and the first one comes first.

The mitigation menu, roughly in order of speed:

  1. Roll back the last deploy. If the timing correlates, do it before you finish arguing about whether it is the cause. A rollback that turns out to be unnecessary costs ten minutes; a diagnosis that takes forty costs forty minutes of customers.
  2. Turn off the feature flag. Seconds, and surgically scoped.
  3. Fail over. Secondary payment provider, replica promotion, secondary region.
  4. Shed load. Disable exports, reports, non-critical consumers; tighten rate limits. Protect the core transaction.
  5. Scale the obvious constraint. More pods, bigger instance, more consumers, if the constraint is genuinely capacity.
  6. Restart. Legitimate for a leaked resource or a wedged process. Note what you lose: the process state that would have explained it. Take a heap snapshot first if you can afford 30 seconds.

The senior discipline is to say out loud: "we are mitigating, not diagnosing. Diagnosis is after." It gives everyone permission to stop theorising.

One caution: mitigations have their own blast radius. Failing over to a cold replica, or restarting a consumer group without checking the offset commit strategy, can turn an availability incident into a data incident. Ask "what could this mitigation break?" for two seconds before doing it. Two seconds, not two minutes.

43.10.2 Communicate on a schedule

The vacuum of silence during an incident gets filled with speculation, and speculation reaches customers. Fix it with a rhythm, not with heroic ad-hoc updates.

Pick an interval by severity: every 15 minutes for a customer-visible outage, every 30 for a degradation. Then post on the interval even when there is nothing new, because "no update, still investigating the payment provider timeout, next update at 14:45" is enormously calming and stops six people from asking.

A good update has four lines and no jargon:
