14:30 UTC - Checkout failures, ~35% of attempts since 14:06.
Impact: customers see an error at payment; carts are preserved.
Now: we have rolled back release 2026.3.11 and are watching error rates.
Next update: 14:45.

Separate the roles. The person typing commands should not also be writing updates to the executive channel. Split them: an incident commander who coordinates and communicates, and responders who investigate. On a small team, the commander can be a non-expert; their job is to run the process, keep the log and protect the responders from interruptions, and that is genuinely valuable work.

Say what you know, what you do not know, and what you are doing next. Never guess at a cause publicly during an incident. "It looks like a database issue" travels to a customer email in eleven minutes and is wrong 40 percent of the time.

43.10.3 Keep a log

Write timestamps as you go, in the incident channel. Every action, every observation, every hypothesis and whether it was ruled out.

14:06 first 5xx spike on /checkout, 12% error rate
14:09 paged; confirmed p99 4.2s on payment-service
14:11 checked deploys: release 2026.3.11 went out 14:02  <- correlation
14:13 pg_stat_activity shows 180 idle in transaction sessions   <- observation
14:15 rolled back 2026.3.11
14:19 error rate back to baseline; idle-in-transaction draining
14:26 hypothesis: new code opens a transaction before an HTTP call to the PSP

Three reasons this matters. During the incident, it stops two people from repeating the same check. After it, it is the postmortem timeline, written for free, while memory is accurate. And it is the only defence against the reconstruction bias that makes everyone believe afterwards that the cause was obvious.

43.10.4 Stay blameless, and mean it

"Blameless" does not mean pretending nobody made a mistake. It means the analysis targets the system that allowed the mistake to reach production, because that is the only part you can change.

An engineer ran a DELETE without a WHERE clause on production. Blame version: the engineer is careless, everyone is reminded to be careful, and it happens again in fourteen months with a different engineer. Blameless version: why did a human have write access to production data from a laptop, why was there no --dry-run step in the tool, why did the query run in a session without a transaction so it could not be rolled back, and why did we not notice for 40 minutes? Four fixable things. The careful-engineer fix is zero fixable things.

The practical test of whether your culture is blameless: does the person closest to the mistake write the postmortem and feel safe doing it? If they are quietly excluded, you have a blame culture with a polite vocabulary, and your next incident will be reported late or hidden.

43.10.5 Follow through

Most organisations are fine at responding and poor at following up. The incident ends, everyone is relieved, the action items go into a document, and 60 percent of them are never done. Then the same incident recurs and the postmortem says "we identified this last time".

Rules that make follow-through real: every action item has one named owner and a date, no owner is "the team", items go into the normal backlog with a link to the incident, and someone reviews open incident actions in a recurring meeting. Cap it: three real action items that get done beat fourteen that decorate a document.

And prioritise by class, not by instance. Do not just add a timeout to the one call that broke. Ask where else you have calls without timeouts, and fix the class with a shared HTTP client that has a default timeout, so the mistake becomes impossible rather than fixed once.

43.10.6 Pressure

Two practical things about your own head, because they change your effectiveness more than any tool.

Slow down externally when things speed up internally. Speak slower, type carefully, read the command before you press enter. The most damaging incident actions I have seen were made by very good engineers moving very fast in the first ten minutes. Say the destructive command out loud to another person before running it. That one habit has saved me twice.

You cannot debug for six hours. After about ninety minutes of an incident, hand over or bring in a second person, deliberately. Fresh eyes see the log line you have scrolled past four times. Tired engineers make the decisions that turn incidents into disasters.

43.11 How seniors communicate

43.11.1 Writing clearly

Most senior impact travels through writing. The rules are boring and effective:

  • Put the conclusion first. People read the first paragraph. Bottom-line-up-front: "I recommend we cap the export endpoint at 5,000 rows and move large exports to a background job. Details below."
  • Numbers, not adjectives. "Slow" is unactionable. "p99 is 4.2 s against our 500 ms target, on 60 RPS" is a decision input.
  • Short sentences. If a sentence has three clauses, it has three sentences hiding in it.
  • Write for the least-informed necessary reader. Define the acronym once. Nobody has ever been annoyed by clarity.
  • Say what you want. Every document ends with the decision you are asking for or the action you want. Documents without an ask get comments, not outcomes.

43.11.2 Explaining a trade-off to a product manager

The failure mode is explaining the mechanism. Product managers do not need to know about B-tree page splits. They need the choice expressed in time, risk and money, and they need you to have an opinion.

Here is a dialogue close to one I have had several times.

PM: Can we add the "download all my data" button this sprint? It looks small.

Engineer: The button is small. The download is not. Our biggest customers have around 400,000 orders. Building that file takes about 90 seconds and roughly 600 MB of memory, and the gateway cuts requests off at 30 seconds. If we do the simple version, it works for most customers and fails for our largest ones, which are the ones most likely to ask for it.

PM: So how long for the version that works?

Engineer: Two options. Option A, four days: the button starts a background job, and the customer gets an email with a link when it is ready, usually within two minutes. That is how every large product does it, so it will not feel odd. Option B, one day: we ship it now with a limit of the last 90 days, which covers about 85 percent of the requests support currently gets, and we add a note about contacting support for more.

PM: What happens if we do the naive version anyway?

Engineer: It works in the demo and fails in production for the accounts that matter, probably during a busy period, and it can take other requests down with it because of the memory. I would not ship that one. If the sprint is fixed, I would take option B this sprint and option A next.

PM: Let's do B now, and put A in next sprint's plan.

Notice: no jargon, real numbers, a named risk, two options with costs, a clear recommendation, and no attempt to win. That conversation takes three minutes and produces a better product decision than a week of tickets.

43.11.3 Saying no with options attached

A flat "no" makes you an obstacle and gets routed around. A "yes" to everything makes you unreliable. The senior pattern is: no to this shape, yes to a shape that works, with the cost of each.

The template: acknowledge the goal, state the specific problem with the request as posed, offer two alternatives with costs, recommend one, and make the trade-off owner's choice explicit.

"I understand we need per-customer pricing live for the campaign on the 14th. Building the full rules engine by then is not realistic; the honest estimate is five weeks and I would be guessing. What we can do by the 14th is hardcode the three tiers marketing has actually asked for, which is four days and covers the campaign, and then decide in March whether the rules engine is worth five weeks based on how often the tiers change. I recommend that. If the full engine is genuinely required for the 14th, then something else in the sprint has to move, and I would need to know what."

That last sentence matters. Scope, time and quality: name which one is moving, and let the person with the authority choose. What you must never do is silently absorb the pressure by cutting quality, because that debt is invisible until it becomes an incident.

43.11.4 Estimating honestly

Estimates are probability distributions that everyone insists on hearing as a single number. Give ranges, with the reason for the width.

  • "Three to five days. The width is because I do not know yet whether the provider's sandbox supports partial refunds. I can find out in two hours, and then I can narrow it."
  • "Two weeks if the data is as clean as the sample suggests; four if it is not. I will know by Wednesday."

Three habits keep you credible. Name the assumption that would blow the estimate up. Say when you will have a better number, and then actually give it. And when you are going to miss, say so as early as you know, not on the due date. Nobody minds a revised estimate on Tuesday. Everyone minds a surprise on Friday afternoon.

Never estimate under social pressure in a meeting. "I'll come back to you this afternoon with a number" is always available and always better than a number you invented to end the silence.

43.11.5 Documenting for the reader in two years

Write for the engineer who joins after you have left. That person has the code, so do not narrate the code. They need what the code cannot tell them:

  • Why it is this way, especially the parts that look wrong.
  • What was tried and rejected.
  • The invariants: "an order in paid must have exactly one payments row with captured status; the reconciliation job in jobs/reconcile.ts enforces this nightly."
  • The operational facts: which alerts exist, what the runbook says, which third parties are involved and what their failure modes are.
  • The traps: "do not add an index on events.payload, we tried, it doubled the write latency; the query it was for now uses the summary table."

Put it in the repository next to the code, not in a wiki that dies. README.md per module, docs/adr/ for decisions, docs/runbooks/ for operations. Documentation that lives with the code gets updated in the same pull request as the change; documentation somewhere else does not.

43.12 How seniors grow others and themselves

43.12.1 Mentoring

Mentoring is not answering questions. It is calibrating how much struggle is productive.

The rule I use: give the question, not the answer, when there is time; give the answer with the reasoning when there is not. "Where would you look first?" beats "check pg_stat_activity" during a calm afternoon. During an incident, say "check pg_stat_activity for idle in transaction, here is why", and teach afterwards.

Two more things that work. Delegate the whole problem, not tasks: "you own the payment retry work, I'm your reviewer" produces growth; "implement this function I designed" produces typing. And be public about your own uncertainty and mistakes. A senior who says "I got this wrong last year and here is what I learned" makes it safe for everyone else to be honest, and honesty is what makes a team fast.

43.12.2 Pairing and design reviews

Pair on the hard part, not the whole day. Ninety minutes on the concurrency design or the tricky migration transfers more than a week of side-by-side typing, and it does not exhaust anybody.

Run design reviews before code exists, not after. A 30-minute conversation over a diagram catches the boundary mistake that would have cost three weeks. The cheapest possible design review is one sentence in a Slack channel: "planning to solve X by doing Y, any objections?" It has saved me more rework than any formal process.

43.12.3 Leaving the codebase better

Not "rewrite everything you touch", which is how you become the person nobody wants to review. The habit is small and constant: while you are in a file, fix the misleading name, add the missing index, delete the dead branch, add the test that was obviously missing, replace the magic number with a named constant.

Also: delete things. Unused endpoints, dead feature flags, unused indexes, obsolete jobs, commented-out code. Every dead thing is something a future engineer must read and be uncertain about. Deletion is the most under-rated senior activity, and Git remembers everything anyway.

43.12.4 Reading source code and postmortems

Two habits that compound faster than any course.

Read the source of the tools you use. When you wonder how TypeORM builds a transaction, or how BullMQ guarantees a job is not processed twice, open the file. It is ordinary TypeScript written by ordinary people. Doing this a few times permanently removes the sense that libraries are magic, and it makes you dramatically better at debugging them.

Read public postmortems. The write-ups published by large infrastructure providers, and the ones your own company writes, are years of expensive experience for an hour of reading. You will notice the same shapes recurring: retry storms, a config change with a wider blast radius than anyone realised, a failover that had never been tested, a queue that filled because a consumer got slower, a certificate nobody owned. Recognising those shapes is most of what "instinct" turns out to be.

43.12.5 Shipping side projects to real production

There is a category of knowledge you cannot get from work if your work hands you a platform: what it costs, what breaks, and what it takes to keep something alive when nobody else is responsible.

Build something small, put it on the internet with a real domain and TLS, add a database, put it behind a CDN, set up an alert, and keep it running for a year. You will learn certificate renewal, backup restores, cost surprises, dependency upgrades, and the specific misery of a disk filling at 04:00. It is the cheapest available simulation of ownership, and the lessons transfer completely.

43.13 Anti-mindsets

The failure modes I see most often, and the correction for each.

Anti-mindset What it looks like Why it hurts The correction
Resume-driven development Choosing Kafka, Kubernetes or GraphQL because it is good for your career The team carries the operational cost for years; you leave in 18 months Choose the boring tool; get your learning from side projects and reading
Cargo cult "Netflix does it this way" Their constraints are not yours: their scale, staffing and failure budget are different by orders of magnitude Ask what problem it solved for them, and whether you have that problem
Premature optimisation Micro-tuning a function that runs 5 times a day; a cache before a measurement Complexity for no gain, and it hides the real bottleneck Measure first. The bottleneck is almost never where you think
Gold plating Building the configurable, pluggable version of a thing with one use case Every reader pays the abstraction tax forever Build for the second use case when it arrives, not the imagined third
Hero culture The same person fixes every incident at 03:00 and is celebrated for it Burnout, a single point of failure, and no incentive to fix root causes Rotate on-call, write runbooks, reward prevention over rescue
"Not my problem" The bug is in another team's service, so it stops with you Customers do not care about your org chart; the problem sits in the gap Drive it to an owner, hand over with context, follow up
Fear of deleting code Commented-out blocks, dead flags, unused endpoints kept "just in case" Every dead line is read, feared and worked around by future engineers Delete it. Git has it. If you are unsure, check the metrics, then delete it
Arguing about formatting Twenty comments on naming, none on the missing timeout Burns review capital on the cheapest issues and misses the expensive ones Automate it: Prettier, ESLint, a linter in CI. Then never discuss it again

Two more worth naming because they wear a disguise. Perfectionism presents as high standards but is often fear of being judged; the tell is a branch that is four weeks old and 90 percent done. And cynicism presents as experience — "we tried that, it won't work" — but it is a way of avoiding the risk of trying. Both are common in strong engineers who have been burned. The antidote to both is shipping something small and reversible this week.

43.14 The senior's daily checklist

Compact versions, for actual use.

Before I finish a design:

  • The requirement is written with a number in it.
  • This is the simplest thing that meets it; I can name what each added component buys.
  • I know what breaks first at 10x and roughly where the wall is.
  • Every dependency has a named behaviour when it is down.
  • Every remote call has a timeout, and every side effect has a duplication defence.
  • I named the source of truth for each important fact.
  • I know the blast radius, and it is acceptable to the business.
  • I classified this as a one-way or two-way door and applied the right amount of process.
  • Alerts, dashboards, runbook and on-call owner exist or are in the plan.
  • I wrote down why, including the option I rejected and the trigger to revisit.

Before I open a pull request:

  • I reviewed it myself, as a stranger, against the concurrency and failure questions.
  • New queries have indexes; new migrations are additive and rollback-safe.
  • Input validated at the boundary; queries scoped to the actor; DTOs not entities.
  • There is at least one test that fails if the core behaviour breaks.
  • The failure branches log identifiers, and the outcome is measurable.
  • The description says what problem this solves, what I considered, and what to watch after deploy.

Before I deploy:

  • Old and new versions can run at the same time.
  • It is rollback-safe, or the PR says explicitly that it is not and why.
  • Migrations are separate from the deploy and bounded in lock time.
  • I know which dashboard I am watching and which number tells me to roll back.
  • Risky behaviour is behind a flag that defaults to off.
  • Someone other than me knows this is going out.

During an incident:

  • Severity declared, channel open, one commander named.
  • Mitigating first; diagnosis is after.
  • Considered rollback and feature flag before anything clever.
  • Timestamped log running in the channel.
  • Updates on a fixed interval, even when there is nothing new.
  • Checked what my mitigation could break before running it.
  • Handing over if I have been on it more than ninety minutes.
  • Postmortem scheduled, timeline captured, three owned action items with dates.

Senior Checklist — Part 43

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I run the architecture, database, distributed, production, security and business question sets automatically on every design
  • I classify decisions as one-way or two-way doors and vary my process accordingly
  • I can write an ADR in twenty minutes that a stranger could act on in two years
  • I build honest trade-off tables, including the criteria that make my preferred option look bad
  • My code reviews label blocking versus preference, and find concurrency and failure bugs rather than style
  • I mitigate before I diagnose, and I communicate on a fixed schedule during incidents
  • I keep a timestamped incident log and run blameless postmortems with owned, dated actions
  • I can explain a technical trade-off to a product manager in three minutes using time, risk and money
  • I give estimates as ranges with the assumption that would break them
  • I say no with options attached, and I name which of scope, time or quality is moving
  • I leave the codebase better, delete dead things, and grow the people around me
  • I can name the anti-mindsets I personally fall into, and the correction for each

Part 43 — Key Takeaways

  • Seniority is measured in removed uncertainty, not in years, syntax or the number of tools you can name.
  • The transferable skill is a question set that fires automatically: can it time out, duplicate, arrive late, arrive out of order, partially succeed; who owns the truth; what happens when the dependency is down.
  • The simplest thing that meets a stated numeric requirement wins; every added component is a permanent tax paid in operations, onboarding and 03:00 debugging.
  • Classify every decision as a one-way or two-way door, and spend process accordingly; both freezing on reversible choices and sprinting through irreversible ones are failures.
  • A timeout is not a failure, it is unknown; that single sentence forces idempotency keys, reconciliation and a defined source of truth.
  • Blast radius matters more than uptime: correctness failures cost far more than availability failures, and juniors systematically underrate them.
  • Data decisions are the ones you cannot take back: partitioning, ownership, index cost, keeping the facts rather than only the derived state.
  • "Done" means running safely in production: alerted on a business signal, deployable, rollback-safe, migratable, debuggable at 03:00, and owned by a named rotation.
  • Write decisions down at the time you make them, with the alternatives and the numeric trigger that would make you revisit; the ADR is for the stranger who arrives in two years.
  • In incidents, mitigate before you diagnose, communicate on a fixed schedule, keep a timestamped log, stay blameless, and fix the class of problem rather than the instance.
  • Express engineering trade-offs in time, risk and money, and always arrive with an opinion and two options.
  • Your throughput caps your value; the people you make better do not, which is why review, pairing, writing and deleting are the job, not overhead.

Part 44 — Junior to Principal: What Is Expected at Each Level

Every company writes its own career ladder, and most of them are vague in the same way: "demonstrates increasing impact and scope". True, and useless on a Monday morning when you want to know what to do differently.

This part is the concrete version. It describes what each level actually looks like in a backend team building NestJS services on PostgreSQL, Redis and Kafka: what you do, what you are trusted to own, what you have stopped getting wrong, and what would get you to the next level. Titles vary between companies — some have no Staff level, some call Principal "Distinguished" — but the behaviours are remarkably consistent, because they are shaped by the same underlying thing: how much uncertainty you can absorb and how far your work travels beyond your own hands.

44.1 The levels in one page

Five dimensions separate the levels. Everything else is downstream of these.

Dimension Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Scope A task A feature or component A system or service Multiple systems, a team's area or a domain An engineering-wide area, or the company's technical direction
Ambiguity Told what to build and often how Told what to build, decides how Told the problem, defines what to build Finds the problem worth solving Decides which problems the organisation should have
Impact Your own output Your team's feature velocity Your team's outcomes and reliability Several teams' outcomes The company's ability to build and operate systems
Influence Learns from others Helps peers Sets the bar on a team; mentors Aligns teams without authority; writes the strategy Changes how the organisation thinks; hires and sets standards
Time horizon Days to a sprint Weeks A quarter to two quarters One to two years Two to five years 
flowchart LR
    J["Junior: a task, days"] --> M["Mid: a feature, weeks"]
    M --> S["Senior: a system, a quarter"]
    S --> St["Staff: several teams, one to two years"]
    St --> P["Principal: the organisation, two to five years"]
    S --> EM["Engineering Manager: people and delivery"]
    St --> D["Director: organisation design"]

44.1.1 The title versus the behaviour

Two things are worth saying plainly.

Titles are calibrated locally. A "Senior Engineer" at a 30-person startup and at a 3,000-person platform company can be two levels apart in either direction. Do not use your title as evidence about yourself, in either direction. Use the behaviours.

Behaviour comes before the title, always. Nobody is promoted to Senior and then starts making senior decisions. The sequence is: you start operating at the next level, you do it consistently for two or three quarters on work that matters, other people notice without you telling them, and then the title catches up. If you are waiting for the title to start behaving differently, you will wait forever. This is the single most common career mistake I see, and it costs people years.

The corollary: if you have been operating at the next level visibly for a year and the title has not followed, that is information about the company, not about you. Ask directly what is missing, get a specific answer, and if the answer is not specific, consider that promotion may be faster elsewhere.

44.1.2 The individual contributor track versus management

Beyond senior, the ladder forks. Both branches are the same seniority; they differ in the material you work with.

The IC track (Staff, Principal) scales your technical judgment: you work through designs, standards, prototypes, reviews and writing. You still code, less than before, and mostly on the hard or risky parts. Your leverage comes from decisions that many people build on.

The management track works through people: hiring, growth, performance, prioritisation, and the health of a team. It is a different job, not a promotion from engineering. The most common mistake is taking it because it looks like the only way up; the second most common is believing you can do it "part time" while remaining the team's main coder.

Two honest signals. If your best days are the ones where you unblocked four people and shaped a plan, management may suit you. If your best days are the ones where you solved something nobody else could and left a design that will hold for three years, stay on the IC track. And note that the switch is reversible in both directions in most healthy companies, though returning to IC after three years of management costs six months of catching up.

44.2 Expectations by engineering area

This is the heart of the part. For each area you get a five-column table with three unlabeled rows, always in the same order:

  1. What they typically do at that level.
  2. What they are trusted to own without supervision.
  3. The failure they have stopped making — often the most diagnostic row.

Then two or three paragraphs of context and one concrete example per level. Read the row for your current level, then read the one to the right; the gap between them is your development plan.

44.2.1 Programming and TypeScript

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Writes working code with review guidance; uses the types the codebase already has Writes clean, tested code independently; uses generics, unions and narrowing correctly Designs types that make invalid states unrepresentable; keeps strict on and knows why Sets language standards across teams; owns shared libraries and lint policy Decides language and runtime direction; judges when TypeScript is not the right tool for a workload
A function or class inside an existing module A feature end to end within a service A service's internal architecture and type contracts The shared kernel: SDKs, error types, config libraries The engineering-wide programming model
Stopped fighting the compiler with any Stopped writing types that merely describe the shape after the fact Stopped clever type gymnastics that nobody else can read Stopped adding abstractions that only the author benefits from Stopped believing a language choice will fix an organisational problem

TypeScript maturity is not measured by knowledge of conditional types. It is measured by whether your types prevent bugs at compile time that would otherwise be caught in production. A senior models an order as a discriminated union where status: 'paid' carries paidAt and paymentId as required fields, so the "paid order with no payment id" bug cannot be written. That is worth more than any amount of mapped-type cleverness.

The other senior marker is knowing where types stop. Data crossing a boundary — HTTP body, queue message, database row, third-party response — is unknown until validated at runtime. An interface asserting that a Kafka payload has a userId is a comment with syntax highlighting, not a guarantee.

  • Junior: implements calculateShippingCost against an existing interface, with tests, after two review rounds.
  • Mid: builds the whole shipping module, including DTOs with class-validator, and handles the nullable-address edge case unprompted.
  • Senior: replaces a status: string with a discriminated union across the order domain, deleting nine defensive if statements and one class of production bug.
  • Staff: writes the shared @company/errors package with typed error codes that three teams' clients depend on, and versions it properly.
  • Principal: decides that the new video-transcoding pipeline is written in Go rather than Node, with a written rationale about CPU-bound workloads, and sets what "supported language" means for the company.

44.2.2 Node.js runtime

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Uses async/await; knows promises resolve later Understands the event loop, microtasks, and why blocking code hurts Diagnoses event-loop lag, memory growth and GC pauses from production evidence Sets runtime standards: versions, flags, container memory ratios Decides where Node belongs in the architecture and where it does not
A handler that awaits correctly A module that does not block the loop The runtime behaviour of a service under load The Node platform baseline across services The runtime strategy and its cost model
Stopped using sync file APIs in a request path Stopped await-ing in a loop where parallelism was safe Stopped guessing at memory issues instead of taking a heap snapshot Stopped letting each team pick a different Node version and flag set Stopped using one runtime for every workload out of habit

The mid-to-senior jump here is diagnostic ability. A mid-level engineer knows the event loop exists; a senior has looked at event_loop_lag_p99 climbing to 400 ms during a report generation and traced it to a synchronous JSON.stringify on a 40 MB object, then moved the work to a worker thread and proved the fix on the graph.

Memory is the other divider. --max-old-space-size set equal to the container limit is the classic OOMKill: V8 delays a major collection because it believes it has room, and the kernel kills the process first. Seniors know the rule of thumb that resident memory runs 150-250 MB above the heap limit, and they set the container limit above that, not equal to it.

  • Junior: fixes a bug by awaiting a promise that was previously fired and forgotten.
  • Mid: replaces a sequential loop of 200 HTTP calls with a bounded-concurrency batch of 10, cutting a job from 90 s to 12 s.
  • Senior: catches a slow memory leak from an unbounded Map cache using heap snapshots taken 30 minutes apart, and adds an LRU bound plus a heap-usage alert.
  • Staff: standardises Node 22 across nine services with a shared base image, one upgrade playbook, and a compatibility matrix for native modules.
  • Principal: writes the position paper on when a workload should leave Node for a JVM or Go service, with cost and latency numbers from real internal benchmarks.

44.2.3 NestJS and application architecture

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Adds controllers and services to existing modules Builds modules with correct providers, guards, pipes and interceptors Designs module boundaries, the request lifecycle and cross-cutting concerns Defines the reference application architecture used by several teams Sets the architectural direction and the criteria for splitting or merging services
An endpoint A feature module A service's structure and its public contracts The shared application template and libraries The system landscape
Stopped putting business logic in controllers Stopped injecting a repository into a controller to save time Stopped letting modules import each other's internals Stopped shipping a template that assumes every service is a CRUD API Stopped solving organisational coupling with technical splits

The senior skill in NestJS is not knowing more decorators. It is deciding what belongs in a guard versus an interceptor versus the service, keeping the domain logic free of framework types, and enforcing module boundaries so the codebase can be split later without a data migration.

Watch for the tell: in a mature codebase, the domain services do not import @nestjs/common except for @Injectable. Framework concerns live at the edges. That single property is what makes a five-year-old codebase upgradable.

  • Junior: adds GET /products/:id to the catalogue controller and wires it to the existing service.
  • Mid: builds the whole promotions module with a ValidationPipe, a caching interceptor and unit tests for the service.
  • Senior: introduces a module-boundary lint rule and a domain-event bus so that the orders module never queries inventory tables directly.
  • Staff: publishes the service template: health checks, graceful shutdown, config schema, logging, tracing, error filter, all wired and tested, so a new service is production-ready on day one.
  • Principal: decides the company runs a modular monolith plus three extracted services rather than fifteen microservices, and writes the criteria for future extractions.

44.2.4 API design

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Adds endpoints following existing patterns Designs a resource with correct status codes, pagination and validation Designs contracts that can evolve: versioning, deprecation, idempotency, error shapes Sets API standards and governance across teams Decides the company's API strategy: public surface, partner model, protocol choices
One endpoint One resource A service's public API and its compatibility guarantees The API style guide and review process The external contract with customers and partners
Stopped returning 200 with an error body Stopped returning entities directly from controllers Stopped making breaking changes without a deprecation path Stopped letting three teams invent three error formats Stopped adding public surface faster than the company can support it

The defining senior insight is that an API is a promise you cannot take back. Once a mobile app in the field consumes your response, that shape is frozen for as long as old versions run, which for mobile is years. Everything follows from that: additive changes only, explicit versioning, deprecation with dates and metrics, and pagination that does not break when data shifts underneath the client.

Error design is the neglected half. A consistent envelope with a stable machine-readable code, a human message, and a correlationId is worth more to your integrators than any amount of endpoint elegance, because it is what they build their retry and alerting logic on.

  • Junior: adds POST /reviews returning 201 with a Location header after being shown the pattern.
  • Mid: designs /orders with filtering, sorting, pagination, and DTO validation that rejects unknown fields.
  • Senior: migrates order history to keyset pagination with a versioned opaque cursor, keeps the old parameters for two releases, and tracks deprecated usage to decide when to remove them.
  • Staff: writes the API style guide — error envelope, pagination, idempotency keys, naming, versioning — and gets four teams to adopt it by making it the default in the service template.
  • Principal: decides the partner integration is webhooks plus a REST API rather than a GraphQL gateway, based on the integration capabilities of actual partners.

44.2.5 SQL and data modelling

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Writes joins and aggregates; uses the ORM for most access Writes efficient multi-table queries; models tables with sensible keys and constraints Models for invariants, growth and change; reaches for raw SQL when the ORM is wrong Sets modelling standards and data ownership rules across services Decides the company's data architecture: what is relational, what is not, who owns what
A query A table and its access patterns A domain's schema and its evolution path The data ownership map and the review bar The data platform strategy
Stopped using SELECT * in application code Stopped modelling with nullable columns instead of proper relations Stopped encoding invariants only in application code Stopped letting services reach into each other's tables Stopped duplicating the same entity in six systems with no owner

Modelling is where the biggest long-term differences appear, because the schema outlives the code. A senior asks what must always be true and pushes it into the database: unique constraints, foreign keys, check constraints, exclusion constraints for overlapping ranges. Application-level validation is a convenience; the database is the only place where a rule cannot be bypassed by a script, a backfill or a second service.

The other senior habit is preserving facts. Store the events that produced the state, not only the state. Almost every "we cannot answer that question" moment in a company's data history is a moment where somebody stored only the current value.

  • Junior: writes a three-table join with a GROUP BY for a report, guided in review.
  • Mid: designs the subscriptions schema with proper foreign keys and a unique constraint on active subscriptions per customer.
  • Senior: adds an append-only subscription_events table, a check constraint enforcing non-negative balances, and range partitioning on the events table before it grows.
  • Staff: publishes the data ownership map — one writer per table, cross-service reads through APIs, views for analytics — and enforces it in design review.
  • Principal: decides the customer master record lives in one system with the others subscribing to change events, ending three years of duplicated customer data.

44.2.6 PostgreSQL operations and performance

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Runs queries; knows an index makes things faster Reads EXPLAIN ANALYZE and adds the right index Diagnoses locks, bloat, vacuum, replication lag, connection exhaustion and plan changes under production pressure Sets database standards, capacity model and review gates for all teams Owns the database strategy: engines, topology, managed versus self-run, DR posture
A query's performance A table's indexes and query patterns A database's health and its operational limits The fleet: sizing, upgrades, pooling, backups The data platform and its risk profile
Stopped testing performance on a 500-row dev database Stopped adding an index per slow query without auditing existing ones Stopped guessing at causes instead of reading pg_stat_activity and pg_stat_statements Stopped letting each team discover connection limits during an incident Stopped treating the database as infrastructure somebody else worries about

The senior level here is defined by comfort with the operational catalogue. When latency triples, they check for lock waits, idle-in-transaction sessions, a plan flip after an ANALYZE, autovacuum falling behind, or a replica lagging — in a deliberate order, using evidence rather than folklore.

Connection management is the most common blind spot. Pods times pool size times the rolling-deploy surge is the number that hits max_connections, and it is discovered during a deploy at peak traffic if nobody computed it in advance. A senior computes it in advance and puts PgBouncer in front when the arithmetic demands it.

  • Junior: adds an index on orders.customer_id after a slow query is pointed out.
  • Mid: reads a plan, spots a Seq Scan with a huge Rows Removed by Filter, and fixes it with a composite index in the right column order.
  • Senior: resolves a production stall by finding 180 idle-in-transaction sessions caused by an HTTP call inside a transaction, then fixes the pattern and adds an alert on the metric.
  • Staff: rolls out PgBouncer and a standard pool-sizing formula across nine services, and runs the major-version upgrade programme with a tested rollback.
  • Principal: decides that analytics moves off the primary to a separate warehouse fed by change data capture, with a cost and staffing plan.

44.2.7 ORM usage

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Uses repository methods and relations as documented Controls eager and lazy loading; avoids N+1; uses the query builder Knows exactly what SQL the ORM emits and when to bypass it; owns transaction boundaries Sets ORM conventions, migration tooling and the escape hatch policy Decides whether an ORM is used at all, and what the persistence strategy is
A repository call A feature's data access A service's persistence layer and its transaction semantics The shared data-access conventions The persistence approach across the estate
Stopped triggering N+1 without noticing Stopped loading whole entity graphs to read two fields Stopped letting the ORM own transaction boundaries implicitly Stopped tolerating three different migration tools in one estate Stopped arguing about ORMs as an identity rather than a trade-off

The senior position on ORMs is unsentimental: they are excellent for the 90 percent of access that is simple CRUD, and actively harmful for complex reads, bulk operations and anything where the exact plan matters. Use the ORM for entity persistence and unit-of-work semantics; drop to raw SQL for reporting queries, upserts at volume, window functions and recursive queries. The tell of maturity is a codebase where both coexist without apology.

Transaction boundaries are the senior's real concern. Who opens the transaction, how long it stays open, whether a network call happens inside it, and whether a retry is safe. Those questions decide whether your database survives a bad afternoon.

  • Junior: uses find with relations and does not know a join was generated.
  • Mid: spots 200 queries in a log for one request and fixes the N+1 with a single leftJoinAndSelect.
  • Senior: moves an outbox insert and the order write into one explicit dataSource.transaction, removes an HTTP call from inside it, and documents the retry semantics.
  • Staff: standardises on one migration tool with a review gate for lock-taking statements, across every service.
  • Principal: sets the direction that read models for reporting are built as SQL views and materialised tables owned by the data team, not as ORM entities.

44.2.8 Caching

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Adds a cache with a TTL where told Chooses keys and TTLs; understands invalidation basics Designs for stampedes, staleness budgets, hot keys and cache-down behaviour Sets caching standards, memory policy and the shared Redis topology Decides the caching strategy and its cost/consistency posture company-wide
A cached value A feature's caching behaviour A service's cache design and failure modes The Redis platform and its limits The consistency model the business accepts
Stopped caching without a TTL Stopped caching data that must be correct immediately Stopped assuming the database can absorb a cold cache Stopped letting every team share one Redis with no eviction policy Stopped paying for caching complexity where correctness was the requirement

The senior questions about a cache are always the same three: what is the staleness budget in seconds, what happens when Redis is unavailable, and can the database survive the cold-start load. A cache designed without answering the third one is an outage amplifier, because the failure of the cache and the overload of the database happen at the same moment.

The second-order skills are stampede protection (a lock or a single-flight so a thousand concurrent misses become one database query), negative caching so a missing key does not hammer the database, and jittered TTLs so a thousand keys do not expire in the same second.

  • Junior: adds a 60-second cache to a product endpoint using @nestjs/cache-manager.
  • Mid: designs the key scheme with a version prefix so a deploy can invalidate a whole namespace, and picks TTLs per data type.
  • Senior: adds single-flight protection with a Redis lock, a stale-while-revalidate path, jittered TTLs, and a fallback that limits concurrent database calls when Redis is down.
  • Staff: separates the shared Redis into cache and session instances with different maxmemory-policy settings, because eviction of sessions was logging people out.
  • Principal: rules that financial balances are never served from cache, and defines which data classes may be cached and for how long.

44.2.9 Messaging and async

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Publishes and consumes messages using existing wiring Builds a consumer with retries, a dead-letter queue and idempotent handling Designs topics, partitions, ordering guarantees, replay and poison-message handling Owns the messaging platform, schema governance and consumer standards Decides whether the company is event-driven, and where the boundaries are
A producer or consumer A queue-backed feature A service's async contracts and their failure behaviour The broker fleet and the event catalogue The company's integration model
Stopped assuming a message is delivered exactly once Stopped acking before the work is durably done Stopped ignoring consumer lag until it becomes an incident Stopped letting teams publish events with no schema or compatibility rules Stopped adding a broker where a synchronous call was correct

The bar for senior is designing for at-least-once delivery as a fact of life. Every handler is idempotent, ordering is achieved by partition key rather than hope, retries have backoff and a limit, and there is a dead-letter path with a documented human procedure. "What happens to a message we cannot process?" has an answer that does not involve losing it.

The other senior skill is capacity thinking about queues. Partition count is chosen from the recovery requirement — how fast must a four-hour backlog drain — not from the steady-state rate. Consumer lag is alerted on in units of time, not messages, because "9 million messages behind" means nothing without a drain rate.

  • Junior: adds a BullMQ job that sends a welcome email when a user registers.
  • Mid: adds exponential backoff, a dead-letter queue, and a processed_messages table so a redelivery does not send a second email.
  • Senior: keys the order events by order_id for per-order ordering, sizes partitions for a 30-minute recovery, and adds a lag alert measured in seconds.
  • Staff: introduces a schema registry with backwards-compatibility checks in CI, ending a class of consumer breakages across five teams.
  • Principal: decides which domains communicate by events and which stay synchronous, and writes the criteria so teams stop relitigating it.

44.2.10 Distributed systems

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Knows services call each other over a network that can fail Handles timeouts and retries; understands eventual consistency Reasons about partial failure, idempotency, ordering, consensus limits and sagas as a matter of routine Designs consistency and failure models spanning teams Sets the company's consistency, latency and availability posture
One call One integration A distributed workflow end to end The interaction model between systems The trade-offs the business is signing up for
Stopped assuming the network is reliable Stopped retrying non-idempotent operations Stopped treating a timeout as a failure rather than as unknown Stopped letting each team invent its own saga pattern Stopped promising strong consistency across systems that cannot provide it

The mid-to-senior step is internalising that partial failure is the normal case, not the exception. Every design gets the interrogation: can it time out, duplicate, arrive late, arrive out of order, partially succeed; what is the source of truth; what happens when the dependency is down. Part 43 — The Senior Engineering Mindset is that question set in full.

The staff-and-above skill is choosing where consistency boundaries sit. Inside a boundary, a database transaction gives you correctness cheaply. Across a boundary, you are paying for eventual consistency with compensations, reconciliation and customer-visible intermediate states. Drawing that boundary in the right place is worth more than any amount of clever saga code.

  • Junior: adds a try/catch around a service call after a review comment.
  • Mid: adds a 2-second timeout and three retries with jitter to the shipping-provider client.
  • Senior: replaces a two-phase-commit fantasy with an outbox plus a saga that has explicit compensation for a failed dispatch, and a reconciliation job.
  • Staff: defines the standard saga and outbox implementation as a shared library so five teams stop writing subtly broken versions.
  • Principal: writes the position that order state is eventually consistent with a 5-second target and payment state is strongly consistent, and gets product and finance to agree.

44.2.11 Reliability

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Fixes bugs; follows the runbook when paged Adds health checks, graceful shutdown, and sensible retries Designs for blast radius: timeouts, bulkheads, circuit breakers, load shedding, degradation Sets SLOs and error budgets; drives reliability programmes across teams Sets the availability posture and what the company will pay for it
A bug fix A service's basic resilience A service's failure behaviour under stress The reliability model of a product area The company's risk appetite
Stopped assuming happy paths Stopped retrying without backoff or a cap Stopped adding redundancy without testing the failover Stopped setting SLOs nobody uses to make decisions Stopped chasing nines without a business case

Senior reliability work is mostly about limiting damage rather than preventing failure. Timeouts stop a slow dependency from becoming your outage. Bulkheads stop one endpoint from consuming every connection. Circuit breakers stop retry storms from finishing off a struggling service. Graceful degradation keeps the core transaction alive while a peripheral feature is off.

Above senior, the work becomes economic: SLOs that reflect what users actually notice, an error budget that gives teams permission to ship when they are within it and forces reliability work when they are not, and honest conversations about what another nine costs.

  • Junior: follows the runbook to restart a stuck consumer at 02:00 and writes what happened in the channel.
  • Mid: adds @nestjs/terminus health checks and graceful shutdown so deploys stop dropping requests.
  • Senior: adds a bulkhead of four concurrent payment calls per pod and a circuit breaker, converting a provider outage from a site-wide failure into slow checkouts.
  • Staff: introduces SLOs for the five customer-facing journeys with error budgets, and gets the alerting rewritten to page only on budget burn.
  • Principal: rejects a multi-region proposal with an analysis showing 99.95 percent single-region meets the contractual requirement at a third of the cost, and defines the conditions that would change the answer.

44.2.12 Security

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Follows auth patterns; does not commit secrets Implements authn and authz correctly; validates input; understands common OWASP issues Threat-models a design; owns authorisation architecture, secret lifecycle and data exposure Sets security standards, review gates and the incident process for vulnerabilities Owns the security posture and its trade-offs with delivery speed
A guarded endpoint A feature's security controls A service's threat model and its blast radius when credentials leak The security baseline across teams The company's risk position and compliance obligations
Stopped trusting client-side checks Stopped forgetting object-level authorisation Stopped treating security as a review step rather than a design input Stopped relying on individual diligence instead of defaults that are safe Stopped treating security as a blocker rather than a design constraint with a budget

The single most valuable senior security habit is asking "who is allowed to call this, and how do I make the wrong answer impossible?" Object-level authorisation — verifying this order belongs to this caller — is the most common serious vulnerability in real systems, and the fix is structural: scope the query, not an if after the fetch.

The second is designing for leaks rather than only against them. Short-lived tokens, narrow scopes, tested rotation, and secrets that no human ever holds. A leaked credential should be an inconvenience, and whether it is one was decided months earlier.

  • Junior: uses the existing JwtAuthGuard and puts the API key in the config rather than in the code.
  • Mid: adds ValidationPipe with forbidNonWhitelisted, scopes queries by customerId, and fixes an IDOR found in review.
  • Senior: threat-models the file-upload feature: signed URLs, MIME validation, size caps, virus scanning, and no user-controlled paths; then adds cross-tenant access tests.
  • Staff: makes the safe path the default: a repository base class that requires a tenant scope, secret scanning in CI, and a dependency policy with an SLA on critical CVEs.
  • Principal: decides the company holds no raw card data and integrates with a provider's hosted fields, removing an entire compliance scope permanently.

44.2.13 Testing

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Writes unit tests for their code Writes integration tests with real dependencies in containers; keeps tests deterministic Designs the test strategy: what to test where, concurrency tests, contract tests, and what not to test Owns test infrastructure, speed and flakiness across teams Sets the quality model and what confidence the company buys at what cost
A test file A feature's test coverage A service's test strategy and its CI feedback loop The testing platform and its economics The organisation's confidence strategy
Stopped writing tests that assert the mock was called Stopped writing tests that pass whether or not the code is correct Stopped chasing a coverage percentage instead of testing invariants Stopped tolerating a flaky suite that everyone has learned to re-run Stopped treating testing as a cost centre rather than as delivery speed

The senior view: tests exist to let you change code confidently, and their value is measured by the bugs they would catch, not by coverage. That leads to a specific shape — a broad base of fast unit tests for logic, a solid middle of integration tests against a real PostgreSQL and Redis in Docker, and a thin top of end-to-end tests for the two or three journeys that must never break.

The tests that separate senior from mid are the ones for the things that are hard to test: 50 concurrent requests asserting stock never goes negative, a duplicate webhook producing one charge, a consumer crash between the database write and the offset commit. Those tests find real money bugs.

  • Junior: writes unit tests for a price calculation with three cases including a zero-quantity edge case.
  • Mid: sets up Testcontainers so the repository tests run against real PostgreSQL, and removes six brittle mocks.
  • Senior: adds a concurrency test that fires 50 parallel reservations and asserts the invariant, catching a race that had been in production for months.
  • Staff: cuts the CI suite from 22 minutes to 6 with parallelisation and a shared database template, and puts flaky tests on a quarantine list with owners.
  • Principal: sets the standard that money-touching paths require property-based or contract tests, and that no service ships without a tested rollback path.

44.2.14 Performance

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Notices something is slow and reports it Profiles a specific endpoint, fixes N+1 queries and obvious waste Works from percentiles and evidence; finds the real constraint; knows when not to optimise Sets performance budgets and capacity models across services Decides where the company invests in performance and what it is worth
A slow function An endpoint's latency A service's latency profile and its saturation points A product area's performance envelope The performance/cost frontier
Stopped optimising based on a guess Stopped using averages to reason about user experience Stopped optimising code when the constraint was I/O or a lock Stopped letting performance regress silently between releases Stopped chasing latency where the business value was elsewhere

The senior habit is refusing to touch anything until there is evidence: a flame graph, a query plan, a lock wait, a saturation metric. Most "slow application" problems are one query, one missing index, one serialised loop, one lock held too long. Rewriting the service is almost never the answer, and the engineers who reach for it are usually the ones who did not measure.

Percentiles are a professional requirement. Averages hide the experience of the users who are suffering. p99 is where the angry emails come from, and p99.9 is where your biggest customers live, because they make the most requests.

  • Junior: reports that the orders page feels slow and shares a screenshot of the network tab.
  • Mid: profiles the endpoint, finds an N+1 producing 340 queries, and fixes it with one join.
  • Senior: shows that p99 latency is dominated by connection-pool queueing rather than query time, resizes the pool, adds a cache for the top queries, and proves the improvement on the graph.
  • Staff: adds performance budgets to CI with a load test on the critical journeys, so regressions fail the build rather than surprising production.
  • Principal: decides that the checkout journey gets a 300 ms p99 budget with the engineering investment to match, and the admin tools explicitly do not.

44.2.15 Observability

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Adds log lines; reads dashboards someone else built Emits structured logs and metrics; builds a useful dashboard Instruments for the 03:00 question; designs alerts on symptoms; owns correlation and tracing Owns the observability platform, its cost and its conventions Decides what the company must be able to see, and what that is worth
A log line A service's dashboards and metrics A service's full observability story, including alerts and runbooks The telemetry pipeline and standards The organisation's operational visibility
Stopped logging strings with no identifiers Stopped logging at the wrong level and burying the signal Stopped alerting on causes rather than on customer symptoms Stopped paying for high-cardinality telemetry nobody queries Stopped treating observability as a tool purchase rather than a practice

The senior standard is simple: when this breaks at 03:00, can someone who has never seen the code find the cause in ten minutes? That requires a correlation id flowing from the gateway through services and into queue messages, structured logs with identifiers, metrics for business outcomes and not only technical ones, and traces on the paths that cross services.

Alert design is where seniority shows most. Page on what the customer feels — error rate, latency, orders per minute dropping — and leave cause metrics for the dashboard you open once you are awake. Every page must be urgent, actionable and documented, or it trains people to ignore pages.

  • Junior: adds a log line at the start of a handler with the user id.
  • Mid: adds a Prometheus counter and histogram for a new endpoint and puts them on the team dashboard.
  • Senior: propagates a correlation id through HTTP, Kafka and BullMQ, adds business-metric alerts, and writes the runbook page for each one.
  • Staff: standardises OpenTelemetry across services with a sampling policy that keeps cost flat while retaining every error trace.
  • Principal: sets the requirement that every customer-facing journey has an owned SLO dashboard, and funds the platform work to make that cheap.

44.2.16 Docker and Kubernetes

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Runs the app in Docker Compose locally Writes a multi-stage Dockerfile; understands probes, limits and manifests Sizes requests and limits from evidence; handles PID 1, graceful shutdown, rollouts and disruption budgets Owns cluster standards, base images and the deployment platform Decides whether the company runs Kubernetes at all, and who operates it
A local environment A service's container and manifests A service's runtime behaviour in the cluster The platform every team deploys onto The infrastructure strategy
Stopped building 1.2 GB images from a full base image Stopped ignoring memory limits until an OOMKill Stopped copying resource limits from another service without measuring Stopped letting each team maintain its own divergent manifests Stopped adopting a platform the organisation cannot staff

The senior details in Kubernetes are unglamorous and decide whether deploys are boring: a readiness probe that flips false before shutdown starts, terminationGracePeriodSeconds longer than the longest in-flight request, preStop sleep to let the load balancer notice, a liveness probe that does not check external dependencies, requests set from observed usage, and memory limits set above the Node heap limit plus overhead.

The most common expensive mistake at mid level is putting the database in the readiness probe. When the database blips, every replica reports unready simultaneously, the load balancer removes them all, and a 20-second database hiccup becomes a full outage.

  • Junior: gets the service running under Docker Compose with PostgreSQL and Redis for local development.
  • Mid: writes a multi-stage Dockerfile that ships a 180 MB image running as a non-root user with a proper init process.
  • Senior: fixes deploy-time 502s with correct readiness, preStop and grace-period settings, and right-sizes CPU requests from a month of usage data.
  • Staff: builds the shared Helm chart and base image with security patching, cutting per-service manifest drift to zero.
  • Principal: decides three low-traffic internal services move to a managed container platform because the Kubernetes operational overhead is not justified for them.

44.2.17 Cloud

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Uses cloud resources that exist; reads the console Provisions resources with infrastructure as code; understands the main managed services Chooses between managed and self-run with cost, lock-in and operational reasoning; designs for zones and failure Owns the cloud account structure, networking, IAM model and cost controls Sets the cloud strategy, vendor relationship and the exit cost the company accepts
A resource A stack for one service A service's cloud footprint and its failure behaviour The landing zone and platform The company's infrastructure position
Stopped clicking things into existence in the console Stopped ignoring which availability zone things live in Stopped assuming managed always means reliable and hands-off Stopped tolerating IAM policies with wildcard permissions Stopped choosing services with a lock-in cost nobody quantified

Senior cloud thinking is mostly a build-versus-buy calculation done honestly. A managed database costs more per month and less per year once you price the engineer time for backups, patching, failover testing and the 03:00 recovery. A managed Kafka is worth its price for most teams. A managed service you use for a trivial workload may not be.

The other senior discipline is failure-domain awareness: which resources are single-zone, what happens when a zone goes away, whether your backups are in a different account, and whether you have actually tested a restore this quarter.

  • Junior: finds the log group in CloudWatch and reads the error.
  • Mid: writes the Terraform for a service's queue, bucket and task definition instead of clicking it together.
  • Senior: designs the S3 upload flow with presigned URLs, lifecycle rules to cheaper storage, and cross-region replication for the documents that legally require it.
  • Staff: builds the multi-account landing zone with per-environment isolation, least-privilege roles, and budget alarms by team tag.
  • Principal: negotiates the committed-use agreement based on a two-year capacity model, and defines which proprietary services are acceptable and which are not.

44.2.18 CI/CD

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Pushes branches; fixes their own red builds Writes pipeline steps; keeps the build green; understands the deployment flow Designs the pipeline: gates, artefacts, environments, migrations, canaries and rollback Owns the delivery platform and the deployment standard across teams Sets how the company ships: frequency, safety, and what is automated versus approved
A commit A pipeline job A service's path to production The delivery platform The engineering delivery model
Stopped leaving the build broken for others Stopped skipping tests to get a release out Stopped coupling schema migrations to application deploys Stopped letting each team invent its own pipeline Stopped adding approval gates that create risk by batching changes

The senior insight is that deployment safety comes from small, frequent, reversible changes rather than from heavyweight approval processes. A team deploying ten times a day with automated tests, canaries and instant rollback is dramatically safer than one deploying monthly behind a change board, because every monthly release contains a hundred changes and nobody knows which one broke it.

Migrations are the usual weak point. They must be independently deployable, backwards compatible, and separate from long backfills. Getting this right is what turns "release night" into a Tuesday afternoon.

  • Junior: fixes the lint failure that broke the pipeline and learns to run it locally first.
  • Mid: adds the integration-test stage with a PostgreSQL service container and caching that halves build time.
  • Senior: separates migrations from deploys, adds a canary stage with automatic rollback on error-rate breach, and documents the rollback-safety rule.
  • Staff: builds the reusable workflow every service uses, with security scanning, SBOM generation and standard environments.
  • Principal: sets the target of deploying on demand with no manual approvals for standard changes, and drives the controls that make an auditor comfortable with it.

44.2.19 Git and collaboration

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Commits, branches, opens pull requests Writes clean history; rebases confidently; reviews peers usefully Keeps changes small and reviewable; sets branching and review norms; unblocks others Aligns workflow across teams; owns monorepo or multi-repo strategy Sets collaboration norms and how the company handles code ownership
Their branch Their feature's history A repository's conventions and review culture The source-control strategy How the organisation collaborates on code
Stopped committing node_modules and secrets Stopped opening 2,000-line pull requests Stopped letting reviews sit for two days Stopped tolerating repositories with no owner Stopped letting tooling choices fragment the engineering organisation

The single highest-leverage collaboration habit at senior level is making changes small. A 200-line pull request gets a real review in twenty minutes; a 2,000-line one gets an approval and a hope. Splitting work into reviewable increments behind a feature flag is a skill, and it is the one that most improves a team's defect rate.

The second is review latency. Reviews are a queue, and queue time dominates delivery time far more than review depth does. A senior who reviews within two hours makes the whole team faster than one who writes brilliant reviews on Thursdays.

  • Junior: learns to write a commit message that explains why, not "fix".
  • Mid: splits a large change into three reviewable pull requests and rebases cleanly on conflicts.
  • Senior: introduces trunk-based development with feature flags, cutting the average branch age from nine days to one.
  • Staff: sets the code-ownership map and review requirements so that shared libraries always get a knowledgeable reviewer.
  • Principal: decides the company consolidates twelve repositories into a monorepo with shared tooling, and sponsors the migration.

44.2.20 System design

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Implements a design somebody else produced Designs a feature within an existing system Designs a system end to end, with capacity numbers, failure behaviour and a migration path Designs across systems and teams; resolves conflicting constraints Sets the target architecture and the sequence to get there
A component A feature's design A service and its contracts A domain's architecture The system landscape and its direction
Stopped starting to code before understanding the problem Stopped designing only the happy path Stopped designing for imagined scale instead of measured requirements Stopped optimising one team's design at another team's expense Stopped producing architecture that the organisation cannot actually build

The senior design signature is arithmetic plus failure analysis. A design document that contains request rates, data volumes, growth projections, the resource that saturates first, and the behaviour when each dependency is unavailable, is a senior design. One that contains boxes and arrows is a picture.

The staff signature is a sequence. Anyone can draw the target state. The valuable artefact is the ordered set of steps that gets a live system from where it is to that target without a big-bang migration, where every intermediate state is shippable and each step is individually justified.

  • Junior: implements the notification worker exactly as specified in the design doc.
  • Mid: designs the coupon-validation flow within the existing order service, including the cache and the invalidation rule.
  • Senior: designs the returns system: schema, API, state machine, saga with compensation, capacity estimate, alerts, and a four-step rollout plan.
  • Staff: designs how orders, inventory and fulfilment interact across three teams, choosing where consistency boundaries sit and getting all three teams to agree.
  • Principal: publishes the two-year target architecture with the migration sequence, and kills two proposed projects that do not fit it.

44.2.21 Incident response

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Follows a runbook; escalates promptly Investigates and mitigates common failures independently Commands an incident: mitigates first, communicates on a schedule, keeps a log, runs the postmortem Improves the incident process; drives cross-team fixes to whole classes of failure Owns the reliability culture and the organisation's learning from failure
A single alert A service's incidents An incident, end to end The incident process and its outcomes How the company learns
Stopped staying silent when stuck Stopped diagnosing while customers are still affected Stopped chasing root cause before mitigating Stopped letting action items expire unowned Stopped tolerating a blame culture wearing a blameless vocabulary

The senior behaviour that matters most is structural, not technical: declare, mitigate, communicate on an interval, log with timestamps, hand over after ninety minutes. Debugging skill is useful, but a well-run incident with an average engineer beats a badly run one with a brilliant engineer almost every time, because the badly run one loses twenty minutes to duplicated work and a wrong public statement.

Above senior, the leverage moves to prevention by class. Not "add a timeout to this call" but "why do we have calls without timeouts at all, and what shared client would make that impossible?"

  • Junior: follows the runbook, restarts the consumer, posts what they did in the channel.
  • Mid: correlates a latency spike with a deploy, rolls back, confirms recovery on the dashboard.
  • Senior: runs a 40-minute checkout outage as commander: rollback in six minutes, updates every fifteen, timeline captured, blameless postmortem with three owned actions.
  • Staff: notices four incidents in a quarter share a cause class, and leads the shared HTTP client project that removes it.
  • Principal: changes how the company runs postmortems, makes them public internally, and ties action items into planning so they actually get done.

44.2.22 Communication and documentation

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Asks clear questions; gives status updates Writes readable pull requests and technical notes; explains their work to the team Writes design docs and ADRs; explains trade-offs to non-engineers; says no with options Writes documents that align multiple teams; influences without authority Writes the documents that set direction for the organisation
Their own updates Their feature's documentation A system's documentation and its decisions A domain's shared understanding The organisation's technical narrative
Stopped going quiet when blocked Stopped writing documents with no ask in them Stopped explaining mechanisms when the audience needed consequences Stopped assuming a document alone creates alignment Stopped writing for peers when the audience is the executive team

Writing is the highest-leverage senior skill and the one most engineers under-invest in. A design document read by twelve people that prevents one wrong architecture is worth more than any month of coding you will ever do. The specific skills: conclusion first, numbers not adjectives, non-goals stated explicitly, and an explicit ask at the end.

The staff-level addition is that documents do not create alignment on their own. Alignment comes from pre-reading with the two people most likely to object, adjusting, and then presenting a position that already survives the hardest questions. A document dropped into a channel with "thoughts?" produces silence and later ambushes.

  • Junior: posts "blocked on the sandbox credentials, asked in #platform, will pick up the tests meanwhile".
  • Mid: writes a pull request description that explains the problem, the approach and what to watch after deploy.
  • Senior: writes the keyset-pagination ADR and explains the trade-off to the product manager in three minutes using time, risk and usage numbers.
  • Staff: writes the event-schema RFC, pre-socialises it with four team leads, and gets adoption without a mandate.
  • Principal: writes the two-page memo that convinces the executive team to fund a year of platform work, in their language.

44.2.23 Mentoring and leadership

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Learns actively; asks for feedback Helps peers; onboards new joiners; reviews thoughtfully Mentors deliberately; raises the team's bar; leads projects without authority Grows senior engineers; multiplies leadership across teams Shapes the engineering culture, hiring bar and technical values
Their own growth A peer's onboarding The team's technical standard The next generation of senior and staff engineers The organisation's engineering identity
Stopped waiting to be told what to learn Stopped answering only what was asked Stopped solving problems that would have grown someone else Stopped being the person who has to be in every design review Stopped confusing personal excellence with organisational capability

The transition into real technical leadership is when you start optimising for what happens without you. Delegating a whole problem rather than tasks, letting a mid-level engineer make a recoverable mistake, and reviewing their design instead of writing it.

There is a trap here worth naming: the indispensable engineer. If every hard problem routes to you, you feel valuable and are actually a bottleneck. The strongest evidence of staff-level leadership is a team that made three good decisions last month without you in the room.

  • Junior: asks for a code-review buddy and acts on the feedback consistently.
  • Mid: onboards a new joiner, pairs with them for a week, and writes the missing setup documentation they needed.
  • Senior: gives a mid-level engineer the payment retry project end to end, reviews the design, and lets them present it.
  • Staff: runs a design-review forum where four teams critique each other's proposals, raising the standard without approving anything personally.
  • Principal: sets the interview bar and the promotion criteria, and personally coaches three staff engineers.

44.2.24 Business and product understanding

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Knows what the ticket asks for Understands the feature's purpose and its users Understands the business model; challenges requirements; proposes cheaper ways to reach the goal Connects technical strategy to business strategy Shapes what the business can do technically, and what it should not attempt
A ticket A feature A product area's technical direction A business line's technical enablement The company's technical possibilities
Stopped implementing without asking why Stopped accepting requirements that contradict each other Stopped building exactly what was asked when a cheaper option met the goal Stopped presenting technical plans without business framing Stopped treating business constraints as interference

The behaviour that changes a career here is turning up with alternatives. "This will take five weeks" ends a conversation. "The full version is five weeks; there is a four-day version that covers the two cases your data says are 96 percent of usage; here is what we would give up" starts a decision. Product managers begin including engineers with that habit in planning, which is where architecture actually gets decided.

Understanding unit economics is the next step: what a customer is worth, what an order costs to process, what an hour of downtime costs. These numbers make technical arguments land instantly with people who control budgets.

  • Junior: asks in refinement why the export needs to include cancelled orders.
  • Mid: notices two requirements conflict on refund timing and gets it resolved before building.
  • Senior: proposes the four-day version that covers 96 percent of the need, with data, and it ships instead of the five-week plan.
  • Staff: shows that the marketplace expansion needs an inventory redesign, and sequences it so the first revenue lands in one quarter rather than three.
  • Principal: tells the executive team that the proposed real-time personalisation product would need an 18-month data platform investment, and proposes a smaller product that ships in a quarter.

44.2.25 Cost awareness

Junior Mid Senior Staff Principal
Unaware of what their code costs to run Knows their service's rough monthly bill and the expensive parts Designs with cost as a constraint; finds and removes waste; can justify spend Owns cost visibility and efficiency programmes across teams Owns the cost model, commitments and the efficiency-versus-velocity balance
Nothing An awareness A service's cost profile A department's spend The company's infrastructure economics
Stopped assuming infrastructure is free Stopped ignoring data transfer and storage growth Stopped over-provisioning "to be safe" without measuring Stopped letting untagged spend hide ownership Stopped optimising cost at the expense of the engineering velocity that earns more

Cost is a design constraint like latency.
