The senior habits are unglamorous and effective: right-size from observed usage rather than fear, set retention on logs and backups, drop unused indexes and idle environments, put lifecycle policies on buckets, and know that cross-availability-zone traffic and NAT gateway data processing are the two line items that surprise everyone.

The counterweight, which principals hold: engineer time usually costs more than compute. Spending three weeks to save $200 a month is a bad trade. Spending three days to save $4,000 a month is an excellent one. Know which you are doing.

  • Junior: does not know the service costs anything.
  • Mid: notices the logging bill tripled after adding debug logging to a hot path, and reduces the level.
  • Senior: cuts a service's bill by 40 percent by right-sizing pods from a month of usage data, adding S3 lifecycle rules, and deleting three unused indexes and two idle staging environments.
  • Staff: introduces mandatory cost tags and per-team dashboards, making spend visible enough that teams self-correct.
  • Principal: buys a three-year committed-use discount against a validated capacity model, saving 28 percent, and blocks a proposed multi-region rollout whose cost had no business justification.

44.3 Moving from mid to senior

This is the most common transition and the one most people get wrong, because they assume the answer is "write better code". It is not. Mid-level engineers are usually already good at code. The gap is elsewhere.

44.3.1 The behaviours that actually get you promoted

You take problems, not tasks. Being handed "improve checkout reliability" and returning with a plan, an owner list, a sequence and results is senior work. Being handed "add a retry to the payment call" and doing it well is mid work. Ask your lead for the problem behind the ticket, and then propose the plan.

You finish things. Not merged: finished. Deployed, verified in production, alerted, documented, and the follow-up work either done or in the backlog with an owner. A large fraction of engineers never get promoted because they leave a trail of 90-percent-complete work that somebody else has to close.

You reduce other people's uncertainty. You write the design down before building it. You send the status update before it is requested. You explain the trade-off to the product manager without being asked. People start to relax when you own something, and that feeling is exactly what a promotion is a formal recognition of.

You think about production before you write code. How will I know it broke, how will I roll it back, what happens at 10x, what happens when this dependency is down. Adding these to your design conversations is the fastest visible change you can make.

You make other people better. Your reviews teach. You pair on hard problems. You wrote the document that stopped three people asking the same question.

You disagree well. You can hold a position with evidence, change your mind when shown better data, and commit fully when overruled. Teams promote people they trust in a disagreement.

44.3.2 The kind of project to own

Look for a project with these properties, and volunteer for it:

  • It is ambiguous. Nobody has fully specified it. That is the point: defining it is the senior work.
  • It touches production seriously. Migrations, reliability, performance under load, a payment path. Work that can hurt is work that demonstrates judgment.
  • It crosses at least one boundary. Another team, or product, or operations. You will have to communicate, not just code.
  • It is bounded. Six to ten weeks. Long enough to matter, short enough to finish inside a review cycle.
  • Its success is measurable. "p99 from 2.1 s to 400 ms", "double charges from 4 per week to zero", "deploys from weekly to daily". Numbers make your case for you.

Good candidates in most teams: fixing the flakiest critical journey, a zero-downtime migration of a big table, adding observability and alerting to an unloved but important service, cutting deploy time and adding rollback safety, or leading the response to a recurring class of incident.

44.3.3 The visible signals

Promotion decisions are made by people who mostly did not watch you work. They rely on artefacts and on what others say about you. So produce artefacts:

  • Design documents and ADRs with your name on them, in the repository.
  • Postmortems you wrote, with actions that were completed.
  • Dashboards and alerts that other people now use.
  • Runbooks that someone else successfully followed at 03:00.
  • Review comments that visibly taught something.
  • A measurable outcome you can state in one sentence with a number.

And make it legible without bragging. A short weekly update in the team channel — "the migration finished, 90 M rows, zero downtime, p99 on order history is now 8 ms, doc here" — is not self-promotion. It is how information reaches the people who make decisions.

44.3.4 A realistic six-month plan

Month Focus Concrete output
1 Production literacy Learn every dashboard for your service; join the on-call shadow rotation; write the missing runbook for the noisiest alert
2 Depth in the database Audit indexes and top queries with pg_stat_statements; fix the two worst; write up before and after numbers
3 Design in writing Write an ADR for a decision your team is about to make; write one design doc and get it reviewed by two people
4 Own an ambiguous project Take a bounded, measurable, production-touching project; define it yourself; publish the plan
5 Deliver and communicate Ship it in increments behind flags; give a 15-minute team talk on what you learned
6 Multiply Mentor one engineer through their own project; improve the review culture with a checklist; ask your lead directly what is still missing

Two notes on this plan. It assumes you keep delivering your normal work; senior behaviour is added on top, not instead. And month 6's "ask directly what is missing" is not optional — ask for the specific gap, in writing, and then close it. Vague answers are a signal to look elsewhere.

44.4 Moving from senior to staff

The senior-to-staff transition is different in kind, not in degree. Senior is the level at which you are complete: a company can hire only senior engineers and function. Staff exists because some problems are bigger than one team, and somebody has to work on those.

That means there is no promotion path made of doing senior work harder. Working more hours, shipping more features and reviewing more pull requests produces an exhausted senior engineer, not a staff engineer.

flowchart TB
    S["Senior: excellent within one team"] --> A["Scope beyond one team"]
    S --> B["Technical strategy: a written direction"]
    S --> C["Influence without authority"]
    S --> D["Glue work others avoid"]
    S --> E["Choosing which problems matter"]
    A --> St["Staff"]
    B --> St
    C --> St
    D --> St
    E --> St

44.4.1 Scope beyond one team

Staff work starts where a problem cannot be solved inside one team's backlog. Examples from real organisations: three teams building three incompatible event schemas; a shared database that four services write to; a 40-minute CI pipeline that costs every team an hour a day; an authentication model that cannot express the permissions the product now needs; a migration off a datastore that six services depend on.

Each of these has a common shape. Every individual team is behaving rationally, the problem lives between them, and no single team can fix it without the others. Somebody has to hold the whole thing, and that somebody is not a manager, because the work is technical.

The practical move is to pick one such problem and start, without asking for a mandate. Write the document that describes the problem clearly, with evidence. That document alone often changes what teams do, and it is the most common way people become staff engineers before they are called one.

44.4.2 Technical strategy

Strategy is an overused word. In engineering it means something specific: a written statement of where we are going technically, why, and what we will not do, that survives contact with the next three quarters of planning.

A useful technical strategy has four parts: the current state described honestly including the parts that embarrass us, the forces that make change necessary (growth numbers, team growth, incident patterns, cost curves, product direction), the target state, and the sequence with the decision points along it.

The sequence is what distinguishes strategy from a wish. "We will move to event-driven communication between order and fulfilment" is a wish. "Quarter one: outbox in the order service and a single consumer, keeping the synchronous call as fallback. Quarter two: fulfilment consumes events and the synchronous call is removed. Quarter three: two more consumers. We stop and reassess if consumer lag exceeds our recovery target or if the schema registry rollout slips." That is a strategy: reversible, staged, with observable checkpoints.

44.4.3 Cross-team influence

You will not have authority over the teams whose behaviour needs to change. Influence at this level is a set of learnable mechanics.

Start from their problems, not yours. A team will not adopt your shared library because it is architecturally correct. They will adopt it because it deletes 400 lines they hate maintaining, or because it fixes an alert that pages them.

Make the good path the easy path. Standards enforced by documents decay. Standards embedded in the service template, the shared library, the lint rule and the CI check hold, because doing the right thing becomes less work than doing the wrong thing.

Pre-socialise everything. Before any proposal goes wide, talk to the two people most likely to object. Either they change your mind, which saves you a public failure, or you incorporate their concern and they become supporters. Proposals that first appear in a big meeting mostly die there.

Give away credit. Cross-team work depends entirely on people wanting to work with you again. Naming the engineer who did the hard part, in public, costs nothing and buys years of cooperation.

Be willing to be the one who writes it down. Half of alignment is somebody being bothered to summarise the meeting, list the decisions and send it out. It is astonishing how much influence that single habit produces.

44.4.4 Writing as a tool

At staff level, writing stops being documentation and becomes the primary way you work. A senior engineer's leverage is bounded by conversations, which are one-to-few and evaporate. A document is one-to-many and persists.

The four documents worth mastering: the problem brief (two pages, the situation with evidence, no solution — often the highest-value thing you will write), the design doc, the RFC for changes that need many teams to agree, and the strategy memo aimed at leadership, framed in delivery speed, risk and cost rather than in technology.

One discipline: write the shortest version that does the job. A two-page memo that everyone reads beats a twenty-page document that three people skim. If it must be long, put a summary and the ask at the top, and assume most readers stop after it.

44.4.5 Glue work

Glue work is the unglamorous connective activity that makes an organisation function: unblocking a stuck integration between two teams, running the design review forum, upgrading a shared dependency everyone depends on, chasing the action items from three incidents, onboarding, writing the summary nobody else wrote.

Two things are true at once, and you need both. Glue work is essential, genuinely staff-level, and organisations fall apart without it. And it is under-credited by default, especially for engineers who are already expected to be helpful, so it can consume you while leaving no evidence you did anything.

Manage that deliberately. Do glue work that is strategic, meaning it removes a recurring problem rather than one instance of it. Make it visible: a written outcome, a metric, a named improvement. And cap the volume: if you have no capacity left for a technical project with your name on it, you have become the team's operations layer, and your next promotion conversation will have nothing to point at.

44.4.6 Choosing which problems to work on

This is the actual staff skill, and it is a judgment about opportunity cost. At senior level, work mostly arrives. At staff level, you choose, and choosing badly wastes a quarter of a very expensive person.

The filter I use, in order:

  1. Would this still matter in a year? Rules out most urgent-feeling things.
  2. Is it a class or an instance? Prefer removing the class.
  3. Will it be done if I do not do it? If a good team will handle it anyway, spend your time elsewhere.
  4. Am I distinctively able to do it? Staff time is scarce; use it where your specific knowledge or credibility matters.
  5. Can I finish it? An unfinished platform migration is worse than never starting: half-migrated systems have all the costs of both.
  6. Does it multiply, or only add? A shared library, a standard or a document keeps producing value after you stop.

And the hardest discipline: say no to the interesting problem that fails these filters. Staff engineers who chase every interesting thing produce a trail of prototypes and no change.

44.5 Staff versus principal

The honest summary: Staff changes how a group of teams builds. Principal changes what the company is capable of building.

At staff, the scope is an organisational one: a department, a product area, a platform. You make several teams collectively better. At principal, the scope is the company: the technical direction, the standards, the hiring bar, the bets that pay off in two to five years, and the ability to say "we should not attempt that" to executives and be believed.

Dimension Staff Principal
Typical scope 3-8 teams, one platform or domain The engineering organisation, or a company-critical domain
Horizon 1-2 years 2-5 years
Main output Designs, standards, strategy for an area, senior engineers grown Direction, technical bets, culture, the standard others enforce
Failure mode Becomes a floating consultant with no shipped outcomes Becomes an ivory-tower architect disconnected from delivery
Relationship to code Codes on the risky or exemplary parts Codes rarely, but reads widely and prototypes to prove a point
Who they influence Team leads, senior engineers, their director Executives, the whole engineering organisation, sometimes the industry

44.5.1 Setting direction

Direction is the principal's product. It answers questions before they are asked: is this company going to be event-driven, do we build platforms or buy them, what is our position on multi-region, which languages do we support, what does "production-ready" mean here, what data do we consider a liability to store.

The test of good direction is that it makes decisions cheaper for everyone else. If four teams each spend a week deciding the same thing independently, direction was missing. If a team can point at a written principle and decide in an hour, direction is working.

Direction that only exists in a principal's head is worthless. It has to be written, repeated until people are bored of hearing it, and embedded in templates, reviews and hiring.

44.5.2 The archetypes

Staff-plus roles come in recognisable shapes. Most people lean towards one, and knowing yours helps you choose work that fits.

The Tech Lead. Leads a team or a group's technical execution. Owns the plan, sequences the work, keeps quality high, is close to delivery. The most common archetype and the easiest to be legible in. Risk: drifting into project management and losing technical depth.

The Architect. Owns the design of a large system or domain over time: interfaces, consistency boundaries, the migration sequence. Deep in one area. Risk: becoming the person who draws diagrams for systems they have never operated. The antidote is to keep shipping and keep taking pages.

The Solver. Parachutes into the hardest problems: the memory leak nobody can find, the corruption bug, the performance wall, the failing migration. Enormous value, highly visible. Risk: no compounding — you solve instances forever and change nothing structurally.

The Right Hand. Works closely with a director or VP on whatever matters most: due diligence on a proposal, a reorganisation's technical implications, a rescue of a failing programme. High leverage, high trust. Risk: your value depends on one relationship, and you can become invisible to everyone else.

None is better. But you should know which one you are being paid for, because the archetypes are evaluated differently and mismatched expectations are the main reason staff engineers feel lost.

44.6 A self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly. The rule: you may only tick a box if you can name a specific instance from the last twelve months. "I could do that" does not count.

Junior

  • I complete assigned tasks without needing the approach re-explained.
  • I write tests for my own code without being asked.
  • I ask for help within an hour of being genuinely stuck, with what I have already tried.
  • I can debug my own code with logs and a debugger before escalating.
  • I follow the team's conventions without needing them repeated in review.

Mid

  • I own a feature end to end: design, code, tests, deploy, verification.
  • I can read EXPLAIN ANALYZE and add the correct index.
  • I write integration tests against real dependencies, not only mocks.
  • I handle failure paths — timeouts, retries, validation — without being reminded.
  • I give code reviews that catch real problems.
  • I understand why the feature exists, not just what it must do.

Senior

  • I have owned a system in production, including its alerts, runbooks and on-call load.
  • I define what to build when handed an ambiguous problem, and write it down.
  • I can name what breaks first at 10x traffic for the systems I own, with numbers.
  • Every design I produce answers: can it time out, duplicate, arrive late, arrive out of order, partially succeed.
  • I have run a production migration on a large table with no downtime.
  • I have commanded an incident: mitigation first, scheduled communication, blameless postmortem, actions completed.
  • I explain trade-offs to non-engineers in time, risk and money, and I arrive with options.
  • I have measurably grown at least one other engineer.
  • I write ADRs and design docs that other people use to make decisions.
  • I say no with alternatives attached, and I name which of scope, time or quality moves.

Staff

  • I have led a technical initiative spanning at least three teams to completion.
  • I have written a technical strategy that changed what teams planned to do.
  • I have changed another team's behaviour without any authority over them.
  • I have built something shared — library, template, standard — that teams adopted voluntarily.
  • I have grown a senior engineer to the point of leading their own cross-team work.
  • I choose my own problems, and I can articulate why I am not working on three other tempting ones.
  • I do strategic glue work and it is visible in written outcomes.
  • I am consulted before major technical decisions in my area, by default.

Principal

  • I have set technical direction that the organisation follows and can cite.
  • I have prevented a large, expensive mistake and can name it.
  • I have made a multi-year technical bet and been accountable for the outcome.
  • I influence executive decisions with technical framing they can act on.
  • I shape hiring standards and promotion criteria.
  • Several senior and staff engineers point to me as a reason they grew.
  • I can say "we should not build this" to leadership and be believed.

A pattern worth noticing when you score yourself: most people find they have gaps below their current level, not only above it. Those gaps are usually the reason the next level feels stuck.

44.7 Common plateaus and how to break them

44.7.1 The strong coder who cannot influence

Symptom. Technically the best on the team. Consistently overruled or ignored. Frustrated that "nobody listens", and often right about the technical substance.

Diagnosis. Influence is not correctness. Being right is roughly a third of it; the rest is framing in the listener's terms, timing, pre-socialising, and having enough credibility deposits that people extend trust. Frequently the pattern is: strong opinions delivered late in a process, in engineering language, to people who care about delivery risk and cost.

How to break it. Write your position down before the decision meeting and share it. Frame in the audience's units — money, dates, risk — not in technology. Talk to the likely objector privately first. Bring two options rather than one verdict. And drop the arguments that do not matter: if you fight equally hard about formatting and about a data-loss risk, people learn to discount you.

44.7.2 The architect who does not ship

Symptom. Produces diagrams, strategies and opinions. Little of it lands. Teams nod politely and then do something else. Increasingly disconnected from what the code actually looks like.

Diagnosis. Credibility at senior-plus levels is renewed by delivery, not by past reputation. Designs from someone who has not operated a system in two years contain the wrong assumptions, and teams can tell.

How to break it. Ship something yourself this quarter, ideally the risky part of your own proposal. Join the on-call rotation. Prototype the design before proposing it, so you find the three things that do not work. And measure your proposals by adoption, not by production: an accepted design nobody implements is not a result.

44.7.3 The firefighter who never prevents fires

Symptom. Heroic. Always in the incident channel. Deeply appreciated. Nothing structurally improves, and the same class of incident recurs quarterly.

Diagnosis. Firefighting is more rewarding in the short term than prevention: it is visible, urgent, and thanked. Prevention is invisible, and its success looks like nothing happening. Some people also come to like it, because it is the part of the job where they feel most competent.

How to break it. Convert instances into classes. After each incident, ask what would make this category impossible, not just this occurrence. Insist on three owned action items with dates and check them at the next retro. Deliberately hand the next incident to someone else and coach them through it. And measure yourself on incidents not happening: pages per week, repeat causes eliminated, mean time to recovery. If your value disappears when the systems are healthy, you have optimised for the wrong outcome.

44.7.4 The specialist who stopped learning

Symptom. Deep expertise in one area, built five to ten years ago. Solves everything with that tool. Dismissive of new approaches, sometimes with good reasons that are no longer current. Scope has quietly narrowed.

Diagnosis. Depth is valuable and this person earned theirs. The failure is refusing to re-validate assumptions. PostgreSQL of five years ago could not do what today's can; the reasons you rejected a technology in 2019 may have been fixed twice since. Expertise decays silently, and its owner is the last to notice.

How to break it. Pick one adjacent area a year and go genuinely deep, to the point of shipping something in it. Re-test your own strong opinions with a small experiment rather than from memory. Read the release notes for the tools you claim to know; the gap between what you believe and what is true is usually shocking. And spend time with engineers who work differently from you — the discomfort is the signal that learning is available.

44.7.5 The general escape from any plateau

All four plateaus share a shape: a strength, over-applied, in an environment that has changed. The exit is always the same three steps. Get honest external feedback, from someone who will actually tell you the truth rather than be kind. Pick the one behaviour with the largest gap and work on it deliberately for a quarter, with a visible output. Then re-check, because you will be tempted to conclude you have fixed it after three good weeks.

Careers are long. A plateau of eighteen months is normal and not a verdict. What is fatal is not noticing you are on one.

Senior Checklist — Part 44

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can place myself honestly on the scope, ambiguity, impact, influence and time-horizon dimensions
  • I have scored myself against the rubric with specific evidence from the last twelve months, not aspirations
  • I know the two or three engineering areas where I am furthest behind my target level
  • I am currently operating one level above my title in at least one visible area
  • I own an ambiguous, production-touching, measurable project rather than a queue of tasks
  • I produce artefacts — ADRs, design docs, postmortems, runbooks — that outlive the conversation
  • I can explain the difference between senior, staff and principal in behaviours, not titles
  • I know which staff archetype fits me and which work I should therefore decline
  • I can name the plateau I am most at risk of, and the behaviour I am practising against it
  • I have asked my lead for the specific gap between me and the next level, and written down the answer

Part 44 — Key Takeaways

  • Levels are defined by five dimensions: scope, ambiguity, impact, influence and time horizon. Everything else follows from them.
  • Behaviour comes before the title, always; nobody is promoted and then starts operating at the new level.
  • The mid-to-senior gap is rarely coding ability. It is production ownership, deciding under ambiguity, writing things down, and finishing work completely.
  • Senior means the organisation can hand you an important, unclear problem and stop worrying about it.
  • Staff is not senior with more hours. It is a different job: problems that span teams, strategy in writing, influence without authority, and choosing what not to do.
  • Principal changes what the company can build; the output is direction that makes everyone else's decisions cheaper.
  • Look at the row to the right of your level in each area table; the difference is your development plan, and you will usually find gaps below your level too.
  • Promotion decisions are made from artefacts and other people's accounts, so produce ADRs, postmortems, runbooks and measurable outcomes, and make them visible without bragging.
  • Glue work is real staff work, but do the strategic kind, make it visible, and cap it so you still have a technical project with your name on it.
  • The four plateaus — the uninfluential expert, the non-shipping architect, the firefighter, the stale specialist — are all one strength over-applied in a changed environment.
  • Choose projects that are ambiguous, production-touching, bounded, cross-boundary and measurable; that combination is what a promotion case is made of.
  • Careers are long; an eighteen-month plateau is normal, and the only fatal version is the one you do not notice.

Part 45 — Senior Backend Interview Preparation

45.0 How senior interviews work

You have built APIs for years. You have been paged at 3 a.m. You have fixed a query that was taking 40 seconds. And then you sit in a senior interview and get asked "what is the difference between type and interface" and you freeze, because the question feels beneath you and you have not said the words out loud in six years.

That is the trap. Senior interviews are not harder versions of junior interviews. They are a different assessment wearing the same clothes. This section tells you what is actually being measured, so that every one of the 260 questions in this Part becomes practice for the real thing rather than flashcard drilling.

45.0.1 The four formats

Almost every senior backend loop is built from four blocks, run in some combination over three to six hours.

flowchart TB
  S["Recruiter screen<br/>30 min"] --> C["Coding / language<br/>45-60 min"]
  C --> D["System design<br/>45-60 min"]
  D --> P["Deep dive on past work<br/>45-60 min"]
  P --> B["Behavioural / leadership<br/>45 min"]
  B --> H["Hiring manager + bar raiser"]

Coding and language. Not LeetCode-hard at senior level in most backend teams. Expect a medium problem plus a runtime conversation: event loop ordering, async correctness, memory, a bug in concurrent code. The code is a pretext for watching how you reason.

System design. The dominant signal. You are given a vague prompt ("design a notification service") and 45 minutes. What is graded is scoping, capacity math, the data model, the failure story, and whether you can say what you would not build.

Deep dive on past work. The most under-prepared round. An interviewer picks one project from your CV and drills for 45 minutes: why that database, what broke, what the numbers were, what you would do differently. It is very hard to fake. Prepare three stories in depth: one performance story, one incident, one design decision you now regret.

Behavioural. Ownership, conflict, mentoring, saying no. At senior level this is not a formality; it is where "strong engineer, would not hire" decisions get made.

45.0.2 What is actually being assessed

Recall is table stakes. The four real signals are:

  1. Trade-off reasoning. Can you name at least two viable options and say why you picked one for this context? A candidate who says "always use Kafka" has told the interviewer they have only used Kafka.
  2. Failure thinking. Do you volunteer what breaks before you are asked? The senior mantra runs under every answer: Can it timeout? Can it fail? Can it become slow? Can it duplicate? Can it return a wrong response? Can it partially succeed?
  3. Ownership and operations. Do you talk about monitoring, rollout, migration and on-call, or do you stop at "the code works"?
  4. Communication. Can a product manager follow you? Can you compress a 40-minute incident into 90 seconds without losing the causal chain?

Notice that none of these require you to remember an API signature.

45.0.3 The answer structure: context, options, decision, consequences

Use one shape for almost every non-trivial answer. It costs nothing to learn and it makes you sound three years more experienced immediately.

flowchart LR
  A["Context<br/>scale, constraints,<br/>what matters here"] --> B["Options<br/>two or three<br/>real candidates"]
  B --> C["Decision<br/>the one you pick<br/>and the reason"]
  C --> D["Consequences<br/>what you gave up,<br/>what breaks, how you<br/>would detect it"]

Worked example. Question: "Would you cache the product page?"

  • Context: "Read-heavy, maybe 4,000 requests per second at peak, product data changes a few times a day, and stale price is a business problem while stale description is not."
  • Options: "Redis cache with a short TTL, CDN edge caching with purge on publish, or a materialised read model in Postgres."
  • Decision: "Redis with a 60-second TTL for the description block, and I do not cache price. Price comes from the pricing service on every request because a wrong price is a refund and a support ticket."
  • Consequences: "I have accepted up to 60 seconds of stale copy, I now need a cache-stampede guard on publish, and I need a cache_hit_ratio metric plus an alert if it drops below 0.8, because a silent cache miss storm looks exactly like a database problem."

Four sentences. That answer signals seniority more than any amount of Redis internals.

45.0.4 How to say "I don't know" well

You will be asked something you do not know. Every senior candidate is; that is often the point. The bad version is bluffing, and interviewers detect it instantly because bluffs have no numbers and no failure modes.

The good version has three parts: admit the boundary, state what you do know that is adjacent, then describe the concrete path to the answer.

"I have not run Citus in production, so I would be guessing about its rebalancing behaviour. What I do know is the general shard-rebalancing problem: you need a routing layer that can point at both old and new shards during the move, and the risky window is the cutover. To answer properly I would read the Citus docs on citus_rebalance_start, then run a rebalance on a staging copy of the real dataset with production-shaped traffic replayed against it, and measure p99 during the move. If that showed a stall, that is a blocker."

That answer is often scored higher than a memorised correct one, because it demonstrates the thing the job actually needs: a method for reducing unknowns.

45.0.5 Red flags interviewers write down

Red flag What the interviewer writes Fix
Absolutes with no trade-off ("never use ORMs", "always microservices") "Dogmatic, single-context experience" Name the context where the opposite is right
Blaming past teams ("the previous devs were idiots") "Will be hard to work with" Describe the constraint they were under, then what you changed
No numbers anywhere "Has not owned anything at scale" Attach one number to every claim: rows, RPS, ms, GB
No failure modes "Happy path engineer" Volunteer the failure before being asked
Cannot scope down "Cannot ship" Say "for v1 I would skip X and here is why that is safe"
Design with no data model "Hand-waves the hard part" Write the tables and the primary keys early
"It depends" with no follow-through "Evasive" Always finish: "it depends on X; assuming X is true, I would do Y"

One more: silence. Thinking quietly for 90 seconds reads as being stuck. Narrate. "I am weighing two options here, give me a second" is free and buys you all the time you need.

The rest of this Part is 260 questions in the shape you will actually meet them, each with the expected answer, why it is asked, the follow-ups that are coming, and the line that separates a senior answer from a competent mid-level one.

45.1 TypeScript

Q1. When do you use type and when do you use interface?

  • Expected answer — Both describe object shapes and both are erased at runtime. interface supports declaration merging (two declarations of the same name combine) and is idiomatic for public object contracts that libraries may want to extend. type is a general alias, so it can express unions, tuples, mapped types, conditional types and primitives, which interface cannot. Practically: use interface for entity and DTO shapes and for anything a consumer might augment; use type the moment you need a union, an intersection of computed types, or a utility-type transformation. Performance differences are negligible in normal code, though very large intersections of type can slow the compiler more than equivalent interfaces. The one behavioural difference that bites is that an interface is not implicitly assignable to an index-signature type like Record<string, unknown>, while a type alias is, because interfaces are open to merging.

  • Why it matters — Shows whether the candidate knows the type system's structural rules or just repeats a blog-post rule.

  • Follow-ups — Why does interface Foo { a: string } fail to satisfy Record<string, unknown> when the equivalent type passes? Where would declaration merging actually help you? Which one would you export from a shared package and why?

  • Senior signal — A senior gives the assignability difference and the library-augmentation use case, and says the choice barely matters inside one service but matters a lot at package boundaries. A mid-level answer stops at "interfaces can be extended, types cannot", which is not even true since types intersect.

Q2. Explain generics and generic constraints with a real backend example.

  • Expected answer — A generic is a type parameter: the function or class is written once and the caller supplies the concrete type. A constraint (extends) narrows what may be supplied so the body can safely use certain properties. In backend code the classic case is a repository or a paginated response wrapper.

    interface HasId { id: string; }

async function findOrFail<T extends HasId>(
  repo: { findOne(where: { id: string }): Promise<T | null> },
  id: string,
): Promise<T> {
  const row = await repo.findOne({ id });
  if (!row) throw new NotFoundException(`entity ${id} not found`);
  return row; // callers get the concrete entity type back, not `any`
}

    Without the constraint the compiler could not know T has an id. Generics preserve the caller's type through the function instead of widening to object. The trap is over-generifying: three type parameters with conditional types in a service class is usually a design smell, not cleverness.

  • Why it matters — Reveals whether the candidate writes reusable typed infrastructure or copy-pastes types.

  • Follow-ups — How do you infer the element type out of Promise<Order[]>? When does a generic default (<T = unknown>) help? What is the cost of a generic that is only ever instantiated once?

  • Senior signal — Mentions that generics are a compile-time-only mechanism with zero runtime cost, and knows when not to use them.

Q3. What is a discriminated union and why is it good for domain modelling?

  • Expected answer — A discriminated (tagged) union is a union of object types that all share a literal-typed field, so the compiler can narrow the union by checking that field. It lets you make illegal states unrepresentable.

    type PaymentResult =
  | { status: 'captured'; transactionId: string; amountMinor: number }
  | { status: 'requires_action'; redirectUrl: string }
  | { status: 'failed'; declineCode: string; retriable: boolean };

function handle(r: PaymentResult) {
  switch (r.status) {
    case 'captured': return log(r.transactionId);      // narrowed
    case 'requires_action': return redirect(r.redirectUrl);
    case 'failed': return r.retriable ? retry() : refundIntent();
  }
}

    Compared with one flat interface full of optional fields, you cannot accidentally read transactionId on a failure. Adding a never exhaustiveness check in the default branch turns a new variant into a compile error instead of a production bug.

  • Why it matters — Separates people who model domains from people who model database rows.

  • Follow-ups — Show the exhaustiveness check with never. How do you serialise this over HTTP and validate it back? What if the discriminant comes from an external API and might be an unknown string?

  • Senior signal — Brings up exhaustiveness enforcement and the boundary problem: unions are only safe if something validates untrusted input into the union at the edge.

Q4. unknown versus any — when do you use each?

  • Expected answer — any switches the type checker off for that value; every property access and call is allowed and errors surface at runtime. unknown is the safe top type: anything is assignable to it, but you can do nothing with it until you narrow it via a type guard, typeof, instanceof or a schema parse. Every value entering the process from outside — request bodies, JSON from Redis, Kafka payloads, third-party SDK responses — should be typed unknown and validated, not cast. any is legitimate only in narrow places: interop with an untyped library while you write the declaration file, or a deliberate escape hatch with a comment. The dangerous property of any is that it is contagious: one any in a chain silently untypes everything downstream, which is why noImplicitAny and lint rules against explicit any earn their keep.

  • Why it matters — Predicts how much runtime type-confusion the candidate will let into a codebase.

  • Follow-ups — Write a type guard for a webhook payload. Why is as a worse tool than a guard? What does unknown do in a catch clause under useUnknownInCatchVariables?

  • Senior signal — Frames it as trust boundaries rather than style, and names the contagion property of any.

Q5. TypeScript uses structural typing. What does that mean and where does it hurt?

  • Expected answer — Two types are compatible if their shapes are compatible, regardless of names or declared inheritance. A function expecting { id: string } accepts any object with a string id. This makes the language pleasant with plain JSON and duck-typed code. Where it hurts is when two domain concepts have the same shape but different meaning: UserId and OrderId are both string, so you can pass one where the other belongs and the compiler is happy. The fix is branded/nominal types, which fake nominality with a phantom field.

    type Branded<T, B> = T & { readonly __brand: B };
type UserId = Branded<string, 'UserId'>;
type OrderId = Branded<string, 'OrderId'>;
const asUserId = (s: string) => s as UserId; // one controlled cast at the edge

    Excess property checks on object literals soften the problem for literals but not for variables.

  • Why it matters — Structural typing causes real, subtle production bugs when identifiers are all strings.

  • Follow-ups — Why does an object literal error on an extra property but a variable does not? How would you brand money amounts? What is the runtime cost of branding?

  • Senior signal — Has actually shipped branded IDs or currency minor-units and can say where the single cast lives.

Q6. Which utility types do you reach for, and what do they compile to?

  • Expected answer — The everyday set: Partial<T> (all properties optional, ideal for PATCH DTOs and update payloads), Required<T>, Readonly<T>, Pick<T, K> and Omit<T, K> (deriving API responses from entities without redeclaring fields), Record<K, V> (lookup maps), ReturnType<F> and Awaited<T> (deriving a service's response type from the function itself), NonNullable<T>, and Parameters<F>. They are built from mapped and conditional types; nothing exists at runtime. The senior habit is deriving instead of duplicating: type OrderResponse = Omit<Order, 'internalNotes' | 'costPrice'> means adding a secret column to the entity does not silently leak it — but only if the response type is derived by Omit, whereas Pick is safer for leak-prevention because a new column is excluded by default. That is the actual trade-off: Omit is convenient, Pick is safe.

  • Why it matters — Shows whether types are maintained by hand (and therefore drift) or derived.

  • Follow-ups — Which is safer for API responses, Pick or Omit, and why? Write DeepPartial<T>. How does Awaited handle nested promises?

  • Senior signal — The Pick-versus-Omit leak argument. That is a production scar, not a textbook fact.

Q7. How do decorators and reflect-metadata work, and how does NestJS use them?

  • Expected answer — A decorator is a function that runs once at class definition time and receives the target (constructor, prototype, property key, parameter index). It can wrap, replace or, most commonly in Nest, just record metadata. reflect-metadata is a polyfill that gives you a metadata store keyed by target plus key, and with emitDecoratorMetadata: true the TypeScript compiler additionally emits design:paramtypes — the runtime constructor parameter types. That emitted array is the whole trick behind Nest's constructor injection: @Injectable() marks the class, and at module bootstrap Nest reads design:paramtypes to learn that OrderService needs a PaymentService, then resolves it from the container. @Get('/orders') stores a path and method on the handler; the router scans that metadata at startup. @UseGuards, @SetMetadata and custom decorators read by Reflector follow the same pattern.

    export const Roles = (...roles: string[]) => SetMetadata('roles', roles);
// guard side: this.reflector.getAllAndOverride<string[]>('roles', [ctx.getHandler(), ctx.getClass()])

    The consequence: interfaces cannot be injected by type, because interfaces vanish at runtime — hence injection tokens.

  • Why it matters — Explains half of NestJS's "magic" and predicts whether the candidate can debug DI failures.

  • Follow-ups — Why can you not inject an interface? What breaks if emitDecoratorMetadata is off? How do you inject an abstract dependency then?

  • Senior signal — Connects design:paramtypes to the injection-token requirement instead of describing decorators abstractly.

Q8. What does strict actually turn on, and is it worth it on a legacy codebase?

  • Expected answer — strict is a bundle: strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, noImplicitThis, alwaysStrict, and useUnknownInCatchVariables. The one that matters most by far is strictNullChecks, because it forces null and undefined to be handled explicitly and eliminates the most common runtime crash class in Node services. On legacy code you do not flip it globally on a Friday; you enable it per-directory using project references or incremental adoption, or turn on individual flags in order — noImplicitAny first, then strictNullChecks with // @ts-expect-error markers that you burn down. strictPropertyInitialization fights with ORM entities, which are populated by the driver rather than the constructor; the honest answer is to use the definite assignment assertion (id!: string) on entity fields rather than disabling the flag everywhere.

  • Why it matters — Migration strategy is a seniority marker; anyone can say "strict is good".

  • Follow-ups — How would you sequence the migration on a 200k-line codebase? What is strictFunctionTypes protecting you from? How do you keep new files strict while old ones are not?

  • Senior signal — Talks about incremental adoption with a measurable burn-down, and admits the ORM friction instead of pretending it does not exist.

Q9. Explain narrowing and control-flow analysis. What defeats it?

  • Expected answer — The compiler tracks how a value's type changes along each code path: typeof x === 'string', x instanceof Error, truthiness checks, in operators, equality against literals, and user-defined guards (function isOrder(v: unknown): v is Order) all narrow. Assertion functions (asserts v is Order) narrow for the rest of the scope. Narrowing is defeated by: reassignment inside a closure the compiler cannot follow, calling a function between the check and the use on a mutable property (if (this.x) { await f(); this.x.y } — after the await, this.x could have changed, and for properties the compiler does reset narrowing across function calls in some cases but notoriously does not for await on locals), destructuring a discriminated union before switching on the tag, and any. The practical rule: narrow into a const local, then use the local.

  • Why it matters — Narrowing failures are where people reach for ! and re-introduce null crashes.

  • Follow-ups — Why does destructuring break discriminated-union narrowing before TS 4.6, and what changed? When is ! acceptable? Show an assertion function for a config value.

  • Senior signal — Gives the "copy to a const" rule and explains why, rather than sprinkling non-null assertions.

Q10. What is declaration merging and when have you needed it?

  • Expected answer — TypeScript merges multiple declarations with the same name in the same scope: interfaces merge their members, namespaces merge, and a namespace can merge with a class or function to add statics. The backend case you actually hit is augmenting third-party types — most often adding user to Express's Request so guards and controllers see the authenticated principal without casting.

    // types/express.d.ts
declare global {
  namespace Express {
    interface Request { user?: { id: string; roles: string[] } }
  }
}
export {};

    It also appears when you add fields to ProcessEnv for typed config, or extend a library's options interface from a plugin. The risk is that it is global and invisible: a merged member appears everywhere, so a wrong or over-permissive augmentation (making user non-optional) makes the compiler lie about unauthenticated routes.

  • Why it matters — Every real Node codebase needs at least one augmentation; doing it badly weakens type safety silently.

  • Follow-ups — Why is the export {} line needed? Should user be optional and why? How do you scope an augmentation so it does not leak to consumers of your package?

  • Senior signal — Insists user stays optional so that unauthenticated paths are still type-checked, and notes the global blast radius.

Q11. Enums versus union literals — which do you use?

  • Expected answer — A numeric enum emits a real runtime object with reverse mappings and its values are just numbers, so a wrong number type-checks; it also does not tree-shake well. A string enum emits an object too, is nominal-ish (a raw string is not assignable to it), and is useful when you need to iterate members or map to a database check constraint. A union of string literals (type OrderStatus = 'created' | 'paid' | 'shipped') emits nothing, compares directly against JSON and database values, works with discriminated unions, and is my default. const enum inlines but breaks with isolatedModules and bundlers, so avoid it in libraries. Practical rule: union literals for domain states that cross the wire and the database; string enums only when you genuinely need the runtime object, and then derive the union from it with `${Status}` or keyof typeof.

  • Why it matters — This choice shows up in every entity and DTO; wrong choices cause serialisation friction for years.

  • Follow-ups — How do you get the list of allowed values at runtime for a class-validator @IsIn? How does this map to a Postgres enum type versus a check constraint? What breaks when you add a value?

  • Senior signal — Connects the type choice to the database representation and to the migration cost of adding a value (Postgres ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE cannot run inside some transaction contexts, whereas a check constraint is a normal migration).

Q12. How do you type async code and errors properly?

  • Expected answer — An async function always returns Promise<T>; declare the T explicitly on public service methods so a refactor cannot silently widen it. TypeScript has no checked exceptions and the catch variable is unknown under strict mode, so error handling must narrow: if (e instanceof HttpException), or a guard on a custom error class hierarchy. For expected failures, prefer a returned result union over throwing, because the compiler can then force the caller to handle it.

    type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };
async function charge(o: Order): Promise<Result<Receipt, 'insufficient_funds' | 'gateway_timeout'>> { /* ... */ }

    Throw for programmer errors and truly exceptional conditions; return a union for domain outcomes such as a declined card. Also type the edges: Promise.all gives a tuple, Promise.allSettled gives a discriminated union you must narrow, and unawaited promises are the top source of floating-promise bugs, so enable @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises.

  • Why it matters — Error typing is where TypeScript's guarantees stop, and how a candidate handles that gap is revealing.

  • Follow-ups — What does unknown in catch change about your error middleware? When would you not use a result type? How do you make sure a finally releasing a DB connection cannot itself throw and mask the original error?

  • Senior signal — Draws the line between exceptions (unexpected, cross-cutting, handled by a filter) and domain outcomes (expected, part of the contract), and mentions floating promises, which is a real production incident source in Node.

45.2 Node.js runtime

This is the section that separates people who use Node from people who can debug it at 3 a.m. Interviewers love it because the answers are checkable and the failure stories are vivid.

Q13. Walk me through the phases of the Node.js event loop.

  • Expected answer — libuv runs the loop in ordered phases, and each turn goes through them: timers (callbacks whose setTimeout/setInterval threshold has elapsed), pending callbacks (some deferred system callbacks such as certain TCP errors), idle/prepare (internal), poll (retrieve new I/O events and run their callbacks; this is where the loop blocks waiting for work), check (setImmediate callbacks), and close callbacks (socket.on('close')). Between every callback — not just between phases — Node drains the microtask queues: process.nextTick first, then promise reactions. The poll phase is the important one: if there are no timers due and no setImmediate pending, the loop parks in epoll_wait/kqueue until an fd is ready or a timeout fires. Everything that "feels async" is one of three things: an fd watched in poll, a task completed on the libuv thread pool, or a timer.

  • Why it matters — Almost every latency mystery in Node ("my p99 is 800 ms but the query is 3 ms") is explained by loop phases and blocking.

  • Follow-ups — Where does a pg query result callback run? Where does fs.readFile complete? What blocks the poll phase from being entered?

  • Senior signal — Says microtasks drain between every callback, and knows the poll phase is where the process idles. A mid-level answer lists phase names from a diagram without the poll-blocking insight.

Q14. What does this print, and why?

console.log('1');
setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0);
setImmediate(() => console.log('3'));
process.nextTick(() => console.log('4'));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('5'));
(async () => { console.log('6'); await null; console.log('7'); })();
console.log('8');

  • Expected answer — Output: 1, 6, 8, 4, 5, 7, 2, 3 — with the caveat that 2 and 3 can swap. Reasoning: synchronous code runs first (1, then the async IIFE runs synchronously up to its first await, printing 6, then 8). The stack empties, so microtasks drain: the nextTick queue has absolute priority, printing 4; then the promise microtask queue in FIFO order, printing 5 and then 7 (the continuation after await null was queued when the IIFE suspended, which was after the .then was registered). Then the loop enters its phases: the timer 2 and the check-phase 3. On the first tick from the main module, whether the 1 ms-clamped timer is already due depends on how long startup took, so 2 before 3 or 3 before 2 are both legal; inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always wins because you are already past the timers phase.

  • Why it matters — This single question exposes whether the mental model is real or memorised.

  • Follow-ups — Why is the 2/3 order non-deterministic only at the top level? What changes if you wrap the last two lines in fs.readFile(__filename, () => { ... })? What happens if process.nextTick recursively schedules itself?

  • Senior signal — Volunteering the non-determinism and the "inside I/O, immediate always beats timeout" rule, plus the starvation hazard of recursive nextTick.

Q15. What is the libuv thread pool, what uses it, and how big should it be?

  • Expected answer — It is a small pool of OS threads (default 4, UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE, max 1024) that libuv uses for work that has no non-blocking kernel API. That includes almost all fs operations, dns.lookup (the getaddrinfo path), crypto.pbkdf2, scrypt, randomBytes in async form, and zlib compression. Network sockets do not use it: TCP/HTTP go through epoll/kqueue in the poll phase. The failure mode is pool saturation: four concurrent pbkdf2 calls with high iterations mean every subsequent file read and DNS lookup queues behind them, so unrelated endpoints get slow while CPU looks fine and the event loop looks idle. Sizing: raise it toward the number of cores times two if your workload is file- or crypto-heavy, but a bigger pool competes for CPU; the better fix is usually to move heavy crypto to worker threads or a dedicated service and to use dns.resolve or a DNS cache instead of dns.lookup.

  • Why it matters — Thread pool saturation is a classic invisible latency source that only experienced Node operators diagnose quickly.

  • Follow-ups — Does an HTTPS request use the pool? How would you prove saturation from metrics? Why does UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE have to be set before the first async call?

  • Senior signal — Distinguishes network I/O (epoll) from pool I/O, and gives a diagnosis path rather than just a tuning knob.

Q16. What does "blocking the event loop" mean and how do you detect it in production?

  • Expected answer — Node runs your JavaScript on one thread. Any synchronous work — a 200 ms JSON.parse of a 20 MB payload, a regex with catastrophic backtracking, crypto.pbkdf2Sync, a for loop over 2 million rows, fs.readFileSync — stops the loop, so no other request progresses, no timer fires, and no health check is answered. Symptoms are p99 latency spikes across all endpoints simultaneously, timeouts on unrelated calls, and readiness probes failing while CPU on one core sits at 100%. Detect it by measuring event loop delay with perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay() (an IntervalHistogram you export as a metric) or toobusy-style sampling, and alert on p99 loop lag above ~50–100 ms. To find the culprit, take a CPU profile (--cpu-prof, node --inspect plus Chrome DevTools, or 0x/clinic flame) during the spike; the flame graph names the synchronous function. Fixes: chunk the work with setImmediate, stream instead of buffering, move to a worker thread, or push it to a background job.

  • Why it matters — This is the single most common Node production pathology.

  • Follow-ups — Which metric would page you? Why does chunking with setImmediate help but setTimeout(fn, 0) in a tight loop is worse? What is a ReDoS and how do you prevent it?

  • Senior signal — Names loop-lag as an SLI with a threshold and describes the profiling workflow, instead of saying "don't write blocking code".

Q17. Worker threads versus cluster — when do you use each?

  • Expected answer — cluster (and the same idea done properly by your orchestrator) forks whole processes that share a listening socket; each has its own V8 heap and event loop. Use it to use all cores for request throughput on a normal I/O-bound API. worker_threads creates threads inside one process, each with its own isolate and loop, communicating by message passing and able to share raw memory via SharedArrayBuffer. Use them for CPU-bound work inside a request path: image resizing, PDF generation, large CSV parsing, heavy crypto, so the main loop stays responsive. Key differences: workers start in ~10–40 ms versus ~50–200 ms for a process, share the process's memory limit, and can transfer ArrayBuffers with zero copy; processes are isolated so one crash does not take the others down. In Kubernetes I usually skip cluster entirely and run one Node process per container with replicas handling the fan-out, because then the scheduler, not my app, owns scaling and restarts.

  • Why it matters — A common design decision, and the Kubernetes answer shows whether the candidate has operated Node in a modern platform.

  • Follow-ups — What is the cost of passing a 50 MB buffer to a worker, and how do you avoid the copy? How do you bound a worker pool? What happens to in-flight requests if a worker throws?

  • Senior signal — Says "one process per container, let the platform scale" and can justify it, and knows about transferable objects.

Q18. Explain streams and backpressure. What goes wrong without them?

  • Expected answer — A stream processes data in chunks with a bounded buffer (highWaterMark, 16 KB by default for byte streams). Backpressure is the mechanism where a slow consumer tells a fast producer to pause: writable.write() returns false when its buffer is full, and a correct producer stops until the 'drain' event. pipe() and, better, pipeline() implement that for you and also propagate errors and destroy the streams on failure, which manual pipe() does not. Without backpressure — for example reading a 2 GB S3 object into memory and then writing it, or ignoring the return value of write() in a loop — the buffer grows unbounded and the process is OOM-killed. A realistic case: exporting 5 million orders to CSV. Streaming from a Postgres cursor through a transform into the HTTP response holds a few megabytes; buffering the array holds several gigabytes and kills the pod.

    await pipeline(queryStream, csvTransform, res); // errors propagate, sockets destroyed

  • Why it matters — Streaming is the difference between an export endpoint that works at 10x growth and one that OOMs.

  • Follow-ups — Why pipeline over pipe? What does highWaterMark mean for an object-mode stream? How do you stream rows out of Postgres with TypeORM or pg?

  • Senior signal — Knows pipe leaks on error, and can tie backpressure to a specific OOM incident with numbers.

Q19. How do you find a memory leak in a Node service?

  • Expected answer — First confirm it is a leak and not just heap growth toward the limit: chart process.memoryUsage().heapUsed and RSS over hours; a leak shows a sawtooth whose troughs rise after each GC. Then capture two heap snapshots minutes apart under load (node --inspect plus Chrome DevTools, or v8.writeHeapSnapshot() triggered by a signal in production), and use the comparison view sorted by delta with "objects allocated between snapshot 1 and 2" — retained size and the retainer path tell you who is holding the memory. Typical culprits I have actually found: an unbounded Map used as a cache with no eviction, event listeners added per request to a long-lived emitter (watch for the MaxListenersExceededWarning), closures captured by a setInterval that is never cleared, request-scoped data pushed into a module-level array for "metrics", and retained references in a global logger context. Also check native/RSS growth separately — a leak outside the JS heap points at Buffers, native addons or fragmentation, and heap snapshots will not show it.

  • Why it matters — Tests real debugging method rather than tool name-dropping.

  • Follow-ups — Snapshot on a 4 GB heap pauses the process; how do you do this safely in production? What is the difference between shallow and retained size? How would you find a Buffer leak?

  • Senior signal — Mentions RSS-versus-heap divergence and the operational cost of taking a snapshot on a live pod, and has a named list of real culprits.

Q20. How does V8 garbage collection work and when do you touch --max-old-space-size?

  • Expected answer — V8 is generational. New objects go into the small new space and are collected by Scavenge, a copying collector that runs often and is fast (sub-millisecond to a few ms) because most objects die young. Survivors are promoted to old space, collected by Mark-Compact with incremental marking and concurrent/parallel phases, so pauses are usually a few milliseconds but can reach tens of milliseconds on large heaps. --max-old-space-size=N (megabytes) sets the old-space ceiling; exceeding it gives FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit — Allocation failed. You raise it when the working set is genuinely large (a big in-process cache, large batch jobs) and the container memory limit is higher — the classic production bug is a container limited to 512 MB with Node defaulting to a larger heap, so the kernel OOM-kills the process before V8 ever GCs. Modern Node reads cgroup limits better, but I still set it explicitly to roughly 75–80% of the container limit, leaving room for Buffers, native memory and the stack.

  • Why it matters — The heap-limit-versus-container-limit mismatch causes silent OOMKilled restarts that people misdiagnose as crashes.

  • Follow-ups — What is the difference between OOMKilled by the kernel and a V8 heap OOM, and how do you tell from the logs? Do Buffers count toward old space? How do you observe GC pauses?

  • Senior signal — The 75–80% rule with the reason, and distinguishing kernel OOM from V8 OOM by the evidence each leaves.

Q21. What happens on an unhandled promise rejection, and what should your policy be?

  • Expected answer — Since Node 15 the default --unhandled-rejections=throw turns an unhandled rejection into an uncaught exception, which terminates the process unless you have an uncaughtException handler. That is the right default: an unhandled rejection means a code path you did not think about, and continuing with unknown state risks corrupt data. My policy is: keep the default, add a process.on('unhandledRejection') handler whose only job is to log with context and then let the process die, run a supervisor (Kubernetes) that restarts it, and make sure graceful shutdown drains in-flight requests. Never swallow. In Nest, most rejections inside a request are caught by the framework and turned into a 500 by the exception filter; the dangerous ones are fire-and-forget calls in event handlers, setInterval bodies and @Cron jobs, which is exactly why no-floating-promises lint is worth enforcing.

  • Why it matters — Reveals attitude to failure: hide it or surface it.

  • Follow-ups — Why is uncaughtException a bad place to keep serving traffic? How does this interact with a readiness probe? What is the difference between the rejection being unhandled and being handled late?

  • Senior signal — Crash-only thinking: log, exit, restart, drain — instead of "catch everything and keep going".

Q22. How do you implement graceful shutdown?

  • Expected answer — On SIGTERM: (1) immediately flip the readiness probe to failing so the load balancer stops sending new requests, and wait a few seconds for endpoints to propagate — this is the step everyone forgets and it is the reason for 502s during deploys; (2) call server.close() so no new connections are accepted while in-flight requests finish, and destroy idle keep-alive sockets; (3) stop consuming from queues and let in-flight messages finish or be nacked for redelivery; (4) stop cron/schedulers; (5) close the database pool and Redis clients; (6) process.exit(0). Everything gets a hard timeout — typically 20–25 seconds against a Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds of 30 — after which you force exit, because a hung shutdown becomes a SIGKILL and a truncated write. Nest gives you this with app.enableShutdownHooks() plus OnApplicationShutdown/beforeApplicationShutdown on providers.

  • Why it matters — Deploy-time 5xx spikes are almost always missing readiness-first shutdown.

  • Follow-ups — Why sleep before server.close()? What happens to a message you have pulled from SQS but not finished? How do keep-alive connections from an ALB complicate this?

  • Senior signal — The readiness-first ordering with the propagation delay, and hard timeouts on every step.

Q23. process.nextTick versus setImmediate — what is the difference and when does it bite?

  • Expected answer — process.nextTick puts the callback on a queue that is drained before promise microtasks and before the loop advances to the next phase — it is not part of the loop at all. setImmediate schedules for the check phase, so it runs after the current poll phase completes. So nextTick is "as soon as the current operation finishes", setImmediate is "on the next loop iteration". It bites in two ways: recursive nextTick starves the event loop completely (I/O never runs, the process hangs while CPU idles), and library authors use nextTick to make a callback consistently asynchronous, which can surprise you with ordering. The safe default in application code is setImmediate when you want to yield to I/O — for example, chunking a large loop so requests keep being served. Use nextTick only to guarantee "always async" semantics for an API that might otherwise call back synchronously.

  • Why it matters — Direct probe of event-loop understanding with a real starvation failure mode.

  • Follow-ups — Write a chunked processor for 1 million rows that yields. What order do nextTick and Promise.resolve().then run in? Which one would you use to defer an error emit?

  • Senior signal — The starvation failure mode and the "use setImmediate to yield to I/O" rule.

Q24. Why do you need HTTP keep-alive agents in Node, and what breaks without them?

  • Expected answer — By default the legacy http.globalAgent did not keep connections alive (this changed in Node 19, where keep-alive is on by default), and fetch/undici pools separately. Without keep-alive, every outbound call does a fresh TCP handshake plus a TLS handshake — roughly 1 RTT plus 1–2 RTTs — which on a 30 ms link adds 60–90 ms per call, and it burns ephemeral ports and file descriptors. With a shared agent (new https.Agent({ keepAlive: true, maxSockets: 100, maxFreeSockets: 20, timeout: 60_000 })), calls reuse warm connections and latency drops to the raw RTT. The failure modes to know: maxSockets too low silently queues requests inside the agent, so you see client-side latency with no server-side latency; keep-alive idle timeout longer than the peer's or the ALB's produces ECONNRESET/socket hang up on the first request after the peer closes, which you fix by setting your idle timeout below theirs and enabling retries on idempotent requests only.

  • Why it matters — Service-to-service latency and mysterious ECONNRESETs both trace back here.

  • Follow-ups — Why must the retry be restricted to idempotent requests? How would you see agent queuing in metrics? What does maxFreeSockets control?

  • Senior signal — The idle-timeout mismatch story and the "queue is invisible unless you instrument the agent" point.

Q25. Can DNS resolution block your Node process?

  • Expected answer — Yes, indirectly. dns.lookup() — which is what http.request, pg, and most clients use under the hood — calls getaddrinfo on the libuv thread pool, not through an async DNS protocol implementation. With the default pool of four threads, four slow lookups (a DNS server timing out at 5 seconds) occupy the entire pool, so all fs operations, crypto and further lookups queue behind them, and the whole service appears to stall even though the event loop is technically free. dns.resolve*() uses c-ares and real async sockets, so it does not consume the pool, but it ignores /etc/hosts and the system resolver order. Mitigations: cache DNS results in-process (cacheable-lookup wired into your agents), keep connections alive so you resolve rarely, raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE, and in Kubernetes reduce ndots churn with an explicit dnsConfig or fully qualified names so you do not do five failed lookups per resolution.

  • Why it matters — DNS is the classic hidden dependency in "everything got slow at once" incidents.

  • Follow-ups — What is ndots:5 doing in a Kubernetes pod and why does it multiply lookups? How would you prove DNS is the problem? Which is safer for a service mesh, lookup or resolve?

  • Senior signal — Connects DNS to thread pool saturation and mentions the Kubernetes ndots amplification, which is a scar you only get from operating clusters.

Q26. Your service starts throwing EMFILE. What is happening and how do you fix it?

  • Expected answer — EMFILE means "too many open files": the process has hit its file-descriptor limit (ulimit -n, often 1024 in a stock container). In Node, sockets, files, pipes and epoll instances are all descriptors. Common causes: a leak of open file handles or sockets (streams never closed on error paths, pipe() without error handling), a client library creating a new connection pool per request, keep-alive with maxSockets: Infinity against a slow upstream so sockets pile up, or genuine high concurrency with an unrealistically low limit. Diagnose with lsof -p <pid> or counting /proc/<pid>/fd, grouped by type — that instantly tells you if it is sockets to one host or files. Fixes in order: fix the leak, bound the pools, then raise the limit (LimitNOFILE/ulimit -n 65535) and confirm the container's limit matches. Raising the limit first just delays the incident and hides the leak.

  • Why it matters — Tests systems knowledge beyond JavaScript and a disciplined diagnosis order.

  • Follow-ups — How do you count descriptors by type? What does EMFILE do to your ability to accept any new connection, including the health check? Why is graceful-fs a band-aid?

  • Senior signal — "Fix the leak before raising the limit", plus knowing the health check dies too, which is why the pod looks unhealthy rather than slow.

Q27. Node is single-threaded. So why do race conditions still happen?

  • Expected answer — Single-threaded means no preemption inside one synchronous block, not no interleaving. Every await is a yield point: between the two halves of an async function, other requests run and can change shared state. So classic races appear: read-modify-write on a module-level Map, two requests both checking "does this email exist?" then both inserting, a cached value refreshed by two requests at once, or a counter incremented after an await. Add multiple processes and pods, and any in-process guard is worthless anyway. The correct fixes are the boring ones: push the invariant into the database (UNIQUE constraint, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, optimistic concurrency with a version column) or into Redis (SET key val NX PX ttl as a lock, INCR for counters). An in-memory mutex is acceptable only for a single-process-local resource such as serialising writes to one file.

    // race: two concurrent calls both see 0 and both write 1
const n = await redis.get(key); await redis.set(key, Number(n) + 1);
// correct: atomic
await redis.incr(key);

  • Why it matters — This misconception ("Node is single-threaded so no locks needed") causes duplicate orders and double charges.

  • Follow-ups — Where exactly is the yield point in your example? Why does a process-local mutex fail with three replicas? How would you make "create user if not exists" correct?

  • Senior signal — Names await as the yield point and immediately moves the invariant to the database, rather than reaching for an application-level lock.

Q28. How do you profile a Node service that is using too much CPU?

  • Expected answer — Start from evidence, not guesses. Confirm it is CPU and not loop lag from I/O by looking at process CPU, event loop delay and GC time together. Then capture a CPU profile from the affected instance: node --cpu-prof for a bounded run, --inspect plus DevTools for a live capture, clinic flame/0x for a flame graph, or a continuous profiler (Pyroscope, Datadog) if you have one, which is far better because you can profile the past rather than trying to reproduce. Read the flame graph by self time first: wide plateaus are the cost. Typical findings are JSON serialisation of oversized responses, class-transformer on big arrays, regex backtracking, synchronous crypto, logging at debug level in a hot path, and unnecessary deep clones. Fix, then re-profile to confirm — and set a regression guard, such as an autocannon benchmark in CI or an alert on CPU per request. Also compare against a baseline: 100% of one core with 40 ms of GC per second is a memory problem wearing a CPU costume.

  • Why it matters — Method beats tools; the answer shows whether they measure or guess.

  • Follow-ups — What does high GC time in the profile tell you? How do you profile a pod you cannot restart? What is the overhead of a continuous profiler?

  • Senior signal — Continuous profiling, self-time-first reading, and closing the loop with a regression guard.

45.3 NestJS

NestJS questions are usually a proxy for "do you understand the framework or do you cargo-cult decorators?" The best answers explain what happens at bootstrap versus per request.

Q29. How does the NestJS DI container work? What kinds of providers are there?

  • Expected answer — At bootstrap Nest scans modules, builds a dependency graph from each provider's metadata, topologically sorts it and instantiates singletons once. Constructor injection works because emitDecoratorMetadata writes design:paramtypes (the runtime constructor types) and Nest looks each token up in the module's injector. Provider forms: useClass (the shorthand providers: [OrderService]), useValue (constants, mocks, an already-built SDK client), useFactory (async or computed construction, with inject: [ConfigService] for its own dependencies), and useExisting (an alias to another token). Because interfaces do not exist at runtime, an abstract dependency needs a token — a string, a Symbol, or better an abstract class used as both type and token:

    export abstract class PaymentGateway { abstract charge(o: Order): Promise<Receipt>; }
{ provide: PaymentGateway, useClass: StripeGateway } // inject by the abstract class

    Resolution is per module: a provider is only injectable where its module is imported and the provider is exportsed.

  • Why it matters — DI errors ("Nest can't resolve dependencies of X") are the number one framework bug, and the fix requires this model.

  • Follow-ups — Read me the error message and tell me the three usual causes. When is useFactory async and what does that do to bootstrap time? How do you inject the same instance under two tokens?

  • Senior signal — Uses abstract classes as tokens for testability and swappability, and can debug a resolution error from first principles.

Q30. Explain injection scopes and what they cost.

  • Expected answer — Scope.DEFAULT is a singleton: one instance for the app's lifetime, shared by all requests. Scope.REQUEST creates a new instance per incoming request, and the whole dependency chain above it is also made request-scoped ("scope bubbling"), because a singleton cannot hold a request-scoped dependency. Scope.TRANSIENT gives every injector a fresh instance. The cost of request scope is real: Nest must instantiate that subtree on every request, which adds allocation and GC pressure, and it disables some optimisations — on a hot path this can be a measurable few percent, and if you accidentally make a controller request-scoped, the entire graph under it is rebuilt per request. It also breaks things that assume singletons, such as a provider that starts a setInterval in onModuleInit. Preferred alternative for "I need the current user or a correlation id": AsyncLocalStorage in a middleware or interceptor, which gives per-request context without per-request instantiation. Use REQUEST scope deliberately, for example a multi-tenant database connection resolved from the request host.

  • Why it matters — Scope bubbling is an easy way to accidentally halve throughput.

  • Follow-ups — What is ContextIdFactory for? How does request scope interact with a @Cron job that has no request? Show the AsyncLocalStorage alternative.

  • Senior signal — Knows about bubbling and offers AsyncLocalStorage, which is the answer of someone who has profiled it.

Q31. How do you design module boundaries in a large Nest application?

  • Expected answer — Modules should follow business capabilities, not technical layers: OrdersModule, PaymentsModule, InventoryModule — not ControllersModule, ServicesModule. Each module exposes a deliberately small public surface via exports (usually one facade service, plus its DTOs), and everything else stays private. Cross-module calls go through those exported facades or, better for anything that is not needed synchronously, through domain events so the caller does not depend on the callee at all. SharedModule/CoreModule should hold only truly cross-cutting things (config, logging, database connection); a god SharedModule that exports everything defeats the point and reintroduces the cycle problem. In practice I keep a rule: if module A imports B and B imports A, one of them is wrong — extract the shared piece or invert with an event.
