This structure is what makes a modular monolith splittable later: the module boundary becomes the service boundary, and the exported facade becomes the API client.

  • Why it matters — Module design is architecture; it decides whether the codebase is refactorable in year three.

  • Follow-ups — Where do shared DTOs live? How do you enforce boundaries in CI? What changes when you extract a module into its own service?

  • Senior signal — Ties module boundaries to future service extraction and mentions automated enforcement (dependency-cruiser, ESLint import rules), not just intentions.

Q32. What is the exact order of the NestJS request lifecycle?

flowchart LR
  A["Middleware"] --> B["Guards"]
  B --> C["Interceptor pre"]
  C --> D["Pipes"]
  D --> E["Handler"]
  E --> F["Interceptor post"]
  F --> G["Response"]
  B -->|"throw"| X["Exception filter"]
  E -->|"throw"| X

  • Expected answer — Incoming request, then: middleware (global first, then module-bound, in registration order) -> guards (global, controller, route) -> interceptors, pre-handler part (the code before next.handle()) -> pipes (parameter transformation and validation) -> the route handler -> interceptors, post-handler part (the RxJS operators applied to the returned stream, in reverse order) -> exception filters if anything threw at any point -> response. Two consequences people get wrong. First, pipes run after guards, so an authorization guard cannot rely on a validated/transformed body — it only has the raw one. Second, interceptors wrap the handler, so the post part runs in reverse nesting order (global outermost), which matters for timing/logging interceptors.

  • Why it matters — Ordering bugs (auth after validation, filters that never fire) are common and this is the map.

  • Follow-ups — Where would you put request-id generation and why? Can a filter catch an error thrown in middleware? Why can a guard not see the DTO instance?

  • Senior signal — Volunteers the guard-before-pipes consequence and the reverse ordering of interceptor post-processing.

Q33. How do you write a custom decorator, and when is one justified?

  • Expected answer — Two kinds. A param decorator built with createParamDecorator extracts something from the execution context, which removes repetitive plumbing from controllers:

    export const CurrentUser = createParamDecorator(
  (data: keyof AuthUser | undefined, ctx: ExecutionContext) => {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request & { user: AuthUser }>();
    return data ? req.user?.[data] : req.user;
  },
);

    A metadata decorator built with SetMetadata (or the typed Reflector.createDecorator()) attaches data a guard or interceptor later reads with reflector.getAllAndOverride(...) across handler and class. Composition helpers like applyDecorators let you bundle @UseGuards(JwtGuard, RolesGuard), @Roles('admin') and Swagger annotations into one @AdminOnly(). Justified when it removes duplicated cross-cutting plumbing from many handlers; not justified when it hides business logic, because a decorator is invisible in a stack trace and hard to unit test.

  • Why it matters — Shows understanding of the metadata system and of when abstraction helps versus obscures.

  • Follow-ups — How does getAllAndOverride differ from get? How do you unit test a param decorator? What breaks if the guard runs before the middleware that sets req.user?

  • Senior signal — The "do not hide business logic in decorators" boundary, and knowing the handler/class metadata merge strategies.

Q34. What is a dynamic module and when do you build one?

  • Expected answer — A dynamic module is a module whose providers are configured at import time. The class exposes static factory methods returning a DynamicModule object: forRoot(options) for app-wide singleton configuration (a database connection, an HTTP client), forRootAsync({ useFactory, inject }) when options depend on ConfigService or an async secret fetch, and forFeature(...) for per-module registrations such as which entities or queues this module uses. Internally you provide the options under a token and inject them into the service. Mark it @Global() only sparingly — global modules make dependencies invisible. You build one when you are packaging reusable infrastructure for multiple apps or teams: an internal KafkaModule, a tenant-resolution module, an audit-logging module. For a single application's own feature module, a plain module plus ConfigService is simpler and you should not over-engineer.

  • Why it matters — Distinguishes library authors from consumers, and tests the configurable-provider pattern.

  • Follow-ups — Implement forRootAsync with useFactory. Why does forFeature exist separately? What does ConfigurableModuleBuilder give you for free?

  • Senior signal — "Do not build a dynamic module for a single app" plus caution about @Global().

Q35. How do exception filters work and how do you design error responses?

  • Expected answer — Nest's built-in filter turns HttpException subclasses into responses and everything else into a 500. A custom filter (@Catch() for everything, @Catch(QueryFailedError) for a specific class) implements catch(exception, host), gets the underlying request/response from the ArgumentsHost, and writes a consistent envelope. I use one global filter that maps domain and infrastructure errors to HTTP once, in one place: EntityNotFoundError to 404, a unique-violation QueryFailedError with code 23505 to 409, a class-validator failure to 422 or 400 with field details, a timeout to 504, everything unknown to 500 with a generated traceId in the body and the full stack only in the logs. That last part matters: never leak stack traces, SQL text or internal hostnames to clients. Order note: filters are matched most-specific-first per level, and a route-level filter overrides the global one for that route.

    @Catch(QueryFailedError)
export class PgExceptionFilter implements ExceptionFilter { /* map 23505 -> 409 */ }

  • Why it matters — Error consistency is an API contract question, and leaking internals is a security issue.

  • Follow-ups — What does your error body look like and why? How do you keep the mapping testable? What status do you return for a business rule violation such as "insufficient inventory"?

  • Senior signal — One central mapping, a trace id linking client-visible errors to logs, and an explicit no-leak rule.

Q36. Which ValidationPipe options do you always set, and why?

  • Expected answer — whitelist: true strips properties with no decorator on the DTO, so a client cannot smuggle extra fields into an object you later pass to an ORM save. forbidNonWhitelisted: true turns that into a 400 instead of silent stripping, which I prefer for internal APIs and avoid for public ones where extra fields should be tolerated. transform: true turns the plain body into a real DTO instance so class-transformer conversions and defaults apply; with transformOptions: { enableImplicitConversion: true } query params become numbers and booleans, though I usually prefer explicit @Type(() => Number) because implicit conversion has surprising edge cases with '0' and empty strings. stopAtFirstError for cheap responses, disableErrorMessages: true in production only if you have a separate detailed log. And crucially, register it globally (app.useGlobalPipes) or via APP_PIPE so no route is accidentally unvalidated. The mass-assignment risk without whitelist is real: { "role": "admin" } posted to a profile update.

  • Why it matters — This is a security question disguised as a configuration question.

  • Follow-ups — Show the mass-assignment attack. Why does APP_PIPE matter over useGlobalPipes for DI? How do you validate nested arrays of objects?

  • Senior signal — Names mass assignment, and knows APP_PIPE allows the pipe to inject dependencies while useGlobalPipes does not.

Q37. What are interceptors good for, and what are they bad at?

  • Expected answer — An interceptor wraps the handler and returns an RxJS stream, so it can act before and after: response shaping (ClassSerializerInterceptor applying @Exclude/@Expose so password hashes never serialise), timing and logging, caching (CacheInterceptor), timeouts (timeout(3000) plus catchError mapping to a 504), retries on idempotent handlers, and transaction management if you are careful. They are bad at anything needing to stop the request before it runs with a domain decision — that is a guard's job — and at per-field validation, which belongs in pipes. The trap: an interceptor that wraps everything in a { data: ... } envelope also wraps file streams and health checks unless excluded, and a global caching interceptor that ignores the authenticated user will serve one user's data to another. Test that specifically.

    return next.handle().pipe(timeout(3000), catchError(e =>
  throwError(() => e instanceof TimeoutError ? new GatewayTimeoutException() : e)));

  • Why it matters — Cross-cutting concerns done in the wrong layer create both bugs and security holes.

  • Follow-ups — How would you add a per-request timeout without breaking streaming responses? Why is a global cache interceptor dangerous with auth? Where do you start the DB transaction?

  • Senior signal — The user-scoped cache poisoning risk, and the guard-versus-interceptor boundary.

Q38. You get a circular dependency error. What do you do?

  • Expected answer — First, treat it as a design smell rather than something to patch. Nest offers forwardRef(() => OtherModule) on both sides of the import and @Inject(forwardRef(() => OtherService)) on the constructor, and that works, but it also disables some resolution guarantees and makes the graph harder to reason about. The better fixes in order: (1) extract the shared piece into a third module both depend on; (2) invert the direction with an event — if OrdersService needs to tell NotificationsService something, emit order.paid via EventEmitterModule or a real broker and let notifications subscribe, so orders no longer imports notifications; (3) pass a callback or use the ModuleRef to resolve lazily at call time (this.moduleRef.get(X, { strict: false })) when there is genuinely a runtime-only relationship. I use forwardRef only as a temporary bridge with a ticket, because a codebase with twenty forwardRefs has no module boundaries left.

  • Why it matters — How someone resolves cycles predicts whether the architecture degrades over time.

  • Follow-ups — Why does forwardRef need to be on both sides? What does the error message tell you about which side to fix? How does the event approach change failure semantics?

  • Senior signal — Treats the cycle as an architecture bug and reaches for event inversion; notes that the event approach changes the call from synchronous-and-transactional to asynchronous-and-eventually-consistent, which is a real trade-off, not a free win.

Q39. Which NestJS microservice transports have you used and how do you choose?

  • Expected answer — @nestjs/microservices supports TCP, Redis (pub/sub), NATS, MQTT, RabbitMQ, Kafka and gRPC, with two messaging styles: request-response (@MessagePattern, client.send(), returns an Observable) and event-based (@EventPattern, client.emit(), fire and forget). Choosing: gRPC for synchronous internal RPC where you want a schema, streaming and low latency; Kafka for high-throughput event streams with replay and ordered partitions; RabbitMQ for work queues with per-message ack, retries and dead-letter exchanges; NATS for lightweight fast messaging; Redis pub/sub only for non-durable fan-out because messages are lost if no one is listening; plain TCP transport basically never in production. The important caveats: client.send() over Kafka creates a reply topic and is usually the wrong shape — Kafka is for events; and consumer offset/ack semantics differ per transport, so "at least once" means you still need idempotent handlers regardless of which one you pick.

  • Why it matters — Transport choice is an architecture decision people often make by familiarity.

  • Follow-ups — How do you handle a poison message in the Rabbit transport? What does Nest do with Kafka offsets by default? When would you keep it a plain HTTP call instead?

  • Senior signal — Warns against request-response over Kafka and says "at least once, so make handlers idempotent" without being asked.

Q40. How do you test a NestJS service and a controller?

  • Expected answer — For a unit test, build a minimal module with Test.createTestingModule({ providers: [OrderService, { provide: PaymentGateway, useValue: mockGateway }, { provide: getRepositoryToken(Order), useValue: mockRepo }] }).compile() and pull the service with module.get. Mock at boundaries — gateways, repositories, clocks — not at internal method level, or the test locks in the implementation. For a controller test, use overrideGuard(JwtGuard).useValue({ canActivate: () => true }) so the HTTP contract is tested without auth plumbing. For integration and e2e, createNestApplication() plus supertest against a real Postgres in Testcontainers, applying the same global pipes and filters as main.ts (a very common bug is a test suite that passes because the global ValidationPipe was never registered in the test app). Use overrideProvider for external HTTP and useRealTimers/fake timers deliberately. And keep the container per test file, resetting data with a truncate or a transaction rollback rather than rebuilding the schema each time.

  • Why it matters — Testing strategy exposes how the person keeps a large codebase changeable.

  • Follow-ups — Why does the e2e app need the same globals as main.ts? How do you make tests fast with a real database? When is mocking the repository a mistake?

  • Senior signal — Mentions the "globals not registered in tests" trap and prefers a real database over mocked repositories for anything query-shaped.

Q41. How do you handle configuration and validate it?

  • Expected answer — ConfigModule.forRoot({ isGlobal: true, validationSchema, cache: true, expandVariables: true }) with a Joi (or class-validator/zod via validate) schema that fails fast at boot if anything is missing or malformed. Fail-fast is the whole point: a service that starts with DB_PASSWORD undefined and then throws on the first request is far worse than one that refuses to start, because Kubernetes will keep the old ReplicaSet during a rolling update if the new pods never become ready. I group config into typed namespaces with registerAs('db', () => ({...})) and inject ConfigType<typeof dbConfig> so consumers get real types instead of configService.get<string>('DB_HOST') stringly-typed lookups. Secrets do not live in .env in production; they come from the platform (Kubernetes secrets from AWS Secrets Manager via External Secrets, or SSM), and the app only reads environment variables. Never log the resolved config object.

  • Why it matters — Config mistakes are a top cause of failed deploys and of leaked credentials.

  • Follow-ups — What breaks if validation happens lazily? How do you rotate a database password without downtime? Why is cache: true recommended?

  • Senior signal — The fail-fast-plus-rolling-update argument, typed namespaces, and secret handling outside .env.

Q42. What lifecycle hooks does Nest give you and what belongs in each?

  • Expected answer — In order: onModuleInit (after the host module's dependencies are resolved — connect clients, warm caches, register consumers), onApplicationBootstrap (after all modules are initialised — safe place for things needing the whole graph, such as starting schedulers), then on shutdown onModuleDestroy, beforeApplicationShutdown (receives the signal; stop accepting work, drain), and onApplicationShutdown (final resource release: close pools, flush the logger). Shutdown hooks only fire if you call app.enableShutdownHooks(), which is the most commonly missed line and the reason "my cleanup never runs". Practical rules: do not do slow work in onModuleInit because it delays readiness for every pod on every deploy; do not start consuming from a queue before the app is fully bootstrapped or you will process a message with a half-built graph; and put "flip readiness to false" in beforeApplicationShutdown, before you close anything.

  • Why it matters — Startup and shutdown correctness is where deploy-time errors live.

  • Follow-ups — Why is enableShutdownHooks opt-in? Where do you register a Kafka consumer? What is the interaction with terminationGracePeriodSeconds?

  • Senior signal — Orders the shutdown steps around readiness and drain, and knows hooks are inert without the opt-in call.

Q43. Express adapter or Fastify adapter?

  • Expected answer — Express is the default and has the largest middleware ecosystem; Fastify is roughly two to three times faster on synthetic JSON benchmarks thanks to schema-based serialisation and a faster router. In practice the adapter is almost never the bottleneck for a real service: if a request does a 4 ms database query and a 1 ms Redis call, the framework overhead of 0.1 ms versus 0.05 ms is noise. I would choose Fastify when the service is a thin, extremely high-RPS proxy or aggregator where serialisation dominates, and when I do not need Express-only middleware. Costs to name: some third-party Nest packages and middleware assume Express, cookie/session/multipart handling uses different plugins, and @Res() semantics differ. Measure before switching an existing app; I have seen a migration produce a 4% end-to-end gain and two weeks of work.

  • Why it matters — Tests whether the candidate reasons about where time actually goes.

  • Follow-ups — What is Fastify's serialisation trick? What breaks if you use @Res() directly? How would you measure whether it is worth it?

  • Senior signal — Refuses to treat a benchmark number as an end-to-end number, and gives a concrete threshold for when the switch pays.

Q44. When would you use @nestjs/cqrs?

  • Expected answer — CQRS separates commands (state changes, no return payload beyond an id or acknowledgement) from queries (reads, no side effects), each with its own handler, plus events published after a command succeeds. @nestjs/cqrs gives you CommandBus, QueryBus, EventBus, AggregateRoot with apply()/commit(), and sagas that turn one event stream into further commands. It pays off when a domain has genuinely complex write rules and many read shapes — an orders domain where the write model enforces inventory, pricing and fraud rules, while reads are served from denormalised projections. It is over-engineering for CRUD: you get three files and a bus for what was a five-line service method, and stack traces become harder to follow. Also be clear that the Nest EventBus is in-process and not durable — if a handler must survive a crash, the event has to go through an outbox and a real broker, not the in-memory bus. That confusion causes silently lost side effects.

  • Why it matters — CQRS is the most commonly over-applied pattern in Nest codebases.

  • Follow-ups — Where does event sourcing come in, and do you need it? How do you keep the read model in sync and what is the staleness budget? What is the failure mode if an in-process event handler throws?

  • Senior signal — States the in-process-bus durability gap and gives a clear "not for CRUD" boundary with an example on each side.

45.4 SQL

SQL rounds separate people who write queries from people who understand what the planner will do with them. Answer with both the semantics and the execution shape.

Q45. Explain the join types, and the three join algorithms Postgres can choose.

  • Expected answer — Logical types: INNER (matching rows only), LEFT/RIGHT OUTER (keep all rows of one side, NULL-fill the other), FULL OUTER (both), CROSS (cartesian product), plus LATERAL which lets the right side reference columns from the left, and semi/anti joins which are what EXISTS/NOT EXISTS compile into. Physical algorithms: nested loop — for each outer row, probe the inner side; excellent when the outer side is tiny and the inner has an index, terrible when the outer row count is large and misestimated. Hash join — build a hash table on the smaller side, probe with the larger; the workhorse for big equality joins, needs memory (work_mem) and spills to disk in batches if it does not fit. Merge join — sort both sides on the join key then walk them together; good when inputs are already sorted, for example both sides arriving from index scans in key order, and for very large joins where hashing would spill. The planner picks by estimated cost; a plan flipping from hash to nested loop after statistics go stale is a classic "the query was fast yesterday" incident.

  • Why it matters — You cannot read EXPLAIN or fix a slow join without this vocabulary.

  • Follow-ups — When is a nested loop with 500,000 outer rows catastrophic, and what does the plan look like? What does work_mem do to a hash join? Give me a case where LATERAL is the right tool.

  • Senior signal — Connects algorithm choice to row estimates and work_mem, and tells the stale-statistics plan-flip story.

Q46. EXISTS versus IN versus a join — which do you use?

  • Expected answer — Semantically, EXISTS is a semi-join: it stops at the first matching row and never duplicates the outer row. IN (subquery) is usually planned identically to EXISTS in modern Postgres, but differs in NULL handling and can be worse when the subquery returns a large, non-unique set. A plain JOIN will multiply outer rows when the inner side has multiple matches, which is a correctness difference, not a performance one, so you need DISTINCT and then you have paid for a sort. My rule: use EXISTS for "does at least one related row exist", use JOIN when you actually need columns from the other table, and use IN with a small literal list. For anti-joins, always NOT EXISTS, never NOT IN, because of NULLs.

    -- customers who have ordered at least once
SELECT c.id, c.email FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

  • Why it matters — The join-duplication bug silently inflates reports and revenue numbers.

  • Follow-ups — Show me the duplication with a concrete example. What plan node does EXISTS produce? When is IN with a 10,000-element array a problem?

  • Senior signal — Leads with the correctness difference (row multiplication) rather than a performance folk rule.

Q47. Explain SQL NULL semantics and the traps.

  • Expected answer — NULL means "unknown", so comparisons yield unknown, not true or false: NULL = NULL is NULL, and a WHERE clause only keeps rows where the predicate is true. Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, or IS DISTINCT FROM when you want NULL-safe inequality. Aggregates skip NULLs: COUNT(col) counts non-null values while COUNT(*) counts rows, and AVG divides by the non-null count. NULL in a UNIQUE index does not conflict with another NULL (each is distinct) unless you use UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT in Postgres 15+. String concatenation with || yields NULL if any operand is NULL, which is how "Dear " turns into nothing in an email template. And CHECK constraints pass when the expression is unknown, so CHECK (amount > 0) does not reject a NULL amount — you also need NOT NULL.

  • Why it matters — NULL bugs are quiet: they produce wrong numbers rather than errors.

  • Follow-ups — Why did my CHECK constraint let a NULL through? What does ORDER BY col do with NULLs and how do you control it? How would you make an "at most one active row per user" constraint that treats NULL correctly?

  • Senior signal — Knows IS DISTINCT FROM, the CHECK-with-NULL gap, and the unique-index NULL rule with the Postgres 15 change.

Q48. What are window functions and when do you reach for one?

  • Expected answer — A window function computes a value across a set of rows related to the current row, without collapsing them the way GROUP BY does. The frame is defined by OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... ROWS/RANGE ...). The ones I use most: ROW_NUMBER() for deduplication and "latest per group", RANK/DENSE_RANK for leaderboards, LAG/LEAD for comparing an event to the previous one (time between order status changes), SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY ...) for running totals, and COUNT(*) OVER () to get a total count alongside a page of rows in one scan.

    SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT o.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) rn
  FROM orders o
) t WHERE rn = 1;   -- latest order per customer

    Cost note: window functions require a sort per partition unless an index provides the order, so on large tables check whether DISTINCT ON (customer_id) with a matching composite index is cheaper.

  • Why it matters — Window functions replace N+1 application loops with one query.

  • Follow-ups — ROWS versus RANGE in a frame — what is the difference and when does it bite? How does DISTINCT ON compare here? Where does the sort show up in EXPLAIN?

  • Senior signal — Offers DISTINCT ON as the Postgres-specific cheaper alternative and knows the default frame is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, which surprises people with ties.

Q49. Are CTEs materialised? How does that affect performance?

  • Expected answer — Before Postgres 12, every WITH clause was an optimisation fence: it was materialised into a temporary result, and predicates from the outer query could not be pushed into it. Since 12, a CTE that is referenced exactly once, is not recursive and has no side effects is inlined by default, so it behaves like a subquery and the planner can push filters down. You can force either behaviour with WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (...) or AS NOT MATERIALIZED. This matters a lot: a CTE that scans 50 million rows and is then filtered by the outer query used to scan all 50 million; inlined, it can use an index. Conversely, materialising on purpose is useful when the CTE is expensive and referenced multiple times, or when you want to stop the planner from re-evaluating a volatile function. Data-modifying CTEs (WITH del AS (DELETE ... RETURNING ...)) are always materialised and all run against the same snapshot, which is a subtlety people get wrong.

  • Why it matters — Version-dependent behaviour that changes query plans by orders of magnitude.

  • Follow-ups — Why do all branches of a data-modifying CTE see the same snapshot, and what bug does that cause? When would you force MATERIALIZED? How do you tell from EXPLAIN whether it inlined?

  • Senior signal — Knows the 12 boundary, both hint keywords, and the same-snapshot rule for writable CTEs.

Q50. Why is OFFSET pagination bad and how does keyset pagination work?

  • Expected answer — LIMIT 20 OFFSET 200000 still has to produce and discard 200,000 rows, so page latency grows linearly with page number; page 10,000 of an orders list can take seconds. It is also unstable: if a row is inserted while a user pages, rows shift and they see duplicates or skip records. Keyset (cursor) pagination instead remembers the last row's sort key and asks for rows after it, which with a matching index is a single index seek plus 20 rows regardless of depth.

    -- page 1
SELECT id, created_at FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;
-- next page, cursor = (last_created_at, last_id)
SELECT id, created_at FROM orders
WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND (created_at, id) < ($2, $3)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;

    The tuple comparison is the trick: it handles ties in created_at correctly and matches a composite index on (tenant_id, created_at DESC, id DESC). Trade-offs: no "jump to page 57", and the cursor must be opaque and signed so clients cannot forge it into someone else's tenant.

  • Why it matters — The single most common list-endpoint scaling bug.

  • Follow-ups — How do you support sorting by an arbitrary user-chosen column? What do you return as the cursor and how do you keep it stable? How would you give the UI a total count without scanning?

  • Senior signal — Uses row-value comparison rather than created_at < $2 OR (created_at = $2 AND id < $3), and mentions cursor opacity as a security concern.

Q51. Explain upsert semantics in Postgres.

  • Expected answer — INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (cols) DO UPDATE SET ... performs an atomic insert-or-update against a specific unique index or constraint (the "conflict target"), which must exist — you cannot upsert on an arbitrary predicate. EXCLUDED refers to the row that would have been inserted. DO NOTHING skips silently and, importantly, returns no row, so RETURNING id gives you nothing on conflict; if you need the id either way, use DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col on a harmless column or follow with a select.

    INSERT INTO inventory (sku, warehouse_id, qty)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (sku, warehouse_id)
DO UPDATE SET qty = inventory.qty + EXCLUDED.qty, updated_at = now()
RETURNING qty;

    Gotchas: the update part takes a row lock, so hot keys serialise; ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE can deadlock when concurrent statements touch multiple conflicting rows in different orders, so sort your batch by key; partial unique indexes need the same WHERE clause in the conflict target; and upsert consumes a sequence value even when it conflicts, so ids get gaps.

  • Why it matters — Upsert is the idiomatic idempotency primitive for consumers and imports.

  • Follow-ups — How do you make a Kafka consumer idempotent with this? Why does the sequence still advance? How do you avoid the deadlock in a 500-row batch?

  • Senior signal — Sorting batch keys to avoid deadlocks, and the DO NOTHING plus RETURNING gap, which is a real production surprise.

Q52. What does FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED do and what would you build with it?

  • Expected answer — SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes a row-level exclusive lock, so another transaction attempting the same rows blocks until commit. Adding SKIP LOCKED makes it silently ignore rows currently locked by others, and NOWAIT makes it error immediately instead of waiting. That turns a table into a concurrent work queue: many workers each grab a different batch without blocking each other.

    WITH claimed AS (
  SELECT id FROM jobs
  WHERE status = 'pending' AND run_at <= now()
  ORDER BY run_at
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  LIMIT 20
)
UPDATE jobs j SET status = 'running', locked_by = $1, locked_at = now()
FROM claimed c WHERE j.id = c.id RETURNING j.*;

    You get exactly-once claiming within the transaction, transactional consistency with your business tables (no dual-write problem), and no extra infrastructure. Limits: it does not scale to hundreds of thousands of jobs per second, dead workers need a lease timeout to reclaim rows, and the table bloats unless you archive completed rows, so add a partial index on status = 'pending' and a retention job.

  • Why it matters — "Do I need Kafka or is Postgres enough?" is a real senior decision and this is the pragmatic middle.

  • Follow-ups — How do you reclaim jobs from a crashed worker? What index makes this fast at 10 million rows? At what throughput would you move to a real broker?

  • Senior signal — Mentions lease reclaim, bloat, the partial index, and a specific throughput threshold rather than "Postgres queues are bad".

Q53. Why does adding a join break my SUM, and how do you fix it?

  • Expected answer — Because a join to a one-to-many table multiplies the parent row, and the aggregate then counts the parent value once per child. Joining orders to both order_items and payments and summing orders.total gives items-count times payments-count times the real value — a classic "our revenue dashboard is 3x too high" incident. Fixes, in order of preference: aggregate each child in its own subquery or lateral before joining; use FILTER clauses or COUNT(DISTINCT ...) when the shape is simple; or aggregate at one grain per query and combine in the application.

    SELECT o.id, o.total, i.item_count, p.paid
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT count(*) item_count FROM order_items WHERE order_id = o.id) i ON true
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT sum(amount) paid FROM payments WHERE order_id = o.id) p ON true;

    COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) masks the symptom but not the SUM problem, so never treat it as the fix.

  • Why it matters — This is the most common source of silently wrong reporting numbers.

  • Follow-ups — Why is SUM(DISTINCT ...) not a fix? How do you spot this in a review? What is the performance profile of lateral subqueries versus pre-aggregated CTEs?

  • Senior signal — Names "grain" explicitly and can tell the story of a wrong dashboard number reaching a stakeholder.

Q54. Write a recursive CTE and say where you would use one.

  • Expected answer — A recursive CTE has an anchor query and a recursive term unioned together, evaluated until the recursive term returns no rows. Real uses: category trees, org charts, bill-of-materials explosion, and following a chain of referrals or reply threads.

    WITH RECURSIVE subtree AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, name, 1 AS depth, ARRAY[id] AS path
  FROM categories WHERE id = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, c.name, s.depth + 1, s.path || c.id
  FROM categories c JOIN subtree s ON c.parent_id = s.id
  WHERE NOT c.id = ANY(s.path) AND s.depth < 20
)
SELECT * FROM subtree;

    The two production concerns are cycles and depth. Bad data with a cycle makes the query run forever and eat memory, so carry a path array and exclude visited ids, and add a depth cap. Use UNION instead of UNION ALL only if you want automatic duplicate elimination, which is slower. For very deep hierarchies read frequently, consider a materialised path or closure table instead, since a recursive CTE on a hot endpoint is expensive.

  • Why it matters — Hierarchies appear in every catalogue and permission system.

  • Follow-ups — What happens with a cycle and how do you prove your guard works? When would you denormalise to a closure table? How do you paginate a tree?

  • Senior signal — Volunteers the cycle guard and depth cap, and knows when to stop using recursion and denormalise.

Q55. COUNT(*) on a 200-million-row table takes 40 seconds. What do you do?

  • Expected answer — First, understand why: because of MVCC, Postgres must check row visibility, so an exact count requires scanning the table or a full index (an index-only scan helps only if the visibility map is mostly all-visible, which needs a recent VACUUM). Then ask what the count is for. If it is a UI "about N results", use reltuples from pg_class (updated by analyze/vacuum, accurate to a few percent) or EXPLAIN's estimated row count for a filtered query. If it is a dashboard total, maintain a counters table or materialised view refreshed periodically, or use an approximate structure like HyperLogLog via postgresql-hll for distinct counts. If it is pagination, drop total counts entirely and use keyset pagination with "load more". If an exact count is genuinely required for correctness (financial reconciliation), run it off a replica during a quiet window and accept the cost. What I refuse to do is put an exact COUNT(*) behind a page-load on a growing table, because the endpoint gets slower every week by design.

  • Why it matters — Tests MVCC understanding plus product judgement.

  • Follow-ups — How accurate is reltuples and what makes it drift? How does an index-only scan avoid the heap and when does it fail to? How would you count rows matching a filter approximately?

  • Senior signal — Reframes the question around what the number is for, and names the visibility map as the reason index-only scans sometimes do not help.

Q56. Why is NOT IN with a subquery dangerous?

  • Expected answer — If the subquery returns even one NULL, NOT IN evaluates to unknown for every row and the query returns zero rows — silently. x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) asks "is x different from 1 and 2 and NULL?", and "different from NULL" is unknown, so the whole conjunction can never be true. NOT EXISTS has no such problem because it is a straightforward anti-join on the correlation predicate. There is a performance dimension too: NOT IN often cannot be planned as an anti-join precisely because of the NULL semantics, so Postgres may build a hashed subplan or re-evaluate it.

    -- dangerous: returns nothing if any customer_id is NULL
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);
-- correct
SELECT * FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

  • Why it matters — A query that returns zero rows instead of erroring is the worst kind of bug.

  • Follow-ups — How would you have caught this in review or in tests? Does NOT IN with a literal list have the same issue? What plan node does NOT EXISTS produce?

  • Senior signal — Explains the three-valued logic rather than saying "NOT IN is slow", and mentions the planner consequence.

Q57. What makes a predicate sargable, and give examples of non-sargable ones.

  • Expected answer — Sargable means the predicate can be used to seek into an index — the indexed column appears bare on one side and is compared to a constant or parameter. Wrapping the column in a function or expression destroys that: WHERE lower(email) = $1, WHERE date(created_at) = '2026-01-01', WHERE amount::text LIKE '1%', WHERE created_at + interval '1 day' > now(), and leading-wildcard LIKE '%foo' all force a sequential scan against a plain B-tree. Fixes: rewrite as a range (created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-02'), move the arithmetic to the constant side, create an expression index (CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))) when the function form is genuinely needed, use citext or a case-insensitive collation, and use pg_trgm GIN indexes for leading-wildcard search. Implicit casts are the sneaky case: comparing a bigint column to a string literal, or varchar to text across a type mismatch, can silently disable the index — check the plan, not the intent.

  • Why it matters — Most "the index isn't being used" tickets are this.

  • Follow-ups — Show the EXPLAIN difference for the timestamp case. When is an expression index better than changing the query? How do you catch implicit casts?

  • Senior signal — Names implicit casts and expression indexes, and insists on reading the plan to confirm.

Q58. How do you query and index JSONB properly?

  • Expected answer — -> returns JSON, ->> returns text, #> and #>> take a path, and the containment operator @> asks "does this document contain this fragment". For indexing, a default GIN index on the whole column (USING gin (payload)) supports @>, ?, ?|, ?&; the jsonb_path_ops operator class is smaller and faster but supports only @>. For equality on one hot key, a B-tree expression index is much cheaper: CREATE INDEX ON events ((payload->>'user_id')). Note that ->> yields text, so numeric comparisons need a cast and a matching index expression.

    CREATE INDEX events_payload_gin ON events USING gin (payload jsonb_path_ops);
SELECT * FROM events WHERE payload @> '{"type":"order.paid","currency":"INR"}';

    The senior position: JSONB is excellent for genuinely variable data (webhook payloads, event envelopes, per-tenant custom fields) and terrible as a substitute for columns. Once a field is queried, filtered or constrained, promote it to a real column with a constraint. Also watch TOAST: large documents are compressed and stored out of line, so selecting a whole 200 KB payload for every row of a list endpoint is a hidden I/O cost.

  • Why it matters — JSONB abuse is a common cause of unindexable, unconstrainable data.

  • Follow-ups — When would you choose jsonb_path_ops? How do you enforce that payload->>'amount' is numeric? What is the write amplification of a GIN index?

  • Senior signal — The "promote queried fields to columns" rule, GIN write cost, and TOAST awareness.

Q59. How do you control transactions in SQL, and what do savepoints buy you?

  • Expected answer — BEGIN, then COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Inside, SAVEPOINT s1 marks a point you can ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s1 without losing the whole transaction, and RELEASE SAVEPOINT discards it. In Postgres, any error aborts the current transaction entirely — subsequent statements fail with "current transaction is aborted" — so a savepoint is the only way to attempt a statement that might fail and continue. That is how ORMs implement nested transactions: TypeORM's nested transaction() and Sequelize's nested transaction both emit savepoints, not real nested transactions. Costs: each savepoint consumes a subtransaction id, and more than 64 subtransactions in one transaction overflows the per-backend cache and can cause severe cluster-wide slowdowns under concurrency (the well-known "subtransaction overflow" pathology). So do not put a savepoint inside a loop over 10,000 rows. Keep transactions short, never hold one open across an HTTP call to a third party, and set statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.

  • Why it matters — Transaction scope discipline is the difference between a healthy and a lock-choked database.

  • Follow-ups — Why is a transaction held open across a payment-gateway call dangerous? What does idle_in_transaction_session_timeout protect? What does the ORM do when you nest transactions?

  • Senior signal — Knows savepoints are subtransactions with a real cluster-level cost, and refuses long transactions with a concrete reason (bloat, lock hold, connection exhaustion).

Q60. What is RETURNING good for?

  • Expected answer — RETURNING makes INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE return the affected rows, so you get generated ids, defaults, computed columns and post-update values in a single round trip instead of a follow-up SELECT. That is both faster (one network round trip, ~0.5–2 ms saved per call, which matters in a loop) and safer: the returned values are the ones this statement actually wrote, with no race against a concurrent update. Combined with conditional updates it becomes a concurrency primitive: an UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'pending' RETURNING id tells you whether you were the one who transitioned the row, which is how you make a state machine safe against duplicate requests.

    UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid', paid_at = now()
WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'pending'
RETURNING id, status, paid_at;   -- zero rows means someone else already paid it

    It also composes with data-modifying CTEs for move-and-audit patterns: delete from one table and insert the returned rows into another in one statement.

  • Why it matters — It replaces read-then-write races with single-statement atomicity.

  • Follow-ups — How does this give you idempotency for a webhook? What does zero returned rows mean and how should the API respond? How do you do this in TypeORM and Sequelize?

  • Senior signal — Uses RETURNING with a guarded WHERE as a lock-free compare-and-set, and interprets zero rows as information rather than an error.

45.5 PostgreSQL

This is the deepest technical section in the Part, because for a senior backend role Postgres knowledge is the highest-leverage differentiator. Twenty-two questions, from storage internals to operations.

Q61. Explain MVCC in PostgreSQL.

  • Expected answer — Multi-Version Concurrency Control means writers never block readers and readers never block writers, because each UPDATE creates a new row version rather than overwriting in place. Every row (tuple) carries hidden system columns xmin (the transaction that created it) and xmax (the transaction that deleted or superseded it). A transaction sees a snapshot: the set of transaction ids that had committed when it took the snapshot, so it shows a tuple if xmin is visible to it and xmax is not. Consequences that matter in production: an UPDATE of one column rewrites the whole row and every index entry unless HOT (heap-only tuple) applies — HOT requires the updated columns to be unindexed and free space on the same page, which is what fillfactor reserves. Dead tuples accumulate and must be reclaimed by VACUUM. And a long-running read transaction pins an old snapshot, which prevents vacuum from cleaning anything newer, so one forgotten analytics query can bloat the whole cluster.

  • Why it matters — MVCC explains bloat, vacuum, long-transaction incidents and why COUNT(*) is slow, all at once.

  • Follow-ups — What is a HOT update and how do you encourage it? Why does a long SELECT on a replica affect the primary (hint: hot_standby_feedback)? What do xmin and xmax look like for an updated row?

  • Senior signal — Connects MVCC to the long-transaction-blocks-vacuum failure mode without prompting, and knows about HOT and fillfactor.

Q62. What does VACUUM do, and how do you deal with table bloat?

  • Expected answer — VACUUM marks space used by dead tuples as reusable and updates the visibility map and free space map; it does not return space to the OS. VACUUM FULL rewrites the table compactly and does return space, but takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, so it is offline. ANALYZE refreshes planner statistics and usually rides along with autovacuum. Autovacuum triggers when dead tuples exceed autovacuum_vacuum_threshold + autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor * reltuples — the default scale factor of 0.2 means a 100-million-row table waits for 20 million dead rows, which is far too late, so on big hot tables I set per-table values like autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01 and raise autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit so it actually keeps up. Diagnose bloat with pg_stat_user_tables (n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum) and the pgstattuple extension. To remove bloat online, use pg_repack, which rebuilds the table with only a brief lock. Root causes of runaway bloat: long-running transactions, abandoned replication slots, hot_standby_feedback with slow replica queries, and very high update rates on a narrow table.

  • Why it matters — Bloat is the slow-motion outage that turns a 2 ms query into a 200 ms one over months.

  • Follow-ups — Why does VACUUM not shrink the file? What does an inactive replication slot do to WAL and vacuum? How would you find the transaction blocking vacuum right now?

  • Senior signal — Per-table autovacuum tuning with real numbers, pg_repack over VACUUM FULL, and naming replication slots as a bloat cause.

Q63. What is transaction id wraparound and why should you care?

  • Expected answer — Transaction ids are 32-bit, so there are about 4 billion of them and visibility is computed on a circular comparison: roughly 2 billion ids "in the past" and 2 billion "in the future". If a tuple's xmin is never frozen and the counter wraps past it, rows that should be visible would appear to be in the future and effectively disappear. To prevent that, Postgres freezes old tuples (marking them as always-visible) during vacuum, driven by vacuum_freeze_min_age and autovacuum_freeze_max_age. If freezing falls too far behind, Postgres starts emitting "database is not accepting commands to avoid wraparound data loss" warnings, then refuses writes until you run a vacuum in single-user mode — a full outage. Newer versions have made the anti-wraparound vacuum less intrusive and Postgres 17+ improves the machinery further, but the failure mode still exists. Monitor age(datfrozenxid) per database and alert well before autovacuum_freeze_max_age (default 200 million). Causes of falling behind: autovacuum permanently cancelled by conflicting DDL, very long transactions, huge cold tables never vacuumed, and prepared transactions left hanging.

  • Why it matters — It is one of the few Postgres failure modes that stops writes completely, and it is entirely preventable by monitoring.

  • Follow-ups — What query would you alert on? Why can an idle prepared transaction cause this? What is the difference between freezing and vacuuming?

  • Senior signal — Has the monitoring query and the alert threshold, and names hanging prepared transactions, which is a scar.

Q64. Explain WAL and checkpoints.

  • Expected answer — Write-Ahead Logging means every change is written to the WAL and flushed to disk before the corresponding data page is. That gives crash recovery: on restart, Postgres replays WAL from the last checkpoint. Committing therefore costs one sequential fsync of the WAL, not random writes of data pages, which is why Postgres commits are fast. A checkpoint flushes all dirty shared buffers to the data files and records a new redo point, bounding recovery time; it is triggered by checkpoint_timeout (default 5 minutes) or by max_wal_size being exceeded. checkpoint_completion_target spreads that I/O over the interval to avoid a write storm. Tuning matters: too-frequent checkpoints cause repeated full-page writes (after a checkpoint, the first write to each page writes the whole page to WAL) and I/O spikes; too-infrequent means long recovery. WAL is also the transport for streaming replication and logical replication, and for PITR via archiving. synchronous_commit = off trades durability (you can lose the last ~200 ms of commits on a crash) for a large throughput gain, which is sometimes acceptable for non-financial write-heavy tables.

  • Why it matters — WAL sits behind durability, replication, backups and half of all write-performance tuning.

  • Follow-ups — What are full-page writes and why do they spike WAL volume after a checkpoint? What does synchronous_commit = remote_apply guarantee? How do you size max_wal_size?

  • Senior signal — Explains full-page writes and gives a scenario where synchronous_commit = off is a defensible trade.

Q65. Walk through the isolation levels Postgres supports and what each prevents.

  • Expected answer — Postgres offers READ COMMITTED (default), REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE; READ UNCOMMITTED is accepted but behaves as READ COMMITTED since dirty reads never happen. READ COMMITTED takes a fresh snapshot at the start of each statement, so two reads in one transaction can differ (non-repeatable read) and a statement can see rows committed mid-transaction. REPEATABLE READ takes one snapshot for the whole transaction; in Postgres it also prevents phantom reads because of the snapshot model, but it does not prevent write skew, and conflicting writes fail with a serialization error (40001) that the application must retry. SERIALIZABLE adds Serializable Snapshot Isolation: Postgres tracks read/write dependencies with predicate locks and aborts transactions that would produce a non-serializable schedule, again with 40001. So the real cost of the stronger levels is not locking, it is that your application must have a retry loop on 40001, with backoff and a cap. My default is READ COMMITTED with explicit locking or constraints where invariants matter, and SERIALIZABLE for a small number of genuinely tricky multi-row invariants.

  • Why it matters — Choosing an isolation level without a retry strategy is a guaranteed production bug.

  • Follow-ups — Show me the retry loop. Why does REPEATABLE READ not stop write skew? What is the throughput cost of SERIALIZABLE under contention?

  • Senior signal — Says "SERIALIZABLE without a retry loop is broken" and can write the loop, including which SQLSTATEs to catch (40001 and 40P01).

Q66. What is a lost update, and how do you prevent it?

  • Expected answer — Two transactions read the same row, each computes a new value from what they read, and both write; the second overwrites the first, so one update is silently lost. Classic case: two support agents editing the same order, or two requests both doing balance = balance - 100 after reading 500, leaving 400 instead of 300. Under READ COMMITTED this is entirely possible if you read and write in separate statements. Three fixes. (1) Do it in one statement so the database re-reads under the row lock: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = $1 AND balance >= 100. (2) Pessimistic locking: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before computing, which serialises but blocks. (3) Optimistic concurrency: a version column and UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2 RETURNING version, where zero affected rows means someone else changed it and you return a 409 so the client can re-fetch. For user-facing edit forms optimistic wins because it does not hold locks across think-time; for money movement inside a short transaction, the single-statement or FOR UPDATE form wins.

  • Why it matters — This is the most common real-world concurrency bug in CRUD applications.

  • Follow-ups — Which one would you use for an inventory decrement and why? How does TypeORM's @VersionColumn implement this? What does the client do on a 409?

  • Senior signal — Picks per situation rather than declaring one universally correct, and specifies the API-level behaviour (409 plus re-fetch), not just the SQL.

Q67. What is write skew and what actually fixes it?

  • Expected answer — Write skew is when two transactions read overlapping data, each checks an invariant that is still true for its own snapshot, and each writes a different row, so no direct write conflict occurs but the combined result violates the invariant. The textbook case is on-call scheduling: both doctors check "at least one other doctor is on call", both see it is true, both go off call, and now nobody is. In a backend, it is "allow at most 3 active subscriptions per account" or "the sum of these bookings must not exceed capacity" — checked with a SELECT count(*), then an INSERT. Row locks do not help because the rows being written did not exist at read time. Fixes: (1) SERIALIZABLE isolation, which is exactly what SSI is designed to catch, with a 40001 retry; (2) lock the parent object so the check is serialised (SELECT ... FROM accounts WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE before counting subscriptions); (3) express the invariant as a constraint the database can enforce — a unique index, an exclusion constraint (EXCLUDE USING gist for non-overlapping booking ranges), or a materialised counter column with a CHECK.

  • Why it matters — It is the concurrency bug that survives naive locking and shows up as "how did this even happen?".

  • Follow-ups — Write an exclusion constraint that prevents double-booking a room. Why does SELECT FOR UPDATE on the queried rows not fix it? What is the retry cost under SERIALIZABLE at 500 TPS?

  • Senior signal — Knows exclusion constraints and the "lock the parent" trick; a mid-level answer stops at "use SERIALIZABLE".

Q68. What causes deadlocks in Postgres and how do you fix them?

  • Expected answer — A deadlock is a cycle: transaction A holds a lock on row 1 and waits for row 2, while B holds row 2 and waits for row 1. Postgres detects it after deadlock_timeout (default 1 second) by building the wait-for graph, then aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40P01. Common real sources: batch updates that touch rows in different orders, ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE on multi-row inserts, foreign-key checks taking share locks on parent rows in different order, and application code that updates a parent and child in different orders in different code paths. Fixes, in order: (1) impose a global lock ordering — always sort ids before updating a batch; (2) shorten transactions so windows do not overlap; (3) take the coarser lock first when you know you will need it; (4) reduce lock strength where possible (FOR NO KEY UPDATE instead of FOR UPDATE when you are not changing the key); (5) add a retry with jitter, because at high concurrency some deadlocks are unavoidable. To debug, set log_lock_waits = on and read the deadlock report in the log, which prints both statements — that usually tells you the ordering violation immediately.

  • Why it matters — Deadlocks appear under load, so they are a production-experience marker.

  • Follow-ups — Read me a deadlock log entry and tell me the fix. Why does a foreign key cause locks on the parent? Would SERIALIZABLE make this better or worse?

  • Senior signal — Sorting ids as the primary fix, plus reading the deadlock report rather than guessing.

Q69. Explain Postgres lock modes and which DDL is safe online.

  • Expected answer — Table-level modes form a conflict matrix; the ones that matter are ACCESS SHARE (taken by SELECT), ROW SHARE (SELECT FOR UPDATE), ROW EXCLUSIVE (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE (VACUUM, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, ANALYZE), SHARE (CREATE INDEX), and ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (most ALTER TABLE, DROP, TRUNCATE, VACUUM FULL), which conflicts with everything including plain SELECT. The production danger is not the DDL duration but the queue: an ALTER TABLE waiting behind a long-running SELECT holds a pending ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request, and every subsequent query queues behind it, so a 5-millisecond migration causes a full outage. Always run migrations with SET lock_timeout = '3s' and retry. Safe-in-modern-Postgres operations: adding a nullable column, adding a column with a non-volatile default (11+, no rewrite), CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, adding a CHECK constraint as NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT separately, and SET NOT NULL backed by a validated check constraint (12+). Unsafe without care: changing a column type, adding a UNIQUE constraint directly (build the index concurrently first, then attach), and DROP COLUMN on a heavily-referenced table.

  • Why it matters — Migration-caused outages are extremely common and entirely avoidable.

  • Follow-ups — Walk me through adding a NOT NULL column with a default to a 500-million-row table with zero downtime. Why does lock_timeout help more than statement_timeout here? What is the lock queue and how do you inspect it?

  • Senior signal — The lock-queue explanation and the lock_timeout-plus-retry migration discipline.

Q70. How do you read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output?

  • Expected answer — Read the tree from the innermost node outward; each node reports cost=startup..total rows=estimated width=bytes and, with ANALYZE, actual time=first..last rows=N loops=L. The key habits: (1) compare estimated versus actual rows — an order-of-magnitude gap is a statistics problem and the true root cause of most bad plans; (2) remember actual time is per loop, so multiply by loops for the real cost of an inner node; (3) BUFFERS shows shared hit (cache) versus read (from the OS/disk) — a node doing 900,000 buffer reads is your I/O; (4) look for the specific smells: Seq Scan on a big table with a selective filter, Rows Removed by Filter in the millions, a Nested Loop with a large outer row count, Sort Method: external merge Disk: 512MB meaning work_mem is too small, and a Bitmap Heap Scan with high lossy block counts. Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE, SETTINGS, FORMAT TEXT) and, on Postgres 16+, GENERIC_PLAN for parameterised statements. Also confirm the plan came from the same parameters and the same work_mem as production, or you are debugging a different query.

  • Why it matters — It is the core diagnostic skill for anyone who owns a database.

  • Follow-ups — Here is a plan with rows=1 estimated and rows=480000 actual — what do you do? Why does loops matter? What does "lossy" mean in a bitmap scan?

  • Senior signal — Starts with the estimate-versus-actual gap rather than the top-line time, and mentions the per-loop multiplication that trips everyone up.

Q71. B-tree, GIN, BRIN, GiST, hash — when do you use which?

  • Expected answer — B-tree is the default and covers equality, ranges, sorting, and prefix LIKE 'abc%' with the right collation; it is what you want 90% of the time. GIN indexes composite values by their elements: full-text search tsvector, jsonb containment, and array membership; it is fast to search and expensive to write (mitigated by the pending list, fastupdate), and it is large. BRIN stores min/max summaries per block range, so it is tiny (kilobytes for a 100 GB table) and only useful when physical order correlates with the value — append-only time-series data on created_at is the perfect case; it is useless after random updates destroy correlation. GiST supports geometric, range and nearest-neighbour queries and backs exclusion constraints, for example non-overlapping booking tstzrange. Hash supports only equality, is WAL-logged and crash-safe since Postgres 10, and is occasionally smaller than B-tree for very large keys, but B-tree is almost always the safer choice. Decision shortcut: equality/range/sort -> B-tree; contains/search inside a document -> GIN; huge append-only table where you can accept coarse filtering -> BRIN; ranges and overlap -> GiST.

  • Why it matters — Index-type choice has 100x effects on size and write throughput.

  • Follow-ups — What is the write amplification of GIN on a high-ingest events table? How would you prove BRIN correlation is good? Why did your BRIN index stop helping after a backfill?

  • Senior signal — Explains BRIN's correlation dependency and GIN's write cost, and gives a real table where each was the right call.

Q72. How do you choose the column order in a composite index?

  • Expected answer — A B-tree on (a, b, c) is sorted by a, then b, then c, so it can be used for predicates on a leading prefix: a, a, b, a, b, c. It cannot seek on b alone. So the rules are: equality columns first, then the range or sort column last. For the query WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND status = $2 AND created_at > $3 ORDER BY created_at DESC, the right index is (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC) — two equalities then the range, which also satisfies the ORDER BY and avoids a sort node. Putting created_at before status means the index can only range-scan on time and then filter, reading far more entries. Selectivity matters less than people think once equality/range ordering is right, but among equality columns put the more selective one first if queries vary, and consider whether one index can serve several queries by prefix — three indexes (a), (a,b), (a,b,c) are wasteful because (a,b,c) covers all three prefixes. Verify with EXPLAIN: look for "Index Cond" (used for seeking) versus "Filter" (checked after fetching), which is the direct evidence of whether a column is actually helping.

  • Why it matters — Index design is the highest-value database skill and this is its core rule.

  • Follow-ups — Why is Filter versus Index Cond the tell? When does DESC in the index definition actually matter? How many indexes is too many on a write-heavy table?

  • Senior signal — The equality-then-range rule stated crisply, the prefix-redundancy insight, and using Index Cond versus Filter as evidence.

Q73. What is a partial index and when is it the right answer?

  • Expected answer — A partial index has a WHERE clause and indexes only the matching rows, so it is smaller, faster to scan and cheaper to maintain. It is the right answer whenever a small, hot subset of a large table is queried constantly. Two patterns I use repeatedly: a job/outbox queue where only pending rows matter, and a "one active row per key" constraint.

    CREATE INDEX jobs_pending ON jobs (run_at) WHERE status = 'pending';
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_default_address ON addresses (user_id) WHERE is_default;

    The first turns a 200-million-row table into a 40,000-entry index that fits in cache; the second enforces a business rule the database can guarantee, which is far better than application checks that race. Requirements: the planner will only use it if it can prove the query predicate implies the index predicate, so the query must contain a matching condition — status = 'pending' written as a bound parameter sometimes fails that proof, which surprises people, so use a literal or check the plan. Also, if the definition uses a mutable expression like now(), it is not allowed, because index predicates must be immutable.

  • Why it matters — Partial unique indexes are the cleanest way to express real business constraints.

  • Follow-ups — Why might a parameterised query miss a partial index? How do you express "only one in-flight payment per order"? What happens to the index when a row's status changes?

  • Senior signal — Uses partial unique indexes as constraints and knows the predicate-proof limitation.

Q74. What is a covering index and what does INCLUDE do?

  • Expected answer — A covering index contains every column a query needs, so Postgres can answer it with an index-only scan and never touch the heap. Since version 11 you can add non-key payload columns with INCLUDE, which keeps them out of the B-tree's ordering and comparison logic but stores them in the leaf pages.

    CREATE INDEX orders_lookup ON orders (tenant_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (status, total_minor);

    The important caveat: index-only scans still consult the visibility map to check whether each page is all-visible; if the table has recently changed and has not been vacuumed, Postgres falls back to heap fetches and the benefit disappears. EXPLAIN shows this as Heap Fetches: 480312. So a covering index on a heavily-updated table needs aggressive autovacuum to pay off. Costs: a wider index means fewer entries per page, more memory, and slower writes, so covering makes sense for a specific high-frequency query, not as a default. INCLUDE is also how you keep a unique index unique on (a) while still covering b.

  • Why it matters — It is the difference between 1 ms and 40 ms on a hot list endpoint, but only if you understand the visibility-map dependency.

  • Follow-ups — What does Heap Fetches in the plan tell you and how do you drive it to zero? When would you put a column in the key rather than INCLUDE? What is the write cost?

  • Senior signal — Knows index-only scans depend on the visibility map and therefore on vacuum, which is the detail that separates reading a blog post from operating a database.

Q75. When does an index make things worse?

  • Expected answer — Every index is a write tax: an INSERT must add an entry to each index, an UPDATE to an indexed column must add entries to those indexes and blocks HOT updates, and each index is more WAL, more disk, more memory competing for shared_buffers, and more work for vacuum. On a table taking 20,000 inserts per second, ten indexes can halve throughput. Indexes also hurt when they are not selective: an index on status where 95% of rows are 'completed' will not be used for that value, and if the planner is tricked into using it the bitmap scan plus heap fetches can be slower than a sequential scan. Small tables (a few hundred rows, one page) are faster to scan than to index. Redundant indexes are pure cost: (a) is subsumed by (a, b). And unused indexes are worse than useless — find them with pg_stat_user_indexes where idx_scan = 0 over a full business cycle, and drop them (after checking they are not backing a constraint, and preferably with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY). My rule: an index needs a query that justifies it, and I re-audit index usage quarterly.

  • Why it matters — Junior engineers add indexes; seniors also remove them.

  • Follow-ups — How do you safely decide an index is unused? What does an index do to a HOT update? How would you measure the write cost before adding one?

  • Senior signal — Talks about removing indexes, the HOT-update interaction, and a full business cycle before trusting idx_scan = 0.

Q76. How do you add an index to a 300-million-row table in production?

  • Expected answer — CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. A plain CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock that blocks all writes for the whole build, which on that table is many minutes of downtime. CONCURRENTLY does two table passes and waits for existing transactions, taking only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, so reads and writes continue. The costs and rules: it cannot run inside a transaction block (which matters because most migration tools wrap migrations in one — TypeORM and Sequelize both do, so you disable that for this migration); it takes roughly two to three times as long; it can fail and leave an INVALID index behind, which you must find (pg_index.indisvalid = false), drop concurrently, and retry; and it waits on long-running transactions, so a stuck analytics query blocks the build indefinitely. Operationally I run it outside the deploy pipeline or in a separate migration step, monitor pg_stat_progress_create_index, run it during a low-traffic window because it consumes significant I/O and maintenance_work_mem, and verify validity plus EXPLAIN afterwards before shipping the code that depends on it.

  • Why it matters — This is the difference between a routine change and an incident.

  • Follow-ups — What do you do when the concurrent build fails halfway? How does this interact with your migration framework's transaction? What order do you ship the index and the query that uses it?

  • Senior signal — Knows the invalid-index cleanup, the transaction-block restriction in migration tools, and ships the index before the code.

Q77. Why are Postgres connections expensive, and what does PgBouncer solve?

  • Expected answer — Each connection is a forked OS process with its own memory (a few megabytes of private memory plus work_mem allocations per sort or hash node, which is per operation, not per connection), and every backend participates in snapshot and lock bookkeeping, so throughput actually degrades past a point — a common rule of thumb is a sweet spot around 2 to 4 x cores active connections, so on 16 cores something like 32 to 64. Node makes this worse: 30 pods times a pool of 20 is 600 connections against a max_connections of 200, and you get FATAL: sorry, too many clients already at exactly the wrong moment. PgBouncer multiplexes many client connections onto few server connections. In transaction pooling mode (the useful one) a server connection is assigned only for the duration of a transaction, so 2,000 clients can share 40 backends. The trade-offs you must state: transaction pooling breaks session state, so no session-level SET, no LISTEN/NOTIFY, no session advisory locks, and prepared statements need care (max_prepared_statements in PgBouncer 1.21+, or disable them in the driver). Sizing: application pool small (say 5–10 per pod), PgBouncer default_pool_size around the database's sweet spot.

  • Why it matters — Connection exhaustion is a top-three Postgres outage cause in containerised environments.

  • Follow-ups — What breaks with transaction pooling in TypeORM or Sequelize? How do you size the app pool versus the bouncer pool? What is RDS Proxy doing differently?

  • Senior signal — Gives concrete numbers and names exactly what transaction pooling breaks, instead of "PgBouncer makes it faster".

Q78. Explain streaming replication and replica lag.

  • Expected answer — The primary streams WAL to standbys, which replay it. Replication is asynchronous by default: the primary commits without waiting, so a standby can be behind by milliseconds normally and by minutes under load or during a big UPDATE. synchronous_commit = on with synchronous_standby_names makes the primary wait for the standby to flush (or apply, with remote_apply), which gives zero data loss on failover at the cost of adding the network round trip to every commit and, critically, making the primary unavailable for writes if the standby dies unless you configure quorum. Lag has three flavours you should measure separately: write, flush and replay lag (pg_stat_replication), plus pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() on the standby. Reading from replicas is the standard scale-out for read-heavy workloads, but it introduces read-your-writes violations: a user creates an order, is redirected to the detail page, the read hits a lagging replica, and they get a 404. Mitigations: route reads that follow a write to the primary for a short window, pass an LSN and wait for the replica to catch up, or make the UI use the response body it already has. Also note hot_standby_feedback = on protects long replica queries from being cancelled but lets replica queries cause bloat on the primary.

  • Why it matters — Read replicas are the most common scaling move and the most common source of confusing "missing data" bugs.

  • Follow-ups — How would you implement read-your-writes? What causes replay lag to spike specifically? What is the failure mode of synchronous replication with one standby?

  • Senior signal — Names read-your-writes as the concrete product bug and knows the hot_standby_feedback trade-off in both directions.

Q79. When and how would you partition a table?

  • Expected answer — Declarative partitioning (PARTITION BY RANGE | LIST | HASH) splits one logical table into physical partitions. The real motivations are operational, not query speed: dropping old data becomes DROP TABLE (instant) instead of a DELETE of 200 million rows that bloats the table for weeks; vacuum, index builds and backups operate per partition; and index sizes stay in memory. Range partitioning by month on an events or orders table is the canonical case. Query speed improves only when the planner can prune partitions, which requires the partition key to be in the WHERE clause — so if your dominant query filters by tenant_id and you partitioned by created_at, you scan every partition and it is slower than before. Costs and gotchas: the partition key must be part of every unique constraint and primary key, so you cannot have a globally unique email unless email is the key; cross-partition foreign keys pointing at a partitioned table were long unsupported (allowed from 12+ with caveats); too many partitions (thousands) slow planning; and you need automation to create future partitions, or writes fail at midnight on the first of the month, which is an incident I have seen twice. Use pg_partman or a scheduled job, and always pre-create several months ahead.

  • Why it matters — Partitioning is often proposed as a fix for the wrong problem.

  • Follow-ups — What happens when a row does not match any partition? How do you migrate an existing 500 GB table to a partitioned one online? What does partition pruning look like in EXPLAIN?

  • Senior signal — Says partitioning is primarily about data lifecycle and maintenance, names the unique-key restriction, and has the missing-future-partition scar.

Q80. How do you use pg_stat_statements?

  • Expected answer — It is an extension that aggregates normalised query statistics: calls, total_exec_time, mean_exec_time, stddev_exec_time, rows, and shared buffer hit/read counts per query fingerprint (literals replaced by $1). The single most useful query is ordering by total_exec_time — not mean_exec_time — because a 2 ms query called 40 million times an hour costs far more than a 4-second report run twice. That is how you find the real hot spot, which is very often an N+1 from the ORM: one query with an enormous calls count.

    SELECT queryid, calls, round(total_exec_time::numeric,0) AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric,2) AS mean_ms, rows
FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 20;

    Complement it with pg_stat_user_tables (sequential scans, dead tuples), pg_stat_activity (what is running now, wait_event_type), and auto_explain with log_min_duration to capture actual plans of slow executions. Reset the view (pg_stat_statements_reset()) around an experiment so you measure a window rather than since-boot. Watch stddev too: a low mean with huge stddev means a plan that flips or a parameter value that is much worse than the rest.

  • Why it matters — It is the shortest path from "the database is slow" to a specific query.

  • Follow-ups — Why order by total rather than mean time? How do you spot an N+1 from this view? What would auto_explain add?

  • Senior signal — Orders by total time, uses stddev to detect plan instability, and knows the N+1 fingerprint.

Q81. What are planner statistics, and why does a plan suddenly flip?

  • Expected answer — ANALYZE samples rows (default default_statistics_target = 100, so 300 x 100 rows) and stores per-column most-common-values lists, histograms, null fraction and distinct-count estimates in pg_statistic. The planner multiplies per-column selectivities assuming independence. Plans flip when the estimate crosses a cost boundary: after a bulk load before autovacuum's analyze catches up, after data distribution shifts (a new large tenant), when correlated columns break the independence assumption (city = 'Mumbai' AND state = 'Maharashtra' estimates a product, so it underestimates by 30x and the planner picks a nested loop that then runs 400,000 times), or when a parameterised statement switches from a custom plan to a generic plan after five executions and the generic estimate is wrong. Fixes: raise default_statistics_target on skewed columns, create extended statistics (CREATE STATISTICS ... (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv) ON city, state FROM addresses), analyze after bulk loads, and where the planner is stubborn, restructure the query or use plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan for the offending prepared statement. Deliberate index hints do not exist in Postgres, which is a design decision, so the fix is always about better information.

  • Why it matters — "It was fast yesterday" is one of the most common production questions and this is the answer.

  • Follow-ups — How do you detect that a plan flipped? What is extended statistics doing exactly? Why does the generic plan appear on the sixth execution?

  • Senior signal — Knows extended statistics and the custom-versus-generic prepared-plan behaviour, both of which are real causes of overnight regressions.

Q82. What do statement_timeout, lock_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout do, and how do you set them?

  • Expected answer — statement_timeout cancels any statement running longer than the limit; it protects against runaway queries eating CPU and, crucially, against a query holding a snapshot that blocks vacuum. lock_timeout fails a statement that has waited too long to acquire a lock, which is what makes migrations safe: without it, an ALTER TABLE queues behind a long read and then blocks every subsequent query. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout kills sessions that opened a transaction and then went idle, which is the classic ORM bug where a transaction is started, an HTTP call is made, and the connection sits open holding locks and pinning an old snapshot. My defaults: a global statement_timeout of 30 s at the role level for the application user, tighter per-endpoint values set on the connection for user-facing paths (2–5 s), a much larger value or none for the reporting role, lock_timeout = 3s plus retry for migrations, and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 60s. Also set a client-side timeout that is longer than the server one so you always get a clean cancellation message rather than a mystery socket hang-up, and remember the application must map the resulting error to a 503 or 504, not a 500.

  • Why it matters — Timeouts are the cheapest availability control in a database and most teams have none.

  • Follow-ups — Why should the client timeout be longer than the server one? Where do you set these per role versus per session? What does the app do when a statement is cancelled mid-transaction?

  • Senior signal — Distinguishes the three precisely, gives concrete values with reasons, and covers the client-side and API-mapping consequences.

45.6 TypeORM

Q83. Explain DataSource, EntityManager and Repository, and when you use the query builder instead.

  • Expected answer — DataSource owns the connection pool and metadata and is created once at startup. EntityManager is the API for all entity operations against a connection; Repository<T> is just an EntityManager scoped to one entity, which is why repo.manager exists.
