Inside a transaction you must use the transactional manager (dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => ...) or a QueryRunner's manager); using the injected repository inside a transaction callback silently runs on a different connection outside the transaction, which is the single most common TypeORM bug and produces writes that do not roll back. I use find/findOne with relations for simple reads, and drop to createQueryBuilder as soon as I need joins with conditions, aggregates, window functions, ON CONFLICT, SKIP LOCKED, or explicit control of the generated SQL. For genuinely complex analytics I use manager.query() with raw parameterised SQL — an ORM is not a query language, and pretending otherwise produces unreadable builder chains.

  • Why it matters — The transactional-manager mistake causes real data-integrity incidents.

  • Follow-ups — Show the wrong and right way to write a transactional service method. What does @Transactional-style AsyncLocalStorage propagation buy you? When do you drop to raw SQL?

  • Senior signal — Leads with the transaction/connection trap and is comfortable abandoning the ORM for the right query.

Q84. How do relations load in TypeORM, and how do you avoid N+1?

  • Expected answer — Relations are lazy by default in the sense that they are simply not loaded; you opt in with relations: ['items'], eager: true on the relation, leftJoinAndSelect in the query builder, or by declaring the property as Promise<T[]> (true lazy relations, which fire a query on access — dangerous in a loop). N+1 happens when you load 100 orders and then touch order.customer for each, producing 101 queries; with a 2 ms query that is 200 ms of pure latency. Detect it by logging queries in development with a per-request count assertion, and in production by pg_stat_statements showing one fingerprint with an enormous calls value. Fixes: join and select in one query; or, when joining explodes rows (one order with 50 items times 3 payments), do two queries and stitch in memory, which is often faster than a wide join. Never set eager: true on a relation used by a list endpoint — it silently joins on every single find, including ones that did not want it.

  • Why it matters — N+1 is the most common ORM performance defect and it scales with data, so it passes tests and fails in production.

  • Follow-ups — Why can take/skip with leftJoinAndSelect return the wrong number of parents, and what does TypeORM do about it? How do you assert query counts in tests? When is two queries better than one join?

  • Senior signal — Knows the pagination-with-join problem (TypeORM uses a distinct id subquery, which changes the plan) and treats query count as a testable budget.

Q85. How do you run transactions correctly in TypeORM?

  • Expected answer — Either dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => { ... }), which commits or rolls back automatically, or an explicit QueryRunner when you need control:

    const qr = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner();
await qr.connect();
await qr.startTransaction('READ COMMITTED');
try {
  const order = await qr.manager.findOne(Order, { where: { id }, lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' } });
  await qr.manager.decrement(Inventory, { sku: order.sku }, 'qty', order.qty);
  await qr.commitTransaction();
} catch (e) { await qr.rollbackTransaction(); throw e; }
finally { await qr.release(); }   // release is mandatory or the pool leaks

    Rules I enforce: every path releases the query runner (a missing release leaks a pooled connection until the pool is exhausted); no HTTP or queue calls inside the transaction; keep it short; use lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' } for row locks and @VersionColumn for optimistic; and catch 40001/40P01 and retry with jitter when using higher isolation. Nested transaction() calls become savepoints, so a rollback of the inner one does not undo the outer, which people misread.

  • Why it matters — Connection leaks and silently non-transactional writes both come from this API.

  • Follow-ups — What happens if you forget release, and how would you detect it? How do you propagate the manager through several services cleanly? What isolation level do you pick for an inventory decrement?

  • Senior signal — The mandatory finally { release() }, no external calls inside the transaction, and an explicit retry policy.

Q86. synchronize: true versus migrations.

  • Expected answer — synchronize: true diffs your entities against the database and applies DDL at startup. It is convenient for a local prototype and catastrophic anywhere else: it can drop columns and tables when an entity changes, it runs unreviewed DDL on boot, it takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks with no lock_timeout, and with multiple pods starting at once, several instances race to alter the same table. Production uses generated, reviewed, versioned migrations (typeorm migration:generate, then hand-edited), run as a separate step in the deploy pipeline — ideally a Kubernetes Job or init step with a single replica and an advisory lock, not on every pod's startup. Generated migrations still need review: TypeORM will happily emit a column type change that rewrites a 200-million-row table. My rules: migrations are forward-only in production with a tested rollback plan (usually roll forward), expand-then-contract for breaking changes (add column, deploy code writing both, backfill, deploy code reading new, drop old), and every migration is tested against a production-sized copy for lock duration.

  • Why it matters — This is the difference between a safe deploy pipeline and data loss.

  • Follow-ups — How do you prevent two pods running migrations simultaneously? Walk me through renaming a column with zero downtime. When is a down-migration a lie?

  • Senior signal — Expand-and-contract, advisory-locked single-runner migrations, and reviewing generated SQL rather than trusting it.

Q87. What is the difference between save, insert, update and upsert?

  • Expected answer — save() is the "smart" one: it checks whether the entity has a primary key and whether it exists, so it may issue a SELECT then an INSERT or UPDATE, and it cascades to relations. That convenience costs an extra round trip and makes the SQL unpredictable, and with a client-supplied UUID primary key it will do a select-then-insert on every create. insert() and update() map directly to single statements, do not cascade, and do not return the full entity by default — much more predictable for hot paths and bulk work. upsert(entities, ['sku','warehouseId']) generates INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, which is what you want for idempotent consumers. Also know that save() on an array executes per-entity queries in a transaction unless chunked, so saving 10,000 rows one by one is a common performance disaster; use insert with chunks or the query builder's .insert().values(rows).orUpdate(...). And remove versus delete: remove loads entities and runs subscribers/cascades, delete issues a single DELETE.

  • Why it matters — Silent extra queries and unpredictable SQL are how ORM-heavy services get slow.

  • Follow-ups — Why is save slow with UUID primary keys, and what do you do instead? How do you bulk insert 100,000 rows? Which of these trigger entity subscribers?

  • Senior signal — Prefers explicit statements on hot paths and knows exactly which calls emit an extra SELECT.

Q88. How do you do optimistic and pessimistic locking in TypeORM?

  • Expected answer — Optimistic: add @VersionColumn() to the entity; TypeORM increments it on every save and adds WHERE version = :v to the update, throwing OptimisticLockVersionMismatchError if zero rows matched. You catch that and return HTTP 409 with the current representation so the client can merge and retry. It costs nothing when there is no contention, which is why it suits user-edited resources. Pessimistic: findOne({ where, lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' } }) emits SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and must be inside a transaction (TypeORM throws otherwise); pessimistic_read gives FOR SHARE, and pessimistic_partial_write maps to FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, which is how you build a job claimer. Choose pessimistic when contention is high and the critical section is short (decrementing stock for a flash sale), optimistic when conflicts are rare and holding a lock across user think-time would be unacceptable. The failure modes to name: pessimistic locks queue and can deadlock, so lock rows in a deterministic order and set lock_timeout; optimistic retries can livelock on a hot row, so cap retries and shed load.

  • Why it matters — This maps directly to Q66 and shows whether database theory reaches their actual code.

  • Follow-ups — What does the client do with the 409? How would you claim jobs with pessimistic_partial_write? What is your retry cap and why?

  • Senior signal — Chooses per contention profile and specifies API behaviour and retry caps rather than just naming the API.

Q89. What are the traps in TypeORM's query builder?

  • Expected answer — Several I hit regularly. (1) take/skip with leftJoinAndSelect cannot just apply LIMIT, because a joined parent spans many rows; TypeORM runs a distinct-ids subquery first, which changes the plan and can be slow, whereas limit/offset apply raw SQL limits and will silently truncate children — know which one you are calling. (2) Parameters must be named and reused carefully; passing the same name twice with different values silently uses the last. (3) where() overwrites, andWhere() appends, so a conditional filter chain that uses where in a loop drops earlier conditions — a data-leak-shaped bug when the dropped condition was tenant_id. (4) Raw string interpolation into where is a SQL injection hole; always use :param. (5) getMany versus getRawMany: the former hydrates entities and de-duplicates, the latter gives flat rows with prefixed aliases, and mixing them up produces surprising row counts. (6) Soft deletes only apply if you use softDelete/withDeleted consistently; a raw query builder join to the same table will happily return deleted rows.

  • Why it matters — These produce wrong data, not just slow data.

  • Follow-ups — Show me the where-in-a-loop bug. When do you want getRawMany? How do you enforce tenant scoping so it cannot be forgotten?

  • Senior signal — Frames the where overwrite and soft-delete gaps as security/tenancy risks and proposes systemic enforcement (a base repository or a global scope) rather than discipline.

Q90. How do you configure and monitor the TypeORM connection pool?

  • Expected answer — With the pg driver, pool options go in extra: max (pool size, default 10), min, idleTimeoutMillis, connectionTimeoutMillis, plus statement_timeout and query_timeout. Sizing is the important part: total connections equals pods times max, and it must fit under max_connections (minus superuser reserved slots) or, better, under your PgBouncer pool. With 20 pods, max: 10 is 200 connections — already at a stock RDS limit. A small pool with a queue is usually better than a large pool: the database gets less contended, and requests wait in your app where you can see and time-box them. Instrument it: export pool total, idle and waiting counts as gauges, and alert on waiting > 0 sustained, because pool saturation looks exactly like "the database is slow" while the database is idle. Always set connectionTimeoutMillis (say 2 s) so a saturated pool fails fast into a 503 instead of piling up. And be aware that with PgBouncer in transaction mode you may need prepare: false or a compatible version, and that idleTimeoutMillis should be lower than any network middlebox idle timeout to avoid stale-socket errors.

  • Why it matters — Pool misconfiguration is one of the top causes of cascading latency in Node services.

  • Follow-ups — Why is a smaller pool often faster? What metric would page you? How does this change behind PgBouncer or RDS Proxy?

  • Senior signal — The "queue in the app, not in the database" argument with a fail-fast timeout, plus pool metrics as an SLI.

45.7 Sequelize

Q91. How do you define models, and how do you manage schema changes?

  • Expected answer — Either sequelize.define('Order', attributes, options) or the class form class Order extends Model with Order.init(attributes, { sequelize, tableName, underscored, paranoid }); with @nestjs/sequelize you use sequelize-typescript decorators (@Table, @Column, @ForeignKey, @BelongsTo). Options that matter: underscored: true to map camelCase attributes to snake_case columns, paranoid: true for soft deletes via deletedAt, timestamps, and freezeTableName. For schema management, sequelize.sync() and especially sync({ alter: true }) are development-only for the same reasons as TypeORM's synchronize — they issue unreviewed DDL, can drop data, and race across replicas. Production uses sequelize-cli migrations checked into the repo and run as a discrete deploy step, with a separate seeders directory for reference data. One Sequelize-specific caution: model definitions and migrations are independent, so they drift silently; the model says a column is allowNull: false while the database never got the constraint. I add a CI check that runs migrations onto an empty database and compares the resulting schema against the models.

  • Why it matters — Model/migration drift is a Sequelize-specific footgun that produces production-only failures.

  • Follow-ups — How do you detect drift? What does paranoid do to your unique constraints? Where do enum changes bite?

  • Senior signal — Names the drift problem and automates the check.

Q92. How do transactions work in Sequelize, and what is CLS?

  • Expected answer — sequelize.transaction(async (t) => { ... }) is the managed form: it commits on resolve and rolls back on throw. Every query inside must receive { transaction: t } or it runs on a different connection outside the transaction — the same trap as TypeORM. Sequelize's answer is CLS (continuation-local storage): set Sequelize.useCLS(namespace) at startup and the transaction is propagated automatically through the async context, so nested service calls join it without threading t through every signature. It is genuinely useful, but you must know its edges: it relies on async context propagation, so code that escapes the context (a callback into a native library, some worker pools, a promise created before the namespace was active) silently drops out of the transaction. Unmanaged transactions (const t = await sequelize.transaction() with explicit t.commit()/t.rollback()) require the same finally discipline as a TypeORM query runner. You can pass isolationLevel and, on Postgres, lock: Transaction.LOCK.UPDATE in a findOne to emit FOR UPDATE.

  • Why it matters — Silent non-transactional writes are the highest-severity ORM bug class.

  • Follow-ups — What happens if you forget { transaction: t } on one query in a batch? How would you test that a rollback really rolls everything back? What are CLS's failure modes?

  • Senior signal — Uses CLS but can name where it leaks, and writes a test that asserts rollback.

Q93. Explain include and how you avoid N+1 and pagination bugs.

  • Expected answer — include produces a join and Sequelize then hydrates nested instances. Without it, touching order.getItems() per row is an N+1. The pagination trap is specific and important: findAll({ include, limit: 20 }) applies LIMIT to the joined rows, so an order with 10 items consumes 10 of your 20 slots and you get 4 orders instead of 20. Sequelize handles this when it can by using a subquery (subQuery: true, its default for hasMany with limit), but the subquery breaks when your where references an included model, and then you must set subQuery: false and handle duplication yourself. findAndCountAll with include counts joined rows unless you pass distinct: true, which is the classic "my total says 340 but there are 34 orders" bug. Practical approach for list endpoints: query the parent ids with the filter and pagination, then fetch children with a second where: { orderId: ids } query and stitch — two predictable queries beat one fragile join.

  • Why it matters — These are wrong-data bugs that pass unit tests with one child row.

  • Follow-ups — What does distinct: true change in the generated SQL? When is separate: true on a hasMany include the right tool? How do you order by a column on an included model with a limit?

  • Senior signal — Knows the subQuery and distinct behaviours by name and prefers the two-query stitch for reliability.

Q94. How do you lock rows and handle concurrency in Sequelize?

  • Expected answer — Inside a transaction, Model.findOne({ where, lock: t.LOCK.UPDATE, transaction: t }) emits SELECT ... FOR UPDATE; LOCK.SHARE gives FOR SHARE, and skipLocked: true adds SKIP LOCKED for queue-style claiming. For counters, prefer atomic operators over read-modify-write: Model.increment({ qty: -1 }, { where: { sku, qty: { [Op.gte]: 1 } }, transaction: t }) compiles to a single UPDATE with a guard, and you check the affected row count to know whether the decrement succeeded. Optimistic locking is available via version: true in the model options, which adds a version column and throws OptimisticLockError on a stale write. The failure modes are the same as everywhere: FOR UPDATE queues and can deadlock, so order your locks consistently and set lock_timeout; increment without the Op.gte guard will happily take stock negative; and a lock without a transaction is silently ignored, which is a quiet correctness hole.

  • Why it matters — Inventory and balance bugs come straight from getting this wrong.

  • Follow-ups — Show me a safe stock decrement including what the API returns when it fails. Why check affected rows? What does skipLocked enable you to build?

  • Senior signal — Uses a guarded single-statement update rather than read-then-write, and checks the affected row count as the decision signal.

Q95. What are hooks and scopes, and where do they hurt?

  • Expected answer — Hooks are lifecycle callbacks (beforeCreate, afterUpdate, beforeBulkDestroy, ...) and scopes are named, reusable query fragments applied with Model.scope('active').findAll() or a defaultScope. They are useful for genuinely mechanical concerns: hashing a password before create, normalising an email, adding tenantId scoping. They hurt in three ways. First, bulk operations do not run individual hooks unless you pass individualHooks: true, so Model.update(..., { where }) skips beforeUpdate per row — audit logs and cache invalidations silently stop working for bulk paths. Second, hooks that do I/O (send an email, publish to Kafka) inside a transaction fire even if the transaction later rolls back, producing notifications for orders that do not exist; side effects belong after commit, ideally via an outbox. Third, a defaultScope is invisible at the call site, so a developer wonders why rows are missing, and Model.unscoped() is easy to forget in one place and leak soft-deleted or other-tenant data. I keep hooks for pure data transformation only and put business side effects in explicit service code.

  • Why it matters — Invisible behaviour is the enemy of a maintainable large codebase.

  • Follow-ups — Where would you publish an order.created event and why not in afterCreate? How does paranoid interact with defaultScope? What breaks with individualHooks at 10,000 rows?

  • Senior signal — The "no I/O in hooks, use an outbox after commit" rule, stated as a hard boundary.

Q96. When do you drop to raw SQL in Sequelize, and how do you do it safely?

  • Expected answer — When the query is analytical, uses window functions, CTEs, ON CONFLICT, SKIP LOCKED, or any Postgres feature the query interface does not model well; when the generated SQL is unpredictable and the query is hot; and for bulk operations where per-row instances would be wasteful. Use sequelize.query(sql, { type: QueryTypes.SELECT, replacements, transaction }) and always use replacements (:name) or bind ($1) rather than string interpolation — bind is stronger because values go to the server as parameters and cannot be reinterpreted as SQL, while replacements are escaped client-side. Return typed rows and map them explicitly rather than pretending they are model instances. Two operational notes: raw queries bypass hooks, scopes and soft-delete filters, so a raw query in a multi-tenant system must include the tenant predicate explicitly, and it is worth centralising these in a repository class so they are reviewable and testable. I also keep raw SQL in files or tagged template constants rather than inline strings, so it is greppable when a column is renamed.

  • Why it matters — Injection and tenancy leaks both hide in raw SQL.

  • Follow-ups — Difference between replacements and bind? How do you keep raw SQL in sync with model changes? How do you test it?

  • Senior signal — Prefers bind, remembers that scopes and soft deletes do not apply, and treats tenancy as a security invariant.

45.8 API design

Q97. Should your API resources mirror your database tables?

  • Expected answer — No. Tables are a storage model optimised for normalisation and write integrity; an API is a contract optimised for the consumer's use cases and for evolving independently of storage. If they are identical, every schema refactor becomes a breaking API change, and clients end up doing five round trips to assemble one screen. Design resources around domain concepts and client workflows: POST /orders/{id}/refunds rather than POST /refund_rows, GET /orders/{id} returning the order with its items and totals even though those live in three tables. Conversely, do not go so far that you build an RPC-over-HTTP mess of verbs; the resource shape is a good default because it gives you caching, idempotency semantics and predictable URLs for free. The test I apply: could I change the storage engine for this entity — split a table, add a cache, move it to another service — without changing the API? If not, the API is leaking storage details.

  • Why it matters — API-storage coupling is a decade-long tax that shows up as "we cannot refactor that table".

  • Follow-ups — How do you model a state transition like cancelling an order? What about a query that needs data from three services? Where do you draw the line before it becomes RPC?

  • Senior signal — The "could I change the storage without changing the contract?" test, plus not over-rotating into pure REST purism.

Q98. How do idempotency keys work and where do you store them?

  • Expected answer — The client generates a unique key per logical operation (a UUID) and sends it as Idempotency-Key. The server, inside a transaction, tries to insert (key, endpoint, request_hash) into an idempotency table with a unique constraint. If the insert succeeds, this is the first attempt: perform the work and store the response body and status against the key. If it conflicts, look up the stored record — if it is complete, replay the saved response; if it is still in progress, return 409 or 425 so the client retries later. Comparing the request hash catches a client reusing a key with a different payload, which should be a 422 rather than silently replaying. Keys are scoped per API consumer and expire (24 hours to 7 days depending on how long clients retry), cleaned by a retention job.

    CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key text PRIMARY KEY, consumer_id uuid NOT NULL, endpoint text NOT NULL,
  request_hash text NOT NULL, status text NOT NULL,
  response_status int, response_body jsonb, created_at timestamptz DEFAULT now());

    The crucial part is that the key record and the business write commit in the same transaction, or a crash between them re-executes the charge.

  • Why it matters — This is the standard defence against double charges, and the details are where people fail.

  • Follow-ups — What happens on a concurrent duplicate that is still in flight? Why must it be one transaction? How does this interact with a downstream payment provider's own idempotency?

  • Senior signal — Same-transaction commit, in-progress handling, request-hash mismatch, and expiry — the four details that make it actually work.

Q99. PUT versus PATCH — how do you decide?

  • Expected answer — PUT replaces the resource with the representation you send, and is idempotent: sending it twice leaves the same state. That means omitted fields should be cleared, which most APIs get wrong by treating PUT as a partial update and thereby breaking the contract. PATCH applies a partial modification; it is not required to be idempotent, though it usually is if the operations are absolute assignments ({"status":"shipped"}) rather than relative ones ({"increment_by":1}). For partial updates I use PATCH with a JSON merge-patch style body, and I define explicitly what null means (clear the field) versus an absent key (leave unchanged), because that ambiguity is the number one source of bugs. In practice, for state transitions I prefer a dedicated sub-resource or action (POST /orders/{id}/cancel) over patching a status field, because the transition has rules and side effects that a generic patch cannot express, and it gives you a clean place to apply idempotency and authorization.

  • Why it matters — Semantics affect retry safety, caching and client expectations.

  • Follow-ups — How do you express "clear this optional field" in JSON? Is PATCH safe to retry after a timeout? Why not just PUT everything?

  • Senior signal — The null-versus-absent rule and preferring explicit action endpoints for state machines.

Q100. Which status codes do you use, and where do people get them wrong?

  • Expected answer — The set I actually use: 200 for a successful read or update with a body; 201 with a Location header for creation; 202 when the work is accepted and asynchronous; 204 for a successful delete or update with no body; 400 for malformed syntax; 401 for missing or invalid authentication; 403 for authenticated but not permitted; 404 for not found — and deliberately for "exists but you may not know it exists", to avoid leaking resource existence; 409 for a state conflict such as an optimistic-lock mismatch or duplicate creation; 422 for semantically invalid input that parsed fine; 429 for rate limiting with Retry-After; 500 for our bug; 503 for overload or a dependency being down, with Retry-After; 504 for an upstream timeout. Common mistakes: returning 200 with {"error": ...} in the body, which defeats every client library, proxy and metric; using 500 for validation failures, which pollutes your error budget and pages someone; and using 403 where 404 avoids an enumeration oracle. The other thing seniors care about is the retryability contract: 429, 502, 503 and 504 mean "retry with backoff", 4xx otherwise means "do not retry", and clients should be able to rely on that.

  • Why it matters — Status codes are the machine-readable half of your contract, and they drive retries and alerting.

  • Follow-ups — What do you return when the request is valid but inventory is insufficient? Which codes count against your availability SLO? What does a client do with a 409?

  • Senior signal — Frames codes as a retryability and alerting contract, not trivia.

Q101. How do you version an API?

  • Expected answer — Three mainstream options: URL path (/v1/orders) — obvious, cache-friendly, easy to route at the gateway, but it duplicates URLs and encourages whole-API version bumps; a custom header or Accept media type (application/vnd.acme.v2+json) — cleaner URLs and per-resource evolution, but harder to test with a browser and easy for proxies to ignore; and date-based versions pinned per consumer (the Stripe model), where the client's registered version selects a chain of request/response transformations. My default for a typical product API is URL versioning at the major level plus additive evolution within a version, because most changes should not need a version at all. The real work is not the scheme, it is the policy: what counts as breaking (removing a field, tightening validation, changing a status code, changing default ordering), how long you support version N-1 (announce, measure usage per consumer, then deprecate with Sunset and Deprecation headers), and how you know who is still calling it — which requires per-consumer, per-version request metrics.

  • Why it matters — Versioning is a lifecycle and organisational problem more than a technical one.

  • Follow-ups — Is adding a required request field breaking? How do you retire v1 when one large customer will not migrate? What is the Stripe approach's hidden cost?

  • Senior signal — Focuses on the deprecation process and measurement, and lists what counts as breaking, including sneaky cases like changing default sort order.

Q102. How should list endpoints paginate?

  • Expected answer — Default to cursor (keyset) pagination for anything that grows: return an opaque next_cursor and a has_more flag, cap limit at something like 100 with a default of 20, and encode the cursor as a signed, base64-encoded tuple of the sort key plus id so clients cannot tamper with it or read into it. Offset pagination is acceptable only for small, bounded collections or admin tools where jumping to page 40 matters — and even then, put a hard cap on the offset. Do not return a total count by default: it forces a second expensive query on every page. Offer it behind an explicit include_total=true flag, or return an approximate count. Also fix the sort: pagination without a deterministic total order (a tiebreaker on the primary key) silently duplicates and skips rows, which is a bug people ship constantly. Document that cursors are opaque and may expire, and version their contents so you can change the sort later.

  • Why it matters — This is the endpoint that breaks first as data grows and the one clients complain about most.

  • Follow-ups — Why must the cursor be signed? How do you support sorting by five different columns? What happens if a row is deleted between pages?

  • Senior signal — Deterministic tiebreaker, opaque signed cursors, and treating total count as opt-in.

Q103. What does a good error response look like?

  • Expected answer — One consistent envelope across the whole API, machine-readable first and human-readable second. I use a shape close to RFC 9457 (application/problem+json): a stable type or code string that clients can switch on and that never changes, a title/message for humans, the HTTP status, a trace_id that appears in our logs, and a structured errors array for field-level validation problems with field, code and message.

    { "type": "https://api.acme.com/errors/insufficient_inventory",
  "title": "Not enough stock for SKU-1183", "status": 409,
  "trace_id": "4f3c...", "errors": [{ "field": "items[0].qty", "code": "max", "message": "only 2 left" }] }

    The rules that matter: codes are part of the contract and are versioned like anything else; never put stack traces, SQL, internal hostnames or upstream provider messages in the body; localise on the client using the code, not by translating message server-side; and make sure the same failure always produces the same code, because clients build retry and UX logic on it.

  • Why it matters — Error contracts determine whether client teams can build good UX or have to string-match your messages.

  • Follow-ups — How do you avoid clients parsing message? What do you log versus return? How do you handle a partial failure in a bulk request?

  • Senior signal — Stable machine codes as a versioned contract plus a trace id bridging client reports to logs.

Q104. Where does validation belong, and what should it cover?

  • Expected answer — In layers, because they catch different things. At the edge: schema validation of shape, types, required fields, string lengths, enum membership and numeric bounds — in NestJS, DTOs with class-validator and a global ValidationPipe with whitelist: true. In the domain: business rules that need context, such as "this coupon is valid for this customer" or "you cannot cancel a shipped order" — these belong in the service, not in a DTO decorator, because they need database state. In the database: the invariants that must hold no matter what code runs — NOT NULL, CHECK (amount_minor > 0), unique indexes, foreign keys. The database layer is the one people skip, and it is the only one that survives a bad migration script, a rogue admin query or a second service writing to the same table. Also validate outputs at boundaries you do not control: a third-party webhook payload gets parsed into a validated type, never trusted. And validate sizes explicitly — max array lengths, max body size — because "500,000 items in one request" is a denial-of-service vector that type validation alone does not stop.

  • Why it matters — Validation strategy is a security question and an architecture question at once.

  • Follow-ups — Give me a rule that must live in the database and say why. How do you keep the DTO and the database constraint in sync? What is the max body size on your API and where is it enforced?

  • Senior signal — Insists on database-level invariants and mentions size limits as a DoS control.

Q105. How would you design rate limiting for a public API?

  • Expected answer — Decide the dimension first: per API key, per user, per IP, or per tenant — usually a combination, with the key as primary and IP as a fallback for unauthenticated endpoints. Then the algorithm: fixed window is cheap but allows a 2x burst across the boundary; sliding window log is exact but memory-heavy; sliding window counter is a good approximation; token bucket is my default because it expresses "sustained rate plus burst" naturally, which is what product people actually want. Implement centrally in Redis so all pods share state — a Lua script doing the read-modify-write atomically, keyed by rl:{key}:{window} with a TTL. Return 429 with Retry-After and the RateLimit-Limit/RateLimit-Remaining/RateLimit-Reset headers so clients can behave well. Differentiate limits by cost: a search endpoint that hits Elasticsearch should cost 10 tokens, a simple GET one. Failure mode to state explicitly: if Redis is down, do you fail open (allow traffic, risk overload) or fail closed (reject everything)? For a public API I fail open with a local in-process fallback limiter, because rejecting all traffic because a cache is down converts a degradation into an outage — but for an expensive or abusable endpoint I fail closed.

  • Why it matters — Rate limiting is one of the few places where the "what if the limiter itself fails" question is unavoidable.

  • Follow-ups — Write the token-bucket Lua sketch. How do you handle a customer who legitimately needs a higher limit? Where do you put the limiter, gateway or app?

  • Senior signal — The fail-open versus fail-closed decision with different answers per endpoint class, and cost-weighted limits.

Q106. How do you design bulk endpoints?

  • Expected answer — First ask whether you need one; often the client is doing an N+1 because the read API is missing a filter. If you do need it, the key decision is failure semantics, and it must be explicit in the contract: all-or-nothing (one transaction, any failure rolls everything back, simple to reason about, but one bad row blocks 999 good ones) or per-item results (207-style response with a per-item status array, more useful for imports, but the client must handle partial success and you must make each item independently idempotent). I usually offer per-item results for imports and all-or-nothing for anything financial. Other essentials: a hard cap on batch size (say 1,000 items) enforced with a 413 or 422, an idempotency key covering the whole batch, per-item client-supplied reference ids echoed back so the client can correlate results, and a size-based body limit. For genuinely large volumes, do not make it synchronous at all — accept the payload, return 202 with a job id, and expose a status endpoint, which is the long-running-operation pattern.

  • Why it matters — Bulk endpoints are where timeouts, partial failure and idempotency all collide.

  • Follow-ups — What does the response look like for 3 failures out of 500? How do you make a retry of a partially-failed batch safe? What is your batch size cap and why?

  • Senior signal — Makes partial-failure semantics an explicit contract decision and links large batches to async processing.

Q107. How do you design and consume webhooks reliably?

  • Expected answer — As a producer: sign every payload (HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body plus a timestamp, sent in a header) so receivers can verify authenticity and reject replays outside a tolerance window; include a stable event_id and event_type; deliver at least once with exponential backoff and jitter over hours, with a dead-letter and a manual replay tool; make delivery asynchronous from the originating transaction using an outbox so you never emit an event for a rolled-back write; and cap the payload, offering an ID that the consumer can fetch instead of embedding large data. As a consumer: verify the signature on the raw body before parsing (this is why frameworks need a raw-body option), respond 2xx within a couple of seconds by enqueueing the work rather than processing inline, deduplicate on event_id with a unique constraint because retries are guaranteed, and never assume ordering — events can arrive out of order, so either carry a version/sequence number or re-fetch the current state. Expose delivery attempts and failures to your customers, because "we sent it" is not enough when they cannot see it.

  • Why it matters — Webhooks concentrate idempotency, ordering, security and retry design into one small surface.

  • Follow-ups — Why verify against the raw body? How do you handle a consumer that is down for six hours? How do you prevent your webhook sender from being an SSRF vector?

  • Senior signal — Outbox on the send side, dedupe plus no-ordering-assumption on the receive side, and SSRF awareness for customer-supplied URLs.

Q108. How do you expose a long-running operation over HTTP?

  • Expected answer — Do not hold the connection. Accept the request, validate it, persist a job with a client-visible id, return 202 Accepted with a Location header pointing at a status resource, and process asynchronously. The status resource returns state (pending, running, succeeded, failed), progress if meaningful, a result link on success and a structured error on failure. Clients poll with a Retry-After hint, or you push completion via a webhook or a WebSocket/SSE channel. Make the submission idempotent with an idempotency key so a client retry after a network timeout does not start a second export. Keep job records long enough for clients to observe the outcome (typically days) and expose cancellation if the operation is expensive. The anti-pattern is a synchronous endpoint with a 300-second gateway timeout: the load balancer, the client library and the browser all have their own timeouts, so the client gives up while the work continues, then retries, and now you are running the same 20-minute report three times.

  • Why it matters — Timeout-driven duplicate work is a very common and expensive production failure.

  • Follow-ups — How do you avoid three concurrent runs of the same export? What do you do if the worker dies mid-job? Poll or push, and why?

  • Senior signal — Explains the layered-timeout retry storm, and combines 202 with idempotency rather than treating them as separate features.

Q109. What counts as a breaking change, and how do you evolve an API without one?

  • Expected answer — Breaking: removing or renaming a field, changing a field's type or format, making an optional request field required, tightening validation, adding a new required header, changing a status code for an existing condition, changing default sort order or default page size, changing error codes, and changing the semantics of an existing field even if the shape is identical. Non-breaking, if clients are tolerant readers: adding optional request fields, adding response fields, adding new endpoints, adding new enum values only if the contract said clients must tolerate unknown values. That last caveat matters: strict client-side schema validation turns additive changes into breaking ones, so publish a tolerant-reader expectation up front. Techniques for evolving: expand-and-contract (add the new field, dual-write, migrate consumers, then remove), feature flags per consumer, a compatibility shim in the gateway that translates old requests to the new internal shape, and measuring actual field usage from logs so you know who would break. Never rely on "nobody uses that field" without data.

  • Why it matters — Backward compatibility discipline is what makes an API a platform rather than a liability.

  • Follow-ups — Is adding an enum value breaking? How do you find out who uses a field? How do you deprecate with a deadline that people actually meet?

  • Senior signal — The tolerant-reader contract and measuring field usage before removal.

Q110. What is contract testing and when is it worth it?

  • Expected answer — Contract testing verifies that a provider and its consumers agree on the interface, without running a full integrated environment. In the consumer-driven form (Pact), each consumer writes tests against a mock provider; those interactions become a contract published to a broker; the provider's CI replays them against the real service and fails if it broke someone. The alternative, schema-first (OpenAPI or protobuf plus a linter that checks for breaking changes between commits), is lighter and catches shape regressions but not semantic expectations. It is worth it when you have several teams and independently deployed services, because the alternative is finding the break in staging, or in production. It is not worth it for one team with a monolith and a single front end — an OpenAPI schema generated from the code plus a few end-to-end tests gives most of the value. The practical requirement people underestimate is process: contract tests only work if the provider's pipeline actually blocks on the broker's verification result, and if there is a can-i-deploy gate. Without that, they are decorative.

  • Why it matters — It shows whether the candidate has worked in a multi-team environment and understands CI gating.

  • Follow-ups — Who owns a failing contract, the consumer or provider? How does this interact with versioning? What does can-i-deploy do?

  • Senior signal — Names the gating requirement and gives a clear "not worth it here" boundary.

45.9 System design

Q111. You get "design a notification service" and 45 minutes. What is your method?

flowchart LR
  A["0-5 min: scope and requirements"] --> B["5-10 min: capacity math"]
  B --> C["10-15 min: API and data model"]
  C --> D["15-30 min: high-level design"]
  D --> E["30-40 min: deep dive on one hard part"]
  E --> F["40-45 min: failure modes and trade-offs"]

  • Expected answer — A fixed method, run out loud, so the interviewer can follow and steer. Step 1: clarify functional scope (which channels, who triggers, do users have preferences, is delivery guaranteed) and non-functional targets (RPS, latency, durability, ordering, retention). Write the assumptions on the board and get them confirmed — an unconfirmed assumption is how designs go wrong for 40 minutes. Step 2: numbers — daily volume, peak-to-average ratio, storage per year. Step 3: the external API and the core tables, because the data model is where most designs quietly fail. Step 4: boxes and arrows with the queue boundaries and the datastore choices justified. Step 5: pick the hardest part (here: deduplication and per-user rate limiting) and go deep. Step 6: what breaks, how you detect it, what you would do differently at 10x. Throughout, state trade-offs explicitly and say what you are not building.

  • Why it matters — Without a method, candidates ramble, run out of time, and never reach the interesting part.

  • Follow-ups — What would you cut for a two-week v1? Which assumption would change the design most if wrong? Where would you have pushed back on the requirements?

  • Senior signal — Manages the clock deliberately, confirms assumptions, and drives to a deep dive rather than drawing more boxes.

Q112. Do the capacity math for a service with 20 million daily active users sending 3 notifications each.

  • Expected answer — 60 million notifications per day. Average is 60e6 / 86,400 ≈ 700 per second. Peak matters more: a 5x peak-to-average ratio for a consumer app gives about 3,500 per second, and a broadcast campaign is not a ratio at all, it is a spike of, say, 5 million in 10 minutes ≈ 8,300 per second, which is the real design point. Storage: a notification record with ids, type, payload reference and timestamps is roughly 400 bytes; 60 million per day is 24 GB per day, 8.7 TB per year — so retention policy is a design decision, not an afterthought; keep 30 days hot (720 GB, fine for one Postgres instance with monthly partitions) and archive the rest to S3. Throughput per worker: if a push send takes 50 ms of mostly I/O and one worker handles 100 concurrent sends, that is ~2,000 per second per worker, so five workers cover the spike with headroom. Bandwidth and third-party limits usually bind first: FCM and your SMS provider have per-second quotas, so the design needs a rate-limited egress stage regardless of what your service can do.

  • Why it matters — Numbers turn a hand-wavy design into an engineering one, and the peak/average distinction is where people are sloppy.

  • Follow-ups — Where did the 5x come from and how would you verify it? What is the cost per month of that storage? What happens when the SMS provider rate-limits you?

  • Senior signal — Designs for the campaign spike rather than the average, and identifies the third-party quota as the true constraint.

Q113. Design the key generation for a URL shortener.

  • Expected answer — Requirements shape it: short (6–8 characters), unguessable enough that people cannot enumerate private links, unique, and generated fast without a central bottleneck. Options. (1) Hash the URL (MD5/SHA) and take the first 7 base62 characters — deterministic and dedupes identical URLs, but collisions must be handled by rehashing with a salt, and identical URLs from different users share a link, which may be wrong for analytics. (2) A central counter encoded in base62 — guaranteed unique and dense, but sequential ids are enumerable and the counter is a single point of contention; mitigate by having each app instance take a block of ids (Redis INCRBY 1000) so it only talks to the counter once per thousand links. (3) Random 7-character base62 (62^7 ≈ 3.5e12) with a unique constraint and retry on conflict — simple, unguessable, and at 1 billion links the collision probability per insert is still tiny (~0.03%), so retries are rare. I would pick (3) for a public product because it is unguessable and needs no coordination, with the database unique index as the correctness backstop and a small retry loop. Add a reserved-word blocklist and profanity filter on generated codes, which is a detail real products always need.

  • Why it matters — It is a compact test of uniqueness-under-concurrency thinking and of security awareness.

  • Follow-ups — Compute the collision probability at 10 billion links. How do you support custom aliases without breaking uniqueness? How do you handle deletion and reuse of codes?

  • Senior signal — Picks based on enumerability and coordination cost, uses the database constraint as the guarantee rather than trusting randomness, and mentions the blocklist.

Q114. Compare rate-limiting algorithms and say how you would run one across 40 pods.

  • Expected answer — Fixed window: count per key per minute; O(1) and trivial, but allows 2x the limit across a boundary (100 at 11:59:59 and 100 at 12:00:00). Sliding window log: store timestamps in a sorted set and count those within the window; exact, but memory grows with the limit and it is the most expensive. Sliding window counter: weight the previous window's count by the fraction of it still in view; approximate within a few percent, cheap, and my usual choice for simple limits. Token bucket: refill at a rate, allow a burst up to capacity; naturally expresses "10 per second with a burst of 50", and it is what most public APIs actually want. Leaky bucket: smooths output to a fixed rate, better for protecting a downstream that cannot burst. Distributed: keep the state in Redis and do the read-modify-write in a single Lua script so it is atomic, keyed by the limit dimension, with a TTL so keys expire. At high volume, cut Redis calls by letting each pod take a local lease of N tokens and reconcile periodically — you trade a little accuracy for a big reduction in round trips. State the failure mode: on Redis failure, fail open with a conservative local limiter for general traffic and fail closed for expensive endpoints.

  • Why it matters — It is the most common "concurrency plus state plus failure" mini-design.

  • Follow-ups — Write the Lua sketch for token bucket. How much error does the local-lease optimisation introduce? What headers do you return?

  • Senior signal — Chooses per requirement, knows the Lua atomicity requirement, and has an answer for the limiter's own failure.

Q115. How do you deduplicate notifications so a user is not messaged twice?

  • Expected answer — Separate three different duplicates. (1) Delivery duplicates from at-least-once messaging: give every notification a deterministic id derived from the triggering event (hash(event_id, user_id, channel)), and make the send path insert that id with a unique constraint before dispatching — a conflict means someone already sent it. (2) Semantic duplicates: five "someone liked your post" events in a minute should be one notification, so add a coalescing window — buffer per (user_id, notification_type, entity_id) for 2 to 5 minutes, then send a rolled-up message ("5 people liked your post"). Implement with a Redis key holding the pending aggregate plus a delayed job, or a small table with a send_after timestamp. (3) Cross-channel duplicates: do not send push and email for the same thing within a window unless the user opted in; keep a per-user, per-type "last sent" record. Combine with per-user rate limits (at most N pushes per hour) and quiet hours in the user's timezone. Crucially, the dedupe key must be stored durably before the external send, and the external provider call must be idempotent or at-least-once-tolerant, because a crash between "provider accepted" and "we recorded it" will otherwise resend.

  • Why it matters — Duplicate notifications are the fastest way to lose user trust, and the answer requires both messaging and product thinking.

  • Follow-ups — What if the provider call succeeds but your write fails? How do you pick the coalescing window? How do quiet hours interact with urgent alerts?

  • Senior signal — Distinguishes delivery from semantic duplication and handles the crash-between-send-and-record window explicitly.

Q116. How do you order messages in a chat system?

  • Expected answer — Do not rely on wall-clock time from clients; phones have skewed clocks and a message can arrive with a timestamp in the past. Order per conversation, not globally, because that is the only ordering users actually perceive. The standard approach is a monotonic per-conversation sequence number assigned by the server: the write path takes a lock or uses a single partition per conversation and assigns seq = last_seq + 1, so all clients agree. In Postgres, that is an UPDATE conversations SET last_seq = last_seq + 1 RETURNING last_seq inside the message insert transaction, which serialises writes per conversation — fine, since a conversation rarely exceeds a few messages per second. If you shard by conversation id in Kafka, the partition gives you ordering for free as long as producer retries are configured for idempotence, otherwise a retry can reorder. Clients need three more things: a client-generated message id for optimistic UI and dedupe, an "unconfirmed" state until the server returns a sequence number, and a gap-detection rule — if a client receives seq 41 and 43, it fetches 42 rather than displaying out of order. For read state, store per-user last_read_seq rather than timestamps.

  • Why it matters — Ordering is the classic distributed-systems problem in a form everyone has an intuition for.

  • Follow-ups — What breaks if you use client timestamps? How do you handle a message edited or deleted after the fact? What does the sequence counter do to write throughput on a busy group chat?

  • Senior signal — Server-assigned per-conversation sequence, gap detection on the client, and awareness that producer idempotence is required for Kafka ordering under retries.

Q117. Fan-out on write or fan-out on read for a social feed?

  • Expected answer — Fan-out on write (push): when a user posts, insert the post id into every follower's feed list (Redis list or a feeds table). Reads are then O(1) and fast, which is what users feel. Cost: a celebrity with 10 million followers generates 10 million writes per post, which is a write storm and expensive storage. Fan-out on read (pull): store posts once and, at read time, query the posts of everyone the user follows, merge and sort. Cheap writes, expensive reads, and the read gets worse as following counts grow. Real systems use a hybrid: push for normal accounts, and for accounts above a threshold (say 100,000 followers) do not fan out — instead, at read time, merge the precomputed feed with a small pull query over the handful of celebrities the user follows. That keeps both sides bounded. Other essentials: feeds are capped (keep the newest ~1,000 entries), fan-out is asynchronous through a queue so posting stays fast, deletions and privacy changes must be reflected at read time by filtering rather than trying to unwind millions of writes, and ranking is applied at read time over a candidate set. Say the staleness budget out loud: a few seconds for a feed is fine, which is what makes async fan-out acceptable.

  • Why it matters — It is the canonical read/write amplification trade-off, and the hybrid answer proves real understanding.

  • Follow-ups — Where do you set the celebrity threshold and how would you measure it? What happens when a user with 5 million followers deletes a post? How do you backfill the feed for a new follow?

  • Senior signal — Proposes the hybrid unprompted and handles deletion by read-time filtering rather than write-time unwinding.

Q118. Design payment idempotency and the ledger.

  • Expected answer — Two separate concerns. Idempotency at the API boundary (see Q98): the client's Idempotency-Key maps to at most one payment attempt, stored in the same transaction as the attempt record. Then the ledger: money is recorded as immutable double-entry journal entries, never as a mutable balance column. Each transaction produces balanced debit and credit lines against accounts (customer wallet, merchant payable, fee revenue, gateway clearing), and the sum of every entry group is zero — a CHECK and a periodic reconciliation job assert that. Balances are derived by summing entries, and materialised into a snapshot table for speed with the snapshot always reconstructible from entries. Nothing is ever updated or deleted; a mistake is corrected with a compensating entry, which preserves the audit trail regulators and finance teams require. Amounts are stored as integer minor units (bigint paise/cents) with an explicit currency column, never floats. State transitions on the payment (pending -> authorized -> captured -> settled, plus failed, refunded) are guarded updates (WHERE status = 'authorized') so duplicate provider callbacks cannot double-capture. Finally, reconcile daily against the provider's settlement file, because your view and theirs will diverge, and the ledger is what makes the difference findable.

  • Why it matters — Money systems are where correctness is non-negotiable, and this is a strong seniority filter.

  • Follow-ups — Why never update a balance in place? How do you handle a refund of a partially captured payment? What does the reconciliation job do when it finds a mismatch?

  • Senior signal — Double-entry, immutability with compensating entries, integer minor units, and daily reconciliation — the four things finance engineering actually requires.

Q119. How do you prevent overselling inventory in a flash sale?

  • Expected answer — Decide the business rule first: is overselling by 1% acceptable with a cancellation, or is it forbidden? For a strict rule, the invariant must live where the writes are serialised. In Postgres, the simplest correct form is a single guarded statement — UPDATE inventory SET available = available - $qty WHERE sku = $1 AND available >= $qty RETURNING available — and zero affected rows means sold out, returned as a 409. This is atomic, needs no explicit lock management, and cannot go negative. The cost is that one row becomes a hot row: at 5,000 requests per second for one SKU, every transaction queues on that row lock, and each waits for the previous commit's fsync, so you cap out at maybe a few thousand per second. Techniques to raise the ceiling: shard the counter into N sub-rows and pick one at random (reducing contention N-fold, at the cost of a slightly harder "is it sold out" check), or move the counter to Redis with DECRBY guarded by a Lua script and treat Redis as the reservation system with Postgres as the durable record, reconciling asynchronously. Add reservations with expiry (stock held for 10 minutes during checkout, released by a job) rather than decrementing only at payment, and a queue/waiting room in front so the spike is shaped rather than absorbed.

  • Why it matters — Hot-row contention under a spike is a very real e-commerce problem with an unavoidable trade-off.

  • Follow-ups — What is the actual throughput limit of a single row and why? How does the Redis approach fail, and what do you lose? How do you expire reservations reliably?

  • Senior signal — Starts from the business tolerance, gives the guarded-update baseline with its concrete throughput ceiling, and only then reaches for sharding or Redis.

Q120. How do you get exactly-once execution of a scheduled job across 10 replicas?

  • Expected answer — You get exactly-once effects, not exactly-once execution, and you say so. The mechanism is a lease: each replica tries to claim the job for a time window, and only the winner runs it. In Postgres that is INSERT INTO job_runs (job_name, run_key) VALUES ($1, $2) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING id where run_key is the scheduled slot (for example daily-invoices:2026-09-09) — one row wins, everyone else gets nothing and skips. Or pg_try_advisory_lock for a coarse "only one instance runs the scheduler" approach. In Redis, SET lock:job val NX PX 60000 with a random token and a Lua compare-and-delete on release. Then handle the hard part: the winner can die mid-run, so the lease must expire and the job must be safe to re-run (idempotent writes, checkpointing progress) — and a lease that expires while the original worker is merely paused by GC means two workers run at once, which is why the work itself must tolerate it, usually via fencing tokens or guarded updates. Also record start and end so you can alert on a job that never completed, which is the failure everyone forgets: a job that silently stops running produces no errors at all.

  • Why it matters — Cron in a replicated deployment is a trap almost every team falls into once.

  • Follow-ups — What happens if the leader is GC-paused for 90 seconds? How do you detect a job that stopped firing? Why is ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING better than checking first?

  • Senior signal — Refuses "exactly once", designs for lease expiry plus idempotent work, and monitors for silent non-execution.

Q121. What is a hot key and how do you deal with one?

  • Expected answer — A hot key is a single key, row or partition receiving a disproportionate share of traffic: one celebrity's profile, one popular product during a sale, one tenant that is 60% of your volume, one Kafka partition because the partition key is country = 'IN'. Symptoms are one Redis node or one shard at 100% while the rest idle, or one partition with growing consumer lag. Remedies depend on read versus write. For hot reads: add a small in-process cache in front of Redis (a two-tier cache with a 1-second TTL absorbs almost all of it), or replicate the key with a suffix (product:123:r{0..9}) and read a random replica. For hot writes: shard the counter as in Q119, batch updates (accumulate in memory and flush every 200 ms), or change the partition key to include a random salt and aggregate downstream. Detect them before they hurt: Redis --hotkeys or MEMORY USAGE sampling, per-partition lag metrics, and top-N key logging at the application layer. And say the design rule: any key derived from user-controlled or naturally skewed data will eventually be hot, so a partitioning scheme needs a documented answer for skew before launch.

  • Why it matters — Skew breaks otherwise-correct scaling designs, and it is invisible in average metrics.

  • Follow-ups — How would you find the hot key at 2 a.m.? What are the consistency costs of a local cache tier? How do you rebalance a hot Kafka partition without losing ordering?

  • Senior signal — Different remedies for read versus write hot keys, and proactive detection rather than reactive firefighting.

Q122. Read replica or cache — how do you choose?

  • Expected answer — They solve different problems. A read replica scales query capacity while keeping full SQL, joins, and transactional freshness within replication lag (usually milliseconds); it needs no invalidation logic, so it cannot go stale in a way you did not design for. A cache scales specific hot reads to sub-millisecond and removes load entirely, but you now own invalidation, stampedes, serialization and a second failure domain. My ordering: first fix the query and the index, because most "we need a cache" situations are a missing index; then add a replica if the workload is broadly read-heavy with varied queries; then add a cache for the narrow set of very hot, expensive, tolerably-stale reads. Concretely: a product detail page hit 5,000 times a second with a 15 ms query is a cache candidate; an admin reporting workload is a replica candidate. Costs to state: a replica doubles database spend and introduces read-your-writes bugs; a cache introduces staleness, stampedes on expiry, and the risk that a cache outage sends 100% of traffic to a database sized for 10%. That last one is the important operational point — always load-test with the cache disabled.

  • Why it matters — This choice is made badly and often, usually by adding Redis to hide a missing index.

  • Follow-ups — What happens to your database when Redis restarts empty? How do you invalidate on write? Would you cache in the application or use a replica for a report that runs every 5 minutes?

  • Senior signal — "Fix the index first", and the cache-cold-start thundering-herd risk with a concrete mitigation.

Q123. Partitioning versus sharding — what is the difference and when do you shard?

  • Expected answer — Partitioning splits one table into pieces within one database instance: the planner prunes, maintenance is per-partition, and transactions and joins still work normally. Sharding splits data across separate database instances: you gain write and storage capacity beyond one machine, and you lose cross-shard transactions, cross-shard joins, global unique constraints, and simple ORDER BY across shards. So partition early and freely for data lifecycle; shard late and reluctantly, only when a single primary genuinely cannot hold the write volume or the working set. Before sharding, exhaust: better indexes, read replicas, caching, moving cold data out, upgrading the instance (modern hardware handles a great deal — a single Postgres box can do tens of thousands of writes per second), and splitting by service rather than by rows, which is usually easier and more valuable. If you must shard, choose the key carefully: it should be present on almost every query (tenant_id for B2B, user_id for consumer), it determines your skew exposure, and changing it later is a migration project. Use consistent hashing or a lookup/directory table so you can rebalance; a modulo scheme makes adding shards a full reshuffle.

  • Why it matters — Premature sharding is one of the most expensive architectural mistakes available.

  • Follow-ups — How do you do a cross-shard report? What is the migration path from unsharded to sharded with no downtime? Why is a directory table better than modulo?

  • Senior signal — A concrete ladder of cheaper options before sharding, and awareness that the shard key is a near-permanent decision.

Q124. When and how would you use a CDN?

  • Expected answer — For anything static or cacheable at the edge: images, JS/CSS bundles, video segments, and increasingly for cacheable API responses. The mechanics: the CDN caches by URL plus the Vary headers, honours Cache-Control (max-age, s-maxage, stale-while-revalidate, stale-if-error), and you invalidate either by purge API or, far better, by content-hashed immutable URLs (app.4f3c9a.js with max-age=31536000, immutable) so you never purge at all. Benefits are latency (an edge PoP 20 ms away instead of an origin 200 ms away), origin offload (a 95% hit ratio means 20x less origin traffic), and absorbing traffic spikes and some DDoS. Things people get wrong: caching authenticated responses without Vary on the auth dimension, which serves one user's data to another; setting a long TTL on HTML so a bad deploy is stuck at the edge for a day; and forgetting stale-if-error, which would have kept the site up when the origin died. For API responses I use short s-maxage (seconds to a minute) with stale-while-revalidate on genuinely public endpoints only, and Cache-Control: private, no-store on anything user-specific.

  • Why it matters — The CDN is the cheapest performance and resilience win available, and also a way to leak data.

  • Follow-ups — How do you cache a personalised page safely? What does stale-while-revalidate do to your origin load during a deploy? How do you handle a purge that must be immediate?

  • Senior signal — Content-hashed immutable assets instead of purging, and the authenticated-response leak risk stated as a security concern.

Q125. A product manager asks for full-text search over 50 million products. What do you build?

  • Expected answer — Start with requirements: what quality of relevance, typo tolerance, faceting, latency target, update freshness, and who maintains it. Options. Postgres full-text (tsvector plus GIN, pg_trgm for fuzzy) is free, transactional, and genuinely good for a few million documents with simple relevance — no extra system, no sync problem. OpenSearch/Elasticsearch gives real relevance tuning, analyzers per language, faceting, aggregations, and horizontal scale, at the price of a cluster to operate, a sync pipeline, and eventual consistency between the source of truth and the index. A managed search product (Algolia, Typesense, Meilisearch) gives excellent relevance and typo tolerance with almost no operations, at a per-record cost that gets expensive at 50 million documents. At 50 million products with faceting, I would go with OpenSearch, keep Postgres as the source of truth, and sync via the outbox and a stream consumer with a full reindex job as the backstop. The parts people underestimate: reindexing strategy with aliases for zero-downtime schema changes, handling the lag between a price change and search reflecting it, and relevance evaluation — you need a labelled query set and a metric, or "improving relevance" is guesswork.

  • Why it matters — It is a build-versus-buy question with real operational consequences.

  • Follow-ups — How do you reindex 50 million documents without downtime? What is the sync lag and does the business accept it? When is Postgres full-text enough?

  • Senior signal — Names the sync pipeline and reindexing as the hard parts rather than the query DSL, and insists on relevance measurement.

Q126. What changes when you go multi-region?

  • Expected answer — Almost everything, so the first question is why: latency for users, regulatory data residency, or disaster recovery? Each implies a different design. For DR only, the cheapest answer is one active region plus asynchronous replication to a warm standby, a documented RTO/RPO (say 15 minutes and 1 minute), and a tested failover runbook — untested failover is not a DR plan. For latency, put read replicas and caches near users but keep writes in one region; most applications are read-heavy and this gets 80% of the benefit with 10% of the complexity. For active-active writes, you have signed up for conflict resolution: either partition ownership by key (each user's data has a home region, writes route there), or accept CRDT/last-write-wins semantics and design the data so conflicts are meaningless. Cross-region latency of 80–150 ms makes synchronous replication painful and any chatty request path unusable, so batch and denormalise. Also budget for the boring things: cross-region data transfer costs real money, schema migrations must now be coordinated, and regional dependency graphs must be verified (a service in eu-west calling an auth service that only exists in us-east has not achieved anything).

  • Why it matters — Multi-region is frequently requested and rarely justified; the analysis matters more than the architecture.

  • Follow-ups — What is your RPO and how do you prove it? How do you route a write for a European user whose home region is down? What breaks first in a multi-region deploy?

  • Senior signal — Starts by challenging the requirement, offers a cheap read-local/write-central option, and mentions testing failover and hidden cross-region dependencies.

Q127. Estimate: how much storage and bandwidth for a video service with 100,000 daily uploads averaging 5 minutes?

  • Expected answer — Do it out loud with round numbers. Ingest: 100,000 x 5 minutes = 500,000 minutes/day. Raw uploads at, say, 20 Mbps for phone 1080p is 150 MB per minute, so 75 TB/day of source — but you would store source cheaply (S3 Glacier-class after processing) or discard it. Transcoded output is what matters: five renditions (240p, 360p, 480p, 720p, 1080p) totalling roughly 6 Mbps combined ≈ 45 MB per minute, so 500,000 x 45 MB ≈ 22 TB/day ≈ 8 PB/year. That number alone tells you the retention and tiering policy is the biggest cost lever in the design. Bandwidth: if each video averages 500 views at 720p (~3 Mbps ≈ 22 MB/minute, say 2 minutes watched) ≈ 45 MB per view, 100,000 x 500 x 45 MB ≈ 2.2 PB/day of egress — which at typical CDN pricing is the dominant cost of the entire business, so the design conversation becomes CDN contracts, caching ratio and adaptive bitrate, not databases. Transcoding compute: 500,000 minutes/day at roughly 0.5x realtime per rendition on a GPU fleet gives an estimate of the worker fleet size.

  • Why it matters — The point is not the exact figure; it is whether you can reason to the dominant cost in two minutes.

  • Follow-ups — Which number would you verify first? How does adaptive bitrate change egress? What would you do to cut cost by half?

  • Senior signal — Rounds aggressively, states assumptions, and finds the number that dominates the design instead of computing everything equally.

Q128. Your system works at today's load. What would you change for 100x?

  • Expected answer — First, refuse to design for 100x speculatively; say what would break in order, and what the next bottleneck would be, because that is how you actually plan. Typical ordering for a Node/Postgres system: (1) the single primary's write capacity and connection count — fix with PgBouncer, batching, and moving high-volume append-only data (events, logs, audit) out of the transactional database; (2) read capacity — replicas and caching; (3) table sizes making vacuum, index builds and backups unmanageable — partition and archive; (4) synchronous cross-service calls creating latency and coupling — move to events with an outbox; (5) hot keys and skew — shard counters, salt partitions; (6) only then shard the database or split services. In parallel, the operational things that must scale with you: observability cardinality and cost, deploy time, migration safety at 100x row counts, and on-call load. Also state what you would deliberately not do now: build for 100x today and you will have paid for complexity you cannot operate, with a design based on guesses about traffic shape. The senior move is to make the next order of magnitude cheap — clean boundaries, an outbox, metrics — not to build the final architecture up front.

  • Why it matters — It tests both scaling knowledge and judgement about when to apply it.

  • Follow-ups — What single metric tells you the first bottleneck is approaching? What is the cost of preparing for 100x too early? What would you do in the next sprint versus the next year?

  • Senior signal — Gives an ordered bottleneck list with the reason each falls over, and explicitly refuses premature complexity while keeping the door open.

45.10 Distributed systems

Q129. State CAP correctly.

  • Expected answer — CAP says that when a network partition occurs, a distributed system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest committed write — technically linearizability) and availability (every non-failing node answers every request). It is not "pick two of three": partition tolerance is not optional, because networks partition whether you like it or not, so the theorem is really a statement about behaviour during a partition. It also applies to a specific operation, not to a whole product: the same system can be CP for payment writes and AP for a "who is online" indicator. And the C in CAP is much stronger than the C in ACID; a system can be ACID-compliant on a single node and still be AP as a cluster. Real examples: a Postgres primary with synchronous replication refuses writes when it cannot reach a quorum (CP); a Redis cluster or a Cassandra ring with a low consistency level keeps serving possibly-stale data (AP). The senior framing is that the interesting question is never "CP or AP" in the abstract, it is "for this operation, what does the user experience if the two halves cannot talk, and which failure is cheaper?"

  • Why it matters — Misquoting CAP is a reliable marker of second-hand knowledge.

  • Follow-ups — Which is your login flow, and which is your analytics ingestion? Is a single-node database CP or AP? What does "available" formally mean here?

  • Senior signal — Says partition tolerance is not a choice, applies CAP per operation, and separates it from ACID.

Q130. What does PACELC add?

  • Expected answer — PACELC extends CAP with the case everyone actually lives in: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else (normal operation), choose Latency or Consistency. That "else" branch is the important half, because partitions are rare while the latency-versus-consistency trade-off is paid on every single request. Synchronous replication to another availability zone adds 1–2 ms; to another region, 80–150 ms — on every commit. Reading from a replica is fast but stale. So a system is described as, for example, PC/EC (a strongly consistent database like Spanner-style systems, consistent even at latency cost), PA/EL (Cassandra or DynamoDB with eventual consistency, favouring latency), or PC/EL (Postgres with async replicas: consistent on the primary, but reads from replicas trade consistency for latency). Framing a design discussion in PACELC terms immediately makes it concrete: "we are choosing EL here because a 120 ms cross-region write on every add-to-cart would cost more conversions than a rare stale read".

  • Why it matters — It moves the conversation from a rare failure case to the everyday design decision.

  • Follow-ups — Where in your system do you pay latency for consistency? Classify your primary datastore. What would you change to move from EC to EL and what would break?

  • Senior signal — Emphasises the "else" branch and attaches millisecond numbers to the trade-off.

Q131. What is partial failure and why does it change how you write code?

  • Expected answer — In a single process, a call either returns or throws. Across a network, there is a third outcome: you do not know. A timeout does not mean the other side did not do the work; it means you did not hear back. The request may have been lost on the way, processed and the reply lost, or still be executing. That single fact drives most distributed design: you cannot treat a timeout as a failure and retry blindly, or you double-charge. So every remote call needs four things: a timeout (never infinite), a decision about whether it is safe to retry, an idempotency mechanism if it is, and a way to reconcile later if you still do not know. Partial failure also means a multi-step operation can stop halfway — the order is created, the payment is captured, and then the inventory service is down. You cannot roll back a captured payment with a database rollback, so you need compensation, an outbox, or a saga. The practical habit: for every remote call in a design review, ask the mantra — can it timeout, can it duplicate, can it partially succeed — and make sure the code has an answer.

  • Why it matters — It is the root cause of the majority of distributed-system bugs.

  • Follow-ups — Your payment call times out. What exactly do you do next? How do you reconcile "unknown" states? Why is a retry without an idempotency key dangerous?

  • Senior signal — Names the unknown-outcome case explicitly and has a reconciliation plan, not just a retry.

Q132. Define idempotency and give three ways to achieve it.

  • Expected answer — An operation is idempotent if performing it more than once has the same effect as performing it once. Note it is about effect, not about the response being byte-identical. Three mechanisms. (1) Natural idempotency: design the operation as an absolute assignment rather than a delta — SET status = 'shipped' is idempotent, increment shipped_count is not. (2) A uniqueness constraint on a deduplication key: derive a deterministic key from the request or event (payment_intent_id, event_id) and let a unique index reject the second attempt; combined with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING this is a single atomic statement. (3) A guarded state transition: UPDATE orders SET status='paid' WHERE id=$1 AND status='pending' RETURNING id — zero rows means someone already did it, and you return the same success response rather than an error, because from the client's perspective the intent was fulfilled. The subtleties seniors mention: the dedupe record must commit in the same transaction as the effect; idempotency keys need a scope and an expiry; and idempotency is not the same as ordering — two different operations arriving out of order are still a problem your design must handle separately.

  • Why it matters — It is the single most reusable technique in distributed backends.

  • Follow-ups — What is the response to a duplicate, and does it matter? How long do you keep keys? How do you make an email send idempotent when the provider has no key support?
