  • Senior signal — Separates idempotency from ordering, and insists on same-transaction commit of the dedupe record.

Q133. What does "at-least-once delivery" actually require of you?

  • Expected answer — It means the broker guarantees a message is delivered one or more times: if a consumer crashes after processing but before acknowledging, the message is redelivered. So the burden shifts to the consumer, which must be idempotent — otherwise a redelivery duplicates a charge, an email or a stock decrement. Practically, an at-least-once consumer must: derive a stable dedupe key from the message (a producer-supplied event_id, never a hash of the arrival time), record it transactionally with the side effect, ack only after the effect is durable, and tolerate out-of-order delivery because a redelivery of message 5 can arrive after message 7. The related modes: at-most-once (ack first, then process — you lose messages on crash, acceptable only for metrics-like data), and "exactly once" which, across a network, is always at-least-once plus deduplication somewhere. Also design for the poison message: after N delivery attempts, route to a dead-letter queue with the error and the original payload, alert on DLQ depth, and provide a replay tool — a consumer that retries a permanently-failing message forever will block a partition or spin forever.

  • Why it matters — It is the delivery mode you will actually be given, and the consumer's obligations are frequently ignored.

  • Follow-ups — Where do you store the dedupe key and for how long? What do you do with a message you cannot process? How do you handle a redelivery that arrives 3 days later?

  • Senior signal — Ack-after-durable-effect, dead-letter with alerting and replay, and awareness that dedupe keys need retention limits.

Q134. Explain the transactional outbox pattern.

  • Expected answer — The problem is the dual write: you need to update your database and publish an event, and there is no transaction spanning both. If you publish first and the commit fails, you emitted an event for something that did not happen; if you commit first and the publish fails, the rest of the system never learns. The outbox fixes it by making the publish part of the same database transaction: insert the event row into an outbox table alongside the business write, commit once. A separate relay then reads unpublished rows and pushes them to the broker, marking them sent — either by polling with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, or by change-data-capture reading the WAL (Debezium), which avoids polling load entirely.

    CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, aggregate_id uuid NOT NULL, event_type text NOT NULL,
  payload jsonb NOT NULL, created_at timestamptz DEFAULT now(), published_at timestamptz);
CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished ON outbox (id) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

    Consequences to state: delivery becomes at-least-once (the relay can publish then crash before marking), so consumers must dedupe; there is publish latency of the polling interval; the table needs an archival job or it grows forever; and ordering is only guaranteed if you publish in id order per aggregate.

  • Why it matters — The dual-write problem is everywhere and the outbox is the standard answer.

  • Follow-ups — Why is the partial index important? Polling or CDC, and what does each cost? How do you guarantee per-aggregate ordering?

  • Senior signal — Volunteers that the outbox produces at-least-once (not exactly-once) and that the table needs retention.

Q135. What is the inbox pattern?

  • Expected answer — The mirror image on the consumer side. When a consumer receives a message, it first inserts the message id into an inbox (processed-messages) table with a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the business effect. If the insert conflicts, the message was already processed and the consumer acks and moves on. This converts at-least-once delivery into effectively-once processing, with the database providing the atomicity that the broker cannot. It matters most when the side effect is a database write, because then everything is in one transaction and there is no window where the effect is durable but the dedupe record is not. When the side effect is external (charging a card, sending an email), you cannot get that atomicity, so you split it: record intent transactionally, perform the external call with its own idempotency key, then record completion — and accept that a crash in the middle leaves an "unknown" record that a reconciliation job resolves. Operationally the inbox table needs a retention policy tied to the broker's maximum redelivery window (keep ids for, say, 7 days), and an index on the id plus a cleanup job.

  • Why it matters — It is the concrete implementation of "make your consumers idempotent", which everyone recommends and few specify.

  • Follow-ups — What is the retention window and how do you choose it? What if the side effect is not a database write? How does this interact with Kafka offset commits?

  • Senior signal — Handles the external-side-effect case honestly rather than pretending the inbox solves it.

Q136. Saga versus two-phase commit.

  • Expected answer — 2PC gives atomicity across resources via a coordinator: prepare, then commit or abort. It gives strong guarantees but holds locks across the whole protocol, blocks if the coordinator dies after prepare (participants sit locked, unable to decide), and requires every participant to support it — which most modern services and brokers do not. It is essentially unusable for cross-service HTTP APIs and is why almost nobody runs it outside a single database or a legacy XA environment. A saga replaces atomicity with a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action: reserve inventory, charge payment, create shipment — and if step three fails, run refund and release-inventory. Two flavours: orchestration, where a central coordinator (a state machine you own) drives each step and knows the whole flow — easier to reason about, monitor and debug, and my usual choice; and choreography, where each service reacts to events with no central brain — less coupling, but the flow exists only in the heads of the people who wrote it, and debugging is painful past three steps. What you give up with sagas: intermediate states are visible, so the system is not isolated; a user can see an order that is paid but not yet shipped, and your UI and business rules must accept that.

  • Why it matters — This is the core "distributed transaction" question and the honest answer is about trade-offs, not technology.

  • Follow-ups — What if the compensation itself fails? How do you make a saga observable? Where do you store saga state?

  • Senior signal — Names the coordinator-blocking failure of 2PC, prefers orchestration for debuggability, and states the loss of isolation as a product-visible consequence.

Q137. How do you design compensating actions?

  • Expected answer — A compensation semantically undoes a completed step; it is not a rollback, because the effect was already visible. Rules I apply. It must be idempotent, since it will be retried. It must be commutative-safe: compensations may run in an order you did not expect, so each should be independently correct. It must handle the case where the forward step's outcome is unknown — so before compensating, query the downstream for the actual state rather than assuming. Some actions cannot be compensated (an email is sent, an SMS delivered, a physical package dispatched), so the design must order steps to put irreversible actions last, after everything reversible has succeeded — that ordering rule is the single most valuable piece of saga design. Where compensation is impossible, use a reservation instead: hold inventory for 15 minutes rather than decrementing, so expiry is the "compensation". Finally, compensations fail too, so you need a terminal state: after N attempts, park the saga in needs_manual_intervention, alert, and give operations a tool — because a saga silently stuck halfway is worse than a loud failure.

  • Why it matters — Compensation design is where saga theory meets messy reality.

  • Follow-ups — Order these steps for a booking flow and justify the order. What is your retry and give-up policy? How does a human resolve a stuck saga?

  • Senior signal — Irreversible actions last, reservations instead of compensations where possible, and an explicit manual-intervention terminal state.

Q138. Explain leader election and fencing tokens.

  • Expected answer — Leader election picks one node to perform a role (run a scheduler, own a shard, coordinate writes), typically via a consensus system (etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul) or a lease in Redis/Postgres. The critical insight is that a lease does not guarantee mutual exclusion: a leader can be alive but stopped — a 45-second GC pause, a hung disk, a network blip — and its lease expires, a new leader is elected, and then the old leader wakes up and writes, believing it is still the leader. Timeouts alone cannot prevent this, because you cannot distinguish a slow node from a dead one. Fencing tokens fix it: every time a lease is granted, the coordinator issues a monotonically increasing token, the leader includes that token in every write to the protected resource, and the resource rejects any write with a token lower than the highest it has seen. The zombie leader's stale token is refused. In practice that means the storage layer must participate — for example a lease_epoch column with UPDATE ... WHERE lease_epoch <= $token, or a conditional write in the object store. If the resource cannot check tokens, you do not have safe mutual exclusion, and you should make the work idempotent instead so a double execution is harmless.

  • Why it matters — The zombie-leader scenario is the classic reason "we have a lock" is not the same as "it is safe".

  • Follow-ups — Why can you not solve this with a shorter lease? Where would the token be checked in a Postgres-backed system? What if the resource is a third-party API?

  • Senior signal — Explains that the resource must enforce the token, and falls back to idempotency when it cannot.

Q139. What is a quorum and why is R + W > N the rule?

  • Expected answer — With N replicas, if a write is acknowledged by W of them and a read consults R of them, then R + W > N guarantees the read set and write set overlap by at least one node, so the read sees the latest acknowledged write (given a way to pick the newest version, such as a version number or timestamp). Common configurations: N=3, W=2, R=2 gives strong-ish reads with tolerance for one node down; W=1, R=1 is fast and eventually consistent; W=N makes writes fail whenever any replica is down. The trade-offs are latency (you wait for the slowest of W) and availability (higher W means fewer failures tolerated for writes). The honest caveats a senior adds: quorum reads are not linearizable on their own — concurrent writes, read repair timing and sloppy quorums with hinted handoff can still surface stale or conflicting values — and quorum systems need conflict resolution (last-write-wins loses data under clock skew; vector clocks or CRDTs preserve it at the cost of complexity). This is why Dynamo-style systems say "eventually consistent" even at R + W > N.

  • Why it matters — It is the vocabulary of every replicated datastore configuration screen.

  • Follow-ups — Why is R + W > N not the same as linearizable? What is a sloppy quorum? How would you choose R and W for a shopping cart?

  • Senior signal — Knows the overlap argument and its limits, and mentions conflict resolution.

Q140. Explain Raft in plain language.

  • Expected answer — Raft keeps a replicated log identical across a cluster. Nodes are in one of three states: follower, candidate, leader. Time is divided into terms; each term has at most one leader. A follower that hears nothing from a leader before its randomised election timeout becomes a candidate, increments the term, and requests votes; a node votes for at most one candidate per term and only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own, so a majority vote elects a leader that cannot be missing committed entries. The leader accepts all client writes, appends them to its log, replicates them, and once a majority has stored an entry it is committed and applied to the state machine; followers learn the commit index from subsequent heartbeats. Consistency comes from the log-matching property: an AppendEntries includes the previous index and term, and a follower rejects it if that does not match, forcing the leader to walk back and overwrite divergent entries. Randomised timeouts prevent split votes. Practical implications: you need an odd number of nodes (3 or 5) because it needs a majority; the cluster is unavailable for writes without a majority; and every write costs a round trip to a majority, which is why cross-region Raft is slow.

  • Why it matters — Raft underlies etcd, Consul and much of Kubernetes, and "explain it simply" tests real understanding.

  • Follow-ups — Why 3 or 5 nodes and not 4? What happens during a network partition of 2 versus 3? How does this affect etcd latency in a multi-AZ cluster?

  • Senior signal — Explains the majority and up-to-date-log voting restriction as the safety mechanism, and connects it to operational sizing.

Q141. Why can you not trust clocks, and what do you use instead?

  • Expected answer — Wall clocks (Date.now()) are synchronised by NTP, so they jump forward, step backward, drift between machines by milliseconds to seconds, and are subject to leap-second handling differences. Two servers' timestamps are not comparable at fine granularity, so "last write wins" by wall clock silently loses data when clocks disagree, and a token that expires "in 60 seconds" may expire immediately on a skewed machine. For measuring durations always use a monotonic clock (process.hrtime.bigint() or performance.now()), which never goes backwards — using Date.now() for latency measurement produces negative durations during an NTP step. For ordering across machines, use logical clocks: a per-entity sequence number, a Lamport clock (a counter carried on messages, giving a consistent total order but not causality), or vector clocks (which capture causality and detect concurrent updates, at the cost of size). Where physical time is unavoidable, bound the uncertainty explicitly — that is what Spanner's TrueTime does, waiting out the uncertainty interval. Practically: never use client-supplied timestamps for ordering, always store timestamptz in UTC, and monitor clock skew across your fleet because it is a real alert.

  • Why it matters — Clock assumptions cause data loss that is nearly impossible to reproduce.

  • Follow-ups — Where does your system currently rely on wall-clock comparison? How would you detect skew? What replaces LWW for a shopping cart merge?

  • Senior signal — The monotonic-versus-wall-clock distinction for durations, plus treating skew as something to monitor.

Q142. Eventual versus strong consistency — how do you decide per feature?

  • Expected answer — Ask what a user or the business loses if a read is stale. Strong consistency is required where a stale read causes an incorrect decision: account balance before a transfer, inventory before committing an order, permission checks, anything a regulator will read. Eventual is fine where staleness is cosmetic or self-correcting: view counts, feeds, search indexes, recommendation lists, analytics dashboards, "3 people are typing". The costs are asymmetric: strong consistency means coordination — a leader, a quorum round trip, or a lock — which costs latency and availability during partitions; eventual consistency means your UI and your business logic must be written to tolerate staleness, which is real design work, not free. The senior move is to make the choice per operation within one product, and to make staleness explicit — a stated staleness budget ("search reflects a price change within 30 seconds") is a requirement you can test and alert on, whereas "it is eventually consistent" is a shrug. Also watch for the trap where an eventually-consistent read feeds a strongly-consistent write: reading stock from a cache and then decrementing is exactly how you oversell.

  • Why it matters — Consistency choices are product decisions with engineering costs; treating them as a purely technical toggle is a mid-level tell.

  • Follow-ups — Pick three features in a product you know and classify them. What is your staleness budget for search, and how would you alert on it? Where does a stale read become a wrong write?

  • Senior signal — Staleness budgets as testable requirements, and spotting the stale-read-then-write hazard.

Q143. How do you provide read-your-writes consistency?

  • Expected answer — The problem: a user updates their profile, is redirected, the read hits a replica or a cache that has not caught up, and they see the old value and think it failed. Options, cheapest first. (1) Return the updated resource in the write response and have the client use it — free, and solves the common case. (2) Sticky routing for a window: after a write, pin that user's reads to the primary (or the same replica) for N seconds, typically via a short-lived cookie or a per-user flag in Redis. (3) LSN/token-based waiting: capture the write position (pg_current_wal_lsn()) and pass it with the read; the read path either routes to the primary or waits until the replica's replay position is past it — precise but requires plumbing through the whole read path. (4) Write-through the cache so the cache is updated in the same operation, rather than invalidating and hoping. In practice I use (1) plus (2): return the resource, and pin session reads to the primary for 5 seconds after a write on that user's data. State the failure mode of sticky routing: it concentrates load on the primary during write-heavy periods, and it does not help a different device belonging to the same user.

  • Why it matters — It is the most common user-visible symptom of read replicas and caching.

  • Follow-ups — What is the cost of routing all post-write reads to the primary? How would you implement the LSN approach in NestJS? Does this help a second user reading the same data?

  • Senior signal — Knows the LSN technique exists but chooses the cheap options and states their limits.

Q144. Design a retry policy.

  • Expected answer — Retries need five decisions. What is retryable: timeouts, connection errors, 429, 502/503/504 — never 400/401/403/404/409/422, because retrying a client error just wastes capacity. Is it safe: only retry non-idempotent operations if you have an idempotency key; otherwise a timeout retry duplicates. How long to wait: exponential backoff with full jitter (sleep = random(0, base * 2^attempt)), because synchronised backoff produces a retry storm where every client retries at exactly the same moment and hammers a recovering service. How many times: a small cap (3–5) plus an overall deadline — a total budget of, say, 10 seconds matters more than the attempt count, and the deadline must be propagated so nested retries do not multiply (3 retries at three layers is 27 requests). What to do when you give up: fail fast to the caller, or move the work to a queue for asynchronous retry with a much longer horizon. Two more things a senior adds: a retry budget (cap retries at, say, 10% of total requests, and stop retrying when the budget is exhausted, which prevents retries from turning a partial outage into a total one), and never retry inside a request the user is waiting on when the deadline is already blown.

  • Why it matters — Naive retries are how a slow dependency becomes a full outage.

  • Follow-ups — Why full jitter rather than plain exponential? How do you propagate a deadline through three services? What is a retry storm and how would you see it in metrics?

  • Senior signal — Full jitter, deadline propagation, and a retry budget — the three things that separate designed retries from a for loop.

Q145. How does a circuit breaker work, and what do you set it to?

  • Expected answer — A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and tracks failures. Closed: calls pass through, failures are counted. When the failure rate crosses a threshold within a window, it trips to open: calls fail immediately without touching the dependency, which stops you from piling threads, connections and latency onto something already broken and gives it room to recover. After a cool-down it moves to half-open, allowing a limited number of trial calls; success closes it, failure reopens it with a longer cool-down. Configuration that actually works: use a failure rate over a rolling window with a minimum request volume (never trip on 2 of 2 requests), something like 50% failures over 20+ requests in 10 seconds, an open period of 5–30 seconds, and count timeouts as failures — a slow dependency is more dangerous than a failing one. Pair it with a bulkhead (a bounded concurrency limit per dependency) so one slow dependency cannot consume the whole event loop or connection pool. And define the fallback: what does the caller do when the circuit is open — serve stale cache, degrade the feature, queue the work, or return 503? A breaker with no fallback plan just converts one error into another.

  • Why it matters — Cascading failure is the dominant outage pattern in service architectures.

  • Follow-ups — Why is a minimum request volume necessary? What is the interaction between breakers and retries? What does your endpoint return when the circuit is open?

  • Senior signal — Rate-based thresholds with a volume floor, bulkheads alongside breakers, and an explicit degraded-mode answer.

Q146. Is exactly-once delivery possible?

  • Expected answer — Exactly-once delivery over a network is impossible in general, and the proof is simple: the sender cannot distinguish "the message was lost" from "the acknowledgement was lost", so it must either resend (risking duplicates) or not (risking loss). What is achievable is exactly-once processing semantics — at-least-once delivery combined with deduplication or idempotent effects at the consumer, so the observable outcome happens once. Kafka's "exactly-once" is precisely this: an idempotent producer (sequence numbers per partition dedupe broker-side retries) plus transactions that atomically commit both the produced messages and the consumer offsets, which gives exactly-once within the Kafka boundary. The moment your consumer writes to Postgres or calls Stripe, that guarantee stops at the edge, and you are back to needing an inbox table or a provider idempotency key. So the senior answer is: "no, and anyone selling it is describing a scope. Tell me where the boundary is, and I will tell you where you still need dedupe." Then name the concrete mechanisms: dedupe keys with unique constraints, guarded state transitions, and reconciliation for the unknown cases.

  • Why it matters — It is a myth that leads teams to skip idempotency because the broker "handles it".

  • Follow-ups — What exactly does Kafka's transactional producer guarantee, and where does it end? Where in your system does at-least-once become effectively-once? What is the cost of Kafka transactions?

  • Senior signal — Distinguishes delivery from processing semantics, and can point at the exact boundary where a vendor's guarantee stops.

45.11 Messaging

Q147. Kafka or RabbitMQ — how do you choose?

  • Expected answer — They are different tools. Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, replicated log: messages are appended, retained for a configured time or size, and consumers track their own offset, so you can replay history and add a new consumer group that reads from the beginning. It excels at high-throughput event streams, event sourcing, and fan-out to many independent consumers. RabbitMQ is a broker with queues and routing: messages are pushed to consumers, acknowledged individually, removed when acked, and routed by exchange type with priorities, TTLs, per-message dead-lettering and delayed delivery. It excels at task queues with complex routing and per-message retry semantics. Practical selectors: do you need replay and multiple independent consumer groups (Kafka), or per-message ack, priorities and delayed retries (Rabbit)? Is ordering per key important (Kafka partitions give it; Rabbit does not across consumers)? What throughput — Kafka comfortably does hundreds of thousands of messages per second per cluster, Rabbit is typically tens of thousands per queue. And the honest option: for many teams, Postgres with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or SQS is the right answer, because a Kafka cluster is a system you must operate.

  • Why it matters — Broker choice is often made by fashion, and running Kafka badly is expensive.

  • Follow-ups — How do you do a delayed retry in Kafka? How do you replay in Rabbit? At what volume would you stop using Postgres as a queue?

  • Senior signal — Frames it as log versus queue, and offers "you may not need either" as a real option.

Q148. How do Kafka partitions relate to ordering and parallelism?

  • Expected answer — A topic is split into partitions; each partition is an ordered, append-only log. Kafka guarantees ordering within a partition only, never across the topic. The partition is chosen by the key's hash (or round-robin when the key is null), so all messages with the same key land in the same partition and are therefore ordered relative to each other. That gives you the standard design rule: key by the entity whose ordering matters — order_id, user_id, conversation_id. Parallelism is bounded by partition count: within a consumer group, each partition is consumed by exactly one consumer, so 12 partitions means at most 12 useful consumers; extra consumers idle. So partition count is a capacity decision made early, since increasing it later re-hashes keys and breaks the ordering guarantee for existing keys in flight. Two more traps: ordering is only preserved on producer retries if enable.idempotence=true (otherwise a retried batch can land after a later one), and a hot key concentrates load on one partition regardless of how many you have.

  • Why it matters — Ordering assumptions that are not backed by keying are a classic silent data bug.

  • Follow-ups — What happens to ordering when you increase partitions from 6 to 12? How do you parallelise beyond partition count? Why does max.in.flight.requests matter for ordering?

  • Senior signal — Connects keying to ordering, partition count to maximum parallelism, and knows the idempotent-producer requirement.

Q149. Explain consumer groups and rebalancing.

  • Expected answer — Consumers with the same group.id share the partitions of a topic; the group coordinator assigns partitions and each is owned by one member. A rebalance happens when a member joins, leaves, or is considered dead (no heartbeat within session.timeout.ms, or it failed to call poll within max.poll.interval.ms). During a classic eager rebalance, all consumers stop consuming while assignments are recomputed — a stop-the-world pause, which on a big group can be seconds and shows up as a latency and lag spike on every deploy. Fixes: use cooperative-sticky assignment so only the moving partitions pause; keep max.poll.records small enough that processing a batch fits comfortably inside max.poll.interval.ms, because slow processing causing a rebalance is the most common cause of an endless rebalance loop; and use static group membership (group.instance.id) so a rolling restart does not trigger a full reassignment. Also remember that after a rebalance you may be handed a partition whose in-flight work you already started, which is another reason handlers must be idempotent.

  • Why it matters — Rebalance storms are a top Kafka operational problem and are usually caused by application-side slowness.

  • Follow-ups — Your consumer takes 8 minutes to process a batch; what happens and how do you fix it? What does cooperative-sticky change? How do you deploy consumers without a rebalance?

  • Senior signal — Diagnoses rebalance loops as a max.poll.interval.ms problem and knows static membership.

Q150. How do you monitor and respond to consumer lag?

  • Expected answer — Lag is the difference between the partition's latest offset and the consumer group's committed offset — how many messages behind you are. Measure it per partition, not just as a topic total, because one lagging partition (a hot key, a stuck consumer, a poison message) is invisible in the sum. Also track lag in time (age of the oldest unprocessed message), which is what the business cares about; "500,000 messages behind" means nothing without throughput, while "we are 14 minutes behind" is actionable. Alert on sustained growth rather than an absolute number, because a spike that drains is normal. When lag grows, the diagnosis tree is: is the producer rate up (check input rate), is the consumer slower (check per-message processing time and downstream latency), is one partition stuck (per-partition view), is the group rebalancing repeatedly (rebalance rate metric), or has the consumer crashed. Remedies: scale consumers up to the partition count, increase partitions (accepting the ordering caveat), make processing cheaper by batching database writes, or shed load by routing to a lower-priority topic. And have a documented answer for "we are 6 hours behind and retention is 24 hours", because that is a data-loss deadline.

  • Why it matters — Lag is the primary SLI for any event-driven system.

  • Follow-ups — Why is time-lag better than count-lag? What do you do when lag exceeds retention? How do you tell producer surge from consumer slowdown?

  • Senior signal — Per-partition and time-based lag, plus the retention deadline as an incident trigger.

Q151. How do you handle poison messages and dead letters?

  • Expected answer — A poison message fails every time — malformed payload, a referenced entity that no longer exists, a bug. Without a plan, it either blocks the partition (Kafka, if you refuse to advance the offset) or loops forever (Rabbit redelivery), and in both cases it stops all progress behind it. The pattern: attempt processing with bounded retries and backoff; classify failures into transient (downstream timeout — retry) and permanent (validation failure, unknown event type — do not retry); on exhaustion, publish the message plus the error, stack, attempt count and original headers to a dead-letter topic or queue, then commit the offset/ack so the stream moves on. Then treat the DLQ as a first-class operational surface: alert on any non-zero depth, keep the original message intact so it can be replayed, build a replay tool that can filter and re-publish, and review the DLQ regularly — an unwatched DLQ is a silent data-loss bucket. For delayed retries in Kafka (which has no per-message delay), use tiered retry topics with increasing delays, consumed by a consumer that sleeps or checks timestamps.

  • Why it matters — This is the difference between a pipeline that degrades gracefully and one that stops.

  • Follow-ups — How do you implement a 5-minute delayed retry in Kafka? What information must the DLQ record carry? Who is on the hook for reviewing it?

  • Senior signal — Classifies transient versus permanent failures, and treats the DLQ as monitored and replayable rather than a graveyard.

Q152. When do you commit offsets, and what are the consequences?

  • Expected answer — Committing before processing gives at-most-once: a crash loses the message. Committing after processing gives at-least-once: a crash between the effect and the commit redelivers, so handlers must be idempotent. Auto-commit (enable.auto.commit=true) commits on a timer regardless of whether processing finished, which quietly gives you both failure modes — messages can be lost if the timer fires before processing completes, and reprocessed if it does not. So for anything that matters, disable auto-commit and commit explicitly after the work is durable, in batches for throughput (commit once per poll batch rather than per message, because commits are network round trips). The stronger pattern when writing to your own database: store the offset in the same transaction as the effect, or use an inbox table keyed by (topic, partition, offset) — then the commit is just an optimisation and correctness does not depend on it. State the consequence clearly: at-least-once plus idempotent handlers is the standard, achievable design; anything else is a special case.

  • Why it matters — Offset strategy is where "we lose messages sometimes" bugs live.

  • Follow-ups — What exactly can go wrong with auto-commit? How do you commit per batch safely? What does the inbox table buy you here?

  • Senior signal — Calls out auto-commit as giving the worst of both, and moves correctness into the database rather than the offset.

Q153. How do you evolve message schemas without breaking consumers?

  • Expected answer — Treat the message as a published contract with more discipline than an HTTP API, because messages are consumed by systems you may not know about and are also replayed from history. Use a schema with a registry (Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema plus Confluent Schema Registry) and enforce a compatibility mode in CI: backward compatible (new consumers can read old messages) is the usual minimum, full compatibility (both directions) if producers and consumers deploy independently in any order. Safe changes: adding an optional field with a default, adding a new event type. Unsafe: removing a field, renaming, changing a type, tightening an enum. Practical rules I enforce: every event carries event_id, event_type, event_version, occurred_at and a producer identifier; consumers ignore unknown fields (tolerant reader); never reuse a field name with new meaning; and if a truly breaking change is needed, publish a new event type in parallel, migrate consumers, then retire the old one — the same expand-and-contract as an API. Remember replay: if you can replay a topic from 30 days ago, your consumer must still parse messages produced by the code from 30 days ago.

  • Why it matters — Schema breakage in an event pipeline can corrupt many downstream systems at once.

  • Follow-ups — What compatibility mode do you set and why? How does replay constrain your schema changes? How do you deprecate an event type?

  • Senior signal — The replay constraint, which is the point people forget, plus a required envelope with event_id for dedupe.

Q154. How do you tune producer and consumer throughput?

  • Expected answer — Producer side: batching is everything — linger.ms (wait a few milliseconds to fill a batch; going from 0 to 5–20 ms often multiplies throughput), batch.size, and compression.type (lz4 or zstd, which usually reduces both network and disk substantially for JSON). acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 for durability, at the cost of a round trip to replicas; acks=1 is faster and can lose data on leader failure. Keep enable.idempotence=true so retries do not duplicate or reorder. Consumer side: max.poll.records and fetch.min.bytes/fetch.max.wait.ms control batch shape; then batch the downstream work — a consumer that does one INSERT per message at 5,000 messages per second is doing 5,000 round trips, whereas batching 500 rows per statement drops that to 10. Parallelism inside a consumer (processing a batch concurrently) is fine as long as you preserve per-key ordering and only commit once the whole batch is durable. And always measure end-to-end: the bottleneck is usually the database or an external API, not the broker, so tuning broker settings when your handler takes 40 ms in Postgres is wasted effort.

  • Why it matters — Throughput tuning is where measurement discipline shows.

  • Follow-ups — What does linger.ms cost you in latency? How do you batch database writes without losing per-message error reporting? Which metric tells you the broker is not the bottleneck?

  • Senior signal — Batching the downstream work, and profiling before tuning broker knobs.

Q155. What retention and replay strategy do you set?

  • Expected answer — Retention (retention.ms, retention.bytes) determines how far back you can replay and how long a broken consumer has to recover. Set it from two requirements: the longest realistic consumer outage you want to survive (a weekend plus a fix is a common 7-day answer), and any need to rebuild a downstream store from history. For topics that represent state rather than events — a compacted "current value per key" topic — use cleanup.policy=compact so the latest value per key is retained forever, which lets a new service bootstrap its state by reading from the beginning. Replay is a capability you must design for, not one you get for free: consumers must be idempotent (replaying charges twice is catastrophic), side effects like emails must be suppressible during a replay, and you need a documented procedure to reset a group's offsets to a timestamp. I also keep a separate archival sink to object storage for long-term history, because keeping 90 days in the broker is expensive compared with S3 and you rarely need broker-speed access to old data.

  • Why it matters — Retention is a data-loss deadline and a recovery capability at once.

  • Follow-ups — What breaks if you replay a topic containing "send email" events? How would you rebuild a read model from a compacted topic? Where do you store history beyond retention?

  • Senior signal — Treats replay as something requiring side-effect suppression, and uses compaction and archival deliberately.

Q156. When would you not use a message broker?

  • Expected answer — When the caller needs the result to continue, a synchronous call is simpler and more debuggable; wrapping it in a broker adds latency, an extra failure domain, and eventual consistency you then have to explain to product. When volume is modest (say under a few hundred jobs per second) and you already run Postgres, a jobs table with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED gives you transactional enqueue with no dual-write problem, no extra infrastructure and easier debugging — you can SELECT your queue. When you need simple background work in a managed environment, SQS or a hosted queue costs almost nothing to operate. And when the team has no experience operating the broker: an under-operated Kafka cluster (no lag alerting, no DLQ, no schema discipline) is worse than no Kafka. The senior framing is that a broker buys you decoupling, buffering, fan-out and replay, and charges you in operational complexity, eventual consistency, ordering caveats and debugging difficulty. If you are not using at least two of the four benefits, you are probably paying the cost for nothing.

  • Why it matters — Anti-hype judgement is explicitly part of the senior bar.

  • Follow-ups — What would make you migrate from a Postgres queue to Kafka? What is the debugging difference in practice? How do you decouple without a broker?

  • Senior signal — A clear cost/benefit test and willingness to recommend the boring option.

45.12 Caching and Redis

Q157. Which Redis data structures do you use, and for what?

  • Expected answer — Strings for cached JSON blobs, counters (INCR) and locks (SET NX PX). Hashes for objects where you update fields independently, and they are memory-efficient for small objects thanks to listpack encoding. Sorted sets for leaderboards, rate-limiter sliding windows (score = timestamp, then ZREMRANGEBYSCORE to trim), and priority queues or delayed jobs (score = run-at time). Lists for simple FIFO queues (LPUSH/BRPOP), though a real broker is usually better. Sets for membership and deduplication. HyperLogLog for approximate unique counts (unique visitors per day in 12 KB, with about 0.8% error) when exactness is not needed. Bitmaps for per-user daily flags at very low memory. Streams (XADD/XREADGROUP) when you want a log with consumer groups and acknowledgement without running Kafka. Geospatial for radius queries. The important skill is picking the structure that makes the operation atomic on the server — ZADD plus ZREMRANGEBYRANK beats reading a list into Node, editing it and writing it back, which is both slower and racy.

  • Why it matters — Choosing the right structure removes whole classes of race conditions.

  • Follow-ups — How would you build a delayed job queue with a sorted set? When is a HyperLogLog acceptable? What is the memory profile of a hash with 1 million fields?

  • Senior signal — Chooses structures to make operations server-side and atomic, and knows the memory characteristics.

Q158. Compare cache-aside, write-through and write-behind.

  • Expected answer — Cache-aside (lazy loading): the application checks the cache, and on a miss reads the database and populates the cache. Simple, resilient (a cache outage degrades to slow, not broken), and only caches what is actually used — my default. Downsides: every miss pays the full cost, the first request after a deploy or eviction is slow, and stale data lingers until TTL or explicit invalidation. Write-through: writes go to the cache and the database together, so the cache is always fresh; it adds latency to every write and caches data that may never be read. Write-behind (write-back): write to the cache and flush to the database asynchronously — fastest writes, but you can lose data if the cache dies before the flush, and it is only acceptable for data you can afford to lose (view counts, last-seen timestamps). In practice I use cache-aside with a TTL as the safety net plus explicit invalidation on write, and I choose the TTL from the business tolerance for staleness, not from habit. One rule worth stating: never make the cache the source of truth by accident — if losing Redis loses data, you have built a database without durability.

  • Why it matters — Cache strategy determines both correctness and blast radius when Redis fails.

  • Follow-ups — Invalidate or update the cache on write, and why? What happens to your database when the cache is flushed? Where would write-behind be acceptable?

  • Senior signal — TTL as a safety net behind explicit invalidation, and the "never accidentally the source of truth" rule.

Q159. What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?

  • Expected answer — A stampede (thundering herd) happens when a hot key expires and hundreds of concurrent requests all miss and all hit the database simultaneously — turning a cache hit path of 0.3 ms into a database spike of hundreds of identical expensive queries, which can take the database down. Three defences, usually combined. (1) Locking / single-flight: the first miss takes a short Redis lock (SET lock:key token NX PX 5000) and recomputes; others either wait briefly and re-read, or serve the stale value. In-process, coalesce concurrent identical requests so one pod issues one query. (2) Early recomputation with jitter: store the value with a logical expiry earlier than the physical TTL, and let a request that sees it is close to expiring refresh it in the background while still serving the current value (probabilistic early expiration). (3) Jittered TTLs: never set the same TTL for a batch of keys populated together, or they all expire in the same second — add ±10% randomness. The related event to plan for is a cold cache after a Redis restart or failover: the whole key space misses at once, so load-test with the cache empty and consider warming the top N keys on startup.

  • Why it matters — It is the most common way a cache causes an outage rather than preventing one.

  • Follow-ups — What does the request that loses the lock race do? How do you implement stale-while-revalidate in Redis? What is your plan for a Redis failover?

  • Senior signal — Serving stale during recompute, TTL jitter, and treating the cold-cache case as a load-test requirement.

Q160. Explain Redis eviction policies and maxmemory.

  • Expected answer — maxmemory caps the dataset size; when it is reached, maxmemory-policy decides what happens. noeviction (the default) returns errors on writes — correct for a queue or a lock store where silently dropping data would be a correctness bug, and catastrophic for a cache because your application starts failing writes. allkeys-lru evicts the least recently used key regardless of TTL — the right choice for a pure cache. volatile-lru/volatile-ttl/volatile-random evict only keys that have a TTL, which is right when you mix cached data with persistent structures in one instance, though it fails hard if you forget to set TTLs and then have nothing to evict. allkeys-lfu (least frequently used) is better than LRU when a small set of keys is genuinely hot and you do not want a one-off scan to evict them. Redis's LRU is approximate, sampling a handful of keys (maxmemory-samples), which is fine in practice. The operational rules: always set maxmemory explicitly (an unbounded Redis gets OOM-killed), monitor evicted_keys and used_memory versus the limit, and do not mix cache and non-cache workloads in one instance precisely because they need different policies.

  • Why it matters — A wrong policy turns a memory pressure event into either data loss or application errors.

  • Follow-ups — Which policy for a session store, and why? What does a rising evicted_keys rate tell you? Why separate cache and queue instances?

  • Senior signal — Ties the policy to the workload and refuses to mix workloads in one instance.

Q161. How do you implement a distributed lock in Redis, and what is Redlock's controversy?

  • Expected answer — The basic single-instance lock is SET lock:resource <random-token> NX PX 30000: atomic acquire with an expiry so a crashed holder does not deadlock. Release must be a Lua script that compares the token before deleting, otherwise you can delete someone else's lock after your own has expired. If the work may exceed the TTL you need a watchdog that extends the lease — and you must handle the case where extension fails. Redlock extends this to N independent Redis nodes, requiring a majority of acquisitions within a bounded time. The controversy (Kleppmann versus antirez) is that Redlock relies on bounded clock drift and bounded process pauses, and neither is guaranteed: a GC pause longer than the TTL means you believe you hold a lock you have lost, so it is not safe for correctness-critical mutual exclusion. The practical senior position: Redis locks are fine for efficiency (avoiding duplicate work, deduplicating a cron run) where a rare double execution is merely wasteful; for correctness (money, inventory), use the database — a row lock, a unique constraint, or a fencing token checked by the resource — because the guarantee has to live where the data lives.

  • Why it matters — Misusing a Redis lock for correctness is a real and expensive mistake.

  • Follow-ups — Write the release script. What is a fencing token and why does Redis not give you one? Give an example where a double execution is acceptable.

  • Senior signal — The efficiency-versus-correctness distinction, and pushing correctness into the database.

Q162. RDB or AOF — how do you configure Redis persistence?

  • Expected answer — RDB takes point-in-time snapshots by forking and writing a compact binary file; restarts are fast and backups are easy, but you lose everything since the last snapshot (potentially minutes), and the fork briefly doubles memory pressure through copy-on-write, which on a large instance can cause a latency spike or an OOM if vm.overcommit_memory is not set. AOF appends every write command to a log, with appendfsync everysec as the usual setting (losing at most about one second) or always (much slower). AOF files are larger and need periodic rewriting to compact, and restart is slower because the log is replayed. Many deployments use both: AOF for durability and RDB for fast restore and backups. The decision follows from what the instance holds: for a pure cache, persistence is often unnecessary — but then you must have a plan for a cold start (see Q159). For a session store or a queue, you need AOF at minimum, and honestly you should question whether that data belongs in Redis at all. In managed services (ElastiCache, Memorystore) you pick from a smaller menu, but the same trade-off applies and you should know your actual RPO.

  • Why it matters — People assume Redis is durable and discover otherwise during an incident.

  • Follow-ups — What is your RPO for this instance? Why does a fork cause a latency spike? What data should not be in Redis at all?

  • Senior signal — Ties persistence choice to the data's role and knows the copy-on-write fork hazard.

Q163. Redis Sentinel or Redis Cluster?

  • Expected answer — Sentinel provides high availability for a single logical dataset: one primary with replicas, and Sentinel processes monitor and promote a replica on failure, with clients discovering the current primary through Sentinel. It does not shard, so your data must fit in one node's memory and one node's throughput. Cluster shards the keyspace across 16,384 hash slots distributed over multiple primaries, each with replicas, and handles both scaling and failover. The costs of Cluster: multi-key operations and transactions only work when keys are in the same slot, which requires hash tags ({user:123}:cart and {user:123}:orders share a slot); Lua scripts must touch only one slot; clients must be cluster-aware and follow MOVED/ASK redirects; and resharding is an operational task. So the rule is to use Sentinel (or a managed equivalent) until you genuinely exceed one node's memory or CPU, then move to Cluster and design keys with hash tags from day one. Also note that many "we need Cluster" cases are actually a hot key or a big key problem, which sharding does not fix.

  • Why it matters — Cluster imposes real constraints on how you name keys, decided before you migrate.

  • Follow-ups — How would you key a rate limiter so it works in Cluster? What breaks in your Lua scripts? What is a MOVED redirect?

  • Senior signal — Hash tags and the multi-key restriction, plus noting that sharding does not solve skew.

Q164. What are pipelining and Lua scripting good for?

  • Expected answer — Redis is fast (typically 0.1–0.5 ms per command in the same AZ), so at scale the dominant cost is round trips: 100 sequential GETs is 100 round trips, maybe 30 ms, while a pipeline sends all 100 in one write and reads one batched response, cutting it to roughly one round trip. MGET/MSET do the same for simple cases. Lua scripts (EVAL/EVALSHA) run atomically on the server, so read-modify-write logic that would be racy from the client becomes safe — this is how you implement token-bucket rate limiting, conditional cache updates, or a compare-and-delete lock release. Rules: keep scripts short because Redis is single-threaded and a slow script blocks every other client (that is the main hazard); use EVALSHA with a cached SHA to avoid resending the body; never call non-deterministic functions in a way that breaks replication; and in Cluster, all keys touched must be in one slot. Also distinguish pipelining from MULTI/EXEC: a transaction queues commands and executes them atomically but cannot branch on intermediate results, which is exactly what Lua adds.

  • Why it matters — Round trips dominate real Redis latency, and atomicity choices determine correctness.

  • Follow-ups — When is MULTI/EXEC not enough? What is the risk of a 50 ms Lua script? How do pipelines interact with errors in the middle?

  • Senior signal — Names round trips as the real cost, and flags single-threaded blocking as the Lua hazard.

Q165. What are the dangerous Redis commands and anti-patterns in production?

  • Expected answer — KEYS * scans the entire keyspace and blocks the server for the duration — on a 10 million key instance that is seconds of total unavailability for every client; use SCAN with a cursor instead. FLUSHALL/FLUSHDB do exactly what they say. DEL on a huge collection blocks while freeing memory; use UNLINK for asynchronous freeing. Large SORT, SMEMBERS on a million-member set, HGETALL on a giant hash, and LRANGE 0 -1 all pull enormous payloads and block. Beyond commands, the anti-patterns are: big keys (a single 500 MB value makes every operation on it slow and makes cluster resharding painful), hot keys (one key taking most of the traffic, so sharding does not help), unbounded key growth with no TTL (memory creeps until eviction or OOM), storing data in Redis that must not be lost, and using Redis pub/sub for anything requiring delivery guarantees, since messages are dropped for disconnected subscribers. Operationally: enable slowlog and check it, rename or disable dangerous commands in production, monitor used_memory, evicted_keys, blocked_clients and latency percentiles, and remember the whole server is single-threaded for command execution.

  • Why it matters — One KEYS * in a support script has caused many outages.

  • Follow-ups — How do you find big keys safely? What replaces pub/sub when you need durability? What does the slowlog tell you?

  • Senior signal — Explains the single-threaded blocking model as the reason all these are dangerous, rather than listing them as trivia.

Q166. How do you choose TTLs, and what is negative caching?

  • Expected answer — A TTL is a staleness budget, so derive it from the business: how wrong can this data be before someone is harmed? Product descriptions can be 10 minutes stale; a price should not be cached at all or only for seconds; a permission check should be very short or explicitly invalidated because a revoked access token cached for an hour is a security incident. Practical guidance: short TTL plus explicit invalidation on write gives freshness with a safety net if invalidation is missed; long TTL alone is only acceptable for immutable data (use content-addressed keys and then TTL barely matters). Always jitter TTLs to avoid synchronised expiry. Negative caching means caching the absence of a result — if a lookup for a missing product hits the database every time, an attacker or a broken client can hammer you with requests for non-existent ids, and the cache provides zero protection. Cache "not found" with a much shorter TTL (say 30 seconds) so a legitimate creation is picked up quickly, and consider a Bloom filter in front for very large key spaces. The related failure is the null-versus-miss ambiguity: store an explicit tombstone value so your code can distinguish "we know it does not exist" from "not cached".

  • Why it matters — TTL choice is where staleness bugs and cache-penetration attacks both originate.

  • Follow-ups — How do you invalidate a cached permission immediately on revocation? How does a Bloom filter help? What is your TTL for a user session and why?

  • Senior signal — Treats TTL as a stated staleness budget, and knows negative caching plus the tombstone-versus-miss distinction.

45.13 Security

Q167. Authentication versus authorization — where does each live in your architecture?

  • Expected answer — Authentication answers "who is this?" and authorization answers "may they do this?". They belong in different places. Authentication happens once at the edge: a gateway or a JwtAuthGuard validates the credential (session cookie, bearer token, mTLS certificate) and attaches a principal to the request. Authorization is layered: coarse checks at the route (@Roles('admin') in a guard) and fine-grained, data-dependent checks in the service, because "can this user cancel this order" needs the order row. The mistake I look for is authorization done only at the route level, which leaves every service method callable with any id — the moment a second entry point exists (a queue consumer, an internal API, a GraphQL resolver), the check is bypassed. So the invariant is: the service method that loads an object also verifies ownership, and ideally the query itself is scoped (WHERE id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2) so a missing check returns nothing rather than someone else's data. Authentication failures are 401, authorization failures are 403 — or 404 when revealing existence is itself a leak.

  • Why it matters — The most common serious API vulnerability is broken object-level authorization, and this is where it starts.

  • Follow-ups — Where exactly do you check that this order belongs to this user? How do you stop a new endpoint from forgetting? What does a queue consumer use as its principal?

  • Senior signal — Pushes the tenant/owner predicate into the query so that forgetting the check fails closed.

Q168. Sessions or JWTs?

  • Expected answer — Server-side sessions store state (a random session id in a cookie, the data in Redis or Postgres). Revocation is instant, the cookie is small, and you can change permissions immediately; the cost is a lookup per request (a sub-millisecond Redis hit) and shared session storage. JWTs are self-contained and signed, so they verify without a lookup, which suits stateless horizontal scaling and cross-service propagation; the cost is that they cannot be revoked before expiry without reintroducing state, and they are frequently implemented badly. My default for a first-party web application is sessions with a HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax cookie, because the operational simplicity and instant revocation are worth more than saving a Redis call. I use JWTs for service-to-service calls and for OAuth access tokens with short lifetimes (5–15 minutes) plus refresh tokens. The hybrid that works well: a short-lived JWT for fast verification plus a revocation list of jti values in Redis checked only for high-value operations, so you get speed with a bounded revocation window.

  • Why it matters — This is one of the most commonly cargo-culted decisions in backend work.

  • Follow-ups — How do you log a user out of all devices with JWTs? What is the revocation window you can live with? What breaks about sessions at 40 pods?

  • Senior signal — Chooses sessions for first-party apps and can articulate why "stateless" is not automatically better.

Q169. What are the common JWT mistakes, and how do refresh tokens work?

  • Expected answer — The mistakes: accepting the alg header from the token (leading to alg: none or an RS256-to-HS256 confusion attack where the public key is used as an HMAC secret) — always pin the expected algorithm server-side; not validating iss, aud and exp; using a weak shared secret; putting sensitive data in the payload, which is base64, not encrypted; long expiry with no revocation path; and storing the token in localStorage, where any XSS steals it. The refresh flow: a short-lived access token (5–15 minutes) plus a long-lived refresh token stored server-side (or at least tracked by id) and sent as an HttpOnly cookie. On refresh, the server verifies the refresh token, issues a new access token and — importantly — rotates the refresh token, invalidating the old one. Rotation plus reuse detection is the key security property: if a rotated token is ever presented again, that means it was stolen, so you revoke the whole token family and force re-authentication. Also key rotation: publish a JWKS with kid so you can roll signing keys without downtime.

  • Why it matters — JWT misconfiguration is a well-known and still-common source of authentication bypass.

  • Follow-ups — Explain the RS256-to-HS256 confusion attack. What does reuse detection do on a legitimate race between two tabs? Where do you store the refresh token in a mobile app?

  • Senior signal — Refresh rotation with reuse detection, algorithm pinning, and JWKS-based key rotation.

Q170. How do you store passwords?

  • Expected answer — With a slow, salted, memory-hard hash: Argon2id is the current recommendation (tune memory around 19–64 MB, iterations and parallelism to about 200–500 ms on your hardware), with bcrypt (cost 12+) as the widely-supported fallback and scrypt as another option. Never MD5, SHA-256 or any fast hash, even salted, because a GPU computes billions per second. The salt is per-user and stored with the hash (bcrypt and Argon2 encode it in the output string), and you should add a server-side pepper kept in a secret store or HSM so a database dump alone is not enough. Verify with a constant-time comparison, which the library does for you. Operationally: re-hash on successful login when the cost parameters have been raised, so the corpus upgrades gradually; never log the password or put it in an error message; enforce length (a 12-character minimum) rather than composition rules, and check against a breached-password list; rate-limit and lock out on repeated failures with a delay that does not reveal whether the account exists. And do the hash on a worker thread or accept that a 300 ms Argon2 call blocks the event loop.

  • Why it matters — It is a solved problem, so getting it wrong signals a lack of security fundamentals.

  • Follow-ups — Why does Argon2 cost matter more than salt length? What does a pepper protect against that a salt does not? How does password hashing interact with the Node event loop?

  • Senior signal — Mentions re-hashing on login, the pepper, and the event-loop cost — the operational details, not just the algorithm name.

Q171. Explain the OAuth2 flows you would use and why.

  • Expected answer — Authorization code with PKCE for all interactive clients — web apps, SPAs and mobile — because the code is exchanged server-side (or with a proof key) so the token never appears in a URL. PKCE (a code verifier and its hash) protects against interception of the code on public clients, and it is now recommended even for confidential clients. Client credentials for machine-to-machine calls where there is no user. Device code for TVs and CLIs. The implicit flow is deprecated (tokens in the URL fragment, no refresh, leaks via history and referrers) and resource owner password credentials is deprecated too, because it requires the user to hand their password to a third-party app. OIDC sits on top of OAuth2 and adds the id_token, a JWT describing the user, plus a discovery document and JWKS. Things to get right regardless of flow: exact-match redirect URI registration (wildcards are how accounts get taken over), the state parameter to prevent CSRF on the callback, the nonce to bind an id_token to the request, and validating aud so a token minted for another client is rejected. And be clear about the distinction: OAuth2 is delegated authorization, OIDC is authentication; using a raw access token as proof of identity is a classic mistake.

  • Why it matters — Almost every product integrates identity, and the failure modes are account takeover.

  • Follow-ups — What attack does state prevent? Why is PKCE needed if you already have a client secret? What is wrong with treating an access token as a login?

  • Senior signal — Names redirect-URI exact matching and the OAuth-versus-OIDC confusion, which is where real breaches come from.

Q172. How do you design authorization for a multi-tenant system?

  • Expected answer — Start with the model: RBAC (roles grant permissions) is simple and covers most products; ABAC (decisions from attributes of user, resource and context) handles rules like "a regional manager can view orders in their region during business hours"; ReBAC (relationship-based, Zanzibar-style) suits deeply nested sharing like documents and folders. Most systems need RBAC plus a few attribute rules, and I would resist building a policy engine before the rules justify it. For tenancy isolation, defence in depth: (1) the tenant id is derived from the authenticated principal, never from a request parameter or header a client can set; (2) every query is scoped by tenant, enforced structurally — a base repository that always adds the predicate, or Postgres row-level security with SET LOCAL app.tenant_id so even a forgotten predicate cannot leak; (3) tests that assert cross-tenant access returns 404; (4) audit logging of access to sensitive resources. For very sensitive domains, separate schemas or databases per tenant give stronger isolation at the cost of migration and connection complexity. The rule I state plainly: shared-table tenancy is fine, but the isolation must be enforced by something other than developer memory.

  • Why it matters — Cross-tenant data leaks are company-ending bugs and they are usually one missing WHERE clause.

  • Follow-ups — How does RLS interact with connection pooling? What test proves isolation? When would you move a tenant to its own database?

  • Senior signal — Structural enforcement (RLS or a base repository) plus tests, rather than trusting code review.

Q173. How does SQL injection happen in an ORM-based codebase, and how do you prevent it?

  • Expected answer — Parameterised queries make injection structurally impossible because values are sent separately from the SQL text and can never be reinterpreted as syntax. Injection still appears in ORM codebases in specific places: raw queries built by string concatenation (manager.query(\SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${email}'`)), query-builder whereclauses with interpolated strings, dynamicORDER BYor column names taken from user input (which *cannot* be parameterised, so they must be validated against an allow-list of known columns),LIKEpatterns assembled by concatenation, and dynamic table names in multi-tenant code. AlsoIN clauses built by joining an array into a string. Prevention: always use bound parameters ($1, :name), allow-list any identifier that must be interpolated, use a lint rule or CodeQL query that flags template literals inside query calls, run SAST in CI, and give the application database user the minimum privileges — no DROP, no access to other schemas, so even a successful injection has a bounded blast radius. Verify by testing: a test that sends '; DROP TABLE users; --` and asserts a normal 404 is cheap insurance.

  • Why it matters — It remains a top vulnerability class, and ORMs create false confidence.

  • Follow-ups — How do you implement a user-selectable sort column safely? Why can't you parameterise a table name? What does least-privilege buy you here?

  • Senior signal — The dynamic-identifier allow-list and least-privilege database user, which are the parts ORMs do not solve.

Q174. Do REST APIs need CSRF protection, and how does CORS relate?

  • Expected answer — It depends entirely on how the credential travels. If authentication uses a cookie, the browser attaches it automatically to cross-site requests, so yes, you need CSRF protection: SameSite=Lax or Strict on the cookie (which blocks most cases), plus a synchroniser token or the double-submit pattern for anything state-changing, and never rely on checking Origin alone. If authentication uses an Authorization: Bearer header, the browser does not attach it automatically, so classic CSRF does not apply — but then you must not also accept the token from a cookie, or you have reintroduced it. CORS is a different mechanism and is often confused with CSRF: it is a browser policy that restricts reading cross-origin responses, not a server-side authorization control. A permissive Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * does not create CSRF, and a strict CORS policy does not prevent it, because a form POST is a simple request that never triggers a preflight. Configure CORS with an explicit origin allow-list, and never reflect the Origin header combined with Allow-Credentials: true, which effectively disables the same-origin policy for every site.

  • Why it matters — The CORS/CSRF confusion is extremely common and leads to both false confidence and broken configs.

  • Follow-ups — Why does SameSite=Lax not cover everything? What is the double-submit pattern and its weakness? What is wrong with reflecting the Origin header?

  • Senior signal — Separates the two mechanisms crisply and knows the origin-reflection-with-credentials anti-pattern.

Q175. What are IDOR and mass assignment, and how do you prevent them?

  • Expected answer — IDOR (insecure direct object reference, or broken object-level authorization) is when an endpoint uses a client-supplied id without checking ownership: GET /invoices/1042 returns someone else's invoice because the handler only did findOne(id). Prevention: scope every lookup by the principal (WHERE id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2), so the check cannot be forgotten; use non-sequential identifiers (UUIDv7 or ULIDs) so enumeration is impractical, though that is defence in depth, not a control; and return 404 rather than 403 where existence itself is sensitive. Mass assignment is when a request body is passed wholesale into an entity: repo.save({ ...body, id }) lets a client set role: 'admin', isVerified: true, balance: 999999 or tenantId. Prevention: explicit DTOs with whitelist: true in the ValidationPipe so unknown properties are stripped, mapping DTO fields to entity fields explicitly rather than spreading, and marking sensitive fields as never-writable from the API. Both classes are best caught structurally — a repository that requires a tenant scope, and a mapping layer between DTO and entity — plus authorization tests as part of the standard test suite for every new endpoint.

  • Why it matters — These are the top two entries on the OWASP API list and both are trivially exploitable.

  • Follow-ups — Write the test that proves an endpoint is not vulnerable. Are UUIDs a security control? How do you prevent a new endpoint from missing the scope?

  • Senior signal — Structural prevention plus a standard authorization test, and being clear that unguessable ids are not authorization.

Q176. How do you manage secrets?

  • Expected answer — Secrets never live in the repository, in a .env committed anywhere, in a Docker image, or in a Kubernetes ConfigMap. They come from a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store, Vault, GCP Secret Manager) and reach the process as environment variables or mounted files, injected by the platform — for example External Secrets Operator syncing into Kubernetes secrets, or IRSA so the pod assumes an IAM role and fetches directly with no static credential at all. Prefer short-lived, automatically-rotated credentials over static ones: RDS IAM authentication or Vault dynamic database credentials mean a leaked credential expires in minutes. Rotation must be designed for: the application should support two valid credentials during a rotation window, or you must sequence "create new, deploy, revoke old". Other essentials: scan the repository history for leaked secrets (gitleaks or GitHub secret scanning) and treat any secret that has ever been committed as compromised — rotate it, do not just delete the commit; redact secrets in logs and in error messages, including in third-party SDK debug output; and audit access to the secret store so you know who read what.

  • Why it matters — Leaked credentials are one of the most common initial access vectors in real breaches.

  • Follow-ups — Walk me through rotating a database password with zero downtime. What do you do the moment a secret is found in Git history? How do you keep secrets out of logs?

  • Senior signal — Dynamic short-lived credentials, dual-credential rotation windows, and treating any committed secret as burned.

Q177. What do you need to know about TLS and mTLS in a backend?

  • Expected answer — TLS gives confidentiality, integrity and server authentication via a certificate chain; TLS 1.3 is the target (fewer round trips, no legacy cipher suites) with 1.2 as the floor. Terminating TLS at a load balancer is normal, but then the hop to your service is plaintext — acceptable inside a private network, and worth encrypting (or using a service mesh) if you have compliance requirements or an untrusted network. mTLS adds client certificate verification, so both sides authenticate; it is the standard for service-to-service identity in a mesh (Istio, Linkerd) and for high-value partner integrations. The operational realities that bite: certificate expiry is a recurring outage cause, so automate renewal (ACME/cert-manager) and alert at 30 and 7 days out; certificate pinning in mobile clients makes rotation dangerous if you pin a leaf rather than an intermediate; internal CAs need their own rotation plan; and clock skew breaks validity checks. In Node specifically: keep the default certificate store rather than setting rejectUnauthorized: false, which people add "temporarily" to fix a self-signed certificate error and then ship — that single flag turns TLS into obfuscation.

  • Why it matters — Expired certificates and disabled verification are both common and both severe.

  • Follow-ups — What happens when your internal CA certificate expires? Why is rejectUnauthorized: false so dangerous? Where does mTLS not help?

  • Senior signal — Treats certificate lifecycle as an operational risk with alerting, and calls out the rejectUnauthorized anti-pattern by name.

Q178. What is SSRF and where does it appear in a backend?

  • Expected answer — Server-Side Request Forgery is when an attacker makes your server issue a request to a destination of their choosing. Backends invite it whenever they fetch a user-supplied URL: webhook registration, "import from URL", avatar fetching by link, PDF or screenshot rendering, and URL preview generation. The impact is severe in cloud environments because your server can reach things the attacker cannot: the instance metadata service (169.254.169.254, which on IMDSv1 hands out IAM credentials), internal admin panels, databases on private IPs, and Kubernetes services. Defences, layered: validate the URL scheme (http/https only) and reject credentials in the URL; resolve the hostname and check the resulting IP against a deny-list of private, loopback, link-local and metadata ranges — then connect to that resolved IP, because otherwise a DNS-rebinding attack changes the answer between check and use; disable redirects or re-validate every hop; enforce timeouts and response size limits; and, most robustly, route all outbound user-driven fetches through an egress proxy with an allow-list, running in a network segment with no access to internal services. Also enforce IMDSv2 so the metadata service requires a PUT-obtained token.

  • Why it matters — SSRF plus cloud metadata is one of the highest-impact bug chains in modern infrastructure.

  • Follow-ups — What is DNS rebinding and why does IP validation alone fail? Which AWS setting mitigates the metadata risk? How do you let customers register arbitrary webhook URLs safely?

  • Senior signal — The check-then-connect-to-the-same-IP detail and the egress proxy, which is what actually holds up.

Q179. How do you handle dependency and supply-chain risk in a Node project?

  • Expected answer — Concretely: commit the lockfile and install with npm ci so builds are reproducible; run npm audit or Snyk/Dependabot in CI with a policy that blocks on high and critical vulnerabilities in production dependencies (and does not block the world on a dev-dependency advisory nobody can exploit); pin base images by digest, not by tag; keep a dependency budget, because every package is code you did not review and node_modules transitively includes hundreds of maintainers. Beyond scanning: use --ignore-scripts where feasible, since post-install scripts are the classic attack vector; generate an SBOM (CycloneDX or SPDX) so that when the next widely-used package is compromised you can answer "are we affected?" in minutes rather than days; prefer packages with a recent release, multiple maintainers and a real test suite; and vendor or fork tiny one-function packages rather than depending on them. On the release side, sign your own artifacts and use provenance attestations. The judgement part: not every advisory is urgent — a prototype-pollution issue in a build-time tool is not the same as a remote-code-execution in your HTTP parser, and treating them identically causes alert fatigue and gets scanning switched off.

  • Why it matters — Supply-chain attacks are increasing and the response depends on preparation, not heroics.

  • Follow-ups — A popular package you depend on is compromised at 9 a.m. What do you do first? How do you decide which advisories block a release? What is an SBOM for?

  • Senior signal — Has a triage policy rather than blanket blocking, and can answer the "are we affected?" question with tooling.

Q180. How do you protect data at rest and handle PII?

  • Expected answer — Layers. Disk-level encryption (RDS/EBS encryption, S3 SSE-KMS) is table stakes and protects against physical and snapshot exposure, but it does not protect against an application-level breach, because the application reads plaintext. So for genuinely sensitive fields — government identifiers, card data, health information — add application-level encryption with keys from KMS, ideally envelope encryption with a per-tenant or per-record data key, and accept that encrypted columns cannot be indexed or searched normally (use a deterministic hash for equality lookup, or a separate blind index). Beyond encryption, the higher-leverage controls are: minimise what you collect and how long you keep it (a retention policy with an actual deletion job), tokenise card data so it never touches your systems (use the payment provider's vault — PCI scope is the strongest argument for not storing something), mask PII in logs and in non-production environments (anonymised database copies, never a production dump on a laptop), restrict who can query production data and audit those queries, and implement deletion and export properly for GDPR/DPDP-style requests, including backups and downstream systems like search indexes and analytics warehouses — which is the part everyone forgets.

  • Why it matters — Data protection is a design and process problem, and the "we encrypt the disk" answer is a mid-level tell.

  • Follow-ups — How do you handle a right-to-erasure request when the data is in three systems and a backup? How do you search an encrypted column? What is in your non-production database?

  • Senior signal — Knows disk encryption does not stop application-level breaches, and treats deletion across downstream systems as the hard part.

45.14 Git

Q181. Merge or rebase?

  • Expected answer — merge creates a commit with two parents, preserving exactly what happened; rebase replays your commits on top of the new base, producing a linear history but rewriting commit hashes. The rule that matters: never rebase commits that others have pulled, because everyone else's history diverges and the fix involves force-pushes and confusion. My practical policy: rebase your own feature branch onto main while you work (so you resolve conflicts incrementally and your branch stays reviewable), then merge into main — either a squash merge for small features, which gives one clean commit per unit of work and a readable main, or a merge commit for larger features where the individual commits carry meaning. The trade-off is honest: linear history makes git log, bisect and blame far easier to read, while merge commits preserve the true development record and make reverting a whole feature a single operation. What I care about more than the policy is that the team has one policy, enforced by branch protection settings, because mixed strategies produce the worst of both.

  • Why it matters — It reveals whether someone has actually collaborated on a busy repository.
