  • Follow-ups — What is the danger of rebasing a shared branch and how do you recover? How does squash merging affect git bisect? When do you want a merge commit?

  • Senior signal — States the shared-history rule, picks a policy for a reason, and cares about enforcement rather than preference.

Q182. What branching strategy would you set up for a team of 12 deploying daily?

  • Expected answer — Trunk-based development: everyone commits to short-lived branches off main, branches live hours to two days, pull requests are small, CI runs on every push, and main is always releasable. Long-lived branches are the enemy — a two-week feature branch guarantees a painful merge and hides work from CI. Incomplete features ship behind feature flags rather than being held back in a branch, which also decouples deploy from release and lets you turn something off without a rollback. GitFlow, with its develop, release and hotfix branches, was designed for versioned software with scheduled releases; for a service deployed daily it adds ceremony and merge overhead for no benefit. What supports this: branch protection requiring review and green CI, a fast pipeline (if CI takes 40 minutes people batch changes and branches grow), automated deploys from main to staging, and a documented rollback that is faster than a fix-forward. The one place I keep release branches is when you must support multiple customer versions simultaneously, which is a different problem.

  • Why it matters — Branching strategy determines integration pain and deployment frequency.

  • Follow-ups — How do you handle a database migration behind a feature flag? What CI duration is acceptable and why? When is GitFlow right?

  • Senior signal — Ties branching to feature flags and CI speed, and separates deploy from release.

Q183. How do you use git bisect?

  • Expected answer — When you know a behaviour worked at commit A and is broken at commit B, bisect binary-searches the range: git bisect start, git bisect bad, git bisect good <sha>, then git checks out the midpoint and you test and mark good/bad. Over 1,000 commits that is about 10 steps. Better, automate it: git bisect run npm test -- path/to/failing.test.ts (or any script exiting 0 for good and non-zero for bad) and walk away — this is where bisect goes from a party trick to a real tool, especially for a performance regression where the script measures a threshold. Practical requirements: commits must be individually buildable and testable, which is an argument for atomic commits and against giant squashes; use git bisect skip for commits that will not build; and remember git bisect reset to return to where you were. I have used it most for regressions with no obvious cause — a subtle behaviour change from a dependency bump, or a query that got 10x slower — where reading diffs would have taken a day and bisect took twenty minutes.

  • Why it matters — It shows a debugging toolkit beyond reading code and adding logs.

  • Follow-ups — What makes a repository bisect-friendly? How would you bisect a flaky failure? What do you do if the bad commit is a merge of 40 changes?

  • Senior signal — Uses bisect run with an automated predicate and connects it back to commit hygiene.

Q184. A bad commit is on main and deployed. revert, reset, or something else?

  • Expected answer — On a shared branch, git revert — it creates a new commit that undoes the change, so history is preserved and nobody has to force-pull. git reset --hard rewrites history and is only appropriate on a local, unpushed branch; doing it on main and force-pushing breaks everyone's clone and destroys the audit trail. If the bad commit is a merge, git revert -m 1 <sha> picks the mainline parent, and you must remember that re-merging that branch later will not reapply the reverted changes unless you revert the revert. Beyond the mechanics, the senior answer covers the deploy: the fastest safe action is usually to roll back the deployment to the previous image (seconds) rather than waiting for a revert commit to build and ship (minutes), and only then land the revert in main so the two do not diverge. If the commit included a database migration, a revert of the code does not undo the schema change, so you need the expand-and-contract discipline that makes the previous version compatible with the new schema — otherwise "roll back" is not actually available and you must fix forward.

  • Why it matters — This is an incident-response question wearing Git clothes.

  • Follow-ups — Why does re-merging a reverted branch lose changes? What if the commit leaked a secret? What makes rollback impossible?

  • Senior signal — Separates rolling back the deployment from reverting the code, and raises migrations as the thing that blocks rollback.

Q185. How do you ship an urgent hotfix while main has unreleased work?

  • Expected answer — Branch from the deployed commit (the tag or SHA currently in production), not from main, because main contains untested work you do not want to ship under pressure. Make the minimal fix, get an expedited review — expedited, not skipped — run CI, deploy, verify with a specific metric or log line rather than "it looks fine", then cherry-pick the fix onto main (or merge the hotfix branch) so it is not lost in the next release. Tag the hotfix so the deployed artifact is identifiable. If a cherry-pick conflicts because main has moved, resolve it deliberately rather than reapplying the change by hand, and add a test that fails without the fix. Afterwards, the important part: a short write-up covering why the bug reached production and what would have caught it, because a hotfix that is not followed by a prevention step guarantees a repeat. If you find yourself hotfixing weekly, the real problem is the pipeline or the test suite, not the process.

  • Why it matters — It tests judgement under time pressure, which is exactly when process gets abandoned.

  • Follow-ups — What do you not skip under pressure? How do you verify the fix worked? What happens if the cherry-pick to main is forgotten?

  • Senior signal — Branches from the deployed SHA, refuses to skip review and tests, and closes the loop with prevention.

Q186. How do you recover work you think you have lost?

  • Expected answer — git reflog first: it records where HEAD and branch tips have been for the last 90 days by default, including commits orphaned by a reset --hard, a bad rebase, a deleted branch or an amended commit. Find the SHA, then git checkout -b recovery <sha> or git reset --hard <sha>. For a rebase specifically, ORIG_HEAD points at where you were before it started. For content that was staged but never committed, git fsck --lost-found can surface dangling blobs. For uncommitted, unstaged changes there is genuinely nothing — which is the practical lesson: commit early and often, even messy commits, because you can always clean history later with an interactive rebase but you cannot recover what was never committed. git stash is also recoverable through the reflog of refs/stash. Worth knowing the boundary: objects unreachable for longer than the reflog expiry can be removed by git gc, so recovery is not indefinite.

  • Why it matters — Everyone destroys work at some point; the recovery habit is the difference between a minute and a day.

  • Follow-ups — How do you recover a branch deleted last week? What does git gc do to your safety net? What is ORIG_HEAD?

  • Senior signal — Knows the reflog expiry boundary and turns the answer into a habit ("commit early, clean later").

Q187. What does good commit and pull-request hygiene look like?

  • Expected answer — Commits should be atomic: one logical change, buildable and testable on its own, which is what makes bisect, revert and code archaeology work. The message explains why, not what — the diff already shows what — with a short imperative subject, a blank line, and a body covering the reasoning, trade-offs and any ticket reference. Conventional Commits are worth adopting if you want automated changelogs and semantic versioning. Pull requests should be small: reviewers genuinely degrade past a few hundred lines, so a 2,000-line PR gets "LGTM" rather than review, which means large PRs are effectively unreviewed. Separate mechanical changes (a rename, a format run) into their own commits or PRs so the substantive diff is readable. In the description, say what changed, why, how you tested it, and what the risk and rollback are. As a reviewer, distinguish blocking concerns from preferences and say which is which; as an author, respond to every comment even if the answer is "good point, follow-up ticket". The measurable goal is a short review turnaround, because a PR sitting for two days is the largest hidden cost in most teams' delivery.

  • Why it matters — Review quality and history quality compound over years.

  • Follow-ups — How do you handle a 3,000-line PR you are asked to review? What belongs in a commit body? How do you speed up review turnaround?

  • Senior signal — Explains why small PRs matter (review degrades with size) and treats review latency as a delivery metric.

Q188. What do you know about monorepos, submodules and rewriting history?

  • Expected answer — A monorepo puts multiple services or packages in one repository, giving atomic cross-project changes, one dependency graph and one CI configuration, at the cost of needing tooling (Nx, Turborepo, Bazel) for affected-only builds, and eventually of repository size. Polyrepos are simpler per project but make cross-cutting changes a coordination exercise across several PRs and deploys. Submodules are the option I avoid: they pin a specific commit of another repository, which sounds right and in practice means detached heads, forgotten updates and confused clones; a package registry or a monorepo solves the same problem better. Git LFS is for large binaries — put them there or, better, in object storage, because a 500 MB asset committed once is in every clone forever. On rewriting history (filter-repo, or filter-branch): it is the only way to purge a leaked secret or a huge accidental file, it rewrites every downstream hash so everyone must re-clone, and it must be paired with rotating the leaked credential, because anyone who cloned before the rewrite still has it. Coordinate it, announce it, and do it once.

  • Why it matters — These are the decisions that make a repository pleasant or painful for years.

  • Follow-ups — When is a monorepo the wrong call? Why is rewriting history not enough after a secret leak? How do you keep CI fast in a monorepo?

  • Senior signal — Rejects submodules with a reason, and pairs history rewriting with credential rotation.

45.15 Docker

Q189. How does Docker layer caching work and how do you exploit it?

  • Expected answer — Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a layer, and a layer is reused if the instruction and all its inputs are unchanged; the moment one layer's cache is invalidated, every layer after it rebuilds. That gives a clear ordering rule: put the things that change least at the top. For a Node service that means copying package.json and the lockfile, running npm ci, and only then copying the source — because copying source first means every code change reinstalls hundreds of megabytes of dependencies, turning a 20-second build into three minutes.

    COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

    Also: use a .dockerignore (excluding node_modules, .git, test fixtures) or the build context alone will be hundreds of megabytes and invalidate caches unpredictably; combine apt-get update and install in one RUN so you never get a stale package index from cache; and in CI enable BuildKit with a registry cache (--cache-from) since CI runners start with an empty local cache. Measure it — build time directly affects how often people deploy.

  • Why it matters — Build time is a developer-productivity multiplier and it is almost always fixable.

  • Follow-ups — Why does RUN apt-get update on its own line cause problems? How do you get cache reuse on ephemeral CI runners? What belongs in .dockerignore?

  • Senior signal — Orders layers by change frequency deliberately and knows the CI cache problem.

Q190. Explain multi-stage builds and what your production image should contain.

  • Expected answer — A multi-stage build uses several FROM stages and copies only the artifacts you need into the final one, so build tools never ship. For a NestJS service: a builder stage on node:22 that installs all dependencies and runs tsc, then a runtime stage that installs only production dependencies and copies dist.

    FROM node:22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev && npm cache clean --force
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]

    The result drops from roughly 1.2 GB to 150–200 MB. Smaller images pull faster (which matters on every scale-up and node replacement), and they have a smaller attack surface — no compilers, no git, no shell utilities for an attacker to use. Consider distroless or Alpine, with the caveat that Alpine uses musl instead of glibc, which occasionally breaks native modules and can change DNS resolution behaviour, so test rather than assume.

  • Why it matters — Image size affects deploy speed, cost and security posture.

  • Follow-ups — What is the Alpine/musl risk for Node? Why does image size affect autoscaling? What is left in your image that should not be?

  • Senior signal — Connects image size to scale-up latency, and knows the Alpine trade-off concretely.

Q191. CMD versus ENTRYPOINT, and why does PID 1 matter for Node?

  • Expected answer — ENTRYPOINT defines the executable; CMD provides default arguments (and is fully replaced by anything you pass on docker run). Use exec form (CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]), never shell form (CMD node dist/main.js), because shell form runs your process as a child of /bin/sh — and then the shell is PID 1, SIGTERM goes to the shell, and your Node process never receives it. That is exactly why "my graceful shutdown never runs" and why pods take the full termination grace period before being SIGKILLed, producing dropped connections on every deploy. PID 1 also has a special role: it must reap zombie processes, which Node does not do, so if your app spawns child processes you want an init (--init on docker run, or tini) as PID 1. The other classic mistake is wrapping the app in npm start: npm becomes PID 1, does not forward signals reliably, and adds a process for no benefit. Run node directly.

  • Why it matters — Signal handling is the difference between clean rolling deploys and 502s.

  • Follow-ups — How would you prove your container receives SIGTERM? Why is npm start a problem in a container? When do you need tini?

  • Senior signal — Connects exec form and PID 1 directly to failed graceful shutdown, which is a scar, not theory.

Q192. Volumes, bind mounts and container storage — what do you use where?

  • Expected answer — The container filesystem is a writable layer that disappears when the container is removed, and writing to it is slower than writing to a volume because of the copy-on-write layer. Named volumes are Docker-managed storage that survives the container and is the right choice for local development databases. Bind mounts map a host path into the container, used for mounting source code during development for hot reload, and for configuration; on macOS and Windows bind mounts are notably slow because of the file-sharing layer, which is why large node_modules should live in a volume rather than being bind-mounted. tmpfs mounts keep data in memory, useful for secrets or scratch space you do not want on disk. In production under Kubernetes, none of this is how you do it: persistent data lives in a PersistentVolumeClaim backed by network storage, or more often not in the pod at all — the container is stateless and the state is in Postgres or S3. The senior framing: containers should be immutable and disposable, so anything written locally must be either cache or logs, and both must be safe to lose.

  • Why it matters — Storage confusion produces both slow development and lost data.

  • Follow-ups — Why is a bind-mounted node_modules slow on macOS? What breaks when two replicas share a volume? Where do your logs go?

  • Senior signal — States the immutable-disposable-container principle and knows local development performance realities.

Q193. How do you run a realistic local environment with Compose?

  • Expected answer — A docker-compose.yml with the application plus its real dependencies — Postgres, Redis, maybe LocalStack for S3 and a broker — on a user-defined network so services resolve each other by service name. Key details that make it actually work: depends_on with condition: service_healthy plus real healthcheck definitions, because depends_on alone only waits for the container to start, not for Postgres to accept connections, which is the source of flaky first-run failures; pinned image versions matching production (postgres:16.4, not postgres:latest) so you do not debug a version difference; named volumes for database data so restarts do not wipe your test data, with a documented down -v to reset; environment variables from a .env that is git-ignored, with a committed .env.example; and a separate compose file or profile for the test dependencies used in CI. The judgement point: Compose is for local development and integration tests, not production. If someone proposes running Compose on an EC2 instance as the production deployment, the honest answer is that it works for a very small system but gives you no rolling deploy, no health-based restarts and no horizontal scaling.

  • Why it matters — Local/production parity determines how many bugs are found before deploy.

  • Follow-ups — Why is depends_on insufficient? How do you seed test data reproducibly? Would you run Compose in production, and when?

  • Senior signal — Healthcheck-gated dependencies and version pinning, plus a clear boundary on production use.

Q194. How do you harden a container image?

  • Expected answer — Run as a non-root user (USER node, or a created user with a fixed UID) so a container escape or a write vulnerability is less useful, and set readOnlyRootFilesystem with an explicit writable emptyDir for anything that must be written. Use a minimal base — distroless or Alpine — so there is no shell, no curl, no package manager for an attacker to pivot with. Pin the base image by digest so a rebuilt tag cannot silently change what you ship. Never put secrets in the image: ENV API_KEY=... and COPY .env . are visible to anyone with the image, and deleting a file in a later layer does not remove it from the earlier one — use BuildKit secret mounts for build-time credentials and runtime injection for the rest. Scan images in CI (Trivy, Grype) and again in the registry, since new CVEs appear for images you already shipped. Drop Linux capabilities and disallow privilege escalation in the runtime security context, and sign images with cosign plus an admission policy if your environment supports it. Finally, rebuild regularly: an image built six months ago has six months of unpatched base-layer CVEs even if your code has not changed.

  • Why it matters — Container security is mostly a small set of defaults that are easy to get right and commonly skipped.

  • Follow-ups — Why does deleting a secret in a later layer not help? What is the practical benefit of a read-only root filesystem? How often do you rebuild?

  • Senior signal — The layer-history point about secrets, and periodic rebuilds for base-image CVEs.

Q195. How do you set memory and CPU limits for a Node container?

  • Expected answer — Two separate systems must agree: the container limit and V8's heap limit. If the container is limited to 512 MB and Node's old-space limit is higher, the kernel OOM-kills the process (exit 137, OOMKilled) with no JavaScript-level error, and you see a restart with no stack trace. So set --max-old-space-size to roughly 75–80% of the container memory limit, leaving room for Buffers, native memory, thread stacks and the runtime itself — for a 1 GB limit, around 768 MB. On CPU: Node is mostly single-threaded for JavaScript, so a CPU limit below 1 core means the process is throttled by cgroup quota, which shows up as bursty latency and unexplained event-loop lag rather than steady slowness; give at least 1 core for a latency-sensitive service and prefer more replicas over more CPU per replica. Also be aware that os.cpus() reports host cores, not your quota, so any library sizing pools by CPU count will over-provision — set UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE and any worker pool size explicitly. Verify by loading the service and watching RSS versus the limit, GC time, and throttling metrics.

  • Why it matters — Silent OOMKilled restarts and CPU throttling are two of the most common and most misdiagnosed container problems.

  • Follow-ups — How do you tell an OOMKilled from a V8 heap OOM? What does CPU throttling look like in your metrics? Why is os.cpus() misleading?

  • Senior signal — The 75–80% heap rule with a reason, and the cgroup-awareness gap in os.cpus().

Q196. What is the difference between a Docker HEALTHCHECK and what you need in production?

  • Expected answer — A Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK runs a command inside the container and marks it healthy or unhealthy; standalone Docker or Compose can restart on that, but Kubernetes ignores it entirely and uses its own probes. That matters because the semantics differ and you need both concepts distinctly: a liveness check answers "is this process wedged and in need of a restart?" and must be cheap and dependency-free — checking the database in a liveness probe means a database blip restarts every pod simultaneously, converting a degradation into an outage. A readiness check answers "should traffic come to me right now?" and should check critical dependencies, so a pod with a broken database connection is removed from the load balancer without being killed. A startup probe covers slow boots so liveness does not kill a pod that is still warming. Logs are the other half: containers should log JSON to stdout and let the platform collect it, never write log files inside the container, and include a request/trace id in every line. The senior point is that health endpoints are an interface with the orchestrator, and getting the liveness/readiness distinction wrong is a self-inflicted outage waiting for its trigger.

  • Why it matters — Probe design is one of the highest-consequence, least-considered pieces of configuration.

  • Follow-ups — What exactly does your liveness endpoint check? What happens when the database is slow and readiness times out on every pod? Where do logs go?

  • Senior signal — The dependency-free liveness rule with the cascading-restart failure story.

45.16 Kubernetes

Q197. What actually happens when you run kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml?

  • Expected answer — kubectl sends the manifest to the API server, which authenticates you, runs admission controllers (validating and mutating webhooks, quota checks, policy engines like OPA/Kyverno), and persists the desired state in etcd. Nothing has run yet — Kubernetes is a set of controllers reconciling desired state against actual state. The Deployment controller sees a new Deployment and creates a ReplicaSet; the ReplicaSet controller sees it needs N pods and creates Pod objects with no node assigned. The scheduler watches for unscheduled pods and picks a node by filtering (does it have enough allocatable CPU and memory, do node selectors, taints, tolerations and affinity rules permit it) and scoring. The kubelet on that node sees a pod assigned to it, pulls the image, asks the container runtime to start it, and reports status back. Meanwhile the endpoints/EndpointSlice controller adds the pod's IP to the Service once its readiness probe passes, and kube-proxy (or a CNI equivalent) programs the node's routing so Service traffic reaches it. The whole model is level-triggered reconciliation, which is why a pod deleted by hand comes back and why "it eventually converges" is the normal mental model.

  • Why it matters — Almost every Kubernetes debugging session is "which controller is stuck and why", and you cannot answer that without this chain.

  • Follow-ups — Your pod is Pending forever — which step failed and how do you check? What is the difference between a Deployment and the ReplicaSet it owns? What does level-triggered mean in practice?

  • Senior signal — Describes controllers and reconciliation rather than reciting object names, and can point at where to look at each step.

Q198. How do you configure liveness, readiness and startup probes for a Node service?

  • Expected answer — Three probes with different jobs. Liveness: "is this process wedged?" — restart is the remedy, so it must be cheap and check nothing external. GET /health/live returning 200 if the event loop is responsive is enough; checking Postgres here means a database blip restarts every pod at once. Typical settings: periodSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 3, timeoutSeconds: 1. Readiness: "should I receive traffic?" — this one should check critical dependencies (database connectivity, a required cache) and should flip to failing during shutdown. Failing readiness removes the pod's IP from the Service endpoints without killing it, which is exactly right for a transient dependency problem. Startup: covers slow boots (migrations, cache warming) with a generous failureThreshold * periodSeconds budget, and while it is running, liveness and readiness are suspended, so a slow start is not mistaken for a hang. The failure mode to name: a readiness probe that checks a shared dependency will fail on every pod simultaneously when that dependency has a hiccup, taking your whole service out of the load balancer for something that was only degraded — so keep the readiness dependency list to things without which the pod is genuinely useless, and consider returning ready-but-degraded for optional dependencies.

  • Why it matters — Probe misconfiguration converts partial degradations into full outages.

  • Follow-ups — Redis is down and your readiness probe checks it. What happens? Why suspend liveness during startup? What does your liveness endpoint measure?

  • Senior signal — The correlated-readiness-failure story and the discipline of a minimal liveness check.

Q199. How do you get a zero-downtime rolling update?

  • Expected answer — The Deployment's RollingUpdate strategy with maxSurge and maxUnavailable controls the pace: maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0 means new pods come up before old ones go down, which costs extra capacity briefly but never reduces serving capacity. Then the details that actually determine whether users see errors. New pods must not receive traffic before they can serve it, which is the readiness probe's job — so minReadySeconds and an accurate readiness check matter. Old pods must stop receiving traffic before they stop serving: when a pod is deleted, endpoint removal and the container's SIGTERM happen concurrently, and endpoint propagation to kube-proxy and any ingress controller takes a second or two, so without care the pod stops accepting connections while traffic is still arriving. The fix is a preStop hook that sleeps 5–10 seconds (or flips readiness and waits) before the application starts draining, plus application-side graceful shutdown that finishes in-flight requests, plus terminationGracePeriodSeconds comfortably longer than your longest request. Also keep connections in mind: with keep-alive, a client may hold a connection to a terminating pod, so the server must send Connection: close during drain.

  • Why it matters — Deploy-time 502s are extremely common and this is precisely why.

  • Follow-ups — Why does a preStop sleep help when the app already handles SIGTERM? What value do you set for the grace period and how do you derive it? How do you verify zero downtime?

  • Senior signal — Knows endpoint removal and SIGTERM race, and prescribes the sleep-then-drain ordering with a derived grace period.

Q200. Requests versus limits, and what are QoS classes?

  • Expected answer — A request is what the scheduler reserves and uses to decide whether a pod fits on a node; a limit is the hard ceiling enforced by cgroups at runtime. For memory, exceeding the limit means the kernel OOM-kills the container (exit 137). For CPU, exceeding the limit means throttling: the container is paused until the next cgroup period, which shows up as spiky p99 latency rather than a clean error. QoS classes follow from these: Guaranteed (requests equal limits for all containers) gets the strongest protection from eviction, Burstable (requests set, limits higher or absent) is the common case, and BestEffort (nothing set) is evicted first under node pressure. My practice: always set memory request equal to memory limit, because memory is incompressible and overcommitting it means the kernel picks a victim under pressure; set a CPU request that reflects steady-state usage; and be deliberate about CPU limits — a low CPU limit on a Node service causes throttling that looks like mysterious latency, and many teams get better tail latency by setting a CPU request with no limit, accepting the noisy-neighbour risk. Derive all of these from observed usage (kubectl top, or the VPA in recommendation mode), not from guesses.

  • Why it matters — Wrong requests waste money or cause evictions; wrong CPU limits cause invisible latency.

  • Follow-ups — Why is memory treated differently from CPU? What does throttling look like in Grafana? How would you right-size 40 services?

  • Senior signal — Memory request equals limit, thoughtful position on CPU limits, and sizing from measured data.

Q201. How does autoscaling work and what do you scale on?

  • Expected answer — The HPA periodically reads a metric and adjusts replica count toward a target: with CPU utilisation, desired = ceil(current * currentMetric / targetMetric). CPU is the default but it is often the wrong signal for a Node service, because an I/O-bound API can be at 30% CPU while its latency is terrible. Better signals via custom or external metrics: requests per second per pod, p95 latency, event-loop lag, or — for workers — queue depth or Kafka consumer lag, which is what KEDA is built for and is the single most useful autoscaling signal for asynchronous workloads because it scales on the backlog rather than on a symptom. Configure the behaviour: fast scale-up (short stabilisation window, allow doubling) and slow scale-down (a 5-minute stabilisation window) so you do not flap and lose warm caches and connections. Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter adds nodes when pods cannot be scheduled, which takes 30 seconds to a few minutes, so for spiky traffic keep some headroom or use low-priority placeholder pods to pre-provision. The failure modes to state: scaling on a metric affected by the scaling itself, an HPA fighting a VPA, and scaling out a service whose bottleneck is the database — where adding pods makes things strictly worse by adding connections.

  • Why it matters — The "we added replicas and it got slower" scenario is common and reveals whether someone understands the bottleneck.

  • Follow-ups — Why is CPU a bad signal for an I/O-bound API? What happens when you scale a service whose database is saturated? How do you handle a 10x spike in 30 seconds?

  • Senior signal — Queue depth and latency as signals, asymmetric scale-up/down behaviour, and the database-bottleneck warning.

Q202. A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. Walk me through debugging it.

  • Expected answer — kubectl describe pod first: the events section usually names the cause and the container statuses show the last exit code and reason. Then kubectl logs <pod> --previous, because the current container may not have produced output yet and the previous crashed instance's logs are what you need. Read the exit code: 0 with a restart means the process exited normally and the container has nothing to keep running (often a wrong command or a script that finished); 1 is an application error, so read the stack trace; 137 is SIGKILL, usually OOMKilled (confirm in describe) or a liveness probe failing; 139 is a segfault, likely a native module. Common causes in order of frequency: a missing or malformed environment variable or secret so config validation fails at boot (which is the fail-fast behaviour working as intended), an unreachable dependency at startup, a memory limit lower than the real working set, a liveness probe that is too aggressive for a slow start (fixed with a startup probe), and an image built for the wrong architecture. If logs are silent, kubectl run the same image with the command overridden to a shell, or attach an ephemeral debug container (kubectl debug), to inspect the environment and filesystem. Related states worth distinguishing: ImagePullBackOff (registry credentials, wrong tag), Pending (no node has room, or a PVC cannot bind), and Init:Error (an init container failed).

  • Why it matters — This is a daily operational task and the diagnosis order shows real experience.

  • Follow-ups — Where do you see OOMKilled specifically? Why --previous? Your pod is Pending with no events — what next?

  • Senior signal — Reads exit codes fluently, uses --previous, and distinguishes the sibling failure states.

Q203. How do ConfigMaps and Secrets work, and how does a config change reach a running pod?

  • Expected answer — Both are key-value objects in etcd. As environment variables they are read once at container start, so a change requires a pod restart — which is why "I updated the ConfigMap and nothing happened" is a frequent confusion. As mounted volumes they are updated in place by the kubelet within roughly a minute, but your process must watch the file and reload; most applications do not, so it still needs a restart. The standard trick is to put a hash of the config into the Deployment's pod template annotations so that changing the ConfigMap changes the pod spec and triggers a normal rolling update — which also gives you a rollback path, since the config change is now part of a revision. Secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted, so you must enable encryption at rest in etcd, restrict RBAC on secret read access (anyone who can create a pod in the namespace can usually mount and read them), and prefer external secret managers via External Secrets Operator or the CSI secrets driver so the source of truth is outside the cluster and rotation is automated. Never put secrets in a ConfigMap, and never log the resolved config.

  • Why it matters — Config delivery and rotation is where "it works in staging" problems and credential leaks both live.

  • Follow-ups — How do you force a rollout when a ConfigMap changes? Are Kubernetes secrets encrypted? How does a rotated database password reach the app?

  • Senior signal — The config-hash annotation pattern and honesty about secret encoding versus encryption.

Q204. How does a request actually reach a pod?

  • Expected answer — From outside: DNS resolves to an ingress load balancer (an ALB or NLB pointing at an Ingress controller, or a Gateway API implementation). The Ingress controller terminates TLS and routes by host and path to a Service. A Service is not a proxy process; it is a stable virtual IP and a set of rules. The endpoints/EndpointSlice controller keeps the list of ready pod IPs behind it, and kube-proxy programs iptables or IPVS rules on every node so that traffic to the Service IP is DNAT'd to one of those pod IPs — many ingress controllers skip this and send traffic directly to pod IPs, which gives better load balancing. Inside the cluster, orders-service.default.svc.cluster.local resolves through CoreDNS to the Service IP. Types: ClusterIP (internal only), NodePort (a port on every node), LoadBalancer (provisions a cloud LB), and headless (clusterIP: None, returning pod IPs directly, which is what StatefulSets use). Two operational details worth knowing: readiness controls endpoint membership, so a failing probe removes a pod from routing; and the default ndots: 5 in the pod's resolv.conf means unqualified lookups try several search domains first, which multiplies DNS traffic and adds latency — a common and fixable source of tail latency.

  • Why it matters — Networking problems are opaque unless you know each hop.

  • Follow-ups — Why is there no process listening on the Service IP? What is a headless Service for? How would you debug "connection refused" between two services?

  • Senior signal — Knows Services are iptables rules rather than proxies, and raises the ndots DNS amplification.

Q205. StatefulSet or Deployment, and would you run Postgres in Kubernetes?

  • Expected answer — A Deployment treats pods as interchangeable: random names, no stable storage, parallel updates. A StatefulSet gives stable network identities (db-0, db-1), stable per-pod PersistentVolumeClaims that survive rescheduling, ordered creation and termination, and a headless Service for direct addressing — everything a clustered stateful system needs. So StatefulSets for databases, Kafka, Zookeeper, Elasticsearch; Deployments for stateless services. On running Postgres in Kubernetes: it is genuinely viable now with a mature operator (CloudNativePG, Zalando, Crunchy) that handles failover, backups, PITR and minor upgrades — but you are taking on database operations, and Kubernetes adds failure modes (a node drain evicting your primary, storage class performance surprises, a PVC that cannot reattach in another AZ). My default recommendation for most teams is managed (RDS, Cloud SQL): the operational burden is where the risk is, not the technology, and a team that is not ready to handle a 3 a.m. failover should not own one. I would run Postgres in-cluster when there is a real reason — cost at scale, data residency, an existing platform team with database expertise — and never as the first stateful thing a team tries.

  • Why it matters — It is a build-versus-buy decision with severe consequences, and the honest answer requires judgement.

  • Follow-ups — What happens to a StatefulSet pod during a node drain? How do PVCs behave across availability zones? What would make you move off RDS?

  • Senior signal — Recommends managed by default with concrete criteria for the exception, and names the Kubernetes-specific failure modes.

Q206. How do you keep a service available during node maintenance?

  • Expected answer — A PodDisruptionBudget declares how much voluntary disruption is acceptable — minAvailable: 2 or maxUnavailable: 1 — and the eviction API respects it, so kubectl drain blocks rather than taking your last two replicas down together. Note the word voluntary: a PDB does not protect against a node crashing, only against drains, cluster upgrades and autoscaler scale-down. Alongside it: topology spread constraints (or pod anti-affinity) to spread replicas across nodes and availability zones, so a single node or zone failure cannot take out every replica — the default scheduler will happily place all three of your pods on one node otherwise. Taints and tolerations keep workloads off nodes they should not use; priority classes decide who gets evicted first under pressure. And graceful termination has to work (see Q199), because a drain sends SIGTERM and then waits only for the grace period. The failure I have seen: a PDB with minAvailable equal to the replica count, which makes drains hang forever and blocks cluster upgrades — so the budget must leave room for at least one pod to move, and it must be paired with enough replicas to make that true.

  • Why it matters — Node maintenance happens constantly in a managed cluster; without these, deploys and upgrades cause outages.

  • Follow-ups — Does a PDB help when a node hardware-fails? What happens if minAvailable equals the replica count? How do you spread across zones?

  • Senior signal — The voluntary-disruption distinction and the self-blocking-PDB scar.

Q207. How do you secure a cluster at the application team's level?

  • Expected answer — Namespaces for isolation and quota, with RBAC granting least privilege: developers get read plus log access in their namespace, deploys happen through CI with a scoped ServiceAccount, and nobody has cluster-admin routinely. Each workload gets its own ServiceAccount — not default — and cloud permissions attach to it (IRSA on EKS, Workload Identity on GKE) so pods get short-lived cloud credentials with no static keys anywhere. NetworkPolicies are important and usually missing: by default every pod can reach every other pod, so a compromised frontend can talk directly to your database; a default-deny ingress policy per namespace plus explicit allows is the fix. Pod Security Admission (restricted profile) or a policy engine blocks privileged containers, host mounts, host networking and running as root. Also: encryption at rest for etcd, audit logging enabled and shipped somewhere, image provenance/admission control if you can, and regular review of who has what — because RBAC accumulates. The framing I use: assume one pod will eventually be compromised, and ask what it can reach; if the answer is "everything", the cluster has no meaningful security boundary.

  • Why it matters — Default Kubernetes is wide open internally, and most teams never close it.

  • Follow-ups — What can a compromised pod do in your cluster today? How does IRSA avoid static credentials? What does a default-deny NetworkPolicy break first?

  • Senior signal — Assumes compromise and reasons about blast radius, and names IRSA/Workload Identity rather than mounting cloud keys.

Q208. Production incident: latency spiked and error rate is up. What do you check in Kubernetes?

  • Expected answer — Work outside-in and change-first. Was there a deploy or config change in the last hour — that is the single highest-prior cause, so check the rollout history and be ready to kubectl rollout undo. Then the service view: kubectl get pods for restarts, CrashLoopBackOff, Pending or Evicted; kubectl top pods and node pressure conditions for resource exhaustion; HPA status to see whether it is at max replicas. Then the dependency view: are errors concentrated on one downstream (traces will tell you immediately), is database CPU or connection count saturated, is a queue backing up. Then the platform view: node events, disk pressure, a node that went NotReady, DNS errors in logs (CoreDNS saturation is a classic cluster-wide latency cause), and network policy or certificate changes. Useful tools: kubectl describe for events, kubectl logs --previous, kubectl debug for an ephemeral container in a pod you cannot exec into (distroless images have no shell), and kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp across the namespace. The habit that matters more than any command: mitigate first (roll back, scale up, shed load, disable the feature flag), diagnose second, and write down the timeline as you go because you will not remember it later.

  • Why it matters — It is the closest thing to a live test of on-call ability.

  • Follow-ups — What is your first action if a deploy went out 20 minutes ago? How do you exec into a distroless container? What do you do when the cluster's DNS is the problem?

  • Senior signal — Mitigate-before-diagnose, change-first hypothesis, and knowing the cluster-level causes (DNS, node pressure) not just the application ones.

45.17 AWS and cloud

Q209. EC2, ECS, EKS or Lambda — how do you choose compute?

  • Expected answer — Start from team and workload, not from fashion. Lambda suits spiky, short, event-driven work — S3 triggers, webhook receivers, glue between services — with no servers to patch and true scale-to-zero; it costs you cold starts, a 15-minute limit, awkward connection pooling against Postgres (hence RDS Proxy), and a debugging experience that is worse than a normal process. ECS on Fargate is the sweet spot for most teams running a handful of long-lived services: containers, no cluster to operate, straightforward autoscaling, and much less to learn than Kubernetes. EKS earns its complexity when you have many services, need the Kubernetes ecosystem (operators, service mesh, Helm, portability), or already have platform engineers; running EKS with three services and no platform team is paying a tax for nothing. EC2 for workloads that need specific instance control — GPUs, huge memory, licence constraints, or a database you insist on self-managing. The honest senior framing: the question is which operational burden you want, and the right answer for a 12-person team shipping a NestJS API is usually Fargate, moving to EKS only when concrete needs appear.

  • Why it matters — Compute choice sets your operational cost and hiring needs for years.

  • Follow-ups — What breaks when Lambda talks to Postgres at scale? What would make you migrate from Fargate to EKS? How do cold starts affect a user-facing API?

  • Senior signal — Frames it as choosing an operational burden and is willing to recommend the less fashionable option.

Q210. Explain IAM roles versus users, and how a pod or task gets credentials.

  • Expected answer — An IAM user is a long-lived identity with static access keys; a role is a set of permissions that an entity assumes temporarily, receiving short-lived credentials via STS. The rule is: no static keys anywhere in a workload. An ECS task gets a task role and the credentials arrive through the container credentials endpoint; an EKS pod uses IRSA (or EKS Pod Identity), where the pod's ServiceAccount is annotated with a role ARN, the pod receives a projected OIDC token, and the SDK exchanges it for temporary credentials; an EC2 instance uses an instance profile via IMDS (enforce IMDSv2 so SSRF cannot trivially steal them). Policies should be least privilege: scope actions and resources narrowly (s3:GetObject on one prefix, not s3:* on *), use conditions, and prefer separate roles per service so a compromise is contained. Also know the evaluation order — an explicit Deny always wins, and permissions boundaries plus SCPs at the organisation level cap what any role can do regardless of its policy. Human access should be federated SSO with assumed roles and MFA, not IAM users with keys in a .aws/credentials file.

  • Why it matters — Leaked static keys are a leading cause of cloud breaches, and the fix is architectural.

  • Follow-ups — How does IRSA avoid a static secret? What does IMDSv2 change for SSRF? How do you scope an S3 policy to one tenant's prefix?

  • Senior signal — Names the token-exchange mechanism rather than "attach a role", and connects IMDSv2 to SSRF.

Q211. What do you need to know about S3 for a backend service?

  • Expected answer — S3 is strongly read-after-write consistent for new objects and overwrites (since 2020), so the old "eventual consistency" workarounds are obsolete, but it is still an object store: no partial updates, no rename (a copy plus delete), and listing is expensive at scale. For uploads, do not proxy file bytes through your API — issue a presigned URL or presigned POST so the client uploads directly to S3, with a short expiry, a content-length range and content-type condition, and a key namespace you control (never let the client choose the full key, or they will overwrite someone else's object). Then have S3 notify you (event notification to SQS/Lambda) rather than trusting the client to tell you it finished. Storage classes and lifecycle rules are the cost lever: Standard for hot, Intelligent-Tiering when access patterns are unknown, Glacier tiers for archives, with lifecycle rules to transition and expire — plus a rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads, which silently accumulate real cost. Security: block public access at the account level, use bucket policies plus SSE-KMS, enable versioning and, for critical data, Object Lock; enable access logging or CloudTrail data events so you can answer "who read this object".

  • Why it matters — Direct-to-S3 uploads and lifecycle policies are two of the most common missed wins.

  • Follow-ups — Why must you control the object key? How do you know an upload completed? What is quietly costing money in an old bucket?

  • Senior signal — Presigned uploads with constraints plus event-driven completion, and the incomplete-multipart cost detail.

Q212. How do you run Postgres on RDS properly?

  • Expected answer — Multi-AZ is availability, not scale: a synchronous standby in another AZ that takes over on failure with a DNS change, typically 60–120 seconds of write unavailability, and your application must reconnect cleanly (which means a connection pool that handles errors and retries idempotent work, and a DNS TTL you do not cache forever). Read replicas are asynchronous and are for scaling reads; they lag, so read-your-writes must be handled (see the distributed-systems section). Backups: automated snapshots plus continuous WAL archiving give point-in-time recovery to any second within the retention window; test a restore, because an untested backup is a hope. Parameter groups are where you set work_mem, max_connections, statement_timeout, log_min_duration_statement and autovacuum tuning — the defaults are conservative and generic. Use RDS Proxy or PgBouncer when many small compute units (Lambda, lots of pods) would otherwise exhaust connections. Monitoring: Performance Insights for wait events and top SQL, plus CloudWatch on CPU, FreeableMemory, ReadIOPS/WriteIOPS, burst balance on gp2, replica lag, and connection count. Upgrades need a plan: minor versions during a window with Multi-AZ to reduce impact, major versions rehearsed on a clone with EXPLAIN comparisons, because a planner change can regress a query.

  • Why it matters — Most teams use managed Postgres and still need to operate it well.

  • Follow-ups — What happens to in-flight transactions during a Multi-AZ failover? How do you test a restore? What is your major-version upgrade plan?

  • Senior signal — Multi-AZ is availability not scale, tested restores, and rehearsing major upgrades for plan regressions.

Q213. SQS, SNS, EventBridge or Kinesis?

  • Expected answer — SQS is a queue: one consumer group, at-least-once delivery, visibility timeouts, dead-letter queues, and FIFO queues when you need ordering and deduplication within a message group (at much lower throughput). Use it for work queues and buffering. SNS is pub/sub fan-out: one publish, many subscribers, no retention — pair it with SQS (the fan-out-to-queues pattern) so each consumer gets its own durable queue. EventBridge is a routing bus with content-based rules, schemas, archives and replay, plus SaaS integrations; it is the better choice for a domain event backbone where consumers come and go, at higher per-event latency than SNS. Kinesis (or MSK for Kafka) is an ordered, partitioned, replayable stream for high-volume data where multiple consumers read at their own position — analytics pipelines, clickstreams, change data capture. Choosing: do you need replay and ordering (Kinesis/Kafka), fan-out to independently-failing consumers (SNS+SQS or EventBridge), or a simple durable work queue (SQS)? And the same caveat as always: everything here is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent, and every queue needs a DLQ with an alarm on depth.

  • Why it matters — Picking the wrong primitive here is expensive to undo once producers exist.

  • Follow-ups — Why SNS to SQS rather than SNS directly to a service? What does an SQS visibility timeout do when processing takes longer than expected? When do you need FIFO?

  • Senior signal — The fan-out-to-queues pattern, visibility-timeout semantics, and DLQ alarms as non-negotiable.

Q214. Explain the VPC pieces a backend engineer must understand.

  • Expected answer — A VPC is a private network with subnets per availability zone. Public subnets have a route to an internet gateway; private subnets do not, and reach the internet through a NAT gateway in a public subnet. Your application and database belong in private subnets; only load balancers live in public ones. Security groups are stateful, instance-level allow-only rules (return traffic is automatically permitted) and can reference other security groups, which is the clean way to say "the database accepts traffic from the app tier". NACLs are stateless, subnet-level, and support deny rules; most teams use the defaults and rely on security groups. Two things that bite: NAT gateways charge per gigabyte processed, so heavy S3 or ECR traffic through NAT is a large and invisible bill — use VPC endpoints (a free gateway endpoint for S3 and DynamoDB, interface endpoints for other services) to keep that traffic off NAT and off the public internet; and cross-AZ data transfer is billed, so chatty services spread across zones cost money. Also plan CIDR ranges with room to grow and avoid overlaps if you will ever peer VPCs or connect on-premises networks.

  • Why it matters — Networking mistakes here show up as both security exposure and surprising bills.

  • Follow-ups — Why is a security group referencing another security group better than a CIDR? What is the cheapest fix for a large NAT bill? Where do you put an RDS instance?

  • Senior signal — VPC endpoints for NAT cost, stateful-versus-stateless distinction, and CIDR planning.

Q215. When is Lambda the wrong choice?

  • Expected answer — When latency consistency matters and cold starts are unacceptable: a cold start for a Node function is typically 100–500 ms, worse inside a VPC historically and worse with a large bundle, and provisioned concurrency fixes it at a cost that erodes the economics. When the workload is steady and high volume — at sustained load, containers on Fargate or EC2 are usually cheaper than per-invocation pricing. When execution exceeds 15 minutes, or needs a lot of memory or local disk. When you need many long-lived connections: every concurrent Lambda holds its own database connection, so 500 concurrent executions is 500 connections, which is why RDS Proxy exists. When the workload needs a persistent in-process cache or a warm connection pool, both of which die with the execution environment. And when the team's debugging, testing and local development story would suffer — a monolith split into 40 Lambdas often produces a distributed system nobody can trace. Where Lambda is excellent: event-driven glue, S3 and DynamoDB triggers, scheduled tasks, image processing, and spiky low-volume APIs where scale-to-zero is real money saved.

  • Why it matters — Serverless enthusiasm without cost and latency analysis produces expensive rewrites.

  • Follow-ups — How do you estimate the crossover point between Lambda and Fargate cost? What does RDS Proxy actually solve? How do you keep a Lambda warm and is that a good idea?

  • Senior signal — Concrete numbers for cold starts and the connection-per-execution problem, plus a fair list of where Lambda genuinely wins.

Q216. ALB or NLB, and what do you configure?

  • Expected answer — An ALB is layer 7: it understands HTTP, routes by host, path and header, terminates TLS, supports HTTP/2 and WebSockets, and integrates with WAF and Cognito. An NLB is layer 4: it forwards TCP/UDP with very low latency, preserves the client IP, handles millions of connections, and gives you a static IP — the right choice for non-HTTP protocols, extreme throughput or when a client needs to allow-list an IP. For a normal API, ALB. Configuration that matters: target group health checks (path, interval, healthy/unhealthy thresholds) determine how fast a bad instance is removed and how a slow start is treated; deregistration delay (default 300 seconds) is the drain window and must exceed your longest request; the ALB idle timeout (default 60 seconds) must be shorter than your Node server's keepAliveTimeout, or the ALB will reuse a connection the server is closing and you get intermittent 502s — this is a well-known Node-behind-ALB failure and the fix is setting server.keepAliveTimeout and headersTimeout above 60 seconds. Also enable access logs, use X-Forwarded-For correctly (trusting only the last hop from the ALB), and prefer target type ip with ECS/EKS for direct pod routing.

  • Why it matters — The keep-alive mismatch causes recurring, hard-to-explain 502s in exactly this stack.

  • Follow-ups — Why do you get 502s with the default Node keep-alive timeout? What does deregistration delay do during a deploy? When do you need an NLB?

  • Senior signal — The keepAliveTimeout versus idle-timeout ordering, which only comes from having debugged it.

Q217. Where does cloud spend actually go, and how would you cut it?

  • Expected answer — Start with data, not intuition: Cost Explorer grouped by service and tag, and a tagging policy that makes per-team and per-environment attribution possible. The usual big items for a backend platform: over-provisioned compute (instances sized for a peak that never comes, or requests set to double actual usage across every pod), RDS instances sized for headroom and never revisited, data transfer — NAT gateway processing, cross-AZ traffic and internet egress, which is frequently the surprise line item — storage that never expires (old snapshots, unpartitioned logs in S3 Standard, CloudWatch log groups with infinite retention), and idle non-production environments running 24/7. The moves, roughly in order of effort-to-savings: right-size from observed metrics, set log and object retention policies, add VPC endpoints to bypass NAT, schedule non-production environments off outside working hours, buy Savings Plans or Reserved Instances for the steady baseline once usage is stable, use Graviton instances (usually 15–25% better price/performance for Node workloads), and use S3 lifecycle tiering. The discipline that makes it stick: a cost dashboard reviewed monthly, an alert on anomalous daily spend, and cost as a line item in design reviews — because the cheapest fix is not building the expensive thing.

  • Why it matters — Cost ownership is an explicit part of senior scope in most companies now.

  • Follow-ups — What is your largest line item and why? How would you attribute cost to teams? What is the risk of buying reservations too early?

  • Senior signal — Measures before cutting, names data transfer as the hidden cost, and treats cost as a design-review input.

Q218. Design a disaster recovery plan.

  • Expected answer — Start with the business numbers: RPO (how much data can we lose) and RTO (how long can we be down), agreed with the business, per system — the payments database and the recommendations cache do not need the same answer. Then pick a strategy that meets them: backup and restore (cheapest, RTO of hours), pilot light (core data replicated, infrastructure defined as code but scaled to zero, RTO of tens of minutes), warm standby (a scaled-down running copy, RTO of minutes), active-active (near-zero RTO, highest cost and complexity). For a typical setup: Multi-AZ RDS covers zone failure automatically, cross-region automated snapshot copies plus PITR cover region loss with an RPO of minutes, infrastructure as code lets you rebuild the stack, and S3 cross-region replication protects object data. Then the part that distinguishes a real plan from a document: test it. Run a restore exercise on a schedule, measure the actual RTO rather than the hoped-for one, and record what was missing — DNS TTLs, secrets that only exist in one region, an unreplicated queue, a hard-coded endpoint. Also cover the non-infrastructure failures: accidental deletion (versioning, soft delete, delayed replication so a bad delete does not replicate instantly), and a compromised account (separate backup account with restricted access).

  • Why it matters — Untested DR is the most common form of imaginary safety.

  • Follow-ups — What is your measured RTO, not your target? How do you protect backups from a compromised admin? What breaks first in a region failover?

  • Senior signal — Business-agreed RPO/RTO per system, tested restores with measured numbers, and protection against deletion as well as outage.

45.18 Testing

Q219. What does your test suite look like for a NestJS service?

  • Expected answer — Weighted toward fast, meaningful tests. A large base of unit tests for pure logic — pricing rules, state machines, validators, mappers — with no framework and no I/O, running in milliseconds. A substantial middle layer of integration tests that exercise a service with a real Postgres (via Testcontainers) and real repositories, mocking only third parties; this is where most of the value is for a backend, because the interesting bugs are in SQL, transactions and constraints, and those are precisely what mocks hide. A thin layer of end-to-end tests through the HTTP surface with supertest against a fully-bootstrapped app, covering the critical user journeys — checkout, login, payment — not every endpoint. Plus contract tests where multiple teams share an interface, and a handful of smoke tests that run against a deployed environment. The framing I use is the "test trophy" rather than a strict pyramid: for backend services, integration tests earn their weight, and a suite of 3,000 heavily-mocked unit tests can pass while the application is completely broken. The constraint is time: the whole suite should run in a few minutes, or people stop running it.

  • Why it matters — Test strategy determines whether a codebase can be changed confidently.

  • Follow-ups — Which layer catches your most common production bugs? How do you keep integration tests fast? What do you do when the suite takes 25 minutes?

  • Senior signal — Argues for integration weight with a reason, and treats suite duration as a first-class constraint.

Q220. What do you mock and what do you refuse to mock?

  • Expected answer — Mock at boundaries you do not own and cannot run: payment gateways, email and SMS providers, third-party HTTP APIs, and time. Do not mock your own database — a mocked repository asserts that you called a method, not that the query is correct, so it cannot catch a wrong join, a missing index-backed constraint, a transaction that does not roll back, or a NOT NULL violation, which are exactly the failures that reach production. Do not mock the framework's own machinery in a way that means your pipes, guards and filters never run in tests. And avoid mocking internal collaborators just to isolate a class: over-mocking couples the test to the implementation, so every refactor breaks tests without any behaviour changing, which trains the team to distrust the suite. For third-party HTTP I prefer a recorded/faked server (nock, MSW, or a WireMock container) over hand-written mocks, because it exercises the real client, serialisation and error handling. And for external providers, add a small number of contract or sandbox tests that run against the real thing on a schedule, so a provider's breaking change is discovered by you rather than by customers.

  • Why it matters — The mocking line determines whether tests give real confidence or theatre.

  • Follow-ups — How do you test that a transaction rolls back? What is wrong with expect(repo.save).toHaveBeenCalled()? How do you catch a provider changing their API?

  • Senior signal — Refuses to mock the database and can name the specific bug classes mocks miss.

Q221. How do you test database code without the suite becoming slow and flaky?

  • Expected answer — Use a real Postgres — Testcontainers spins one up per suite, or a shared local instance with per-worker databases. Run migrations once at startup rather than per test. Then isolate tests: the fastest reliable approach is to wrap each test in a transaction and roll back at the end, which is very quick but breaks if the code under test manages its own transactions or if you need to test commit behaviour; the alternative is truncating the affected tables between tests (TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE), which is slower but always correct. Never share mutable fixture data across tests, and never rely on test ordering. Parallelism: give each Jest worker its own database (test_db_1, test_db_2) so tests do not fight over rows, which is the single biggest speed win. Seed with factories that create only what a test needs rather than a giant shared fixture, so a test's preconditions are visible in the test itself. And test the things only a real database can show: unique-violation handling, cascade behaviour, concurrent updates with two connections, and that a failing step actually rolls back the whole unit of work.

  • Why it matters — Database tests are where most backend confidence comes from, and where most suite slowness comes from too.

  • Follow-ups — How do you test a deadlock or a concurrent update? Transaction rollback or truncate, and when does each fail? How long should 500 integration tests take?

  • Senior signal — Per-worker databases for parallelism and a clear-eyed comparison of the isolation strategies.

Q222. Why are tests flaky, and how do you deal with flakiness?

  • Expected answer — Causes, in the order I usually find them: shared mutable state between tests (a database row, a module-level cache, a mocked singleton not reset); time — tests that depend on Date.now(), timezones, or a sleep that is usually long enough; async leaks where a promise is not awaited so an assertion runs before the effect; ordering dependence, exposed the moment you shuffle or parallelise; real network calls to a flaky third party; and genuine race conditions in the code, which are the valuable ones. The policy matters as much as the fixes: a flaky test is a broken test, because a suite people re-run until it goes green provides no signal. So quarantine it immediately (skip it with a ticket and an owner), fix it within a bounded time, and track flake rate as a metric. Never add a blanket retry to hide it — retries turn a real intermittent bug into an invisible one. Practical prevention: fake timers and an injected clock instead of Date.now(), deterministic seeded random, no sleep in tests (wait on a condition instead), reset all state in beforeEach, and run the suite in random order in CI so ordering dependence is found early.

  • Why it matters — Flakiness silently destroys the value of an entire test suite.

  • Follow-ups — Would you ever retry a test in CI? How do you test code that uses Date.now()? How do you find an ordering dependency?

  • Senior signal — Treats flakiness as a broken-signal problem with a policy, and rejects blanket retries.

Q223. How do you test event-driven and queue-based code?

  • Expected answer — Split it into layers. The handler itself is a plain function that takes a message and does work — test it directly, including the duplicate case (call it twice with the same message and assert the effect happened once) and the malformed-message case. The wiring — that the consumer subscribes to the right topic, deserialises correctly, acks and dead-letters — is an integration test with a real broker container or the framework's testing support, asserting on observable effects rather than internal calls. For the producer side, assert that the outbox row is written in the same transaction as the business change, and separately that the relay publishes it. Avoid the common trap of tests that await sleep(2000) and hope: poll for the expected condition with a timeout instead, so the test is both faster and less flaky. Also test the ordering and failure behaviour explicitly: what happens when messages arrive out of order, when a handler throws, when the same message arrives after a redelivery. And keep a contract test on the message schema so a producer change that breaks consumers is caught in CI rather than at 2 a.m.

  • Why it matters — Async code is where teams' test coverage is weakest and production surprises are highest.

  • Follow-ups — How do you assert "exactly one email was sent" for a duplicated message? How do you avoid sleeps? Where do you test the DLQ path?

  • Senior signal — Tests idempotency and out-of-order arrival explicitly, and polls conditions instead of sleeping.

Q224. How do you test time-dependent behaviour and scheduled jobs?

  • Expected answer — Inject the clock. A Clock provider with a now() method (or a DateProvider token in Nest) means tests can set the time explicitly, and production code never calls Date.now() directly. Use fake timers (jest.useFakeTimers() with advanceTimersByTime) for code that uses setTimeout/setInterval, remembering to restore real timers afterwards or every later test inherits a frozen clock. Test the edges deliberately, because that is where the bugs are: daylight-saving transitions, month and year boundaries, leap days, timezone conversion for a user in a different zone from the server, and expiry exactly at the boundary. Store and compute in UTC (timestamptz in Postgres) and convert only at the presentation edge. For scheduled jobs, separate the schedule from the work: test the work as an ordinary function, and test the schedule wiring lightly. Add the operational test too — a job that silently stops running produces no failures, so assert on a "last successful run" record and alert on staleness rather than assuming the cron fired.

  • Why it matters — Time bugs are subtle, seasonal, and often only reproduce in production.

  • Follow-ups — Your billing job double-charged on the DST change. How would a test have caught it? Why is timestamptz important? How do you know a nightly job ran?

  • Senior signal — Injected clock plus explicit edge cases, and monitoring for jobs that stop firing.

Q225. How do you manage test data?

  • Expected answer — Factories, not fixtures. A factory function creates a valid entity with sensible defaults and lets the test override only the fields it cares about (createOrder({ status: 'pending', total: 5000 })), so the test reads as a statement about behaviour rather than a wall of unrelated setup, and adding a required column means changing one factory rather than 300 tests. Each test creates the data it needs and does not depend on anything left behind. Avoid a giant shared seed file: it becomes load-bearing, nobody dares change it, and tests start depending on incidental values. For end-to-end and staging environments, generate data with the same factories rather than restoring a production dump — production data in a test environment is a compliance incident waiting to happen, and if you must use it, it has to be anonymised properly (not just masked names, since ids and relationships re-identify people). Keep test data creation fast: bulk-insert where possible, and do not create 500 rows when 3 prove the point, except in the specific tests that exist to check behaviour at scale.

  • Why it matters — Test data design decides whether a suite stays maintainable at 2,000 tests.

  • Follow-ups — What breaks when tests share a seeded user? How do you build data for a pagination test? What is your policy on production data in lower environments?

  • Senior signal — Factories with overrides, no shared seed, and a clear compliance line on production data.

Q226. What does code coverage tell you, and what does it not?

  • Expected answer — Coverage measures which lines and branches executed during the suite. It is useful as a negative signal: a critical module at 10% coverage is genuinely untested and worth attention. It is a poor positive signal, because executing a line is not the same as asserting anything about it — you can reach 100% with tests that have no assertions at all, and coverage says nothing about whether you tested the right inputs, the error paths, or the concurrent case. Chasing a number produces low-value tests written for the metric, especially on generated code, DTOs and mappers, and it creates resistance to deleting dead code. So I set a floor rather than a target (say, do not let coverage drop on changed files), exclude generated and trivial code, and look at coverage per module rather than one global percentage. Mutation testing (Stryker) is the stronger signal: it changes your code deliberately — flipping a comparison, removing a call — and checks whether any test fails; surviving mutants show tests that execute code without verifying it. It is slow, so run it periodically or on the critical modules only, not on every commit.

  • Why it matters — Coverage targets are a common source of wasted effort and false confidence.

  • Follow-ups — Would you enforce 80% coverage as a gate? What is a surviving mutant telling you? Which modules do you actually want near-complete coverage on?

  • Senior signal — Uses coverage as a negative signal only, and knows mutation testing as the real quality check.

Q227. How do you do performance testing, and where does it fit in CI?

  • Expected answer — Distinguish the types: a load test at expected peak to verify the SLO holds; a stress test past the limit to find where it breaks and confirm it degrades gracefully rather than collapsing; a soak test running for hours to reveal leaks, connection exhaustion and slow bloat; and a spike test for sudden traffic, which is what breaks autoscaling assumptions. Tools: k6 or Gatling for scripted scenarios, autocannon for a quick endpoint check. What makes it meaningful: realistic data volume (a query that is fast on 10,000 rows and terrible on 10 million), realistic traffic mix and think time rather than a single endpoint hammered flat out, and warm caches or explicitly cold ones depending on what you are testing. In CI, run a short smoke-level benchmark on every merge to catch a gross regression (a p95 that doubled), and a full load test on a schedule or before a major release against an environment sized like production — full load tests are too slow and too noisy for every commit. Always measure the system, not just the API: during the test, watch database CPU, connection counts, event loop lag and queue depth, because the interesting result is usually which component saturated first.

  • Why it matters — Performance regressions are cheap to prevent and expensive to discover in production.

  • Follow-ups — What data volume do you test against and why? What would you alert on in a CI benchmark? How do you keep load tests from being noisy?

  • Senior signal — Names the four test types with distinct purposes and watches downstream saturation, not just response times.

Q228. What does "testing in production" mean responsibly?

  • Expected answer — It means accepting that no pre-production environment fully reproduces production — real data distributions, real traffic patterns, real third-party behaviour — and building controls so that production verification is safe. The tools: feature flags to decouple deploy from release, so code ships dark and is enabled for internal users, then 1%, then everyone, with an instant kill switch; canary deploys where a small percentage of traffic hits the new version while you compare error rate and latency against the baseline, with automated rollback on regression; shadow traffic, mirroring real requests to the new version without using its responses, which is excellent for validating a rewritten query path; synthetic monitoring, scripted journeys running continuously so you detect breakage before users report it; and chaos experiments — deliberately killing a pod, adding latency to a dependency — run in a controlled window with a hypothesis and an abort condition. The prerequisites matter more than the techniques: you need good observability to see the difference, a fast and reliable rollback, and blast-radius control so an experiment cannot take out everyone. Without those, "testing in production" is just shipping bugs to customers.

  • Why it matters — This is where modern delivery practice and operational maturity meet.

  • Follow-ups — What is your rollback time? How do you canary a database migration? What is the prerequisite for a chaos experiment?

  • Senior signal — Names the prerequisites (observability, rollback, blast-radius control) rather than just listing techniques.

45.19 Performance

Q229. A product manager says "the API is slow". What do you do?

  • Expected answer — Refuse to guess, and turn it into a measurable statement first: which endpoint, for which users, at what time, and slow compared with what? Then look at the data in a fixed order. (1) Is it real and where — per-endpoint p50/p95/p99 latency over time, so you know whether it is everything (infrastructure, event loop, database, a shared dependency) or one route (a query, a new feature). (2) When did it start, and what changed then — a deploy, a config change, a data volume crossing a threshold, a traffic increase, a third-party degradation. (3) Where is the time going — a distributed trace of a slow request breaks the total into service, database, cache and external calls, which usually ends the investigation in a minute. Without tracing, fall back to per-layer metrics: database query time from pg_stat_statements, event loop lag, external call latency. (4) Is it latency or queueing — a saturated connection pool or worker pool shows as time waiting, not time working, and that distinction changes the fix completely. Only then form a hypothesis, test it, fix, and verify with the same metric you started from.

  • Why it matters — Diagnostic method is the most transferable performance skill.

  • Follow-ups — What if there is no tracing? How do you distinguish queueing from slow work? What number do you report back to the PM?

  • Senior signal — Starts from percentiles and change correlation, and separates waiting from working.

Q230. Why do averages lie, and which percentiles do you track?

  • Expected answer — An average hides the shape of the distribution. If 95 requests take 20 ms and 5 take 2 seconds, the mean is 119 ms — a number no user experienced, and it looks fine on a dashboard while one in twenty users is having a terrible time. Track p50 (the typical experience), p95 and p99 (the tail, which is where timeouts, retries and abandonment live), and the max. Tail latency matters disproportionately because a single page often makes ten backend calls, so a p99 of 2 seconds means roughly one in ten page loads is slow. Track it per endpoint and per dependency, because a global percentile is dominated by whichever route has the most traffic. Two subtleties a senior adds: percentiles do not average or add — you cannot compute a service's p99 by averaging the p99s of its instances, which is why you aggregate histogram buckets rather than pre-computed percentiles; and the metric must be measured where the user is, since server-side timing excludes queueing at the load balancer, TLS handshakes and network time. Also watch the shape: a bimodal distribution (fast cache hits, slow misses) needs a different fix from a uniformly slow one.

  • Why it matters — Choosing the wrong statistic makes real problems invisible.

  • Follow-ups — Why can't you average p99s across pods? What does a bimodal latency histogram usually mean? Where exactly do you measure latency?

  • Senior signal — The non-averageability of percentiles and the "ten calls per page" tail amplification argument.

Q231. Walk me through fixing a slow endpoint that does too many queries.
