  • Expected answer — Confirm the count first: log or count queries per request in development, or find the fingerprint with a huge calls value in pg_stat_statements. A typical N+1 is 1 + 200 queries at 2 ms each, so 400 ms of pure round trips even though every query is "fast" — which is why the database looks healthy while the endpoint is slow. Fix in order of leverage: (1) load the related data in one query — a join with leftJoinAndSelect, or two queries plus an in-memory stitch when the join multiplies rows badly; (2) make sure the resulting query is indexed for its actual predicate and sort, verified with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) rather than assumed; (3) reduce what you select — pulling 40 columns including a 200 KB JSONB payload to render a list is a large hidden cost; (4) paginate with keyset instead of offset; (5) cache only after the query is as good as it can be, because caching a bad query hides it until the cache misses. Then guard the fix: an assertion on query count in the integration test for that endpoint, so the N+1 cannot silently return in six months.

  • Why it matters — This is the single most common backend performance defect.

  • Follow-ups — When is two queries better than one join? How do you assert query count in a test? Why not just add a cache?

  • Senior signal — Adds a regression guard, and orders the fixes so caching comes last.

Q232. My service is slow but CPU is low and the database is idle. What is happening?

  • Expected answer — Almost always queueing somewhere. The usual suspects: a saturated database connection pool, where requests wait for a connection while the database itself is bored — visible as a non-zero waiting count on the pool; a saturated HTTP agent (maxSockets reached) queueing outbound calls; the libuv thread pool blocked by crypto or file operations; a bounded worker pool with a backlog; or an upstream dependency that is slow, so your requests sit waiting on I/O. Little's Law is the tool: concurrency = arrival rate x service time, so if requests take 200 ms and you receive 100 per second, you need 20 concurrent slots; with a pool of 10, half the requests wait and latency doubles. The fix is not automatically "make the pool bigger" — a bigger database pool can make things worse by contending inside Postgres. The right move is to measure where the wait is (instrument pool waiting, agent queue depth, event loop lag), then either reduce service time (faster query), increase capacity where it genuinely helps, or shed load with a fail-fast timeout so the queue cannot grow unbounded. An unbounded queue always converts a small slowdown into a total outage.

  • Why it matters — Queueing effects are counter-intuitive and cause the most confusing incidents.

  • Follow-ups — Apply Little's Law to a real number. Why can a bigger pool be worse? What does a fail-fast timeout buy you?

  • Senior signal — Reaches for Little's Law and bounded queues with fail-fast, rather than raising limits.

Q233. How do payload size and serialisation affect performance?

  • Expected answer — More than people expect, because JSON.stringify is synchronous and blocks the event loop: serialising a 10 MB response can take tens of milliseconds during which nothing else in the process runs, so one large endpoint degrades every other request. Fixes: return less — field selection or sparse fieldsets so clients ask for what they need, pagination with sane limits, and never embed a large JSONB blob in a list response. Compression (gzip or brotli) reduces bytes on the wire substantially for JSON, but it costs CPU per response, so terminate it at the load balancer or CDN when you can rather than burning application CPU. For very large responses, stream rather than buffer — pipeline from a database cursor through a transform to the response keeps memory flat. Also watch class-transformer: plainToInstance on a 5,000-item array is surprisingly expensive, and a ClassSerializerInterceptor applied globally to a large payload is a common invisible cost. Measure the actual sizes: an endpoint whose p95 response is 2 MB is a design problem, not a tuning problem, and the honest fix is usually a narrower contract.

  • Why it matters — Serialisation cost is invisible in query metrics and blocks the single thread.

  • Follow-ups — Where would you enable compression and why? How would you profile serialisation cost? What is the biggest response your API returns?

  • Senior signal — Knows stringify blocks the loop and that class-transformer on big arrays is a real cost centre.

Q234. Where do you add a cache, and what do you check first?

  • Expected answer — Only after the underlying operation is as fast as it reasonably can be, because a cache in front of an unindexed query hides the problem until the day the cache is cold and the database falls over. Then choose the layer by what you are caching: CDN or HTTP cache headers for public, cacheable responses (cheapest and furthest from your servers); a shared Redis cache for hot, expensive, tolerably-stale data used by all pods; a small in-process cache with a very short TTL for extremely hot keys, which absorbs the top of the distribution and cuts Redis round trips, at the cost of per-pod staleness; and a materialised view or precomputed table in Postgres for expensive aggregations. Before adding any of them, answer four questions: what is the staleness budget, how is it invalidated on write, what happens when the cache is empty or unavailable, and how will you know the hit ratio. That last one matters — a cache with a 40% hit ratio is usually a design mistake and should be visible on a dashboard, along with the load test you ran with the cache disabled to confirm the origin can survive a cold start.

  • Why it matters — Caching is the most common source of both big wins and subtle correctness bugs.

  • Follow-ups — What is your hit ratio and is it good? What happens when Redis restarts? How do you invalidate on a write from another service?

  • Senior signal — The four questions as a gate, and load testing with the cache off.

Q235. How do you reduce round trips?

  • Expected answer — Count them first: a request that makes 12 sequential calls at 5 ms each spends 60 ms doing nothing but waiting. Techniques: parallelise independent calls with Promise.all instead of awaiting in sequence, which is often a one-line change worth 50% of the latency; batch — MGET instead of N GETs, Redis pipelines, a single WHERE id = ANY($1) instead of N selects, and a DataLoader-style per-request batcher that coalesces lookups automatically; denormalise the read path so one query returns what a screen needs rather than five; co-locate — keep chatty services in the same availability zone, since a cross-AZ hop is around 1 ms and a cross-region hop 80–150 ms, which makes a chatty design unusable across regions; and keep connections warm with keep-alive agents so you are not paying handshakes. The senior addition is knowing when not to parallelise: firing 200 concurrent database queries from one request is a good way to exhaust the pool and hurt every other request, so bound the concurrency (a p-limit style semaphore) and be explicit about the limit.

  • Why it matters — Round trips dominate latency in distributed systems, and the fixes are cheap.

  • Follow-ups — Where would Promise.all be dangerous? How does DataLoader work? What is the latency cost of a cross-region call?

  • Senior signal — Bounds the concurrency when parallelising, and quotes real per-hop latency numbers.

Q236. What causes tail latency, and how do you attack it?

  • Expected answer — The tail is rarely the same cause as the median. Common sources: garbage collection pauses; event loop blocking from a synchronous operation on some requests (a large payload, a slow regex); queueing behind a saturated pool; a cold cache or a first-request-after-eviction; a slow shard, a hot key or a hot row in the database; a lock wait; connection setup on a cold keep-alive pool; DNS timeouts; noisy neighbours and CPU throttling in a container; and retries — a request that timed out at 1 second and retried appears as a 2-second request. The attack: instrument enough to attribute the tail (traces sampled to include slow requests specifically — tail-based sampling exists for exactly this), then treat each cause on its merits. Structural remedies worth knowing: hedged requests (send a second request to another replica if the first is slower than p95 and take the first answer) trade a few percent extra load for a much better tail; bounded queues with fail-fast so a slow path does not accumulate; per-dependency timeouts tighter than the overall request budget; and reducing variance at the source, since the tail is usually variance rather than mean slowness.

  • Why it matters — Tail latency is what users and downstream services actually feel.

  • Follow-ups — How do you make sure your traces include the slow requests? When are hedged requests a bad idea? How does a retry show up in your latency histogram?

  • Senior signal — Tail-based sampling and hedged requests, plus recognising retries as a tail contributor.

Q237. How do garbage collection and memory affect latency in Node?

  • Expected answer — Minor (scavenge) collections are frequent and cheap, typically well under a millisecond; major mark-compact collections are less frequent and can pause for tens of milliseconds on a large heap, which lands directly in your p99. So the practical levers are about allocation rate and heap size rather than GC flags. Reduce allocation: avoid creating large temporary arrays and objects per request, do not deep-clone big payloads, reuse Buffers where sensible, and stream instead of materialising. Watch heap growth: a heap that keeps climbing means either a leak or an in-process cache with no bound, and as the heap grows major GC pauses grow with it — this is why an unbounded in-memory cache degrades latency long before it causes an OOM. Instrument it: export heapUsed, heapTotal, RSS and GC pause time (via perf_hooks PerformanceObserver on the gc entry type) and correlate GC pauses with latency spikes; if 40 ms of every second is GC, you have found your tail. Sizing: set --max-old-space-size to about 75–80% of the container limit, and prefer more smaller instances over one huge heap, because a 4 GB heap has worse pause characteristics than four 1 GB heaps.

  • Why it matters — GC is an invisible latency source that people blame on the database.

  • Follow-ups — How would you prove GC is causing a latency spike? Why prefer smaller heaps? What allocates most in a typical request?

  • Senior signal — Measures GC pause time as a metric and prefers smaller heaps for pause behaviour.

Q238. How do you do capacity planning and protect a service under overload?

  • Expected answer — Planning: measure the per-instance capacity by load testing to the point where latency degrades (not to the point of failure), take that as the safe throughput, and size for peak with headroom — typically 30–40% — so that a node loss or a traffic surge does not immediately breach the SLO. Account for the real peak (campaigns, month-end, a marketing email) rather than the daily average, and revisit as the data grows, since capacity per instance falls as tables grow. Protection under overload matters just as much, because demand eventually exceeds capacity: load shedding — reject excess requests quickly with 429 or 503 plus Retry-After rather than accepting everything and timing out, since a queue of doomed requests is worse than a fast rejection; priority — shed low-value traffic first (background sync, analytics, non-critical endpoints) and protect checkout and login; bounded queues everywhere so backlogs cannot grow without limit; circuit breakers and bulkheads so a failing dependency cannot consume all capacity; and autoscaling with the understanding that it takes minutes, so shedding covers the gap. The principle to state: a system that degrades predictably under overload is far more valuable than one that is slightly faster and collapses.

  • Why it matters — Graceful degradation under overload is a defining senior/SRE concern.

  • Follow-ups — What do you shed first and how do you decide? Why is rejecting better than queueing? How much headroom do you keep and why?

  • Senior signal — Explicit load shedding with prioritisation, and headroom justified by failure scenarios.

45.20 Observability and SRE

Q239. Metrics, logs and traces — what is each for?

  • Expected answer — Metrics are cheap, aggregated numeric time series: they tell you that something is wrong and are what you alert on, because they are low cardinality, cheap to store for a long time and fast to query. Logs are discrete events with detail: they tell you what happened for a specific request, and they are where you look once metrics point you somewhere. Traces connect the spans of a single request across services: they tell you where the time went and which hop failed, which is the fastest path from "the API is slow" to a specific dependency. The three are complementary and the workflow between them is what matters: an alert fires on a metric, you open the dashboard to see the scope, you jump to exemplar traces for slow or failing requests, and then to the logs for that trace id. That linkage — trace id in every log line, exemplars linked from metrics — is what turns three tools into one investigation, and its absence is why teams with all three still take an hour to diagnose. Add profiles as a fourth signal when you can, since continuous profiling answers "which code" the way tracing answers "which service".

  • Why it matters — Owning production means being able to answer questions quickly, not having tools installed.

  • Follow-ups — What links your logs to your traces? Why not alert on logs? What would you add first to a service with none of these?

  • Senior signal — Describes the investigation workflow and the linkage between signals, not a list of tools.

Q240. What does good logging look like in a Node service?

  • Expected answer — Structured JSON to stdout, one object per line, with the platform handling collection — never log files inside a container, and never console.log in production code. Every line carries a consistent set of fields: timestamp, level, service, version, environment, trace_id/span_id, request_id, user_id or tenant_id where applicable, and the message plus structured context ({ orderId, durationMs, statusCode }) rather than an interpolated sentence you cannot query. Levels used with discipline: error for things a human must act on, warn for recoverable anomalies, info for business-significant events (order created, payment captured), debug off in production but enablable per-request or per-service without a redeploy. Correlation is the essential part: generate or accept a request id at the edge, propagate it with AsyncLocalStorage so every log line and every downstream call carries it, and return it to clients in the error body so a support ticket maps to logs instantly. And redact: never log tokens, passwords, card numbers, full request bodies with PII, or connection strings — with a redaction list in the logger, not a rule in a wiki. Finally, treat volume as a cost: sample high-frequency success logs, keep errors unsampled.

  • Why it matters — Logging is the tool used most during an incident and the one most often useless.

  • Follow-ups — How does a log line get a trace id in NestJS? What would you sample and what never? How do you enable debug logging for one customer?

  • Senior signal — AsyncLocalStorage correlation, structured context over interpolated strings, and redaction as code.

Q241. Explain distributed tracing and how you would instrument a NestJS service.

  • Expected answer — A trace is a tree of spans, each with a start time, duration, attributes and a parent; the root span is created at the entry point and context is propagated to downstream calls through headers (W3C traceparent). With OpenTelemetry, the Node SDK auto-instruments HTTP, pg, Redis, and common libraries, so you get a useful trace with very little code; you then add manual spans around meaningful business operations and attach attributes (order.id, tenant.id, payment.provider) so traces are searchable by things you care about. Propagation is the part that breaks: an async boundary that loses context — a queue message, a setTimeout, a worker thread — needs the trace context carried explicitly in the message envelope and re-attached in the consumer, or your trace stops at the producer. Sampling is the cost control: head-based sampling at 1–10% is cheap but misses rare slow requests; tail-based sampling decides after the fact and can keep all errors and all slow traces, which is what you actually want, at the cost of running a collector that buffers. Also emit exemplars linking metrics to traces, and always sample errors at 100%.

  • Why it matters — Tracing is the highest-leverage observability investment in a multi-service system.

  • Follow-ups — How do you propagate context through a Kafka message? What sampling strategy do you use and why? What attributes make traces searchable?

  • Senior signal — Async-boundary context propagation and tail-based sampling with errors always kept.

Q242. Which metrics do you export for a service?

  • Expected answer — Use RED for request-driven services: Rate (requests per second), Errors (failed requests, split by 4xx and 5xx because they mean different things), Duration (a latency histogram), each labelled by route and method. Use USE for resources: Utilisation, Saturation, Errors — for a Node service that means CPU, memory and heap, event loop lag, database pool in-use and waiting counts, HTTP agent socket counts, and per-dependency call rate and latency. Then the business and pipeline metrics that actually tell you the system is doing its job: orders created per minute, payment success ratio, queue depth and consumer lag, job success and failure counts, and the age of the oldest unprocessed item. That last category is what catches the failures no infrastructure metric sees — every pod healthy, CPU fine, and zero orders for twenty minutes because a feature flag or an upstream broke. Keep labels low-cardinality (route templates like /orders/:id, never raw URLs with ids), export from every instance and aggregate centrally, and make sure the histogram buckets match your SLO thresholds so you can compute the SLI directly.

  • Why it matters — The right metric set determines whether you detect incidents or hear about them from customers.

  • Follow-ups — What business metric would have caught your last incident? Why split 4xx from 5xx? How do you choose histogram buckets?

  • Senior signal — Insists on business-level metrics and matches histogram buckets to the SLO.

Q243. Why do people compute percentiles wrong?

  • Expected answer — Two classic mistakes. First, averaging percentiles: taking p99 from each of 20 pods and averaging them gives a number with no statistical meaning; the correct approach is to export a histogram (bucketed counts) from each instance, sum the buckets centrally, and compute the quantile from the merged histogram — which is what Prometheus histogram_quantile over rate(..._bucket[5m]) does. Summaries, by contrast, compute quantiles client-side and therefore cannot be aggregated across instances, which is the main reason to prefer histograms in a distributed system. Second, bucket resolution: a histogram can only give you an answer within its bucket boundaries, so if your buckets jump from 1 s to 10 s, a p99 in that range is a linear interpolation and essentially a guess — choose buckets around your SLO thresholds (for a 300 ms target, have boundaries at 100, 250, 300, 500, 1000 ms). Related traps: computing a percentile over too short a window on low-traffic endpoints, where a handful of requests makes p99 meaningless; and forgetting that p99 over 5 minutes at 10 requests per second is the 30th-slowest request, so it moves a lot.

  • Why it matters — Wrong percentile math silently invalidates dashboards and SLOs.

  • Follow-ups — Histogram or summary, and why? Where would you put buckets for a 200 ms SLO? What is wrong with p99 on a low-traffic endpoint?

  • Senior signal — Histograms for aggregatability plus bucket placement tied to the SLO — details that only come from building this.

Q244. What is metric cardinality and why does it matter?

  • Expected answer — Cardinality is the number of distinct label-value combinations, and each combination is a separate time series to store, index and query. Adding a user_id label to a metric with a million users creates a million series; adding a raw URL with ids does the same; combining endpoint x status x region x customer multiplies. The consequences are practical and expensive: the metrics backend's memory grows with active series, queries slow down, ingestion costs rise steeply, and in the worst case a single bad deploy that adds a high-cardinality label takes down the monitoring system — which is especially painful because it happens exactly when you need it. Rules: labels must be bounded and enumerable (route template, method, status class, service, environment, version); anything unbounded (ids, emails, full URLs, error messages, timestamps) belongs in logs or traces, not in metric labels. If you need per-customer visibility, either restrict it to your largest few tenants with an explicit allow-list, or answer that question with traces and logs. Set limits and alerts on series count per job so you find out before the bill or the outage.

  • Why it matters — Cardinality explosions are a common self-inflicted observability outage.

  • Follow-ups — How would you get per-tenant latency without exploding cardinality? What limits would you configure? What is the cost model of your metrics backend?

  • Senior signal — Offers a concrete alternative for high-cardinality questions rather than just saying "do not do it".

Q245. Define SLI, SLO and error budget, and how you would set them.

  • Expected answer — An SLI is a measured indicator of user-visible behaviour — for example the proportion of requests to the checkout API that succeed in under 300 ms, measured at the load balancer. An SLO is the target for that indicator over a window, such as 99.9% over 28 days. The error budget is the allowed shortfall: 99.9% over 28 days is about 40 minutes of full unavailability, or an equivalent amount of partial degradation. Setting them: start from what users actually feel — availability and latency of the critical journeys, not CPU — pick a small number (two or three per service), measure current performance for a few weeks before committing to a number, and choose a target you can actually meet, because an SLO nobody meets is ignored and an SLO always met is too loose to inform decisions. The point is the decision rule it creates: budget remaining means you can take deployment risk and ship features; budget exhausted means you stop feature work and spend on reliability. That makes reliability a negotiated, visible trade-off with the business rather than an argument between engineering and product. Alert on burn rate (a fast burn over an hour for pages, a slow burn over days for tickets), not on every individual error.

  • Why it matters — SLOs are how senior engineers make reliability a decision instead of a debate.

  • Follow-ups — What does 99.9% mean in minutes? What happens when the budget is exhausted? Why alert on burn rate rather than error count?

  • Senior signal — Frames the error budget as a decision rule and knows multi-window burn-rate alerting.

Q246. How do you design alerts people will not ignore?

  • Expected answer — Alert on symptoms, not causes: page on "checkout error rate above threshold" or "SLO burn rate is high", not on "CPU above 80%", because high CPU may be harmless while a silent failure at low CPU is an outage. Every page must be actionable and urgent — if the responder's correct action is "acknowledge and look at it tomorrow", it is a ticket, not a page. Include context in the alert itself: what is broken, which service and environment, the current and threshold values, a link to the dashboard and the runbook, and recent deploys. Use multi-window burn-rate alerting so a brief blip does not page and a slow steady burn still does. Ruthlessly delete or fix alerts that fire repeatedly without action, because alert fatigue is the real failure mode — an on-call engineer receiving 30 pages a week stops reading them, and the one that mattered is lost. Track pages per on-call shift as a metric the team owns and treat a rising number as a defect. Also alert on absence: no orders in 15 minutes, a nightly job that did not report success, a queue that stopped being consumed — silent failures produce no errors at all.

  • Why it matters — Alert quality determines whether on-call is sustainable and whether incidents are caught.

  • Follow-ups — Give me an example of a cause-based alert you would delete. How do you detect a silent failure? What is an acceptable number of pages per week?

  • Senior signal — Symptom-based alerting, alerting on absence, and treating alert volume as a tracked defect.

Q247. What belongs on a service dashboard?

  • Expected answer — One dashboard that answers "is this service healthy and, if not, where is the problem?" in about thirty seconds, arranged top to bottom from user-visible to internal. Top row: SLO status and error budget remaining, request rate, error rate split by class, and latency percentiles — the RED signals. Second row: dependencies — database query latency and connection pool usage, cache hit ratio, external API latency and error rate, queue depth and consumer lag. Third row: runtime and resources — CPU, memory and heap, event loop lag, GC time, pod count and restarts. Overlay deploy and config-change annotations on every graph, because "what changed" is the first question in every incident and a vertical line answers it instantly. Keep it to one screen; a dashboard with 60 panels is a dashboard nobody reads. Have a second, deeper dashboard for investigation, and keep the top-level one stable so people build muscle memory. The test I apply: hand it to someone who has never seen the service and ask them to tell you whether it is healthy — if they cannot, it is decoration.

  • Why it matters — Dashboards are used under stress; design for that.

  • Follow-ups — What is missing from most dashboards you have seen? Why annotate deploys? How do you keep dashboards from rotting?

  • Senior signal — Deploy annotations, one-screen discipline, and the "can a stranger read it" test.

Q248. Walk me through how you run an incident.

  • Expected answer — Declare it early — under-declaring costs far more than over-declaring. Assign roles even in a small team: an incident commander who coordinates and decides (and does not debug), one or two people investigating, and a communications role posting updates on a cadence, say every 15–30 minutes, to a single channel so stakeholders stop interrupting the responders. Mitigate before diagnosing: roll back the recent deploy, disable the feature flag, scale up, shed load, fail over — restoring service is the goal, and root cause can wait. Form explicit hypotheses and test them one at a time rather than several people changing things simultaneously; record every action with a timestamp in the channel, which becomes the timeline for the postmortem and prevents "did anyone already restart that?". Keep a bias toward reversible actions, and if a change does not help, revert it before trying the next. When the symptom is resolved, say so explicitly, keep monitoring for a defined period, and only then stand down. Then schedule the postmortem while it is fresh. The two most common failures are not declaring soon enough and debugging in a group with no coordination.

  • Why it matters — Incident handling is a directly observable senior behaviour.

  • Follow-ups — Who makes the call to roll back? What do you tell stakeholders at 20 minutes with no diagnosis? How do you avoid three people changing things at once?

  • Senior signal — Mitigate-first, explicit roles, and a written timeline as you go.

Q249. What makes a good postmortem?

  • Expected answer — Blameless, factual and actionable. Blameless means the analysis targets the system, not the person: "the deploy pipeline allowed a migration with no lock timeout to reach production" rather than "X ran a bad migration" — because in a blaming culture people hide information and you lose the ability to learn. Contents: a plain-language summary, customer impact quantified (how many users, how long, what they experienced, revenue where relevant), a detailed timeline from first symptom to resolution including detection and mitigation times, contributing factors (plural — real incidents have several, and "human error" is never a root cause but a prompt to ask why the system permitted it), what went well, and action items. The action items are where most postmortems fail: each needs an owner, a due date and a ticket, they should be prioritised by whether they prevent, detect faster, or mitigate faster, and someone must track completion — a document full of unowned "we should" items is theatre. Two metrics worth tracking across incidents: time to detect and time to mitigate, since improving detection often has a bigger effect than preventing the specific cause, which rarely recurs identically.

  • Why it matters — Whether an organisation learns from failure is largely decided by this document.

  • Follow-ups — What do you do when the action items are never completed? How do you handle a postmortem where someone clearly made a mistake? What do you measure across incidents?

  • Senior signal — Multiple contributing factors, owned and tracked actions, and detect/mitigate time as improvement targets.

Q250. What does "production ready" mean to you?

  • Expected answer — A checklist I would actually apply before a service takes real traffic. Correctness and safety: input validation, authorization on every endpoint including object-level checks, idempotency on anything that creates or charges, database constraints for the real invariants. Resilience: timeouts on every outbound call, bounded retries with jitter, circuit breakers on critical dependencies, graceful shutdown with readiness-first draining, and known behaviour when each dependency is down. Operability: structured logs with correlation ids, RED metrics plus business metrics, tracing, a dashboard, symptom-based alerts tied to an SLO, and a runbook for each alert. Deployability: automated CI with tests, reversible migrations using expand-and-contract, a rolling deploy, and a rollback that has been executed at least once rather than assumed. Capacity and cost: a load test establishing per-instance capacity, resource requests and limits set from measurements, autoscaling configured, and a cost estimate. Security: no secrets in the image or repository, least-privilege credentials, dependency scanning, TLS everywhere. Data: backups with a tested restore and a retention policy. Nothing on that list is exotic, and shipping without it is how a team ends up owning a service they cannot operate.

  • Why it matters — It is the single best summary of whether someone has actually run systems in production.

  • Follow-ups — Which item is most often missing in your experience? What would you cut for an internal tool? How do you enforce this without it becoming bureaucracy?

  • Senior signal — Answers as a concrete checklist with scars behind each item, and can say which parts are negotiable for which risk level.

45.21 Behavioural and leadership

These ten are not memorisation questions. A rehearsed script is obvious within two sentences, and interviewers probe until they find the real story. What follows is the structure to fill with your own material, plus what a strong answer contains. Prepare six or seven real stories with numbers, and map them onto these prompts rather than inventing one answer per question.

The default frame is STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result), with one senior amendment: end with Reflection — what you learned and what you would do differently. Keep the situation to two sentences, spend most of the time on your actions and reasoning, and always land a measurable result.

Q251. Tell me about the hardest production incident you have handled.

  • Expected answer — Structure: what the system was and its scale (one sentence with numbers), what the symptom was and how it was detected, the impact in user and business terms, what you did to mitigate and in what order, how you found the cause, and what changed afterwards. Good looks like: a clear timeline with times attached; mitigation described before diagnosis, showing you restore service first; specific evidence used at each step ("the p99 doubled but the database was idle, so I looked at pool saturation"); honesty about the wrong turns and how long they cost; and a concrete prevention outcome — an alert added, a limit set, a design changed — with evidence it worked. Weak looks like: a vague story with no numbers, a hero narrative where you alone fixed it, blaming another team, or ending at the fix with no follow-through.

  • Why it matters — It is the closest proxy for on-call competence and for how you behave under pressure.

  • Follow-ups — What would have caught it earlier? What did you do wrong during the incident? What happened to the action items?

  • Senior signal — Mitigate-before-diagnose, quantified impact, credit shared with the team, and a prevention step that actually shipped.

Q252. Tell me about a technical decision you later reversed.

  • Expected answer — Structure: the original decision and the reasoning that made it sensible at the time, what evidence later showed it was wrong, the cost of the reversal, how you made the call, and what you changed about how you decide. Good looks like: taking ownership without self-flagellation; showing the original decision was defensible given what was known, which is far more credible than "I was stupid"; naming the specific signal that triggered the reversal (an operational cost, a latency number, a hiring problem); describing how you migrated back safely rather than just declaring the change; and extracting a transferable lesson, typically about reversibility — "I now ask which decisions are one-way doors and only those get a long design review". Weak looks like: claiming never to have reversed anything, or a trivial example like a library choice with no consequences.

  • Why it matters — It tests intellectual honesty and whether you learn from evidence rather than defending positions.

  • Follow-ups — How long did you wait before reversing, and was that too long? Who disagreed with the reversal? What would you have needed to know earlier?

  • Senior signal — Distinguishes reversible from irreversible decisions and adjusts the process, not just the outcome.

Q253. Describe a time you disagreed with your manager or tech lead.

  • Expected answer — Structure: the decision, why you disagreed and what evidence you had, how you raised it, what happened, and how you behaved afterwards. Good looks like: disagreeing on substance with data rather than preference; raising it privately and directly first; genuinely engaging with their reasoning, including constraints you may not have seen (budget, timeline, politics, a commitment already made); proposing an alternative rather than only objecting; and — critically — committing fully once the decision was made, even when it went against you, while agreeing on what evidence would prompt a revisit. That "disagree and commit, with a trigger to re-open" behaviour is exactly what senior means here. Weak looks like: a story where you were right and everyone else was foolish, or one where you quietly complied and then said "I told you so", or one where you escalated immediately without a direct conversation.

  • Why it matters — Senior engineers must be able to push back without being corrosive.

  • Follow-ups — What if you had been the one who was wrong? When would you escalate above your manager? How did the relationship look afterwards?

  • Senior signal — Data-driven disagreement, real engagement with constraints, and committing cleanly with a defined revisit trigger.

Q254. How do you mentor engineers?

  • Expected answer — Structure: a specific person, where they were and where they needed to be, what you actually did over what period, and the measurable outcome. Good looks like: concrete mechanisms rather than platitudes — pairing on a real problem, giving a stretch task with a safety net, reviewing code with explanations of why instead of prescriptions, letting them own a design document and asking questions rather than rewriting it, deliberately not taking over during their first incident. It should include how you adapted to the individual (someone lacking confidence needs different support from someone lacking depth), how you gave difficult feedback, and an outcome you can point to: they led a project, they were promoted, they now own an area. Good answers also mention what you learned from mentoring and where you failed at it. Weak looks like: "I answer questions in the team channel", or claiming credit for someone else's growth.

  • Why it matters — At senior level your impact through others is a large part of the job.

  • Follow-ups — Tell me about someone you could not help. How do you give feedback that is hard to hear? How do you avoid becoming the bottleneck?

  • Senior signal — Resists solving the problem for them, adapts the approach per person, and can name a failure as well as a success.

Q255. Tell me about pushing back on scope or a deadline.

  • Expected answer — Structure: what was asked, why it was not achievable as stated, how you presented that, what alternative you offered, and the outcome. Good looks like: pushing back with options rather than a refusal — "we can ship the full scope by March, or this reduced scope by January with these three things deferred, or the full scope by January with two more engineers; here is what I recommend and why"; making the trade-off visible in the stakeholder's terms (revenue, risk, customer commitments) rather than in engineering terms; being specific about what "done" means for each option, including operational readiness, not just feature completion; and flagging the risk early rather than at the deadline. It should also show you took the business constraint seriously rather than treating the request as unreasonable by default. Weak looks like: "I told them it was impossible", padding estimates silently, or agreeing and then missing the date.

  • Why it matters — Scope negotiation is a core senior skill and a common failure point.

  • Follow-ups — What if they said no to all your options? How early did you raise it? What did you cut and how did you decide?

  • Senior signal — Offers a menu with honest trade-offs in business language, and raises risk early rather than at the deadline.

Q256. How do you estimate work?

  • Expected answer — Structure: your method, an example where it worked, an example where it did not, and what you changed. Good looks like: decomposing until the pieces are small enough to reason about, because large estimates are guesses; estimating in ranges or confidence levels rather than single numbers ("two to three weeks, and I will know by Thursday which end after I have spiked the migration"); explicitly listing unknowns and buying information cheaply with a timeboxed spike; including the parts people forget — code review, testing, migration, deployment, monitoring, documentation and the inevitable interruptions, which is why a "three-day" task takes two weeks; using historical data from similar work instead of optimism; and re-forecasting publicly as you learn rather than defending the original number. It should also cover communicating uncertainty to non-engineers without either false precision or uselessly wide ranges. Weak looks like: "I add 50% buffer", or refusing to estimate at all.

  • Why it matters — Estimation accuracy affects everyone's planning, and how you handle uncertainty is the real signal.

  • Follow-ups — What is your biggest estimation miss and why? How do you estimate something you have never done? How do you handle pressure to lower an estimate?

  • Senior signal — Ranges with an explicit information-gathering plan, re-forecasting in public, and counting the non-coding work.

Q257. How do you deal with technical debt?

  • Expected answer — Structure: how you identify and categorise it, how you get time for it, a specific example with the before-and-after numbers, and how you prevent it accumulating. Good looks like: distinguishing deliberate, well-understood debt taken for speed (fine, if tracked with a repayment plan) from accidental debt caused by ignorance or drift (a different problem needing learning or standards); prioritising by pain, not by aesthetics — debt that slows delivery, causes incidents or blocks a roadmap item is worth fixing, while ugly-but-stable code that nobody touches is not; making the cost visible in business language ("this module causes about one incident a month and doubles the time for any change in this area") so the trade-off is a business decision rather than an engineering plea; and paying it down incrementally alongside feature work — the boy-scout rule, strangler-fig migrations, and a standing allocation — rather than requesting a three-month rewrite, which almost never gets approved and rarely finishes when it does. Weak looks like: "we need a rewrite", or complaining about debt without ever quantifying its cost.

  • Why it matters — Debt management is where engineering judgement meets stakeholder communication.

  • Follow-ups — When is a rewrite the right answer? How do you say no to a refactor someone wants? What debt are you deliberately carrying right now?

  • Senior signal — Quantifies debt in delivery and incident terms and pays it down incrementally rather than demanding a rewrite.

Q258. Tell me about a conflict with another team.

  • Expected answer — Structure: the situation and each side's actual interest, what you did to resolve it, the outcome, and how the relationship ended up. Good looks like: genuine curiosity about the other team's constraints and incentives before assuming bad faith — most cross-team conflict is two teams optimising for different, individually-reasonable goals; moving the conversation from positions ("you must build this") to interests ("we need this latency by Q3; what options do you have?"); getting the disagreement into a shared written document with data so it stops being a personality clash; escalating with both parties present and framed as "we need a decision" rather than complaining upward about someone; and accepting an outcome that is not what you wanted while keeping the working relationship, since you will need them next quarter. Weak looks like: a story where the other team was simply unreasonable, or one resolved by going over their heads.

  • Why it matters — Most senior work crosses team boundaries, and the failure mode is expensive.

  • Follow-ups — What was their side of the story? When do you escalate, and how? What would you do differently?

  • Senior signal — Can articulate the other team's position fairly, and escalates transparently rather than politically.

Q259. Tell me about a time you said no.

  • Expected answer — Structure: what was asked, why you declined, how you communicated it, what you offered instead, and the outcome. Good looks like: saying no to the thing, not the person, with a reason grounded in impact — "adding this would put the checkout path behind an unproven dependency; here is the risk and here are two safer ways to get the same outcome"; being specific about what you would have to stop doing if you said yes, which turns a refusal into a prioritisation conversation; saying it early and directly rather than slow-rolling; and being willing to be overruled gracefully with the risk documented. Strong examples include refusing to ship something unsafe (no rollback path, no authorization on a new endpoint, a migration that would lock a large table during peak), refusing scope that would break a commitment already made, and refusing to add a technology the team cannot operate. Weak looks like: saying no as a reflex, or saying yes to everything and then failing quietly.

  • Why it matters — The ability to decline well is what stops a senior engineer from becoming a bottleneck or a rubber stamp.

  • Follow-ups — What happened when you were overruled? How do you say no to your own manager? What do you always say yes to?

  • Senior signal — Turns "no" into a prioritisation and risk conversation, and documents the risk when overruled.

Q260. Tell me about a significant failure and what you learned.

  • Expected answer — Structure: what you were responsible for, what went wrong, your specific contribution to it, the impact, and the durable change you made. Good looks like: choosing a genuinely significant failure rather than a safe one — a project that did not deliver, a design that had to be replaced, an outage you caused, a hire or a delegation that went badly; owning your part precisely without either excusing it or performing guilt; explaining the decision process that led there, since that is what generalises; and describing a specific behaviour change with evidence it stuck, for example "I now write a one-page design with explicit assumptions and get two reviewers before starting anything that will take more than two weeks, and I have done that for the last four projects". The best answers also include what the organisation changed, not only what you changed personally. Weak looks like: a disguised strength ("I care too much"), a failure that was really someone else's, or a lesson with no evidence it changed anything.

  • Why it matters — It is the clearest test of self-awareness, and self-awareness predicts growth.

  • Follow-ups — What did you do in the first 24 hours after realising? Who else was affected and how did you handle that? Has the lesson been tested since?

  • Senior signal — Picks a real failure, owns a precise share of it, and can point to a changed behaviour that has been tested.

45.22 Three mock interview loops

Run these against a partner, out loud, on a timer. Reading answers silently builds recognition, not recall — and interviews test recall under mild stress. Record yourself once; you will hear the filler words and the missing numbers immediately.

Score each dimension 1 to 4: 1 = missing or wrong, 2 = mid-level (correct but no trade-offs or failure modes), 3 = senior (trade-offs, failure modes, numbers), 4 = strong senior (production scars, unprompted risks, clean communication). A hire signal at senior level is an average of 3 or above with no 1s on a core dimension.

45.22.1 Loop A — 45-minute coding and Node deep dive

Timing

Minutes Activity
0-3 Warm-up: what have you built with Node, and at what scale?
3-15 Coding: implement an in-memory rate limiter (token bucket) with a clean interface and tests in mind
15-25 Extend it: make it correct across 40 pods; discuss Redis, Lua atomicity, failure modes
25-38 Node runtime deep dive (questions below)
38-43 Debugging scenario
43-45 Candidate questions

The exact questions to run

  1. Implement class TokenBucket { constructor(capacity, refillPerSec); tryConsume(n = 1): boolean } using a monotonic clock, and say why you chose lazy refill over a timer. (Q114, Q141)
  2. Now make it correct across 40 pods. Write the Redis Lua sketch and explain the atomicity requirement. (Q114, Q164)
  3. What happens if Redis is down — fail open or closed, and does the answer differ by endpoint? (Q105)
  4. Predict the output of the ordering snippet in Q14 and explain each line.
  5. Where does fs.readFile complete versus an HTTP response, and what is the libuv thread pool? (Q13, Q15)
  6. This endpoint's p99 is 900 ms while the query takes 4 ms. Name five possible causes. (Q16, Q229, Q232)
  7. Node is single-threaded — why did we still get duplicate orders? (Q27)
  8. Walk me through a graceful shutdown in Kubernetes, in order. (Q22, Q199)
  9. Debugging: memory grows 40 MB per hour and the pod is OOMKilled every 14 hours. What do you do, in order? (Q19, Q20)

Rubric

Dimension 1 2 3 4
Code quality Does not compile mentally; no types Works; unclear naming; no edge cases Typed, small, testable; handles clock and boundary cases Also discusses testability and a concurrency test
Event loop model Guesses ordering Recites phases Explains microtask draining and poll blocking Predicts output correctly and explains the non-determinism
Failure thinking None offered Only when prompted Volunteers timeout, duplicate, partial failure Names the specific metric that would detect each
Debugging method "Add logs" Names a tool Ordered hypothesis-driven method with evidence Adds the regression guard afterwards
Communication Silent or rambling Answers only what is asked Narrates reasoning, checks assumptions Compresses well and adapts to the interviewer's level

45.22.2 Loop B — 45-minute system design

Prompt: "Design a notification service for a food-delivery product: push, SMS and email, 20 million daily active users, driven by order lifecycle events."

Timing

Minutes Activity What the interviewer is scoring
0-5 Requirements and scope; what is explicitly out Does the candidate ask before designing?
5-10 Capacity math: volume, peak, storage, provider limits Are there numbers, and is peak treated separately?
10-16 API and data model; the events consumed Is the data model concrete with keys and indexes?
16-28 High-level design: ingestion, dedup, preferences, scheduling, per-channel senders Are queue boundaries and datastores justified?
28-38 Deep dive: deduplication, coalescing, per-user rate limits, provider throttling Depth on one hard problem
38-43 Failure modes, monitoring, what changes at 10x Operational thinking
43-45 Trade-offs the candidate would revisit Self-critique

The exact questions to run

  1. What are the functional requirements, and what are you deliberately not building in v1? (Q111)
  2. Do the capacity math including a broadcast campaign of 5 million in 10 minutes. (Q112)
  3. Show me the tables. What is the primary key of the notification record and why? (Q97, Q118)
  4. A user must never receive the same notification twice. How? (Q115, Q132)
  5. Five "order updated" events arrive in 60 seconds. What does the user see? (Q115)
  6. The SMS provider rate-limits you to 100 per second. What happens to the other 8,200? (Q112, Q238)
  7. Your consumer is 40 minutes behind and retention is 24 hours. What do you do? (Q150, Q155)
  8. Where is the transactional boundary between "order paid" and "notification queued"? (Q134)
  9. What are your SLIs, and what would page you at 3 a.m.? (Q245, Q246)
  10. What breaks first at 10x, and what would you change? (Q128)

Rubric

Dimension 1 2 3 4
Scoping Starts drawing immediately Asks a few questions Confirms assumptions and states non-goals Negotiates requirements and challenges one
Capacity math None Average only Peak, storage, growth, per-year cost Identifies the binding constraint (provider limits)
Data model Vague boxes Tables listed Keys, indexes, access patterns, retention Partitioning and archival designed in
Failure design None Mentions retries Idempotency, DLQ, backpressure, degraded modes Names detection for each failure
Trade-offs Absolutes One option per decision Two or three options with a justified choice Explains what would change the choice
Time management Runs out at 20 min Uneven Reaches deep dive and failure modes Drives the clock deliberately

45.22.3 Loop C — 45-minute PostgreSQL deep dive

Timing

Minutes Activity
0-5 Scale context: largest table, RPS, instance size you have operated
5-15 Query and index design against a given schema
15-25 Read and fix an EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan
25-35 Concurrency and transactions
35-43 Operations: vacuum, migrations, connections, replication
43-45 Candidate questions

The exact questions to run

  1. Given orders(id, tenant_id, status, created_at, total_minor) at 400 million rows, design the index for WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND status = 'pending' AND created_at > $2 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Justify the column order. (Q72)
  2. The same endpoint uses OFFSET 200000. Rewrite it and say what you lose. (Q50)
  3. Here is a plan with rows=1 estimated and rows=480000 actual on a nested loop. What happened and what do you do? (Q70, Q81)
  4. Two requests both decrement stock to 0 and we oversold. Give me three fixes and pick one. (Q66, Q119)
  5. Explain write skew and give me a constraint-based fix. (Q67)
  6. We need to add a NOT NULL column with a default to that 400-million-row table with zero downtime. Walk me through it. (Q69, Q76)
  7. Autovacuum has not run on this table for six days and queries are getting slower. Why, and what do you check? (Q61, Q62)
  8. We have 30 pods with a pool of 20 each and max_connections = 200. What happens, and what do you change? (Q77, Q90)
  9. Reads moved to a replica and users report their new order is missing. Explain and fix. (Q78, Q143)
  10. What timeouts do you set on the application database user, and why three different ones? (Q82)

Rubric

Dimension 1 2 3 4
Index design Guesses columns Right columns, wrong order Equality-then-range with a reason; verifies with EXPLAIN Considers covering, partial, and write cost
Plan reading Cannot read it Reads total time only Compares estimated versus actual, uses BUFFERS and loops Diagnoses statistics and proposes extended stats
Concurrency Application-level locks Knows FOR UPDATE Chooses per contention profile; names isolation and retries Uses constraints and guarded updates; discusses hot-row throughput
Operations No exposure Knows the terms Vacuum, CONCURRENTLY, lock_timeout, pooling with numbers Has run these under load and has scars
Trade-offs Absolutes One answer States costs of each choice Says when Postgres is the wrong tool

Senior Checklist — Part 45

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can structure any answer as context, options, decision, consequences
  • I can say "I don't know" and describe exactly how I would find out
  • I have three prepared stories with real numbers: a performance win, an incident, and a decision I reversed
  • I can run a 45-minute system design to a deep dive without running out of time
  • I can predict Node event-loop output and explain the non-determinism
  • I can read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and name the fix
  • I can design idempotency for a payment endpoint from memory
  • I can state CAP and PACELC correctly and apply them per operation
  • I can define SLI, SLO and error budget and say what happens when the budget is gone
  • I attach a number to every claim I make in an interview

Part 45 — Key Takeaways

  • Senior interviews assess trade-off reasoning, failure thinking, ownership and communication — not recall. Depth without judgement reads as mid-level.
  • Structure every substantial answer as context, options, decision, consequences. Four sentences in that shape beat four minutes of unstructured detail.
  • Attach a number to every claim: rows, RPS, milliseconds, gigabytes, rupees. Numbers are the difference between "we scaled it" and "we took p99 from 900 ms to 80 ms at 4,000 RPS".
  • Volunteer failure modes before you are asked. Run the mantra under every answer: can it timeout, fail, become slow, duplicate, return a wrong response, partially succeed?
  • "I don't know" plus a concrete plan to find out scores higher than a confident guess. Bluffing is detected instantly because bluffs have no numbers and no failure modes.
  • Absolutes are the most reliable red flag. Name the context where the opposite choice is correct, then choose.
  • The database section is where senior candidates separate: MVCC, vacuum, EXPLAIN, locking, index design and connection limits are the highest-leverage knowledge you can carry.
  • Exactly-once delivery does not exist. At-least-once plus idempotent effects is the achievable design, and idempotency is the single most reusable technique in distributed backends.
  • In system design, scope down before you scale up. Saying what you will not build in v1 is a stronger signal than another box on the diagram.
  • Behavioural rounds are not a formality at senior level. Prepare real stories with impact, your specific contribution, and evidence that the lesson stuck.
  • Practise out loud, on a timer, with a partner. Recognition is not recall, and interviews test recall under mild stress.
  • The best preparation is operating a system and paying attention while you do it. Every scar in this Part came from an incident someone had to explain the next morning.

Part 46 — Practical Projects: From Auth Service to Microservices Platform

46.0 How to use these projects

Reading about backpressure, saga compensation and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED does not make you senior. Shipping something that keeps working at 3 a.m. does. This part gives you six projects that, built in order, take you from a single well-made service to a distributed platform you actually have to operate. Each one is a real system, not a tutorial: it has numbers, a schema, failure modes and a definition of done.

Build them in order. This is not a menu. Project 1 (authentication) teaches token state, expiry, replay and rate limiting — which Project 2 assumes when it puts a cart behind a logged-in user. Project 2 teaches the modular monolith, the outbox and inventory reservations — which Project 4 assumes when it runs a saga across those modules. Project 4 teaches idempotency keys, ledgers and webhooks — which Project 6 assumes when it splits them across the network. Project 5 (your own job processor) teaches you what BullMQ and Kafka are doing for you, so that in Project 6 you can argue about them instead of trusting them. If you skip ahead, you will build the microservices platform on top of concepts you never internalised, and you will produce exactly the thing this book keeps warning you about: distribution without competence.

The definition of done matters more than the feature list. Every project ends with a ### Definition of done checklist. That checklist is the assignment. The feature list is only the excuse to build something worth operating. A cart that works but has no metric for "reservation expired without an order" is not done. A payment flow that works but cannot survive a duplicated webhook is not done. Nobody in an interview will ask whether you implemented wishlists. Several will ask what happens when the payment provider sends the same charge.succeeded twice, or what your p99 was and how you knew.

Review your own work with the questions from Part 43. When you think a project is finished, wait two days, then read your own pull request as if a stranger wrote it, using the review questions from Part 43. Ask them out loud: where is the transaction boundary, what happens on retry, what is unbounded, which index serves this query, what is the blast radius if this throws. You will find things. Write the findings down before you fix them — the list of what you missed is a better map of your weaknesses than any course syllabus.

Keep an incident diary. One markdown file per project, appended to every time something surprises you. Format: what you saw, what you thought it was, what it actually was, how you found out, what you changed. "Login latency jumped to 900 ms after I raised argon2 memory to 64 MiB; the container had a 512 MiB limit and four workers, so it OOMKilled under load; dropped to 19 MiB per OWASP and pinned parallelism to 1." Six months of that file is more valuable than six months of tutorials, and it is what you will actually talk about in senior interviews, because it is evidence rather than vocabulary.

Deploy each one somewhere real. Not docker compose up on your laptop — somewhere with a public hostname, TLS, a real domain, a health check, a rollout and a rollback. A three-node k3s cluster on the cheapest VMs you can rent, or a managed Kubernetes cluster you tear down at night, or even a single VM with Docker Compose behind Caddy for the first two projects. The point is that you meet certificate expiry, DNS propagation, image pull failures, a readiness probe you got wrong, and the moment when a migration locks a table on a machine you cannot attach a debugger to. Local development hides every operational lesson.

Suggested time, working evenings. Assume six to eight hours a week.

Project Evenings Calendar time The bar
1. Authentication 12 to 16 3 to 4 weeks Refresh rotation with reuse detection provably works
2. E-commerce backend 20 to 28 6 to 8 weeks Keyset pagination and inventory reservations under concurrency
3. Notification system 14 to 20 4 to 5 weeks A poisoned message lands in the DLQ and you replay it
4. Payment and orders 20 to 28 6 to 8 weeks The ledger balances after a partial refund and a duplicate webhook
5. Job processing 16 to 24 5 to 6 weeks A worker is killed mid-job and another takes over the lease
6. Microservices platform 30 to 40 8 to 12 weeks One trace spans six services and you can explain every span

That is roughly nine months of evenings. Do not rush it, and do not build all six half-way. One finished project with a real definition of done beats six repositories with a README and a TODO.

46.1 Project 1 — Production-grade authentication system

46.1.1 Goal and what you will learn

You will build an authentication service that a real product could sit on: registration, login, short-lived access tokens, rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection, device and session management, email verification, password reset, TOTP multi-factor, role-based access control, rate limiting, brute-force lockouts, an audit log, "Login with Google" over OIDC, and JWKS key rotation.

Authentication is the ideal first project because the feature list is small and the engineering is not. Every hard backend theme shows up in a system you can hold in your head:

  • Cryptography you must not invent. Argon2id parameters, constant-time comparison, hashing tokens at rest.
  • State with a lifetime. Access tokens expire, refresh tokens rotate, email tokens are single-use, sessions end. Anything with a lifetime has a race at the boundary.
  • Replay and idempotency. What happens when the same refresh token arrives twice, from two tabs, 40 ms apart on a flaky mobile network? That is not a hypothetical; it is the single most common bug in home-made auth.
  • Stateless versus stateful tradeoffs. Access tokens are verified without a database hit, which is why revocation is hard, which is why the denylist exists, which is why TTLs are short.
  • Rate limiting and abuse. Credential stuffing is real traffic, not a thought experiment.
  • Third-party dependency. Google can be slow or down. Your login must degrade, not die.
  • Key rotation. Signing keys must roll without logging anyone out. Doing that once teaches you more about deployment ordering than any blog post.

By the end you should be able to draw the refresh rotation flow from memory, explain why the refresh token is hashed in the database, and say precisely what happens to the other five devices when one device's token is stolen.

46.1.2 Requirements

Functional

  1. Register with email and password; password is checked against a minimum length of 12 and a breached-password list; account starts pending_verification.
  2. Verify email with a single-use token valid for 24 hours.
  3. Log in with email and password; if MFA is enabled, return an MFA challenge instead of tokens.
  4. Issue an access token (JWT, 10 minutes) and a refresh token (opaque, 30 days) bound to a session.
  5. Rotate the refresh token on every use; detect reuse of an already-rotated token and revoke the entire token family.
  6. List active sessions with device, IP country, created and last-seen timestamps; revoke one session or all sessions ("logout everywhere").
  7. Request a password reset; a single-use token valid for 30 minutes; changing the password revokes every session.
  8. Enrol TOTP with a QR payload and 10 single-use recovery codes; require a TOTP code at login when enabled.
  9. RBAC: roles with permissions, a @Roles decorator and a guard; admin can list users and force-logout.
  10. Rate limit by IP and by account; lock an account after repeated failures with exponential backoff.
  11. Write an append-only audit event for every security-relevant action.
  12. "Login with Google" via OIDC authorization code with PKCE; link to an existing account when the email matches and is verified.
  13. Publish JWKS at /.well-known/jwks.json with at least two keys during rotation.

Non-functional (the numbers you design against)

Property Target Why it drives design
Login p99 under 350 ms Argon2id at OWASP settings costs about 100 to 150 ms of CPU; that budget forbids extra sequential queries
Token verification p99 under 3 ms, no database call The other services verify JWTs locally against cached JWKS
Refresh p99 under 60 ms One transaction, two indexed statements
Peak load 500 logins/s, 2,000 refreshes/s, 20,000 verifications/s Verification must never touch this service; refresh must not lock hot rows
Availability 99.95 percent for verification-adjacent endpoints, 99.9 percent for login If login is down, nothing new starts; if JWKS is down, everything breaks
Argon2id m=19456 KiB, t=2, p=1 OWASP minimum; fits a 512 MiB container with 4 workers
Access token TTL 600 s Bounds the damage from a stolen token to 10 minutes
Refresh token TTL 30 days absolute, 14 days idle Balance between security and users hating you
Rate limits 10 login attempts per 5 min per IP+email; 100 per hour per IP Slows credential stuffing without breaking offices behind one NAT
Lockout 10 consecutive failures locks 15 min, doubling to 24 h Attackers get expensive; real users get a reset link
Audit retention 400 days, partitioned monthly Compliance asks for a year; partitions make deletion free

46.1.3 Architecture

flowchart TB
  client["Web and mobile clients"] --> edge["Load balancer and TLS"]
  edge --> api["Auth API - NestJS"]
  api --> pg[("PostgreSQL - primary")]
  api --> redis[("Redis - limits, lockouts, denylist")]
  api --> google["Google OIDC provider"]
  api --> outbox["Outbox table in PostgreSQL"]
  outbox --> relay["Outbox relay worker"]
  relay --> broker["Kafka topic auth.events"]
  broker --> mailer["Email worker"]
  mailer --> smtp["Email provider"]
  other["Other services"] --> jwks["GET /.well-known/jwks.json"]
  jwks --> api

Five things in that picture are deliberate.

The access token never comes back to this service. Other services fetch JWKS once, cache it for five minutes, and verify signatures locally. That is why 20,000 verifications per second do not appear in the auth service's load. The cost is revocation latency: a revoked token stays valid until it expires, which is why the TTL is 10 minutes and why a denylist exists for the rare "revoke now" case.

Refresh tokens are opaque and stateful. They are random 32-byte values, stored hashed, and every use rotates them inside one transaction. Stateless refresh tokens cannot be revoked, and revocation is the whole point of having them.

Email is not sent inside the request. Registration writes the user and an outbox row in the same transaction, and a relay publishes to Kafka. If the email provider is down, registration still succeeds. If we sent the email inline, a provider timeout would either roll back a created user or leave a user with no email — both are bugs you will meet in production.

Redis holds only data we can lose. Rate-limit counters, lockout counters, and the short-lived denylist. If Redis is empty after a restart, the worst outcome is that an attacker gets a few extra attempts. Nothing that must survive lives there.

Google is on the critical path only for one endpoint. The OIDC callback has a 3-second timeout and a circuit breaker; password login is unaffected when Google is slow.

46.1.4 Database schema

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgcrypto;

CREATE TYPE user_status AS ENUM ('pending_verification', 'active', 'locked', 'disabled');

CREATE TABLE users (
  id             uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email          citext NOT NULL,
  email_verified_at timestamptz,
  status         user_status NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending_verification',
  display_name   text,
  created_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT users_email_unique UNIQUE (email),
  CONSTRAINT users_email_shape CHECK (position('@' in email) > 1)
);

-- Credentials are separate from users: a user may have a password, a Google
-- identity, both, or neither. One row per credential type per user.
CREATE TABLE credentials (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id       uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  provider      text NOT NULL,              -- 'password' | 'google'
  subject       text,                        -- provider subject id, null for password
  password_hash text,                        -- argon2id encoded string, null for oidc
  password_changed_at timestamptz,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT credentials_user_provider_unique UNIQUE (user_id, provider),
  CONSTRAINT credentials_provider_subject_unique UNIQUE (provider, subject),
  CONSTRAINT credentials_shape CHECK (
    (provider = 'password' AND password_hash IS NOT NULL AND subject IS NULL)
    OR (provider <> 'password' AND subject IS NOT NULL AND password_hash IS NULL)
  )
);

CREATE TABLE sessions (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id       uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  device_label  text,
  user_agent    text,
  ip_country    char(2),
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  last_seen_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  revoked_at    timestamptz,
  revoked_reason text
);
CREATE INDEX sessions_active_idx ON sessions (user_id, last_seen_at DESC)
  WHERE revoked_at IS NULL;

CREATE TABLE refresh_tokens (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  session_id    uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES sessions(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  family_id     uuid NOT NULL,              -- all descendants of one login
  token_hash    bytea NOT NULL,             -- sha256 of the opaque token
  parent_id     uuid REFERENCES refresh_tokens(id),
  issued_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  expires_at    timestamptz NOT NULL,
  used_at       timestamptz,                -- set when rotated
  revoked_at    timestamptz,
  CONSTRAINT refresh_tokens_hash_unique UNIQUE (token_hash)
);
CREATE INDEX refresh_tokens_family_idx ON refresh_tokens (family_id);
CREATE INDEX refresh_tokens_live_idx ON refresh_tokens (session_id)
  WHERE used_at IS NULL AND revoked_at IS NULL;

CREATE TABLE mfa_secrets (
  user_id       uuid PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  secret_enc    bytea NOT NULL,             -- AES-GCM ciphertext of the TOTP secret
  secret_nonce  bytea NOT NULL,
  confirmed_at  timestamptz,
  recovery_hashes text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',  -- sha256 hex of unused codes
  last_used_step bigint,                    -- replay guard: last accepted 30 s step
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TYPE email_token_kind AS ENUM ('verify_email', 'reset_password');

CREATE TABLE email_tokens (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id     uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  kind        email_token_kind NOT NULL,
  token_hash  bytea NOT NULL,
  expires_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
  consumed_at timestamptz,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT email_tokens_hash_unique UNIQUE (token_hash)
);
-- One live token per user per kind: re-requesting invalidates the old one.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX email_tokens_one_live_idx ON email_tokens (user_id, kind)
  WHERE consumed_at IS NULL;

CREATE TABLE roles (
  id          smallint PRIMARY KEY,
  name        text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  permissions text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'
);

CREATE TABLE user_roles (
  user_id     uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  role_id     smallint NOT NULL REFERENCES roles(id),
  granted_by  uuid REFERENCES users(id),
  granted_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, role_id)
);

CREATE TABLE audit_events (
  id          bigserial,
  occurred_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  user_id     uuid,
  actor_id    uuid,
  action      text NOT NULL,        -- 'login.success', 'token.reuse_detected', ...
  ip_hash     bytea,                -- HMAC of IP, never the raw IP
  user_agent  text,
  metadata    jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  PRIMARY KEY (id, occurred_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (occurred_at);

CREATE TABLE audit_events_2026_09 PARTITION OF audit_events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-09-01') TO ('2026-10-01');
CREATE INDEX audit_events_2026_09_user_idx
  ON audit_events_2026_09 (user_id, occurred_at DESC);
erDiagram
  USERS ||--o{ CREDENTIALS : has
  USERS ||--o{ SESSIONS : owns
  USERS ||--o| MFA_SECRETS : enrols
  USERS ||--o{ EMAIL_TOKENS : receives
  USERS ||--o{ USER_ROLES : assigned
  ROLES ||--o{ USER_ROLES : grants
  SESSIONS ||--o{ REFRESH_TOKENS : issues
  REFRESH_TOKENS ||--o| REFRESH_TOKENS : rotates_into
  USERS {
    uuid id PK
    citext email
    user_status status
    timestamptz email_verified_at
  }
  REFRESH_TOKENS {
    uuid id PK
    uuid session_id FK
    uuid family_id
    bytea token_hash
    timestamptz used_at
  }

46.1.5 APIs

Method Path Auth Request Success Errors Idempotent
POST /auth/register none {email,password,displayName} 201 {userId} 409 email taken, 422 weak password, 429 No; duplicate email returns 409
POST /auth/verify-email none {token} 204 400 invalid, 410 expired/consumed Yes; second call returns 410
POST /auth/login none {email,password,deviceLabel} 200 {accessToken,refreshToken,expiresIn} or 200 {mfaRequired:true,challengeId} 401 bad credentials, 423 locked, 429 No
POST /auth/mfa/verify challenge {challengeId,code} 200 {accessToken,refreshToken} 401 bad code, 410 challenge expired No; code is single-use per step
POST /auth/refresh refresh token {refreshToken} 200 {accessToken,refreshToken} 401 unknown/expired, 401 + family revoked on reuse No; rotation is by design single-use
POST /auth/logout access token {} 204 401 Yes
POST /auth/logout-all access token {} 204 401 Yes
GET /auth/sessions access token — 200 [{id,device,lastSeenAt,current}] 401 Yes
DELETE /auth/sessions/:id access token — 204 401, 404 Yes
POST /auth/password/forgot none {email} 202 always 429 Yes; always 202 to avoid user enumeration
POST /auth/password/reset none {token,newPassword} 204 400, 410 expired, 422 weak Yes; second use returns 410
POST /auth/mfa/enrol access token {} 200 {otpauthUri,recoveryCodes} 401, 409 already enrolled No
POST /auth/mfa/confirm access token {code} 204 401 bad code Yes
DELETE /auth/mfa access + password {password} 204 401 Yes
GET /auth/oidc/google/start none ?redirect= 302 to Google 400 bad redirect Yes
GET /auth/oidc/google/callback none ?code&state 302 to app with tokens 400 state mismatch, 502 provider down No; code is single-use at Google
GET /auth/me access token — 200 {id,email,roles,permissions} 401 Yes
GET /admin/users access + admin ?cursor&limit 200 {items,nextCursor} 401, 403 Yes
POST /admin/users/:id/force-logout access + admin {} 204 401, 403, 404 Yes
GET /.well-known/jwks.json none — 200 {keys:[...]} — Yes; cached 300 s

Two rules run through that table. Everything that a client can retry after a network timeout is either idempotent or returns a specific, non-scary error on the second attempt. And POST /auth/password/forgot always returns 202, whether or not the email exists, because anything else is a user-enumeration oracle.
