    command: ["node","dist/worker.js"]     # cancel timer, outbox relay, reconciliation
    environment: *env

Build mockpay yourself and make it hostile. It should support: succeeding after a delay, timing out with no response, returning 500 then succeeding on the idempotent retry, sending the webhook twice, sending the webhook before the HTTP response, sending a webhook for an unknown intent, and sending a webhook with a bad signature. Every failure mode in section 46.4.14 should be reproducible by flipping MODE. This container is where your confidence comes from.

46.4.12 CI/CD

jobs:
  verify:
    services:
      postgres: { image: postgres:16, env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev, POSTGRES_DB: pay_test }, ports: ["5432:5432"], options: --health-cmd "pg_isready -U postgres" --health-interval 5s --health-retries 10 }
      redis:    { image: redis:7, ports: ["6379:6379"] }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci && npm run lint && npx tsc --noEmit
      - run: npm run migration:run
      - run: npm run test:unit
      - run: npm run test:money           # property tests on ledger and refund arithmetic
      - run: npm run test:integration     # Testcontainers + mockpay
      - run: npm run test:race -- --repeat 200   # cancel-vs-capture race, 200 iterations
      - run: npm run test:e2e
  build:
    needs: verify
    steps:
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with: { push: true, tags: "ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/payments:${{ github.sha }}" }
      - uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with: { image-ref: "ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}/payments:${{ github.sha }}", severity: "CRITICAL,HIGH", exit-code: "1" }
      - run: npx @cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm --output-file sbom.json
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: sbom, path: sbom.json }
  deploy:
    needs: build
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    environment: production            # requires manual approval
    steps:
      - run: kubectl apply -f k8s/ && kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/pay-migrate --timeout=300s
      - run: kubectl rollout status deploy/pay-api deploy/pay-saga deploy/pay-workers --timeout=600s
      - run: ./scripts/smoke-payments.sh   # 1-cent order end to end against a sandbox, then refund it
      - run: ./scripts/ledger-invariant.sh # fails the deploy if any transaction is unbalanced

Two things separate this pipeline from the earlier ones: the production environment gate, so a human approves anything that touches money, and the post-deploy ledger invariant check, which turns "the deploy broke accounting" from a month-end discovery into a five-minute rollback.

46.4.13 Observability

Metrics: payment_intents_total{result}; payment_confirm_duration_seconds (with the provider span as a separate histogram so you can see whose latency it is); payment_result_total{result="captured|declined|timeout|transient"}; psp_breaker_state; webhook_received_total{type,signature_ok} and webhook_duplicate_total; saga_active gauge by state, saga_duration_seconds, saga_compensations_total{step} — the last one is the metric that tells you your design is wrong when it climbs; orders_auto_cancelled_total; ledger_unbalanced_transactions gauge (must be 0); refunds_total{kind="full|partial"}; reconciliation_mismatches_total{kind}; outbox_lag_seconds.

Log fields: traceId, orderId, paymentId, sagaId, step, providerIntentId, idempotencyKey (hashed), amountCents, currency, errorClass, attempt, latencyMs. Never log card data, tokens or the raw webhook body of a payment method. Log the idempotencyKey as a hash so support can correlate without it being reusable from a log aggregator.

Traces: the confirm trace shows idempotency.begin, pg.select for update, psp.confirm (the long one), pg.update payment, outbox.insert. The saga trace links to it by correlation_id. When a customer says "it took forever", you can say precisely how much of it was the provider.

Dashboards: a money row (captures, refunds, net, by currency, versus yesterday); a health row (confirm p50/p95/p99, decline rate, timeout rate, breaker state); a saga row (active by state, oldest running, compensations); a reconciliation row (matched, mismatched, unexplained, by day).

Alerts: ledger_unbalanced_transactions > 0 (page immediately); any saga in running older than 30 minutes (page); decline rate above 30 percent for 10 minutes, which usually means the provider changed something (page); webhook signature failures above 1 per minute (security page); reconciliation_mismatches_total > 0 unexplained after the daily run (ticket, escalating to page after 24 hours); orders_auto_cancelled_total spiking, which means checkout is broken upstream.

46.4.14 Failure scenarios

Failure Expected behaviour How you test it
Provider times out on confirm 504 to the client with status: unknown; payment stays processing; webhook or reconciler settles it; no second charge MODE=silent on mockpay; assert exactly one capture
Provider returns 500 then succeeds on retry The idempotent retry returns the same intent; one charge, one ledger transaction MODE=flaky
Webhook arrives twice Second insert conflicts; no second ledger entry; webhook_duplicate_total increments MODE=double_webhook
Webhook arrives before the API response Payment is already captured; the confirm handler sees the terminal state and returns it Force ordering in an integration test
Cancel job fires while capture is in flight The FOR UPDATE lock serialises them; outcome is consistently paid-or-cancelled Race test, 200 iterations
Saga runner pod dies mid-step Another replica picks the saga up after next_run_at; the step is re-run idempotently SIGKILL the runner in a chaos test
Outbox relay down for an hour Orders still process; events are delayed; outbox_lag_seconds alerts; nothing is lost Stop the relay, restart, assert all events published
Refund exceeds captured amount 409 with code: refund_exceeds_captured; nothing posted to the ledger Unit and integration tests
Provider webhook signature invalid 401, event stored with signature_ok = false, security alert fires, no state change Send a tampered payload
Reconciliation finds a charge you never saw Reported as missing_local; a human decides; the system never auto-creates a payment Inject the row in the settlement fixture
Database failover mid-transaction The transaction aborts; the client retries with the same idempotency key and gets the original outcome Kill the primary during the race test
Clock skew of 5 minutes on a pod Webhook timestamp window rejects valid events; alert on signature failures reveals it Shift the container clock in staging

46.4.15 Scaling strategy

1x — 500 orders/day. One API pod, one saga runner, one worker, one PostgreSQL. The provider is the slowest thing in the system by two orders of magnitude, so nothing you do to your own code matters yet. Spend the effort on correctness: this is the scale at which you should build the ledger and the reconciler, because doing it later means backfilling history.

10x — 5,000 orders/day, 50/s peak. Three API pods, two saga runners (safe because of SKIP LOCKED), two relay replicas. The provider's rate limit becomes visible; the token bucket earns its keep. payment_attempts and ledger_entries grow to a few million rows a month, which is nothing, but start the monthly partitions now while the tables are small enough to convert in a maintenance window.

100x — 50,000 orders/day, 500/s peak, several currencies and providers. The write path is still tiny by database standards (500 writes/s), so PostgreSQL is fine; the pressure moves to three places. First, provider concurrency: you will need multiple merchant accounts or providers, which turns the adapter list into a routing decision (by currency, by card scheme, by cost, by health). Second, the saga runner poll: at thousands of active sagas, polling every second with LIMIT 50 is not enough — increase the batch, shard the poll by hashtext(correlation_id) % N per replica, or move to an event-driven wake-up where the outbox relay signals the runner. Third, reconciliation: parsing a daily settlement file of 50,000 rows in memory stops being reasonable; stream it, COPY it into a staging table, and do the comparison in SQL with a full outer join, which is both faster and easier to explain to finance.

What does not change with scale: the ledger stays authoritative, the invariant check stays continuous, and nobody is ever allowed to UPDATE a ledger row.

46.4.16 Security checklist

  • No card data ever touches your servers: the client tokenises with the provider's SDK and you receive only a token. This is what keeps you in PCI SAQ-A instead of a full audit.
  • Webhook HMAC verified with timingSafeEqual, a 5-minute timestamp window, and the raw body (verify before any JSON parsing that could normalise bytes).
  • Provider credentials in a secret manager, rotated, with separate sandbox and live keys and a startup check that the key environment matches the deploy environment.
  • Idempotency keys are client-generated UUIDs, scoped per route, and reuse with a different body returns 409.
  • Amounts are bigint minor units, computed server-side from the order, never taken from the request body.
  • Every refund requires an authorisation check: the owner for self-service refunds within policy, an admin role plus a second approval above a threshold.
  • Refund amount validated against captured_cents - refunded_cents inside the same transaction that writes the refund.
  • The application database role has INSERT but no UPDATE or DELETE on ledger_entries and webhook_events.
  • Rate limits on /payments/* per user and per IP; card-testing attacks look like many small distinct payments and must be alarmed on.
  • Full order and payment audit trail retained for the legally required period; deletion requests remove PII but keep financial records.
  • Admin endpoints require a separate role, are rate-limited, and log actor, target and reason for every action.
  • Reconciliation reports and settlement files are treated as sensitive data at rest.

46.4.17 Stretch goals

Multiple payment providers with routing rules and automatic failover, which turns the adapter into a real strategy pattern with cost and success-rate inputs. 3-D Secure with its extra asynchronous redirect state. Multi-currency with FX rates pinned at capture. Payouts to sellers in a marketplace model, which adds a second ledger dimension. Dispute and chargeback handling, including the evidence deadline as a scheduled job. Subscriptions with retry schedules and dunning emails, which is the same saga with a different clock. Invoice PDF generation. Idempotency key expiry and cleanup. Finally, write the finance-facing month-end report from the ledger only, and have someone who is not you check it against the provider dashboard — that exercise finds bugs no test suite will.

46.4.18 Definition of done

  • All 11 functional requirements implemented, with the saga defined as data and executed by a restartable runner.
  • End-to-end idempotency: client key, service key, provider key; proven by the double-submit and timeout tests.
  • FOR UPDATE on the order row for every transition, with the conditional UPDATE as a second guard.
  • Cancel-versus-capture race test green over 200 iterations with no mixed outcomes.
  • Double-entry ledger with a continuous invariant check that has never reported a non-zero imbalance.
  • Partial refunds correct, capped, and reflected in both orders and the ledger.
  • Webhook handler verifies HMAC on the raw body, is idempotent, and tolerates out-of-order arrival.
  • Reconciliation job runs daily, reports mismatches in three categories, and auto-corrects nothing.
  • Mock provider supports all six hostile modes and every failure-table row is reproducible locally.
  • Chaos test passes the three invariants after 500 checkouts with random pod kills.
  • Dashboards for money, health, sagas and reconciliation; the unbalanced-ledger alert drilled in staging.
  • Deployed with a manual approval gate, a migration Job, a post-deploy ledger check, and a tested rollback.
  • Runbook: what to do on a stuck saga, a provider outage, a signature-failure spike, and an unexplained mismatch.

46.5 Project 5 — Distributed job processing system

46.5.1 Goal and what you will learn

You will build a job processing system on PostgreSQL — the thing you have used a dozen times without knowing what is inside it. Claiming with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, leases with heartbeats and takeover, retries with backoff, priorities, cron schedules that survive time zones and daylight saving, DAG dependencies executed in topological order, idempotent execution keys of (job_id, scheduled_for), a dead-letter queue, execution history partitioned by month, a leader-elected scheduler using an advisory lock, an admin API and metrics.

Then you will implement one queue in BullMQ as well, run the same workload through both, and write down an honest comparison: durability, throughput, transactional enqueue, and operational effort. Not a winner — a comparison. Senior engineers get asked "why did you not just use Redis?" and the good answer contains numbers.

What this project teaches:

  • Exactly-once is a lie; at-least-once plus idempotency is the truth. You will build the mechanism that makes that sentence practical: a unique execution key.
  • Leases beat locks for long work. A held lock dies with its connection at the worst moment. A lease with a heartbeat lets a healthy system take over from a dead worker in seconds, deterministically.
  • Time is the hardest input. A cron entry of 30 2 * * * in Europe/Berlin does not run on the March morning when 02:30 does not exist, and runs twice in October if you are careless.
  • Dependencies are a graph, and graphs have cycles. You will detect them at write time and cap them at read time.
  • Leader election is three lines of SQL. pg_try_advisory_lock gives you a single scheduler without ZooKeeper, etcd or a consensus library, and understanding exactly what it guarantees (and does not) is worth more than the code.
  • Operating a queue is most of the work. Depth, age, throughput, failure rate, stuck jobs, poison jobs, and a way to retry one job by hand at 3 a.m.

46.5.2 Requirements

Functional

  1. Enqueue a job with a type, payload, priority (1 highest to 9 lowest), run_after time, and an optional unique key.
  2. Workers claim jobs in priority then time order, in batches, without ever handing the same job to two workers.
  3. A claimed job holds a lease; the worker heartbeats every 10 seconds; a lease that expires is taken over.
  4. Failed jobs retry with exponential backoff and jitter, up to a per-type maximum; then go to the DLQ.
  5. Cron schedules with an IANA timezone create job instances; a missed window is caught up (configurable) or skipped.
  6. Jobs may depend on other jobs; a job becomes runnable only when all its dependencies have succeeded; execution follows topological order; cycles are rejected at creation.
  7. Every execution is recorded with a unique key (job_id, scheduled_for), so a duplicate claim can never produce a duplicate side effect.
  8. Execution history is queryable and partitioned by month with a retention policy.
  9. Exactly one scheduler is active across all replicas, elected with a PostgreSQL advisory lock.
  10. Admin API: list, inspect, retry, cancel, pause a queue, drain, requeue from the DLQ.
  11. Prometheus metrics for depth, age, throughput, latency, failures and lease takeovers.
  12. One queue also implemented on BullMQ, running the same job type, with the same admin surface.

Non-functional

Property Target Consequence
Throughput 2,000 jobs/s claimed and completed on a 4 vCPU database Batch claims, no per-job transaction round trips
Claim latency p99 under 20 ms for a batch of 20 One statement, one index
Enqueue latency p99 under 5 ms A single insert, no triggers
Duplicate execution zero side effects, even under takeover Unique (job_id, scheduled_for) execution key
Takeover time under 60 s after a worker dies 30 s lease, 10 s heartbeat, reaper every 10 s
Scheduler skew a cron job fires within 5 s of its target instant Scheduler ticks every second, advisory-locked
History retention 90 days hot, then dropped Monthly partitions
DLQ zero jobs older than 24 hours unreviewed Alert plus a replay endpoint
Availability queue accepts enqueues while all workers are down Enqueue only writes a row

46.5.3 Architecture

flowchart TB
  api["Producer services"] --> enq["Enqueue API"]
  enq --> pg[("PostgreSQL - jobs, runs, schedules")]
  sched["Scheduler replicas"] --> lock["pg_try_advisory_lock"]
  lock --> pg
  sched --> pg
  w1["Worker 1"] --> pg
  w2["Worker 2"] --> pg
  w3["Worker N"] --> pg
  reaper["Lease reaper"] --> pg
  pg --> dlq["dead_letter table"]
  admin["Admin API and CLI"] --> pg
  metrics["Prometheus"] --> exporter["Metrics exporter"]
  exporter --> pg
  bull["BullMQ comparison queue"] --> redis[("Redis")]

The design has no broker, no coordinator process and no leader for the workers. Every worker independently runs the same loop: claim a batch, execute, heartbeat, complete or fail. Coordination is entirely in the database, which is the point — the queue inherits PostgreSQL's durability, transactions and backup story, and you can enqueue a job in the same transaction that writes the business row it refers to.

Only the scheduler needs to be a singleton, because two schedulers would create two instances of the same cron occurrence. That singleton is enforced with a session-level advisory lock, not with a config flag saying "run this on pod 0".

46.5.4 Database schema

CREATE TYPE job_status AS ENUM
  ('waiting','ready','running','succeeded','failed','cancelled','dead');

CREATE TABLE job_queues (
  name         text PRIMARY KEY,
  paused       boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  max_attempts smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 5,
  lease_seconds int NOT NULL DEFAULT 30,
  concurrency_hint int NOT NULL DEFAULT 10
);

CREATE TABLE jobs (
  id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  queue         text NOT NULL REFERENCES job_queues(name),
  type          text NOT NULL,
  payload       jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  priority      smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 5 CHECK (priority BETWEEN 1 AND 9),
  status        job_status NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ready',
  run_after     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  scheduled_for timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),   -- logical occurrence instant
  unique_key    text,                                  -- dedupe on enqueue
  attempt       smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  max_attempts  smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 5,
  worker_id     text,
  lease_expires_at timestamptz,
  depends_remaining int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,            -- counter, kept by triggers/updates
  schedule_id   bigint,
  last_error    text,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT jobs_unique_key UNIQUE (queue, unique_key),
  CONSTRAINT jobs_lease_shape CHECK (
    (status = 'running') = (lease_expires_at IS NOT NULL AND worker_id IS NOT NULL))
);

-- THE index. Every claim query must use exactly this one.
CREATE INDEX jobs_claim_idx ON jobs (queue, priority, run_after, id)
  WHERE status = 'ready';
CREATE INDEX jobs_lease_idx ON jobs (lease_expires_at)
  WHERE status = 'running';
CREATE INDEX jobs_waiting_idx ON jobs (id) WHERE status = 'waiting';

CREATE TABLE job_dependencies (
  job_id        bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES jobs(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  depends_on_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES jobs(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  PRIMARY KEY (job_id, depends_on_id),
  CONSTRAINT no_self_dependency CHECK (job_id <> depends_on_id)
);
CREATE INDEX job_dependencies_reverse_idx ON job_dependencies (depends_on_id);

CREATE TABLE schedules (
  id           bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  name         text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  queue        text NOT NULL REFERENCES job_queues(name),
  type         text NOT NULL,
  cron         text NOT NULL,                    -- '30 2 * * *'
  timezone     text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'UTC',      -- IANA name
  payload      jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  priority     smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 5,
  catchup      boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,   -- create missed occurrences?
  enabled      boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
  last_fired_for timestamptz,                    -- last logical occurrence created
  next_fire_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT schedules_tz_valid CHECK (timezone <> '')
);
CREATE INDEX schedules_due_idx ON schedules (next_fire_at) WHERE enabled;

-- Append-only history. The unique key is the idempotency guarantee.
CREATE TABLE job_runs (
  id           bigserial,
  job_id       bigint NOT NULL,
  scheduled_for timestamptz NOT NULL,
  attempt      smallint NOT NULL,
  worker_id    text NOT NULL,
  status       text NOT NULL,             -- running | succeeded | failed | lost
  started_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  finished_at  timestamptz,
  duration_ms  int,
  error        text,
  PRIMARY KEY (id, started_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (started_at);

CREATE TABLE job_runs_2026_09 PARTITION OF job_runs
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-09-01') TO ('2026-10-01');
-- One successful execution per logical occurrence, ever.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX job_runs_2026_09_exec_key
  ON job_runs_2026_09 (job_id, scheduled_for) WHERE status = 'succeeded';
CREATE INDEX job_runs_2026_09_job_idx ON job_runs_2026_09 (job_id, started_at DESC);

CREATE TABLE dead_letters (
  id           bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  job_id       bigint NOT NULL,
  queue        text NOT NULL,
  type         text NOT NULL,
  payload      jsonb NOT NULL,
  attempts     smallint NOT NULL,
  last_error   text NOT NULL,
  died_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  replayed_at  timestamptz
);
CREATE INDEX dead_letters_open_idx ON dead_letters (died_at) WHERE replayed_at IS NULL;
erDiagram
  JOB_QUEUES ||--o{ JOBS : holds
  JOBS ||--o{ JOB_RUNS : executed_as

  waiting --> ready
  ready --> running
  running --> succeeded

  running --> failed
  failed --> ready
  failed --> dead
  ready --> cancelled
  waiting --> cancelled
  succeeded --> [*]
  dead --> [*]
  cancelled --> [*]

waiting means "dependencies not satisfied". running -> ready is the lease takeover path. failed -> ready is the retry path after backoff. failed -> dead happens when attempts are exhausted.

GET /metrics internal — Prometheus text 200 Yes

Enqueue is deliberately a plain INSERT with no side effects, which means a producer can call it inside its own business transaction using its own connection — the killer feature of a database-backed queue, and the reason this project exists.

claim.service.ts — the one query everything depends on.

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

export interface ClaimedJob {
  id: string; queue: string; type: string; payload: unknown;
  attempt: number; scheduled_for: string; max_attempts: number;
}

@Injectable()
export class ClaimService {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  /**
   * Claims up to `batch` jobs atomically. SKIP LOCKED means concurrent workers
   * step over rows another worker has locked instead of queueing behind them,
   * which is what turns a table into a queue.
   */
  async claim(queue: string, workerId: string, batch: number, leaseSeconds: number): Promise<ClaimedJob[]> {
    return this.ds.query(
      `UPDATE jobs j
          SET status = 'running',
              worker_id = $2,
              attempt = j.attempt + 1,
              lease_expires_at = now() + make_interval(secs => $4),
              updated_at = now()
        WHERE j.id IN (
          SELECT c.id
            FROM jobs c
            JOIN job_queues q ON q.name = c.queue
           WHERE c.queue = $1
             AND c.status = 'ready'
             AND c.run_after <= now()
             AND q.paused = false
           ORDER BY c.priority ASC, c.run_after ASC, c.id ASC
           LIMIT $3
           FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
        )
        RETURNING j.id, j.queue, j.type, j.payload, j.attempt,
                  j.scheduled_for, j.max_attempts`,
      [queue, workerId, batch, leaseSeconds],
    );
  }
}

Three details make this correct and fast. The inner SELECT carries FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so two workers never collide. The ORDER BY matches jobs_claim_idx exactly, so the plan is an index scan of a handful of rows, not a sort of the queue. And the UPDATE increments attempt at claim time, not at failure time — a worker that dies without reporting anything has still consumed an attempt, which is what stops an infinitely crashing job from looping forever.

worker.runner.ts — the loop, with the idempotency key.

import { Injectable, Logger, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { ClaimService } from '../queue/claim.service';
import { HandlerRegistry } from './handlers/handler.registry';
import { backoffMs } from '../queue/backoff';

@Injectable()
export class WorkerRunner implements OnModuleInit {
  private readonly log = new Logger(WorkerRunner.name);
  private readonly workerId = `${process.env.HOSTNAME ?? 'local'}:${process.pid}`;
  private running = true;

  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource, private readonly claims: ClaimService,
              private readonly handlers: HandlerRegistry) {}

  onModuleInit() { void this.loop(); }

  private async loop() {
    while (this.running) {
      const jobs = await this.claims.claim('default', this.workerId, 20, 30);
      if (jobs.length === 0) { await sleep(500 + Math.random() * 500); continue; }
      await Promise.all(jobs.map((j) => this.execute(j)));
    }
  }

  private async execute(job: ClaimedJob) {
    // Reserve the execution key first. A duplicate claim of the same logical
    // occurrence fails here and the job is completed without side effects.
    const reserved = await this.ds.query(
      `INSERT INTO job_runs (job_id, scheduled_for, attempt, worker_id, status)
       VALUES ($1,$2,$3,$4,'running')
       ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING id`,
      [job.id, job.scheduled_for, job.attempt, this.workerId],
    );

    const started = Date.now();
    try {
      const handler = this.handlers.get(job.type);
      await handler.handle(job.payload, { jobId: job.id, attempt: job.attempt });
      await this.ds.query(
        `WITH done AS (
           UPDATE jobs SET status='succeeded', lease_expires_at=NULL, worker_id=NULL,
                           updated_at=now() WHERE id=$1 RETURNING id)
         UPDATE job_runs SET status='succeeded', finished_at=now(), duration_ms=$2
          WHERE job_id=$1 AND attempt=$3`,
        [job.id, Date.now() - started, job.attempt]);
      await this.releaseDependents(job.id);
    } catch (err) {
      const message = (err as Error).message.slice(0, 2000);
      const dead = job.attempt >= job.max_attempts;
      await this.ds.query(
        `UPDATE jobs
            SET status = CASE WHEN $3 THEN 'dead' ELSE 'ready' END,
                run_after = now() + make_interval(secs => $4),
                lease_expires_at = NULL, worker_id = NULL, last_error = $2, updated_at = now()
          WHERE id = $1`,
        [job.id, message, dead, backoffMs(job.attempt) / 1000]);
      if (dead) await this.toDeadLetter(job, message);
      this.log.warn(`job ${job.id} attempt ${job.attempt} failed: ${message}`);
    }
  }
}
const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

lease.reaper.ts — takeover, and why the lease must be shorter than your patience.

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Interval } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

@Injectable()
export class LeaseReaper {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  /** Runs on every replica; the statement is safe to run concurrently. */
  @Interval(10_000)
  async reap() {
    const rows = await this.ds.query(
      `WITH expired AS (
         SELECT id, attempt, max_attempts FROM jobs
          WHERE status = 'running' AND lease_expires_at < now()
          ORDER BY lease_expires_at LIMIT 500 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
       ), marked AS (
         UPDATE job_runs r SET status='lost', finished_at=now()
           FROM expired e WHERE r.job_id = e.job_id AND r.status='running'
           RETURNING r.job_id
       )
       UPDATE jobs j
          SET status = CASE WHEN j.attempt >= j.max_attempts THEN 'dead' ELSE 'ready' END,
              worker_id = NULL, lease_expires_at = NULL,
              run_after = now(), last_error = 'lease_expired', updated_at = now()
         FROM expired e WHERE j.id = e.id
       RETURNING j.id, j.status`,
      [],
    );
    if (rows.length) this.metrics.leaseTakeovers.inc(rows.length);
  }
}

A lease of 30 seconds with a 10-second heartbeat means a killed pod's jobs are runnable again within 40 seconds. Make the lease long enough that a normal GC pause or a slow query never expires it (a 2-second lease will cause phantom takeovers and double execution attempts), and short enough that a dead worker does not strand a job for minutes. For handlers that legitimately run for 20 minutes, extend the lease from inside the handler on the heartbeat, not by setting a 30-minute lease globally.

leader.service.ts — one scheduler, three lines.

import { Injectable, OnModuleDestroy } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource, QueryRunner } from 'typeorm';

const LOCK_KEY = 918_273_645;    // any stable bigint; document it

@Injectable()
export class LeaderService implements OnModuleDestroy {
  private runner?: QueryRunner;
  private leader = false;

  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  /** Session-level lock: held until this connection closes, so a crash releases it. */
  async tryAcquire(): Promise<boolean> {
    if (this.leader) return true;
    this.runner ??= this.ds.createQueryRunner();
    await this.runner.connect();
    const [{ pg_try_advisory_lock: ok }] =
      await this.runner.query('SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock($1)', [LOCK_KEY]);
    this.leader = ok;
    return ok;
  }

  isLeader() { return this.leader; }

  async onModuleDestroy() {
    if (this.runner && this.leader) {
      await this.runner.query('SELECT pg_advisory_unlock($1)', [LOCK_KEY]);
    }
    await this.runner?.release();
  }
}

Be precise about what this guarantees. The lock is tied to a connection. If the pod is network-partitioned but alive, PostgreSQL will drop the connection when TCP keepalives fail (tune tcp_keepalives_idle), and another pod becomes leader — but the old pod may not have noticed yet. So the scheduler must also be idempotent: it creates occurrences with ON CONFLICT (queue, unique_key) DO NOTHING where unique_key = 'schedule:{id}:{scheduledFor}'. Leader election reduces duplicate work; the unique key prevents duplicate effects. Never rely on election alone.

Cron with timezone and DST. Compute the next occurrence in the schedule's zone, convert to UTC, store it. Two rules cover the awkward cases: if the local time does not exist (spring forward), run at the first valid instant after the gap; if the local time occurs twice (autumn fall-back), run on the first occurrence only, which you enforce for free because unique_key contains the logical scheduledFor in UTC and the second occurrence produces a different UTC instant — so decide explicitly and write a test for both days of the year. When the scheduler was down and catchup is true, create every missed occurrence in order; when it is false, jump to the next future occurrence and record a schedule_skipped metric. Nothing makes an operator angrier than a system that silently ran 400 catch-up jobs at 09:00 Monday.

DAG dependencies. dependsOn is validated at enqueue with a recursive CTE that walks the existing graph and rejects a cycle:

WITH RECURSIVE reach AS (
  SELECT depends_on_id AS id, 1 AS lvl FROM job_dependencies WHERE job_id = $1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT d.depends_on_id, r.lvl + 1
    FROM job_dependencies d JOIN reach r ON d.job_id = r.id
   WHERE r.lvl < 50
)
SELECT 1 FROM reach WHERE id = $2 LIMIT 1;   -- would create a cycle

A job with dependencies is created waiting with depends_remaining = count. When a job succeeds, releaseDependents decrements its dependents and flips any that reach zero to ready:

UPDATE jobs SET depends_remaining = depends_remaining - 1,
                status = CASE WHEN depends_remaining - 1 = 0 THEN 'ready' ELSE status END
 WHERE id IN (SELECT job_id FROM job_dependencies WHERE depends_on_id = $1)
   AND status = 'waiting';

Topological order falls out of this without a sort: a node only becomes runnable when its in-degree reaches zero, which is Kahn's algorithm executed by the queue itself. If a dependency ends dead, its dependents are cancelled with reason upstream_failed — decide that policy explicitly, because "hang forever" is the default if you do not.

46.5.7 PostgreSQL design decisions

Transactions. The claim is one statement, therefore one implicit transaction, therefore atomic. Do not wrap the claim and the execution in one transaction: holding a transaction open for the duration of a 40-second job pins an xid, blocks vacuum, and turns your queue table into a bloated mess. Claim in one transaction, execute outside any transaction, complete in another. That is the whole reason leases exist.

Locks. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is the entire concurrency design. Without SKIP LOCKED, twenty workers queue behind one lock and throughput collapses to one job at a time. With it, each worker gets a different set of rows on the first try. The reaper uses the same pattern so several reapers can run.

Indexes. jobs_claim_idx (queue, priority, run_after, id) WHERE status = 'ready' is the only index the hot path uses, and the partial predicate keeps it tiny: at 2,000 jobs/s with 200 ms average execution, only a few hundred rows are ready at any moment even though the table holds millions. jobs_lease_idx partial on running drives the reaper. jobs_waiting_idx supports dependency release. Resist adding a general index on status — it is low-cardinality, huge, and the planner will not use it.

Bloat and vacuum. A queue table is the worst case for MVCC: every row is inserted, updated three or four times, and deleted. Set aggressive autovacuum on jobs specifically:

ALTER TABLE jobs SET (
  autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02,
  autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 0,
  autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.02,
  fillfactor = 70
);

fillfactor = 70 leaves room on each page for HOT updates, so an UPDATE that does not change an indexed column can reuse the same page and skip index maintenance. This single setting can double the throughput of a busy queue table, and almost nobody knows it exists. Move completed jobs out to job_runs and delete them from jobs in nightly batches, so jobs stays in the low hundreds of thousands of rows.

Partitioning. job_runs by month, with the unique execution-key index defined per partition. Note the consequence: the uniqueness guarantee is per partition, so a scheduled_for at a month boundary retried on the other side of midnight on the 1st could execute twice. Fix it by partitioning on scheduled_for instead of started_at when your jobs can retry across a month boundary, or accept and document the window. This is exactly the kind of subtlety that separates a system you understand from one you copied.

Migrations. Adding a status enum value, changing the claim index, or changing lease semantics all need care because workers are running old and new code simultaneously during a rollout. The rule: index changes go first with CONCURRENTLY, semantic changes go behind a config flag, and the claim query is never changed in the same release as the index it uses.

46.5.8 Redis usage

The PostgreSQL queue uses Redis for exactly three things, and none of them are the queue:

Key Structure TTL Purpose
metrics:queue:{name}:depth String 15 s Cached depth so /queues does not COUNT(*) a big table on every dashboard refresh
worker:{id}:seen String 60 s Live worker roster for the admin UI
lock:partitions SET NX PX 60000 60 s One replica creates next month's partitions

The BullMQ comparison queue, by contrast, uses Redis for everything: the job data, the states (wait, active, delayed, completed, failed), the priority sorted set, and the atomic move scripts. That is the honest difference — one design uses Redis as a convenience, the other as the system of record.

46.5.9 Messaging usage, and the BullMQ comparison

Implement one real queue both ways. A good candidate is report.generate: it takes 5 to 60 seconds, must not run twice for the same (reportId, day), and matters enough that losing one is noticed.

// BullMQ version: the whole queue is three files.
import { Processor, WorkerHost, InjectQueue } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { Queue, Job } from 'bullmq';

@Processor('reports', { concurrency: 10 })
export class ReportProcessor extends WorkerHost {
  async process(job: Job<{ reportId: string; day: string }>) {
    // BullMQ guarantees at-least-once. The dedupe is still yours to build.
    return generateReport(job.data.reportId, job.data.day);
  }
}

// Enqueue with a deterministic jobId: BullMQ ignores a duplicate id while the job
// exists, which is dedupe with an expiry, not a durable unique constraint.
await this.queue.add('generate', data, {
  jobId: `report:${data.reportId}:${data.day}`,
  attempts: 5,
  backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 2000 },
  removeOnComplete: { age: 3600, count: 1000 },
  removeOnFail: 5000,
});

Run both under the same load — 200,000 jobs, 20 workers, a handler that sleeps 50 ms — and measure. Then fill in this table from your own numbers, not from mine:

Dimension PostgreSQL queue BullMQ on Redis
Throughput (measured, 4 vCPU db / 2 GiB Redis) roughly 2,000 to 4,000 jobs/s with batch claims; limited by write amplification and vacuum roughly 10,000 to 20,000 jobs/s; limited by Redis single-thread and Lua script time
Enqueue latency 1 to 3 ms 0.2 to 0.5 ms
Durability Full: WAL, replication, PITR, backups you already run Depends on config; AOF everysec can lose a second; RDB can lose minutes; a failover can lose in-flight state
Transactional enqueue Native. INSERT the job in the same transaction as the business row. No orphan jobs, no lost jobs, ever Impossible. You need an outbox anyway, which means you end up with a database table regardless
Delayed and scheduled jobs run_after column, trivially queryable and correctable with SQL Built-in delayed set; correcting 10,000 scheduled jobs means writing a script against Redis
Priorities ORDER BY priority on an index; exact Supported, with a documented throughput cost on the priority set
Dependencies and DAGs Yours to build (this project) FlowProducer gives parent/child flows out of the box
Visibility and ad-hoc queries Anything you can express in SQL: "all failed jobs of type X with payload containing customer Y" Redis key scans, or the paid UI; ad-hoc queries are painful
Operational effort Vacuum tuning, partition maintenance, one more hot table on your primary A separate Redis to size, secure, monitor and fail over; memory is the hard limit
Failure blast radius Queue problems can slow your main database Redis OOM stops the queue; noeviction is mandatory or jobs vanish
Tooling Whatever you build Mature UI, metrics, rate limiting, flows, repeatable jobs
Time to first working queue Two evenings Twenty minutes

The honest conclusion: below roughly 500 jobs per second, and whenever enqueue must be transactional with a database write, the PostgreSQL queue is the better engineering choice — fewer moving parts, better durability, better debuggability, and no second datastore to operate. Above a few thousand jobs per second of small, fire-and-forget work, Redis-backed queues win on raw cost per job and give you a lot of features for free. Most teams are in the first category and reach for the second out of habit. Now you can say that with numbers instead of an opinion.

sequenceDiagram
  participant W1 as WorkerA
  participant DB as Postgres
  participant R as Reaper
  participant W2 as WorkerB
  W1->>DB: claim batch, lease 30s
  DB-->>W1: job 4711 attempt 1
  W1->>DB: heartbeat extend lease
  Note over W1: pod is OOMKilled
  R->>DB: find running with expired lease
  DB-->>R: job 4711
  R->>DB: mark run lost, job back to ready
  W2->>DB: claim batch
  DB-->>W2: job 4711 attempt 2
  W2->>DB: insert job_runs job_id scheduled_for
  W2->>DB: succeeded

46.5.10 Testing strategy

Unit: backoff with jitter (bounded, monotonic in expectation), cron next-occurrence across DST in both directions, cycle detection, dependency counter arithmetic. Integration with Testcontainers: everything about claiming, leasing and reaping, because none of it can be tested with mocks. E2E: the admin API and a real DAG execution.

The ten cases:

  1. No double claim — 20 concurrent workers claim from a queue of 10,000 jobs; every job is claimed exactly once and the union of claims equals the queue.
  2. Lease takeover — claim a job, kill the worker with SIGKILL, assert another worker picks it up within 60 s with attempt = 2 and a lost run row.
  3. Idempotent execution key — force a takeover while the first worker is still finishing; the unique index means only one succeeded run row exists and the side effect happened once.
  4. Backoff schedule — a job failing five times has run_after gaps of roughly 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, 16 s, 32 s within jitter bounds, then lands in the DLQ.
  5. Priority ordering — enqueue 1,000 priority-9 jobs then 10 priority-1 jobs; the priority-1 jobs are all claimed in the next batch.
  6. DAG order — a diamond graph A then B and C then D; assert D starts only after both B and C succeed, and that a failure of B leaves D cancelled with upstream_failed.
  7. Cycle rejection — creating A depends on B when B already depends on A returns 422 and writes nothing.
  8. Cron DST — a 30 2 * * * schedule in Europe/Berlin produces exactly one occurrence on the spring-forward day and exactly one on the fall-back day; assert the UTC instants.
  9. Single scheduler — start three scheduler replicas; assert exactly one holds the advisory lock and exactly one occurrence per cron tick is created, then kill the leader and assert another takes over within 5 s.
  10. Throughput and no bloat — process 200,000 jobs; assert sustained throughput above your target and that pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup on jobs returns below 10 percent within a minute of the run ending.

46.5.11 Docker

services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    command: ["postgres","-c","max_connections=200","-c","shared_buffers=512MB",
              "-c","autovacuum_naptime=10s","-c","track_io_timing=on"]
    environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev, POSTGRES_DB: jobs }
    ports: ["5432:5432"]
    healthcheck: { test: ["CMD-SHELL","pg_isready -U postgres -d jobs"], interval: 5s, retries: 10 }
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: ["redis-server","--appendonly","yes","--appendfsync","everysec",
              "--maxmemory","1gb","--maxmemory-policy","noeviction"]
    ports: ["6379:6379"]
  api:
    build: { context: ., target: runtime }
    command: ["node","dist/main.js"]
    environment: &env
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:dev@postgres:5432/jobs
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
    depends_on: { postgres: { condition: service_healthy } }
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
  worker:
    build: { context: ., target: runtime }
    command: ["node","dist/worker.js"]
    environment: *env
    deploy: { replicas: 4 }
  scheduler:
    build: { context: ., target: runtime }
    command: ["node","dist/scheduler.js"]
    environment: *env
    deploy: { replicas: 3 }          # three replicas, one leader, on purpose
  bull-worker:
    build: { context: ., target: runtime }
    command: ["node","dist/bull-worker.js"]
    environment: *env
  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:latest
    ports: ["3001:3000"]
  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:latest
    volumes: ["./ops/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro"]
    ports: ["9090:9090"]

Running three scheduler replicas locally is deliberate: it makes leader election a thing you can observe with docker compose logs rather than a thing you hope works in production.

46.5.12 CI/CD

jobs:
  verify:
    services:
      postgres: { image: postgres:16, env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev, POSTGRES_DB: jobs_test }, ports: ["5432:5432"], options: --health-cmd "pg_isready -U postgres" --health-interval 5s --health-retries 10 }
      redis:    { image: redis:7, ports: ["6379:6379"] }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci && npm run lint && npx tsc --noEmit
      - run: npm run migration:run
      - run: npm run test:unit
      - run: npm run test:concurrency -- --workers 20 --jobs 10000
      - run: npm run test:integration
      - run: npm run test:e2e
      - run: npm run bench:queue -- --jobs 50000 --report bench.json
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: bench, path: bench.json }
  deploy:
    needs: verify
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps:
      - run: kubectl apply -f k8s/ && kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/jobs-migrate --timeout=300s
      - run: kubectl rollout status deploy/jobs-api deploy/jobs-worker deploy/jobs-scheduler --timeout=600s
      - run: ./scripts/smoke-jobs.sh   # enqueue, wait for success, check metrics endpoint

Publish bench.json on every run and plot it over time. A performance regression in the claim query is invisible in unit tests and obvious in a chart — and this is the one project where the claim query's plan is the product.

Rolling deploys need terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60 and a SIGTERM handler that stops claiming, finishes in-flight jobs, and exits. Without it, every deploy manufactures lease takeovers and inflates your attempt counts.

46.5.13 Observability

Metrics: job_queue_depth{queue,status}; job_queue_oldest_ready_seconds{queue} — the single best queue health metric, because depth without age tells you nothing; job_claimed_total{queue}; job_completed_total{queue,type,result}; job_duration_seconds{type} histogram; job_wait_seconds{queue} from run_after to claim; job_attempts histogram; job_lease_takeovers_total; job_dead_total{type}; dlq_depth and dlq_oldest_seconds; scheduler_is_leader (0 or 1 per pod; the sum across pods must always be 1); schedule_fire_skew_seconds; and the database's own pg_stat_user_tables{relname="jobs"} dead-tuple ratio scraped by the exporter.

Log fields: traceId, jobId, queue, type, attempt, workerId, scheduledFor, durationMs, result, errorClass. Log claim batches at debug with sizes, not one line per job, or a 2,000 jobs/s system will generate more log volume than work.

Traces: the producer's trace context is stored on the job payload as traceparent and restored by the worker, so a report generated by a nightly cron links back to the API call that scheduled it. This is unreasonably useful and costs ten lines.

Dashboards: queue row (depth and age per queue, claim rate, completion rate); health row (failure rate by type, attempts distribution, takeovers); scheduler row (leader gauge, fire skew, occurrences created, catch-up count); database row (dead tuples on jobs, autovacuum runs, claim query p99 from pg_stat_statements).

Alerts: job_queue_oldest_ready_seconds > 300 for a latency-sensitive queue (page); sum(scheduler_is_leader) != 1 for 2 minutes (page — either nobody is scheduling or two are); job_lease_takeovers_total rate above 1 per minute sustained (usually workers being OOMKilled); dlq_oldest_seconds > 86400 (ticket); dead-tuple ratio on jobs above 30 percent for 15 minutes (vacuum is losing); schedule_fire_skew_seconds > 60 (the scheduler is starved).

46.5.14 Failure scenarios

Failure Expected behaviour How you test it
Worker pod OOMKilled mid-job Lease expires, run marked lost, job retried by another worker within 60 s, execution key prevents a duplicate side effect SIGKILL in an integration test; assert one succeeded run
Handler hangs forever Lease is not heartbeated past the handler timeout; the runner aborts the handler at leaseSeconds * 0.8 and fails the job Handler that awaits a never-resolving promise
Database failover Claims fail, workers back off and retry, no jobs lost, some leases expire and are retried Kill the primary during the concurrency test
Two schedulers both think they are leader Impossible to fully prevent under partition; duplicate occurrence blocked by unique_key; metric sum(scheduler_is_leader) alarms Simulate by forcing the lock query to return true on two pods
Poison job crashes every worker Attempts exhaust, job goes dead, DLQ alert; the queue keeps moving Handler that throws immediately
Queue paused during an incident Claims return nothing; enqueue still works; depth grows; resume drains Admin API test
Table bloat after a 1M-job burst Autovacuum with the aggressive settings recovers within minutes; throughput returns Bench run, then measure n_dead_tup over time
Next month's job_runs partition missing Inserts fail loudly, jobs fail rather than silently losing history; alert on partition existence catches it beforehand Drop the partition in staging
Clock skew of 2 minutes on one worker run_after comparisons happen in the database, so worker clock skew is harmless; only log timestamps look odd Shift a container clock and observe
Redis down (BullMQ queue only) The BullMQ queue stops entirely; the PostgreSQL queue is unaffected Stop Redis during the bench; note the difference in the comparison table

46.5.15 Scaling strategy

1x — 50,000 jobs/day, about 1/s. One worker pod with concurrency 10, one scheduler set, default vacuum settings. The claim query returns in under a millisecond and the queue table stays small. Honestly, a setInterval would work at this scale; you are building the machinery to learn it.

10x — 500,000 jobs/day, 20/s peak. Four worker pods, batch claims of 20, the aggressive autovacuum settings, and the nightly move of completed jobs out of jobs. Watch job_queue_oldest_ready_seconds, not depth. Split queues by workload shape — fast jobs and slow jobs must not share a queue, or one 10-minute report starves 5,000 emails.

100x — 5 million jobs/day, 2,000/s peak. Now the claim statement is the bottleneck, and three moves matter. First, batch harder: claim 50 to 100 rows per statement, which amortises the round trip and the index descent. Second, reduce write amplification: fillfactor, fewer status updates per job, and completion via a single statement. Third, partition the work: either separate queues on separate tables, or hash-partition jobs by queue so different workloads do not share heap pages and vacuum pressure. Beyond about 5,000 jobs/s of small jobs on one primary, stop: either move that specific workload to a Redis-backed or Kafka-backed queue, or shard the queue database. Recognising the ceiling and naming it is the senior move; pretending PostgreSQL scales infinitely as a queue is not.

One more scaling note that surprises people: SELECT count(*) for depth becomes the most expensive query in the system at scale. Approximate it from pg_class.reltuples, or keep counters, and cache it for 15 seconds.

46.5.16 Security checklist

  • Job payloads validated per type with a registered schema; an unknown type is rejected at enqueue, not at execution.
  • Payloads never contain secrets; they contain references, and the worker fetches credentials from the secret manager.
  • Handlers run with the least privilege they need; the worker's database role is distinct from the API's.
  • The enqueue API requires a service token, and a token is scoped to the queues and types it may use.
  • Admin endpoints (retry, cancel, pause, dlq/replay) require an admin role and log actor and reason.
  • Payload size capped (for example 256 KB); large inputs go to object storage and the payload carries a key.
  • Cron expressions and timezones validated against an allow-list of zones; a bad expression cannot create an infinite schedule.
  • DLQ payloads redacted for fields marked sensitive in the type's schema, because the DLQ is the most-read table during an incident.
  • Rate limits on enqueue per caller so a looping producer cannot fill the table and take the database down.
  • Retention and deletion of job_runs covers personal data in error messages; truncate errors and scrub them.

46.5.17 Stretch goals

Job cancellation that actually interrupts a running handler using an AbortSignal propagated from a cancellation flag checked on heartbeat. Rate-limited queues (no more than N jobs of type X per minute) implemented with a token bucket inside the claim statement. Unique-in-flight semantics (only one sync:{tenantId} running at a time) via a partial unique index on (type, unique_key) WHERE status IN ('ready','running'). Fan-out and fan-in jobs with a parent that completes when all children do. A workflow DSL that compiles to a DAG. Priority ageing so low-priority jobs cannot starve forever. A worker autoscaler driven by job_queue_oldest_ready_seconds through KEDA. Finally, run the same benchmark against a third option — SQS or Kafka as a work queue — and extend the comparison table to three columns.

46.5.18 Definition of done

  • All 12 functional requirements implemented, including the BullMQ comparison queue running the same job type.
  • Concurrency test with 20 workers and 10,000 jobs shows exactly-once claiming, run 20 times in CI.
  • Lease takeover proven with a SIGKILL test; takeover within 60 s; the execution key prevents duplicate effects.
  • DAG execution correct for a diamond graph, including the upstream-failure policy; cycles rejected at enqueue.
  • Cron correctness proven for both DST transitions in a real timezone, with asserted UTC instants.
  • Exactly one scheduler leader across three replicas, with failover under 5 seconds, proven by test.
  • job_runs partitioned monthly with automated creation and an alert on absence; the month-boundary uniqueness caveat documented.
  • Autovacuum and fillfactor tuned on jobs; dead-tuple ratio stays under 20 percent during the 200,000-job bench.
  • Benchmark published in CI with numbers for both implementations; the comparison table filled in from your own measurements.
  • Metrics, dashboards and all six alerts in place; sum(scheduler_is_leader) != 1 drilled in staging.
  • Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM verified: a rolling deploy causes zero lease takeovers.
  • Deployed to a real cluster with separate API, worker and scheduler deployments and a tested rollback.
  • Runbook: stuck queue, poison job, DLQ replay, leader stuck, vacuum falling behind.

46.6 Project 6 — Microservices-based commerce platform

46.6.1 Goal and what you will learn

You will take the modular monolith from Project 2 and the payment system from Project 4 and cut them into services: a gateway BFF plus auth, catalog, orders, payments, inventory and notification. A Kafka event backbone with a written schema-compatibility policy. A PostgreSQL database per service, with no shared tables and no cross-service joins. Sagas that now span the network. Authentication and rate limiting at the gateway. Service-to-service authentication. OpenTelemetry tracing across every hop. Kubernetes manifests or a Helm chart per service. A CI/CD pipeline per service with contract tests. Shared dashboards. A chaos test plan. And a strangler-fig migration plan that gets you from the monolith to this without a big-bang rewrite.

The goal is not to convince you that microservices are good. It is to make you competent enough to have the argument. By the end you will have felt, in your own hands, that:

  • Every in-process call you replace with a network call gains four new failure modes: slow, failed, duplicated, and partially applied. The mantra from the rest of this book stops being a slogan here.
  • A database per service is the actual boundary. Shared tables are the thing that makes "microservices" a distributed monolith with extra latency.
  • Events are a public API. Once another team consumes your event, its shape is a contract, and you need a compatibility policy before you need a schema registry.
  • Sagas across the network need timeouts, compensation and observability, and the observability is the hard part.
  • Tracing is not optional at six hops. Without a trace id that survives HTTP and Kafka, debugging becomes archaeology.
  • The operational surface multiplies. Six pipelines, six databases, six sets of dashboards, six on-call runbooks. That cost is real and you should be able to quantify it.

46.6.2 Requirements

Functional

  1. All Project 2 and Project 4 capabilities still work end to end: browse, search, cart, checkout, payment, refund, notification.
  2. The gateway is the only public entry point; it authenticates, rate-limits, and composes responses for the client.
  3. Each service owns its data; no service reads another service's database.
  4. Services communicate synchronously (HTTP or gRPC) only where the caller needs an answer now; everything else is an event.
  5. Checkout is a saga orchestrated by the orders service across payments and inventory, with compensation.
  6. All events are published through per-service outboxes and consumed idempotently through per-service inboxes.
  7. Every request carries a trace context across HTTP and Kafka; every span is attributable to a service and a version.
  8. Each service deploys independently with its own pipeline, its own migrations and its own rollback.
  9. Contract tests fail a producer's build if it breaks a consumer's expectations.
  10. A documented schema-compatibility policy governs every topic.
  11. A chaos test plan exercises each cross-service dependency failing.
  12. A strangler-fig plan describes the sequence from monolith to platform with no big-bang cutover.

Non-functional

Property Target Notes
Checkout end to end p95 under 3 s including the provider Budget: gateway 20 ms, orders 80 ms, inventory 40 ms, payments 2.4 s, slack 400 ms
Product page p95 under 200 ms at the gateway Composed from catalog plus inventory, with a stale-tolerant cache
Availability, read path 99.95 percent Catalog must survive orders being down
Availability, checkout 99.9 percent It depends on four services and a provider
Inter-service timeout 800 ms default, 2 s for payments confirm Shorter than the caller's own budget, always
Event lag p99 under 5 s from produce to consume Beyond that, users notice stale state
Deploy frequency any service, any time, no coordination The reason for doing this at all
Rollback time under 3 minutes per service helm rollback plus a compatible schema
Trace coverage 100 percent of checkout requests sampled Tail-based sampling elsewhere

46.6.3 Architecture

flowchart TB
  client["Web and mobile"] --> gw["Gateway BFF"]
  gw --> auth["Auth service"]
  gw --> cat["Catalog service"]
  gw --> ord["Orders service"]
  gw --> inv["Inventory service"]
  ord --> pay["Payments service"]
  ord --> inv
  pay --> psp["Payment provider"]
  cat --> catdb[("catalog db")]
  ord --> orddb[("orders db")]
  pay --> paydb[("payments db")]
  inv --> invdb[("inventory db")]
  auth --> authdb[("auth db")]
  notif["Notification service"] --> notifdb[("notify db")]
  kafka["Kafka backbone"] --> notif
  ord --> kafka
  pay --> kafka
  inv --> kafka
  cat --> kafka

The gateway is a backend for frontend: it terminates authentication, applies rate limits, fans out to two or three services, and returns one response shaped for the client. It holds no business logic and no database. When a product page needs catalog data plus live stock, the gateway makes two parallel calls with a 300 ms budget each and degrades: if inventory is slow, the page renders with stockStatus: "unknown" rather than failing.

Synchronous calls exist in exactly three places: gateway to services, orders to inventory (reserve and commit need an answer), and orders to payments (the customer is waiting). Everything else is an event. That rule is worth writing on the wall, because every extra synchronous edge multiplies your availability: three services at 99.9 percent in series give 99.7 percent, and nobody notices the arithmetic until the incident review.

sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant G as Gateway
  participant O as Orders
  participant I as Inventory
  participant P as Payments
  participant K as Kafka
  participant N as Notifications
  C->>G: POST /checkout with token
  G->>G: verify JWT, rate limit
  G->>O: POST /orders s2s token traceparent
  O->>I: POST /reservations 800ms budget
  I-->>O: reservation held
  O->>P: POST /payments/intents
  P-->>O: intent requires_confirmation
  O-->>G: 201 order pending_payment
  C->>G: POST /payments/pi_1/confirm
  G->>P: confirm
  P->>K: payment.captured via outbox
  K->>O: consume payment.captured
  O->>I: POST /reservations/commit
  O->>K: order.paid
  K->>N: send confirmation email

46.6.4 Database schema

The schema work in this project is not new tables; it is the cut. Each service gets its own PostgreSQL database, its own migrations, its own connection pool and its own credentials.

Service Owns Duplicates as read model Never touches
auth users, credentials, sessions, refresh_tokens, roles — everything else
catalog categories, products, variants, reviews — inventory levels
inventory inventory, inventory_reservations, stock_movements variant_ref (id, sku, active) prices
orders orders, order_items, order_events, sagas, saga_steps product_snapshot on each item, user_ref (id, email hash) inventory rows
payments payments, payment_attempts, ledger_*, webhook_events order_ref (id, total, currency) order items
notification notifications, deliveries, templates, preferences, inbox user_contact (email, phone, locale, timezone) orders

Every service also gets the same two infrastructure tables:

-- One per service database. The transactional bridge to Kafka.
CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id            bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  event_id      uuid NOT NULL UNIQUE DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  aggregate     text NOT NULL,
  aggregate_id  text NOT NULL,
  type          text NOT NULL,          -- 'order.paid'
  schema_version int NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  payload       jsonb NOT NULL,
  trace_context text,                   -- W3C traceparent captured at write time
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  published_at  timestamptz
);
CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished_idx ON outbox (id) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

-- One per service database. Consumer-side idempotency.
CREATE TABLE inbox (
  consumer     text NOT NULL,
  event_id     uuid NOT NULL,
  topic        text NOT NULL,
  handled_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (consumer, event_id)
);
CREATE INDEX inbox_cleanup_idx ON inbox (handled_at);

And the read-model tables that replace the joins you lost. Orders can no longer join products, so it snapshots what it needs at order time:

-- orders service: what the customer actually bought, frozen forever.
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id     uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  variant_id   bigint NOT NULL,
  sku          text NOT NULL,
  title        text NOT NULL,           -- snapshot, not a join
  image_url    text,
  unit_price_cents bigint NOT NULL,     -- snapshot: the price they agreed to
  quantity     int NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, variant_id)
);

-- inventory service: a slim projection of catalog, kept by consuming catalog events.
CREATE TABLE variant_ref (
  variant_id   bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  sku          text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  active       boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
  updated_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  source_event uuid                       -- last event applied, for debugging
);

-- notification service: contact details, kept by consuming auth events.
CREATE TABLE user_contact (
  user_id      uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  email        citext,
  phone_e164   text,
  locale       text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'en',
  timezone     text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'UTC',
  updated_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

Snapshotting is not denormalisation for performance; it is correctness. An order line must show the price the customer paid, not today's price, and a service that joins live catalog data into old orders will eventually show a customer a receipt that does not match their card statement.

erDiagram
  ORDERS ||--o{ ORDER_ITEMS : snapshots
  ORDERS ||--o| SAGAS : coordinated_by
  ORDERS ||--o{ OUTBOX : publishes
  PAYMENTS ||--o{ LEDGER_ENTRIES : posts
  PAYMENTS ||--o{ INBOX : consumes
  INVENTORY ||--o{ INVENTORY_RESERVATIONS : holds
  INVENTORY ||--o{ VARIANT_REF : projects
  NOTIFICATIONS ||--o{ USER_CONTACT : reads
  ORDER_ITEMS {
    uuid order_id FK
    bigint variant_id
    text title
    bigint unit_price_cents
  }
  VARIANT_REF {
    bigint variant_id PK
    text sku
    boolean active
    uuid source_event
  }

46.6.5 APIs

Public, at the gateway. Same shapes as Projects 2 and 4, so clients do not change during the migration. The gateway adds composition endpoints.

Method Path Auth Composes Degradation Codes
GET /api/products/:slug optional catalog + inventory Renders without stock if inventory times out 200, 404, 503
GET /api/search optional catalog none 200, 422
POST /api/cart/items optional catalog price check + cart 409 if catalog is unavailable 200, 404, 409, 503
POST /api/checkout required orders (which fans out) none; checkout requires everything 201, 409, 502, 504
POST /api/payments/:id/confirm required payments none 200, 202, 402, 504
GET /api/orders/:id required orders + payments status Shows order without payment detail if payments is down 200, 403, 404
GET /api/me/notifications required notification Empty list with a warning header 200

Internal, service to service. Not public, authenticated with a service token, with an explicit timeout and idempotency contract.

Caller Callee Endpoint Timeout Idempotency Failure policy
gateway any GET /internal/health 300 ms — Remove from pool
gateway auth GET /internal/jwks 500 ms — Cached 300 s, stale allowed
orders inventory POST /internal/reservations 800 ms Idempotency-Key: order:{id} Retry once, then fail the saga
orders inventory POST /internal/reservations/:id/commit 800 ms key = reservation id Retry with backoff; saga step, safe forever
orders inventory POST /internal/reservations/:id/release 800 ms key = reservation id Compensation; retry until success
orders payments POST /internal/payments/intents 1 s Idempotency-Key: order:{id} Fail the saga; compensate the reservation
orders payments POST /internal/payments/:id/refund 2 s Idempotency-Key: refund:{orderId}:{n} Compensation; retry forever with alert
catalog inventory none — — Uses events only

Notice what is missing: nobody calls the notification service synchronously. Notifications are always an event, because a notification that fails must never fail the business action that caused it.

46.6.6 NestJS modules

A monorepo (Nx or npm workspaces) with one deployable per service and shared libraries that are versioned, not shared by reaching into each other's source.

platform/
  apps/
    gateway/        src/  Dockerfile  helm/
    auth/           src/  Dockerfile  helm/  migrations/
    catalog/        ...
    inventory/      ...
    orders/         ...
    payments/       ...
    notification/   ...
  libs/
    contracts/      events/*.ts  (typed event payloads + version)
    http-client/    resilient-client.ts (timeout, retry, breaker, propagation)
    kafka/          producer.ts consumer.ts outbox-relay.ts inbox.ts
    observability/  otel.ts logger.ts metrics.ts
    auth-guards/    jwt.guard.ts service-token.guard.ts roles.guard.ts

libs/http-client/resilient-client.ts — every synchronous hop goes through this.

import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { context, propagation, SpanStatusCode, trace } from '@opentelemetry/api';
import { CircuitBreaker } from './circuit-breaker';

export class UpstreamTimeout extends Error {}
export class UpstreamUnavailable extends Error {}

@Injectable()
export class ResilientClient {
  private readonly log = new Logger(ResilientClient.name);
  private readonly breakers = new Map<string, CircuitBreaker>();

  async call<T>(opts: {
    service: string; method: string; path: string; body?: unknown;
    timeoutMs: number; idempotencyKey?: string; retries?: number;
  }): Promise<T> {
    const breaker = this.breakers.get(opts.service)
      ?? this.breakers.set(opts.service, new CircuitBreaker({ failureThreshold: 5, halfOpenAfterMs: 15_000 })).get(opts.service)!;
    if (breaker.isOpen()) throw new UpstreamUnavailable(`${opts.service}_breaker_open`);

    const headers: Record<string, string> = {
      'content-type': 'application/json',
      authorization: `Bearer ${await this.serviceToken(opts.service)}`,
      ...(opts.idempotencyKey ? { 'idempotency-key': opts.idempotencyKey } : {}),
    };
    // Inject W3C traceparent so the callee's spans join this trace.
    propagation.inject(context.active(), headers);

    const span = trace.getTracer('http-client').startSpan(`${opts.service} ${opts.method} ${opts.path}`);
    const attempts = (opts.retries ?? 0) + 1;
    for (let i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) {
      const ac = new AbortController();
      const t = setTimeout(() => ac.abort(), opts.timeoutMs);
      try {
        const res = await fetch(`http://${opts.service}${opts.path}`, {
          method: opts.method, headers, signal: ac.signal,
          body: opts.body ? JSON.stringify(opts.body) : undefined,
        });
        if (res.status >= 500) throw new UpstreamUnavailable(`http_${res.status}`);
        breaker.recordSuccess(); span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.OK });
        return (await res.json()) as T;
      } catch (err) {
        breaker.recordFailure();
        const timedOut = (err as Error).name === 'AbortError';
        if (i === attempts) {
          span.recordException(err as Error);
          span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR });
          throw timedOut ? new UpstreamTimeout(`${opts.service}_timeout`) : err;
        }
        await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 100 * i + Math.random() * 100));
      } finally { clearTimeout(t); span.end(); }
    }
    throw new UpstreamUnavailable('unreachable');
  }
}

Retries are opt-in and only for idempotent calls. Retrying POST /internal/payments/intents without an idempotency key is how you create two payment intents for one order. The rule in the codebase: retries > 0 requires idempotencyKey, enforced by a type constraint or a runtime assertion.

libs/auth-guards/service-token.guard.ts — service-to-service authentication.

import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, ForbiddenException, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Reflector } from '@nestjs/core';
import { jwtVerify, createRemoteJWKSet } from 'jose';

/** Short-lived service JWTs issued by auth, aud = callee, sub = caller service. */
@Injectable()
export class ServiceTokenGuard implements CanActivate {
  private readonly jwks = createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(process.env.AUTH_JWKS_URL!));

  constructor(private readonly reflector: Reflector, private readonly me: string) {}

  async canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): Promise<boolean> {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    const token = (req.headers.authorization ?? '').replace(/^Bearer /, '');
    const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, this.jwks, {
      issuer: 'https://auth.internal', audience: this.me,
    });
    const allowed = this.reflector.get<string[]>('allowedCallers', ctx.getHandler()) ?? [];
    if (allowed.length && !allowed.includes(String(payload.sub))) {
      throw new ForbiddenException({ code: 'caller_not_allowed', caller: payload.sub });
    }
    req.caller = payload.sub;
    return true;
  }
}

A network policy that says "only pods labelled app=orders may reach inventory:3000" is the second layer; the token is the first. Do both. mTLS through a service mesh is the third, and worth it only once you have more services than people.

libs/kafka/outbox-relay.ts — the same relay, now in six services.

@Injectable()
export class OutboxRelay {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource, private readonly producer: Producer,
              private readonly topicFor: (type: string) => string) {}

  @Interval(500)
  async tick() {
    await this.ds.transaction(async (em) => {
      const rows = await em.query(
        `SELECT id, event_id, type, aggregate_id, payload, schema_version, trace_context
           FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL
          ORDER BY id LIMIT 200 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`);
      if (!rows.length) return;
      await this.producer.send({
        topic: this.topicFor(rows[0].type),
        messages: rows.map((r: any) => ({
          key: r.aggregate_id,
          value: JSON.stringify(r.payload),
          headers: {
            eventId: r.event_id, eventType: r.type,
            schemaVersion: String(r.schema_version),
            traceparent: r.trace_context ?? '',
          },
        })),
      });
      await em.query(`UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() WHERE id = ANY($1)`,
        [rows.map((r: any) => r.id)]);
    });
  }
}

Note that messages from one batch may span several topics in a real implementation; group them by topic before sending. And note the trace_context column: it is what makes an event's consumer span attach to the trace of the HTTP request that caused it, which is the difference between a trace that ends at the outbox and one that reaches the email.

46.6.7 PostgreSQL design decisions

A database per service, physically separate. Not a schema per service in one instance, at least not permanently: shared instances mean shared connection limits, shared vacuum pressure, shared failover and, eventually, someone writing a cross-schema join "just this once". Start with separate databases on one instance during the migration if budget requires, and split instances before the second team joins.

No distributed transactions. There is no BEGIN that spans orders and inventory. The saga replaces it, and every step is a local transaction plus an idempotent remote call. Say this out loud when someone proposes two-phase commit: XA across services couples their availability, which is the thing you were trying to avoid.

Eventual consistency, with names. After order.paid, the notification service knows within a few seconds. Between those moments the system is inconsistent, and that is fine as long as it is bounded and observable. Set an SLO on event lag (p99 under 5 s), alarm on it, and make the UI honest ("we are preparing your confirmation") rather than pretending.

Migrations, per service, per pipeline. Each service runs its own migration Job before its own rollout. Expand-contract is now mandatory rather than good practice, because two versions of a service run simultaneously during every rollout and a consumer may lag a version behind a producer for hours. The order is always: add the new nullable column, deploy code that writes both, backfill in batches, deploy code that reads new, then drop the old in a later release. Never in one deploy.

Connection pools. Six services times three pods times a pool of 10 is 180 connections; each database sees only its own share now, which is one of the quiet benefits of the split. Set max per pod deliberately and add PgBouncer per database when a service scales past about 100 connections.

Reference data drift. variant_ref in inventory is a projection built from catalog events. It will drift — a missed event, a bug, a topic retention expiry during an outage. Build a nightly reconciliation job that compares projections against the owner and reports differences, and expose projection_drift_rows as a metric. Every event-driven system that has run for two years and never reconciled is quietly wrong somewhere.

46.6.8 Redis usage

Owner Key Purpose TTL
gateway rl:{userOrIp}:{route} Rate limiting at the edge, sliding window in Lua 60 s
gateway jwks:auth Cached JWKS so every request does not call auth 300 s
gateway compose:product:{slug} Composed product payload 30 s
catalog product:{slug}, category:tree Same as Project 2 300 s
inventory stock:{variantId} Read-mostly stock badge 15 s
orders lock:order:{id} Advisory lock across multi-step flows 15 s
payments breaker:psp, idem:{route}:{key} As in Project 4 varies
notification buckets, breakers, ws:user:{id} As in Project 3 varies

Each service gets its own Redis logical database or its own instance. A shared Redis with shared key prefixes is a shared failure domain and, worse, a shared namespace where one team's FLUSHDB during a local debugging session takes down someone else's rate limiter. The gateway's Redis is the most critical one: if it is down, choose fail-open for rate limiting and fail-closed for nothing.

46.6.9 Messaging usage

Topics and ownership. One producing service per topic. Nobody writes to a topic they do not own.

Topic Owner Partitions Key Consumers Retention
auth.events.v1 auth 6 user_id notification, orders 7 days
catalog.events.v1 catalog 12 product_id inventory, search indexer 7 days
inventory.events.v1 inventory 12 variant_id catalog, orders 7 days
order.events.v1 orders 12 order_id payments, notification, analytics 30 days
payment.events.v1 payments 12 order_id orders, notification, analytics 30 days
*.dlq each 3 original key none; drained by the replay tool 30 days

Schema-compatibility policy. Write it down, put it in the repository, and enforce it in CI. The policy:

  1. Every event has eventId, eventType, schemaVersion, occurredAt, aggregateId and a data object.
  2. Schemas live in libs/contracts, one file per event and version, published as a versioned package.
  3. Backward compatible changes only within a major version: add optional fields, add enum values that consumers treat as unknown, never rename, never change a type, never make an optional field required, never remove a field consumers use.
  4. A breaking change means a new topic (order.events.v2) and a period where the producer writes both. Consumers migrate on their own schedule; the old topic is retired only when its consumer-group lag has been zero and its consumer list empty for two weeks.
  5. Consumers must ignore unknown fields. This one rule prevents most breakages.
  6. CI runs a compatibility check comparing the schema on the branch with the schema on main and fails the build on a backward-incompatible change without a version bump.

Confluent Schema Registry with Avro or Protobuf enforces this mechanically; a JSON Schema file plus a CI check enforces it well enough for a platform this size. Pick one and make it non-negotiable.

Consumer groups, retries, DLQ. One consumer group per service per topic, named {service}-{topic}. Handlers are idempotent through the inbox table. Retries use the retry-topic ladder from Project 3 (30 s, 5 min, 30 min, DLQ). Consumer lag is a first-class alert per group, because in a distributed system lag is how "everything is green but nothing works" manifests.

Outbox and inbox everywhere. Every producing service writes to its outbox inside the business transaction; every consuming service records the eventId in its inbox inside the handling transaction. Six services, twelve tables, one pattern. The uniformity is the point: an on-call engineer who understands it in one service understands it in all of them.

46.6.10 Testing strategy

The test pyramid changes shape. Unit and integration tests stay per service, but a whole new layer appears between them and end-to-end: contract tests.

  • Unit — pure logic, as before.
