  • Integration (per service) — Testcontainers with that service's PostgreSQL, Redis and Redpanda; the service's own HTTP surface and consumers.
  • Contract (consumer-driven) — with Pact or an equivalent, the orders service (consumer) declares "when I POST /internal/reservations with this body, I expect a 201 with {reservationId, expiresAt}". That expectation becomes a pact file; the inventory service's pipeline replays it against the real service and fails if it no longer holds. Do the same for events: a consumer declares the fields it reads, and the producer's build verifies its schema still provides them. This is the mechanism that lets six teams deploy independently without a shared staging traffic jam.
  • End-to-end (few, high value) — five journeys against a fully composed environment: browse to order to paid to notified; cancel unpaid; refund; login and session revocation; search after a catalog update propagates.

The ten most important test cases:

  1. Cross-service saga happy path — checkout completes; assert order paid, reservation committed, ledger balanced, notification sent, and one trace containing all six services.
  2. Inventory times out during reserve — orders retries once, then fails the saga with 409; no orphan reservation; the customer sees a clear error.
  3. Payments succeeds but orders never hears — drop the payment.captured event; the reconciliation job in orders detects a captured payment with an unpaid order within 5 minutes and completes the saga.
  4. Duplicate event delivery — replay 10,000 events from a topic; inbox dedupe means zero duplicate side effects and zero duplicate emails.
  5. Contract break is caught — remove a field from order.paid in the producer; the notification service's pact verification fails the producer's build.
  6. Schema evolution works — add an optional field, deploy the producer first, and assert old consumers are unaffected; then add a required field and assert CI blocks it.
  7. Gateway degradation — kill inventory; product pages still render with unknown stock, checkout returns a clean 503, and no gateway thread pool is exhausted.
  8. Auth key rotation across services — rotate the signing key; every service picks up the new JWKS within 300 s with zero rejected valid tokens.
  9. Compensation across the network — force commit-reservation to fail permanently; the saga refunds the payment and restocks; the final state is consistent and the customer is notified.
  10. Trace completeness — assert programmatically that a checkout trace contains spans from gateway, orders, inventory, payments, Kafka producer, Kafka consumer and notification, with one trace id.

46.6.11 Docker

Each service keeps its own Dockerfile (the multi-stage shape from Project 1). Local development uses one compose file with profiles so you can run a subset:

x-service: &service
  build: { context: ., dockerfile: apps/${SVC}/Dockerfile }
  environment: &common
    KAFKA_BROKERS: redpanda:9092
    OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: http://otel-collector:4318
    AUTH_JWKS_URL: http://auth:3000/.well-known/jwks.json
  depends_on: [redpanda, otel-collector]

services:
  redpanda:
    image: redpandadata/redpanda:latest
    command: ["redpanda","start","--smp","2","--memory","2G","--overprovisioned",
              "--kafka-addr","PLAINTEXT://0.0.0.0:9092","--advertise-kafka-addr","PLAINTEXT://redpanda:9092"]
  pg-auth:      { image: postgres:16, environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev, POSTGRES_DB: auth } }
  pg-catalog:   { image: postgres:16, environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev, POSTGRES_DB: catalog } }
  pg-inventory: { image: postgres:16, environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev, POSTGRES_DB: inventory } }
  pg-orders:    { image: postgres:16, environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev, POSTGRES_DB: orders } }
  pg-payments:  { image: postgres:16, environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev, POSTGRES_DB: payments } }
  pg-notify:    { image: postgres:16, environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev, POSTGRES_DB: notify } }
  redis:        { image: redis:7-alpine }
  otel-collector:
    image: otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:latest
    volumes: ["./ops/otel-collector.yaml:/etc/otelcol-contrib/config.yaml:ro"]
    ports: ["4318:4318"]
  jaeger:  { image: jaegertracing/all-in-one:latest, ports: ["16686:16686"] }
  grafana: { image: grafana/grafana:latest, ports: ["3001:3000"] }
  gateway:
    build: { context: ., dockerfile: apps/gateway/Dockerfile }
    environment: { <<: *common, REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379 }
    ports: ["8080:3000"]
  orders:
    build: { context: ., dockerfile: apps/orders/Dockerfile }
    environment: { <<: *common, DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:dev@pg-orders:5432/orders }
  # ...one block per service, same shape

Be honest about the cost: this compose file starts fifteen containers and needs about 8 GiB of RAM. That is a real tax on every developer's laptop and on every new joiner's first day, and it is one of the items in section 46.6.19.

Kubernetes, one Helm chart per service. The chart is a small template with per-service values:

# apps/orders/helm/values.yaml
replicaCount: 3
image: { repository: ghcr.io/acme/orders, tag: "" }        # set by CI to the SHA
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 384Mi }
  limits:   { cpu: "1",  memory: 768Mi }
probes:
  liveness:  { path: /health/live,  initialDelaySeconds: 10, periodSeconds: 10 }
  readiness: { path: /health/ready, periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 3 }
podDisruptionBudget: { minAvailable: 2 }
hpa: { enabled: true, minReplicas: 3, maxReplicas: 20, targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 65 }
migrationJob: { enabled: true, command: ["node","dist/migrate.js"] }
env:
  KAFKA_BROKERS: kafka-bootstrap:9092
  OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: orders
secrets: [DATABASE_URL, SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY]
networkPolicy:
  ingressFrom: [gateway]
  egressTo: [pg-orders, kafka, inventory, payments]

/health/live returns 200 if the process is alive. /health/ready returns 503 when the database pool cannot serve or Kafka producer is disconnected — but not when a downstream service is down, or one slow dependency will cascade into every pod in the cluster being marked unready at once. That distinction has caused more self-inflicted outages than any other Kubernetes setting.

46.6.12 CI/CD

One pipeline per service, triggered by path filters so a catalog change does not rebuild payments.

name: orders
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["apps/orders/**", "libs/**"]
  pull_request:
    paths: ["apps/orders/**", "libs/**"]

jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres: { image: postgres:16, env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev, POSTGRES_DB: orders_test }, ports: ["5432:5432"], options: --health-cmd "pg_isready -U postgres" --health-interval 5s --health-retries 10 }
      redis:    { image: redis:7, ports: ["6379:6379"] }
      redpanda: { image: redpandadata/redpanda:latest, ports: ["9092:9092"] }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx nx lint orders && npx nx typecheck orders
      - run: npx nx test orders
      - run: npm run schema:compat -- --service orders     # event compatibility gate
      - run: npx nx run orders:test-integration
      - run: npx nx run orders:pact-consumer                # publish consumer pacts
      - run: npx nx run orders:pact-verify                  # verify pacts others hold on us
  build:
    needs: verify
    steps:
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with: { file: apps/orders/Dockerfile, push: true, tags: "ghcr.io/acme/orders:${{ github.sha }}" }
      - uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with: { image-ref: "ghcr.io/acme/orders:${{ github.sha }}", severity: "CRITICAL,HIGH", exit-code: "1" }
      - run: npx @cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm --output-file sbom.json
  deploy-staging:
    needs: build
    steps:
      - run: helm upgrade --install orders apps/orders/helm --namespace staging --set image.tag=${{ github.sha }} --wait --timeout 5m
      - run: ./scripts/smoke.sh https://orders.staging.internal
      - run: npx nx run e2e:checkout --env staging
  can-i-deploy:
    needs: deploy-staging
    steps:
      - run: npx pact-broker can-i-deploy --pacticipant orders --version ${{ github.sha }} --to-environment production
  deploy-production:
    needs: can-i-deploy
    environment: production
    steps:
      - run: helm upgrade --install orders apps/orders/helm --namespace prod --set image.tag=${{ github.sha }} --wait --timeout 10m
      - run: ./scripts/smoke.sh https://orders.internal || helm rollback orders --namespace prod

can-i-deploy is the gate that makes independent deployment safe: it asks the contract broker whether this version of orders is compatible with the versions of its providers and consumers currently in production. Without it, "deploy independently" quietly means "break each other independently".

Migrations run as a Helm pre-upgrade hook Job per service. Rollback is helm rollback, which is fast — but only safe if the migration was expand-only, which is why the expand-contract rule is enforced by review and, ideally, by a migration linter.

46.6.13 Observability

Tracing is the backbone. Every service initialises OpenTelemetry at boot, before any other import:

// libs/observability/otel.ts - imported first in every main.ts
import { NodeSDK } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-node';
import { getNodeAutoInstrumentations } from '@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node';
import { OTLPTraceExporter } from '@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-http';
import { Resource } from '@opentelemetry/resources';

export function startTelemetry(serviceName: string) {
  const sdk = new NodeSDK({
    resource: new Resource({
      'service.name': serviceName,
      'service.version': process.env.GIT_SHA ?? 'dev',
      'deployment.environment': process.env.ENV ?? 'local',
    }),
    traceExporter: new OTLPTraceExporter({ url: `${process.env.OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT}/v1/traces` }),
    instrumentations: [getNodeAutoInstrumentations({
      '@opentelemetry/instrumentation-fs': { enabled: false },   // noisy, useless here
    })],
  });
  sdk.start();
  process.on('SIGTERM', () => void sdk.shutdown());
}

Auto-instrumentation covers HTTP, PostgreSQL, Redis and KafkaJS. What it cannot do is bridge the outbox: the event is written now and published later, so you capture traceparent into the outbox.trace_context column at write time and restore it as the parent when the relay produces. Do that, and a single trace runs from the customer's click, through orders, into Kafka, out to notification, and ends at the email provider call. That trace is the single most valuable artefact this project produces.

Metrics, standardised across services through the shared library, so every dashboard works for every service: http_server_duration_seconds{service,route,status}, http_client_duration_seconds{service,upstream,status}, breaker_state{service,upstream}, kafka_consumer_lag{service,topic,group}, outbox_lag_seconds{service}, inbox_duplicates_total{service}, saga_active{state}, projection_drift_rows{projection}, plus each service's business metrics.

Log fields, standardised: timestamp, level, service, version, env, traceId, spanId, requestId, caller, userId, route, status, durationMs, outcome. Ship them to one place with the trace id indexed, so you can pivot from a slow trace to its logs in one click.

Shared dashboards. Build three, and make them the same for every service: a service dashboard (RPS, error rate, latency percentiles, saturation, dependency latencies, breaker states) templated by service name; a platform dashboard (all services' error budgets, the slowest dependency edge, Kafka lag across all groups, outbox lag across all services); and a journey dashboard (checkout funnel with per-step latency taken from traces, so a product manager can see where customers are lost).

Alerts. Per service: error rate above 2 percent for 5 minutes; p99 above the SLO for 10 minutes; readiness failures. Platform-wide: any consumer group lag above 10,000 or growing for 15 minutes; any outbox lag above 120 s; breaker open for more than 5 minutes; projection_drift_rows > 0; saga stuck over 30 minutes. Route alerts to the owning service's on-call, and make the platform-wide ones page the platform rota — otherwise every Kafka alert wakes six people.

46.6.14 Failure scenarios

Failure Expected behaviour How you test it
Inventory service down Product pages render without stock; checkout returns 503 with code: inventory_unavailable; breaker opens; no cascading thread exhaustion Scale inventory to 0 replicas; run the journey suite
Inventory slow, 3 s responses 800 ms timeout fires; orders fails fast; gateway p99 unaffected for browse Inject latency with a toxiproxy sidecar or a chaos mesh delay
Kafka unavailable for 20 minutes Services keep serving; outbox grows; outbox_lag_seconds alarms; on recovery everything drains in order with no loss Stop brokers during a soak test
Consumer group rebalance storm Lag spikes then recovers; no duplicate side effects thanks to the inbox Roll a consumer deployment repeatedly under load
One service deployed with a breaking event change can-i-deploy blocks it in CI; if forced, consumers log unknown-schema and DLQ the message rather than crashing Deliberately break a schema in a staging branch
Auth down Existing tokens keep working for up to 10 minutes via cached JWKS; new logins fail; the rest of the platform serves Scale auth to 0; assert browse and checkout with an existing token
Payments captures but order.paid never publishes Reconciliation in orders finds captured payments with unpaid orders within 5 minutes and completes the saga Drop the event in a test harness
Network partition between orders and inventory Reserve times out; saga compensates; reservation may exist in inventory and is released by its own expiry sweeper Partition with a network policy mid-checkout
Gateway Redis down Rate limiting fails open with an alert; JWKS served from in-process cache; requests continue Stop the gateway's Redis
Cluster node loss with 3 of 9 pods PDBs and multi-AZ spread keep every service serving; HPA replaces pods Drain a node during the load test
Database failover on one service That service returns 503 for 10 to 30 s; others unaffected; breakers prevent cascade Failover the orders database in staging
Clock skew across services Token validation and HMAC windows fail; NTP alert fires Skew one node's clock by 10 minutes

Chaos test plan. Run it monthly in staging under a 100 req/s synthetic load, one experiment at a time, with a written hypothesis and an abort condition:

  1. Kill 30 percent of pods of one service (hypothesis: no user-visible errors).
  2. Add 500 ms of latency to one dependency edge (hypothesis: breakers trip, p99 degrades under 20 percent, no cascade).
  3. Blackhole one service entirely (hypothesis: documented degradation only).
  4. Stop Kafka for 15 minutes (hypothesis: zero data loss, full drain within 10 minutes).
  5. Fail over one database (hypothesis: under 60 s of errors for that service only).
  6. Fill a disk on one broker (hypothesis: producers back off, alerts fire, no silent loss).
  7. Deploy a deliberately broken image (hypothesis: readiness fails, rollout halts, no traffic served).
  8. Expire a service token signing key early (hypothesis: alert fires, documented recovery under 10 minutes).

Record the result of every experiment. A chaos plan you run once is theatre; one you run monthly and whose findings change the code is engineering.

46.6.15 Scaling strategy

1x — the platform you just built. Three replicas per service, one database each, a three-broker Kafka, one Redis per service. The bottleneck at this scale is you: six pipelines, six on-call runbooks and fifteen containers on a laptop. Be able to say, honestly, that the monolith would have served this traffic on two pods.

10x — 8,000 req/s at the gateway. Scale services independently, which is now the payoff: catalog goes to 20 pods because it takes most of the read traffic; payments stays at 3 because it is bounded by the provider. Kafka partitions increase for the busy topics (plan them at creation). Add read replicas per service database where the read/write ratio justifies it. The gateway becomes the thing to watch: it fans out, so its concurrency and its outbound connection pools are the first saturation point, and it needs its own HPA on both CPU and in-flight requests.

100x — 80,000 req/s, multi-region. Now the interesting decisions arrive. Catalog reads move to the edge with a CDN and a stale-while-revalidate policy. Search moves out of PostgreSQL into a dedicated cluster fed by catalog.events. Kafka gets tiered storage or shorter retention plus an archive. The write path is regionalised: either an active-passive design with one write region and read replicas everywhere (simple, correct, higher write latency for distant users) or an active-active design with per-region ownership of order ids and a conflict policy (fast, and a genuinely hard distributed-systems problem). Choose active-passive unless someone can articulate why the extra complexity is worth it in revenue.

The scaling insight that matters: at 100x, the platform's limits are almost never CPU. They are partition counts you chose two years ago, connection pools, a single hot row somewhere, a provider's rate limit, and how quickly a human can understand a trace during an incident.

46.6.16 Security checklist

  • The gateway is the only ingress; service pods have no public route, enforced by network policy and by ingress configuration.
  • End-user JWTs are verified at the gateway; services re-verify rather than trusting a header, because a compromised pod inside the mesh must not be able to impersonate a user.
  • Service-to-service auth with short-lived JWTs (5 minutes), aud set to the callee, sub to the caller, and an explicit allowed-callers list per endpoint.
  • Network policies default-deny; every allowed edge is declared in the service's chart and reviewed.
  • mTLS between services if a mesh is in place; TLS to every database and broker regardless.
  • Secrets from a secret manager (External Secrets, Vault or cloud-native); no secrets in charts, images or environment files in git.
  • Per-service database credentials with least privilege; no service can read another's database even if it wanted to.
  • Rate limits at the gateway per user and per IP, plus per-service internal limits so one misbehaving service cannot exhaust another.
  • Kafka ACLs: a service may produce only to the topics it owns and consume only what it declares.
  • Event payloads contain no unnecessary personal data; use ids and let the consumer look up what it needs, or accept the duplication deliberately and document it for deletion requests.
  • Images signed and scanned; only signed images admitted by policy; SBOM published per build.
  • Audit logging at the gateway (who called what) and inside each service for privileged actions.
  • A documented deletion procedure that reaches every service holding a copy of a user's data, including projections and Kafka retention.

46.6.17 Stretch goals

A service mesh (Istio or Linkerd) for mTLS, retries and traffic shifting, then a measurement of what it cost in latency and complexity. Canary deployments with automated analysis on error rate and latency. gRPC for the internal hops, with a measurement of the payload-size and latency difference against JSON. CQRS with a dedicated read model for the order history. Event sourcing for one aggregate only, so you feel the difference rather than reading about it. Multi-tenancy with per-tenant quotas. A developer platform: one command that spins up a namespace with only the services you are changing and stubs the rest. Cost attribution per service, which changes architectural conversations more than any diagram. And a written architecture decision record for every major choice, because in eighteen months nobody will remember why the gateway does composition and not the client.

46.6.18 Definition of done

  • Six services plus a gateway, each with its own database, pipeline, chart, dashboards and runbook.
  • All Project 2 and Project 4 journeys pass end to end against the composed platform.
  • No service reads another service's database; enforced by credentials and verified by a review checklist.
  • Outbox and inbox in every service; a 10,000-event replay produces zero duplicate side effects.
  • Written schema-compatibility policy, enforced by a CI check that blocks incompatible changes.
  • Consumer-driven contract tests with can-i-deploy gating production deploys.
  • One checkout trace contains spans from all six services, including across Kafka; asserted by an automated test.
  • Saga across services completes, compensates correctly, and never leaves a mixed state under the race tests.
  • Reconciliation jobs for the two riskiest projections, with a drift metric that has been at zero for a week.
  • Chaos plan executed at least once end to end, with written results and at least two fixes that came out of it.
  • Independent deploys demonstrated: three services deployed in one afternoon with no coordination and no downtime.
  • Strangler-fig plan written, with the monolith still able to serve every route until the last cutover.
  • Section 46.6.19 written from your own experience, not copied from mine.

46.6.19 What got harder

This is the section to write with complete honesty, because it is the one a hiring manager will read most carefully. Everything below genuinely got worse when the monolith became a platform. For each, the mitigation that actually works.

1. Local development. One npm run start:dev became fifteen containers and 8 GiB of RAM. Mitigation: a docker compose profile per journey so you run three services, not fifteen; contract stubs generated from pacts for the ones you are not changing; and a shared development namespace in the cluster with per-developer overrides.

2. Debugging. A bug that used to be one stack trace is now spread across four services and a topic. Mitigation: tracing with propagated context everywhere including the outbox, one log store with traceId indexed, and a rule that every error response carries a traceId the customer can quote.

3. Transactions. BEGIN ... COMMIT across orders and inventory no longer exists. Every multi-service change is a saga with compensation, and compensation is code nobody exercises except during incidents. Mitigation: sagas defined as data, every step idempotent, compensation paths covered by tests that run on every build, and a saga_compensations_total metric so you know when they actually fire.

4. Data consistency. The catalog says a product is active; inventory's projection has not caught up; a customer buys something that no longer exists. Mitigation: bounded staleness with an SLO on event lag, nightly reconciliation jobs per projection with a drift metric, and UI copy that is honest about eventual consistency.

5. Testing. End-to-end tests need the whole platform, so they are slow and flaky, and the temptation is to delete them. Mitigation: invest in contract tests so that end-to-end tests can be few (five journeys), and treat a flaky e2e test as a production bug, not a test bug — nine times out of ten it is telling you about a real race.

6. Deployment coordination. Independent deploys are only independent if the contracts hold. Our first breaking event change took down notifications for 40 minutes. Mitigation: the schema policy, the CI compatibility gate, can-i-deploy, and the rule that consumers ignore unknown fields.

7. Latency. Checkout gained about 120 ms of pure network and serialisation overhead compared with the monolith's in-process calls. Mitigation: keep synchronous hops to a minimum (three, in this design), set explicit budgets per hop, parallelise fan-out at the gateway, and accept the rest as the price of the architecture. Say the number out loud; it stops the argument from being about feelings.

8. Failure modes multiplied. Every synchronous edge added timeout, partial failure and retry-duplication. Mitigation: the ResilientClient as the only way to make a call, timeouts shorter than the caller's budget, idempotency keys on every retryable write, and breakers so a slow service fails fast rather than exhausting its callers.

9. Operational surface. Six pipelines, six databases to back up and patch, six sets of alerts, six runbooks, plus Kafka. On-call got noticeably harder. Mitigation: uniformity — one chart template, one metrics library, one logging shape, one runbook template — so that knowing one service means knowing all of them. Ruthlessly delete alerts that never lead to action.

10. Cost. Infrastructure roughly tripled: more pods with per-pod overhead, six databases instead of one, a Kafka cluster, more inter-AZ traffic, more observability data. Mitigation: right-size requests and limits from real usage, use one database instance with several databases until traffic justifies splitting, sample traces (tail-based, keeping all errors), and put a cost-per-service dashboard in front of the team.

11. Onboarding. A new engineer used to be productive in two days; now they need a mental model of six services and an event backbone. Mitigation: an architecture decision record per major choice, one diagram that is actually maintained, a "your first change" guide that touches exactly one service, and pairing for the first cross-service change.

12. Reasoning about correctness. In the monolith, a foreign key guaranteed a product existed. Now it is an event you hope arrived. Mitigation: accept that constraints do not cross service boundaries, replace them with reconciliation and monitoring, and be explicit in design reviews about which invariants are enforced and which are merely observed.

The strangler-fig migration plan. You do not rewrite. You put the gateway in front of the monolith and move one route at a time:

  1. Deploy the gateway in front of the monolith. It proxies 100 percent of traffic and does nothing else. Now you have a place to stand. Add authentication and rate limiting here first.
  2. Extract auth. It has the fewest inbound dependencies. The monolith starts verifying JWTs against the new service's JWKS instead of its own tables. Run both for a week with a comparison log.
  3. Extract notification. It is asynchronous and nobody blocks on it, so a mistake is cheap. The monolith publishes order.placed to Kafka; the new service consumes. Turn off the monolith's email code only after a week of shadow running where both send to a test inbox and you diff them.
  4. Extract catalog reads. The gateway routes GET /products/* to the new catalog service, which reads a replicated copy while the monolith still owns writes. Compare responses in shadow mode. Then move writes and stop dual-writing.
  5. Extract inventory. The riskiest one, because it owns money-adjacent state. Move the tables, expose the internal API, and change the monolith's InventoryService to a thin HTTP client — which is trivial precisely because Project 2 forbade cross-module table access. This is where that lint rule pays for itself.
  6. Extract payments, then orders. Payments first (it is already isolated behind webhooks and a provider), orders last, because orders is the orchestrator and should be the final thing to move.
  7. Delete the monolith's code path by path, not in one commit. Keep the route in the gateway pointing at the monolith until the new service has served that route in production for two weeks with equal or better error rates.

At every step: dual-run, compare, and keep the old path deployable for one rollback window. If you cannot roll back a step in ten minutes, the step is too big. Splitting the monolith is not one project; it is fifteen small ones, and the discipline of keeping the system shippable throughout is the actual senior skill on display.

Senior Checklist — Part 46

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I have built refresh-token rotation with reuse detection and proven it with a test
  • I can prevent overselling under concurrency with an atomic conditional update, and prove it with 50 parallel requests
  • I can explain why my inventory lock ordering makes deadlocks impossible
  • I have written a consumer that is idempotent through an inbox table, and killed it mid-flight to prove it
  • I can implement quiet hours correctly across a DST transition in a named IANA timezone
  • I can build a double-entry ledger and a continuous invariant check that has never fired
  • I know exactly what my system does when a payment provider times out mid-charge
  • I can write a claim query with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and explain every clause and the index it uses
  • I can implement lease-based takeover and explain why leases beat locks for long-running work
  • I can elect a leader with a PostgreSQL advisory lock and explain what it does not guarantee
  • I can compare a PostgreSQL queue with BullMQ using my own measured numbers
  • I can propagate a trace across HTTP and Kafka, including through an outbox
  • I can write a schema-compatibility policy and enforce it in CI
  • I can describe a strangler-fig migration in steps that are each individually reversible
  • I can name twelve things that got harder when I split the monolith, and the mitigation for each

Part 46 — Key Takeaways

  • Build the projects in order; each one assumes the concepts the previous one taught, and skipping ahead means distributing systems you do not yet understand.
  • The definition of done, not the feature list, is the assignment: metrics, alerts, a runbook, a real deployment and a tested rollback are part of "finished".
  • Authentication teaches every hard theme in miniature: hashing, expiry, replay, rotation, revocation, rate limiting and key management, all in a system small enough to hold in your head.
  • Overselling, double charging and duplicate notifications are all the same bug — a race that application code cannot win — and the fix is always in the database: an atomic conditional update, a unique constraint, or a row lock.
  • At-least-once delivery plus an inbox table is how you get effectively-once behaviour; there is no exactly-once transport, and anyone who says otherwise is selling something.
  • The outbox pattern is the only correct way to publish an event about a database change: same transaction, then relay, then dedupe at the consumer.
  • Money needs a double-entry ledger with a continuous zero-sum invariant check, and financial rows are append-only forever; reversals are entries, not updates.
  • A PostgreSQL queue with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, leases and heartbeats is the right choice below a few thousand jobs per second and whenever enqueue must be transactional with a business write.
  • Leader election reduces duplicate work; a unique execution key prevents duplicate effects. You need both, and only the second one is a guarantee.
  • Every synchronous call you move across the network gains four failure modes: slow, failed, duplicated and partially applied. Count your synchronous edges and keep them few.
  • A database per service is what makes microservices real; shared tables produce a distributed monolith with worse latency and the same coupling.
  • Events are a public API: write the compatibility policy, enforce it in CI, and make consumers ignore unknown fields.
  • Tracing propagated across HTTP, Kafka and the outbox is the single most valuable thing you build in a distributed system, because it is the only way debugging stays possible.
  • Splitting a monolith makes local development, debugging, transactions, consistency, testing, latency, cost and onboarding all harder; do it when independent deployment and independent scaling are worth that bill, and be able to name the bill.

Part 47 — Real-World Architecture Patterns

A pattern is not a library and not a framework. It is a named shape of a solution that has been rediscovered so many times that giving it a name saves everyone an hour of whiteboard time. When you say "we will put the outbox in front of Kafka", four people in the room stop arguing about dual writes and start arguing about the table schema, which is the argument worth having.

This part is a working catalogue. Thirty patterns, each with the same ten sub-sections, so you can skim to the one you need and read only the parts that matter to your decision. The two sub-sections most engineers skip are the two that save you: When NOT to use and Edge cases and failure modes. Patterns are dangerous exactly because they sound smart. A pattern applied to a problem you do not have is pure cost: more code, more moving parts, more pages at 03:00, and no benefit.

Several of these patterns are covered in depth elsewhere in the book. Circuit breakers, retries, timeouts and backpressure belong to Part 20 — Reliability Engineering. Outbox, inbox, saga and idempotency belong to Part 19 — Distributed Transactions. Cache-aside, rate limiting and token buckets belong to Part 16 — Caching and Redis. Here they get a short, catalogue-style entry with a different example, so this part works as a reference you can read end to end without duplicating three hundred pages.

One rule runs through everything below. Before you adopt a pattern, ask the senior questions: Can it time out? Can it fail? Can it become slow? Can it duplicate? Can it return a wrong response? Can it partially succeed? A pattern that does not improve at least one of those answers is decoration.

47.1 API Gateway

Problem

You have twelve services behind one product. Every one of them needs TLS termination, authentication, rate limiting, request logging, CORS headers, request size limits and a stable public hostname. If each service implements all of that, you have twelve copies of your auth logic, twelve places where a security fix must land, and twelve different opinions about what a 429 body looks like. Clients also suffer: the mobile app must know that orders live at orders.internal, payments at payments.internal, and that one of them moved last week.

Solution

Put one component at the edge that owns everything cross-cutting and routes to internal services by path or host. Clients see one origin (api.shop.com). The gateway authenticates the caller once, attaches a verified identity header, enforces global limits, and forwards the request. Internal services trust the gateway and stop re-implementing the edge.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  M["Mobile app"] --> GW["API Gateway"]
  W["Web app"] --> GW
  P["Partner API client"] --> GW
  GW -->|"/orders/*"| OS["Order Service"]
  GW -->|"/payments/*"| PS["Payment Service"]
  GW -->|"/catalog/*"| CS["Catalog Service"]
  GW --> AU["Auth: JWKS verify"]
  GW --> RL["Redis: rate limit counters"]

Example

A Kubernetes ingress that terminates TLS, applies a global rate limit, caps body size and strips any client-supplied identity header before it reaches the service.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: public-api
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "200"          # per client IP
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-burst-multiplier: "3"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "2m"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "15"  # seconds
    # never let a client forge the identity the gateway injects
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/configuration-snippet: |
      proxy_set_header X-Auth-User-Id "";
      proxy_set_header X-Request-Id $request_id;
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts: ["api.shop.com"]
      secretName: api-shop-tls
  rules:
    - host: api.shop.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend: { service: { name: order-service, port: { number: 80 } } }
          - path: /payments
            pathType: Prefix
            backend: { service: { name: payment-service, port: { number: 80 } } }

Inside NestJS, the service trusts the gateway's headers only when the request arrived on the internal port, and never parses the raw Authorization header again:

@Injectable()
export class GatewayIdentityGuard implements CanActivate {
  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    const userId = req.headers['x-auth-user-id'];
    if (typeof userId !== 'string' || userId.length === 0) {
      throw new UnauthorizedException('missing gateway identity');
    }
    req.principal = { userId, scopes: String(req.headers['x-auth-scopes'] ?? '').split(',') };
    return true;
  }
}

Advantages

  • One place for TLS, auth, rate limiting, CORS, body limits and access logs.
  • Clients get one stable hostname; internal topology can change freely.
  • Security fixes land once. So do observability defaults such as a generated X-Request-Id.
  • Cheap protocol translation at the edge: public HTTP/JSON, internal gRPC or HTTP/2.

Disadvantages

  • It is a single point of failure and a single point of config failure. A bad route rule takes down everything.
  • It becomes a dumping ground. "Just add the coupon logic in the gateway" is how gateways turn into monoliths with a Lua plugin system.
  • One more network hop: typically 1 to 3 ms in-region, more if it lives in another AZ.
  • Deploy coupling: everyone waits for the gateway team.

When to use

  • More than about three public-facing services.
  • You need consistent auth and rate limiting across services.
  • You have external partners and want one documented origin and one set of error shapes.

When NOT to use

  • A single service. An ingress or load balancer already gives you TLS and routing; calling it a "gateway" adds a team, not a capability.
  • As a place for business logic. If the gateway needs to know what a coupon is, the boundary is wrong.
  • As a database proxy. Gateways that join data across services become the slowest, most fragile thing you own.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • JWKS fetch failure: the gateway cannot verify tokens and rejects everything. Cache keys for at least an hour and serve stale on fetch error.
  • Header spoofing: a client sends X-Auth-User-Id: 1. If you forget to strip it, you have an authentication bypass. Strip on entry, always.
  • Config rollout: an invalid route reload can drop live connections. Validate config in CI and roll out gradually.
  • Slow upstream: without per-route timeouts, one slow service consumes all gateway worker connections and takes the others with it.
  • Body buffering: gateways that buffer large uploads run out of memory or disk. Stream, and cap size.

Senior perspective

The gateway is a policy enforcement point, not an application. The test I apply in review: if a change to the gateway requires knowing a domain concept, reject it. The second test: can we run without it? Internal service-to-service calls should not go through the public gateway; that turns a north-south component into an east-west bottleneck and doubles your blast radius. Also budget for the boring work — gateway config is production code and needs review, versioning and a rollback plan just like the services behind it.

47.2 Backend-for-Frontend

Problem

One API cannot serve a mobile app, a web app and a partner integration well. Mobile wants a tiny payload over a flaky 4G link and hates round trips. Web wants rich objects and can afford them. Partners want a stable, versioned, slow-moving contract. Serving all three from one REST API produces endpoints with fifteen optional query flags, payloads that carry fields nobody uses, and a change freeze because "the partner might break".

Solution

Give each client type its own thin backend. The BFF owns the shape of the response for exactly one consumer: it calls internal services, aggregates, trims fields and adapts protocols. It contains no business rules — only composition and presentation for its client.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  IOS["iOS app"] --> BM["Mobile BFF"]
  AND["Android app"] --> BM
  WEB["Web SPA"] --> BW["Web BFF"]
  PART["Partner system"] --> BP["Partner API"]
  BM --> OS["Order Service"]
  BM --> CS["Catalog Service"]
  BW --> OS
  BW --> CS
  BW --> RS["Review Service"]
  BP --> OS

Example

A mobile BFF endpoint that builds the whole "order detail" screen in one call, with a hard budget on the fan-out.

@Controller('mobile/v1/orders')
export class MobileOrderController {
  constructor(
    private readonly orders: OrderClient,
    private readonly catalog: CatalogClient,
    private readonly shipping: ShippingClient,
  ) {}

  @Get(':id/screen')
  async orderScreen(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string, @Principal() p: Principal) {
    const order = await this.orders.getForUser(id, p.userId); // 404 if not theirs
    // Fan out in parallel; degrade instead of failing the screen.
    const [products, tracking] = await Promise.all([
      this.catalog.getManyBrief(order.items.map((i) => i.productId)).catch(() => []),
      this.shipping.getTracking(order.id).catch(() => null),
    ]);
    return {
      id: order.id,
      status: order.status,
      totalMinor: order.totalMinor,
      currency: order.currency,
      // mobile only needs thumbnail + name, not the 40-field product object
      items: order.items.map((i) => {
        const prod = products.find((x) => x.id === i.productId);
        return { name: prod?.name ?? 'Item', thumb: prod?.thumbUrl ?? null, qty: i.qty };
      }),
      tracking: tracking && { carrier: tracking.carrier, eta: tracking.eta },
    };
  }
}

Advantages

  • Each client evolves at its own pace; the mobile team ships without a partner-contract review.
  • Payload sizes drop dramatically. A 180 KB generic response often becomes 8 KB.
  • Round trips collapse: one screen, one request. On a 4G link at 120 ms RTT, replacing five calls with one saves roughly half a second.
  • Client-specific concerns (pagination style, image sizes, date formatting) stop leaking into domain services.

Disadvantages

  • More deployables. Three BFFs means three pipelines, three dashboards, three on-call surfaces.
  • Duplication between BFFs is real and mostly acceptable; policing it creates a shared library that recouples everything.
  • Business logic creeps in. Every BFF eventually grows a "just this one rule".

When to use

  • Two or more client types with genuinely different needs (mobile plus web plus partner).
  • Mobile clients where payload size and round trips matter.
  • When one client's release cycle is blocking another's.

When NOT to use

  • One client. A BFF for a single SPA is just your API with an extra hop.
  • When the "difference" is one field. Sparse fieldsets (?fields=) or GraphQL solve that more cheaply.
  • When the BFF would need write-side business rules. Those belong in the owning service.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Partial dependency failure: decide per field whether to degrade or fail. The example returns the order without tracking rather than a 500.
  • Fan-out amplification: one BFF request becoming 30 internal calls turns a traffic spike into an internal DDoS. Cap concurrency and batch.
  • Timeout budget: if the client timeout is 5 s, the BFF must time out downstream calls at roughly 1.5 s so it can still assemble a response.
  • Auth confusion: the BFF must pass the user's identity downstream, not a service account, or you lose per-user authorization.

Senior perspective

A BFF is a presentation layer that happens to run on a server. I keep them deliberately dumb and deliberately owned by the client team — if the mobile engineers cannot deploy their own BFF, you have built a second gateway with extra steps. The failure I have seen most often is the BFF quietly becoming the place where "we needed data from two services so we joined them here", and six months later it holds the real order-total calculation. Guard that boundary in code review: a BFF may reshape, filter, cache and merge. It may not decide.

47.3 Service discovery

Problem

Service A needs to call service B. In a container platform, B's pods come and go every deploy, get new IPs, scale from 3 to 30 during a sale and back down at night. Hardcoding IPs is impossible; hardcoding a hostname works only if something keeps that name pointing at healthy instances.

Solution

A registry maps a logical name to the current set of healthy network addresses. Instances register on start and deregister on stop (or are health-checked out), and callers resolve the name at call time. Two flavours: client-side discovery (the caller asks the registry and picks an instance itself) and server-side discovery (the caller talks to a stable virtual address and something else load balances). Kubernetes gives you server-side discovery for free via Service plus DNS.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  A["Order Service pod"] -->|"DNS: payment-service"| DNS["Cluster DNS"]
  DNS --> SVC["Service: ClusterIP 10.96.4.7"]
  SVC --> EP["Endpoints from readiness probes"]
  EP --> P1["payment pod 1"]
  EP --> P2["payment pod 2"]
  EP --> P3["payment pod 3"]

Example

Kubernetes discovery in practice: a headless-free Service plus a readiness probe that controls membership, and a Node client that respects DNS TTL rather than caching an IP forever.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: payment-service
spec:
  selector: { app: payment }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 3000 }]
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: payment }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: payment } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: payment } }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.internal/payment:1.42.0
          readinessProbe:                 # failing this removes the pod from Endpoints
            httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: 3000 }
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 2
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec: { command: ["sleep", "10"] }   # drain before the process dies
// Node keeps HTTP connections alive, which pins you to old pods after a deploy.
// Cap socket lifetime so the agent re-resolves DNS and picks up new endpoints.
export const paymentAgent = new https.Agent({
  keepAlive: true,
  maxSockets: 50,
  maxFreeSockets: 10,
  timeout: 5_000,
});
setInterval(() => paymentAgent.destroy(), 60_000); // force fresh DNS every minute

Advantages

  • Deploys, scaling and node failures become invisible to callers.
  • Health checks and discovery are the same mechanism: unready means unrouted.
  • Works uniformly for every language and framework in the fleet.

Disadvantages

  • The registry is critical infrastructure. When DNS is wrong, everything is wrong.
  • Client-side discovery pushes load-balancing logic (and bugs) into every service.
  • DNS caching in Node, the JVM and connection pools defeats it silently.

When to use

  • Any dynamic environment: Kubernetes, ECS, autoscaling groups.
  • Whenever instance counts change without a deploy.

When NOT to use

  • Two fixed servers behind a load balancer. A DNS record is enough.
  • Do not run Consul or etcd yourself if your platform already provides discovery. You are adopting a quorum system, and quorum systems page you.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Stale DNS: a pod is gone but the caller has its IP cached, so every call fails until the cache expires. This is the most common "half the requests fail after deploy" cause.
  • Keep-alive pinning: long-lived connections keep hitting old pods. Bound socket lifetime, as above.
  • Registration without readiness: an instance that registers before it can serve traffic causes a burst of 502s on every deploy.
  • Split brain: a network partition makes the registry report instances that are unreachable from the caller's zone.
  • Thundering herd on registry restart: all clients re-resolve at once.

Senior perspective

Discovery is where deploys visibly hurt. Almost every "we get 502s for 30 seconds during rollout" incident traces to three missing details: a readiness probe that returns ready too early, no preStop drain delay, and a keep-alive agent holding sockets to dead pods. Fix those three and rolling deploys become boring. I also refuse to build custom registries; if the platform offers one, use it, and spend your budget on the health-check semantics instead.

47.4 Sidecar

Problem

Every service needs the same operational capabilities: log shipping, metrics scraping, TLS between services, secret rotation, traffic capture. Implementing them as libraries means every service must be rebuilt and redeployed whenever the capability changes, and every language needs its own version.

Solution

Run the capability as a separate container in the same pod, sharing the network namespace and (optionally) a volume with the application. The app stays ignorant; the sidecar handles the concern. This is how service meshes, log shippers and secret agents work.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  subgraph Pod
    APP["NestJS container"] -->|"localhost:9091"| SC["Sidecar: envoy proxy"]
    APP -->|"writes /var/log/app.log"| VOL["Shared volume"]
    LS["Sidecar: log shipper"] --> VOL
  end
  SC --> EXT["Other services with mTLS"]
  LS --> ELK["Log backend"]

Example

A log-shipping sidecar sharing an emptyDir with the app, so the app writes plain JSON lines and never learns what a log backend is.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: order }
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: applogs
          emptyDir: { sizeLimit: 512Mi }   # bound it, or a log loop fills the node
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.internal/order:2.9.1
          env: [{ name: LOG_DESTINATION, value: "/var/log/app/app.log" }]
          volumeMounts: [{ name: applogs, mountPath: /var/log/app }]
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" }
            limits:   { memory: "1Gi" }
        - name: log-shipper
          image: registry.internal/vector:0.39.0
          args: ["--config", "/etc/vector/vector.toml"]
          volumeMounts:
            - { name: applogs, mountPath: /var/log/app, readOnly: true }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "50m", memory: "64Mi" }
            limits:   { memory: "128Mi" }

Advantages

  • Language agnostic. One sidecar serves Node, Go and Java services identically.
  • Upgrade the capability by changing an image tag, not by rebuilding twenty apps.
  • Strong isolation: a crashing log shipper does not take the app's heap with it.

Disadvantages

  • Every pod pays the sidecar's CPU and memory. At 500 pods, a 128 MB sidecar is 64 GB of cluster memory.
  • Startup and shutdown ordering is genuinely hard: the app may start before the proxy is ready, or the proxy may die before the app finishes draining.
  • Debugging gains a layer. "Which container dropped my request?" becomes a real question.

When to use

  • Cross-cutting infrastructure concerns in a polyglot fleet.
  • mTLS, traffic shaping and retries you want uniform and out of application code.
  • Log or metric collection where the app should stay unaware.

When NOT to use

  • Business logic. A sidecar that computes prices is a distributed monolith in a trench coat.
  • Small clusters where a DaemonSet (one agent per node) does the job at a fraction of the memory.
  • When the capability is one line of app config. Do not deploy a proxy to add a header.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Startup race: the app calls out before the proxy has its config and gets connection refused. Use startup probes and retry the first calls.
  • Shutdown race: Kubernetes stops the proxy first and in-flight requests fail. Use preStop sleeps on the sidecar too, or native sidecar containers.
  • Resource starvation: the sidecar's limit is hit and it is OOMKilled, taking the pod's traffic with it.
  • Disk fill: a shared emptyDir with no sizeLimit and a log loop evicts every pod on the node.

Senior perspective

Sidecars are the right answer when the concern is infrastructural and uniform. They become the wrong answer the moment somebody asks "can we put the retry policy for this one endpoint in the mesh?" — now half your reliability behaviour lives in YAML that the service team cannot read or test. My rule: application-visible behaviour (timeouts, retries, idempotency) stays in the application, where it can be unit-tested; invisible plumbing (mTLS, log shipping, metrics) goes to the sidecar.

47.5 Ambassador

Problem

Your service calls a third-party payment provider over the internet. That call needs TLS pinning, connection pooling, retries with jitter, a circuit breaker, credential rotation, request signing and per-tenant rate limiting. Implementing that inside every service that touches the provider spreads security-critical code everywhere, and each implementation is subtly different.

Solution

The ambassador is a sidecar specialised for outbound calls: a local proxy that owns the relationship with a remote dependency. The app talks plain HTTP to localhost; the ambassador does TLS, auth, retries, breaking and metrics. It is the outbound twin of the gateway.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  subgraph Pod
    APP["Payment Service"] -->|"http://localhost:8081/charge"| AMB["Ambassador proxy"]
  end
  AMB -->|"mTLS + signed request"| PSP["Stripe or Adyen API"]
  AMB --> SEC["Secret manager for key rotation"]
  AMB --> MET["Metrics: latency, breaker state"]

Example

An Envoy ambassador that owns the outbound circuit breaker and timeout for the provider, so the app's HTTP client stays trivial.

# envoy ambassador: one cluster per external dependency
static_resources:
  listeners:
    - address: { socket_address: { address: 127.0.0.1, port_value: 8081 } }
      filter_chains:
        - filters:
            - name: envoy.filters.network.http_connection_manager
              typed_config:
                "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.network.http_connection_manager.v3.HttpConnectionManager
                stat_prefix: psp
                route_config:
                  virtual_hosts:
                    - name: psp
                      domains: ["*"]
                      routes:
                        - match: { prefix: "/" }
                          route:
                            cluster: psp_upstream
                            timeout: 8s                 # hard outbound budget
                            retry_policy:
                              retry_on: "5xx,reset,connect-failure"
                              num_retries: 2
                              per_try_timeout: 3s
                http_filters: [{ name: envoy.filters.http.router }]
  clusters:
    - name: psp_upstream
      connect_timeout: 2s
      type: LOGICAL_DNS
      lb_policy: ROUND_ROBIN
      circuit_breakers:
        thresholds:
          - max_connections: 100
            max_pending_requests: 50      # queue cap: fail fast instead of piling up
            max_retries: 10
      transport_socket:
        name: envoy.transport_sockets.tls
        typed_config:
          "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.transport_sockets.tls.v3.UpstreamTlsContext
          sni: api.stripe.com

Advantages

  • One audited implementation of TLS, signing and credential handling for a sensitive dependency.
  • Uniform outbound metrics: you can see provider latency per pod without instrumenting each app.
  • Credential rotation without redeploying applications.

Disadvantages

  • Reliability policy moves out of the code and into config the app team may not own.
  • An extra process to size, monitor and upgrade per pod.
  • Local-only trust: anything in the pod can now call the provider without credentials.

When to use

  • A small number of high-value external dependencies (payments, KYC, carrier APIs).
  • Polyglot services calling the same provider.
  • Strict requirements for pinning, signing or egress auditing.

When NOT to use

  • One service calling one API. A well-written HTTP client with a timeout and a breaker is simpler and testable in Jest.
  • Internal service-to-service calls, where a mesh or plain client already covers it.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Retry duplication: the app retries and the ambassador retries, so two retries become six requests to the provider. Decide once where retries live.
  • Silent breaker: the ambassador opens its circuit and the app sees only 503s with no idea why. Export breaker state to the app's dashboards.
  • Credential expiry: rotation fails and every call gets 401 at once.
  • Localhost trust: a compromised container in the pod can charge cards. Keep the ambassador's listener bound to 127.0.0.1 and the pod's containers minimal.

Senior perspective

I use ambassadors for exactly one thing: external dependencies where the security envelope matters more than the retry policy. When the main motivation is "we want retries", that is a library, not a proxy. The failure I have watched twice is nested retries during a provider brownout: the provider slows to 6 seconds, the app retries three times, the ambassador retries twice per attempt, and a 200 RPS service throws 1,200 RPS at a struggling partner and gets rate limited into a full outage. Write down where retries happen, and make everything else pass through.

47.6 Health check

Problem

The orchestrator, the load balancer and the on-call engineer all need to answer two different questions: "is this process alive?" and "should this process receive traffic right now?" Conflating them is how you get pods restarted during a database blip, or traffic sent to a pod whose connection pool is still empty.

Solution

Expose separate endpoints with separate semantics. Liveness answers "is the process wedged, should it be killed?" and must check almost nothing. Readiness answers "can I serve traffic right now?" and may check the dependencies the pod cannot function without. Startup gives a slow-booting app time before liveness applies. A fourth, deep check is for humans and dashboards, never for the orchestrator.

Architecture

flowchart TB
  K["Kubelet"] -->|"GET /health/live"| L["Liveness: event loop responsive"]
  K -->|"GET /health/ready"| R["Readiness: PG pool ok, migrations done"]
  LB["Load balancer"] -->|"GET /health/ready"| R
  OPS["Operator or dashboard"] -->|"GET /health/deep"| D["Deep: PG, Redis, Kafka, provider"]
  R --> PG["PostgreSQL"]
  D --> PG
  D --> RD["Redis"]
  D --> KF["Kafka"]

Example

@nestjs/terminus with a deliberately shallow liveness check and a readiness check that includes only hard dependencies.

@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
  constructor(
    private readonly health: HealthCheckService,
    private readonly db: TypeOrmHealthIndicator,
    private readonly mem: MemoryHealthIndicator,
    private readonly redis: RedisHealthIndicator, // custom indicator
  ) {}

  // Liveness: no I/O. If this responds, the event loop is not blocked.
  @Get('live')
  @HealthCheck()
  live() {
    return this.health.check([() => this.mem.checkHeap('heap', 1_200 * 1024 * 1024)]);
  }

  // Readiness: only what we cannot serve a single request without.
  @Get('ready')
  @HealthCheck()
  ready() {
    return this.health.check([
      () => this.db.pingCheck('postgres', { timeout: 800 }),
    ]);
  }

  // Deep: for humans. Redis being down degrades us; it must not un-ready every pod.
  @Get('deep')
  @HealthCheck()
  deep() {
    return this.health.check([
      () => this.db.pingCheck('postgres', { timeout: 1500 }),
      () => this.redis.isHealthy('redis'),
    ]);
  }
}

Advantages

  • Rolling deploys stop serving 502s: unready pods never receive traffic.
  • Wedged processes get restarted automatically instead of paging someone.
  • Clear operational semantics: "unready" is a routing decision, "dead" is a restart decision.

Disadvantages

  • Wrong checks cause outages that pure crashes never would (see below).
  • Health endpoints leak information if they expose versions and dependency names publicly.
  • They add load: a 5-second probe interval across 200 pods is 40 requests per second of pure overhead if each one queries the database.

When to use

  • Always, for anything behind an orchestrator or load balancer.

When NOT to use

  • Never skip them. But do not check optional dependencies in readiness, and do not check anything remote in liveness.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Correlated failure: readiness checks PostgreSQL; PostgreSQL fails over for 20 seconds; every pod in the fleet goes unready simultaneously and the service is hard-down instead of degraded. This is the classic self-inflicted outage.
  • Liveness that calls the database: a slow query makes the kubelet kill healthy pods, which increases load, which slows queries further. A restart loop under load.
  • Probe timeout longer than period: probes queue up and the verdict lags reality.
  • Ready before warm: pod reports ready with an empty connection pool and a cold JIT, so the first 200 requests are slow or fail.
  • Unbounded deep check: a /health that calls six dependencies with no timeouts hangs, and the probe times out, un-readying a perfectly good pod.

Senior perspective

Health checks are the highest-leverage 30 lines in your service, and the easiest to get catastrophically wrong. My defaults: liveness checks nothing external and returns in under a millisecond; readiness checks only the primary datastore, with a short timeout and a small failure tolerance; readiness flips to false during graceful shutdown before the server stops accepting, and stays false for at least one probe interval so the load balancer has time to notice. And I always ask the question that catches the classic mistake: if this dependency is down, do I want every replica removed from the load balancer at the same time? If the answer is no — and for caches, search and analytics it is always no — that dependency does not belong in readiness. Part 48 revisits this as an anti-pattern in its own right.

47.7 Circuit breaker

Problem

A downstream service is failing or has become very slow. Your service keeps calling it. Each call occupies a connection, a promise, an event-loop slot and a request context for the full timeout — say 5 seconds. At 200 requests per second, after 5 seconds you have 1,000 in-flight requests waiting on a dependency that is not coming back. Your memory climbs, your own latency explodes, and callers upstream start timing out on you. One sick service has made three healthy ones sick.

Solution

Wrap the call in a state machine that counts failures. After a threshold, the breaker opens and calls fail immediately without touching the network. After a cool-down it goes half-open and lets a small number of probe requests through. Success closes it; failure re-opens it. The point is not to fix the dependency; it is to fail fast and free your own resources. Part 20 — Reliability Engineering covers the thresholds, the tuning and the interaction with retries in depth; this entry is the catalogue view.

Architecture

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Closed
  Closed --> Open: "failure rate above 50 percent in 20 calls"
  Open --> HalfOpen: "after 30s cool-down"
  HalfOpen --> Closed: "3 consecutive probe successes"
  HalfOpen --> Open: "any probe fails"

Example

A breaker around the shipping-rate provider, with the fallback that actually matters: a cached or default answer, not an exception.

import CircuitBreaker from 'opossum';

@Injectable()
export class ShippingRateService {
  private readonly breaker: CircuitBreaker<[string, number], Quote>;

  constructor(private readonly http: HttpService, private readonly cache: Cache) {
    this.breaker = new CircuitBreaker(
      (zip: string, weightG: number) => this.callProvider(zip, weightG),
      {
        timeout: 2_000,            // a slow call counts as a failure
        errorThresholdPercentage: 50,
        volumeThreshold: 20,       // never trip on 2 requests
        resetTimeout: 30_000,      // cool-down before half-open
      },
    );
    // Fallback must be cheap and local. Never call another remote service here.
    this.breaker.fallback((zip: string) => this.cache.getFlatRate(zip) ?? FLAT_RATE_DEFAULT);
    this.breaker.on('open', () => this.metrics.inc('breaker_open', { dep: 'shipping' }));
    this.breaker.on('halfOpen', () => this.metrics.inc('breaker_half_open', { dep: 'shipping' }));
  }

  quote(zip: string, weightG: number): Promise<Quote> {
    return this.breaker.fire(zip, weightG);
  }
}

Advantages

  • Bounded resource usage during a dependency outage. Latency stays flat instead of climbing to the timeout.
  • The failing dependency gets breathing room to recover instead of being hammered.
  • Explicit, observable state: breaker_open on a dashboard is a much better signal than a latency graph.

Disadvantages

  • One more thing to tune wrongly. Too sensitive and it trips on normal noise; too lax and it never helps.
  • Open breakers turn partial failures into total ones for that feature.
  • Per-process state: with 40 pods you have 40 independent breakers, each needing its own volume of traffic to trip.

When to use

  • Any remote call that can be slow: third-party APIs, cross-service calls, cross-region calls.
  • Where a degraded answer exists (cached price, default shipping rate, "try again later" state).

When NOT to use

  • Around your primary database. If PostgreSQL is down you have no service; a breaker only changes the error message while hiding the real signal.
  • On calls that must be exactly-once and have no fallback — failing fast just moves the problem.
  • Low-traffic endpoints, where the breaker never sees enough calls to decide anything meaningful.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Half-open stampede: the cool-down expires and every pod probes at the same instant, re-killing a recovering dependency. Add jitter to resetTimeout.
  • Slow, not failing: a dependency returning 200s in 9 seconds never trips an error-count breaker. Count timeouts as failures, which is why timeout above is set.
  • Breaker plus retry: retries inside the breaker inflate load and confuse the failure count. Retry outside, or not at all.
  • Shared breaker for multiple endpoints: one failing endpoint opens the breaker for the healthy ones. Key breakers per dependency and per operation class.

Senior perspective

The question I ask before adding a breaker is: what do we do when it is open? If the answer is "return a 500", the breaker bought you resource protection and nothing else — which is still worth it, but say so explicitly. If the answer is "serve last known price", you have a real resilience improvement and the breaker is the mechanism. I also insist on emitting breaker state as a metric with the dependency name as a label. In an incident, "shipping breaker opened at 02:14" collapses twenty minutes of investigation into one glance.

47.8 Retry

Problem

Networks drop packets. Pods get rescheduled. A database fails over for eight seconds. A provider returns 503 for one request in a thousand. Failing the user's checkout because of a transient blip is a bad trade when a second attempt would have worked.

Solution

Retry, but only for failures that can plausibly succeed on a second attempt, with exponential backoff plus jitter, a hard cap on attempts, a total time budget, and only on operations that are idempotent or protected by an idempotency key. Part 20 — Reliability Engineering has the full treatment including budgets and retry storms; here is the shape and one concrete implementation.

Architecture

flowchart TB
  C["Call attempt"] --> R{"Result"}
  R -->|"2xx"| OK["Return"]
  R -->|"4xx except 429"| FAIL["Fail immediately"]
  R -->|"5xx, timeout, 429"| B{"Attempts left and budget left"}
  B -->|"no"| FAIL
  B -->|"yes"| W["Wait: base times 2^n plus jitter"]
  W --> C

Example

A retry helper with a deadline, which is the part most implementations forget: three retries at 4 seconds each is a 12-second call your caller already gave up on.

type RetryOpts = { attempts: number; baseMs: number; deadlineMs: number };

export async function retry<T>(fn: (attempt: number) => Promise<T>, o: RetryOpts): Promise<T> {
  const deadline = Date.now() + o.deadlineMs;
  let lastErr: unknown;
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= o.attempts; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fn(attempt);
    } catch (err) {
      lastErr = err;
      if (!isRetryable(err) || attempt === o.attempts) throw err;
      // full jitter: random between 0 and the exponential cap
      const cap = o.baseMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1);
      const wait = Math.floor(Math.random() * cap);
      if (Date.now() + wait >= deadline) throw err;   // no time left, stop pretending
      await sleep(wait);
    }
  }
  throw lastErr;
}

const isRetryable = (e: unknown) =>
  e instanceof TimeoutError ||
  (e instanceof HttpError && (e.status >= 500 || e.status === 429)) ||
  (e as NodeJS.ErrnoException)?.code === 'ECONNRESET';

Advantages

  • Turns most transient failures invisible: a database failover becomes a 300 ms latency bump instead of 4,000 errors.
  • Cheap to add, and pairs naturally with idempotency keys.
  • Jitter spreads load so recovering dependencies are not re-flooded.

Disadvantages

  • Multiplies load exactly when the system is least able to take it.
  • Hides real problems from your error rate until they become severe.
  • Increases tail latency: a p99 that includes two backoffs looks terrible.

When to use

  • Idempotent reads, and writes protected by an idempotency key or a unique constraint.
  • Known-transient errors: connection resets, 503s, lock timeouts, leader elections.
  • Between your own services, where you control both retry policy and capacity.

When NOT to use

  • Non-idempotent writes with no dedupe. Retrying POST /charges without a key charges the card twice.
  • Deep in a call chain where every layer also retries. Three layers of 3 retries is 27 requests. Retry at exactly one layer, usually the outermost that owns the user's deadline.
  • On 4xx errors. A 400 will be a 400 forever.
  • When a queue would be better: if the work can be asynchronous, enqueue it and let the worker retry with a proper backoff schedule.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Retry storm: a brownout causes every client to retry, tripling load and turning a slow dependency into a dead one. Cap with a token-bucket "retry budget" — for example, allow retries only up to 10 percent of successful call volume.
  • Retries on a full queue: pointless work while the real problem is capacity.
  • Duplicate side effects: emails sent twice, stock decremented twice.
  • Budget exhaustion: the user's 3-second timeout expires while attempt two is still backing off.
  • Retrying a poisoned request: a malformed payload that always fails burns your retry budget forever.

Senior perspective

Retries are the single easiest way to convert a small incident into a large one, and they still belong in every serious system. The discipline is in three rules I apply without exception: retry only where the operation is idempotent, retry at exactly one layer of the stack, and always retry against a deadline rather than a count. The fourth rule is a monitoring one — graph attempts separately from requests. A service whose retry ratio quietly rose from 1.02 to 1.4 over a month is telling you something before it pages you.

47.9 Bulkhead

Problem

Your API serves both a fast product-detail endpoint and a slow report endpoint. Both use the same 20-connection PostgreSQL pool and the same Node event loop. One morning the report query starts taking 30 seconds. Reports occupy all 20 connections. Now product detail — a 2 ms query — cannot get a connection either. A slow feature has taken down a fast one. The name comes from ships: a hull is divided into watertight compartments so one breach does not sink the vessel.

Solution

Partition resources so that a failure in one workload cannot consume the resources of another. Partition connection pools, thread or worker pools, queues, and in extreme cases whole deployments.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  IN["Incoming requests"] --> RT{"Route class"}
  RT -->|"interactive"| P1["Deployment: api-web, PG pool 20"]
  RT -->|"reports"| P2["Deployment: api-reports, PG pool 5"]
  RT -->|"partner batch"| P3["Deployment: api-partner, PG pool 5"]
  P1 --> PG["PostgreSQL primary"]
  P2 --> RR["Read replica"]
  P3 --> RR

Example

Two TypeORM DataSources in one NestJS app: a small, replica-backed pool with a hard statement timeout for reports, and the main pool untouched by them.

@Module({
  imports: [
    TypeOrmModule.forRoot({
      name: 'default',
      type: 'postgres',
      url: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
      extra: { max: 20, connectionTimeoutMillis: 2_000, statement_timeout: 5_000 },
    }),
    TypeOrmModule.forRoot({
      name: 'reporting',                       // separate bulkhead
      type: 'postgres',
      url: process.env.DATABASE_REPLICA_URL,   // different server too
      extra: { max: 5, connectionTimeoutMillis: 1_000, statement_timeout: 60_000 },
    }),
  ],
})
export class DatabaseModule {}

@Injectable()
export class ReportService {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource('reporting') private readonly ds: DataSource) {}
  // Worst case: 5 stuck report queries. Checkout still has all 20 primary connections.
}

The same idea at the queue level with BullMQ: separate queues and separate worker concurrency, so a flood of image resizes cannot starve payment webhooks.

new Worker('payments-webhook', handler, { concurrency: 10, connection });
new Worker('image-resize',    handler, { concurrency: 4,  connection });  // capped on purpose

Advantages

  • Failures stay local. A stuck workload degrades one feature instead of the product.
  • Makes capacity explicit: you can state "reports may use at most 5 connections".
  • Enables different tuning per workload — long statement timeouts for reports, short ones for checkout.

Disadvantages

  • Lower total utilisation. Reserved capacity sits idle when its workload is quiet.
  • More configuration and more deployables to reason about.
  • Sizing is guesswork until you have production data, and wrong sizes cause artificial queuing.

When to use

  • Mixed workloads on shared resources: interactive plus batch, internal plus partner traffic.
  • Multi-tenant systems where one tenant can generate pathological load.
  • Any time you can name a workload that is allowed to be slow.

When NOT to use

  • A single homogeneous workload. Partitioning 20 connections into four pools of five just lowers your ceiling.
  • As a substitute for fixing the slow query. Bulkheads contain damage; they do not repair it.
  • Under tight memory budgets, where each extra pool and process costs real RAM.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Undersized bulkhead: the reserved pool is too small and the workload queues even when the system is idle overall.
  • Shared underlying resource: two pools on the same PostgreSQL instance still compete for CPU, buffers and locks. Real isolation may need a replica.
  • Event loop is the real bulkhead: in Node, a CPU-heavy handler blocks everything in the process regardless of pool separation. Isolation there means separate processes or worker threads.
  • Connection limit overrun: 40 pods times 25 connections is 1,000 connections against a max_connections of 200. Bulkheads need a global budget, usually via PgBouncer.

Senior perspective

Bulkheads are how you buy the right to have slow features. Once I can say "reports run on the replica, with five connections and a sixty-second statement timeout", the report team is free to write expensive queries and the checkout team stops caring. The most valuable bulkhead in a Node system is usually the crudest one: a separate deployment. Same image, different --role flag, different replica count, different HPA target. It costs a few hundred megabytes of memory and removes an entire class of incident.

47.10 Rate limiter

Problem

Any endpoint open to the internet will eventually be hit far harder than you planned: a partner's buggy retry loop, a scraper, a credential-stuffing attack, or your own mobile app after a push notification. Without a limit, the first symptom is your database at 100 percent CPU and every customer affected by one caller.

Solution

Count requests per subject (API key, user, IP) per window and reject once the count exceeds the allowance, with a 429 and a Retry-After. The counter must be shared across pods, which in practice means Redis. Part 16 — Caching and Redis and the rate limiter case study in Part 40 cover algorithms, tiering and headers in detail; this entry is the architectural placement.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  C["Client"] --> GW["Gateway limiter: coarse per IP"]
  GW --> API["NestJS service"]
  API --> RL["Redis: per-subject counters"]
  RL -->|"allowed"| H["Handler"]
  RL -->|"denied"| R429["429 with Retry-After"]

Example

Two layers, which is the part people miss. A cheap global limit at the edge, and a precise business limit in the app with @nestjs/throttler backed by Redis so all pods share one counter.

@Module({
  imports: [
    ThrottlerModule.forRootAsync({
      useFactory: () => ({
        throttlers: [
          { name: 'short', ttl: 1_000, limit: 20 },     // burst protection
          { name: 'long',  ttl: 60_000, limit: 300 },   // sustained rate
        ],
        storage: new ThrottlerStorageRedisService(process.env.REDIS_URL),
      }),
    }),
  ],
  providers: [{ provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: ThrottlerGuard }],
})
export class AppModule {}

@Controller('auth')
export class AuthController {
  // Auth endpoints get a much tighter limit than the global default.
  @Throttle({ short: { ttl: 60_000, limit: 5 } })
  @Post('login')
  login(@Body() dto: LoginDto) { /* ... */ }
}

Advantages

  • Protects capacity and cost from a single bad actor.
  • Turns credential stuffing from feasible into impractical.
  • Becomes a product feature: documented tiers for free and paid partners.

Disadvantages

  • Adds a Redis round trip (0.3 to 0.8 ms in-AZ) to every request.
  • Shared IPs behind corporate NAT or carrier-grade NAT punish innocent users.
  • Wrong limits are invisible until a customer complains about 429s during their peak.

When to use

  • Every public endpoint. Especially login, password reset, OTP send and search.
  • Multi-tenant APIs where fairness matters.
  • Expensive endpoints: exports, reports, anything that fans out.

When NOT to use

  • Internal service-to-service calls where the right control is concurrency limiting and backpressure, not rejection.
  • As your only defence against abuse. A limiter does not stop a distributed attack from 50,000 IPs; that needs WAF and bot management.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Redis down: decide fail-open or fail-closed per route. Fail-open on product browsing, fail-closed on login.
  • Hot key: one enormous tenant makes a single Redis key a bottleneck. Shard the key or use per-pod local limits with a global ceiling.
  • Clock skew between pods when using fixed windows causes double allowance at boundaries. Sliding window or token bucket fixes it.
  • Retry-After ignored: clients that retry immediately turn a limit into a hot loop. Emit the header and expect it to be ignored anyway.

Senior perspective
