Rate limiting is one of the very few controls that protects you from problems you did not predict. I put a generous global limit on day one — high enough that nobody notices, low enough that a runaway loop cannot melt the database — and tighten specific endpoints as they earn attention. Two design details matter more than the algorithm: the limiter must never be able to take the API down (so its failure mode is a per-route policy decision), and it must return honest headers so partners can self-regulate instead of filing tickets.

47.11 Token bucket

Problem

Fixed-window counters are simple and wrong at the edges: a client with a limit of 100 per minute can send 100 at 11:59:59 and 100 at 12:00:00, delivering 200 requests in one second. Meanwhile a real client's traffic is bursty by nature — a page load fires eight requests at once and then nothing for a minute. A limiter that forbids bursts breaks legitimate usage; one that ignores them permits abuse.

Solution

Model the allowance as a bucket of tokens with a capacity (burst size) and a refill rate (sustained rate). Each request removes tokens equal to its cost. If tokens are unavailable, reject or wait. Capacity and rate are two independent dials: "300 per minute, burst 20" is expressible, unlike a fixed window. Part 16 derives the algorithm; here is the placement and the atomic implementation.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  RF["Refill: rate tokens per second"] --> B["Bucket: capacity 20"]
  REQ["Request cost 1 to 5"] --> CHK{"tokens >= cost"}
  B --> CHK
  CHK -->|"yes"| ALLOW["Deduct and allow"]
  CHK -->|"no"| DENY["429 with Retry-After"]
  ALLOW --> B

Example

The whole pattern in one Redis Lua script. Atomicity matters: read-then-write from Node lets two pods spend the same token.

-- KEYS[1] = bucket key, ARGV = capacity, refillPerSec, nowMs, cost, ttlSec
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local capacity, rate = tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now, cost      = tonumber(ARGV[3]), tonumber(ARGV[4])
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or capacity
local ts     = tonumber(b[2]) or now
-- lazy refill: no background job, we compute elapsed time on read
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + ((now - ts) / 1000.0) * rate)
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= cost then tokens = tokens - cost; allowed = 1 end
redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], tonumber(ARGV[5]))   -- idle buckets disappear
-- returns: allowed, tokens left, ms until one token is available
return { allowed, math.floor(tokens), math.floor(math.max(0, (cost - tokens) / rate * 1000)) }
const [allowed, remaining, retryAfterMs] = await this.redis.evalsha(
  this.sha, 1, `rl:{${apiKey}}:search`, 20, 5, Date.now(), 5, 3600,
); // capacity 20, 5 per second, this request costs 5 units

Advantages

  • Bursts allowed on purpose, up to a number you chose.
  • Lazy refill means no background timer and O(1) memory per subject (about 120 bytes).
  • Per-request cost falls out naturally: a search costs 5, a read costs 1.
  • One round trip and one atomic operation.

Disadvantages

  • Two parameters to explain to partners instead of one.
  • Redis-dependent for correctness across pods.
  • Floating-point token accounting needs care with very low rates.

When to use

  • Public APIs with documented burst and sustained limits.
  • Outbound throttling toward a provider that publishes "200 requests per second".
  • Any place where you want to smooth rather than block: a leaky-bucket variant queues instead of rejecting.

When NOT to use

  • When you need a strict "no more than N in any rolling 60 seconds" guarantee for compliance. Use a sliding-window log; the bucket permits a burst on top of the rate.
  • Single-process tools, where an in-memory counter is fine and Redis is overkill.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Clock skew: nowMs supplied by the client pod can jump backwards. Use Redis TIME inside the script if pods drift.
  • Key expiry mid-burst: a bucket that expires refills to full capacity, granting a free burst. Set the TTL longer than the full refill time.
  • Cluster slots: use a hash tag ({apiKey}) so all keys for a subject live on one shard and the script stays single-slot.
  • Cost larger than capacity: a request costing 30 against a 20 bucket can never succeed. Validate at config time.

Senior perspective

I default to token bucket for everything user-facing because it matches how real clients behave: bursty, then quiet. The two numbers also make good contract language — "5 requests per second sustained, bursts of 20" is something a partner engineer can implement against. Where I have been burned is Redis Cluster: without hash tags the script touches multiple slots and fails in production but not in your single-node dev Redis. Test limiters against the topology you actually run.

47.12 Backpressure with bounded queues

Problem

Producers are faster than consumers. An upload endpoint accepts files faster than the resizer can process them; a Kafka consumer reads faster than it can write to PostgreSQL; a Node stream reads a 2 GB file faster than it can push to S3. Unbounded buffering absorbs the difference — until it does not. The classic Node failure is an in-memory array that grows until the pod is OOMKilled, losing every item in it.

Solution

Make every buffer bounded, and make "full" mean something. When the buffer is full, the producer must slow down, block, or be rejected. This is backpressure: the signal that flows backwards from a slow consumer to a fast producer. Part 20 covers load shedding and admission control; here is the queue-shaped version.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  P["Producer: HTTP handler"] -->|"enqueue"| Q["Bounded queue: max 1000"]
  Q --> W["Worker pool: concurrency 8"]
  W --> DB["PostgreSQL"]
  Q -->|"queue full"| REJ["503 Service Unavailable with Retry-After"]
  W -->|"lag metric"| HPA["Autoscaler"]

Example

A bounded in-process queue for a write-behind path, plus the Kafka consumer equivalent where backpressure means pausing the partition instead of buffering.

@Injectable()
export class EventIngestService {
  private readonly queue: Batch[] = [];
  private readonly MAX = 1_000;              // bounded, on purpose
  private draining = false;

  enqueue(batch: Batch): void {
    if (this.queue.length >= this.MAX) {
      this.metrics.inc('ingest_shed');
      throw new ServiceUnavailableException('ingest saturated'); // shed, do not buffer
    }
    this.queue.push(batch);
    void this.drain();
  }

  private async drain(): Promise<void> {
    if (this.draining) return;
    this.draining = true;
    try {
      while (this.queue.length) {
        const chunk = this.queue.splice(0, 100);
        await this.repo.insertMany(chunk);    // one round trip per 100 rows
      }
    } finally {
      this.draining = false;
    }
  }
}
// KafkaJS: real backpressure is pausing the partition, not growing an array.
await consumer.run({
  partitionsConsumedConcurrently: 3,
  eachBatch: async ({ batch, resolveOffset, heartbeat, pause }) => {
    if (this.db.pool.waitingCount > 20) {
      const resume = pause();                 // stop fetching from this partition
      setTimeout(resume, 5_000);
      return;
    }
    for (const m of batch.messages) {
      await this.handle(m);
      resolveOffset(m.offset);
      await heartbeat();                      // avoid rebalance during slow batches
    }
  },
});

Advantages

  • Memory usage becomes predictable and provable, not hopeful.
  • Overload turns into explicit, observable rejection (503, shed counter) instead of a silent death.
  • Queue depth becomes a first-class autoscaling and alerting signal.

Disadvantages

  • You must decide what to do when full, and every option is unpleasant: reject, block, or drop.
  • Bounded queues surface capacity problems loudly and early, which feels worse than it is.
  • Blocking producers can propagate stalls upstream if you did not intend that.

When to use

  • Every producer-consumer boundary: HTTP to worker, Kafka to database, stream to storage.
  • Ingest endpoints where traffic spikes are expected.
  • Anywhere memory is bounded (containers) and input is not.

When NOT to use

  • Never skip bounding. But do not add an in-process queue at all when a durable broker is the right answer: an in-memory queue loses everything on restart, and "we buffer in memory for durability" is not a plan.
  • When the work must not be dropped and the producer cannot be slowed — then you need durable buffering with disk, not a bigger array.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • The queue that isn't: Promise.all over 50,000 items is an unbounded queue with extra steps. Use a concurrency limiter.
  • Consumer lag masking: pausing partitions stops lag from growing in memory but grows it in the broker. Alert on consumer lag, not just RAM.
  • Rebalance during pause: a paused consumer that stops heartbeating is kicked out of the group, causing a rebalance storm.
  • Shed the wrong traffic: dropping checkout while accepting analytics. Prioritise by request class before you shed.
  • Silent drops: dropping without a metric turns data loss into a mystery three weeks later.

Senior perspective

Backpressure is the pattern that separates systems that degrade from systems that die. My review question for any queue, buffer, array or Promise.all in a service is simply: what is the maximum size of this, and what happens when it is reached? If the author cannot answer with a number, the code is an outage waiting for a traffic spike. The corollary is that rejecting work is a legitimate, healthy behaviour. A service returning 503 on 2 percent of ingest requests while serving the other 98 percent at normal latency is doing its job perfectly; a service that accepts everything and then falls over serves zero percent.

47.13 Outbox

Problem

An order is placed. You must write the order row to PostgreSQL and publish order.created to Kafka. These are two different systems with no shared transaction. Whichever you do first, there is a window where a crash leaves them inconsistent: an order that nobody was told about, or an event about an order that does not exist. This is the dual-write problem, and it will bite you at a rate roughly proportional to your deploy frequency.

Solution

Write the event into the same database transaction as the business change, into an outbox table. A separate relay reads unpublished rows and publishes them to the broker, marking them sent. The database transaction guarantees the event exists if and only if the order exists. Publication becomes at-least-once, which is why consumers need idempotency. Part 19 — Distributed Transactions covers the relay, ordering and cleanup in full; this entry gives the shape and a distinct example.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  API["Order Service"] -->|"one transaction"| DB[("PostgreSQL")]
  DB --> T1["orders row"]
  DB --> T2["outbox row"]
  REL["Relay: poller or CDC"] -->|"SELECT unpublished FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED"| DB
  REL -->|"publish"| K["Kafka topic order.events"]
  REL -->|"mark published_at"| DB
  K --> CON["Consumers"]

Example

The table, the write inside the transaction, and the relay query. Note SKIP LOCKED, which lets several relay pods share the table without blocking each other.

CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  aggregate_id  UUID        NOT NULL,
  event_type    TEXT        NOT NULL,
  payload       JSONB       NOT NULL,
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  published_at  TIMESTAMPTZ
);
-- partial index: only unpublished rows are ever scanned, so it stays tiny
CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished_idx ON outbox (id) WHERE published_at IS NULL;
async placeOrder(dto: PlaceOrderDto): Promise<Order> {
  return this.dataSource.transaction(async (em) => {
    const order = await em.save(em.create(Order, { ...dto, status: 'PENDING' }));
    await em.insert(OutboxEvent, {
      aggregateId: order.id,
      eventType: 'order.created',
      payload: { orderId: order.id, userId: order.userId, totalMinor: order.totalMinor },
    });
    return order; // both rows commit together, or neither does
  });
}
-- relay: batch of 200, several pods can run this concurrently
WITH batch AS (
  SELECT id FROM outbox
  WHERE published_at IS NULL
  ORDER BY id
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  LIMIT 200
)
SELECT o.* FROM outbox o JOIN batch b ON b.id = o.id ORDER BY o.id;

Advantages

  • Atomic by construction. No lost events, no phantom events.
  • Works with any broker, and with none: the outbox is also a perfectly good audit log.
  • The relay is independently scalable and restartable; a crash mid-publish costs a duplicate, not a loss.

Disadvantages

  • At-least-once only. Every consumer must be idempotent or you will process duplicates.
  • Extra write per business operation, extra table growth, and a table that needs pruning.
  • Publication latency is the poll interval (typically 100 ms to 1 s) unless you use CDC.

When to use

  • Any time a database write and a message publish must both happen.
  • When you are currently doing await repo.save(); await kafka.send(); and hoping.

When NOT to use

  • When the event does not need to be reliable — analytics pings, "user viewed page". Fire and forget is cheaper and honest.
  • When the write itself is the event and consumers can read from CDC directly.
  • Single-service systems with no broker, where an in-process event emitter inside the same transaction boundary is enough.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Ordering: per-aggregate ordering requires publishing in id order per key and using aggregate_id as the Kafka partition key. Global ordering is not achievable with parallel relays.
  • Table bloat: a busy outbox at 500 events per second is 43 million rows a day. Delete published rows older than a few days, or partition by day and drop partitions.
  • Relay down: events accumulate silently. Alert on max(now() - created_at) for unpublished rows, not on row count.
  • Broker down: the relay must retry without marking rows published, and must not spin at full speed.
  • Long transactions: an open transaction holding outbox rows blocks the relay's view; keep transactions short.
  • Duplicate publish: a crash between publishing and marking sends the row again. Expected; consumers dedupe.

Senior perspective

The outbox is the least glamorous pattern in this catalogue and the one I have argued for most often. The counter-argument is always "but we can just publish after commit, the window is milliseconds". That window is real, and at 100 deploys a month with pods being terminated mid-request, it will produce orders that never reached fulfilment. The debugging cost of one such incident exceeds the implementation cost of the outbox. The operational detail people forget is retention: put the cleanup job in the same pull request as the table, or you will meet the outbox again as a disk-full alert.

47.14 Transactional inbox

Problem

The outbox gives you at-least-once delivery, so a consumer will see order.created twice. If the consumer's job is "charge the card" or "decrement stock", processing it twice is a real financial or inventory error. Consumers must be idempotent, and "make the handler idempotent" is easy to say and hard to do for handlers that touch several tables.

Solution

Record every consumed message id in an inbox table, in the same transaction as the side effects. If the insert violates the primary key, this message was already processed and you skip it. The database's uniqueness guarantee becomes your deduplication guarantee, with no extra infrastructure. Part 19 covers the interplay with offsets and retries; here is the practical shape.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  K["Kafka: order.created"] --> C["Consumer"]
  C -->|"begin tx"| DB[("PostgreSQL")]
  DB --> I["INSERT inbox message_id"]
  I -->|"conflict"| SKIP["Already processed, commit and ack"]
  I -->|"inserted"| SE["Apply side effects"]
  SE --> CM["Commit, then ack offset"]

Example

One transaction, two guarantees: dedupe and side effect. Note that the offset is committed only after the database transaction succeeds.

@Injectable()
export class OrderCreatedConsumer {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  async handle(msg: KafkaMessage): Promise<void> {
    const messageId = msg.headers?.['message-id']?.toString();
    if (!messageId) throw new Error('message-id header required');

    await this.ds.transaction(async (em) => {
      const res = await em
        .createQueryBuilder()
        .insert()
        .into(InboxMessage)
        .values({ messageId, consumer: 'reserve-stock', receivedAt: new Date() })
        .orIgnore()                       // ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
        .execute();

      if (res.raw.length === 0) return;   // duplicate: do nothing, commit cleanly

      const event = JSON.parse(msg.value!.toString()) as OrderCreated;
      // Side effects live in the same transaction as the dedupe row.
      await em.decrement(Stock, { sku: event.sku }, 'available', event.qty);
      await em.insert(StockLedger, { sku: event.sku, delta: -event.qty, ref: event.orderId });
    });
  }
}
CREATE TABLE inbox_message (
  consumer    TEXT        NOT NULL,
  message_id  TEXT        NOT NULL,
  received_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (consumer, message_id)   -- per-consumer dedupe, same event, many consumers
);
CREATE INDEX inbox_received_idx ON inbox_message (received_at);  -- for pruning

Advantages

  • Exactly-once effects on top of at-least-once delivery, without a distributed transaction.
  • Uses only PostgreSQL guarantees you already trust.
  • Gives you a queryable record of what was consumed and when, which is priceless during incidents.

Disadvantages

  • One more table to prune. At 2,000 messages per second that is 172 million rows a day.
  • Only protects effects inside that one database. It cannot make an outbound HTTP call idempotent.
  • Adds a write to every message, raising consumer cost and WAL volume.

When to use

  • Any consumer with non-idempotent side effects: money, stock, emails, external calls.
  • Whenever the delivery guarantee is at-least-once, which is essentially always.

When NOT to use

  • When the handler is naturally idempotent: a full-state upsert (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE of the whole row) needs no inbox.
  • When the side effect is in a different system than the dedupe table, because then it is not atomic anyway; use an idempotency key at that system's boundary instead.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Ack before commit: acking the offset before the transaction commits loses the message on crash. Commit database first, always.
  • Missing message id: relying on payload hashing breaks when a producer adds a timestamp field. Require an explicit id header.
  • Retention shorter than replay: pruning after 7 days then replaying a 30-day-old topic reprocesses everything. Match retention to your replay policy.
  • Consumer rename: changing the consumer value re-processes the entire history.
  • Hot table: heavy inserts and heavy deletes cause bloat. Partition by day and drop partitions instead of DELETE.

Senior perspective

The inbox is a two-line change with a five-year payoff. The subtlety I always check in review is transaction scope: the dedupe insert and the side effects must be the same transaction, and the offset commit must be strictly after. I have seen a version where the dedupe row was written with a separate connection "for speed" — it deduped perfectly and lost the side effects on every rollback. Also: prefer natural idempotency where you can get it. If the handler can be written as an upsert of a full state, that is better than an inbox, because it needs no cleanup job and survives replays of any age.

47.15 Saga

Problem

Placing an order spans four services: payment authorises the card, inventory reserves stock, shipping books a slot, notification emails the customer. There is no distributed transaction across them — and even if there were (two-phase commit), holding locks across four services and a network for the duration of a checkout is an availability disaster. Yet the business needs the whole thing to either complete or be visibly undone.

Solution

Model the flow as a sequence of local transactions, each with a defined compensating action. If step three fails, run the compensations for steps two and one, in reverse. Consistency becomes eventual and semantic: you do not roll back a captured payment, you issue a refund. Two styles: choreography (services react to each other's events) and orchestration (one component owns the state machine). Part 19 covers both in depth; this entry gives the shape.

Architecture

sequenceDiagram
  participant O as Orchestrator
  participant P as Payment
  participant I as Inventory
  participant S as Shipping
  O->>P: authorize(orderId, amount)
  P-->>O: authorized(authId)
  O->>I: reserve(orderId, items)
  I-->>O: reserved
  O->>S: bookSlot(orderId)
  S-->>O: failed no capacity
  O->>I: releaseReservation(orderId)
  O->>P: voidAuthorization(authId)
  O->>O: mark order FAILED with reason

Example

An orchestrator step table plus the handler, so the saga survives a pod restart. The state is in PostgreSQL, not in a variable.

CREATE TABLE saga_instance (
  id           UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  saga_type    TEXT NOT NULL,
  order_id     UUID NOT NULL,
  step         TEXT NOT NULL,          -- AUTHORIZE, RESERVE, SHIP, DONE, COMPENSATING
  state        JSONB NOT NULL,         -- authId, reservationId, ...
  attempts     INT  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  next_run_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX saga_due_idx ON saga_instance (next_run_at) WHERE step <> 'DONE';
async advance(saga: SagaInstance): Promise<void> {
  try {
    switch (saga.step) {
      case 'AUTHORIZE': {
        const auth = await this.payment.authorize(saga.orderId, saga.state.amountMinor, {
          idempotencyKey: `${saga.id}:authorize`,      // safe to retry this step
        });
        return this.moveTo(saga, 'RESERVE', { ...saga.state, authId: auth.id });
      }
      case 'RESERVE': {
        const r = await this.inventory.reserve(saga.orderId, saga.state.items, {
          idempotencyKey: `${saga.id}:reserve`,
        });
        return this.moveTo(saga, 'SHIP', { ...saga.state, reservationId: r.id });
      }
      case 'SHIP': {
        await this.shipping.book(saga.orderId, { idempotencyKey: `${saga.id}:ship` });
        return this.moveTo(saga, 'DONE', saga.state);
      }
    }
  } catch (err) {
    if (isRetryable(err) && saga.attempts < 5) return this.scheduleRetry(saga, err);
    return this.compensate(saga, err);   // release reservation, void authorization
  }
}

Advantages

  • No distributed locks, so services stay independently available.
  • Every step is a normal local transaction your team already understands.
  • The saga table is a live, queryable record of every in-flight order and where it is stuck.

Disadvantages

  • You must design a compensation for every step, and some are not truly reversible (an email is sent; a refund is not an un-charge).
  • Intermediate states are visible to users and to other services.
  • The failure matrix grows fast: N steps means N compensations plus the cases where a compensation itself fails.
  • Testing is genuinely hard. Every step needs a "what if this fails after the remote side succeeded" test.

When to use

  • Multi-service business processes with real money or inventory at stake.
  • Long-running flows (minutes to days) where holding a transaction is impossible.

When NOT to use

  • Inside one service and one database. Use a single ACID transaction. A saga there is pure cost.
  • For two steps where the second is retryable and idempotent — just retry until it succeeds.
  • When the business genuinely requires atomic visibility ("the customer must never see a half-created order"). Redesign the boundaries instead; that is usually a sign the split is wrong.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Compensation fails: the refund API is down. You need a dead-letter path and a human queue, not an infinite retry.
  • Duplicate step execution: the orchestrator crashes after the remote call but before recording it. This is why every step carries an idempotency key derived from the saga id.
  • Out-of-order events in choreography: payment.captured arrives before order.created. Handlers must tolerate it or buffer.
  • Stuck sagas: a step whose event never arrives sits forever. Add a timeout per step and a "sagas older than 15 minutes" alert.
  • Partial compensation: stock released but authorization not voided, so the customer's card holds funds for a week.

Senior perspective

Sagas are what you get when you split a transaction across services, and the honest framing is that they are the cost of that split, not a benefit of it. Before writing one I always ask whether the two steps could live in the same service and the same transaction. Very often they could, and the saga disappears. When the saga is genuinely needed, three things make it survivable: state persisted in a table rather than in memory, an idempotency key on every outbound step, and a dashboard showing sagas by step and age. That last one turns "some orders are stuck" from a two-day investigation into a two-minute query.

47.16 Idempotency key

Problem

The mobile app sends POST /payments. The response is lost to a flaky network. The app retries. Without protection, the customer is charged twice. This is not a rare edge case: on mobile networks, 0.5 to 2 percent of requests get a lost response, and every retry layer in your stack multiplies the chance.

Solution

The client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it as a header. The server stores the key with the result of the first successful execution. A repeat with the same key returns the stored result instead of executing again. The database's unique constraint does the hard part.

Architecture

flowchart TB
  REQ["POST /payments with Idempotency-Key"] --> INS{"INSERT key row"}
  INS -->|"inserted"| EXEC["Execute in same transaction"]
  EXEC --> STORE["Store status and response body"]
  STORE --> R201["201 Created"]
  INS -->|"conflict, completed"| REPLAY["200 with stored response"]
  INS -->|"conflict, in progress"| R409["409 or 425, client retries later"]

Example

The table and the interceptor. The key detail is the three-state handling: new, completed, and in progress (two concurrent retries).

CREATE TABLE idempotency_key (
  key           TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id       UUID        NOT NULL,
  endpoint      TEXT        NOT NULL,
  request_hash  TEXT        NOT NULL,      -- detects key reuse with a different body
  status        TEXT        NOT NULL,      -- IN_PROGRESS | COMPLETED
  response_code INT,
  response_body JSONB,
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
@Injectable()
export class IdempotencyInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  async intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Promise<Observable<unknown>> {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    const key = req.headers['idempotency-key'];
    if (!key) throw new BadRequestException('Idempotency-Key header required');
    const hash = sha256(JSON.stringify(req.body));

    const existing = await this.repo.claim(key, req.user.id, req.route.path, hash);
    if (existing?.status === 'COMPLETED') {
      if (existing.requestHash !== hash) throw new ConflictException('key reused with different body');
      ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse().status(existing.responseCode);
      return of(existing.responseBody);                 // replay, do not execute
    }
    if (existing?.status === 'IN_PROGRESS') {
      throw new ConflictException('request already in progress');  // client retries later
    }
    return next.handle().pipe(
      tap((body) => this.repo.complete(key, 201, body)),
      catchError((e) => { void this.repo.release(key); return throwError(() => e); }),
    );
  }
}

Advantages

  • Makes retries safe, which makes every other reliability pattern usable.
  • Cheap: one indexed insert per request.
  • Turns "did my payment go through?" from a support ticket into a repeat call with the same key.

Disadvantages

  • Clients must generate and persist keys correctly, which requires a contract and documentation.
  • The stored response can become stale if the resource changes afterwards.
  • Keys need retention management, and the table grows with traffic.

When to use

  • Every non-idempotent public write: payments, orders, transfers, refunds, sending messages.
  • Webhook receivers, where the provider guarantees at-least-once delivery.
  • Any endpoint your own retry logic might call twice.

When NOT to use

  • GET, PUT with full state, and DELETE by id, which are already idempotent by definition.
  • Where a natural business key exists and can be a unique constraint (UNIQUE (user_id, cart_id) prevents double order creation without any extra machinery). Prefer the natural key.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Concurrent duplicates: two retries arrive 5 ms apart. The IN_PROGRESS state and the unique constraint are what stop double execution; without them, both pass the "does it exist" check.
  • Client reuses a key with a different body: without the request hash you would replay the wrong response. Reject with 409.
  • Crash mid-execution: the row stays IN_PROGRESS forever and blocks the customer. Add a TTL or a sweeper that releases stale claims.
  • Key scope too wide: a global key namespace lets one tenant guess another's key. Scope by user id.
  • Retention too short: a client retrying after 48 hours re-executes. State the window in your API docs (24 hours is typical).

Senior perspective

I treat the idempotency key as a public API contract, documented alongside authentication. The design decision that matters is who generates it: it must be the client, generated once per logical intent and reused across retries. A key generated per HTTP attempt is worthless. In review I also look for the response being stored, not just the key — replaying with an empty 200 body breaks clients that expect the payment id. And I always pair it with the natural-key question: if a unique constraint on the business data gives the same protection, take it, because constraints never expire and never need a sweeper.

47.17 Change Data Capture

Problem

Six systems need to know when a product changes: the search index, the cache, the analytics warehouse, the recommendation service, a partner feed and the audit log. Writing six publish calls into the product service couples it to all of them, and every one of those calls is a dual write that can be lost. Meanwhile the outbox relay's polling adds latency and load.

Solution

Read the database's own replication log — in PostgreSQL, the write-ahead log via logical replication — and turn committed row changes into a stream of events. Nothing is added to the application. Debezium is the common implementation; it publishes before and after images to Kafka. CDC can also carry your outbox table, which gives you outbox semantics with sub-second latency and no polling.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  APP["Order Service"] --> PG[("PostgreSQL")]
  PG --> WAL["Write-ahead log"]
  WAL --> SLOT["Logical replication slot"]
  SLOT --> DBZ["Debezium connector"]
  DBZ --> K["Kafka topics per table"]
  K --> ES["Elasticsearch indexer"]
  K --> DW["Warehouse loader"]
  K --> CIN["Cache invalidator"]

Example

The PostgreSQL side and a Debezium connector configured in outbox mode, which is the configuration I recommend in almost every case.

ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_level = 'logical';           -- requires restart
-- REPLICA IDENTITY FULL gives you the "before" image, at a WAL size cost
ALTER TABLE products REPLICA IDENTITY FULL;
CREATE PUBLICATION cdc_pub FOR TABLE products, outbox;
SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('debezium_orders', 'pgoutput');
-- watch this, it is the number that causes disk-full incidents
SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(
  pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained
FROM pg_replication_slots;
{
  "name": "orders-outbox",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
    "plugin.name": "pgoutput",
    "slot.name": "debezium_orders",
    "publication.name": "cdc_pub",
    "table.include.list": "public.outbox",
    "transforms": "outbox",
    "transforms.outbox.type": "io.debezium.transforms.outbox.EventRouter",
    "transforms.outbox.route.by.field": "event_type",
    "transforms.outbox.table.field.event.key": "aggregate_id",
    "heartbeat.interval.ms": "10000"
  }
}

Advantages

  • Zero application code. New consumers appear without touching the producing service.
  • Sub-second latency, far better than a 1-second poller.
  • Captures every change including manual UPDATEs run by an engineer at 02:00, which application-level events miss.
  • Guaranteed consistent with committed data, because it is the commit log.

Disadvantages

  • You are now publishing your schema. A column rename becomes a breaking change for six consumers.
  • Replication slots retain WAL. A stopped connector with an active slot fills the disk and takes the primary down. This is the number one CDC outage.
  • Operational weight: Kafka Connect is another cluster to run, monitor and upgrade.
  • Snapshotting a 500 GB table on first start puts real load on the database.

When to use

  • Fanning changes to search, cache, analytics and other read models.
  • Carrying an outbox table, where you get clean events and CDC's latency.
  • Migrating data to a new system while the old one keeps writing (see Strangler Fig).

When NOT to use

  • As your primary integration contract for raw tables. Publishing products row images makes every consumer depend on your physical schema; use the outbox transform so you publish events you designed.
  • For a handful of consumers in one service, where an in-process emitter is enough.
  • When nobody on the team can operate Kafka Connect at 03:00.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Slot retention: connector stops, restart_lsn freezes, WAL grows without bound. Alert on retained WAL bytes, and always set max_slot_wal_keep_size.
  • Schema evolution: adding a nullable column is fine; renaming or dropping breaks consumers. Version your event payloads.
  • Failover: a physical replica promoted to primary does not carry logical slots in older PostgreSQL versions, so CDC stops silently after failover.
  • Snapshot storms: an accidental connector reset re-snapshots a huge table and floods Kafka.
  • Transaction boundaries: consumers see individual row changes, not transactions, so a multi-row change appears as separate events out of business order unless you use the outbox transform.
  • Toast columns: unchanged large values arrive as a placeholder unless REPLICA IDENTITY FULL is set, which surprises consumers expecting full rows.

Senior perspective

CDC is the highest-leverage integration tool in the box and the one with the sharpest operational edge. My strong preference is CDC-over-outbox rather than CDC-over-tables: you keep an explicit, versioned event contract, and consumers never depend on a column you might want to rename. On the operations side, there is exactly one alert I insist on before CDC goes to production: retained WAL per replication slot, paging at a threshold you can survive. I have seen a stopped Debezium task over a long weekend take a primary to 100 percent disk. Nothing else about CDC is as urgent as that graph.

47.18 Anti-corruption layer

Problem

You integrate with a 15-year-old ERP. Its concept of "customer" has 60 fields, three status codes that mean "active", dates as YYYYMMDD strings, and a CUST_TYPE of 'W' that means wholesale. If those shapes leak into your domain, every service in your system learns the ERP's vocabulary, and the day you replace the ERP you rewrite everything. The same happens with any external model: a payment provider, a legacy monolith, a partner feed.

Solution

Put a translation layer at the boundary that speaks the foreign model on one side and your domain model on the other. Nothing beyond the layer knows the foreign vocabulary. It is a coordinate transform for concepts, and it is the single most valuable thing you can do when integrating with a system you do not control.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  subgraph YourDomain
    OS["Order Service"] --> ACL["Anti-corruption layer"]
  end
  ACL -->|"SOAP, CUST_TYPE W"| ERP["Legacy ERP"]
  ACL -->|"REST, snake_case"| PSP["Payment provider"]
  OS --> DOM["Domain model: Customer, Money, OrderStatus"]

Example

A port, an adapter and a mapper. The domain sees Customer; only the adapter has ever heard of CUST_TYPE.

// Domain-owned interface (the port). Lives in the domain module.
export interface CustomerDirectory {
  findById(id: CustomerId): Promise<Customer | null>;
}

// Adapter: the only file allowed to know the ERP exists.
@Injectable()
export class ErpCustomerDirectory implements CustomerDirectory {
  constructor(private readonly erp: ErpSoapClient) {}

  async findById(id: CustomerId): Promise<Customer | null> {
    const raw = await this.erp.getCustomer({ CUST_ID: id.value }); // throws ErpFault
    if (!raw || raw.DEL_FLG === 'Y') return null;
    return this.toDomain(raw);
  }

  private toDomain(r: ErpCustomerRecord): Customer {
    return new Customer({
      id: CustomerId.of(r.CUST_ID),
      name: r.CUST_NAME.trim(),
      // three ERP codes collapse into one domain concept
      status: ['A', 'AC', '01'].includes(r.STATUS) ? 'ACTIVE' : 'INACTIVE',
      segment: r.CUST_TYPE === 'W' ? 'WHOLESALE' : 'RETAIL',
      creditLimit: Money.fromMinor(Number(r.CRED_LIM) * 100, 'EUR'),
      createdAt: parse(r.CRT_DT, 'yyyyMMdd', new Date()),
    });
  }
}

Advantages

  • Your domain model stays clean and expressive regardless of what you integrate with.
  • Replacing the foreign system means rewriting one adapter, not the application.
  • Testing gets easy: unit-test the mapper with real recorded payloads; stub the port everywhere else.
  • Foreign failures are translated too, so the domain sees CustomerUnavailableError, not ErpFault.

Disadvantages

  • Boilerplate. Two models and a mapper for every integrated concept.
  • An extra hop of indirection when debugging.
  • Mapping is where subtle bugs hide: a wrong status collapse can silently change business behaviour.

When to use

  • Any integration with a system you do not control: legacy monolith, ERP, partner API, acquired company's platform.
  • Strangler Fig migrations, where the ACL is what lets old and new coexist.
  • Any bounded-context boundary where the two contexts disagree about a word's meaning.

When NOT to use

  • Between two services your own team owns with a shared, well-designed contract. Then the ACL is a second name for the same model.
  • For trivially-shaped data. A single string field does not need a mapper class.
  • When "translation" is really business logic — deciding whether a customer gets credit is a domain rule, not a mapping.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Lossy mapping: the foreign model has a state yours cannot express, so information is silently dropped. Log and alert on unmapped values rather than defaulting them.
  • New enum value: the ERP adds STATUS = 'P' and your mapper quietly returns INACTIVE. Fail loudly on unknown values in non-critical paths, and alert.
  • Encoding and locale: dates without timezones, decimal commas, non-UTF-8 payloads.
  • Foreign failures leaking: a SOAP fault propagating into an HTTP 500 with a stack trace from the ERP client.
  • Performance: the ACL becomes a chatty proxy, calling the ERP once per item in a loop. Batch inside the adapter.

Senior perspective

The anti-corruption layer is the cheapest insurance in software architecture. It costs a mapper file per concept; it buys you the ability to replace a vendor without rewriting your product. The signal that you skipped it is unmistakable: search your codebase for a foreign vocabulary word like CUST_TYPE and count the files. If the answer is more than one, the foreign model has already colonised your domain. I also make the adapter own translation of errors and timeouts, not just data. When the domain layer catches ErpFault, the boundary has leaked even though the field names were mapped.

47.19 CQRS

Problem

One model serves two very different jobs. Writes need validation, invariants and normalised tables: an order with items, addresses and discounts spread across six tables. Reads need a flat, denormalised shape: the order list screen wants order number, customer name, item count, total and status in one row, sorted and paginated, at 3,000 requests per second. Serving both from one model means either your writes carry denormalised baggage or your reads join six tables on every request.

Solution

Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate the write model from the read model. Commands change state through the domain model; queries read from a shape built for reading. That is the whole idea. The read side may be a different query in the same database, a materialized view, a separate table, a replica, or a separate datastore entirely — those are increasing levels of commitment, and most teams should stop at the first or second.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  C["Command: PlaceOrder"] --> CH["Command handler"]
  CH --> WM["Write model: normalized tables"]
  WM --> EV["Domain event"]
  EV --> PRJ["Projector"]
  PRJ --> RM["Read model: order_list_view"]
  Q["Query: GET /orders"] --> QH["Query handler"]
  QH --> RM

Example

The lightweight version that pays for itself. Same database, separate read table maintained by a projector, so the list screen is a single indexed scan.

-- read model: one row per order, exactly what the list screen renders
CREATE TABLE order_list_view (
  order_id      UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id       UUID        NOT NULL,
  order_number  TEXT        NOT NULL,
  customer_name TEXT        NOT NULL,
  item_count    INT         NOT NULL,
  total_minor   BIGINT      NOT NULL,
  status        TEXT        NOT NULL,
  placed_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX olv_user_recent ON order_list_view (user_id, placed_at DESC);
// Write side: NestJS CQRS command handler, normalized entities, invariants enforced.
@CommandHandler(PlaceOrderCommand)
export class PlaceOrderHandler implements ICommandHandler<PlaceOrderCommand> {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource, private readonly bus: EventBus) {}

  async execute(cmd: PlaceOrderCommand): Promise<string> {
    const order = await this.ds.transaction(async (em) => {
      const o = Order.place(cmd);              // domain invariants live here
      await em.save(o);
      await em.insert(OutboxEvent, { aggregateId: o.id, eventType: 'order.placed', payload: o.toEvent() });
      return o;
    });
    this.bus.publish(new OrderPlacedEvent(order.id));
    return order.id;
  }
}

// Read side: no entities, no joins, no domain objects. Just the shape the UI needs.
@QueryHandler(ListOrdersQuery)
export class ListOrdersHandler implements IQueryHandler<ListOrdersQuery> {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  execute(q: ListOrdersQuery) {
    return this.ds.query(
      `SELECT order_id, order_number, customer_name, item_count, total_minor, status, placed_at
         FROM order_list_view
        WHERE user_id = $1 AND ($2::timestamptz IS NULL OR placed_at < $2)
        ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT $3`,
      [q.userId, q.cursor, q.limit],
    );
  }
}

Advantages

  • Reads become trivial and fast: 1 to 3 ms index scans instead of 40 ms six-table joins.
  • Read and write sides scale independently. Add read replicas or cache the read model without touching writes.
  • The write model can stay strictly normalised and rich, without denormalisation for the UI.
  • Query handlers stop importing domain entities, which removes a large class of accidental coupling.

Disadvantages

  • The read model is eventually consistent unless you update it in the same transaction. A user who just placed an order may not see it in their list, which is a support ticket generator.
  • Two models to keep in sync, plus a projector to operate, monitor and rebuild.
  • More code for the same feature. A simple CRUD entity becomes a command, a handler, an event, a projector and a read table.
  • Debugging gains a question: "is the data wrong, or is the projection behind?"

When to use

  • Read and write loads differ by an order of magnitude, or in shape.
  • The read shape is genuinely different from the write shape (dashboards, feeds, search, reporting).
  • Read traffic must scale independently, for example a public catalogue with an internal admin write path.

When NOT to use

  • Most CRUD applications. This deserves saying plainly: if your reads are "select the entity by id and show its fields", CQRS makes the system worse. You add eventual consistency, a projector, a rebuild procedure and double the code, in exchange for nothing. The default is one model, one table, an index, and SELECT.
  • When users expect read-after-write consistency everywhere and you cannot route those reads to the write model.
  • When the team is small. Two models means two things to change for every feature, forever.
  • As a synonym for "we use the @nestjs/cqrs package". Command and query classes over the same tables are a code-organisation choice, not CQRS, and that is fine — just do not claim architectural benefits you did not buy.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Read-after-write: the user places an order and the list is empty. Mitigate by reading from the write model for that one screen, or by writing the read row in the same transaction.
  • Projector lag: a slow projector makes every read stale. Emit projection_lag_seconds and alert on it.
  • Projection bug: a bad projector corrupts the read model. You need a documented, tested rebuild that runs in acceptable time. At 200 million rows, "rebuild" is a two-day operation you must plan for.
  • Duplicate events: projectors must be idempotent, typically by upserting keyed on the aggregate id.
  • Out-of-order events: apply a version number and ignore events older than the row's current version.

Senior perspective

CQRS is two ideas wearing one name, and conflating them causes most of the damage. The first idea — "the shape you read is not the shape you write" — is nearly always right and costs almost nothing: a denormalised table or a materialized view, updated by a projector, with a rebuild script. The second idea — separate databases, separate services, asynchronous projection, eventual consistency everywhere — is a serious distributed-systems commitment and should be justified by a number: read RPS, write RPS, or a query that cannot be made fast any other way. When someone proposes CQRS, I ask which of the two they mean. If they cannot say, they mean the first one and should build only that.

47.20 Event sourcing

Problem

Your orders table stores the current state. A customer disputes a charge and asks what the order looked like on the 3rd. You cannot answer: the row was updated in place and the previous values are gone. An updated_at column and a partial audit table give you fragments. Meanwhile the business keeps asking questions your schema was never designed for — "how many carts had an item removed before checkout?" — and each one needs a new column and a backfill.

Solution

Store the sequence of events as the source of truth instead of the current state. OrderPlaced, ItemAdded, PaymentAuthorized, ItemRemoved, OrderShipped. Current state is derived by replaying events (usually with periodic snapshots for speed). The event log is append-only and immutable, which gives you a perfect audit trail and the ability to build new read models over history that nobody thought of at the time.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  CMD["Command"] --> AGG["Aggregate: rebuild from events, validate"]
  AGG --> APP["Append new events"]
  APP --> ES[("event_store: append only")]
  ES --> SNAP["Snapshot every 100 events"]
  ES --> PRJ["Projectors"]
  PRJ --> RM1["order_current_view"]
  PRJ --> RM2["analytics: cart abandonment"]

Example

The store, the optimistic-concurrency guard that makes it correct, and the rehydration.

CREATE TABLE event_store (
  stream_id   UUID        NOT NULL,          -- one stream per aggregate
  version     INT         NOT NULL,          -- 1,2,3... per stream
  event_type  TEXT        NOT NULL,
  payload     JSONB       NOT NULL,
  metadata    JSONB       NOT NULL,          -- causationId, correlationId, actor
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (stream_id, version)           -- this is the concurrency control
);
CREATE TABLE snapshot (
  stream_id UUID PRIMARY KEY, version INT NOT NULL, state JSONB NOT NULL
);
async append(streamId: string, expectedVersion: number, events: DomainEvent[]): Promise<void> {
  await this.ds.transaction(async (em) => {
    const rows = events.map((e, i) => ({
      streamId, version: expectedVersion + i + 1,
      eventType: e.type, payload: e.payload,
      metadata: { correlationId: this.ctx.correlationId, actor: this.ctx.userId },
    }));
    try {
      await em.insert(EventRow, rows);
    } catch (err) {
      // PK violation means someone else appended since we loaded: retry the command
      if ((err as any).code === '23505') throw new ConcurrencyError(streamId, expectedVersion);
      throw err;
    }
  });
}

async load(streamId: string): Promise<Order> {
  const snap = await this.snapshots.findOne({ where: { streamId } });
  const from = snap?.version ?? 0;
  const events = await this.events.find({ where: { streamId, version: MoreThan(from) }, order: { version: 'ASC' } });
  return events.reduce((agg, e) => agg.apply(e), Order.fromSnapshot(snap));
}

Advantages

  • Complete, immutable history. Every state change, who caused it, and when. Compliance and dispute resolution become trivial.
  • Time travel: reconstruct any past state exactly.
  • New read models over old data. Add a projection today that answers a question about last year.
  • Optimistic concurrency falls out of the primary key, with no locks.
  • Debugging is exceptional: you can replay a production stream locally and watch the bug happen.

Disadvantages

  • Every query becomes a projection. There is no ad-hoc SELECT ... WHERE status = 'X' over the truth.
  • Schema evolution is genuinely hard. A five-year-old event must still be replayable, so you carry upcasters forever.
  • Deleting data is architecturally awkward, which collides with GDPR erasure. The usual answer, crypto-shredding, is real work.
  • Snapshotting, stream sizing, replay performance and projection rebuilds are all operational burdens you now own.
  • The talent pool is small. Most engineers joining your team have never done this.

When to use

  • Domains where history is the business: ledgers, accounting, trading, insurance claims, medical records, audit-heavy compliance.
  • Where regulators require proof of what happened, not just what is true now.
  • Where temporal queries and behavioural analytics have clear, funded business value.

When NOT to use

  • Almost every CRUD application. This is the strongest warning in this part. If your domain is "users edit their profile, admins manage products, customers place orders and view them", event sourcing will make your system slower to build, harder to query, harder to hire for, and harder to change — with no benefit you cannot get from an audit table.
  • When you need ad-hoc queries against current state. You will build a projection for every question, forever.
  • When "we might need the history someday" is the justification. Add an audit table (orders_history written by a trigger, or a pgaudit-style log). It gives you 90 percent of the value for 2 percent of the cost.
  • When erasure requirements are strict and the team has not designed crypto-shredding.
  • When the team is under five engineers, or when nobody has operated an event-sourced system before.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Huge streams: an aggregate with 200,000 events takes seconds to load. Snapshot, or the aggregate boundary is wrong.
  • Event schema drift: a renamed field breaks replay of old events. Version events and write upcasters, and test replay of the oldest event in CI.
  • Projection rebuild time: rebuilding from 500 million events can take days. Measure it before you need it in an incident.
  • Concurrency retries: a hot aggregate (a popular product's stock) causes constant version conflicts. Split the aggregate or move to a different model, such as sharded counters.
  • GDPR erasure: an immutable log conflicts with "delete my data". Encrypt personal fields per subject and destroy the key.
  • Poison event: a projector that throws on one malformed event stalls the whole projection.

Senior perspective

Event sourcing is a specialist tool that produces exceptional results in a narrow set of domains and quiet misery everywhere else. I have used it well in a payments ledger, where "what was the balance at 14:03 on the 12th" is a daily business question, and I have watched it applied to a product catalogue where it added six months to a roadmap and a permanent tax on every feature. My test is a single question: does the business ask questions about the past that the current state cannot answer, and is someone paid to answer them? If yes, event source that one bounded context and nothing else. If no, use a normal table plus an append-only history table written by a trigger, and spend the saved time on features. Note also that event sourcing and CQRS are separate decisions that got married by convention: you can do CQRS without event sourcing, and you almost always should.

47.21 Materialized view and read model

Problem

The seller dashboard shows revenue for the last 30 days grouped by day and category. The query joins orders, order_items, products and categories, aggregates 4 million rows, and takes 2.8 seconds. Forty sellers load the dashboard every morning at 09:00. Your database CPU chart has a spike shaped exactly like the sales team's routine.

Solution

Compute the result once and store it. PostgreSQL's MATERIALIZED VIEW does this natively with an explicit refresh; a hand-rolled summary table updated by a projector or a trigger gives you more control and incremental updates. Either way you trade freshness for latency, and you choose the trade explicitly.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  O["orders"] --> MV["Materialized view: seller_daily_revenue"]
  OI["order_items"] --> MV
  P["products"] --> MV
  REF["Refresh job: every 15 minutes"] --> MV
  API["Dashboard API"] -->|"2.8s becomes 4ms"| MV
  API -->|"today so far"| LIVE["Live query on last 24h only"]

Example

A concurrent refresh (which needs a unique index, and does not block readers) and the hybrid query that keeps today live.

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW seller_daily_revenue AS
SELECT o.seller_id,
       date_trunc('day', o.placed_at) AS day,
       p.category_id,
       count(DISTINCT o.id)           AS orders,
       sum(oi.qty * oi.unit_price_minor) AS revenue_minor
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p     ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.status IN ('PAID','SHIPPED','DELIVERED')
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3;

-- REFRESH CONCURRENTLY requires a unique index on the view
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX sdr_pk ON seller_daily_revenue (seller_id, day, category_id);
CREATE INDEX sdr_seller_day ON seller_daily_revenue (seller_id, day DESC);

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY seller_daily_revenue;  -- readers keep working
-- Hybrid: fast history from the view, live numbers for today only.
SELECT day, category_id, revenue_minor FROM seller_daily_revenue
 WHERE seller_id = $1 AND day >= current_date - 29 AND day < current_date
UNION ALL
SELECT current_date, p.category_id, sum(oi.qty * oi.unit_price_minor)
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
 WHERE o.seller_id = $1 AND o.placed_at >= current_date AND o.status IN ('PAID','SHIPPED','DELIVERED')
 GROUP BY p.category_id;

Advantages

  • Enormous latency wins: 2,800 ms becomes 4 ms, and the database CPU spike disappears.
  • No application code for the plain materialized view case. It is one DDL statement.
  • Refresh cost is paid once, not once per viewer.
  • CONCURRENTLY means no read downtime during refresh.

Disadvantages

  • Stale by design. You must decide and communicate the staleness window.
  • REFRESH recomputes everything: on a large view it can take minutes and burn significant I/O.
  • No incremental refresh in PostgreSQL, so very large views need a hand-rolled summary table instead.
  • The view is invisible to developers who do not know it exists, so they write the slow query again.

When to use

  • Dashboards, reports, leaderboards, aggregates over large tables.
  • Expensive queries whose inputs change far less often than they are read.
  • Any query where 15-minute-old data is business-acceptable.

When NOT to use

  • Data that must be current to the second (account balance, stock availability at checkout).
  • When the underlying query is slow because of a missing index. Fix the index first: a materialized view over a badly indexed query hides the real problem and doubles the storage.
  • When the refresh takes longer than the acceptable staleness. A 20-minute refresh cannot deliver 15-minute freshness.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Refresh overlap: the next refresh starts while the previous is running, doubling load. Take an advisory lock.
  • Non-concurrent refresh: plain REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and blocks every reader. In production, always CONCURRENTLY.
  • Bloat: concurrent refresh writes a full new copy and leaves dead tuples. Watch table size and autovacuum.
  • Silent staleness: the refresh job dies and the dashboard shows Tuesday's numbers on Friday. Store and display refreshed_at, and alert on its age.
  • Replica lag on top of staleness: a view read from a lagging replica is stale twice.

Senior perspective

The materialized view is the cheapest big win in the entire catalogue and it is systematically underused because it feels unfashionable next to a streaming pipeline. Before anyone builds a projection service, I want to see why REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY on a schedule is insufficient. Two disciplines make them safe in production: always expose the refresh timestamp to the UI so staleness is visible rather than surprising, and always alert on refresh age rather than trusting the cron. And the discipline that makes them honest: check the index first. Roughly half the "we need a materialized view" requests I have reviewed were a missing composite index.

47.22 Cache-aside

Problem

The product page is read 8,000 times per second. Each read is a 12 ms PostgreSQL query joining product, price and inventory. That is 96 database seconds of work per wall-clock second, which no single primary will serve. The data changes a few times a day.

Solution

The application checks the cache first. On a miss it reads the database, writes the result to the cache with a TTL, and returns it. On a write it invalidates or updates the entry. Also called lazy loading, this is the default caching pattern because the cache never needs to know about the database. Part 16 — Caching and Redis covers stampedes, TTL strategy, serialization and eviction in depth; this entry is the catalogue view with the invalidation detail that matters most.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  R["Read request"] --> C{"Redis GET"}
  C -->|"hit, 0.4ms"| RET["Return"]
  C -->|"miss"| DB[("PostgreSQL, 12ms")]
  DB --> SET["Redis SETEX ttl 300"]
  SET --> RET
  W["Write request"] --> DBW[("UPDATE")]
  DBW --> DEL["Redis DEL key after commit"]

Example

Cache-aside with single-flight protection, so a cold key under 8,000 RPS does not send 8,000 identical queries to PostgreSQL.

@Injectable()
export class ProductReadService {
  private readonly inflight = new Map<string, Promise<Product>>();

  async getProduct(id: string): Promise<Product> {
    const key = `product:v3:${id}`;                 // version in the key: deploy = clean slate
    const hit = await this.redis.get(key);
    if (hit) return JSON.parse(hit) as Product;

    // Single flight: one loader per key per pod, everyone else awaits it.
    const existing = this.inflight.get(key);
    if (existing) return existing;

    const p = (async () => {
      try {
        const product = await this.repo.findFull(id);
        if (!product) throw new NotFoundException();
        // jittered TTL so a batch of keys does not expire in the same second
        const ttl = 300 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 60);
        await this.redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(product), 'EX', ttl);
        return product;
      } finally {
        this.inflight.delete(key);
      }
    })();
    this.inflight.set(key, p);
    return p;
  }

  async updatePrice(id: string, priceMinor: number): Promise<void> {
    await this.ds.transaction((em) => em.update(Product, id, { priceMinor }));
    await this.redis.del(`product:v3:${id}`);       // AFTER commit, never before
  }
}

Advantages

  • Database load collapses. At a 97 percent hit rate, 8,000 RPS becomes 240 RPS on PostgreSQL.
  • Latency drops from 12 ms to under 1 ms for the common path.
  • Simple and resilient: if Redis is empty or down, everything still works, just slower.
  • Only requested data is cached, so memory tracks actual access patterns.

Disadvantages

  • Stale reads for up to the TTL. You must decide what staleness the business tolerates.
  • Cache invalidation is genuinely hard, especially for derived and list data.
  • Cold start after a Redis restart means full database load at once.
  • Every cached shape is a second representation to keep compatible across deploys.

When to use

  • Read-heavy data with a read-to-write ratio above roughly 10 to 1.
  • Expensive-to-compute results where slight staleness is acceptable.
  • Protecting the database from predictable hot keys.

When NOT to use

  • Write-heavy data. Constant invalidation means you pay cache cost and get no hits.
  • Data that must be strictly consistent: account balances, stock at the moment of checkout, permission checks after a revoke.
  • When the query is 12 ms because of a missing index. Add the index; a cache over a bad query hides it until the cache is cold during an incident, which is the worst possible moment.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Stampede: a hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once. Single flight plus jittered TTL, as above.
  • Invalidate before commit: deleting the key before the transaction commits lets a concurrent read repopulate the cache with the old value, which then lives for the whole TTL. Always invalidate after commit.
  • Redis down: with no timeout on the Redis call, the cache becomes slower than the database. Set a 50 to 100 ms timeout and treat failures as misses.
  • Hot key: one product on the front page saturates one Redis shard. Add a short-lived local cache in front.
  • Shape change: a deploy changes the cached object's fields and old entries crash the new code. Version the key prefix.
  • Unbounded memory: caching without TTL or eviction policy fills Redis and triggers evictions of the wrong keys. Set maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru.

Senior perspective

Cache-aside is right roughly nine times out of ten, and the two decisions that matter are the TTL and the invalidation point. On TTL, I start from the business question — "how stale can this be before someone is harmed?" — and pick the largest number that answers it, because every second of TTL is database load removed. On invalidation, the rule is absolute: invalidate after commit, never before, and never inside the transaction. The other habit worth building is measuring hit rate per key prefix. An aggregate hit rate of 95 percent can hide a prefix at 20 percent that is costing you more in Redis round trips than it saves.

47.23 Sharded counters

Problem

A viral post's like counter. UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1 WHERE id = $1 at 5,000 requests per second means 5,000 transactions serialising on one row. Every writer takes a row lock; each must wait for the previous to commit. PostgreSQL will happily do maybe 1,000 to 3,000 updates per second on a single row under ideal conditions, and far fewer with replication and fsync. Beyond that, lock waits climb, connections pile up, and the whole pool is stuck behind one row. This is the classic hot row.

Solution

Split the counter into N rows. Each writer picks a shard (randomly, or by hashing the actor id) and increments that. Reading sums the shards. Contention drops by a factor of N, at the cost of read complexity and exact-at-any-instant precision.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  W1["Writer"] -->|"hash mod 16"| S3["shard 3"]
  W2["Writer"] -->|"hash mod 16"| S11["shard 11"]
  W3["Writer"] -->|"hash mod 16"| S3
  S3 --> T["post_like_shard table"]
  S11 --> T
  RD["Read count"] -->|"SUM over 16 rows"| T
  RD --> CA["Cached total, TTL 5s"]

Example

The table, the write and the read, with the rollup that keeps reads cheap.

CREATE TABLE post_like_shard (
  post_id  UUID   NOT NULL,
  shard_id SMALLINT NOT NULL,          -- 0..15
  count    BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  PRIMARY KEY (post_id, shard_id)
);

-- write: contention is now 1/16th per row
INSERT INTO post_like_shard (post_id, shard_id, count)
VALUES ($1, (hashtext($2::text) & 15), 1)     -- $2 = user_id, deterministic shard
ON CONFLICT (post_id, shard_id) DO UPDATE SET count = post_like_shard.count + 1;

-- read: 16 rows, one index scan, about 0.2 ms
SELECT sum(count) FROM post_like_shard WHERE post_id = $1;
// Even cheaper: count in Redis, roll up to PostgreSQL periodically.
await this.redis.hincrby(`likes:${postId}`, String(shard), 1);       // 0.3 ms, no locks
// every 10s a rollup job drains the hash into post_like_shard for durability

Advantages

  • Removes the hot-row bottleneck. Sixteen shards turn 3,000 writes per second into a theoretical 48,000.
  • Simple, boring SQL. No new infrastructure.
  • Shard count is tunable per counter: 4 for moderately warm, 64 for viral.

Disadvantages

  • Reads cost N row lookups instead of one, so a list of 50 posts becomes 800 lookups without a rollup or cache.
  • Exact instantaneous totals are harder; the sum is consistent but the shape encourages caching, which reintroduces staleness.
  • Decrements can make an individual shard negative, which looks alarming even when the sum is right.
  • More rows: 10 million posts times 16 shards is 160 million rows.

When to use

  • Genuinely hot single-row counters: likes, views, stock reservations on a flash-sale item, rate counters.
  • Write rates above roughly 500 per second against one logical row.

When NOT to use

  • Ordinary counters. A product with 40 orders a day does not need sharding; you have added 16 rows and a sum for nothing.
  • When approximate counts are acceptable and Redis alone will do. INCR on one Redis key handles 100,000 per second without any sharding.
  • When the counter needs to enforce a limit (stock must not go below zero). A sum over shards cannot be checked atomically; use a single row with a CHECK constraint, or Redis with a Lua script.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Read amplification: a feed of 50 posts summing 16 shards each. Maintain a rollup total updated every few seconds, and read that.
  • Shard count change: going from 16 to 64 makes old counts live in the wrong shards. Totals stay correct because you sum all shards, but never re-shard by re-hashing.
  • Redis rollup loss: if Redis is the write path and it restarts before the rollup, you lose counts. Acceptable for likes, unacceptable for anything billed.
  • Negative shards: after decrements, a shard can go negative. Clamp only the sum, never the shard.
  • Autovacuum pressure: hot-updated rows generate dead tuples. Set a lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor on the table.

Senior perspective

Sharded counters are a targeted fix for a specific, measurable symptom: lock waits on one row. I do not apply them pre-emptively, because they cost read complexity forever. The trigger is data — pg_stat_activity showing sessions blocked on a Lock wait event for the same tuple, or pg_locks pointing at one row. When that appears, the decision is between sharding in PostgreSQL and moving the counter to Redis with periodic rollup. My default for social-style counters is Redis plus rollup, because it is faster and cheaper. My default for anything that touches money or stock is PostgreSQL, because durability beats throughput and I would rather solve contention by changing the model than by risking a lost increment.

47.24 Fan-out on write versus on read

Problem

A social feed. When a user opens the app, they must see recent posts from everyone they follow, newest first, in under 200 ms. Two obvious designs exist and they are opposites. Compute the feed when someone posts (push a copy into every follower's timeline), or compute it when someone reads (query the posts of everyone they follow and merge). Choosing wrong costs you either write amplification or read latency, and at scale both are severe.

Solution

Fan-out on write precomputes timelines: one post by a user with 900 followers becomes 900 inserts, and reads are a single indexed scan. Fan-out on read computes at query time: writes are one insert, reads merge N sources. The real answer for most large systems is a hybrid: fan out on write for normal users, and fan out on read for the small number of accounts with enormous follower counts.

Architecture

flowchart TB
  POST["User posts"] --> DEC{"follower count"}
  DEC -->|"under 10k: fan-out on write"| Q["Enqueue fanout job"]
  Q --> TL["Insert into each follower timeline"]
  DEC -->|"over 10k: celebrity, no fanout"| ONLY["Store post only"]
  READ["User opens feed"] --> M["Merge: precomputed timeline"]
  M --> CEL["Plus live query of followed celebrities"]
  CEL --> OUT["Sorted merged feed"]

Example

The hybrid, which is what you would actually build. Fan-out is a background job with a cap; celebrities are merged at read time.

// WRITE PATH: fan out to followers, in batches, off the request path.
@Processor('fanout')
export class FanoutProcessor {
  @Process({ concurrency: 8 })
  async handle(job: Job<{ postId: string; authorId: string }>) {
    const followerCount = await this.follows.countFollowers(job.data.authorId);
    if (followerCount > 10_000) return;             // celebrity: read-time merge instead

    let cursor: string | null = null;
    do {
      const page = await this.follows.pageFollowers(job.data.authorId, cursor, 1_000);
      await this.timeline.insertMany(page.ids.map((uid) => ({
        userId: uid, postId: job.data.postId, createdAt: job.data.createdAt,
      })));                                          // 1000 rows per round trip
      cursor = page.next;
    } while (cursor);
  }
}

// READ PATH: precomputed rows plus a live query for followed celebrities.
async feed(userId: string, before: Date, limit = 30): Promise<Post[]> {
  const [own, celebs] = await Promise.all([
    this.timeline.page(userId, before, limit),                    // 1 index scan, ~2ms
    this.posts.recentByAuthors(await this.follows.celebrityIds(userId), before, limit),
  ]);
  return merge(own, celebs).sort(byCreatedAtDesc).slice(0, limit);
}

Advantages

  • Fan-out on write: reads are one indexed scan, so feed latency is flat and predictable regardless of how many people you follow. Read traffic dominates in social products by 100 to 1, so optimising reads is usually right.
  • Fan-out on read: writes are cheap and instant, storage is minimal, and there is no timeline to rebuild when follow graphs change.
  • Hybrid: bounds the worst case of both.

Disadvantages

  • Fan-out on write: write amplification. An account with 40 million followers generates 40 million inserts per post. Storage multiplies: 500 million timeline rows for a modest network. Unfollowing means deleting rows or filtering at read time.
  • Fan-out on read: latency grows with the number of followed accounts. A user following 3,000 accounts triggers a merge across 3,000 sources; p99 becomes unacceptable.
  • Hybrid: two code paths, a threshold to tune, and merge logic that must be correct at page boundaries.

When to use

  • Fan-out on write: read-heavy feeds, modest follower counts, latency-critical reads.
  • Fan-out on read: write-heavy or low-read systems, symmetric graphs (group chats, small teams), and any case where storage cost dominates.
  • Hybrid: any real social product past a few million users.

When NOT to use

  • Do not fan out on write when the follower distribution has a long tail you cannot cap; you will build a job that runs for an hour on a single post.
  • Do not fan out on read when the average user follows hundreds of accounts and expects a 200 ms feed.
  • Do not build either for a product with 5,000 users. A single SELECT ... WHERE author_id = ANY($1) ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 30 with a good composite index serves that perfectly for years.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Follower spike: an account gains a million followers in a day and the fan-out queue backs up for hours. Cap fan-out and fall back to read-time merge.
  • Timeline drift: a deleted post must vanish from millions of timelines. Filter deleted posts at read time rather than chasing rows.
  • New follow: a fresh follow shows no history unless you backfill; a backfill of recent posts on follow is the usual compromise.
  • Ordering across sources: merging precomputed and live results at a cursor boundary can drop or duplicate items. Merge on a stable sort key, not on offset.
  • Storage growth: timeline tables grow without bound. Trim to the most recent 1,000 entries per user; nobody scrolls further.

Senior perspective

This is the clearest example in the catalogue of a decision driven purely by numbers, and the numbers are follower distribution and read-to-write ratio. Get those two from the data before arguing. In every social system I have worked on, the distribution was heavy-tailed enough that a pure strategy failed — median follower count in the tens, maximum in the millions — which is why the hybrid is not a clever optimisation but the only design that survives. The other thing I insist on early is timeline trimming, because unbounded per-user timelines are how a feed feature turns into a storage bill nobody budgeted for.

47.25 Competing consumers

Problem

Order confirmation emails arrive on a queue at 400 per second during a flash sale. One worker processes 30 per second because each email involves a template render and an SMTP call. The queue grows by 370 messages per second. Customers get their confirmation an hour late, and the backlog does not clear until 03:00.

Solution

Run many identical consumers against the same queue. The broker delivers each message to exactly one of them, so throughput scales roughly linearly with worker count until some other resource becomes the bottleneck. This is the fundamental scaling pattern for asynchronous work, and it is why queues exist.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  P["Producers"] --> Q["Queue: emails"]
  Q --> W1["Worker 1"]
  Q --> W2["Worker 2"]
  Q --> W3["Worker 3"]
  Q --> WN["Worker N"]
  W1 --> SMTP["Email provider"]
  W2 --> SMTP
  W3 --> SMTP
  WN --> SMTP
  Q --> LAG["Lag metric"] --> HPA["Autoscaler: scale on queue depth"]

Example

A BullMQ worker with bounded concurrency, plus the Kubernetes autoscaler that scales on queue depth rather than CPU (workers waiting on SMTP use almost no CPU, so CPU-based scaling never triggers).

new Worker(
  'emails',
  async (job) => {
    await this.mailer.send(job.data);   // idempotent: provider dedupes on messageId
  },
  {
    connection,
    concurrency: 10,                     // per pod; 12 pods gives 120 in flight
    limiter: { max: 500, duration: 1000 }, // respect the provider's 500/s contract
    lockDuration: 30_000,                // longer than the slowest send
  },
);
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata: { name: email-workers }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { name: email-worker }
  minReplicaCount: 2
  maxReplicaCount: 30
  triggers:
    - type: redis
      metadata:
        address: redis.prod:6379
        listName: "bull:emails:wait"
        listLength: "100"      # add a pod per 100 waiting jobs

Advantages

  • Throughput scales with worker count; adding capacity is a replica-count change.
  • Natural load levelling: producers never wait for consumers.
  • Fault tolerance is built in: a crashed worker's unacknowledged message is redelivered to another.
  • Rolling deploys are invisible to producers.

Disadvantages

  • Message order across consumers is lost. Two updates to the same order can be processed out of sequence.
  • At-least-once delivery means duplicates, so handlers must be idempotent (see the transactional inbox).
  • The bottleneck moves. Twenty workers hammering one PostgreSQL connection pool or one third-party rate limit is worse than five.

When to use

  • Any independent, parallelisable unit of work: emails, thumbnails, webhooks, exports, indexing.
  • Load spikes that should not be felt by the producer.

When NOT to use

  • When strict ordering per entity is required, unless you partition by key (Kafka partitions, or a per-entity lock).
  • When the downstream cannot take the concurrency. Scaling workers 10x against a database that can serve 2x is how you take down the database with a background job.
  • For work that must happen inside the user's request, such as validation that decides the HTTP response.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Visibility timeout too short: a slow job's lock expires, the message is redelivered, and two workers process it simultaneously. Set lockDuration above p99 processing time and renew for long jobs.
  • Poison message: one bad payload crashes every worker in turn, looping forever. That is what dead-letter queues are for.
  • Rebalancing storms in Kafka: every deploy triggers a rebalance and pauses consumption. Use cooperative sticky assignment and a sane session.timeout.ms.
  • Downstream saturation: workers scale up and exhaust the connection pool. Bulkhead the pool per worker type.
  • Unbounded scale-up: KEDA scales to 200 pods and hits the provider's rate limit, which returns 429s that you then retry.

Senior perspective

Competing consumers is the pattern people think they get for free by using a queue, and mostly they do. The two things that are not free are ordering and idempotency, and both must be decided before the first message flows. My default is to assume no ordering, make every handler idempotent, and use a partition key only where the business genuinely requires per-entity sequencing. The operational default I insist on is scaling on queue depth or consumer lag, never on CPU: I/O-bound workers sit at 5 percent CPU while a backlog grows for two hours, and CPU-based autoscaling will happily do nothing the entire time.

47.26 Retry queue

Problem

A webhook delivery to a partner fails because their endpoint is down for maintenance. Retrying immediately fails again. Retrying in a tight loop inside the worker blocks that worker for the duration of the backoff, so a handful of failing messages consume your whole worker pool while thousands of healthy messages wait behind them.

Solution
