Move the failed message out of the main queue and into a delayed queue, to be redelivered after a backoff. The worker returns immediately and picks up the next message. Backoff grows per attempt, so the retry schedule might be 30 s, 2 min, 10 min, 1 h, 6 h. Some brokers support this natively (BullMQ delayed jobs, SQS with a delay queue, RabbitMQ with a dead-letter exchange and TTL); Kafka needs explicit retry topics.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  M["Main queue: webhooks"] --> W["Worker"]
  W -->|"success"| DONE["Ack"]
  W -->|"retryable failure"| R1["retry.30s"]
  R1 -->|"delay elapsed"| M
  W -->|"attempt 5 failed"| DLQ["Dead-letter queue"]
  R1 --> R2["retry.5m"] --> M

Example

BullMQ with per-job backoff, plus the Kafka pattern of tiered retry topics, which is the version people get wrong.

await this.webhookQueue.add('deliver', payload, {
  attempts: 6,
  backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 30_000 },  // 30s, 1m, 2m, 4m, 8m
  removeOnComplete: 1000,
  removeOnFail: false,                              // keep failures for inspection
});
// Kafka: separate topics per delay tier. Never sleep inside a consumer:
// a paused poll loop triggers a rebalance and stalls the whole partition.
const TIERS = [
  { topic: 'webhooks.retry.1m',  delayMs: 60_000 },
  { topic: 'webhooks.retry.10m', delayMs: 600_000 },
  { topic: 'webhooks.retry.1h',  delayMs: 3_600_000 },
];

async onFailure(msg: KafkaMessage, attempt: number): Promise<void> {
  const tier = TIERS[attempt - 1];
  if (!tier) return this.producer.send({ topic: 'webhooks.dlq', messages: [msg] });
  await this.producer.send({
    topic: tier.topic,
    messages: [{ ...msg, headers: { ...msg.headers, attempt: String(attempt + 1),
      'not-before': String(Date.now() + tier.delayMs) } }],
  });
}
// The retry-tier consumer checks not-before; if the time has not come, it pauses
// the partition until it has, which is safe because the tier topic is ordered by time.

Advantages

  • Failing work stops blocking healthy work.
  • Backoff gives the downstream time to recover instead of hammering it.
  • Retry state is durable: a worker crash does not lose the schedule.
  • Attempt counts and delays are visible and tunable in production without a deploy.

Disadvantages

  • Ordering is lost for retried messages. A retried order.updated can land after a newer one.
  • More topics or queues to create, monitor and reason about.
  • Long backoffs mean the effect happens much later than the cause, which confuses debugging and users.

When to use

  • Deliveries to systems you do not control: webhooks, partner APIs, payment providers.
  • Any failure class that is genuinely transient over minutes to hours.

When NOT to use

  • For failures that will never succeed: validation errors, 404s, malformed payloads. Send those straight to the DLQ; retrying them for six hours is pure waste.
  • When the message has a business deadline shorter than the backoff, such as a one-time password.
  • When retrying is unsafe because the handler is not idempotent.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Retry loop with no cap: a message that always fails cycles forever, consuming capacity indefinitely. Always terminate at the DLQ.
  • Sleeping in a consumer: await sleep(600000) inside a Kafka handler stops heartbeats and triggers a rebalance that stalls the consumer group.
  • Retry amplification: every failure during a downstream outage lands in the retry queue, and when the downstream recovers they all fire at once and knock it over again. Add jitter to delays.
  • Message expiry: a retry scheduled for 6 hours later against a broker with a 4-hour retention silently disappears.
  • Growing payloads: appending diagnostic headers on each retry until the message exceeds the broker's size limit.

Senior perspective

The rule I apply is: classify the failure before you schedule the retry. A 422 from a partner is permanent and belongs in the dead-letter queue immediately; a 503 or a connection reset is transient and belongs in the retry tier. Systems that skip this classification spend most of their retry capacity on messages that can never succeed, and then have no capacity left during a real outage. The second rule is that the retry schedule is a product decision: how long should we keep trying to deliver a partner's webhook before we give up and page someone? Get an answer from the business, and encode it as the tier list.

47.27 Dead-letter queue

Problem

A message fails permanently: a schema change made the payload unparseable, a referenced order was hard-deleted, or a bug throws on one specific edge case. Without somewhere to put it, you have two bad options — drop it silently (data loss you will discover in an audit) or keep retrying (a poison message that blocks the partition or burns capacity forever).

Solution

After a bounded number of attempts, move the message to a dedicated queue or topic with its full context: original payload, error message, stack trace, attempt count, timestamps and correlation id. The main flow continues. Humans and tools then inspect, fix and replay.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  Q["Main queue"] --> W["Worker"]
  W -->|"attempts exhausted"| DLQ["DLQ with error context"]
  DLQ --> AL["Alert: DLQ depth above 0"]
  DLQ --> INS["Inspect: query by error type"]
  INS --> FIX["Fix code or data"]
  FIX --> RP["Replay tool: DLQ back to main queue"]
  RP --> Q

Example

A dead-letter record that is actually useful during an incident, and the replay endpoint that makes it a workflow rather than a graveyard.

async deadLetter(msg: KafkaMessage, err: Error, attempts: number): Promise<void> {
  await this.producer.send({
    topic: 'orders.dlq',
    messages: [{
      key: msg.key,
      value: msg.value,                                   // original payload, untouched
      headers: {
        'original-topic': 'orders.events',
        'original-partition': String(msg.partition ?? ''),
        'original-offset': msg.offset,
        'error-class': err.constructor.name,
        'error-message': err.message.slice(0, 500),
        'attempts': String(attempts),
        'failed-at': new Date().toISOString(),
        'correlation-id': msg.headers?.['correlation-id'] ?? '',
        'consumer-version': process.env.APP_VERSION ?? 'unknown',
      },
    }],
  });
  this.metrics.inc('dlq_messages', { topic: 'orders.events', error: err.constructor.name });
}
// Replay is a first-class, guarded operation, not a script somebody writes at 03:00.
@Post('admin/dlq/:topic/replay')
@Roles('sre')
async replay(@Param('topic') topic: string, @Body() dto: ReplayDto) {
  const msgs = await this.dlq.read(topic, { since: dto.since, errorClass: dto.errorClass, limit: dto.limit ?? 100 });
  for (const m of msgs) {
    await this.producer.send({ topic: m.originalTopic, messages: [{ key: m.key, value: m.value }] });
  }
  return { replayed: msgs.length };   // consumers are idempotent, so replay is safe
}

Advantages

  • No silent data loss, and no poison message stalling the pipeline.
  • Failures become a queryable dataset: "17,000 messages failed with ProductNotFound between 14:00 and 14:20" is a diagnosis in one query.
  • Replay after a fix restores correctness without manual data entry.

Disadvantages

  • Only works if someone watches it. An unmonitored DLQ is a very tidy way to lose data.
  • Replay requires idempotent consumers, or you double-process.
  • Storing full payloads in the DLQ can duplicate sensitive data into a less-protected place.

When to use

  • Every consumer, without exception. This is not optional infrastructure.

When NOT to use

  • Never skip it. But do not use a DLQ as a substitute for validation: if 30 percent of messages dead-letter, the contract is broken and the DLQ is hiding it.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Unmonitored DLQ: the classic. Alert on depth greater than zero, and on rate.
  • DLQ for the DLQ: the dead-lettering itself fails because the broker is down. Fall back to writing the failure to a database table or structured log.
  • Replay storms: replaying 200,000 messages at once takes down the very service that could not handle them. Replay with rate limiting.
  • Stale replays: replaying week-old price.changed events overwrites current prices with old ones. Check event timestamps before replaying anything order-dependent.
  • PII duplication: DLQ payloads inherit personal data, so retention and access control must match the source topic.

Senior perspective

The DLQ is where I judge a team's operational maturity. Anyone can create the topic; the mature version has three more things: an alert that fires on the first message, headers rich enough to diagnose without opening the payload, and a tested replay path with rate limiting and role-based access. I have seen a DLQ with 1.2 million messages accumulated over eight months that nobody had ever looked at — every one of them a customer order that never shipped. Set the alert on the day you create the topic, not later.

47.28 Claim check

Problem

Your event carries a 40 MB video, a 12 MB CSV import, or a base64 PDF. Kafka's default message limit is 1 MB and raising it hurts everything: broker memory, replication bandwidth, consumer buffer sizes and rebalance times. SQS caps at 256 KB. Even where a big message fits, every consumer of that topic now pays to transfer bytes it may not need, and your broker becomes an expensive, badly-shaped blob store.

Solution

Store the payload in object storage and put only a reference in the message: bucket, key, size, checksum, content type. Consumers that need the bytes fetch them; consumers that only need the metadata never pay. The message goes from 40 MB to 400 bytes. The name comes from a coat check: you carry the ticket, not the coat.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  P["Producer"] -->|"PUT object"| S3["S3 bucket"]
  P -->|"publish reference"| K["Kafka: media.uploaded"]
  K --> C1["Transcoder: fetches bytes"]
  K --> C2["Audit consumer: metadata only"]
  C1 -->|"GET object"| S3
  S3 --> LC["Lifecycle rule: delete after 30 days"]

Example

Producing the claim check and consuming it, with the details that make it safe: checksum, size limit and a scoped, expiring URL.

async publishUpload(file: Express.Multer.File, userId: string): Promise<void> {
  const key = `uploads/${userId}/${randomUUID()}`;
  const checksum = createHash('sha256').update(file.buffer).digest('hex');

  await this.s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({
    Bucket: this.bucket, Key: key, Body: file.buffer,
    ContentType: file.mimetype, ChecksumSHA256: Buffer.from(checksum, 'hex').toString('base64'),
    Metadata: { userId },
  }));

  // 380 bytes instead of 40 MB
  await this.producer.send({
    topic: 'media.uploaded',
    messages: [{ key: userId, value: JSON.stringify({
      bucket: this.bucket, key, sizeBytes: file.size,
      contentType: file.mimetype, checksumSha256: checksum,
      uploadedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    }) }],
  });
}

async consume(ref: ClaimCheck): Promise<void> {
  if (ref.sizeBytes > 500 * 1024 * 1024) throw new TooLargeError(ref.key);  // guard memory
  const obj = await this.s3.send(new GetObjectCommand({ Bucket: ref.bucket, Key: ref.key }));
  await pipeline(obj.Body as Readable, this.transcoder.createSink());        // stream, never buffer
}

Advantages

  • Messages stay small, so broker throughput, retention cost and rebalance times all stay healthy.
  • Consumers that need only metadata skip the transfer entirely.
  • Object storage is the right tool for blobs: cheap, durable, lifecycle-managed, and it supports ranged reads and streaming.
  • Retention policies decouple: keep events for a year, keep blobs for 30 days.

Disadvantages

  • Two systems must stay consistent. A message pointing at a deleted object is a broken event.
  • Extra latency per consumer: an S3 GET is 20 to 80 ms versus reading bytes already in the message.
  • Access control gets more complex; each consumer needs bucket permissions.
  • Replaying old events may find the objects expired.

When to use

  • Any payload above roughly 100 KB: images, video, documents, large exports, bulk import files.
  • Where multiple consumers need the same large payload, so it is downloaded only by those that use it.

When NOT to use

  • Small payloads. A 2 KB order event does not need a claim check; you have added a network call and a failure mode for nothing.
  • When the consumer must be able to process from the message alone with no external dependency, for example a strictly air-gapped audit consumer.
  • When object lifetime cannot be guaranteed to exceed message retention plus replay window.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Dangling reference: the lifecycle rule deletes the object after 30 days, then someone replays a 60-day-old event. Align lifecycle with replay policy, and handle NoSuchKey as a permanent failure, not a retry.
  • Write-then-publish race: publishing before the PUT completes gives consumers a 404. Always store first, publish second.
  • Partial upload: a multipart upload that failed leaves an incomplete object. Verify the checksum on read.
  • Memory blowup: a consumer that buffers a 2 GB object into a Node Buffer gets OOMKilled. Stream, and enforce a size guard.
  • Permission drift: a new consumer without bucket access fails on every message.

Senior perspective

The claim check is one of those patterns that seems obvious after you have had the alternative incident: a team raised max.message.bytes to 50 MB to ship PDFs through Kafka, and six months later broker memory pressure during a rebalance caused a two-hour consumer outage. The rule I write into event guidelines is a hard cap — messages over 100 KB must use a claim check — enforced by a producer-side check that throws. The other detail is ordering: store the object, verify it, then publish. Reversing those two produces intermittent 404s that are maddening to debug because they only happen under load.

47.29 Leader election

Problem

You run six replicas of a service for availability. One of its jobs is a nightly reconciliation that must run exactly once, and another is a poller that drains a table. With six replicas, both run six times: six duplicate reports, six workers fighting over the same rows, six emails to the finance team. Scaling for availability broke a job that assumes singularity.

Solution

Elect one replica as leader; only the leader performs the singleton work. Election uses a shared store with an atomic primitive and a lease that expires, so if the leader dies another takes over within seconds. Options in order of increasing weight: a PostgreSQL advisory lock, a Redis lease with SET NX PX, a Kubernetes Lease object, or a proper consensus store like etcd.

Architecture

flowchart TB
  P1["Pod 1"] -->|"try acquire lease"| L["Lease store: Redis or PG"]
  P2["Pod 2"] -->|"try acquire lease"| L
  P3["Pod 3"] -->|"try acquire lease"| L
  L -->|"granted, ttl 15s"| P1
  P1 -->|"renew every 5s"| L
  P1 --> JOB["Run singleton job"]
  L -->|"lease expired"| P2
  P2 --> JOB

Example

The simplest thing that works well in a PostgreSQL shop: a session-level advisory lock. The lock disappears automatically if the connection dies, which is exactly the failure semantics you want.

@Injectable()
export class ReconciliationJob {
  private readonly LOCK_KEY = 918_273_645;   // arbitrary but fixed per job

  @Cron('0 2 * * *')                          // fires on every replica
  async run(): Promise<void> {
    const runner = this.ds.createQueryRunner();
    await runner.connect();
    try {
      // Non-blocking: returns immediately. Only one connection in the cluster wins.
      const [{ pg_try_advisory_lock: got }] = await runner.query(
        'SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock($1)', [this.LOCK_KEY]);
      if (!got) return this.logger.debug('another replica holds the lock, skipping');

      await this.reconcile();                 // safe: exactly one replica is here
    } finally {
      await runner.query('SELECT pg_advisory_unlock($1)', [this.LOCK_KEY]);
      await runner.release();                 // releasing the connection also frees the lock
    }
  }
}
// Redis variant for non-PostgreSQL work, with the renewal that makes it a lease.
const acquired = await redis.set('leader:indexer', this.podName, 'NX', 'PX', 15_000);
if (acquired) {
  this.renewTimer = setInterval(async () => {
    // renew ONLY if we still own it; a plain PEXPIRE can extend someone else's lease
    await redis.eval(
      `if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], 15000) else return 0 end`,
      1, 'leader:indexer', this.podName);
  }, 5_000);
}

Advantages

  • Lets you scale replicas for availability without duplicating singleton work.
  • Automatic failover: a crashed leader's lease expires and another replica takes over in seconds.
  • The advisory-lock version needs no new infrastructure at all.

Disadvantages

  • Leadership is never perfectly safe. Between a leader pausing (GC, CPU throttle) and its lease expiring, two processes can believe they are leader.
  • The leader is a capacity bottleneck: singleton work does not scale.
  • Failover has a gap. With a 15-second lease, nothing runs for up to 15 seconds.

When to use

  • Cron jobs and schedulers on multi-replica deployments.
  • Single-writer processes: a CDC relay, a partition assigner, a cache warmer.
  • Coordination where a broker's consumer-group semantics do not apply.

When NOT to use

  • Where the work is parallelisable. Do not elect a leader to consume a queue; use competing consumers.
  • Where a database constraint or SKIP LOCKED gives you safety without coordination — that is almost always the better answer for "drain a table".
  • As a substitute for idempotency. Assume split brain will happen and make the work safe anyway.
  • Do not build your own consensus. If you truly need strong leadership guarantees, use etcd or the platform's primitives.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Split brain: a leader is CPU-throttled for 20 seconds; its lease expires; a new leader starts; the old one wakes up and continues, believing it still leads. Fence the work with a monotonically increasing token, or make it idempotent.
  • Clock skew: TTL-based leases assume roughly synchronised clocks. Renew at one third of the TTL to leave margin.
  • Lock never released: an application-level lock in a table with no expiry, held by a crashed pod, blocks the job forever. Advisory locks and Redis leases both expire; table-based locks usually do not.
  • Leader overload: all singleton work concentrated on one pod that then falls behind on its health checks.
  • Renewal failure: Redis blips for 3 seconds, the renewal fails, the lease is lost mid-job. Detect loss and abort cleanly rather than finishing blind.

Senior perspective

My first question is always whether the work truly needs a single runner. Half the time the honest answer is "we need it to not run twice", and the right tool is a uniqueness constraint or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, not an election. When election is genuinely needed, I use pg_try_advisory_lock in PostgreSQL shops because it is free, correct and self-cleaning. The thing I never rely on is the guarantee itself: leader election reduces the probability of duplicate execution; idempotency eliminates the consequence. Build both, and you can sleep through a lease expiry.

47.30 Strangler Fig

Problem

A ten-year-old monolith runs the business. It is 400,000 lines, has no tests worth the name, and touches one database with 300 tables. A rewrite is estimated at eighteen months, during which no new features ship. Every big-bang rewrite you have witnessed either shipped two years late or was cancelled. Yet the monolith cannot be maintained much longer.

Solution

Grow the new system around the old one and let it take over route by route, exactly as a strangler fig grows around its host tree. Put a routing layer in front. Move one capability at a time to a new service; the router sends that path to the new system and everything else to the old. Repeat until the monolith serves nothing, then delete it. The system stays live and shippable throughout, and every step is individually reversible.

Architecture

flowchart LR
  C["Clients"] --> R["Router at the edge"]
  R -->|"/catalog/*"| NEW["New Catalog Service"]
  R -->|"/checkout/*, /admin/*"| OLD["Legacy monolith"]
  NEW --> NDB[("New catalog DB")]
  OLD --> ODB[("Legacy DB")]
  NDB -.->|"CDC sync during transition"| ODB
  ACL["Anti-corruption layer"] --- NEW

Example

The migration in three states, expressed as router config. The middle state — dual read with comparison — is the one that makes this safe.

# Stage 1: shadow. New service receives a copy, its response is compared, never returned.
- match: { prefix: /catalog }
  route: { cluster: legacy }
  request_mirror_policies:
    - cluster: catalog_new
      runtime_fraction: { default_value: { numerator: 100, denominator: HUNDRED } }

# Stage 2: canary. 5 percent of real traffic served by the new service.
- match: { prefix: /catalog }
  route:
    weighted_clusters:
      clusters:
        - { name: catalog_new, weight: 5 }
        - { name: legacy,      weight: 95 }

# Stage 3: cut over. Legacy kept warm for a one-line rollback for two weeks.
- match: { prefix: /catalog }
  route: { cluster: catalog_new }
// Shadow comparison: log differences, never fail the user's request.
@Injectable()
export class ShadowComparator {
  async compare(path: string, legacy: unknown, next: Promise<unknown>): Promise<void> {
    try {
      const candidate = await Promise.race([next, timeout(1_500)]);
      const diff = diffIgnoring(legacy, candidate, ['generatedAt', 'traceId']);
      if (diff.length) this.metrics.inc('shadow_mismatch', { path, field: diff[0].path });
    } catch {
      this.metrics.inc('shadow_error', { path });   // shadow failures never affect users
    }
  }
}

Advantages

  • The business keeps shipping. No feature freeze, no eighteen-month bet.
  • Risk is decomposed: each capability is a small, independently reversible migration.
  • You learn the real requirements from live traffic instead of from the old code's comments.
  • Rollback is a routing change, measured in seconds.

Disadvantages

  • Two systems run in parallel for a long time — often years — and both need maintenance, on-call and deploys.
  • Data synchronisation between old and new is the hard part, and it is where the real cost lives.
  • Migration fatigue is a genuine organisational risk. Half-finished strangler migrations are extremely common, and a permanently half-migrated system is worse than either endpoint.

When to use

  • Any migration of a live, revenue-carrying system.
  • Replacing a vendor platform, a legacy monolith, or an old database.
  • When downtime is unacceptable and a rewrite is unaffordable.

When NOT to use

  • Small systems. If the whole thing is 8,000 lines and can be rewritten in three weeks with a maintenance window, do that.
  • When the boundaries are not yet understood. Strangling requires knowing where to cut; if you cannot name the capability, do the domain work first.
  • When nobody will fund finishing it. Starting a strangler migration without a committed end date and an owner produces the worst outcome in this catalogue: permanent duality.

Edge cases and failure modes

  • Shared database: the new service reads the legacy schema directly, which is fast to build and creates the exact coupling you were escaping. Use an ACL and plan the data split.
  • Dual writes during transition: writing to both systems is a dual-write problem; use CDC one way instead, and make one system authoritative for each entity at all times.
  • Behavioural drift: the new service is 99 percent identical, and the 1 percent is a pricing rule that costs money. That is what the shadow stage is for.
  • Session and auth split: users bouncing between systems lose their session. Share the token format from day one.
  • Stalled migration: the last 10 percent of routes are the ugliest, so they never move. Schedule them first if you can, or budget explicitly for them.
  • Rollback after data divergence: once the new system has written data the old cannot read, routing rollback is no longer safe. Know the point of no return and announce it.

Senior perspective

Strangler Fig is not really a technical pattern; it is a risk-management pattern that happens to be implemented with a router. The technical work is easy compared to the organisational work of maintaining momentum over eighteen months. Two practices make the difference. First, always run the shadow stage — comparing real responses on real traffic finds requirements no one documented, and it is the only cheap way to discover them. Second, publish a burndown of routes still served by the legacy system, visible to leadership, updated automatically. Migrations that are measured get finished; migrations that are merely intended become permanent.

47.31 A pattern selection matrix

Patterns are answers. This table starts from the question, which is how the decision actually arrives.

Problem you have Candidate patterns Pick this one when
Twelve services, each doing its own auth and TLS API Gateway, service mesh Gateway when the concern is north-south and public; mesh when it is east-west and mTLS
Mobile needs small payloads, web needs rich ones BFF, GraphQL, sparse fieldsets BFF when the clients differ in shape and release cadence; fieldsets when they differ by a few fields
Instances change IP on every deploy Service discovery, static DNS Discovery whenever the platform is dynamic; static DNS for two fixed hosts
A dependency is slow and dragging you down Circuit breaker, timeout, bulkhead Timeout always; breaker when a fallback exists; bulkhead when one workload must not starve another
Transient network failures cause user-visible errors Retry, retry queue, idempotency key Retry inline for sub-second blips; retry queue when backoff exceeds the request budget
One slow endpoint takes down fast ones Bulkhead, separate deployment, rate limiter Separate deployment when the workloads are named and different; bulkhead within a process otherwise
Abusive or runaway clients Rate limiter, token bucket, load shedding Token bucket for public APIs with bursts; shedding when you are saturated regardless of who is calling
Producer faster than consumer Bounded queue with backpressure, competing consumers Backpressure first, always; add consumers when the bottleneck is consumer capacity
DB write and event publish must both happen Outbox, CDC Outbox when you want a designed event contract; CDC-over-outbox when you also need sub-second latency
Consumers see duplicate messages Transactional inbox, natural upsert, idempotency key Natural upsert when the handler can be a full-state write; inbox when side effects span tables
A business flow spans four services Saga, merge the services, single transaction Merge first if you can; saga only when the split is genuinely required
Client retries cause double charges Idempotency key, unique business constraint Constraint when a natural key exists; idempotency key for open-ended public writes
Six systems need to know about row changes CDC, outbox, dual writes CDC over an outbox table; never dual writes
Integrating a legacy or vendor model Anti-corruption layer Always, when you do not control the other model
Reads and writes have different shapes and loads CQRS light (read table), materialized view, index Index first; materialized view next; separate read model only when the first two fail
The business asks questions about the past Event sourcing, audit table, CDC to warehouse Audit table for 90 percent of cases; event sourcing only for ledger-like domains
A dashboard query takes 2.8 seconds Materialized view, better index, cache Index first; materialized view when the query is an aggregate over lots of rows
Read-heavy data, expensive query Cache-aside, read replica, materialized view Cache-aside when staleness is acceptable and the key space is bounded
One row is a write bottleneck Sharded counters, Redis counter, batching Redis plus rollup for social counters; PostgreSQL shards when durability matters
Feed must be fast for everyone Fan-out on write, on read, hybrid Hybrid past a few million users; on read below that
Emails are backing up during a sale Competing consumers with queue-depth autoscaling Always, unless per-entity ordering is required
A message can never succeed Dead-letter queue Always. Alert on depth greater than zero
Payload is 40 MB Claim check Any payload over about 100 KB
A cron runs on all six replicas Leader election, SKIP LOCKED, external scheduler SKIP LOCKED when it is queue-shaped; advisory lock for true singletons
A ten-year-old monolith must be replaced Strangler Fig, rewrite Strangler for anything live and revenue-carrying
Deploys cause 30 seconds of 502s Health checks plus drain, discovery Readiness probe, preStop delay, bounded socket lifetime. All three

Two meta-rules for reading this table. First, the row's first candidate is usually the cheap one; try it before the expensive one. Second, if none of the candidates makes the answer to a senior question better — can it time out, fail, slow down, duplicate, return wrongly, partially succeed — then the honest choice is the pattern that is not in the table: do nothing, and keep the simpler system.

Senior Checklist — Part 47

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can name the cheaper alternative to every pattern I propose, and say why it is insufficient
  • I can explain why most CRUD applications should not use CQRS or event sourcing
  • I can write an outbox table, relay query and retention job from memory
  • I can explain why readiness must not check optional dependencies
  • I can state the maximum size of every queue and buffer in my service
  • I know where retries happen in my stack, and that it is exactly one layer
  • I can describe the rollback path for a Strangler Fig migration, including the point of no return
  • I can compute follower distribution before choosing fan-out on write or read
  • I have an alert on DLQ depth and on replication-slot retained WAL

Part 47 — Key Takeaways

  • A pattern is a named trade, not an upgrade. Applying one to a problem you do not have is pure cost.
  • The two sub-sections that save you are "When NOT to use" and "Edge cases and failure modes". Read those first.
  • Gateways and BFFs are presentation and policy layers. The moment either learns a business rule, the boundary is wrong.
  • Health checks cause more self-inflicted outages than crashes do: liveness checks nothing remote, readiness checks only hard dependencies.
  • Retry at exactly one layer, against a deadline rather than a count, and only where the operation is idempotent.
  • Every buffer needs a maximum and a defined behaviour when full. Rejecting work is healthy; dying is not.
  • The outbox solves the dual-write problem for the price of one table and a cleanup job. Almost nothing else does.
  • At-least-once delivery is the norm, so idempotency is not optional — prefer a natural unique constraint, then an inbox, then an idempotency key.
  • CQRS as "the read shape differs from the write shape" is nearly always right and nearly free. CQRS as separate stores and asynchronous projection is a distributed-systems commitment that needs a number to justify it.
  • Event sourcing is excellent for ledgers and quietly ruinous for CRUD. If "we might want history" is the reason, write an audit table instead.
  • Check the index before you build the cache, the materialized view or the projection. Roughly half of those requests are a missing composite index.
  • Leader election lowers the probability of duplicate work; idempotency removes its consequence. Build both.
  • Strangler Fig is risk management with a router. The shadow-comparison stage is where the unknown requirements are found.
  • The simplest architecture that meets the requirement wins, and the pattern catalogue exists to help you skip the ones you do not need.

Part 48 — Backend Anti-Patterns and Why They Hurt

Nobody sits down and writes an anti-pattern on purpose. Every one of the things in this part started as a reasonable decision by a competent engineer under time pressure, and most of them were correct at the size the system was then. The SELECT * was fine when the table had six columns. The shared database was fine when there was one team. The retry was fine before there were four layers of them.

That is why every entry here starts by explaining the good intention. If you only learn the list of forbidden things, you will forbid them in code review and then invent them again in a new shape. If you learn the pressure that produces them, you will recognise the shape before it becomes a schema migration you cannot undo.

Each anti-pattern below has five sub-sections: what it looks like in code, why it is dangerous with the concrete production consequence, how it happens, the fix, and how to detect it in review or in metrics. That last one matters most. Reviews catch what a human happens to notice on a Tuesday; metrics catch what is actually happening at 03:00, which is a different and more honest list.

A word on tone. Calling something an anti-pattern is not calling the author careless. Almost every example in this part is drawn from code I have written, reviewed and approved, or shipped myself. The value is in noticing them earlier next time.

48.1 God service

What it looks like

// order.service.ts - 4,200 lines, 61 public methods, 23 injected dependencies
@Injectable()
export class OrderService {
  constructor(
    private readonly orderRepo: Repository<Order>,
    private readonly userRepo: Repository<User>,
    private readonly productRepo: Repository<Product>,
    private readonly inventoryRepo: Repository<Stock>,
    private readonly paymentGateway: StripeClient,
    private readonly mailer: MailerService,
    private readonly sms: TwilioClient,
    private readonly pdf: InvoicePdfGenerator,
    private readonly analytics: SegmentClient,
    private readonly search: ElasticClient,
    private readonly fraud: FraudScoreClient,
    private readonly loyalty: LoyaltyService,
    /* ...11 more... */
  ) {}

  async placeOrder(dto: PlaceOrderDto) { /* 340 lines */ }
  async cancelOrder(id: string) { /* 180 lines */ }
  async refund(id: string) { /* 210 lines */ }
  async recalculateLoyaltyTier(userId: string) { /* ... */ }
  async exportMonthlyRevenueCsv(month: string) { /* ... */ }
  async syncProductToSearchIndex(sku: string) { /* ... */ }
}

Why it is dangerous

Every change to any part of the ordering domain touches this file, so every pull request conflicts with every other pull request. On one team I worked with, order.service.ts averaged 4.2 merge conflicts per week and the file's test suite took 6 minutes because instantiating the service required mocking 23 dependencies. Worse, the blast radius is total: a bug in the CSV export code path can throw inside a shared helper used by placeOrder, and a memory leak in the PDF generator takes down checkout. When the class is this large, nobody reads the whole thing before changing it, so behaviour is discovered by incident rather than by reading.

The scaling consequence is just as bad. You cannot give the invoice PDF path more memory or fewer replicas than the checkout path, because they are the same object in the same process.

How it happens

It starts as good cohesion. All order logic in one place is genuinely easier to find than order logic spread over nine files. Then a feature arrives that is "sort of about orders" — loyalty tiers, which are earned by ordering — and adding a method to an existing service takes ten minutes while creating a new module takes an afternoon and a discussion about naming. Each individual addition is defensible. The growth is invisible because nobody ever sees the whole file at once; they see a 40-line diff.

The fix

Split by reason to change, not by noun. Ask who requests changes to each method. Checkout rules come from the payments team, loyalty tiers from growth, CSV exports from finance. Those are three services with three owners.

// Each service has one reason to change and a handful of dependencies.
@Injectable()
export class PlaceOrderService {          // owns the checkout transaction only
  constructor(
    private readonly orders: OrderRepository,
    private readonly pricing: PricingService,
    private readonly inventory: InventoryPort,
    private readonly outbox: OutboxWriter,   // side effects become events
  ) {}

  async execute(cmd: PlaceOrderCommand): Promise<OrderId> { /* 40 lines */ }
}

Move the non-transactional side effects (email, SMS, analytics, search indexing) behind events published to the outbox. That alone typically removes half the dependencies, because most of them were never part of the transaction in the first place.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • A constructor with more than about seven injected dependencies. This is the single most reliable smell.
  • Any service file over roughly 500 lines, or with more than 15 public methods.
  • Git signal: run git log --format= --name-only | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20. Files at the top of that list are change magnets.
  • Test setup longer than the test.
  • In review, ask: "which team will request the next change to this file?" If there is more than one answer, it is already a god service.

48.2 God or fat controller

What it looks like

@Controller('orders')
export class OrderController {
  @Post()
  async create(@Body() body: any, @Req() req: Request) {
    if (!body.items || body.items.length === 0) throw new BadRequestException('no items');
    if (body.items.length > 50) throw new BadRequestException('too many items');

    const user = await this.userRepo.findOne({ where: { id: req.user.id } });
    if (!user || user.status !== 'ACTIVE') throw new ForbiddenException();

    let total = 0;
    for (const item of body.items) {
      const p = await this.productRepo.findOne({ where: { id: item.productId } });
      if (!p) throw new NotFoundException(`product ${item.productId}`);
      if (p.stock < item.qty) throw new ConflictException('out of stock');
      total += p.price * item.qty;                       // float arithmetic on money
      if (user.tier === 'GOLD') total -= p.price * item.qty * 0.1;
    }
    if (total > 100000 && !user.verified) throw new ForbiddenException('verify first');

    const order = await this.orderRepo.save({ userId: user.id, total, status: 'NEW' });
    await this.mailer.send(user.email, 'order-confirmation', { order });
    return order;
  }
}

Why it is dangerous

The business rules — gold tier discount, the 100,000 verification threshold, the stock check — live in an HTTP handler. They cannot be unit tested without an HTTP layer, cannot be reused by the admin API or the CSV importer, and cannot be called by a background job. When the mobile team needs the same order creation flow with a slightly different payload, the rules get copy-pasted into a second controller, and six months later the two copies disagree about the gold discount. That disagreement is a real revenue bug, and it is invisible until a customer notices.

There is also a correctness problem hiding in plain sight: the stock check and the save are not in a transaction, so two concurrent requests both pass the check and both succeed. Under a flash sale at 300 requests per second, this oversells consistently.

How it happens

The endpoint started with three lines. Adding one if to a controller is the shortest path from a ticket to a deployed feature, and every reviewer approves a four-line diff. There is no moment where somebody decides to put business logic in the controller; it accretes one condition at a time. NestJS makes it easy in the good sense, which is also the dangerous sense.

The fix

Controllers do four things and nothing else: validate input shape, extract the principal, call one application service, map the result to an HTTP response.

@Controller('orders')
export class OrderController {
  constructor(private readonly placeOrder: PlaceOrderService) {}

  @Post()
  @UsePipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, transform: true }))
  async create(@Body() dto: PlaceOrderDto, @Principal() p: Principal): Promise<OrderResponse> {
    const order = await this.placeOrder.execute({ userId: p.userId, items: dto.items });
    return OrderResponse.from(order);          // no rules, no repositories, no mailer
  }
}

export class PlaceOrderDto {
  @IsArray() @ArrayMinSize(1) @ArrayMaxSize(50)
  @ValidateNested({ each: true }) @Type(() => OrderItemDto)
  items!: OrderItemDto[];
}

Shape validation moves to the DTO where class-validator handles it declaratively. Business rules move to the service where they can be tested in milliseconds and reused by the admin API, the importer and the queue consumer.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Any repository, ORM entity or third-party client injected into a controller.
  • The word if appearing more than twice in a handler.
  • @Body() body: any — untyped bodies are almost always accompanied by manual validation.
  • A handler longer than about 15 lines.
  • Test signal: if the controller's tests need a database, the logic is in the wrong place.

48.3 Anemic domain model

What it looks like

@Entity()
export class Order {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id!: string;
  @Column() status!: string;
  @Column('int') totalMinor!: number;
  @Column({ nullable: true }) cancelledAt!: Date | null;
  // ...and nothing else. No methods. A struct with decorators.
}

// Every rule about orders lives somewhere else, and is repeated.
async cancel(id: string) {
  const o = await this.repo.findOneOrFail({ where: { id } });
  if (o.status === 'SHIPPED') throw new BadRequestException('already shipped');
  if (o.status === 'CANCELLED') throw new BadRequestException('already cancelled');
  o.status = 'CANCELLED';
  o.cancelledAt = new Date();
  await this.repo.save(o);
}

// admin-order.service.ts - the same rule, subtly different
async adminCancel(id: string) {
  const o = await this.repo.findOneOrFail({ where: { id } });
  if (o.status === 'DELIVERED') throw new BadRequestException('delivered');
  o.status = 'CANCELLED';                    // forgot cancelledAt, allows cancelling SHIPPED
  await this.repo.save(o);
}

Why it is dangerous

The entity cannot protect its own invariants, so every caller must remember the rules. There were two call sites here and they already disagree: the admin path lets you cancel a shipped order and forgets to set cancelledAt. In a real system there are eight call sites — the API, the admin panel, a Kafka consumer, a cron job, a data-fix script — and the rules drift across all of them. The failure mode is silent data corruption: orders in states the business believes are impossible, discovered months later when a report does not balance.

How it happens

ORMs encourage it. TypeORM and Sequelize entities look like database rows, so people treat them as rows. Layered-architecture tutorials say "entities hold data, services hold logic", which sounds like separation of concerns and is actually procedural programming with extra classes. It also works at small scale, which is the most persuasive argument of all.

The fix

Put the rules where the data is. The entity decides whether a transition is legal.

@Entity()
export class Order {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id!: string;
  @Column({ type: 'text' }) private status!: OrderStatus;
  @Column({ type: 'timestamptz', nullable: true }) private cancelledAt!: Date | null;

  cancel(reason: CancellationReason, now = new Date()): void {
    if (this.status === 'SHIPPED' || this.status === 'DELIVERED') {
      throw new OrderCannotBeCancelled(this.id, this.status);   // one rule, one place
    }
    if (this.status === 'CANCELLED') return;                    // idempotent by design
    this.status = 'CANCELLED';
    this.cancelledAt = now;
    this.record(new OrderCancelled(this.id, reason));
  }

  get isCancellable(): boolean { return this.status === 'NEW' || this.status === 'PAID'; }
}

Now both call sites become order.cancel(reason) and it is impossible to get it wrong. Note this is not "put everything in the entity" — cross-aggregate logic and orchestration still belong in services. It is "invariants live with the data they protect". Part 7 — Domain-Driven Design covers where the line sits.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Entities with only getters, setters and decorators.
  • The same if (status === ...) condition appearing in more than one file. Grep for a status literal and count files.
  • Services that mutate an entity's fields directly (o.status = ...) rather than calling a method.
  • A state machine that exists only in a diagram on a wiki, never in code.

48.4 N+1 queries

What it looks like

const orders = await this.orderRepo.find({ where: { userId }, take: 50 });   // 1 query
for (const order of orders) {
  order.items = await this.itemRepo.find({ where: { orderId: order.id } });  // 50 queries
  for (const item of order.items) {
    item.product = await this.productRepo.findOne({ where: { id: item.productId } }); // 200 more
  }
}

Lazy relations make it invisible: with TypeORM lazy loading or a Sequelize getter, the loop above can look like order.items.map(i => i.product.name) and still issue 250 queries.

Why it is dangerous

Each query is cheap; the round trips are not. At 1.5 ms per query in the same AZ, 251 queries is 376 ms of pure latency for one request. Add a 3 ms cross-AZ hop and it is 750 ms. Now serve 200 requests per second: that is 50,200 queries per second against a database sized for 2,000, and every one of them holds a pool connection. The endpoint that tested fine with three orders in development times out in production with fifty.

The characteristic incident: an endpoint's latency is fine for months, then a single power user with 400 orders opens their history and the connection pool is exhausted for everyone. The dashboard shows database CPU at 90 percent with no slow queries, because every individual query is 1.5 ms. This is why N+1 hides so well.

How it happens

The loop reads beautifully. for (const order of orders) { order.items = ... } expresses exactly what you mean, and the ORM makes the query invisible. The developer tested with a seeded database containing three orders, where 4 queries and 16 queries feel identical. Lazy loading, marketed as a convenience, is specifically the feature that hides the cost.

The fix

Fetch related data in one round trip, either with a join or with a batched second query.

// Option 1: one query with joins. Best for small fan-out.
const orders = await this.orderRepo.find({
  where: { userId },
  relations: { items: { product: true } },   // TypeORM emits a single LEFT JOIN query
  take: 50,
});

// Option 2: two queries, batched. Better when the join multiplies rows badly.
const orders = await this.orderRepo.find({ where: { userId }, take: 50 });
const items = await this.itemRepo.find({ where: { orderId: In(orders.map(o => o.id)) } });
const products = await this.productRepo.find({ where: { id: In(items.map(i => i.productId)) } });
const byId = new Map(products.map(p => [p.id, p]));
// stitch in memory: 3 queries total regardless of order count

For GraphQL or any per-item resolver, use DataLoader, which batches per request tick. Part 24 — Performance Engineering covers the batching patterns in detail.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Any await inside a for or map over database results. This is the review rule; it catches almost every case.
  • Enable query logging in tests and assert a query count: expect(queryCount).toBeLessThan(5).
  • Metrics: db_queries_per_request as a histogram. An endpoint whose p99 query count is 250 is an N+1, no investigation needed.
  • APM traces: a flat wall of identical short spans is the visual signature.
  • pg_stat_statements: a query with an enormous calls count and a tiny mean_exec_time is the N+1's inner query.

48.5 SELECT *

What it looks like

// TypeORM's default: selects every column of every entity in the relation graph
const users = await this.userRepo.find({ relations: { profile: true, addresses: true } });
SELECT * FROM users u
JOIN profiles p ON p.user_id = u.id
WHERE u.created_at > now() - interval '7 days';

Why it is dangerous

The users table has 34 columns including bio (average 2 KB), preferences jsonb (4 KB) and avatar_base64 (a legacy column averaging 60 KB that nobody removed). Selecting 10,000 users transfers 660 MB instead of the 400 KB you needed for id, email and name. That is network time, Node heap, JSON serialization CPU and garbage collection pressure — and on a t3.large-sized service, a single such request can push heap past the limit and cause an OOMKilled.

It also defeats index-only scans. A covering index on (created_at, id, email) can answer a targeted query entirely from the index at 0.3 ms; SELECT * forces a heap fetch per row and turns it into 40 ms. And it makes schema changes dangerous in a different way: adding a large column to a table silently degrades every existing query.

How it happens

It is the default. repo.find() selects everything and requires zero thought; listing columns requires knowing which ones you need and updating the list when requirements change. In SQL, SELECT * is what you type while exploring, and exploration code becomes production code. It is also genuinely convenient when the table is narrow, which most tables are at the start.

The fix

Select what you use.

const users = await this.userRepo.find({
  select: { id: true, email: true, name: true },     // 3 columns, not 34
  where: { createdAt: MoreThan(sevenDaysAgo) },
  take: 1000,
});

// Or a query builder for list endpoints, returning plain objects rather than entities
const rows = await this.userRepo.createQueryBuilder('u')
  .select(['u.id AS id', 'u.email AS email', 'u.name AS name'])
  .where('u.created_at > :d', { d: sevenDaysAgo })
  .limit(1000)
  .getRawMany();
-- and the index that makes it index-only
CREATE INDEX users_recent_covering ON users (created_at DESC) INCLUDE (id, email, name);

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for SELECT * in raw SQL and for .find( without a select option in list endpoints.
  • EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) showing Heap Fetches on a query you expected to be index-only.
  • Response payload size metrics. A list endpoint returning 4 MB is returning columns nobody renders.
  • Watch shared read buffer counts in EXPLAIN BUFFERS: wide rows mean more pages, and more pages means more I/O.
  • In review, ask which fields the caller actually renders. If the answer is "three", the query should select three.

48.6 No indexes

What it looks like

@Entity()
export class Order {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') id!: string;
  @Column() userId!: string;             // no @Index, queried on every dashboard load
  @Column() status!: string;             // filtered on constantly
  @Column() createdAt!: Date;            // sorted on constantly
}
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

Why it is dangerous

With 200 rows in development this is instant. With 8 million rows in production, PostgreSQL sequentially scans the whole table, sorts the matches and takes 20: a plan that reads roughly 900 MB and takes 2.4 seconds.

Limit  (cost=402318.42..402318.47 rows=20 width=312) (actual time=2412.9..2412.9 rows=20 loops=1)
  ->  Sort  (cost=402318.42..402412.10 rows=37472 width=312) (actual time=2412.9..2412.9 rows=20)
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 34kB
        ->  Seq Scan on orders  (actual time=0.31..2380.4 rows=41 loops=1)
              Filter: (user_id = '...'::uuid)
              Rows Removed by Filter: 8017442
              Buffers: shared read=114203

Note Rows Removed by Filter: 8017442. Every one of those rows was read from disk to find 41. Now run this at 50 requests per second: the database saturates its I/O, every other query queues behind it, and the whole product goes down because of one missing line of DDL. This is, by a wide margin, the most common cause of "the database is slow" incidents.

How it happens

Development databases are tiny. A seq scan over 200 rows is faster than an index scan, so nothing is slow, and nobody adds an index for a problem that does not exist yet. ORM entity definitions do not force you to think about access paths — @Column() is complete and valid without one. And indexes are invisible in code review because they live in a migration file that reviewers skim.

The fix

Index the way you query. Composite, in the order that matches your filter and sort.

-- equality column first, then the sort column
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_user_recent ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);
Limit  (actual time=0.048..0.061 rows=20 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using orders_user_recent on orders  (actual time=0.046..0.057 rows=20)
        Index Cond: (user_id = '...'::uuid)
        Buffers: shared hit=8

2,412 ms becomes 0.06 ms, and buffer reads go from 114,203 to 8. Always CONCURRENTLY in production so the build does not lock writes. Part 12 — Database Indexing covers column ordering, partial indexes and covering indexes properly.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • pg_stat_user_tables: high seq_scan with high n_live_tup is the definition of a missing index.
    SELECT relname, seq_scan, idx_scan, n_live_tup
FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE n_live_tup > 100000 ORDER BY seq_scan DESC LIMIT 10;
  • pg_stat_statements ordered by total_exec_time: the top query is usually missing an index.
  • auto_explain with log_min_duration = 200ms in staging, so slow plans are logged before production sees them.
  • In review: for every new query, ask which index serves it. If nobody can name one, the migration is incomplete.

48.7 Indexing everything

What it looks like

-- the reaction to the previous incident
CREATE INDEX ON orders (user_id);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (status);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (updated_at);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (total_minor);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (currency);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (channel);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (user_id, status);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (status, created_at);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (user_id, created_at);
-- 18 indexes on a table with 12 columns

Why it is dangerous

Indexes are not free; they are a write tax. Every INSERT updates every index, and every UPDATE updates every index whose columns changed (and can break HOT updates entirely). On a table with 18 indexes, an insert that took 0.4 ms takes 3.1 ms, and a bulk load of a million rows goes from 7 minutes to 50. Write throughput drops by a factor of five for indexes that are never used.

Storage compounds it: 18 indexes on an 80 GB table can add 140 GB, which no longer fits in RAM, so the buffer cache thrashes and read performance degrades too. And currency — a column with three distinct values across 8 million rows — will never be used by the planner anyway, because a seq scan is cheaper than reading a third of the table through an index.

The subtler harm is planner confusion: with a dozen overlapping candidate indexes, PostgreSQL sometimes picks a worse one, and plans become unstable across statistics refreshes.

How it happens

It is the overcorrection after a missing-index outage. "We were down for an hour because of a missing index" naturally becomes "index everything so it cannot happen again". It also happens through ORM decorators: @Index() on a field is one word, and adding it feels like diligence. Nobody ever removes an index, because removing one feels risky and adding one felt safe.

The fix

Index based on measured query patterns, and delete the rest.

-- find indexes that have never been used since the last stats reset
SELECT s.relname AS table, s.indexrelname AS index,
       s.idx_scan, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid)) AS size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes s
JOIN pg_index i ON i.indexrelid = s.indexrelid
WHERE s.idx_scan = 0 AND NOT i.indisunique AND NOT i.indisprimary
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid) DESC;

DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_currency_idx;   -- after confirming across a full business cycle

Also collapse redundancy: an index on (user_id, created_at) already serves queries filtering on user_id alone, so the single-column (user_id) index is dead weight. And prefer partial indexes for skewed data: CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING' is a fraction of the size and serves the queue query perfectly.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • idx_scan = 0 in pg_stat_user_indexes after a full business cycle, including month-end reporting.
  • Total index size approaching or exceeding table size: pg_indexes_size('orders') versus pg_table_size('orders').
  • Left-prefix duplicates: an index whose columns are a prefix of another index's columns.
  • Insert latency creeping up on a table nobody has changed. Graph write latency per table.
  • In review: a migration adding an index should name the query it serves. No named query, no index.

48.8 Distributed monolith

What it looks like

Twelve services, one release train. Deploying order-service requires deploying pricing-service and inventory-service in the same window because they share a DTO package that just changed. The CI pipeline is one repository-wide job that runs 40 minutes and deploys all twelve.

// @company/shared-types v4.2.0 - imported by all 12 services
export interface Order {
  id: string;
  status: 'NEW' | 'PAID' | 'SHIPPED';   // adding 'REFUNDED' breaks every consumer's exhaustive switch
  items: OrderItem[];
  internalPricingSnapshot: PricingSnapshot;   // an internal type, now public
}

Why it is dangerous

You pay every cost of distribution — network latency, partial failure, serialization, distributed debugging, twelve deploy pipelines, twelve on-call surfaces — and receive none of the benefits, because you cannot deploy, scale or fail independently. This is strictly worse than a monolith. A monolith with a bad module boundary is a refactor; a distributed monolith with a bad boundary is a coordinated multi-team release.

The concrete production consequence is deploy velocity collapse. A team I worked with went from 20 deploys per week as a monolith to 3 per week after the split, because each release needed a version-compatibility matrix and a rollback plan across four services. Incident recovery time doubled: a rollback now required rolling back four services in the correct order.

How it happens

The intention is good and the mechanism is a shared library. Splitting a monolith into services duplicates types, so somebody extracts a shared-types package to avoid duplication (DRY, correctly applied at the wrong boundary). Then shared validation. Then shared database entities. Each extraction removes duplication and adds coupling, and coupling across a network is far more expensive than duplication within a process.

The fix

Duplicate the types. Across a service boundary, duplication is the correct choice: each service defines the subset of the contract it actually consumes, and versions it independently.

// inside order-service: only the fields this service uses, owned by this service
export interface PricingResult {
  totalMinor: number;
  currency: string;
  // no 'internalPricingSnapshot' - if pricing changes its internals, we do not care
}

Share only stable, versioned wire contracts (OpenAPI specs, protobuf files, Avro schemas), never internal domain types. Enforce backward compatibility in CI with a schema-compatibility check. If a change requires a coordinated deploy, that is a design bug, not a scheduling problem — Part 32 — Backward Compatibility covers expand-contract for exactly this.

And be honest about the alternative: if the services genuinely cannot be decoupled, merge them back. A modular monolith with enforced internal boundaries is a legitimate, senior destination, not a defeat.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • A shared package that all services depend on and that changes more than monthly.
  • Any release process with the words "deploy in this order".
  • Deploy frequency per service. If services always deploy together, they are one service.
  • A service that cannot start unless three others are running — check whether integration tests require the whole stack.
  • In review: "can this change ship alone?" If not, note why.

48.9 Microservices too early

What it looks like

A pre-product-market-fit startup with four engineers and eleven repositories: user-service, auth-service, notification-service, product-service, cart-service, order-service, payment-service, search-service, api-gateway, shared-lib, infra. Total traffic: 40 requests per minute.

Why it is dangerous

Every feature now spans three repositories and needs three pull requests, three reviews and three deploys. A change that would take two hours in a monolith takes two days. With four engineers and eleven services, nobody owns anything properly, and every service has a different logging format because they were each set up in a hurry.

The operational tax is real money and real time: eleven CI pipelines, eleven sets of dashboards, eleven Kubernetes deployments and eleven idle service footprints. At 40 requests per minute you are paying roughly 400 dollars a month in infrastructure that a single 2 vCPU instance would serve, plus the far larger cost of engineering time spent on distributed-systems problems that your traffic does not justify.

Worst of all, the boundaries are wrong. You do not yet know your domain, and service boundaries are the most expensive thing in software to move. Fixing a bad module boundary is a refactor in an afternoon; fixing a bad service boundary is a data migration, an API deprecation and a quarter.

How it happens

Two good intentions. First, engineers who have felt the pain of a badly-factored monolith want to avoid repeating it, and microservices are marketed as the cure. Second, "we will need to scale" — which is true eventually and irrelevant now. Conference talks describe architectures built by companies with 300 engineers and 100,000 requests per second, and the architecture is copied without the context. Resume-driven development is real too, and worth naming without shame.

The fix

Start with a modular monolith: one deployable, one database, strict internal module boundaries with explicit public interfaces per module.

// src/modules/orders/index.ts - the ONLY file other modules may import from
export { OrdersModule } from './orders.module';
export { PlaceOrderService } from './application/place-order.service';
export type { OrderSummary } from './application/order-summary.dto';
// internals (entities, repositories, private services) are not exported

Enforce it mechanically, so it is not a matter of discipline:

{
  "rules": {
    "no-restricted-imports": ["error", {
      "patterns": [{
        "group": ["**/modules/*/!(index)", "**/modules/*/**"],
        "message": "Import modules only through their public index.ts"
      }]
    }]
  }
}

Extract a service when you have a specific reason: a genuinely different scaling profile, a different runtime need, an independent team that is blocked, or a compliance boundary. One reason, one service, one extraction at a time. Part 5 — Software Architecture covers the modular monolith in depth and Part 49 gives the decision tree.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Services per engineer above roughly one. Below three engineers per service, you have an ownership problem.
  • Total requests per second divided by service count. Under 10 RPS per service, distribution is not buying you anything.
  • Features that routinely touch more than two repositories.
  • The phrase "we should extract this into a service" appearing in a design doc without a named scaling, team or compliance reason.

48.10 Shared database between services

What it looks like

// order-service
const user = await this.dataSource.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1', [userId]);

// user-service, same database, same table
await this.userRepo.update(userId, { tier: 'GOLD' });

// analytics-service, also writing
await this.dataSource.query('UPDATE users SET last_seen_at = now() WHERE id = $1', [userId]);

Why it is dangerous

The database schema becomes an undocumented public API with three owners and no versioning. When the user service renames tier to loyalty_tier, the order service breaks at runtime, in production, with no compile-time warning and no contract test to catch it. You cannot deploy the rename at all without a coordinated release, which puts you back in the distributed monolith.

Worse consequences arrive under load. Locking is now cross-service: a long-running analytics UPDATE on users blocks the checkout path's SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, so a reporting job takes down ordering. Connection budgets are shared too — three services with 20-connection pools across 15 pods each is 900 connections against a max_connections of 300, and the third service to start simply cannot connect.

And the ownership question becomes unanswerable: when users.tier holds a wrong value, which of the three services wrote it?

How it happens

It is the fastest path, and it starts during a migration. When you extract a service from a monolith, splitting the data is by far the hardest part, so the first version keeps the shared database "temporarily". Temporary lasts years. It is also genuinely convenient: joining across service data in one query is easy, and building an API to fetch it is work.

The fix

One database per service, with data crossing boundaries through APIs or events.

// order-service no longer reads the users table
@Injectable()
export class OrderEnrichmentService {
  constructor(private readonly users: UserServiceClient) {}

  async enrich(order: Order): Promise<EnrichedOrder> {
    const user = await this.users.getSummary(order.userId);   // versioned API contract
    return { ...order, customerName: user.name, tier: user.tier };
  }
}

For read-heavy access where an API call per request is too slow, replicate the data you need into your own store via events, and own that copy:

-- order-service's own table, updated from user.tier_changed events
CREATE TABLE user_projection (
  user_id     UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,
  tier        TEXT NOT NULL,
  updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);

When you cannot split immediately, take the intermediate step: give each service its own database user with grants only on the tables it owns, plus read-only views for what it needs. That converts an invisible coupling into an explicit, auditable one, and it can be done in an afternoon.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • More than one service's credentials pointing at the same database host and schema. Audit connection strings.
  • pg_stat_activity grouped by application_name: more than one application name on a table is the smell.
  • Migrations in one repository altering tables owned by another.
  • Lock waits in pg_locks where the blocking and blocked sessions come from different applications.

48.11 Synchronous call chains

What it looks like

sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant A as API
  participant O as Orders
  participant P as Pricing
  participant I as Inventory
  participant T as Tax
  C->>A: POST /checkout
  A->>O: create order
  O->>P: get price
  P->>T: get tax rate
  T-->>P: rate
  P-->>O: price
  O->>I: reserve stock
  I-->>O: reserved
  O-->>A: order
  A-->>C: 201

Five services deep, all synchronous, all blocking.

Why it is dangerous

Availability multiplies downward. Five services at 99.9 percent each gives 99.5 percent for the chain, which is 3.6 hours of downtime per month instead of 43 minutes. Latency adds up: if each hop has a p99 of 120 ms, the chain's p99 is not 120 ms but closer to 400 ms, because the slowest hop dominates and tail latencies compound.

The failure mode is worse than the arithmetic. If tax-service slows to 3 seconds, every service in the chain holds an open request waiting for it, consuming connections and event-loop slots all the way up to the client. One leaf service can exhaust the resources of four upstream services simultaneously. This is precisely the cascade that Part 20 — Reliability Engineering exists to prevent.

How it happens

It is the natural translation of a function call into a network call. The monolith had pricingService.getPrice() calling taxService.getRate(), and after extraction those became HTTP calls with identical structure. Nobody redesigned the flow; they changed the transport. Each individual call is also perfectly reasonable in isolation — the problem is only visible when you draw the whole chain, which nobody does.

The fix

Three moves, in order of preference. First, flatten: have the API call services in parallel rather than in a chain.

// Depth 2 instead of 5, and the slowest call sets the latency, not the sum.
const [price, stock, tax] = await Promise.all([
  this.pricing.getPrice(items, { timeoutMs: 300 }),
  this.inventory.check(items, { timeoutMs: 300 }),
  this.tax.getRate(address, { timeoutMs: 300 }),
]);

Second, make non-critical steps asynchronous. Does the tax rate need to be fetched live, or can it be cached for an hour, or computed after the order is accepted? Most chain links are synchronous out of habit rather than requirement.

Third, where a step must be synchronous, give it a strict timeout budget that shrinks as you go deeper, and a fallback:

Client timeout        5000 ms
  API gateway         4000 ms
    Order service     2500 ms
      Pricing          800 ms  (cached tax rate, no further hop)
      Inventory        800 ms

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Distributed traces: sort by span depth. Any trace deeper than three service hops deserves a design review.
  • Compute the theoretical availability of each critical path and compare it to your SLO.
  • Grep for sequential await calls to different service clients that could be Promise.all.
  • Alert on "requests where more than one downstream service was called sequentially".

48.12 Retry storms

What it looks like

// client library: retries 3 times
const response = await this.http.get(url, { retries: 3 });

// service layer: also retries 3 times
await retry(() => this.client.fetchUser(id), { attempts: 3 });

// worker: also retries
await queue.add(job, { attempts: 3 });

Three layers, three attempts each: one logical request becomes up to 27 calls to the downstream service.

Why it is dangerous

Retries multiply load exactly when the system is least able to absorb it. Here is the incident shape, and it is always the same. At 02:14 the payment service's p99 rises from 80 ms to 900 ms because of a slow query. Callers start timing out at 1 second and retry. Load on the payment service triples instantly, from 400 RPS to 1,200 RPS. Its connection pool saturates, latency goes to 8 seconds, and now every request times out, so every request is retried the maximum number of times: 400 RPS of real traffic becomes 3,600 RPS of attempts. A service that was merely slow is now completely dead, and it stays dead after the slow query is fixed, because the retry backlog keeps it saturated. Recovery requires shedding traffic at the edge.

How it happens

Each retry layer was added by a different person solving a different real problem, months apart, and none of them knew about the others. HTTP client libraries often retry by default, which means one of the three layers is invisible in your code entirely. The intention — "make transient failures invisible to users" — is correct at every single layer.

The fix

Retry at exactly one layer, and add a retry budget so retries can never exceed a fraction of normal traffic.

// Retry budget: allow retries only while they are under 10 percent of successful calls.
@Injectable()
export class RetryBudget {
  private tokens = 0;
  onSuccess(): void { this.tokens = Math.min(this.tokens + 0.1, 100); }   // earn budget
  tryConsume(): boolean {
    if (this.tokens < 1) return false;                                    // budget exhausted
    this.tokens -= 1;
    return true;
  }
}

async callWithBudget<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  try {
    const r = await fn();
    this.budget.onSuccess();
    return r;
  } catch (e) {
    if (!isRetryable(e) || !this.budget.tryConsume()) throw e;   // fail fast when unhealthy
    return fn();
  }
}

Disable retries in the HTTP client library explicitly (retries: 0) so the one retry layer is visible. Add jitter so retries do not synchronise. Combine with a circuit breaker so that when the downstream is clearly unhealthy, you stop calling it altogether instead of retrying into it.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • The ratio of outbound_requests_total to logical_operations_total. Healthy is near 1.0; anything above 1.2 sustained is a warning; above 2.0 is a storm forming.
  • Downstream request rate rising while your own inbound rate is flat. That gap is retries.
  • Grep every HTTP client construction for default retry settings.
  • In review: for each new retry, ask "what else retries in this path?" and require an answer.

48.13 Infinite retries

What it looks like

async processMessage(msg: Message): Promise<void> {
  while (true) {                       // "it will succeed eventually"
    try {
      await this.handle(msg);
      return;
    } catch (err) {
      this.logger.warn('retrying', err);
      await sleep(1000);
    }
  }
}

Or the queue-configuration version: attempts: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, or a consumer that never acknowledges a failing message so the broker redelivers it forever.

Why it is dangerous

A message that can never succeed — a malformed payload, a reference to a hard-deleted product, a schema field the consumer does not understand — blocks the pipeline forever. In an ordered Kafka partition, one poison message stops every message behind it: the partition's lag grows without bound while the consumer logs the same error 86,400 times a day. I have seen a single unparseable event stall an order-fulfilment partition for eleven hours overnight, holding up 40,000 orders, because the retry loop never gave up and no alert fired on "same error repeating".

Even without ordering, infinite retries burn a worker slot permanently. Ten poison messages against a pool of ten workers is a total outage of that pipeline, and the metrics look fine: CPU is low, no errors are being returned to anyone, the queue simply stops draining.

How it happens

The intention is data safety: "we must never lose a message". That is a good instinct, and the infinite loop is the naive implementation of it. It is reinforced by the fact that during testing, every retry eventually succeeded, because every test failure was transient.

The fix

Bound attempts and route exhausted messages to a dead-letter queue, which preserves the message without blocking the pipeline. That satisfies the original "never lose data" intention properly.

const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5;

async processMessage(msg: Message, attempt = 1): Promise<void> {
  try {
    await this.handle(msg);
  } catch (err) {
    if (!isRetryable(err)) return this.deadLetter(msg, err, attempt);   // permanent: stop now
    if (attempt >= MAX_ATTEMPTS) return this.deadLetter(msg, err, attempt);
    const delay = Math.min(2 ** attempt * 1000, 60_000) * (0.5 + Math.random());
    await this.retryQueue.add(msg, { delay, attempt: attempt + 1 });
  }
}

Classify errors first: a 422 or a JSON parse failure is permanent and should dead-letter on attempt one, not attempt five.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Any while (true) or recursive retry with no attempt counter.
  • Queue configuration with no attempts limit or no dead-letter target.
  • Metrics: consumer lag rising steadily while the error rate is constant and non-zero. That combination is a poison message.
  • Log signal: the same error message with the same correlation id appearing more than a handful of times. Alert on it.
  • Message age: max(now - message.timestamp) for in-flight messages. A message older than an hour is stuck.

48.14 No timeouts

What it looks like

// axios with no timeout: waits until the OS gives up, which can be 2 hours
const { data } = await axios.get(`${PRICING_URL}/prices/${sku}`);

// pg pool with no statement_timeout: a query can run until the connection dies
const rows = await this.pool.query('SELECT ... FROM huge_table WHERE unindexed = $1', [v]);

// fetch with no AbortController
const res = await fetch(url);

Why it is dangerous

Without a timeout, a slow dependency does not fail — it accumulates. Node's default socket timeout is effectively unbounded for an established connection, and the OS-level TCP keepalive can take over two hours to notice a dead peer. During that time each waiting request holds a socket, a promise chain, a request context and often a database connection.

Here is the arithmetic that ends services: 200 requests per second into a dependency that has stopped responding. After 30 seconds you have 6,000 in-flight requests, each holding roughly 30 KB of context, which is 180 MB of heap that will never be freed. After 60 seconds the pod is OOMKilled. Kubernetes restarts it, the new pod picks up traffic, and it dies too. Meanwhile the connection pool is exhausted, so requests that do not even touch the slow dependency start failing. One unresponsive third-party API takes down a service that only used it for an optional feature.

How it happens

Nobody omits a timeout deliberately; libraries default to none, and the default is invisible. In development the dependency is always fast, so the missing timeout has no observable effect. Setting a timeout also requires choosing a number, which requires knowing the dependency's latency profile, which requires data nobody has yet — so it gets deferred.

The fix

Set timeouts everywhere, at every layer, defaulting to aggressive.

// HTTP client: connect and total budget, configured once in the module
@Module({
  imports: [HttpModule.register({ timeout: 2_000, maxRedirects: 2 })],
})
export class PricingModule {}

// PostgreSQL: server-side limits so a runaway query cannot outlive its client
TypeOrmModule.forRoot({
  extra: {
    connectionTimeoutMillis: 2_000,   // waiting for a pool connection
    statement_timeout: 5_000,         // server kills the query
    idle_in_transaction_session_timeout: 10_000,  // kills forgotten open transactions
    query_timeout: 5_000,
  },
});

// Anything else: wrap it
const withTimeout = <T>(p: Promise<T>, ms: number, label: string) =>
  Promise.race([p, new Promise<never>((_, rej) =>
    setTimeout(() => rej(new TimeoutError(label, ms)), ms).unref())]);

Choose numbers from data: set the timeout at roughly p99 plus 50 percent, and make timeouts shorter the deeper you go so the budget shrinks along the chain.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for axios.get(, fetch(, new Pool( and check each for a timeout. A CI lint rule can enforce it.
  • Latency histograms with no ceiling. If your p99.9 latency has no natural maximum, nothing is bounding it.
  • In-flight request gauge (http_client_requests_in_flight). A number that only goes up is the signature.
