  • Heap growth correlated with downstream latency in your dashboards.
  • Check idle in transaction sessions in pg_stat_activity — long-lived ones mean a missing session timeout.

48.15 No idempotency

What it looks like

@Post('payments')
async charge(@Body() dto: ChargeDto) {
  const charge = await this.stripe.charges.create({    // no idempotency key
    amount: dto.amountMinor,
    currency: dto.currency,
    source: dto.token,
  });
  await this.paymentRepo.save({ chargeId: charge.id, orderId: dto.orderId });
  return charge;
}

Why it is dangerous

Every layer above this endpoint retries: the mobile client on a dropped connection, the load balancer on a 502, the client's own "tap again because nothing happened". On mobile networks roughly 0.5 to 2 percent of requests lose their response, so at 10,000 payments a day you can expect 50 to 200 duplicate submissions. Without protection, that is 50 to 200 double charges per day: refunds, chargebacks, support tickets, and in regulated markets a compliance incident.

The same problem in a less obvious place is often worse. A webhook consumer that decrements stock without deduplication will oversell during any broker redelivery, and the discrepancy shows up as a physical inventory mismatch weeks later that nobody can trace to a cause.

How it happens

The happy path works perfectly, and every test exercises the happy path. Duplicates are a property of the network, not of the code, so they are invisible in unit tests, invisible in staging, and only appear at production volume. It also feels like the client's problem: "the app should not send it twice" is true and useless, because the app cannot know whether the first request arrived.

The fix

Make the operation idempotent at the boundary. Prefer a natural unique constraint where one exists, because it never expires and needs no cleanup.

-- one payment per order, enforced by the database
ALTER TABLE payments ADD CONSTRAINT payments_order_unique UNIQUE (order_id);
@Post('payments')
async charge(@Body() dto: ChargeDto, @Headers('idempotency-key') key: string) {
  if (!key) throw new BadRequestException('Idempotency-Key required');

  return this.ds.transaction(async (em) => {
    const claimed = await em.createQueryBuilder().insert().into(IdempotencyKey)
      .values({ key, userId: dto.userId, status: 'IN_PROGRESS' }).orIgnore().execute();
    if (claimed.raw.length === 0) {
      const prior = await em.findOneOrFail(IdempotencyKey, { where: { key } });
      if (prior.status === 'IN_PROGRESS') throw new ConflictException('in progress');
      return prior.responseBody;                    // replay, do not charge again
    }
    // Pass the key downstream too: the provider dedupes on its side as well.
    const charge = await this.stripe.charges.create(
      { amount: dto.amountMinor, currency: dto.currency, source: dto.token },
      { idempotencyKey: key },
    );
    await em.save(Payment, { chargeId: charge.id, orderId: dto.orderId });
    await em.update(IdempotencyKey, { key }, { status: 'COMPLETED', responseBody: charge });
    return charge;
  });
}

For consumers, use the transactional inbox from Part 19 — Distributed Transactions: insert the message id in the same transaction as the side effects.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Any POST endpoint that creates money, stock or messages without a unique constraint or an idempotency key.
  • Query for duplicates directly: SELECT order_id, count(*) FROM payments GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1. Run it as a scheduled data-quality check, not just once.
  • Payment provider dashboards showing duplicate charges within a short window for the same customer.
  • Support ticket categories. "Charged twice" appearing at all means the mechanism is missing.
  • In review, apply the mantra: can it duplicate? If the handler is not safe when called twice with identical input, it is not finished.

48.16 Logging sensitive data

What it looks like

@Post('login')
async login(@Body() dto: LoginDto) {
  this.logger.log(`login attempt: ${JSON.stringify(dto)}`);      // password in the log
  const user = await this.auth.validate(dto);
  this.logger.debug('user loaded', user);                        // password hash, email, phone
  return this.jwt.sign({ sub: user.id });
}

// and the interceptor that logs every request body "for debugging"
this.logger.log({ method: req.method, url: req.url, body: req.body, headers: req.headers });

Why it is dangerous

Logs go everywhere. They are shipped to a log aggregator, replicated, backed up, retained for a year, and readable by every engineer, every contractor with dashboard access and every system that ingests them. A password written to a log is a password in fifteen systems, none of which were designed to store credentials. The headers line above logs the Authorization header, so every bearer token in your system is now in plaintext in a searchable index.

The regulatory consequence is concrete: under GDPR this is unlawful processing, and the remediation is not "stop logging it" but "find and purge every copy from every backup", which is often technically impossible. Under PCI DSS, logging a full card number is an immediate compliance failure that can cost you your ability to take payments. I have seen a company spend three weeks of engineering time and a five-figure legal bill because one debug line logged a request body containing national ID numbers.

How it happens

Debugging. Someone had a production bug they could not reproduce, added JSON.stringify(dto) to see the payload, shipped it, fixed the bug and never removed the line. Or a generic logging interceptor was written to log "everything" because at the time the payloads were harmless. Nobody re-reads logging code when a new field is added to a DTO, so the day someone adds ssn to a request body, it starts flowing into the logs silently.

The fix

Redact structurally, not by remembering. Use an allowlist where you can, and a redaction layer that is applied by the logger itself so no individual log call has to be careful.

import pino from 'pino';

export const logger = pino({
  redact: {
    paths: [
      'req.headers.authorization', 'req.headers.cookie',
      '*.password', '*.passwordHash', '*.token', '*.refreshToken',
      '*.card.number', '*.cvv', '*.ssn', '*.taxId',
      'body.password', 'body.token',
    ],
    censor: '[REDACTED]',
  },
});

// And never log whole objects. Log the identifiers you need to correlate.
this.logger.log({ event: 'login_attempt', userId: user.id, ip: hashIp(req.ip) });

Add a test that asserts sensitive fields never appear in serialized log output, and make DTOs opt in to logging with a @Loggable()-style marker rather than opting out.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep the codebase for JSON.stringify(dto), logger.*(req.body), logger.*(user) and ...req.headers.
  • Run a scheduled scan over the log index for patterns: card-number regexes, "password", Bearer ey, national ID formats. Alert on any hit.
  • In review, reject any log line that logs an entire object it did not construct itself.
  • Check log volume per endpoint. An endpoint producing kilobytes per request is logging bodies.

48.17 Giant transactions, and transactions that call external APIs

What it looks like

await this.dataSource.transaction(async (em) => {
  const orders = await em.find(Order, { where: { status: 'PENDING' } });  // 50,000 rows
  for (const order of orders) {
    const charge = await this.stripe.charges.create({ ... });   // network call INSIDE tx
    await this.mailer.send(order.email, 'receipt', { order });  // another one
    order.status = 'PAID';
    await em.save(order);
  }
});

Why it is dangerous

Two separate disasters in one block.

The transaction is enormous: 50,000 rows locked for the duration. Every one of those rows is unavailable to other writers, so any customer trying to modify their own pending order blocks. It also pins the oldest running transaction's snapshot, which stops autovacuum from cleaning dead tuples across the whole database — table bloat grows, and on a busy system you can add tens of gigabytes in an hour. In extreme cases it pushes you toward transaction ID wraparound protection, which forces an emergency vacuum.

The external calls are worse. Stripe's p99 is around 900 ms; 50,000 of them is over twelve hours of held transaction. If the process crashes at order 30,000, the database rolls back all 30,000 status updates, but Stripe has already charged 30,000 cards. The database and the outside world are now permanently inconsistent, and there is no automatic way to reconcile because you rolled away the record of what you did.

How it happens

Transactions feel like a safety blanket: wrapping more in one feels safer, and "all or nothing" sounds like the responsible choice. Batch jobs naturally grow from 50 rows to 50,000 without anyone revisiting the transaction boundary. And the external call ends up inside because the code was written top to bottom, in the order the steps happen.

The fix

Keep transactions short, local and free of network calls. Chunk the work, and move side effects outside via an outbox.

// 1. Claim a small batch in its own short transaction.
const batch = await this.ds.transaction(async (em) =>
  em.query(`UPDATE orders SET status = 'PROCESSING', claimed_at = now()
             WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status = 'PENDING'
                          ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 100)
             RETURNING id, email, total_minor`));

// 2. Do the slow, external work OUTSIDE any transaction, with an idempotency key.
for (const order of batch) {
  const charge = await this.stripe.charges.create(
    { amount: order.total_minor, currency: 'eur' },
    { idempotencyKey: `order-charge-${order.id}` },     // safe if we crash and retry
  );
  // 3. Commit the result in a tiny transaction, and queue the email via the outbox.
  await this.ds.transaction(async (em) => {
    await em.update(Order, order.id, { status: 'PAID', chargeId: charge.id });
    await em.insert(OutboxEvent, { aggregateId: order.id, eventType: 'order.paid', payload: { ... } });
  });
}

Now the longest transaction is a few milliseconds, a crash loses at most one order's bookkeeping (recoverable via the idempotency key), and email sending happens in a worker.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for HTTP clients, mailers and queue clients used inside a transaction( callback. This is a mechanical, high-value lint rule.
  • pg_stat_activity: alert when now() - xact_start exceeds 30 seconds for any session.
    SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS age, state, left(query, 80)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 5;
  • Monitor pg_stat_database.xact_commit duration and table bloat (n_dead_tup) — bloat growth with normal traffic points at long transactions.
  • In review, ask how many rows the transaction touches at production scale, not at seed-data scale.

48.18 Premature optimisation

What it looks like

// A hand-rolled LRU with a custom doubly-linked list, 240 lines,
// written before anyone measured the query it caches.
class OptimizedProductCache {
  private head: Node | null = null;
  private tail: Node | null = null;
  private map = new Map<string, Node>();
  // ...manual pointer manipulation, an off-by-one in eviction, no tests for eviction
}

// Or: a bespoke binary serialization format "because JSON is slow",
// used on an endpoint serving 4 requests per minute.

Why it is dangerous

You pay complexity now for a benefit you have not verified exists. The cost is concrete: 240 lines of pointer manipulation is a permanent tax on every future reader, it has a bug in eviction that leaks memory under a specific access pattern, and it is untested because testing an LRU properly is fiddly. Meanwhile the actual bottleneck — measured later — was a missing index that took one line to fix.

The deeper harm is that premature optimisation usually optimises the wrong thing. In a Node backend, application CPU is rarely the bottleneck; I/O and database work dominate by an order of magnitude. Micro-optimising a loop that accounts for 0.3 percent of request time while a 40 ms query runs next to it is measurably pointless, and the complexity you added makes the real fix harder to see.

How it happens

Good instincts, wrong timing. Engineers who have been burned by slow systems want to prevent it, and optimisation is a satisfying, tractable kind of work — far more satisfying than measuring. It also masquerades as seniority: writing a clever cache looks more impressive in review than adding an index. And it is often invisible as optimisation at all; it is framed as "doing it properly the first time".

The fix

Measure first, always. Then optimise the top item, and only that one.

// Before optimising, get the number. This is the whole discipline.
const start = process.hrtime.bigint();
const result = await this.slowThing();
this.metrics.histogram('operation_duration_ms', Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - start) / 1e6,
  { operation: 'product_lookup' });

Use pg_stat_statements for database time, an APM flame graph or node --cpu-prof for CPU, and a load test to establish the baseline. Then write down the target ("p99 under 200 ms at 500 RPS") before changing anything, so you know when to stop. And prefer the boring fix: an index, a Promise.all, a cache-manager entry with a TTL, or simply fetching fewer columns. Use lru-cache from npm rather than writing one.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • A performance-motivated pull request with no before-and-after numbers. Ask for them; if they do not exist, the change is speculative.
  • Hand-rolled implementations of things that exist as well-tested libraries: caches, pools, schedulers, serializers.
  • Comments containing "for performance" with no benchmark reference.
  • Complexity that only makes sense at a scale you do not have. Ask what RPS the code is designed for and compare it to your actual traffic.

48.19 Overengineering

What it looks like

// Five layers of abstraction so we can "swap the database later"
export interface IRepositoryFactory { create<T>(t: Type<T>): IRepository<T>; }
export interface IRepository<T> { find(spec: ISpecification<T>): Promise<T[]>; }
export interface ISpecification<T> { toCriteria(): ICriteria; and(o: ISpecification<T>): ISpecification<T>; }
export class ProductNameSpecification implements ISpecification<Product> { /* 60 lines */ }
export class ProductActiveSpecification implements ISpecification<Product> { /* 40 lines */ }
export class SpecificationToTypeOrmTranslator { /* 300 lines of query building */ }

// The one and only usage, five years later:
const products = await this.factory.create(Product)
  .find(new ProductNameSpecification(name).and(new ProductActiveSpecification()));
// which is: SELECT * FROM products WHERE name ILIKE $1 AND active = true

Why it is dangerous

Every abstraction is a cost paid on every read, every debugging session and every onboarding. A new engineer must learn five bespoke concepts before they can add a WHERE clause. Stack traces pass through four layers of indirection, so a null-pointer error takes twenty minutes to trace instead of two. And the flexibility is almost always unused: in fifteen years I have seen a team actually swap its relational database exactly once, and the abstraction layer did not help because the real coupling was in transactions, migrations and query semantics, not in the repository interface.

The measurable consequence is velocity. Features take longer, estimates inflate, and the team starts routing around the abstraction with "temporary" raw queries, which leaves you with two ways to do everything.

How it happens

It comes from real pain and good books. Someone was burned by a system that hardcoded a vendor, read about hexagonal architecture, and applied it thoroughly and sincerely. Abstraction also feels like the professional choice; adding an interface is never questioned in review, while removing one is. And "we might need it later" is unfalsifiable, so it always wins the argument.

The fix

Apply YAGNI with a rule of three: abstract when you have three real implementations, or one implementation plus a signed contract for the second. Until then, write the direct version.

@Injectable()
export class ProductRepository {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Product) private readonly repo: Repository<Product>) {}

  findActiveByName(name: string): Promise<Product[]> {
    return this.repo.find({ where: { name: ILike(`%${name}%`), active: true }, take: 50 });
  }
}

This is still testable (stub the class), still swappable (change one file), and readable in ten seconds. Keep interfaces for genuine ports — a payment provider, an email sender, a storage backend — where a second implementation already exists or is a test double you actually need.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Interfaces with exactly one implementation and no test double that needs them.
  • Abstraction layers whose only caller is one line of application code.
  • A ratio: count files touched per feature. If a simple field addition touches seven files, the layering is too deep.
  • Onboarding time. If a competent engineer needs two weeks to make their first meaningful change, complexity is the cause.
  • In review, ask for the concrete second implementation. "We might" is not one.

48.20 Unbounded in-memory caches

What it looks like

@Injectable()
export class GeoService {
  private cache = new Map<string, Location>();     // never evicts, never expires

  async resolve(ip: string): Promise<Location> {
    if (this.cache.has(ip)) return this.cache.get(ip)!;
    const loc = await this.geoApi.lookup(ip);
    this.cache.set(ip, loc);                        // one entry per unique IP, forever
    return loc;
  }
}

Why it is dangerous

The key space is unbounded, so the cache is a memory leak with a helpful name. At 300,000 unique IPs a day and roughly 200 bytes per entry, that is 60 MB per day per pod. On a 512 MB container the pod is OOMKilled around day six, and because it happens gradually the graph looks like normal growth until the restart. Restarts then produce a cold cache and a burst of geo API calls, which may hit a rate limit and cause a second, unrelated-looking incident.

How it happens

new Map() is the obvious way to cache, and at the time the key space looked small — the developer was thinking about country codes, not IPs. Nobody asks "how many distinct keys can this have?" because the code works perfectly in every test.

The fix

Bound every in-process cache by size and time, and prefer a shared cache when the data is shared.

import { LRUCache } from 'lru-cache';

private cache = new LRUCache<string, Location>({
  max: 10_000,                       // hard entry cap
  ttl: 60 * 60 * 1000,               // one hour
  maxSize: 20 * 1024 * 1024,         // and a byte budget
  sizeCalculation: (v) => JSON.stringify(v).length,
});

For anything shared across pods, use Redis with a TTL and an eviction policy (maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru), as in Part 16 — Caching and Redis.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for new Map(, new Set( and object literals used as caches at class or module scope. Every one needs a bound.
  • nodejs_heap_size_used_bytes trending upward monotonically between restarts, with a sawtooth at deploys.
  • Pods restarting on a regular cadence with OOMKilled in their termination reason.
  • In review: ask for the maximum number of distinct keys. No answer means no bound.

48.21 Request-scoped everything

What it looks like

@Injectable({ scope: Scope.REQUEST })          // and so is every service it depends on
export class OrderService {
  constructor(@Inject(REQUEST) private readonly req: Request,
              private readonly pricing: PricingService) {}   // now also request-scoped
}

Why it is dangerous

In NestJS, request scope is contagious: any provider that injects a request-scoped provider becomes request-scoped itself, all the way up the graph. That means the entire dependency tree is instantiated per request. At 2,000 requests per second with 40 providers each, you are constructing 80,000 objects per second, which is pure garbage-collector pressure. Measured overhead is typically 15 to 30 percent added latency, and GC pauses lengthen visibly at p99. It also breaks anything that assumed singleton state: connection pools, in-memory caches, breakers and rate-limit counters are all recreated per request and therefore useless.

How it happens

Someone needs the current user or a correlation id inside a deep service, and request scope is the documented way to inject REQUEST. It works immediately, and the performance cost is invisible until load testing — which usually happens after the pattern has spread.

The fix

Use AsyncLocalStorage for ambient request context and keep providers singleton.

export const requestContext = new AsyncLocalStorage<{ userId?: string; correlationId: string }>();

@Injectable()
export class ContextMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {
  use(req: Request, _res: Response, next: NextFunction) {
    requestContext.run({ userId: req.user?.id, correlationId: req.headers['x-request-id'] as string ?? randomUUID() }, next);
  }
}

@Injectable()                                    // singleton, fast
export class OrderService {
  get correlationId() { return requestContext.getStore()?.correlationId; }
}

Better still, pass what you need explicitly as a parameter. Explicit arguments are cheaper and easier to test than any ambient mechanism.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for Scope.REQUEST and Scope.TRANSIENT. Each occurrence needs a justification.
  • Latency regression after a refactor with no algorithmic change.
  • GC metrics: rising nodejs_gc_duration_seconds and scavenge frequency with flat traffic.
  • Singletons that stop working — a rate limiter whose counters always read zero is the classic symptom.

48.22 Business logic in ORM hooks

What it looks like

@Entity()
export class Order {
  @AfterInsert()
  async notifyAndCharge() {
    await mailer.send(this.email, 'order-created');   // side effect inside a lifecycle hook
    await stripe.charges.create({ amount: this.totalMinor });
    await analytics.track('order_created', { id: this.id });
  }
}

Sequelize's hooks: { afterCreate } and TypeORM subscribers produce the same shape.

Why it is dangerous

The side effects fire inside the ORM's save path, which is usually inside a transaction. A slow email provider now holds a database transaction open (see 48.17). A failure in the hook rolls back the order, so a transient mail error loses a paid order. And the behaviour is invisible: await repo.save(order) gives no hint that it charges a card, so a test fixture that creates an order charges a real card in staging. I have watched a data-backfill script send 40,000 emails because it inserted rows through the ORM.

How it happens

Hooks look like the perfect place for "things that always happen when an order is created", and they genuinely enforce that consistency. The intention — never forget the notification — is right; the mechanism couples persistence to business process.

The fix

Hooks may compute derived persistence data (a slug, a checksum, updated_at). Anything with an external effect goes through an explicit application service and an outbox event.

async placeOrder(cmd: PlaceOrderCommand) {
  return this.ds.transaction(async (em) => {
    const order = await em.save(Order.place(cmd));
    await em.insert(OutboxEvent, { aggregateId: order.id, eventType: 'order.placed', payload: order.toEvent() });
    return order;                       // email and charge happen in workers, later
  });
}

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for @AfterInsert, @AfterUpdate, @BeforeInsert, addHook, and TypeORM EntitySubscriber classes; check each for I/O.
  • Any import of an HTTP client, mailer or queue inside an entity file.
  • Symptom: a migration or backfill script triggering user-visible side effects.

48.23 synchronize: true in production

What it looks like

TypeOrmModule.forRoot({
  type: 'postgres',
  url: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  autoLoadEntities: true,
  synchronize: true,          // "keeps the schema in sync automatically"
});

Why it is dangerous

TypeORM's synchronize compares entities to the live schema and issues whatever DDL it thinks closes the gap — including DROP COLUMN. Rename a property in an entity and it drops the old column and creates a new empty one; your data is gone with no migration to reverse and no record of what happened. On a deploy with two replicas starting simultaneously, both run DDL concurrently and can deadlock on ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks, taking the application down at startup. There is no review step, no dry run and no rollback.

How it happens

It is in the getting-started documentation and it makes local development delightful. The .env for staging gets copied to production, or the flag is set from a variable that defaults to true. Nobody notices until the first destructive change.

The fix

TypeOrmModule.forRoot({
  synchronize: false,                 // never true outside a disposable local database
  migrationsRun: process.env.RUN_MIGRATIONS === 'true',   // and run them from one place
  migrations: ['dist/migrations/*.js'],
});

Generate migrations locally (typeorm migration:generate), review the SQL as code, and run them as a separate Kubernetes Job before the rolling deploy — not from application startup, so replicas cannot race. Part 31 — Database Migrations covers safe, zero-downtime patterns.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep every config for synchronize and alter: true (Sequelize's equivalent). Fail CI if either is truthy when NODE_ENV=production.
  • Schema drift: compare production DDL against the migration history in CI.
  • Unexpected ALTER TABLE statements in the PostgreSQL log at application startup.

48.24 Swallowed errors

What it looks like

try {
  await this.inventory.reserve(orderId, items);
} catch (e) {
  // TODO: handle
}

try { await this.cache.set(key, value); } catch {}      // silent

Why it is dangerous

The system continues as though the operation succeeded. Orders are confirmed with no stock reserved, so you oversell and only discover it at fulfilment. There is no log, no metric and no trace, so debugging starts from the symptom (angry customers) rather than the cause, and typically takes days. Empty catch blocks are how a 20-minute bug becomes a 3-day investigation.

How it happens

An exception was crashing something in development, and catching it made the crash stop. The // TODO is sincere. It also happens defensively: "the cache is optional, so a failure should not break the request" — which is correct reasoning with a missing second half, namely recording that it happened.

The fix

Every catch does at least one of three things: handle it meaningfully, rethrow (possibly wrapped), or log and count it. Never nothing.

try {
  await this.cache.set(key, value);
} catch (err) {
  this.metrics.inc('cache_write_failed', { key_prefix: prefix });    // optional but visible
  this.logger.warn({ err, key }, 'cache write failed, continuing');
}

try {
  await this.inventory.reserve(orderId, items);
} catch (err) {
  throw new OrderCannotBeFulfilled(orderId, { cause: err });          // not optional: fail
}

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • ESLint no-empty with allowEmptyCatch: false; grep for catch {} and catch (e) {}.
  • Search for catch blocks with no logger, throw or metrics call in the body.
  • Symptom in metrics: an operation whose success count is far below its attempt count while the error rate is zero.

48.25 Fire-and-forget promises

What it looks like

@Post()
async create(@Body() dto: CreateDto) {
  const order = await this.orders.create(dto);
  this.mailer.sendConfirmation(order);      // no await, no catch
  this.analytics.track('order_created');    // same
  return order;
}

Why it is dangerous

An unhandled promise rejection in Node 15 and later terminates the process by default. So a transient SMTP failure does not just skip an email; it crashes the pod, killing every other in-flight request. Even when it does not crash, the work is unobserved: nobody knows how many confirmation emails were never sent, because there is no error path and no metric. And during a rolling deploy the pod exits while the promise is still pending, so the work silently disappears.

How it happens

Not awaiting is the easy way to keep an endpoint fast, and it usually works. The failure needs a rejection, which needs the dependency to fail, which does not happen in development.

The fix

Either await it, or hand it to something durable. For genuinely optional work, mark the intent explicitly and attach a handler.

// Durable: survives a pod restart, retries, dead-letters.
await this.mailQueue.add('confirmation', { orderId: order.id }, { attempts: 5 });

// Truly fire-and-forget: never unhandled, always counted.
void this.analytics.track('order_created').catch((err) =>
  this.logger.warn({ err }, 'analytics track failed'));

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • ESLint @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises. This one rule catches nearly every instance; turn it on today.
  • process.on('unhandledRejection') counter exported as a metric.
  • Pods restarting with exit code 1 and no obvious cause in application logs.

48.26 Hard deletes with no audit trail

What it looks like

@Delete(':id')
async remove(@Param('id') id: string) {
  await this.orderRepo.delete(id);        // row is gone, along with any way to explain it
}

Why it is dangerous

The data is unrecoverable outside a backup restore, which for a large database is hours of downtime to recover one row. Foreign keys either block the delete (a runtime error users see) or cascade (silently removing order items, payments and shipments). Financial and legal records frequently must be retained for seven years, so a hard delete on an invoice is a compliance breach. And when a customer asks "who cancelled my order and when?", the honest answer is that nobody can know.

How it happens

DELETE is what the ORM offers and what the word "delete" means. Soft deletes require a flag, a filter on every query and a cleanup policy, which is more work for what looks like the same outcome.

The fix

Soft-delete business records, and record who did it.

@Entity()
export class Order {
  @DeleteDateColumn({ type: 'timestamptz' }) deletedAt?: Date;   // TypeORM filters these out
  @Column({ nullable: true }) deletedBy?: string;
  @Column({ nullable: true }) deletionReason?: string;
}

await this.orderRepo.softDelete(id);          // sets deletedAt; queries exclude it by default

Add a partial index so the common query stays fast (CREATE INDEX ... WHERE deleted_at IS NULL), and a scheduled job that hard-deletes rows past their retention period so GDPR erasure remains possible. For genuine erasure requests, delete or crypto-shred the personal fields and keep the financial record.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for .delete(, .remove(, DELETE FROM on business tables.
  • ON DELETE CASCADE on any table containing financial or user-facing history.
  • In review, ask: who is allowed to delete this, and what does the audit log say afterwards?

48.27 Magic strings for states

What it looks like

if (order.status === 'PENDING') { /* ... */ }
if (order.status === 'pending') { /* never true, silently */ }
await this.repo.update(id, { status: 'PAYED' });     // typo, accepted by the database

Why it is dangerous

The compiler cannot help you. A typo becomes a row in a state nothing handles, so the order stops moving and no error is raised anywhere. It surfaces days later as "these 300 orders are stuck", and fixing it needs a data migration plus a code fix. Case mismatches produce conditions that are simply never true, which is the hardest kind of bug to see in review because the code looks correct.

How it happens

String literals are frictionless. The first status was added in one place, then a second, and by the time there are eight nobody wants to do the refactor to an enum.

The fix

Make illegal states unrepresentable at both layers.

export const ORDER_STATUS = ['NEW', 'PAID', 'SHIPPED', 'DELIVERED', 'CANCELLED'] as const;
export type OrderStatus = typeof ORDER_STATUS[number];

@Column({ type: 'enum', enum: ORDER_STATUS })
status!: OrderStatus;         // TypeScript rejects 'PAYED' at compile time
-- and the database rejects it too, for anything that bypasses the application
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_status_chk
  CHECK (status IN ('NEW','PAID','SHIPPED','DELIVERED','CANCELLED'));

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for quoted status values across the codebase and count distinct spellings.
  • A data check: SELECT DISTINCT status FROM orders should return exactly the values in your enum. Run it as a scheduled data-quality assertion.
  • Columns typed text or varchar that hold a fixed vocabulary and have no CHECK constraint.

48.28 Environment-specific code branches

What it looks like

async charge(amount: number) {
  if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production') {
    return this.stripe.charges.create({ amount });
  }
  return { id: 'fake_charge', status: 'succeeded' };     // staging never exercises the real path
}

if (process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production') {
  app.use(cors({ origin: '*' }));                        // and this ships if the env var is missing
}

Why it is dangerous

The code that runs in production is code that has never been tested, because every environment below production ran the other branch. Staging becomes worthless as a signal: it proves the fake path works. The failure is discovered by customers, on the day of release.

There is a security edge too. If NODE_ENV is unset — a surprisingly common misconfiguration in containers, since the default is development in many frameworks — you ship the permissive branch to production. Wide-open CORS, disabled auth guards and verbose error responses have all reached production this way.

How it happens

It is the quickest way to avoid charging real cards in development, and the alternative (a proper stub implementation behind an interface, or a provider sandbox) takes an afternoon to set up.

The fix

Same code everywhere; different configuration and different implementations, chosen at wiring time.

@Module({
  providers: [{
    provide: PAYMENT_GATEWAY,
    useClass: process.env.PAYMENT_DRIVER === 'stub' ? StubPaymentGateway : StripePaymentGateway,
  }],
})
export class PaymentModule {}

The code path is identical in every environment; only the injected adapter differs, and the adapter is a first-class, tested class. Better still, use the provider's sandbox mode so even staging exercises the real client code with test credentials.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for NODE_ENV outside configuration and bootstrap files. In application logic it is almost always this anti-pattern.
  • Any branch whose production side has no test coverage. Coverage reports make these obvious.
  • In review: "which environment tested this line?"

48.29 Configuration in code

What it looks like

const DB_HOST = 'prod-db-01.internal';
const RATE_LIMIT = 100;
const FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT = false;
const STRIPE_KEY = 'sk_live_51H...';       // committed to git, forever

Why it is dangerous

Changing any operational value requires a code change, a review, a build, and a deploy: fifteen minutes at best, during an incident when you need fifteen seconds. Raising a rate limit to absorb a partner's migration becomes a release. The same artifact can no longer be promoted across environments, because the environment is baked into it, which breaks the fundamental build-once-deploy-many principle. And secrets in code are secrets in git history, on every laptop and in every fork, permanently — rotating them is the only remedy.

How it happens

A constant is the fastest way to make something work, and it starts as one value that "will never change". Configuration infrastructure feels like overhead on day one.

The fix

Configuration comes from the environment, validated at startup so a bad value fails immediately rather than at 03:00.

@Module({
  imports: [ConfigModule.forRoot({
    validationSchema: Joi.object({
      DATABASE_URL: Joi.string().uri().required(),
      RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN: Joi.number().integer().min(1).default(100),
      STRIPE_SECRET_KEY: Joi.string().pattern(/^sk_/).required(),
    }),
    validationOptions: { abortEarly: false },     // report every problem at once
  })],
})
export class AppModule {}

Secrets come from a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, sealed Kubernetes secrets), never from the repository. Values that must change without a deploy — feature flags, limits, kill switches — belong in a runtime configuration store or a flag service.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Secret scanning in CI (gitleaks, trufflehog, GitHub secret scanning) on every push and on history.
  • Grep for hostnames, URLs containing .internal, and anything matching sk_live, AKIA, -----BEGIN.
  • A hardcoded number used in a decision (limits, timeouts, thresholds) is configuration in disguise.
  • Operational test: can you change the rate limit without a deploy? If not, it is in the wrong place.

48.30 List endpoints with no pagination

What it looks like

@Get('orders')
async findAll() {
  return this.orderRepo.find();      // every order, ever
}

Why it is dangerous

The endpoint is fine for eighteen months and then becomes an outage. At 8 million orders with 300-byte rows, one request materialises roughly 2.4 GB of JavaScript objects, serialises them to JSON and holds the whole thing in heap before the first byte reaches the client. The pod is OOMKilled in seconds. It is also a free denial-of-service primitive: any authenticated user can take the service down by refreshing a page, and no rate limiter will save you because one request is enough.

How it happens

The table had 40 rows during development and the frontend "just needs all of them" for a dropdown. Pagination is extra work on both sides for no visible benefit at that size, and nobody revisits the endpoint later because it never errors — it just gets slower until it stops.

The fix

@Get('orders')
async findAll(@Query() q: ListOrdersDto) {
  return this.orderRepo.find({
    where: { userId: q.userId },
    take: Math.min(q.limit ?? 25, 100),     // hard server-side ceiling, always
    order: { createdAt: 'DESC' },
  });
}

The ceiling must be enforced by the server, not requested by the client. Make the default page size small and return a cursor. For genuine bulk export, use a streaming endpoint or an asynchronous job that writes to object storage.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for .find() and .findAll() with no take or limit.
  • Response size histogram per endpoint; alert on any response above a few megabytes.
  • Query row-count metrics: pg_stat_statements.rows / calls above a few thousand for an interactive endpoint.

48.31 Deep OFFSET pagination

What it looks like

SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 200000;

Why it is dangerous

OFFSET does not skip rows cheaply. PostgreSQL fetches and discards all 200,000 rows before returning 20, so page 1 takes 2 ms and page 10,000 takes 1.8 seconds. Crawlers and export scripts walk deep pages methodically, so the slow case is not rare — it is a background process hitting it thousands of times a day. There is also a correctness bug: if a row is inserted between page requests, rows shift and the client sees an item twice or misses one entirely.

How it happens

OFFSET is what pagination looks like in every tutorial, and the UI needs page numbers. The performance cliff is invisible until someone actually browses deep.

The fix

Keyset (cursor) pagination: filter on the last seen sort key instead of counting rows.

-- page 1
SELECT id, created_at FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;
-- next page: pass the last row's (created_at, id) back as a cursor
SELECT id, created_at FROM orders
 WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2)          -- row-value comparison, uses the index
 ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;

With an index on (created_at DESC, id DESC) every page costs the same 2 ms, whether it is page 1 or page 10,000. Include a tiebreaker column so the ordering is total and stable. Part 49 gives the decision tree for when OFFSET is still acceptable (small, bounded, admin-only tables).

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for OFFSET and for TypeORM's skip: with a value that can grow.
  • Latency by page number. If p99 rises with the page parameter, this is why.
  • Duplicated or missing items reported by clients during active writes.

48.32 Floating point for money

What it looks like

@Column('float') price!: number;                  // or 'double precision', or plain number

const total = items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price * i.qty, 0);
// 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.30000000000000004

Why it is dangerous

Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly. Errors accumulate across additions and multiplications, so an invoice of 1,000 line items can be off by several cents. That is not a rounding curiosity; it is a reconciliation failure. Payment providers reject mismatched amounts, accounting will not balance, and in regulated markets an unbalanced ledger is a reportable defect. I have seen a month-end close delayed by two days over a 4-cent discrepancy that took an engineer a day to trace to a float column.

How it happens

number is the only numeric type in JavaScript, and float is the obvious column type for something with a decimal point. It works perfectly in every test, because test values are small and few.

The fix

Store money as integer minor units, or as NUMERIC, and always with a currency.

ALTER TABLE order_items ADD COLUMN unit_price_minor BIGINT NOT NULL;   -- cents
ALTER TABLE order_items ADD COLUMN currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL;
-- NUMERIC(19,4) is the alternative when fractional minor units are needed
export class Money {
  private constructor(readonly minor: bigint, readonly currency: string) {}
  static fromMinor(minor: number | bigint, currency: string) { return new Money(BigInt(minor), currency); }
  plus(o: Money) {
    if (o.currency !== this.currency) throw new CurrencyMismatch(this.currency, o.currency);
    return new Money(this.minor + o.minor, this.currency);
  }
}

Note that TypeORM and Sequelize return NUMERIC as a string in Node to avoid precision loss. Do not "fix" that by parsing it to a float.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Query the catalogue: SELECT table_name, column_name, data_type FROM information_schema.columns WHERE data_type IN ('real','double precision') AND column_name ~ '(price|amount|total|cost|fee|balance)'.
  • Grep for parseFloat near money field names.
  • Reconciliation check: sum line items and compare to the stored order total. Any drift proves it.

48.33 JSON blobs instead of a schema

What it looks like

@Column('jsonb') data!: Record<string, unknown>;   // everything about the order lives here
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE data->>'status' = 'PAID' AND (data->>'total')::numeric > 100;

Why it is dangerous

The database can no longer help you. There are no NOT NULL constraints, no foreign keys, no type checking, and no default index, so the query above is a sequential scan with a cast on every row. Because nothing enforces shape, the column accumulates variants: some rows have total, older ones have totalAmount, a few have both with different values. Every consumer needs defensive code, and no migration can fix rows whose shape you cannot enumerate.

How it happens

Schema changes feel slow, and jsonb means shipping without a migration. It is genuinely the right tool for sparse, variable, non-queried attributes — the mistake is using it for the core, queried fields because it is convenient today.

The fix

Columns for anything you filter, sort, join or constrain on. jsonb for genuinely variable extras.

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id           UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id      UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  status       TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('NEW','PAID','SHIPPED','CANCELLED')),
  total_minor  BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (total_minor >= 0),
  metadata     JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'    -- vendor extras, campaign tags, A/B data
);
CREATE INDEX orders_metadata_gin ON orders USING gin (metadata jsonb_path_ops);

Part 49 covers the flip side: PostgreSQL with jsonb is very often the document database you actually needed — the point is to choose deliberately, per column.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for ->> in WHERE clauses. Filtering on an extracted JSON field is the signal.
  • EXPLAIN showing a seq scan with a jsonb filter.
  • Data check: SELECT DISTINCT jsonb_object_keys(data) FROM orders — a long, inconsistent list means the shape has drifted.

48.34 Polling a queue table without SKIP LOCKED

What it looks like

const jobs = await this.ds.query(
  `SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE`);

Why it is dangerous

FOR UPDATE without SKIP LOCKED makes every worker queue behind the first one. With ten worker pods you get the throughput of one, plus nine idle processes holding open transactions. Under load, lock waits grow until lock_timeout or the connection pool is exhausted, and the queue backs up while CPU sits idle. Without FOR UPDATE at all it is worse in a different way: every worker selects the same rows and processes each job ten times.

How it happens

FOR UPDATE is the documented way to lock rows, and SKIP LOCKED is a less well-known modifier. With one worker in development, neither problem appears.

The fix

UPDATE jobs SET status = 'RUNNING', locked_at = now(), locked_by = $1
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id FROM jobs
   WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND run_after <= now()
   ORDER BY priority DESC, id
   FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED           -- each worker takes a different batch
   LIMIT 10
)
RETURNING *;

SKIP LOCKED lets each worker claim rows nobody else holds, so throughput scales with worker count. Add a locked_at reaper for workers that die mid-job, and an index on (status, run_after) filtered to pending rows.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for FOR UPDATE without SKIP LOCKED in any polling loop.
  • pg_stat_activity showing several sessions in wait_event_type = 'Lock' on the same table.
  • Queue throughput that does not improve when you add workers. That is the definitive test.

48.35 Cron on every replica

What it looks like

@Injectable()
export class ReportJob {
  @Cron('0 6 * * *')          // runs on all 6 replicas at 06:00
  async sendDailyReport() { await this.mailer.sendToFinance(await this.buildReport()); }
}

Why it is dangerous

Six replicas means six emails, six full report queries hitting the database simultaneously, and six sets of any side effects. When the job writes data, you get six copies or six racing writers. When it calls a paid API, you pay six times. The consequence scales with your availability: the more replicas you add for reliability, the worse the duplication gets, which is a genuinely perverse incentive.

How it happens

@nestjs/schedule works per process and there is no warning that the process is one of many. It is correct in development, where there is exactly one instance.

The fix

Guard singleton work with a lock. In a PostgreSQL shop the cheapest correct option is a session advisory lock, which releases automatically if the pod dies.

@Cron('0 6 * * *')
async sendDailyReport(): Promise<void> {
  const runner = this.ds.createQueryRunner();
  await runner.connect();
  try {
    const [{ pg_try_advisory_lock: got }] =
      await runner.query('SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock($1)', [4711]);
    if (!got) return;                       // another replica is doing it
    await this.mailer.sendToFinance(await this.buildReport());
  } finally {
    await runner.query('SELECT pg_advisory_unlock($1)', [4711]);
    await runner.release();
  }
}

Alternatives: a Kubernetes CronJob that runs a dedicated pod, or enqueueing a job with a deterministic id so the queue deduplicates it. Part 47 covers leader election properly, including why you still want the work to be idempotent.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for @Cron and check each against replica count.
  • Duplicate rows or duplicate notifications with timestamps within the same second.
  • A job-run counter labelled by pod name. More than one pod per scheduled tick is the proof.

48.36 One giant utils module

What it looks like

// utils.ts - 2,800 lines, imported by 140 files
export function formatDate() {}
export function calculateVat() {}          // business logic, hiding in "utils"
export function slugify() {}
export function getStripeClient() {}       // creates a client at import time
export function isEligibleForFreeShipping() {}

Why it is dangerous

Importing one helper pulls in the whole module and everything it imports, so a unit test for a date formatter instantiates a Stripe client and needs an API key. Circular imports appear as soon as a domain module imports utils and utils imports a domain type, and in TypeScript those surface as undefined at runtime in a way that is genuinely hard to diagnose. The module also becomes a merge-conflict magnet and a dumping ground: calculateVat is a domain rule that nobody will ever find in a file called utils.

How it happens

The first two helpers genuinely had no home. Once the file exists, it is the path of least resistance for the third, and there is never a moment where adding one more feels wrong.

The fix

Group by domain, not by "miscellaneous". formatDate goes to shared/date.ts with no dependencies. calculateVat goes to the pricing module, because it is a business rule. getStripeClient becomes a NestJS provider, not a function with import-time side effects. Keep leaf helpers dependency-free so importing them is cheap and testable.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Any file named utils, helpers, common or misc over about 200 lines.
  • Import fan-in: a module imported by more than 50 files deserves splitting.
  • madge --circular src/ to find the cycles it causes.

48.37 Ignoring replication lag

What it looks like

await this.writeDb.save(order);                       // primary
const saved = await this.readDb.findOne(order.id);    // replica, 200 ms behind
return saved;                                          // undefined

Why it is dangerous

Read replicas lag: normally 5 to 50 ms, but during a bulk update, a long vacuum or a network hiccup, seconds to minutes. Code that writes then immediately reads from a replica returns stale data or nothing at all. The user creates a resource and the next screen says it does not exist, so they create it again — now you have duplicates. Worse, an authorization check reading a revoked permission from a lagging replica grants access that was withdrawn a minute ago.

How it happens

Routing reads to replicas is a standard, correct scaling move, usually applied globally with a slaves/replication configuration. The read-after-write case is a small subset of traffic that nobody separates out.

The fix

Route by consistency requirement, not by verb. Anything the current user just wrote, and anything security-relevant, reads from the primary.

// TypeORM lets you force the primary per query
const saved = await this.ds
  .createQueryBuilder(Order, 'o')
  .setQueryRunner(this.ds.createQueryRunner('master'))   // read from primary
  .where('o.id = :id', { id: order.id })
  .getOne();

Monitor the lag and stop routing to a replica that exceeds a threshold:

SELECT client_addr, state,
       (pg_current_wal_lsn() - replay_lsn) AS lag_bytes
FROM pg_stat_replication;

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Export pg_replication_lag_seconds and alert above a few seconds.
  • Grep for a read immediately following a write in the same handler.
  • Intermittent 404s right after a successful create, especially under load. That symptom is almost always this.

48.38 Mocking the database in "integration" tests

What it looks like

const mockRepo = { find: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue([{ id: '1', total: 100 }]) };
const module = await Test.createTestingModule({
  providers: [OrderService, { provide: getRepositoryToken(Order), useValue: mockRepo }],
}).compile();
// "integration test" that never touches PostgreSQL

Why it is dangerous

The test asserts that your mock returns what you told it to return. It cannot catch the things that actually break in production: a missing index, a constraint violation, a wrong column type, a transaction that does not roll back, a NULL where the code expects a value, a migration that was never applied, or an ORM query that generates invalid SQL. Teams with 90 percent coverage built this way still ship schema bugs weekly, and the coverage number actively hides the gap.

How it happens

Mocks are fast and require no infrastructure, and setting up a real database in CI used to be genuinely painful. The test file gets labelled "integration" because it wires several classes together, which feels like integration.

The fix

Run the real database with Testcontainers, or a disposable PostgreSQL service in CI. Keep unit tests mocked and fast; make integration tests real.

let container: StartedPostgreSqlContainer;

beforeAll(async () => {
  container = await new PostgreSqlContainer('postgres:16-alpine').start();
  dataSource = new DataSource({ type: 'postgres', url: container.getConnectionUri(),
    entities: [Order], migrations: ['src/migrations/*.ts'] });
  await dataSource.initialize();
  await dataSource.runMigrations();          // migrations are tested too, for free
}, 60_000);

it('rejects a duplicate order for the same cart', async () => {
  await repo.save({ cartId: 'c1', userId: 'u1' });
  await expect(repo.save({ cartId: 'c1', userId: 'u1' }))
    .rejects.toMatchObject({ code: '23505' });   // the real unique constraint fires
});

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for getRepositoryToken combined with useValue in files named *.integration.spec.ts or *.e2e-spec.ts.
  • CI runtime: an integration suite that finishes in under a second is not touching a database.
  • Track escaped defects by category. Constraint and migration bugs reaching production means this layer is missing.

48.39 Deploying with no rollback plan

What it looks like

A release checklist that ends at "deploy to production", plus a migration in the same release that does ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN legacy_total;.

Why it is dangerous

At 14:20 the new version starts throwing 500s on checkout. The obvious move is to roll back the application — but the previous version reads legacy_total, which no longer exists, so rolling back makes things worse. You are now debugging forward under maximum pressure, which typically turns a five-minute incident into a two-hour one. The most expensive minutes in engineering are the ones spent discovering that rollback is impossible.

How it happens

Deploys usually work. Rollback plans cost time to write and rehearse for an event that has not happened yet, and destructive migrations are bundled with the code change because that is the natural unit of work.

The fix

Make every release reversible by construction, using expand and contract.

Release N     add new nullable column, dual-write, deploy code that reads either
Release N+1   backfill, switch reads to the new column, verify
Release N+2   stop writing the old column
Release N+3   drop the old column   <- only now, and only after N+2 is proven stable

Never combine a destructive migration with a code change. Keep the previous container image warm, know the rollback command, and put a kill switch (a feature flag) in front of risky behaviour so you can disable it in seconds without any deploy. Rehearse a rollback in staging so the runbook is real rather than aspirational. Part 31 and Part 32 cover this in detail.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Any migration containing DROP COLUMN, DROP TABLE, ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE or a NOT NULL addition in the same release as code changes.
  • Measure mean time to rollback. If nobody knows it, there is no plan.
  • In review, ask: what is the exact command to undo this, and has anyone run it?

48.40 No rate limiting on auth endpoints

What it looks like

@Post('login')                       // no throttling, no lockout, no CAPTCHA
async login(@Body() dto: LoginDto) { return this.auth.login(dto.email, dto.password); }

Why it is dangerous

Credential stuffing is automated and cheap. With a leaked-password list, an attacker can try 200 requests per second against your login endpoint; at typical reuse rates of 1 to 2 percent, a list of a million credentials yields thousands of valid accounts within hours. The same applies to password reset (email enumeration and inbox flooding), OTP send (SMS costs that are literally billed to you, often exploited as toll fraud), and OTP verify (a 6-digit code is trivially brute-forced without a limit).

There is a secondary self-inflicted risk: bcrypt at cost factor 12 takes about 250 ms of CPU per attempt by design, so an unlimited login endpoint is also a CPU exhaustion vector. A few hundred concurrent attempts will saturate the service.

How it happens

Rate limiting is treated as a cross-cutting infrastructure concern to be added later, and auth endpoints are built early, before that infrastructure exists.

The fix

Tight, layered limits keyed by more than one dimension.

@Post('login')
@Throttle({ default: { ttl: 60_000, limit: 5 } })       // per IP
async login(@Body() dto: LoginDto, @Ip() ip: string) {
  await this.lockout.assertNotLocked(dto.email);         // per account, independent of IP
  try {
    return await this.auth.login(dto.email, dto.password);
  } catch (e) {
    await this.lockout.recordFailure(dto.email);         // exponential backoff per account
    throw new UnauthorizedException('invalid credentials');  // same message either way
  }
}

Limit per IP and per account, because a distributed attack rotates IPs while targeting one account, and a stuffing attack uses one IP against many accounts. Add CAPTCHA after a few failures, and alert on failure-rate spikes.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • List every unauthenticated endpoint and check each for a limit. Login, register, reset, OTP send, OTP verify, invite accept.
  • Metric: failed logins per minute. A step change is an attack in progress.
  • Distinct emails attempted per IP per hour, and distinct IPs per email per hour. Both are strong stuffing signals.
  • SMS spend per hour, which is often the first place OTP abuse becomes visible.

48.41 Trusting client-side validation

What it looks like

@Post('orders')
async create(@Body() body: any) {
  // "the frontend already validates this"
  return this.orders.create({ userId: body.userId, priceMinor: body.priceMinor });
}

Why it is dangerous

The browser is not part of your system; it is an environment the attacker controls entirely. curl bypasses every frontend check in one command. Here, priceMinor comes from the client, so an attacker buys a laptop for one cent. userId comes from the client, so they place orders as somebody else. These are not theoretical: price tampering and horizontal privilege escalation through client-supplied identifiers are among the most commonly exploited web vulnerabilities.

The mass-assignment variant is just as bad: passing an unfiltered body into repo.save() lets a caller set role: 'ADMIN' or isVerified: true if those columns exist.

How it happens

The frontend does validate, visibly and well, so the backend check feels redundant. Frontend and backend are often built by the same person in the same sprint, and duplicating rules feels like a DRY violation.

The fix

Validate everything server-side, and derive identity and price from the server, never from the payload.

export class CreateOrderDto {
  @IsArray() @ArrayMinSize(1) @ArrayMaxSize(50)
  @ValidateNested({ each: true }) @Type(() => OrderItemDto)
  items!: OrderItemDto[];                 // note: no userId, no price
}

@Post('orders')
@UsePipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true, transform: true }))
async create(@Body() dto: CreateOrderDto, @Principal() p: Principal) {
  return this.orders.create({
    userId: p.userId,                      // from the verified token, never the body
    items: dto.items,                      // prices looked up server-side from the catalogue
  });
}

whitelist: true strips unknown properties and forbidNonWhitelisted: true rejects them outright, which kills mass assignment.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Grep for @Body() body: any, and for any DTO containing a price, a role, a status or a user id.
  • Check that ValidationPipe is applied globally with whitelist and forbidNonWhitelisted.
  • Data check: compare stored order totals against catalogue prices. Any mismatch is either a bug or an exploit.
  • In review, ask which fields come from the client and which from the token. Identity and money must come from the server.

48.42 Secrets in git

What it looks like

// config/production.ts, committed in 2021
export default { stripeKey: 'sk_live_51H...', dbPassword: 'Pr0d!2021', jwtSecret: 'supersecret' };

Why it is dangerous

Git history is permanent and distributed. The secret exists in every clone, every fork, every CI cache and every backup, and deleting the line in a later commit changes nothing. Public repositories are scanned continuously by bots: a leaked AWS key is typically exploited within minutes, usually to spin up compute for crypto mining, and the bill arrives before the alert does. A leaked jwtSecret is worse than a leaked database password, because anyone can mint a valid admin token and no log will show anything unusual.

Rewriting history with filter-repo does not fix it either, since you cannot un-distribute what people already cloned. The only real remedy is rotation.

How it happens

It is the fastest way to make the application run, and the value starts as a development placeholder that is later replaced with a real one "temporarily". .env files get committed because a new team member could not get set up without them.

The fix

# 1. Rotate first. The old secret must be assumed compromised forever.
# 2. Then remove it from the working tree and load from the environment.
echo ".env*" >> .gitignore
git rm --cached .env
# 3. Prevent recurrence
pip install pre-commit && pre-commit install     # with a gitleaks hook

Load secrets at runtime from AWS Secrets Manager, Vault or Kubernetes secrets mounted as files, and commit a .env.example with empty values so onboarding still works.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • gitleaks detect --source . --log-opts="--all" scans the entire history, not just HEAD.
  • Enable push protection and secret scanning on the repository host.
  • Grep for the obvious prefixes: sk_live, AKIA, ghp_, -----BEGIN RSA, xoxb-.
  • Audit provider dashboards for keys that have never been rotated.

48.43 latest image tags

What it looks like

containers:
  - name: api
    image: registry.internal/order-service:latest
    imagePullPolicy: Always

Why it is dangerous

latest is a moving pointer, so you do not know what is running. Two pods of the same deployment can run different code if they pulled at different times, which produces bugs that reproduce on one pod and not another. Rollback is impossible: kubectl rollout undo restores a manifest that still says latest, so it redeploys the same broken image. And a pod rescheduled at 03:00 silently picks up whatever was pushed last, meaning an unreviewed image can reach production without any deploy having happened.

How it happens

It removes a step. Nobody has to update a manifest for every release, and it works fine when there is one environment and one person deploying.

The fix

image: registry.internal/order-service:2.14.3@sha256:9f2a...   # tag plus digest
imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent

Tag with the git SHA or a semantic version produced by CI, and pin the digest so the tag cannot be moved underneath you. Enable registry tag immutability so a published tag can never be overwritten.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{..image}' | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -c ':latest'
  • An admission policy (OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno) that rejects latest outright.
  • Compare the running image digest against the release record. Any drift is this problem.

48.44 Missing readiness probes

What it looks like

containers:
  - name: api
    image: registry.internal/order-service:2.14.3
    ports: [{ containerPort: 3000 }]
    # no readinessProbe, no preStop

Why it is dangerous

Kubernetes adds the pod to the Service endpoints as soon as the container starts, before Nest has finished bootstrapping, before the connection pool is warm and before migrations have been checked. Every rolling deploy therefore produces a burst of 502s lasting as long as your startup time — typically 5 to 20 seconds per pod, multiplied across the rollout. The mirror problem happens at shutdown: without a preStop delay, the pod stops accepting connections before the load balancer notices, so in-flight requests are severed.

The result is a company that believes deploys inherently cause errors and therefore deploys rarely, which makes every release bigger and riskier.

How it happens

Probes are optional and the deployment works without them. The 502s appear for a few seconds and are attributed to "normal deploy noise".

The fix

readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: 3000 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 2
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: 3000 }
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 2            # allows 60s to boot without liveness killing it
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec: { command: ["sleep", "10"] }   # keep serving while endpoints propagate
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45

Pair it with app.enableShutdownHooks() in NestJS so in-flight requests drain cleanly.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • kubectl get deploy -o json | jq '.items[].spec.template.spec.containers[] | select(.readinessProbe == null) | .name'
  • A 5xx spike correlated with every deploy. If your error graph has periodic spikes at release times, this is almost certainly why.
  • Compare pod ready time against application "listening" log time.

48.45 Health checks that call every dependency

What it looks like

@Get('health')
@HealthCheck()
check() {
  return this.health.check([
    () => this.db.pingCheck('postgres'),
    () => this.redis.isHealthy('redis'),
    () => this.kafka.isHealthy('kafka'),
    () => this.http.pingCheck('stripe', 'https://api.stripe.com/healthcheck'),
    () => this.http.pingCheck('search', 'https://es.internal:9200/_cluster/health'),
  ]);
}

Wired to the readiness probe.

Why it is dangerous

This converts any dependency's partial degradation into your total outage. Elasticsearch goes yellow for 40 seconds during a shard rebalance; the check fails on every pod simultaneously; Kubernetes removes every pod from the Service; your API returns nothing at all — even though 95 percent of your endpoints never touch search. You have taken a degraded feature and turned it into a hard down, and you did it to yourself with a monitoring endpoint.

It also creates load and a dependency on a third party's availability for your own routing decisions. At 200 pods and a 5-second period, that is 40 requests per second to Stripe's endpoint purely for health checking, which will get you rate limited.

How it happens

"Health" sounds like it should mean "everything is fine", and a thorough check feels more responsible than a shallow one. The distinction between "can I serve traffic" and "is everything downstream healthy" is subtle until the first self-inflicted outage teaches it.

The fix

Separate the endpoints by consumer and semantics.

@Get('health/live')   @HealthCheck()
live() { return this.health.check([]); }             // process is alive, no I/O

@Get('health/ready')  @HealthCheck()
ready() {                                             // only what we cannot serve without
  return this.health.check([() => this.db.pingCheck('postgres', { timeout: 800 })]);
}

@Get('health/deep')   @HealthCheck()
deep() {                                              // for dashboards and humans only
  return this.health.check([
    () => this.db.pingCheck('postgres', { timeout: 1500 }),
    () => this.redis.isHealthy('redis'),
    () => this.search.isHealthy('search'),
  ]);
}

The test to apply to every readiness dependency: if this is down, do I want all replicas removed from the load balancer simultaneously? For caches, search and analytics the answer is always no.

How to detect it in review or in metrics

  • Read the readiness endpoint and count remote calls. More than one is a warning; anything optional is a bug.
  • Any external hostname in a probe path.
  • Incident review signal: an outage where the dependency was degraded but your own core paths were fine.
  • Check that every health check has a timeout shorter than the probe period.

48.46 The anti-pattern smell test

Most anti-patterns are discovered through a symptom, not through reading code. This table runs backwards from the symptom to the cause, and gives the one check that confirms it in under five minutes.

Smell Likely anti-pattern The quick check that confirms it
One file appears in every pull request God service (48.1) git log --format= --name-only | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
Endpoint slow only for large accounts N+1 queries (48.4) Count queries per request in a trace; look for a wall of identical spans
Database CPU high, no slow queries N+1 or missing index (48.4, 48.6) pg_stat_statements ordered by calls, then by total_exec_time
Latency fine in staging, terrible in production No indexes (48.6) EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and look for Rows Removed by Filter
Writes got slower with no code change Indexing everything (48.7) idx_scan = 0 rows in pg_stat_user_indexes
Response payloads are megabytes SELECT * or no pagination (48.5, 48.30) Response size histogram per endpoint
Memory climbs steadily, pod restarts every few days Unbounded cache (48.20) or no timeouts (48.14) Heap graph shape plus in-flight request gauge
Pod dies with no error in logs Fire-and-forget promise (48.25) unhandledRejection counter; exit code 1
Services must be deployed in a fixed order Distributed monolith (48.8) Does any service depend on a shared package that changes weekly
Feature needs three repositories and three PRs Microservices too early (48.9) Services per engineer; RPS per service
A reporting job takes down checkout Shared database (48.10) or no bulkhead pg_stat_activity grouped by application_name during the incident
One slow dependency and everything is slow Sync call chains (48.11) or no timeouts (48.14) Trace depth; grep clients for missing timeouts
Downstream traffic higher than your inbound traffic Retry storm (48.12) Ratio of outbound requests to logical operations
Consumer lag grows, error rate constant Infinite retries on a poison message (48.13) Same correlation id repeating in logs; max message age
Customers charged twice No idempotency (48.15) GROUP BY order_id HAVING count(*) > 1
Orders stuck in an impossible state Magic strings (48.27) or anemic model (48.3) SELECT DISTINCT status versus the enum
Table bloat growing with normal traffic Giant transactions (48.17) max(now() - xact_start) in pg_stat_activity
Adding workers does not increase throughput No SKIP LOCKED (48.34) Sessions waiting on Lock for the same table
Six identical emails at 06:00 Cron on every replica (48.35) Job-run counter labelled by pod
404 immediately after a successful create Replication lag (48.37) pg_stat_replication lag bytes at that timestamp
High test coverage, schema bugs still ship Mocked database in integration tests (48.38) Integration suite runtime under one second
Rollback made the incident worse No rollback plan (48.39) Did the release include a destructive migration
Login failures spike from many IPs No auth rate limiting (48.40) Distinct emails per IP per hour
A cheap order for an expensive product Trusting the client (48.41) Compare stored totals against catalogue prices
Two pods behave differently on the same version latest tag (48.43) Compare running image digests
5xx spike on every deploy Missing readiness probe (48.44) Deployments with readinessProbe == null
Total outage when search degraded Health check calls everything (48.45) Count remote calls in the readiness endpoint

How anti-patterns cascade into an outage

No single anti-pattern usually causes a major incident. Outages are chains, and the chain below is the most common one in backend systems. Each link is individually defensible; together they take down a company.

flowchart TB
  A["Slow query appears: missing index"] --> B["Downstream p99 rises to 3s"]
  B --> C["No timeouts: callers wait indefinitely"]
  C --> D["Retries at 3 layers: load multiplies 9x"]
  D --> E["Connection pool exhausted"]
  E --> F["Unrelated endpoints now fail: no bulkhead"]
  F --> G["Readiness probe checks the database"]
  G --> H["All replicas marked unready at once"]
  H --> I["Service removed from load balancer: total outage"]
  I --> J["Rollback blocked: destructive migration shipped"]
  J --> K["Recovery measured in hours, not minutes"]

Read it as a list of independent brakes you could have installed. A timeout at step C caps the damage. A retry budget at D stops the amplification. A bulkhead at F preserves the healthy endpoints. Removing the database from the readiness probe at G means the service degrades instead of disappearing. A reversible migration at J turns a two-hour incident into a two-minute one. You do not need all five; any one of them shortens the outage substantially, which is exactly why the fixes in this part are worth doing before you need them.

Senior Checklist — Part 48

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can name the good intention behind every anti-pattern here, not just the fix
  • I can spot an N+1 in a pull request without running the code
  • I can prove a missing index with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output
  • I know how many indexes each of my hot tables carries, and which are unused
  • Every outbound call in my service has a timeout, and I can point to each one
  • Retries happen at exactly one layer of my stack and are covered by a budget
  • Every queue, cache and buffer in my service has a documented maximum size
  • My readiness probe does not check any optional dependency
  • My last release could have been rolled back in under five minutes, and I have tested that
  • No secret has ever been committed to a repository I own, and I can prove it with a history scan
  • My integration tests run against a real PostgreSQL instance

Part 48 — Key Takeaways

  • Nobody writes an anti-pattern on purpose. Every one starts as a reasonable decision that outlived the conditions that justified it.
  • The most expensive anti-patterns are invisible at development scale: N+1, missing indexes, no pagination, unbounded caches and no timeouts all work perfectly with seed data.
  • A constructor with more than seven dependencies, an await inside a loop, and an empty catch block are the three highest-yield things to look for in review.
  • Missing indexes cause more "the database is slow" incidents than anything else; indexing everything is the overcorrection that quietly halves your write throughput.
  • Distribution multiplies costs before it multiplies benefits. A distributed monolith is strictly worse than the monolith it came from, and a shared database is the coupling that creates it.
  • Retries, timeouts and idempotency are one decision, not three: retry only what is idempotent, always against a deadline, at exactly one layer.
  • Never call an external API inside a database transaction, and never let a transaction span thousands of rows.
  • Logs, git history and backups are forever. Assume anything written to them can never be unwritten.
  • Floating point is not money, magic strings are not states, and jsonb is not a schema for anything you filter on.
  • Health checks and probes cause self-inflicted outages more often than crashes do. Readiness must never depend on an optional service.
  • Coverage from mocked databases measures nothing that breaks in production. Test against a real PostgreSQL instance.
  • A release is not finished until you can undo it. Destructive migrations must never ship with the code that stops using the column.
  • Outages are chains, not single failures. Any one brake in the chain converts a multi-hour incident into a minor blip.

Part 49 — Architecture Decision Framework

Most architecture arguments are not really disagreements about technology. They are disagreements about which constraint matters most, held by people who never said their constraint out loud. One person is optimising for hiring, another for latency, a third for the cloud bill. All three are right, and the argument cannot be resolved by discussing PostgreSQL.

This part is a set of decision procedures. For each of the twenty-one decisions below you get the same six things: a decision tree you can walk in ninety seconds, an explicit list of conditions mapped to choices, a trade-off table across nine dimensions, the signals that tell you the choice was wrong, the realistic migration path if it was, and a short note on how a senior engineer actually approaches it.

Three principles run underneath all of them.

The default is the boring choice. PostgreSQL, a modular monolith, REST, containers, managed services. Not because they are best in every case, but because they are best in most cases and the burden of proof belongs on the exception. When you deviate, write down the specific requirement that forced it.

Reversibility is a first-class criterion. Decisions differ enormously in how expensive they are to unmake. Choosing GraphQL is a few weeks to undo; choosing DynamoDB with a single-table design is a year. Spend your analysis budget in proportion to irreversibility, and where a decision is cheap to reverse, just decide and move.

Every choice has a "signals you chose wrong" list, and you should write it before you decide. A decision without falsification criteria is a belief. Writing down "if our p99 is still above 400 ms in three months, this was wrong" is what turns architecture from opinion into engineering.

49.1 SQL versus NoSQL

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["Do you know all your query patterns and will they stay fixed"] -->|"no"| PG["PostgreSQL"]
  A -->|"yes"| B{"Do you need transactions across entities"}
  B -->|"yes"| PG
  B -->|"no"| C{"Is your write or read volume beyond one big node"}
  C -->|"no"| PG
  C -->|"yes"| D{"Is the access pattern a single key lookup"}
  D -->|"yes"| KV["DynamoDB or Redis"]
  D -->|"no"| E{"Is it time series or append-heavy analytics"}
  E -->|"yes"| TS["TimescaleDB or ClickHouse"]
  E -->|"no"| DOC["Document store, or PostgreSQL with jsonb"]

If... then choose
