If you need ACID transactions across multiple entities and rich ad-hoc queries
   -> Choose PostgreSQL
If you need single-digit-millisecond key lookups at extreme scale with one access pattern
   -> Choose DynamoDB or Redis
If your documents are variable in shape but you still need joins, constraints and SQL
   -> Choose PostgreSQL with jsonb columns
If you are storing 500,000 metric points per second with time-window queries
   -> Choose TimescaleDB, ClickHouse or a dedicated TSDB
If you need full-text relevance ranking across millions of documents with facets
   -> Choose Elasticsearch alongside PostgreSQL, never instead of it
If your data is a graph and your queries are variable-depth traversals
   -> Choose a graph database, but only after testing recursive CTEs in PostgreSQL
If you do not yet know the shape of your data or your queries
   -> Choose PostgreSQL, always

The most under-used answer on that list is the third. PostgreSQL with jsonb is very often the document database people actually needed: schemaless columns where you want them, real constraints and joins where you need them, GIN indexes for containment queries, and one system to operate.

CREATE TABLE products (
  id          UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  sku         TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,             -- structured where it matters
  price_minor BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (price_minor >= 0),
  attributes  JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'       -- schemaless where it helps
);
CREATE INDEX products_attr_gin ON products USING gin (attributes jsonb_path_ops);

-- containment query, index-backed, roughly 1 to 3 ms on millions of rows
SELECT id, sku FROM products WHERE attributes @> '{"colour":"red","size":"XL"}';

Trade-offs

Dimension PostgreSQL Document store (MongoDB) Key-value (DynamoDB, Redis)
Consistency Strong, ACID, serializable available Tunable; multi-document transactions exist but are costly Item-level atomic; cross-item needs application work
Latency 1 to 5 ms typical indexed query 1 to 5 ms typical Under 1 ms for a key lookup
Throughput Tens of thousands of TPS on one node; scales with replicas and partitions High with sharding Effectively unbounded with partitioning
Operational cost Well understood; managed options everywhere Sharding and balancing need real expertise Very low if managed; you own capacity planning
Team skill Nearly every backend engineer knows SQL Moderate; misuse is common Data modelling is genuinely hard and unforgiving
Flexibility Excellent for new queries; jsonb covers variable shapes Good for shape changes, weaker for new access patterns Poor. New access patterns need new tables or GSIs
Money cost Cheapest per GB; a single instance goes far Higher per node Pay per request; cheap at low volume, expensive at high read volume
Ecosystem Enormous: ORMs, migrations, BI, extensions Good Good within its cloud, weak outside
Failure modes Connection exhaustion, lock contention, bloat, replication lag Unbalanced shards, hot chunks, unindexed scans Hot partitions, throttling, unbounded item growth

Signals you chose wrong

  • You picked NoSQL and are now doing joins in application code, fetching three collections to render one screen.
  • You are writing eventual-consistency reconciliation jobs to fix data a transaction would have kept correct.
  • Product asks a new question and the answer is "we cannot query that without a migration or a new index table".
  • You picked PostgreSQL and one table is 4 TB with 200,000 writes per second on a single hot key, and partitioning has not helped.
  • Your DynamoDB bill is dominated by read capacity, which usually means you are using it as a query engine.

How to change your mind later

Moving from NoSQL to PostgreSQL is the common direction and is very doable: dual-write for a period, backfill historically with a batch job, verify with a comparison script that reads both and reports differences, then switch reads behind a feature flag and stop writing the old store. Budget one to three months for a medium dataset.

Moving from PostgreSQL to a key-value store is harder because you are giving up joins and transactions that application code has relied on for years. The realistic path is to move one access pattern at a time: identify the specific hot table, put the new store in front as a read cache first, then move writes once the read path is proven. Never migrate the whole database.

The cheapest insurance is a repository layer that keeps SQL in one place per aggregate. Not a generic abstraction over all databases, which is the overengineering trap from Part 48, just a boundary where the queries live.

Senior perspective

I have never regretted starting on PostgreSQL, and I have several times watched teams spend a year escaping a NoSQL choice made in month two for scale that arrived in year four, if ever. The question that settles it is not "how much data will we have" but "will our query patterns change". If the answer is yes, and for any product still finding its market it is always yes, then the flexibility of SQL is worth more than the throughput of a key-value store. Choose the specialised store when you have a specific, measured access pattern that PostgreSQL demonstrably cannot serve. That is a real and legitimate situation; it is just much rarer than the architecture blogs suggest.

49.2 Monolith versus microservices

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["How many engineers"] -->|"under 15"| MM["Modular monolith"]
  A -->|"15 or more"| B{"Are teams blocked by each other's deploys"}
  B -->|"no"| MM
  B -->|"yes"| C{"Do you have clear bounded contexts"}
  C -->|"no"| DDD["Do the domain work first, then split"]
  C -->|"yes"| D{"Is there a different scaling or compliance need"}
  D -->|"yes"| MS["Extract that service only"]
  D -->|"no"| MM

If... then choose

If you have fewer than 15 engineers, or you are pre product-market fit
   -> Choose a modular monolith
If one component needs 20x the replicas of everything else at peak
   -> Extract that one component as a service
If a component has a different compliance boundary, such as card data
   -> Extract it, and keep the boundary narrow
If independent teams are genuinely blocked waiting on each other's release train
   -> Extract along the team boundary, one service at a time
If a component needs a different runtime, such as Python for machine learning
   -> Extract it
If your reason is "microservices are the modern architecture"
   -> Choose a modular monolith
If you already have a distributed monolith and cannot deploy services separately
   -> Merge them back, then re-split along the real boundaries

The default middle path deserves its own paragraph. A modular monolith is one deployable with hard internal boundaries: each module exposes a small public interface, imports across module internals are blocked by a lint rule, and each module owns its own tables that no other module queries directly. You get almost all of the design benefit of microservices — clear ownership, explicit contracts, testable boundaries — with none of the distributed-systems cost. It is also the ideal precondition for extraction: a module with a clean interface and its own tables becomes a service in a week.

{
  "rules": {
    "no-restricted-imports": ["error", {
      "patterns": [{
        "group": ["**/modules/*/src/**", "**/modules/*/!(index)"],
        "message": "Cross-module imports must go through the module's public index.ts"
      }]
    }]
  }
}

Trade-offs

Dimension Modular monolith Microservices
Consistency Single database, real transactions across modules Distributed; sagas, outbox, eventual consistency
Latency In-process calls, nanoseconds Network hops, 1 to 10 ms each, compounding
Throughput Scale the whole app together; usually fine Scale each service independently; efficient at high scale
Operational cost One pipeline, one dashboard, one on-call rotation N of everything, plus tracing, discovery, mesh
Team skill Standard backend skills Requires distributed-systems and platform expertise
Flexibility Refactor boundaries in an afternoon Boundaries are expensive to move; contracts must be versioned
Money cost One deployment, high utilisation Idle capacity per service; typically 2 to 4x infrastructure
Ecosystem Everything works out of the box Needs a platform investment to be pleasant
Failure modes One process; a memory leak affects everything Partial failure, cascades, retry storms, version skew

Signals you chose wrong

  • You chose microservices and every feature touches three repositories, or you have more services than engineers.
  • Services must be deployed in a specific order, which means you built a distributed monolith (see Part 48).
  • You chose a monolith and a single module's memory or CPU profile now forces you to over-provision everything.
  • Deploy frequency is falling because the blast radius of one release has become frightening.
  • Teams are queuing for a shared release train, and the queue is measured in days.

How to change your mind later

Monolith to services is the easy direction if the modules were clean: extract one module, give it its own database schema, replace direct calls with an API or events, run both in parallel behind a router (Strangler Fig, Part 47), then delete the old code. Expect four to eight weeks for the first service, much less for later ones because the platform work is done.

Services back to a monolith is unfashionable and entirely reasonable. It is also mechanically simpler than people expect: merge the repositories, replace HTTP clients with direct calls, consolidate the databases with a schema per former service. The hard part is political, not technical. Several well-known engineering organisations have done this and reported large cost and latency improvements.

Senior perspective

The question I ask is never "monolith or microservices" but "what specifically is blocked today". If nothing is blocked, the answer is a modular monolith and the conversation is over. If something is blocked, the answer is to extract exactly the thing that is blocked, and nothing else. Service boundaries are the most expensive artefact in software to move — far more expensive than a schema or an API — so you want to draw them with knowledge you can only get by operating the system for a year. The modular monolith is how you buy that year without accumulating the mess that makes people reach for microservices in the first place.

49.3 REST versus GraphQL

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["Who consumes this API"] -->|"third parties and partners"| R["REST"]
  A -->|"our own clients"| B{"Do clients need widely varying field sets"}
  B -->|"no"| R
  B -->|"yes"| C{"Are there many client types with different screens"}
  C -->|"no"| BFF["REST plus a BFF"]
  C -->|"yes"| D{"Can you own caching and query-cost limits"}
  D -->|"no"| BFF
  D -->|"yes"| G["GraphQL"]

If... then choose

If your API is public, versioned and consumed by partners you do not control
   -> Choose REST
If mobile clients need many different field subsets and screens change often
   -> Choose GraphQL
If you have one web client and a stable set of screens
   -> Choose REST
If clients complain about over-fetching but there are only two or three shapes
   -> Choose REST with sparse fieldsets or a BFF per client
If you need HTTP caching, CDN caching and simple observability by URL
   -> Choose REST
If you are aggregating many backend services for many frontends
   -> Choose GraphQL as a gateway layer, with strict cost limits
If your team has never operated GraphQL in production
   -> Choose REST, and revisit in a year

Trade-offs

Dimension REST GraphQL
Consistency Resource-shaped, predictable payloads Client-shaped; the same entity can arrive in many shapes
Latency Multiple round trips for composed screens One round trip; resolver fan-out can hide N+1
Throughput Easy to cache at CDN and reverse proxy Hard to cache; usually POST, so CDN caching is mostly off
Operational cost Low; every tool understands it Needs query cost analysis, depth limits, persisted queries
Team skill Universal Requires understanding resolvers, DataLoader and schema design
Flexibility Adding a field is easy; adding a shape needs an endpoint Excellent; clients compose what they need
Money cost Low Higher compute per request; unbounded queries are a cost risk
Ecosystem Enormous, including OpenAPI tooling Good and mature, but narrower
Failure modes Over-fetching, endpoint sprawl, chatty clients N+1 in resolvers, malicious deep queries, 200 responses containing errors

Signals you chose wrong

  • You chose REST and your mobile team maintains a list of 14 calls to render one screen.
  • Your REST API has endpoints like /orders?include=items,user,shipping&fields=... — you are reimplementing GraphQL badly.
  • You chose GraphQL and your p99 is dominated by resolver N+1 because nobody added DataLoader.
  • Your CDN hit rate went to zero after the migration and origin traffic tripled.
  • A single client query can read 200,000 rows because there is no depth or cost limit.

How to change your mind later

REST to GraphQL is additive and low risk: put a GraphQL layer in front that resolves by calling the existing REST endpoints or services, migrate clients screen by screen, keep REST for partners forever. Nothing needs to be deleted.

GraphQL to REST is more work but bounded: generate REST endpoints for the queries clients actually run — persisted-query logs tell you exactly which those are, usually a few dozen — and migrate clients one at a time. Persisted queries are also the thing that makes the migration measurable, which is a good reason to enable them on day one regardless.

Senior perspective

GraphQL solves a client-diversity problem. If you do not have that problem, it is a tax: you pay in caching, observability and query-cost defence, and you receive flexibility you were not going to use. The strongest predictor I have found is the number of distinct client applications with independent release cycles. One client, choose REST. Four clients on three platforms with a design system that changes quarterly, GraphQL earns its keep. And whichever you choose, the discipline that matters is the same: know the cost of every request the client can construct, and cap it.

49.4 REST versus gRPC

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["Is the caller a browser or a third party"] -->|"yes"| R["REST over HTTP and JSON"]
  A -->|"no, internal service"| B{"Is payload size or latency a measured problem"}
  B -->|"no"| R
  B -->|"yes"| C{"Do you need streaming in either direction"}
  C -->|"yes"| G["gRPC"]
  C -->|"no"| D{"Do you have polyglot services needing generated clients"}
  D -->|"yes"| G
  D -->|"no"| R

If... then choose

If browsers call it directly, or partners integrate with it
   -> Choose REST over HTTP and JSON
If two internal services exchange millions of messages per day and bytes matter
   -> Choose gRPC
If you need bidirectional or server-side streaming between services
   -> Choose gRPC
If you have services in TypeScript, Go and Java that must share a contract
   -> Choose gRPC, and let protoc generate the clients
If your services are all Node and the traffic is under a few thousand RPS
   -> Choose REST; the gain is not worth the tooling
If you want a strict, machine-checked contract with backward-compatibility rules
   -> Choose gRPC, or REST with OpenAPI and a contract test in CI

Trade-offs

Dimension REST and JSON gRPC and protobuf
Consistency Contract by convention or OpenAPI Contract enforced by generated code
Latency Higher: JSON parsing plus HTTP/1.1 overhead Lower: binary encoding, HTTP/2 multiplexing; typically 20 to 40 percent faster in-region
Throughput Good Better; payloads often 30 to 60 percent smaller
Operational cost Trivial to debug with curl and browser tools Needs grpcurl, reflection, and proxies that speak HTTP/2
Team skill Universal Requires learning protobuf, codegen and streaming semantics
Flexibility Add a field freely Add a field freely if you follow protobuf rules; renumbering breaks everything
Money cost Higher bandwidth and CPU for serialization Lower bandwidth; relevant at high volume or cross-AZ
Ecosystem Everything Strong for backend, weak in browsers without grpc-web and a proxy
Failure modes Silent contract drift, over-fetching Version skew between generated stubs, load balancing needs L7 awareness

A practical note on load balancing: gRPC uses long-lived HTTP/2 connections, so a plain L4 load balancer pins a client to one server and traffic becomes badly skewed. You need client-side load balancing or an L7 proxy that understands HTTP/2. This surprises teams in production more than any protocol detail.

Signals you chose wrong

  • You chose gRPC and every debugging session starts by installing a tool to read a payload.
  • Browser clients need grpc-web plus a translating proxy, which you now operate.
  • One backend pod receives 80 percent of gRPC traffic because of connection pinning.
  • You chose REST and serialization CPU is a visible fraction of your service's profile, or cross-AZ bandwidth is a line item you can see on the bill.
  • Internal payloads exceed a megabyte and JSON parsing shows up in flame graphs.

How to change your mind later

Run both. A NestJS service can expose an HTTP controller and a gRPC controller over the same application service with no duplication of logic.

@Controller()
export class PricingGrpcController {
  constructor(private readonly pricing: PricingService) {}   // same service as the REST controller

  @GrpcMethod('PricingService', 'GetPrice')
  getPrice(req: GetPriceRequest): Promise<PriceReply> {
    return this.pricing.getPrice(req.sku, req.quantity);
  }
}

Migrate callers one at a time, keep REST for anything external, and delete nothing until traffic is zero.

Senior perspective

gRPC is a performance and contract tool for internal, high-volume, polyglot communication. Reach for it when you have measured a serialization or bandwidth problem, or when you genuinely need streaming, or when generated clients across three languages would remove a class of integration bugs. Do not reach for it because it is faster in a benchmark: at 500 RPS between two Node services, the difference is invisible next to your database time, and you have paid a real debuggability cost. My usual arrangement is REST at the edge, gRPC only on the two or three internal paths where the numbers justify it.

49.5 Synchronous versus asynchronous

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["Does the caller need the result to continue"] -->|"yes"| B{"Can the work finish in under 1 second reliably"}
  A -->|"no"| ASY["Asynchronous: queue or event"]
  B -->|"yes"| SYN["Synchronous call"]
  B -->|"no"| C{"Can you return an accepted status and a status endpoint"}
  C -->|"yes"| ASY
  C -->|"no"| D["Redesign: the requirement is probably wrong"]

If... then choose

If the user cannot proceed without the answer, and it takes under a second
   -> Choose synchronous
If the work is slow, external, or allowed to fail and be retried
   -> Choose asynchronous with a durable queue
If you need a strict ordering guarantee per entity across services
   -> Choose asynchronous with a partition key, not synchronous chains
If the operation must be transactional with your own database write
   -> Choose synchronous inside one transaction, or the outbox pattern
If a spike of traffic must not take down the downstream
   -> Choose asynchronous, so the queue absorbs the burst
If you are calling a third party whose latency you do not control
   -> Choose asynchronous, or synchronous with a hard timeout and a fallback
If the answer must appear on the same screen and there is no acceptable loading state
   -> Choose synchronous, and make it fast enough

Trade-offs

Dimension Synchronous Asynchronous
Consistency Immediate, read-your-write Eventual; the client sees an intermediate state
Latency Caller waits for the slowest hop Caller returns in milliseconds; work completes later
Throughput Limited by the slowest dependency Limited by consumer capacity; producers never block
Operational cost Simple: one request, one trace Broker, consumers, lag monitoring, DLQ, replay tooling
Team skill Universal Requires idempotency, ordering and backpressure understanding
Flexibility Adding a consumer means changing the caller New consumers subscribe without touching the producer
Money cost Lower for low volume Broker cost, but far better utilisation under spiky load
Ecosystem Everything Mature but requires deliberate tooling
Failure modes Cascading timeouts, retry storms, availability multiplication Duplicates, out-of-order delivery, consumer lag, poison messages

Signals you chose wrong

  • Your checkout endpoint has a p99 of 4 seconds because it waits for an email provider.
  • A downstream outage takes your API down even though the feature is optional.
  • You chose asynchronous and users constantly refresh because they cannot tell whether their action worked.
  • Support tickets say "I clicked pay and nothing happened", which means the async design has no status feedback.
  • You are building a synchronous polling loop over an async result, which is the worst of both.

How to change your mind later

Synchronous to asynchronous is straightforward and can be incremental: publish the work as a message and return 202 Accepted with a status URL, then move the caller to poll or subscribe. The hard part is the user experience, not the code — you need a visible pending state.

Asynchronous to synchronous is harder because clients have built around eventual results. The usual bridge is to keep the async pipeline and add a synchronous read-your-write path for the initiating user only, reading from the write model rather than the projection.

Senior perspective

The test I apply is: does the user's next action depend on this result? Sending a confirmation email does not block anything, so it is asynchronous, full stop. Authorising a payment does block, so it is synchronous with a strict timeout and a clear failure path. Most systems get this wrong in one specific way: they do too much synchronously inside the request because it was easier to write, and then discover under load that their checkout availability is the product of six third-party availabilities. Moving optional work out of the request path is usually the single highest-leverage reliability change available to a team, and it costs one queue.

49.6 Redis versus PostgreSQL for caching, sessions, queues, locks and counters

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["What is the workload"] -->|"cache"| C{"Is the data derivable and loss tolerable"}
  C -->|"yes"| RD["Redis"]
  C -->|"no"| PG["PostgreSQL"]
  A -->|"sessions"| S{"Do you need instant revocation and low latency"}
  S -->|"yes"| RD
  S -->|"no"| PG
  A -->|"queue"| Q{"Under 1000 jobs per second and already on PostgreSQL"}
  Q -->|"yes"| PGQ["PostgreSQL with SKIP LOCKED"]
  Q -->|"no"| RD
  A -->|"locks"| L{"Is correctness critical"}
  L -->|"yes"| PGL["PostgreSQL advisory lock"]
  L -->|"no"| RD
  A -->|"counters"| N{"Must every increment be durable"}
  N -->|"yes"| PG
  N -->|"no"| RD

If... then choose

If you need a cache with TTLs, eviction and sub-millisecond reads
   -> Choose Redis
If you need sessions with instant revocation across many pods
   -> Choose Redis, with a PostgreSQL record of the user for audit
If you need a job queue under about 1,000 jobs per second and already run PostgreSQL
   -> Choose PostgreSQL with SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
If you need a job queue above that, with delays, priorities and retries built in
   -> Choose Redis with BullMQ, or a real broker
If you need a mutual exclusion lock where losing it would corrupt data
   -> Choose a PostgreSQL advisory lock, because it is tied to a transaction you trust
If you need a best-effort lock to avoid duplicate work
   -> Choose Redis with SET NX PX and a fencing token
If you need counters that must never be lost, such as billing units
   -> Choose PostgreSQL, sharded if the row is hot
If you need counters for likes, views or rate limits
   -> Choose Redis, with periodic rollup into PostgreSQL

Trade-offs

Dimension Redis PostgreSQL
Consistency Single-threaded per shard, atomic per command; replication is asynchronous so failover can lose writes ACID, durable, synchronous commit available
Latency 0.2 to 1 ms 1 to 5 ms for an indexed query
Throughput 100,000+ ops per second per node 10,000 to 50,000 TPS with good schema and hardware
Operational cost Simple until clustering; memory sizing matters Well understood; more knobs but more tooling
Team skill Easy to start, easy to misuse (unbounded keys, blocking commands) Universal
Flexibility Data structures are the API; no ad-hoc queries Any query you can express in SQL
Money cost Memory is expensive per GB Disk is cheap; the same data costs far less
Ecosystem Excellent for caching, queues, rate limiting, streams Everything, plus extensions
Failure modes Eviction under memory pressure, failover data loss, hot keys, blocking commands stalling the loop Connection exhaustion, lock contention, bloat, replication lag

The point people miss is that Redis failover can lose recently acknowledged writes, because replication is asynchronous. That is entirely fine for a cache and completely unacceptable for the only copy of a payment record. Choose per workload, not per system.

Signals you chose wrong

  • Redis is your source of truth for something you cannot rebuild, and you have no idea what a failover would cost you.
  • Your Redis memory keeps growing because keys have no TTL, and evictions are now dropping data you needed.
  • You built a job queue on PostgreSQL and it is doing 5,000 jobs per second, generating enormous table bloat and vacuum pressure.
  • You used a Redis lock for a financial invariant and cannot explain what happens during a network partition.
  • Your PostgreSQL cache table is being updated more often than it is read.

How to change your mind later

Cache: trivially reversible. Delete the cache lookup, keep the database query. Always write the code so the cache is optional and a miss is correct.

Sessions: move from Redis to database-backed sessions or the reverse by writing to both for one session lifetime (typically 30 days for refresh tokens), then switching reads.

Queues: PostgreSQL to Redis or a broker is a producer and consumer swap. Keep draining the old table until empty, then delete it. Plan a day, not a sprint.

Counters: dual-increment for a period, compare totals, then cut over. Divergence between the two tells you exactly how much you were losing.

Senior perspective

I treat Redis as a performance tool and PostgreSQL as a correctness tool, and the decision then answers itself workload by workload. The mistake I see most is a queue built on Redis with no durability configuration, used for work that must not be lost — orders, payments, notifications with legal significance. The mirror mistake is a queue on PostgreSQL that outgrew it, where DELETE churn on the jobs table causes bloat that eventually hurts unrelated queries. Both are fine choices in their range; the failure is not revisiting the choice when the volume changed. Put a number on the boundary when you decide, so future-you knows when to move.

49.7 Kafka versus RabbitMQ versus SQS versus Redis Streams

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["Do you need to replay history or have many independent consumers"] -->|"yes"| K["Kafka"]
  A -->|"no"| B{"Do you need complex routing, priorities or per-message TTL"}
  B -->|"yes"| R["RabbitMQ"]
  B -->|"no"| C{"Are you on AWS and want zero operations"}
  C -->|"yes"| S["SQS, with SNS for fan-out"]
  C -->|"no"| D{"Do you already run Redis and need a simple durable stream"}
  D -->|"yes"| RS["Redis Streams"]
  D -->|"no"| R

If... then choose

If consumers must replay events from days ago, or new consumers must read history
   -> Choose Kafka
If you need ordered, partitioned event streams at hundreds of thousands of messages per second
   -> Choose Kafka
If you need routing rules, priority queues, per-message TTL and delayed delivery
   -> Choose RabbitMQ
If you want a queue with no servers to operate and you are already on AWS
   -> Choose SQS, with SNS or EventBridge when you need fan-out
If you need FIFO ordering per key with exactly-once processing on AWS
   -> Choose SQS FIFO, and accept the 300 messages per second per group limit
If you already run Redis, need a durable-ish stream, and volumes are moderate
   -> Choose Redis Streams
If you need a background job queue with retries, delays and a dashboard
   -> Choose BullMQ on Redis; it is a job queue, not an event bus
If you are a small team and cannot name a reason for Kafka
   -> Choose SQS or RabbitMQ

The distinction that resolves most of these arguments: Kafka is a log, the others are queues. In a log, consuming does not remove the message, many consumer groups read the same data independently, and you can rewind. In a queue, a message is delivered and deleted. If you have said the words "we need to replay", you want a log. If you have said "we need each job done once by one worker", you want a queue.

Trade-offs

Dimension Kafka RabbitMQ SQS Redis Streams
Consistency Ordered per partition, at-least-once, exactly-once within Kafka transactions Ordered per queue, at-least-once At-least-once standard, FIFO variant ordered Ordered per stream, at-least-once
Latency 5 to 20 ms typical 1 to 5 ms 10 to 100 ms Under 1 ms
Throughput Millions per second with partitions Tens of thousands per queue Effectively unlimited, per-queue quotas apply Hundreds of thousands, single-node bound
Operational cost High: brokers, ZooKeeper or KRaft, rebalancing, retention tuning Moderate: clustering and queue mirroring need care Near zero Low, but memory-bound and you own persistence config
Team skill Steep learning curve; consumer groups and offsets are subtle Moderate; AMQP concepts Trivial Easy if you already run Redis
Flexibility Excellent for new consumers over existing data Excellent routing topologies Simple; fan-out needs SNS or EventBridge Basic consumer groups
Money cost Expensive: 3 brokers minimum, plus storage Moderate Pay per request; cheap at low volume Memory cost per retained entry
Ecosystem Huge: Connect, Streams, CDC, schema registry Mature, many client libraries AWS-native integrations Small
Failure modes Rebalance storms, consumer lag, partition skew, disk fill from retention Queue backlog memory pressure, split-brain in clusters Visibility timeout misuse, 256 KB limit, in-flight caps Memory eviction dropping entries, no partition parallelism

Signals you chose wrong

  • You chose Kafka and run a three-broker cluster for 50 messages per second. The cluster costs more than the feature.
  • You chose Kafka and nobody has ever replayed a topic, and there is exactly one consumer group.
  • You chose SQS and now need ordering and replay, so you are building an event store on top of DynamoDB.
  • You chose RabbitMQ and your queue depth regularly grows into millions, pushing the broker into memory alarms and flow control.
  • You chose Redis Streams for financial events and discovered that a failover can lose acknowledged entries.

How to change your mind later

The producer and consumer interfaces are the migration surface, so wrap them from day one.

export interface EventPublisher {
  publish(topic: string, key: string, payload: unknown, headers?: Record<string, string>): Promise<void>;
}

@Injectable()
export class KafkaPublisher implements EventPublisher { /* ... */ }
@Injectable()
export class SqsPublisher implements EventPublisher { /* ... */ }

To migrate, dual-publish to both systems for a period, move consumers one at a time, verify counts match, then stop the old publisher. For queues this is usually a two-week exercise. Moving to Kafka is harder than moving away, because Kafka's ordering and partitioning assumptions leak into consumer design — plan for the consumers to be rewritten, not ported.

Senior perspective

Kafka is excellent and most teams that adopt it do not need it. The honest test is a single question: name the consumer that will replay history, or name the second consumer group. If you cannot, you want a queue, and a queue you do not operate is better than one you do. I start teams on SQS or RabbitMQ, and I move them to Kafka when a real requirement appears — usually CDC, an analytics pipeline, or a third independent consumer of the same events. That migration is a known, bounded project. Running Kafka for two years "because we will need it" is an unbounded operational tax paid in advance.

49.8 PostgreSQL search versus Elasticsearch

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["How many searchable documents"] -->|"under 1 million"| PG["PostgreSQL full-text search"]
  A -->|"1 to 20 million"| B{"Do you need relevance tuning, facets or fuzzy matching"}
  B -->|"no"| PG
  B -->|"yes"| C{"Can you operate another stateful cluster"}
  C -->|"no"| PG2["PostgreSQL with trigram and ranking, plus a plan to revisit"]
  C -->|"yes"| ES["Elasticsearch or OpenSearch"]
  A -->|"over 20 million with high query volume"| ES

If... then choose

If you have under a million documents and need decent keyword search
   -> Choose PostgreSQL full-text search with a GIN index on tsvector
If you need typo tolerance and autocomplete at moderate scale
   -> Choose PostgreSQL with pg_trgm, which handles both surprisingly well
If you need per-field boosting, synonyms, faceted aggregation and relevance tuning
   -> Choose Elasticsearch or OpenSearch
If search is the product, not a feature
   -> Choose Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, and staff it
If you need search across data that must be transactionally consistent with writes
   -> Choose PostgreSQL, because an external index is always slightly behind
If you have a two-person team and no on-call capacity for a second cluster
   -> Choose PostgreSQL and revisit at a measured threshold
-- PostgreSQL search that is genuinely good enough for most products
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(name, '')), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(description, '')), 'B')
  ) STORED;                                    -- maintained automatically, no triggers
CREATE INDEX products_search_gin ON products USING gin (search_vector);

SELECT id, name, ts_rank(search_vector, q) AS rank
FROM products, websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1) q
WHERE search_vector @@ q
ORDER BY rank DESC LIMIT 20;                   -- roughly 5 to 20 ms on a million rows

Trade-offs

Dimension PostgreSQL FTS Elasticsearch / OpenSearch
Consistency Transactional with your data; always current Near real-time, typically 1 second refresh; can lag much more under load
Latency 5 to 50 ms up to a few million rows 5 to 30 ms at far larger scale
Throughput Shares capacity with your OLTP workload Dedicated cluster, scales horizontally
Operational cost None beyond what you already run A stateful cluster: shards, replicas, heap tuning, rolling upgrades
Team skill SQL you already know Query DSL, analyzers, mappings, cluster operations
Flexibility Limited relevance tuning; no built-in faceting beyond SQL aggregation Very rich: analyzers, synonyms, boosting, aggregations, vector search
Money cost Zero extra Three nodes minimum for production; often the second largest infrastructure line
Ecosystem Extensions like pg_trgm, unaccent, pgvector Kibana, ingest pipelines, huge plugin ecosystem
Failure modes Slow queries competing with OLTP; large GIN index maintenance Index lag, split brain, yellow cluster during rebalance, mapping explosions, reindexing pain

Signals you chose wrong

  • Search queries appear at the top of pg_stat_statements and are slowing down checkout. Your search workload is now competing with your transactional workload.
  • Users complain that results are irrelevant and you have no lever to tune ranking beyond ts_rank.
  • You run Elasticsearch and it holds a copy of one table with 40,000 rows, queried 20 times an hour.
  • Your Elasticsearch index is regularly out of sync with PostgreSQL and nobody can say by how much.
  • You have a reindex procedure that nobody has run in a year and that takes an unknown amount of time.

How to change your mind later

PostgreSQL to Elasticsearch is a well-worn path: add CDC or an outbox-driven indexer, backfill with a batch job, run both behind a search interface, compare result quality on real queries, then switch reads with a feature flag. Two to six weeks. Keep PostgreSQL search working as a fallback for at least a quarter — when the cluster goes yellow, degraded search beats no search.

Elasticsearch to PostgreSQL happens more often than people admit, usually as a cost or complexity reduction when the data turned out to be small. It is easy: build the tsvector column, compare relevance on your top thousand queries, switch.

Either way, put search behind an interface with one method (search(query, filters, page)), so the swap touches one class.

Senior perspective

Most products describe their need as "search" when they mean "filter with a text box". PostgreSQL full-text search plus pg_trgm handles that beautifully up to a few million rows, and it has the enormous advantage of being transactionally consistent — no indexer, no lag, no reindex runbook. I ask for a number before agreeing to a search cluster: document count, query rate, and one concrete relevance requirement that PostgreSQL cannot meet. When search is genuinely the product, Elasticsearch is the right tool and you should staff it properly. When search is a text box above a list, adding a second stateful cluster is one of the most expensive ways to solve a small problem.

49.9 TypeORM versus Sequelize versus raw SQL

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["Is the query simple CRUD on one aggregate"] -->|"yes"| ORM["ORM: TypeORM or the alternative your team knows"]
  A -->|"no"| B{"Does it involve window functions, CTEs or heavy aggregation"}
  B -->|"yes"| SQL["Raw SQL, or a query builder"]
  B -->|"no"| C{"Is it a hot path where the plan must be predictable"}
  C -->|"yes"| SQL
  C -->|"no"| ORM

If... then choose

If you are doing standard create, read, update and delete on entities with relations
   -> Choose an ORM, because migrations, relations and change tracking are real value
If you need window functions, recursive CTEs, lateral joins or complex aggregation
   -> Choose raw SQL, parameterised, living in a repository class
If you need the exact query plan to be stable under load on a hot path
   -> Choose raw SQL and check it with EXPLAIN ANALYZE in a test
If you want type-safe SQL without an ORM's abstraction
   -> Choose Kysely, which is a typed query builder, not an ORM
If you want a modern schema-first workflow with excellent generated types
   -> Choose Prisma, accepting less control over the emitted SQL
If you want something between Prisma and raw SQL with a SQL-shaped API
   -> Choose Drizzle
If your team already knows one of these and it is not on fire
   -> Choose the one your team knows

The honest position is that this is the least important decision in this part, and it consumes the most argument. Every option listed can serve a production system well. The mix that works is: an ORM for entity CRUD and migrations, raw SQL for the twenty queries that matter. Both, in the same codebase, on purpose.

@Injectable()
export class OrderRepository {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  // ORM for CRUD: relations, cascades and change tracking earn their keep here.
  findWithItems(id: string) {
    return this.ds.getRepository(Order).findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { items: true } });
  }

  // Raw SQL for analytics: no ORM expresses this well, and the plan must be stable.
  topProductsByRevenue(sellerId: string, days: number) {
    return this.ds.query(
      `SELECT p.id, p.name, sum(oi.qty * oi.unit_price_minor) AS revenue_minor,
              rank() OVER (ORDER BY sum(oi.qty * oi.unit_price_minor) DESC) AS position
         FROM order_items oi
         JOIN orders o   ON o.id = oi.order_id AND o.status = 'PAID'
         JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
        WHERE p.seller_id = $1 AND o.placed_at > now() - ($2 || ' days')::interval
        GROUP BY p.id, p.name
        ORDER BY revenue_minor DESC LIMIT 20`,
      [sellerId, days],
    );
  }
}

Trade-offs

Dimension TypeORM Sequelize Raw SQL
Consistency Transactions and change tracking built in; some surprising cascade behaviour Solid transaction API, explicit locking support Complete control, and complete responsibility
Latency Overhead is small but relation loading can be wasteful Similar Lowest; exactly the query you wrote
Throughput Fine until N+1 or eager loading bites Same Best, and predictable
Operational cost Migrations included; synchronize is a foot-gun Migrations via umzug; alter: true is the same foot-gun You own migrations separately
Team skill Decorators and TypeScript-first; familiar to NestJS developers Mature, more JavaScript-idiomatic Requires real SQL skill on the team
Flexibility Query builder covers a lot; complex SQL is awkward Similar Unlimited
Money cost Indirect: wasteful queries cost database capacity Same Efficient queries cost less to run
Ecosystem First-class NestJS integration First-class NestJS integration Universal
Failure modes N+1 from lazy relations, synchronize data loss, opaque generated SQL Same class of problems, plus looser typing SQL injection if you interpolate, drift from entity definitions

Signals you chose wrong

  • You spend more time fighting the ORM's generated SQL than you would spend writing SQL.
  • Your hot endpoints all bypass the ORM already, and the ORM is now only doing findOne.
  • You chose raw SQL everywhere and have hand-written 300 nearly identical CRUD queries with subtle differences.
  • Nobody on the team can read EXPLAIN output, and query performance is nobody's job.
  • You are choosing an ORM to avoid learning SQL. That never ends well; SQL is the durable skill.

How to change your mind later

You do not need to migrate wholesale. Introduce the new tool for new modules and leave the old one in place; two data-access approaches in one codebase is normal and healthy. If you must migrate fully, do it module by module behind repository classes, and keep migrations in whichever tool owns the schema — the schema is the coupling point, not the query API.

The genuinely irreversible mistake is not choosing the wrong ORM. It is scattering ORM calls through controllers and services so there is no boundary to migrate. Keep data access in repository classes and any of these decisions becomes reversible in weeks.

Senior perspective

I care far more about where data access lives than which library performs it. Repository classes, parameterised queries, no ORM calls in controllers, and an EXPLAIN check on anything that touches a large table — those practices make every library on this list work fine. What I look for in a candidate's answer is whether they know what SQL their ORM emits. Engineers who can enable query logging, read the generated SQL and explain the plan write good code in any of these tools; engineers who cannot will write N+1 queries in all of them.

49.10 ECS versus Kubernetes

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["Do you have a platform team or a dedicated infrastructure owner"] -->|"no"| B{"Is the workload simple HTTP services and workers"}
  A -->|"yes"| K["Kubernetes"]
  B -->|"yes"| C{"Are you on AWS only"}
  B -->|"no"| K
  C -->|"yes"| E["ECS Fargate, or App Runner for the simplest cases"]
  C -->|"no"| CR["Cloud Run or a managed container platform"]
  K --> D{"Do you need multi-cloud, operators, or a rich ecosystem"}
  D -->|"no"| E

If... then choose

If you run on AWS, deploy stateless services, and have no platform team
   -> Choose ECS on Fargate
If you want the least possible operations for a single containerised web service
   -> Choose App Runner or Cloud Run
If your workload is event-driven, spiky, and each execution is short
   -> Choose Lambda
If you need operators, custom resources, service mesh, or portability across clouds
   -> Choose Kubernetes
If you have more than about 30 services and several teams deploying independently
   -> Choose Kubernetes; the ecosystem starts paying for itself
If you need GPUs, complex scheduling, or stateful workloads with operators
   -> Choose Kubernetes
If your reason is that Kubernetes is what serious companies use
   -> Choose ECS, and revisit when you can name the feature you need

Trade-offs

Dimension ECS (Fargate) Kubernetes (EKS/GKE) Lambda / Cloud Run / App Runner
Consistency Simple task model, predictable Rich but complex; many ways to express the same thing Simplest; the platform owns the model
Latency No cold starts with running tasks No cold starts Cold starts: 100 ms to several seconds for Lambda; Cloud Run is usually faster
Throughput Scales fine; scaling is slower to react Fast HPA, KEDA on any metric Scales to very high concurrency automatically
Operational cost Low: AWS runs the control plane and you write task definitions High: upgrades, CNI, ingress, RBAC, node pools, cluster autoscaler Lowest
Team skill Learnable in days Weeks to months to be safe in production Hours
Flexibility Limited to the ECS model Anything; you can extend the API itself Constrained: execution limits, no long-lived connections in Lambda
Money cost Fargate is roughly 20 percent more per vCPU than EC2 Control plane fee plus node cost; better bin-packing at scale Pay per use: very cheap when idle, expensive under sustained load
Ecosystem AWS-native only Enormous: Helm, operators, ArgoCD, mesh Cloud-native only
Failure modes Task placement failures, slow scaling, limited scheduling control CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, evictions, misconfigured RBAC, upgrade breakage Cold starts, concurrency limits, timeout ceilings, connection-pool exhaustion against PostgreSQL

Signals you chose wrong

  • You run Kubernetes for four services and someone spends a day a week on cluster upgrades.
  • You cannot name a Kubernetes feature you use that ECS lacks.
  • You chose ECS and are building custom tooling that reimplements Kubernetes primitives such as jobs, cron and config reloading.
  • You chose Lambda for a service that holds database connections, and PostgreSQL is at max_connections because every concurrent invocation opened one.
  • Your serverless bill exceeds what an always-on container would cost, which happens around continuous moderate load.

How to change your mind later

Container platforms are among the most reversible decisions here, provided your application is a well-behaved twelve-factor container: configuration from the environment, logs to stdout, no local state, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM. Migrating ECS to Kubernetes is largely a translation of task definitions to Deployments, plus rebuilding CI/CD. Expect two to six weeks for a small fleet.

Lambda to containers is harder if you used platform-specific triggers and idioms heavily. Keep handlers thin and put the logic in plain classes, and the port becomes a new entry point rather than a rewrite.

Senior perspective

Kubernetes is a platform for building platforms, and it is superb when you have the problems it solves: many teams, many services, heterogeneous workloads, a need for custom automation. It is a poor trade for a team of eight running five services, because you take on a full-time operational surface to gain flexibility you will not exercise. My rule of thumb is roughly thirty services or three independent deployment teams before Kubernetes clearly wins on merit. Below that, ECS Fargate or Cloud Run gives you 90 percent of the value with about 10 percent of the operational load, and the migration later is genuinely straightforward if you kept your containers boring.

49.11 Cache versus database (and when the real fix is a better index)

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["Query is slow"] --> B{"Have you run EXPLAIN ANALYZE"}
  B -->|"no"| EX["Run it first"]
  B -->|"yes"| C{"Is there a sequential scan or a bad join order"}
  C -->|"yes"| IDX["Add or fix the index. Stop here"]
  C -->|"no"| D{"Is the query inherently expensive, such as a big aggregate"}
  D -->|"yes"| E{"Is stale data acceptable"}
  D -->|"no"| F["Fix the query: fewer columns, better pagination, batching"]
  E -->|"yes"| CA["Cache or materialized view"]
  E -->|"no"| RR["Read replica, or precompute in the write path"]

If... then choose

If EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan on a large table
   -> Add the right index. Do not cache
If the query is fast but called 8,000 times per second on the same key
   -> Choose a cache with a TTL
If the query is an aggregate over millions of rows and 15-minute staleness is fine
   -> Choose a materialized view, refreshed concurrently
If the data must be current to the second and the query is unavoidably heavy
   -> Precompute it on the write path into a summary table
If read volume is the problem and staleness of a few hundred milliseconds is fine
   -> Choose a read replica
If you are caching to hide an unindexed query
   -> Fix the index. The cache will fail you during a cold start, which is the worst moment

Trade-offs

Dimension Better index Cache Read replica
Consistency Perfect; it is the same data Stale up to the TTL, plus invalidation bugs Stale by replication lag, typically 5 to 50 ms
Latency 0.1 to 5 ms 0.2 to 1 ms Same as primary
Throughput Improves both reads and the whole system Enormous read amplification Linear with replica count for reads
Operational cost One migration Redis to run, invalidation to maintain, hit rate to watch Another database instance, lag to monitor
Team skill Requires reading EXPLAIN Requires cache-invalidation discipline Requires read-write routing discipline
Flexibility Helps every query that matches the access path Helps only the cached shape Helps all reads
Money cost Free; small storage and write overhead Memory is expensive per GB A full extra instance
Ecosystem Native Mature Native
Failure modes Wrong column order does nothing; too many indexes slow writes Stampede, stale data, cold start, hot key, Redis down Lag spikes, read-your-write bugs, failover confusion

Signals you chose wrong

  • Your cache hit rate is 60 percent and the misses are still slow, which means you cached instead of fixing the query.
  • A Redis restart causes a full outage because the database cannot survive the cold-start load. That is proof the cache is hiding a capacity problem.
  • You added a cache and the p99 barely moved, because the slow path was the 3 percent of requests that miss.
  • You added an index and write latency doubled, which means you added the wrong one or too many.
  • You have a cache invalidation bug list, and it keeps growing.

How to change your mind later

Caches are the most reversible thing in this part: remove the lookup, keep the query. Always write cache code so that a miss is correct and a Redis failure degrades to the database with a short timeout.

Removing an index is one statement (DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY), but verify with pg_stat_user_indexes first, over a full business cycle including month-end.

Adding a read replica is easy; removing the routing logic afterwards is the part people forget to clean up.

Senior perspective

The order of operations matters more than the choice: measure, index, query shape, then cache. I have reviewed dozens of "we need Redis" proposals, and roughly half were a missing composite index. Caching an unindexed query is genuinely dangerous, because you have moved the load off the database and removed the signal that would have told you the query was bad — until a deploy or a Redis restart empties the cache and the database meets full traffic for the first time. That is the incident. Fix the query first, then cache what is still expensive, and always be able to say what happens to your database when the cache is empty.

49.12 Offset versus keyset pagination

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["Does the UI need arbitrary page numbers"] -->|"no"| K["Keyset pagination"]
  A -->|"yes"| B{"Is the result set small and bounded"}
  B -->|"yes, under a few thousand rows"| O["Offset is fine"]
  B -->|"no"| C{"Can the UI change to infinite scroll or next and previous"}
  C -->|"yes"| K
  C -->|"no"| H["Offset with a hard page ceiling, plus a search filter to narrow results"]

If... then choose

If the client scrolls forward through a feed or list
   -> Choose keyset pagination with a cursor
If the table is large and the sort key is indexed
   -> Choose keyset pagination
If an admin screen shows a few hundred rows and needs page numbers
   -> Offset is fine; do not over-engineer it
If rows are inserted frequently while users page through them
   -> Choose keyset, because offset will duplicate and skip rows
If you are exporting a large dataset with a script
   -> Choose keyset, or a server-side cursor, never deep offset
If your API is public and you cannot control client behaviour
   -> Choose keyset and return an opaque cursor, so clients cannot construct deep offsets
// Opaque cursor: encode the sort key so clients cannot craft arbitrary offsets.
const encode = (o: { placedAt: string; id: string }) =>
  Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(o)).toString('base64url');

async page(userId: string, cursor?: string, limit = 25) {
  const after = cursor ? JSON.parse(Buffer.from(cursor, 'base64url').toString()) : null;
  const rows = await this.ds.query(
    `SELECT id, placed_at, total_minor FROM orders
      WHERE user_id = $1
        AND ($2::timestamptz IS NULL OR (placed_at, id) < ($2, $3))
      ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
      LIMIT $4`,
    [userId, after?.placedAt ?? null, after?.id ?? null, Math.min(limit, 100) + 1],
  );
  const hasMore = rows.length > limit;
  const page = rows.slice(0, limit);
  return { items: page, nextCursor: hasMore ? encode(page[page.length - 1]) : null };
}

Trade-offs

Dimension Offset Keyset (cursor)
Consistency Rows shift when data changes: duplicates and skips Stable; the cursor anchors to a row, not a position
Latency Degrades linearly: page 1 at 2 ms, page 10,000 at 1.8 s Constant: every page costs the same
Throughput Deep pages burn database CPU and I/O Index range scan, minimal work
Operational cost None None, but needs a suitable composite index
Team skill Trivial Slightly more thought; needs a tiebreaker column
Flexibility Jump to any page, show total pages Forward and backward only; no page numbers, and total counts are expensive
Money cost Wasted database capacity at depth Efficient
Ecosystem Every UI component supports it Common in modern APIs; some UI libraries need adapting
Failure modes Timeouts at depth, duplicate and missing rows, easy denial of service by requesting a huge offset Cursor invalid after the anchor row is deleted; needs a total order to be correct

Signals you chose wrong

  • Latency correlates with the page number in your dashboards.
  • Users report seeing the same item twice while scrolling an active list.
  • A crawler or export script regularly requests OFFSET 500000 and your database notices.
  • You chose keyset and the product genuinely needs "page 47 of 210", so you are now maintaining a fake page-number mapping.
  • Your keyset query returns inconsistent results because the sort key is not unique and you never added a tiebreaker.

How to change your mind later

Support both at the API level during a transition: accept either ?page= or ?cursor=, and return both nextCursor and, where cheap, a total count. Migrate clients one screen at a time and then remove the offset branch. This is a one-sprint change in most codebases.

Going from keyset back to offset is trivial but rarely a good idea. The usual compromise for an admin screen that wants page numbers is offset with a hard ceiling (OFFSET capped at a few thousand) plus better filters, so users narrow the result set instead of paging through it.

Senior perspective

Keyset pagination is one of the highest ratio of benefit to effort changes available in a backend: constant latency, correct results under concurrent writes, and immunity to a trivial denial-of-service vector, all for one composite index and a cursor encoder. The only real objection is page numbers, and that is usually a design habit rather than a user need — nobody navigates to page 47; they refine their filter. When the product genuinely needs counts and page numbers, offset over a bounded, filtered result set is a perfectly reasonable answer. The failure is deep offset over an unbounded table, which is a performance cliff that arrives silently, months after the code was written.

49.13 JWT versus sessions

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["Do you need to revoke access immediately"] -->|"yes"| B{"Can you tolerate a store lookup per request"}
  A -->|"no"| C{"Are there many services that must verify identity independently"}
  B -->|"yes"| S["Server-side sessions"]
  B -->|"no"| H["Short-lived JWT plus a revocation list"]
  C -->|"yes"| J["JWT, short expiry, refresh tokens in a store"]
  C -->|"no"| S

If... then choose

If you run one application and want the simplest correct thing
   -> Choose server-side sessions in Redis with an httpOnly cookie
If you must revoke a user's access within seconds, for example on a ban
   -> Choose sessions, or JWTs with a 5-minute expiry and a revocation check
If many independent services must verify identity without calling an auth service
   -> Choose JWT signed with an asymmetric key, verified locally against JWKS
If you are building a public API for third-party clients
   -> Choose OAuth 2 with short-lived JWT access tokens and opaque refresh tokens
If you have a mobile app that must stay logged in for weeks
   -> Choose short-lived access tokens plus a rotating refresh token stored server-side
If your reason for JWT is that it is stateless and therefore scalable
   -> Choose sessions; a Redis lookup is 0.3 ms and you are not at the scale where that matters

The practical answer for most systems is a hybrid: a short-lived JWT access token (5 to 15 minutes) that services verify locally, plus a long-lived refresh token that is stored server-side, single-use and rotated. You get local verification for the hot path and real revocation at the refresh boundary.

@Injectable()
export class TokenService {
  async issue(userId: string, sessionId: string) {
    const accessToken = await this.jwt.signAsync(
      { sub: userId, sid: sessionId, scope: 'user' },
      { expiresIn: '10m', algorithm: 'RS256' },          // services verify with the public key
    );
    const refreshToken = randomBytes(32).toString('base64url');
    await this.redis.set(`rt:${sha256(refreshToken)}`, JSON.stringify({ userId, sessionId }),
      'EX', 60 * 60 * 24 * 30);                           // opaque, revocable, rotated on use
    return { accessToken, refreshToken };
  }

  async revokeSession(sessionId: string) {
    await this.redis.set(`revoked:${sessionId}`, '1', 'EX', 900);  // covers the access-token window
  }
}

Trade-offs

Dimension Server-side sessions JWT
Consistency Always current; a change to permissions takes effect on the next request Stale until expiry; claims are a snapshot from issue time
Latency One store lookup, 0.3 to 1 ms Signature verification, roughly 0.1 ms with a cached key
Throughput Bounded by the session store, which is very high with Redis No store to bound it
Operational cost A session store to run, size and back up Key management, rotation and JWKS distribution
Team skill Simple and familiar Easy to implement insecurely: alg: none, missing audience checks, long expiry
Flexibility Change session content freely at any time Claims are fixed until the token is reissued
Money cost Memory for sessions, typically small Effectively zero
Ecosystem Built into every framework Universal across languages and platforms
Failure modes Session store outage logs everyone out; sticky-session mistakes Cannot revoke, token theft is high-impact, clock skew, key rotation breakage, oversized cookies

Signals you chose wrong

  • Support asks you to ban a user and the honest answer is "in 24 hours, when their token expires".
  • Your JWT has grown to 4 KB of permissions and now every request carries it, and some proxies reject the header size.
  • You built a JWT denylist checked on every request, which is a session store with extra cryptography.
  • You chose sessions and a Redis failover logged out every user during business hours, with no graceful degradation.
  • Your access tokens live for 30 days "for convenience", which means a stolen token is valid for a month.

How to change your mind later

Sessions to JWT: issue both for a transition period. The session cookie keeps working while clients start sending the bearer token, and services accept either. Once traffic on the cookie path is zero, remove it. Two to four weeks.

JWT to sessions: harder because clients hold tokens you cannot recall. Keep verifying existing JWTs until the longest expiry has passed, issue sessions for new logins, and shorten the JWT expiry immediately so the tail is short. Plan for one token lifetime plus a margin.

The design decision that makes both directions cheap is to hide the mechanism behind a guard and a Principal object, so application code never parses a token or reads a session directly.

Senior perspective

The stateless argument for JWT is usually applied to a problem nobody has. A Redis session lookup costs less than a millisecond and gives you instant revocation, server-side session data, and the ability to see who is logged in — properties that matter to security teams and to customer support. Where JWT genuinely earns its place is a multi-service architecture in which each service must verify identity without a network call, or a public API where third parties hold tokens. My default is sessions for a single application, and short-lived asymmetric JWTs plus server-side refresh tokens for anything distributed. And whichever you choose, the expiry is the security control: a 10-minute access token makes most theft scenarios survivable, and a 30-day one does not.

49.14 UUID versus bigint keys

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["Are ids exposed to clients or in URLs"] -->|"yes"| B{"Would sequential ids leak business information"}
  A -->|"no"| BI["bigint identity"]
  B -->|"yes"| U["UUIDv7, or bigint plus a separate public id"]
  B -->|"no"| BI
  U --> C{"Do clients or offline systems generate ids"}
  C -->|"yes"| U2["UUIDv7, generated client-side"]
  C -->|"no"| U3["UUIDv7 generated by the database"]

If... then choose

If ids are internal only and never appear in a URL or an API response
   -> Choose bigint generated always as identity
If ids appear in URLs and sequential values would leak volume or allow enumeration
   -> Choose UUIDv7, which is time-ordered and index-friendly
If clients, mobile apps or offline systems must create ids before syncing
   -> Choose UUID, generated on the client
If you merge data from multiple databases or shards
   -> Choose UUID, because bigint sequences will collide
If you have a very large, write-heavy table and index size matters
   -> Choose bigint, and expose a separate public identifier
If you are considering random UUIDv4 as a primary key on a hot table
   -> Choose UUIDv7 instead; random insert order is the problem, not the width

The important modern detail: UUIDv4 is random, so inserts land in random positions of the B-tree, which causes page splits, poor cache locality and index bloat. UUIDv7 embeds a timestamp prefix, so inserts are approximately sequential and behave much more like a bigint. If you need UUIDs, use v7.

-- bigint: 8 bytes, sequential, minimal index bloat
CREATE TABLE events (
  id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  ...
);

-- UUIDv7 as a primary key, with a bigint surrogate for internal joins if needed
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          UUID PRIMARY KEY,          -- generated in the application as v7
  public_ref  TEXT GENERATED ALWAYS AS ('ORD-' || substr(id::text, 1, 8)) STORED,
  ...
);

Trade-offs

Dimension bigint identity UUIDv7 UUIDv4
Consistency Unique per table per database Globally unique Globally unique
Latency Fastest lookups and joins Close to bigint; slightly larger comparisons Slower inserts due to random page access
Throughput Highest; sequential appends Near bigint Notably worse on large write-heavy tables
Operational cost Sequences need care when merging databases None Index bloat and more frequent vacuum
Team skill Trivial Requires choosing a v7 library Trivial, and trivially misused
Flexibility Cannot be generated offline or merged across shards Generated anywhere, merged freely Same
Money cost 8 bytes; smallest indexes 16 bytes; roughly 2x index size on the key 16 bytes plus bloat, often 30 to 40 percent larger indexes in practice
Ecosystem Universal Well supported; uuidv7 libraries are stable and PostgreSQL 18 has a built-in generator Universal
Failure modes Enumeration attacks, information leakage, collisions when merging Timestamp leaks creation time, which is usually fine Index fragmentation, slow bulk inserts, cache pressure

Numbers worth knowing: on a 100 million row table, a bigint primary key index is roughly 2.1 GB, a UUID one roughly 3.7 GB, and every foreign key referencing it doubles in size too. That difference decides whether your working set fits in RAM.

Signals you chose wrong

  • You chose bigint and your public URLs are /orders/48211, so a competitor can measure your order volume by placing two orders a day apart.
  • You have an IDOR vulnerability made trivially exploitable because ids are guessable.
  • You chose UUIDv4 and insert throughput on your largest table has degraded steadily as it grew, with high n_dead_tup and frequent index bloat.
  • You are merging two databases after an acquisition and your bigint sequences collide.
  • Your total index size has become the reason your instance no longer caches the working set.

How to change your mind later

This is one of the most expensive decisions to reverse, because every foreign key, every stored reference and every external integration carries the id.

The realistic path is additive: add the new column alongside the old one, populate it, add a unique index, then migrate foreign keys one table at a time using the expand-and-contract pattern from Part 31. Keep both columns for months. External systems that stored your ids may never migrate, so plan to accept both forms at your API boundary indefinitely.

A cheaper alternative that avoids the whole migration: keep bigint internally and add an external identifier column (a UUID or a short random string) used exclusively in URLs and APIs. You get non-enumerable public ids and small internal indexes. This is my usual recommendation when the concern is only exposure.

Senior perspective

The decision is less about UUID versus bigint and more about whether internal and external identifiers should be the same thing. They usually should not. Internal keys want to be small, sequential and cheap to join; external identifiers want to be unguessable and stable. Using one value for both means you optimise for neither. Where I do use UUID as the primary key is in distributed or offline-capable systems, where the ability to generate an id anywhere is genuinely valuable — and there I insist on v7, because v4 primary keys on a large write-heavy table are a performance problem that arrives quietly and is painful to fix later.

49.15 Read replica versus cache

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["What is saturated"] -->|"database CPU from many different queries"| RR["Read replica"]
  A -->|"database CPU from a few repeated queries"| CA["Cache"]
  RR --> B{"Can the reads tolerate 5 to 50 ms of lag"}
  B -->|"no"| PR["Keep on the primary, or precompute"]
  B -->|"yes"| RR2["Route analytics and list reads to the replica"]
  CA --> C{"Is the key space small and the hit rate high"}
  C -->|"no"| RR
  C -->|"yes"| CA2["Cache-aside with a TTL"]

If... then choose

If many different queries are collectively saturating the primary
   -> Choose a read replica; it scales the whole read workload, not one shape
If a handful of queries dominate and they repeat on the same keys
   -> Choose a cache; the hit rate will be high and the win is larger
If reporting and analytics compete with transactional traffic
   -> Choose a read replica, and put reports on it with a long statement timeout
If you need sub-millisecond reads
   -> Choose a cache; a replica is still a database round trip
If the data changes constantly and every read must be fresh
   -> Choose a replica, because lag is milliseconds while a cache TTL is seconds
If you need both, which is common
   -> Cache the hot shapes, put the long tail on a replica, keep writes and read-your-write on the primary

Trade-offs

Dimension Read replica Cache (Redis)
Consistency Lags by replication delay, usually 5 to 50 ms, seconds under load Stale for the TTL; invalidation bugs make it worse
Latency Same as the primary, 1 to 5 ms 0.2 to 1 ms
Throughput Linear with replica count for reads Enormous for cached shapes; nothing for the rest
Operational cost Another instance to monitor, patch and fail over; lag alerting Redis to run, plus invalidation logic in every write path
Team skill Read-write routing discipline Cache-invalidation discipline, which is harder
Flexibility Serves any query, including ones you have not written yet Serves only what you explicitly cache
Money cost A full extra database instance, often the largest single line item Memory is expensive per GB but you need far less of it
Ecosystem Native to PostgreSQL and every managed service Mature
Failure modes Lag spikes during bulk writes, read-your-write bugs, stale authorization decisions, failover confusion Stampede on expiry, cold start after restart, hot keys, evictions dropping needed data

Signals you chose wrong

  • You added a replica and the primary's CPU did not drop, which means your load is writes, not reads. No number of replicas will help.
  • You added a cache and the hit rate is 40 percent, which means the key space is too large or the TTL too short.
  • Users see stale data on screens where they just made a change, because a global "reads go to the replica" rule was applied without exception.
  • Replication lag spikes to 30 seconds during your nightly batch, and your morning traffic reads yesterday's data.
  • Redis eviction rate is non-zero, which means you are silently losing entries you assumed were cached.

How to change your mind later

Both are additive and removable. Removing a replica means changing routing and terminating the instance. Removing a cache means deleting the lookup. The critical discipline in both cases is that the code must remain correct without them: a cache miss reads the database, and a replica outage falls back to the primary.

Write routing as an explicit per-query choice rather than a global default. Then moving a query between primary, replica and cache is a one-line change with an obvious blast radius.

Senior perspective

The diagnostic question is what kind of load you have. A replica scales breadth — many different queries — while a cache scales depth on a few hot shapes. Teams often add a replica when three queries account for 80 percent of the load, which is the case where a cache would have been far cheaper and far more effective. The reverse mistake is caching a long tail of rarely-repeated queries and achieving a 30 percent hit rate for a lot of invalidation complexity. Look at pg_stat_statements before deciding: if the top five queries dominate total execution time, cache; if the load is spread across fifty queries, replicate. And in both cases, route read-your-write traffic to the primary explicitly, because that single rule prevents most of the confusing bugs either option introduces.

49.16 Partitioning versus sharding

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["Is one table too large to manage"] -->|"yes"| B{"Does one server still have enough CPU, memory and I O"}
  A -->|"no"| N["Neither. Index and archive first"]
  B -->|"yes"| P["Partitioning within one PostgreSQL instance"]
  B -->|"no"| C{"Can you split by a natural key such as tenant or region"}
  C -->|"yes"| S["Sharding across instances"]
  C -->|"no"| D["Reduce data first: archive, summarise, or move cold data out"]

If... then choose

If one table has hundreds of millions of rows and queries filter by time
   -> Choose range partitioning by time, and drop old partitions instead of deleting rows
If you must delete old data regularly and DELETE is causing bloat and vacuum pressure
   -> Choose partitioning, because DROP PARTITION is instant and generates no bloat
If maintenance operations such as VACUUM and REINDEX no longer fit in a window
   -> Choose partitioning
If a single server can no longer handle the write throughput or the working set
   -> Choose sharding, and only then
If you are a multi-tenant SaaS and tenants are naturally isolated
   -> Choose sharding by tenant, which is by far the easiest sharding to operate
If your problem is a slow query on a 20 million row table
   -> Choose neither. Add the right index

Partitioning splits one table into pieces inside one database; sharding splits your data across separate databases. Partitioning is a maintenance and query-pruning tool. Sharding is a capacity tool and a significant architectural commitment.

-- Range partitioning by month: pruning plus instant retention management
CREATE TABLE events (
  id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
  occurred_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  payload JSONB NOT NULL
) PARTITION BY RANGE (occurred_at);

CREATE TABLE events_2026_09 PARTITION OF events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-09-01') TO ('2026-10-01');

-- retention: instant, no bloat, no vacuum storm
DROP TABLE events_2026_03;

Trade-offs

Dimension Partitioning Sharding
Consistency Full ACID; it is still one database Cross-shard transactions are not available in practice
Latency Faster with partition pruning; slower if a query cannot prune Fast within a shard; cross-shard queries are scatter-gather and slow
Throughput Bounded by one server Scales linearly with shards
Operational cost Moderate: partition creation automation, constraint management High: routing, rebalancing, per-shard migrations, per-shard backups
Team skill Learnable in a week Requires real expertise; every operation becomes N operations
Flexibility Any query still works Queries must include the shard key or fan out
Money cost Same server N servers, plus operational headcount
Ecosystem Native PostgreSQL, pg_partman for automation Citus, Vitess, or application-level routing you maintain
Failure modes Queries that cannot prune scan every partition; too many partitions slow planning; unique constraints must include the key Hot shards, rebalancing downtime, cross-shard joins, a failed shard taking down a subset of customers

Signals you chose wrong

  • You partitioned and query plans got slower, because queries do not filter on the partition key so every partition is scanned.
  • You have 3,000 partitions and planning time now dominates execution time.
  • You sharded and one shard holds 60 percent of the data because the shard key is skewed.
  • Your application does scatter-gather queries across all shards for common screens, which means the shard key is wrong.
  • You sharded when the real problem was a missing index or an unarchived history table.

How to change your mind later

Partitioning an existing table is done online with expand and contract: create the partitioned table, copy data in batches, dual-write during the transition, then swap names in a short transaction. For a 500 GB table, plan several days of background copying and one brief cutover.

Sharding is the hardest reversal in this part. Going from one database to shards is a months-long project touching every query. Going back is equally hard. The mitigations are to route everything through a data-access layer that takes an explicit shard key, and to delay sharding as long as possible by exhausting the cheaper options first: better indexes, archiving cold data, read replicas, partitioning, and vertical scaling. A single modern PostgreSQL instance with 64 vCPUs and fast NVMe storage handles far more than most teams assume.

Senior perspective

Partitioning is a routine tool and you should reach for it as soon as retention management becomes painful — DROP TABLE on last quarter's partition instead of a DELETE that generates 200 GB of bloat is reason enough. Sharding is a different category: it is a commitment that changes how every future feature is written, because every query must carry the shard key. I treat it as the last option, after archiving, partitioning, replicas and a bigger instance. When it is genuinely required, sharding by tenant is the version worth having, because the shard key is obvious, the data is naturally isolated, and you gain per-tenant blast-radius isolation as a bonus.

49.17 Serverless versus containers

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["What is the traffic shape"] -->|"spiky, bursty or near zero much of the day"| SL["Serverless"]
  A -->|"steady and continuous"| CT["Containers"]
  SL --> B{"Does the work hold database connections or long-lived state"}
  B -->|"yes"| C{"Can you use a connection proxy such as RDS Proxy or PgBouncer"}
  C -->|"no"| CT
  C -->|"yes"| SL2["Serverless with a pooled connection layer"]
  B -->|"no"| SL2
  SL2 --> D{"Is a cold start of 100 ms to 2 s acceptable"}
  D -->|"no"| CT

If... then choose

If traffic is spiky or near zero for most of the day
   -> Choose serverless; you pay only for what runs
If the workload is event-driven glue, such as reacting to an S3 upload
   -> Choose serverless
If traffic is steady and continuous above roughly one request per second sustained
   -> Choose containers; the economics flip
If you need long-lived connections, WebSockets or in-process caches
   -> Choose containers
If the work regularly runs longer than the platform's execution limit
   -> Choose containers
If cold-start latency on a user-facing path is unacceptable
   -> Choose containers, or keep a provisioned concurrency floor
If you need one runtime for both HTTP and background workers with shared code
   -> Choose containers; a NestJS image can run as an API or a worker with a flag

Trade-offs

Dimension Serverless (Lambda) Containers (ECS, Kubernetes)
Consistency Same code, but each invocation is isolated; no shared in-process state Shared process state, in-memory caches, warm pools
Latency Cold starts of 100 ms to 2 s; warm invocations are fast Consistently warm; no cold-start class of problem
Throughput Scales to thousands of concurrent executions in seconds Scales in tens of seconds; needs headroom planning
Operational cost Very low; no servers, patching or capacity planning Moderate; images, rollouts, autoscaling, probes
Team skill Low to start; hard to debug distributed event flows Standard backend and platform skills
Flexibility Constrained: execution time limits, payload limits, no persistent connections Anything you can run in Linux
Money cost Cheap when idle, expensive under sustained load; the crossover is usually a few hundred thousand invocations per day Fixed cost regardless of traffic; better value at steady load
Ecosystem Deep cloud integration with triggers and events Portable, huge ecosystem
Failure modes Cold starts, concurrency limits, connection exhaustion against PostgreSQL, timeout ceilings, retry semantics that surprise people OOMKilled, CrashLoopBackOff, slow scaling under a spike

The database connection issue deserves emphasis because it is the most common serverless production failure.
