Each concurrent Lambda holds its own PostgreSQL connection; 500 concurrent invocations means 500 connections against a max_connections of 200, and the database rejects them all. The fix is a proxy (RDS Proxy or PgBouncer in transaction mode), and it must be in the design from the start.

Signals you chose wrong

  • Your Lambda bill exceeds what two containers would cost, which means sustained load.
  • You added provisioned concurrency to remove cold starts, which is paying for always-on compute inside a pay-per-use model.
  • PostgreSQL is at its connection limit and the connections come from function invocations.
  • Your function times out at 15 minutes and you are splitting work into artificial chunks to fit.
  • You chose containers and pay for 20 idle pods overnight for a workload that runs twice an hour.

How to change your mind later

Keep business logic in plain classes and treat the handler as a thin adapter. Then a function becomes a container by adding an HTTP entry point, and a container becomes a function by adding a handler file.

// Shared, platform-free application service
export class ResizeImageService { async execute(input: ResizeInput): Promise<ResizeResult> { /* ... */ } }

// Lambda adapter
export const handler = async (event: S3Event) =>
  service.execute({ bucket: event.Records[0].s3.bucket.name, key: event.Records[0].s3.object.key });

// Container adapter: a NestJS worker consuming the same events from a queue
@Processor('resize')
export class ResizeProcessor { @Process() run(job: Job<ResizeInput>) { return service.execute(job.data); } }

With that structure, migrating in either direction is a week of adapter and pipeline work rather than a rewrite.

Senior perspective

Serverless is a billing model and a scaling model before it is anything else, and the decision usually comes down to duty cycle. Below roughly 20 percent utilisation, paying per invocation is cheaper and simpler; above that, a container running continuously wins on both cost and latency. I use serverless enthusiastically for event glue — image processing, webhook receivers, scheduled jobs, S3 triggers — and containers for the core API, because APIs hold connections, benefit from warm caches, and cannot afford cold starts on a checkout path. The mistake I have watched most often is building an entire product on functions and then discovering that the connection pool, the cold starts and the local development story each cost more than the servers ever would have.

49.18 Managed service versus self-hosted

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["Is this component core to your product differentiation"] -->|"yes"| B{"Do you have the expertise and headcount to run it well"}
  A -->|"no"| M["Managed"]
  B -->|"no"| M
  B -->|"yes"| C{"Is the managed cost more than roughly one engineer per year"}
  C -->|"no"| M
  C -->|"yes"| D{"Do you need control the managed version does not offer"}
  D -->|"yes"| SH["Self-hosted"]
  D -->|"no"| M

If... then choose

If it is a database, a broker, a cache or a search cluster and you have no dedicated team
   -> Choose managed
If the managed version costs less than the fully loaded cost of the engineer who would run it
   -> Choose managed
If you need an extension, a version or a configuration the managed service forbids
   -> Choose self-hosted, and budget the operational time honestly
If compliance or data residency rules forbid the managed option
   -> Choose self-hosted
If the component is your competitive advantage and you must tune it deeply
   -> Choose self-hosted
If you are self-hosting to save money and have not costed on-call, upgrades and backups
   -> Choose managed; the saving is usually imaginary

Trade-offs

Dimension Managed Self-hosted
Consistency Provider guarantees, documented and contractual Whatever you configure and verify yourself
Latency Sometimes a small penalty from proxies and multi-tenancy Can be tuned; co-location with your application is possible
Throughput Bounded by instance classes and provider quotas Bounded only by hardware and your skill
Operational cost Patching, backups, failover and monitoring are included You own upgrades, backups, restore testing, failover drills and 03:00 pages
Team skill Basic operational literacy Deep expertise in that specific system, sustained over years
Flexibility Constrained: fixed versions, allowlisted extensions, limited parameters Total
Money cost Typically 20 to 100 percent more than raw compute Cheaper on paper; the real cost is engineer time and incidents
Ecosystem Integrated with the cloud's identity, networking and observability Portable; no lock-in
Failure modes Provider outages you cannot fix, quota surprises, forced upgrade windows, limited debugging access Everything is your failure mode: disk full, failed failover, an untested backup

The comparison people skip: a fully loaded senior engineer costs roughly 150,000 to 250,000 per year. If self-hosting a database consumes 20 percent of one engineer's time in steady state — a conservative estimate once you include upgrades, capacity work and incidents — that is 30,000 to 50,000 per year of hidden cost, before the first outage.

Signals you chose wrong

  • You self-host and your last successful restore test was never, or more than a year ago.
  • A major version upgrade has been deferred for two years because nobody wants to own it.
  • Your on-call rotation is dominated by pages from infrastructure you chose to run yourself.
  • You chose managed and are paying for capacity you cannot tune, with a bill growing faster than traffic.
  • The managed service blocks an extension you now need, and there is no workaround.

How to change your mind later

Self-hosted to managed is usually straightforward for stateful systems that support standard replication: set up logical replication into the managed instance, let it catch up, then cut over during a short maintenance window. For PostgreSQL this is a well-trodden path with tools like AWS DMS or plain logical replication. Expect a few weeks including rehearsal.

Managed to self-hosted is more work because you must build the operational apparatus first: backups, restore testing, monitoring, alerting, upgrade procedure and a runbook. Build all of that before migrating, not after. Two to three months is realistic.

Avoid provider-specific features that have no open equivalent unless you have decided the lock-in is acceptable. Being on standard PostgreSQL, standard Redis and standard Kafka protocols is what keeps this decision reversible.

Senior perspective

The question is not "can we run this" — a competent team can run almost anything for a month. It is "will we still run this well in year three, after the person who set it up has left". Operational excellence is a sustained commitment, and most teams systematically underestimate it because the costs arrive as interruptions rather than invoices. I default to managed for anything stateful and only self-host when there is a specific, written reason: a required extension, a compliance boundary, or a scale at which the managed premium genuinely exceeds a salary. And I apply one test to any self-hosting proposal: show me the restore. If the team cannot restore a backup to a fresh instance and prove the data is intact, they are not running that system, they are hosting it and hoping.

49.19 Build versus buy

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["Is this a source of competitive advantage"] -->|"no"| B{"Does a mature vendor cover 80 percent of the need"}
  A -->|"yes"| C{"Can you actually staff it for years"}
  B -->|"yes"| BUY["Buy"]
  B -->|"no"| D{"Is the remaining 20 percent worth building the whole thing"}
  C -->|"no"| BUY
  C -->|"yes"| BUILD["Build"]
  D -->|"no"| BUY2["Buy, and build the gap on top"]
  D -->|"yes"| BUILD

If... then choose

If it is payments, and you would otherwise handle card numbers
   -> Buy. Stripe, Adyen or Braintree. PCI scope alone justifies it
If it is authentication for a standard product with social login and MFA
   -> Buy, or use a library. Auth0, Cognito, Clerk, or Passport with your own store
If it is authorization with complex, product-specific rules
   -> Build. Permission models are domain logic and vendors fit them badly
If it is search and you need keyword plus facets at ordinary scale
   -> Buy a managed cluster, or use PostgreSQL. Do not build a search engine
If it is transactional email and SMS
   -> Buy. Deliverability is a specialist business you cannot replicate
If it is notification orchestration, such as preferences, batching and channels
   -> Build the orchestration, buy the delivery
If the vendor's pricing at your projected scale exceeds two engineers per year
   -> Model it carefully; buying can still win, but the maths deserves attention
If your differentiation depends on it and the vendor constrains you
   -> Build, and accept the ongoing cost with open eyes

The nuance is that build versus buy is rarely all or nothing. The pattern that works is to buy the commodity layer and build the thin domain layer on top: buy card processing, build your order and refund lifecycle; buy identity, build your permission model; buy email delivery, build your preference and batching logic.

// Buy the delivery, build the orchestration you actually care about.
@Injectable()
export class NotificationService {
  constructor(
    private readonly prefs: PreferenceRepository,   // yours: quiet hours, channels, opt-outs
    private readonly email: EmailProvider,          // theirs: SendGrid or SES
    private readonly sms: SmsProvider,              // theirs: Twilio
  ) {}

  async notify(userId: string, event: NotifiableEvent): Promise<void> {
    const p = await this.prefs.get(userId);
    if (!p.allows(event.type)) return;                       // your rules
    if (p.isQuietHours(new Date())) return this.queue.schedule(userId, event, p.nextWindow());
    for (const channel of p.channelsFor(event.type)) {
      await this.dispatch(channel, userId, event);           // provider is an implementation detail
    }
  }
}

Trade-offs

Dimension Build Buy
Consistency Exactly your semantics Vendor semantics you must adapt to
Latency Local, no third-party hop An external call, typically 50 to 300 ms, plus their availability
Throughput Bounded by your capacity Bounded by their rate limits and plan
Operational cost Yours forever, including 03:00 pages Theirs, mostly; you still own the integration
Team skill Requires domain expertise you may not have, such as deliverability or fraud Requires integration skill only
Flexibility Total Constrained by their roadmap and API
Money cost Salary, ongoing; large and invisible on the infrastructure bill A visible invoice, often growing with usage
Ecosystem You own the tooling Documentation, SDKs, dashboards and support included
Failure modes Bugs in a domain you do not specialise in; the author leaves Vendor outage, price increase, deprecation, acquisition, rate limits

Signals you chose wrong

  • You built it and the maintainer has left; nobody understands the fraud rules or the retry logic any more.
  • You built authentication and are now reading OAuth specifications to fix an edge case, which is not your product.
  • You bought it and spend more time working around the vendor's model than you would have spent building.
  • Vendor cost is growing faster than revenue, which usually means per-unit pricing on a unit you generate a lot of.
  • You bought a platform and have built a large adapter layer to make it behave — you are paying twice.

How to change your mind later

Always integrate a vendor behind your own interface. This single practice is what makes the decision reversible.

export interface PaymentGateway {
  authorize(cmd: AuthorizeCommand): Promise<Authorization>;
  capture(authId: string, amountMinor: number): Promise<Capture>;
  refund(captureId: string, amountMinor: number, reason: string): Promise<Refund>;
}

Build to buy is easy: implement the interface with the vendor's SDK, run both in parallel with a percentage split, then remove your implementation.

Buy to build, or vendor to vendor, is harder mainly because of data: tokenised cards, user credentials and historical records live on their side. Ask about export and migration before you sign, and check whether card tokens are portable (most major providers support a supervised token migration; it takes weeks and paperwork). For authentication, plan a password-rehash-on-next-login migration, because you cannot export password hashes from most identity vendors.

Senior perspective

The test I use is whether a customer would ever choose you because of this component. Nobody picks a food delivery app because of its email sending or its card processing; they might pick it for its routing algorithm or its inventory accuracy. Build the second kind and buy the first. The trap on the build side is that these systems look simple at the demo stage — sending an email is one API call, checking a password is one comparison — and the real cost is in the long tail: deliverability reputation, bounce handling, PCI scope, MFA recovery flows, fraud rules, regulatory change. That tail is where a vendor's entire company is focused and where your team has an afternoon. The trap on the buy side is skipping the interface, which turns a reversible decision into a permanent one.

49.20 Feature flag versus branch

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["How long until this ships to everyone"] -->|"under 2 days"| BR["Short-lived branch"]
  A -->|"longer"| B{"Does it change user-visible behaviour"}
  B -->|"yes"| FF["Feature flag, merged to main behind the flag"]
  B -->|"no"| C{"Does it touch shared code many people edit"}
  C -->|"yes"| FF
  C -->|"no"| BR
  FF --> D{"Do you need gradual rollout or per-tenant control"}
  D -->|"yes"| FFS["Flag service with targeting"]
  D -->|"no"| FFC["Config-based flag is enough"]

If... then choose

If the change is small and merges within a day or two
   -> Choose a short-lived branch and a normal pull request
If the work spans weeks and touches files other people are editing
   -> Choose trunk-based development with a feature flag
If you need to release to 5 percent of users and watch the metrics
   -> Choose a flag with percentage targeting
If you need to enable a feature for one enterprise customer first
   -> Choose a flag with per-tenant targeting
If you need an instant kill switch for a risky code path
   -> Choose a flag, and treat the kill switch as part of the feature's definition of done
If the change is a pure refactor with no behaviour change
   -> Choose a branch; a flag adds branching complexity for no benefit
If the change is a database migration
   -> Choose neither: use expand and contract; flags cannot roll back a dropped column
@Injectable()
export class CheckoutController {
  constructor(private readonly flags: FeatureFlagService) {}

  @Post()
  async checkout(@Body() dto: CheckoutDto, @Principal() p: Principal) {
    // Evaluate once, log the decision, so traces and metrics can be split by variant.
    const useNewPricing = await this.flags.isEnabled('pricing-engine-v2', {
      userId: p.userId, tenantId: p.tenantId,
    });
    return useNewPricing
      ? this.newPricing.checkout(dto, p)
      : this.legacyPricing.checkout(dto, p);
  }
}

Trade-offs

Dimension Long-lived branch Feature flag
Consistency The branch drifts from main; the merge is a big-bang event One codebase; everyone sees the same code
Latency No runtime cost A flag evaluation per request, sub-millisecond if cached locally
Throughput No effect Negligible with a local cache; a remote call per request would be a mistake
Operational cost Painful merges, conflicts and rebases Flags must be cleaned up, or they accumulate
Team skill Familiar to everyone Requires discipline about flag lifecycle and testing both paths
Flexibility All or nothing at merge time Gradual rollout, targeting, instant rollback without a deploy
Money cost Engineer time lost to merge conflicts A flag service subscription, or a simple self-built one
Ecosystem Git LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith, or a config table
Failure modes Merge hell, a three-week integration, conflicts nobody can resolve Flag debt, untested combinations, a flag left on for a subset of users forever

Signals you chose wrong

  • Your branch is three weeks old and rebasing takes half a day.
  • The merge required a two-day "integration period" that nobody scheduled.
  • You have 60 flags and nobody knows which are safe to remove.
  • A flag defaulted to off in a new environment and a feature silently disappeared in production.
  • Your tests cover only one side of each flag, so the other path is effectively untested code shipping to users.

How to change your mind later

Branch to flag: merge what you have behind a flag that is off, then continue on main. This is almost always an improvement and can be done mid-project.

Flag to branch is rarely wanted. What you actually want is flag removal: once a feature is at 100 percent and stable for a couple of weeks, delete the flag and the dead path in a dedicated pull request. Put an expiry date on every flag at creation and fail CI when a flag passes it. That single rule is what prevents flag debt from becoming the next generation of environment-specific branches from Part 48.

Senior perspective

Trunk-based development with flags is the practice most strongly associated with high-performing teams, and the reason is simple: integration pain grows superlinearly with branch age, so merging daily makes it disappear. The cost is flag hygiene, and teams that fail here end up with a codebase full of conditionals nobody can reason about. I insist on three rules: every flag has an owner and an expiry date, both branches of a flag are tested, and the flag's default when the service is unreachable is written down and matches the safe behaviour. And I keep flags out of database migrations entirely — a flag can hide a code path, but nothing can hide a dropped column, which is why expand and contract exists.

49.21 Multi-AZ versus multi-region

Decision tree

flowchart TB
  A["What are you protecting against"] -->|"instance or datacentre failure"| AZ["Multi-AZ"]
  A -->|"whole region failure"| B{"Can you tolerate hours of downtime in that rare case"}
  A -->|"user latency across continents"| C{"Are reads mostly local"}
  B -->|"yes"| AZ2["Multi-AZ plus cross-region backups"]
  B -->|"no"| MR["Multi-region"]
  C -->|"yes"| RD["Multi-AZ primary plus read replicas in other regions"]
  C -->|"no"| MR

If... then choose

If you need protection from a single machine, rack or availability zone failing
   -> Choose multi-AZ. This is the default for anything in production
If your SLA allows a few hours of downtime in a genuine regional outage
   -> Choose multi-AZ plus cross-region backups and a tested restore
If regulation requires data to stay in a jurisdiction
   -> Choose per-region deployments with data partitioned by region
If users on another continent suffer 200 ms of latency on reads
   -> Choose read replicas or a CDN in that region, not full multi-region writes
If the business genuinely cannot tolerate a regional outage, such as payments infrastructure
   -> Choose active-passive multi-region with a tested failover
If you think you need active-active multi-region writes
   -> Verify the requirement first; this is the most expensive architecture in this part

Be precise about the failure you are buying insurance against. Multi-AZ protects against the common case: a host failure, a rack failure, a zone-level network or power event. Those happen. Full regional outages are rare, typically a few hours long, and affect large parts of the internet simultaneously — which changes the business conversation, because your competitors are usually down too.

Trade-offs

Dimension Multi-AZ Multi-region active-passive Multi-region active-active
Consistency Synchronous replication; no data loss on failover Asynchronous; expect seconds of data loss on failover Conflict resolution required; strong consistency is expensive or impossible
Latency Sub-millisecond between zones Normal in the active region Cross-region writes cost 80 to 150 ms
Throughput Unaffected Unaffected Coordination overhead reduces it
Operational cost Minimal; a checkbox on managed services Real: failover runbook, drills, DNS strategy Very high: conflict handling, data partitioning, split-brain design
Team skill Standard Requires disaster-recovery discipline Requires senior distributed-systems expertise
Flexibility Fine for almost everything Adds regional deployment complexity Constrains every data model decision
Money cost Roughly 2x database cost, small application cost Roughly 2x total infrastructure, mostly idle 2 to 3x plus significant engineering time
Ecosystem Native everywhere Supported but manual Few managed options; usually bespoke
Failure modes Zone failure handled automatically; failover takes 30 to 120 seconds Stale replica, DNS caching delays failover, untested runbook fails Split brain, conflicting writes, partial regional failure is worse than total

Signals you chose wrong

  • You have a multi-region setup and have never tested a failover, which means you have paid for it and do not have it.
  • You built active-active and spend engineering time on write conflicts for a product where a five-minute outage would be tolerable.
  • You are single-AZ in production and one zone event took you offline for three hours.
  • Your recovery point objective is "we do not know", because backups are cross-region but the restore has never been timed.
  • You went multi-region for latency when a CDN and regional read replicas would have delivered most of the benefit.

How to change your mind later

Single-AZ to multi-AZ is usually a configuration change on managed services, with one failover-length interruption. Do it now if you have not.

Multi-AZ to multi-region active-passive is a project: cross-region replicas, an infrastructure-as-code deployment for the second region, a DNS or global-load-balancer failover strategy, and a written, rehearsed runbook. Two to four months, and the rehearsal is the part that makes it real.

Active-passive to active-active is a re-architecture, not a deployment change: you must decide, per entity, how conflicts are resolved or how data is partitioned so conflicts cannot occur. The realistic version for most products is regional data partitioning — European customers live in Europe, American customers live in America, and each region is authoritative for its own users. That gives you locality and regulatory compliance without global write coordination.

Senior perspective

Start by asking what the business actually loses per hour of downtime, and compare it to the cost of the architecture. For most products, multi-AZ plus cross-region backups plus a restore that someone has actually performed and timed is the right answer, and the money saved is better spent on the reliability problems that cause real outages: bad deploys, missing indexes, retry storms and unbounded queues. Regional failure is not what takes most companies down; their own changes are. I have also never seen an untested failover work on the first attempt during a real incident, so if you do build multi-region, budget for quarterly drills. An untested disaster-recovery plan is a slide, not a capability.

49.22 A general decision-making template

Every decision in this part follows the same shape, and you can apply it to decisions this book does not cover. Write it down — the writing is what forces the thinking, and the artefact is what stops the same argument recurring in six months with new people.

The template has six parts:

  1. Context. What is happening, what forced the decision now, and what constraints are non-negotiable. Include numbers: current traffic, current latency, team size, budget. A decision record with no numbers is an opinion.
  2. Options. At least three, including "do nothing" or "keep the current approach". If you cannot state a genuine third option, you have not explored the space.
  3. Criteria and weights. Pick four to seven criteria that matter for this decision and weight them so they sum to 100. Weighting is where the real disagreement lives, and surfacing it early is the whole point.
  4. Decision. What you chose and, crucially, what you are giving up. Name the criterion you deliberately sacrificed.
  5. Consequences. What becomes easier, what becomes harder, what new work this creates, and what would tell you the decision was wrong.
  6. Revisit date. A specific date and a specific trigger. Not "when we scale" but "on 2027-03-01, or when write throughput exceeds 5,000 per second, whichever comes first".

Keep it to one page. Store it in the repository as docs/adr/NNNN-title.md so it is versioned with the code it describes. Never edit a decided record; supersede it with a new one that links back, so the history of reasoning survives.

A worked ADR

# ADR 0014: Job queue for order fulfilment

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-09-09
- Deciders: Backend team, SRE, Head of Engineering
- Supersedes: none

## Context

Order fulfilment currently runs inline in the checkout request. Checkout p99 is
2.8 s, of which 1.9 s is the warehouse API call and the label-printing call. On
2026-08-14 the warehouse API was degraded for 40 minutes and checkout availability
fell to 91 percent, costing an estimated 38,000 EUR in abandoned orders.

Current scale: 240 orders per minute at peak, 12 fulfilment steps per order,
roughly 172,000 messages per day. Team: 9 backend engineers, 1 SRE, no dedicated
platform team. We already run PostgreSQL 16 (RDS) and Redis 7 (ElastiCache). We
do not run Kafka today.

Constraint: no order may be lost. Duplicate processing is acceptable because
fulfilment steps are idempotent via the warehouse reference id.

## Options considered

1. PostgreSQL job table with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
2. BullMQ on the existing Redis
3. Amazon SQS (standard queues) with SNS for fan-out
4. Kafka (MSK) with one topic per fulfilment stage
5. Do nothing: keep fulfilment inline and add timeouts plus a circuit breaker

## Criteria and weights

| Criterion | Weight | Why it matters here |
|---|---|---|
| Durability of queued work | 30 | Losing an order is the worst outcome we can have |
| Operational burden | 25 | One SRE; we cannot absorb a new stateful cluster |
| Delivery time | 20 | The incident is recent; leadership wants this within one quarter |
| Retry and delay features | 15 | Warehouse outages need backoff over hours, plus a DLQ |
| Cost at 3x current volume | 10 | Must stay under 500 EUR per month |

## Scoring

| Option | Durability (30) | Ops (25) | Delivery (20) | Features (15) | Cost (10) | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL SKIP LOCKED | 30 | 20 | 20 | 6 | 10 | 86 |
| BullMQ on Redis | 15 | 20 | 18 | 15 | 9 | 77 |
| SQS | 30 | 25 | 16 | 11 | 8 | 90 |
| Kafka on MSK | 30 | 5 | 8 | 9 | 3 | 55 |
| Do nothing | 0 | 25 | 20 | 0 | 10 | 55 |

## Decision

We will use **Amazon SQS** standard queues, one queue per fulfilment stage, with a
dead-letter queue after 5 attempts and an outbox table in PostgreSQL so that
enqueueing is transactional with the order write.

We explicitly give up **ordering** and **replay**. Fulfilment steps are commutative
and idempotent, so ordering is not required, and we have no consumer that needs to
re-read history. If either becomes a requirement, this decision is superseded.

We rejected Kafka because we cannot operate it with the staffing we have, and none
of the properties that make Kafka worth its cost - replay, many independent consumer
groups, very high throughput - apply to 172,000 messages per day.

We rejected BullMQ because Redis replication is asynchronous and a failover can lose
acknowledged jobs, which conflicts with the "no order may be lost" constraint.

## Consequences

Easier:
- Checkout returns as soon as the order is persisted; expected p99 drops to about 400 ms.
- A warehouse outage delays fulfilment instead of failing checkout.
- Fulfilment workers scale independently on queue depth.

Harder:
- Customers no longer see immediate fulfilment status; the UI needs a pending state.
- We now own a DLQ, its alerting and a replay tool.
- Every consumer must be idempotent; we will add an inbox table keyed by message id.
- Local development needs ElasticMQ or LocalStack to emulate SQS.

New work created:
- Outbox table and relay (2 weeks)
- Consumer framework with inbox dedupe and DLQ routing (2 weeks)
- Pending-state UI (1 week, frontend team)
- Runbook and DLQ alerting (3 days)

We were wrong if:
- Queue depth alerts fire more than twice a month in steady state.
- We need message ordering within 6 months.
- SQS cost exceeds 500 EUR per month before traffic triples.
- Checkout p99 does not fall below 600 ms after rollout.

## Revisit

2027-03-09, or earlier if sustained volume exceeds 2 million messages per day, or if
a second consumer group needs to read the same stream independently.

Notice what makes this record useful a year later. The numbers are specific enough to check. The rejected options say why they were rejected in terms of this context, not in general. The sacrifice is named explicitly. And the "we were wrong if" section is falsifiable, so the revisit is a real review rather than a re-argument from scratch.

Senior Checklist — Part 49

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I state the constraint I am optimising for before I argue about technology
  • I can name the boring default for every decision, and what would justify deviating
  • I write down falsifiable "signals you chose wrong" criteria before deciding
  • I weight my criteria explicitly, and I know which criterion I sacrificed
  • I can describe the realistic migration path away from every choice I have made
  • I keep vendors, ORMs, brokers and caches behind an interface so decisions stay reversible
  • I know the cost of each choice in money and in engineer time, not just in latency
  • I set a revisit date with a numeric trigger, not "when we scale"
  • I have written at least one ADR that a colleague could act on without me
  • I can explain to a product manager why the simpler option is the responsible one

Part 49 — Key Takeaways

  • Most architecture arguments are unstated disagreements about which constraint matters. Name the constraint and the argument usually resolves itself.
  • The default is the boring choice: PostgreSQL, a modular monolith, REST, containers, managed services. Deviating requires a written, specific reason.
  • Spend analysis effort in proportion to irreversibility. Caches and flags are cheap to undo; service boundaries, primary keys and sharding are not.
  • PostgreSQL with jsonb is very often the NoSQL you actually needed, and PostgreSQL full-text search is very often the search cluster you did not need.
  • A modular monolith with enforced module boundaries is the correct middle path, and the best possible precondition for extracting services later.
  • Kafka is a log, everything else in that comparison is a queue. If you cannot name the replay or the second consumer group, you want a queue.
  • Choose synchronous only when the user's next action depends on the result. Moving optional work out of the request path is usually the biggest reliability win available.
  • Fix the index before you add the cache. Caching an unindexed query removes the signal and keeps the debt, and the bill arrives when the cache is cold.
  • Keyset pagination gives constant latency and correct results for the price of one composite index. Deep OFFSET is a cliff that arrives silently.
  • Sessions give you revocation for 0.3 ms. JWT earns its place when many services must verify identity without a network call.
  • Managed versus self-hosted is a question about year three, not month one. If you cannot demonstrate a restore, you are not operating that system.
  • Buy the commodity, build the differentiator, and always integrate the vendor behind your own interface so the decision stays reversible.
  • Multi-AZ is the default; multi-region is insurance whose premium is paid in complexity and whose value is zero if the failover is never tested.
  • A decision without falsification criteria and a revisit date is a belief. Write the ADR, name what you sacrificed, and set the trigger that makes you look again.

Part 50 — The Knowledge Map and Learning Roadmap

Backend engineering is not a list of technologies. It is a dependency graph, and most people learn it in the wrong order: they start with a framework, then a database library, then a container, and only years later discover that everything they found confusing about all three was a consequence of something in operating systems, networking or the relational model that nobody had shown them.

This part is the map. It shows what depends on what, in what order to learn it, how long each stage realistically takes, and what to read alongside. It closes the book, so it also tries to say the honest things about a career that a list of parts cannot.

50.1 The knowledge map

The chain from theory to practice looks linear when written as a sentence — computer science, then programming, then operating systems, networking, backend development, databases, distributed systems, system design, cloud, DevOps, observability, SRE, architecture, leadership — but that is not how the dependencies actually run. Concurrency in the Node runtime is what makes database transaction anomalies intuitive. PostgreSQL internals are what make indexing make sense. Messaging is what makes sagas necessary. Observability is what makes both incident response and production debugging possible.

Here is the real shape, in three views.

50.1.1 Foundations into application engineering

flowchart TB

    P2 --> P12["Part 12 Indexing"]
    P1 --> P16["Part 16 Caching and Redis"]

Two dependencies in that diagram are worth calling out, because they are the ones people skip.

Part 3 into Part 21 into Part 13. The event loop is why a single Node process can serve 2,000 concurrent requests, and it is also why fifty of those requests can be inside the same read-modify-write sequence on the same row at the same time. If you do not understand the runtime's concurrency model, database isolation levels read like trivia. Once you do, they read like the solution to a problem you have personally caused.

Part 4 into Part 20. Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers and backpressure are not framework features. They are consequences of what TCP does and does not promise you. A retry that makes an outage worse makes perfect sense once you have seen a connection queue fill.

50.1.2 The data path

The spine here is Part 11. PostgreSQL internals — the page layout, MVCC, the visibility map, the write-ahead log, autovacuum, the planner — is the single highest-return investment in the book for a backend engineer. Indexing stops being a list of index types and becomes obvious. Transactions stop being isolation-level trivia and become "which row versions can this snapshot see". Bloat, replication lag, plan flips and lock waits stop being mysteries and become things you can predict from first principles.

Note also that Part 13 feeds Part 19. Sagas exist because a database transaction cannot span two services. You cannot understand why the outbox pattern exists until you understand exactly what a local transaction gives you for free.

The pattern to notice: everything in the top half of this graph converges on the bottom. Part 43 is not a separate soft-skills topic bolted onto the end of a technical book. It is what the technical parts turn into once you have enough of them: the questions in Part 43 are only answerable by someone who knows what a timeout does to a connection pool, what a partial saga leaves behind, and what a missing index costs at a billion rows.

Three reading notes on this table.

Prerequisites are about comprehension, not permission. You can read Part 27 on Kubernetes without Part 3. You will retain about a third of it, and you will not understand why a memory limit interacts with the V8 heap, which is exactly the thing that will page you.

The foundation rows are the ones that keep paying. Parts 1, 2, 3, 4, 9 and 30 describe things that have been true for decades and will still be true when NestJS is a historical curiosity. Everything above them is an implementation of them.

"Staff" level in this table does not mean harder. It means the content is about judgment across systems and organisations rather than about mechanisms. A strong mid-level engineer can read Part 48 and enjoy it; they will get ten times more from it after operating something for two years.

50.2 The learning roadmap

Five stages. Each one has a goal, a reading order, a thing to build, skills you must be able to demonstrate rather than recognise, a realistic time estimate for someone working full time as a developer and studying seriously outside that, and an exit test.

flowchart LR
    S1["Stage 1 Beginner foundation"] --> S2["Stage 2 Backend engineer"]
    S2 --> S3["Stage 3 Advanced backend engineer"]
    S3 --> S4["Stage 4 Senior backend engineer"]
    S4 --> S5["Stage 5 Staff engineer"]
    S1 -.->|"3 to 6 months"| S2
    S2 -.->|"9 to 18 months"| S3
    S3 -.->|"12 to 24 months"| S4
    S4 -.->|"2 to 4 years"| S5

The time estimates assume you are also doing a job. They are honest rather than encouraging: someone telling you that you can be a senior backend engineer in six months is selling something. The good news is that the stages overlap with paid work, so most of the time is not extra.

50.2.1 Stage 1 — Beginner foundation

Goal. Understand what happens underneath before you learn any framework's opinion about it. You should be able to explain what a process is, what happens between typing a URL and receiving bytes, what a table with a primary key really is, and why one algorithm is slower than another.

Read in this order. Part 30 (Git) first, because you need it from day one. Then Part 1, Part 2, Part 3, Part 4, Part 9, Part 10. Do not skip Part 3 because it looks like operating-systems theory; it is the part that explains every future confusing thing about Node.

Build alongside. Not a project yet — exercises. Implement an LRU cache from scratch. Write a small HTTP server with Node's http module, no framework, and handle a POST body yourself. Create a PostgreSQL schema for a blog with proper foreign keys and write ten queries against it by hand, including joins and aggregates. Use psql, not a GUI.

You must be able to demonstrate.

  • Explain the difference between a process, a thread and the event loop, and why blocking code hurts a Node server.
  • Walk through DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP for a single request, naming the round trips.
  • Write a query with a join, a GROUP BY and a HAVING without looking anything up.
  • Explain why a hash map lookup is O(1) and a sorted array search is O(log n), and where each appears in a real backend.
  • Use Git for branching, rebasing, and recovering a commit you thought you lost.

Time. Three to six months, part time.

Ready for the next stage when. You can explain to another person, without notes, what happens between a browser request and a database row being returned, including where the time goes.

50.2.2 Stage 2 — Backend engineer

Goal. Build and ship a complete, correct API on your own: modelled, validated, tested, containerised, deployed, and not embarrassing.

Read in this order. Part 5, Part 6, Part 8, Part 14, Part 16, Part 23, Part 26, Part 29, Part 36, Part 33. Read Part 22 (Security) at least to the end of authentication, authorisation and injection; you cannot ship a login system responsibly without it.

Build alongside. The first Part 46 project: the production-grade authentication system. Registration, login, password hashing, refresh-token rotation with reuse detection, email verification, rate limiting, and a full test suite. Then deploy it somewhere real with a domain and TLS, and keep it running.

You must be able to demonstrate.

  • A NestJS service with modules, DTO validation, guards, interceptors and an exception filter, where the domain logic does not depend on the framework.
  • Correct HTTP semantics: status codes, idempotency of PUT, pagination, error envelopes.
  • Integration tests that run against real PostgreSQL and Redis in containers.
  • A multi-stage Dockerfile producing a small non-root image, and a CI pipeline that runs tests and builds it.
  • Password hashing, token lifetimes and authorisation checks you can defend in a review.

Time. Nine to eighteen months, overlapping with a working job.

Ready for the next stage when. You have shipped something to real users, and when it broke you fixed it yourself using logs and metrics rather than by guessing.

50.2.3 Stage 3 — Advanced backend engineer

Goal. Understand your database and runtime deeply enough to predict behaviour rather than discover it. Start being the person others ask about performance and correctness.

Read in this order. Part 11, Part 12, Part 13, Part 21, Part 24, Part 25, Part 15, Part 17, Part 18, Part 27, Part 28, Part 34, Part 35, Part 41. This is the densest stretch of the book and the one that changes how you see everything.

Build alongside. Extend the Part 46 line of projects into an order and inventory system with money in it: transactions, concurrent stock reservation, background jobs, idempotent webhook handling from a payment provider, and a cache with a real invalidation strategy. Then generate ten million rows and make it fast. The volume is the point; a correct system at 5,000 rows teaches you almost nothing.

You must be able to demonstrate.

  • Read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and say why a plan is bad and what index would fix it.
  • Cause a deadlock deliberately, read it in the PostgreSQL log, and fix it by ordering lock acquisition.
  • Prove a race condition with 50 parallel requests, then fix it with an atomic statement and a check constraint.
  • Find a memory leak with two heap snapshots and name the retaining path.
  • Instrument a service with structured logs, metrics and traces, and debug a real slowdown using them.
  • Estimate the storage, connections and partitions a system needs, with arithmetic on paper.

Time. Twelve to twenty-four months.

Ready for the next stage when. Someone brings you a production performance problem and you find the cause from evidence, in under an hour, without changing random things.

50.2.4 Stage 4 — Senior backend engineer

Goal. Own systems, not features. Design under ambiguity, operate what you build, and make the people around you better.

Read in this order. Part 7, Part 19, Part 20, Part 22 in full, Part 31, Part 32, Part 37, Part 38, Part 40, Part 42, Part 43, Part 44, Part 39, Part 49.

Build alongside. The later Part 46 projects, where the system becomes distributed: an outbox, a saga with compensation across two services, a real message broker, zero-downtime migrations on a large table, and an on-call setup for yourself with genuine alerts that wake you. Then deliberately break it: kill the broker, fill the disk, add 300 ms of latency to the database, and see whether your system degrades or collapses.

You must be able to demonstrate.

  • Run a zero-downtime migration on a table with tens of millions of rows, including the rollback plan.
  • Design a multi-service workflow with explicit idempotency, compensation and reconciliation.
  • Write an ADR that a stranger can act on in two years.
  • Command an incident: mitigate, communicate on a schedule, keep a log, run a blameless postmortem with completed actions.
  • Explain a trade-off to a non-engineer in time, risk and money, with two options and a recommendation.
  • Design a system end to end in 45 minutes with capacity numbers and failure behaviour.

Time. Two to four years from Stage 3, mostly gated by exposure rather than reading. You cannot learn incident command from a book; you can only prepare so that the incidents teach you efficiently.

Ready for the next stage when. Your team makes good decisions in your absence, and problems that span teams start finding their way to you.

50.2.5 Stage 5 — Staff engineer

Goal. Work above one team: strategy, standards, influence without authority, and problems nobody owns.

Read in this order. Part 47, Part 48, then re-read Part 5, Part 7, Part 40 and Part 43 with a different question in mind — not "how does this work" but "how do I get five teams to do this consistently". Part 44 sections 44.4 and 44.5 are the map.

Build alongside. Not a personal project. A cross-team artefact: a shared library or service template that other teams adopt voluntarily, a written technical strategy that changes plans, a migration programme spanning several services, or a standard embedded in tooling.

You must be able to demonstrate.

  • A written strategy with a staged sequence and observable checkpoints, that teams actually followed.
  • Changing another team's behaviour with no authority, and being able to explain how.
  • Growing a senior engineer to the point where they lead their own cross-team work.
  • Choosing not to work on three tempting problems, and articulating why.

Time. Two to four years, and it is not guaranteed by effort; it also requires an organisation with problems of that size.

50.2.6 A six-month plan, week by week

This assumes roughly eight to ten focused hours a week outside work, and that you are somewhere around Stage 2 ending or Stage 3 beginning. Adjust the reading, keep the shape: read, build, prove.

Week Read Build Prove it
1 Part 11.1-11.5 (pages, tuples, MVCC) Seed a 10 M row orders table with generate_series Explain MVCC and dead tuples to a colleague
2 Part 11 rest (WAL, vacuum, planner) Watch pg_stat_user_tables during a bulk update Show bloat growing, then vacuum it away

50.2.7 A twelve-month plan

The six-month plan builds depth. The twelve-month plan turns depth into seniority, which needs breadth and visible ownership.

Month Theme Reading Output that proves it
1 PostgreSQL internals and indexing 11, 12 An index audit of a real system, with before and after numbers
2 Transactions and concurrency 13, 21 A concurrency bug found and fixed in production code, with a test
3 Performance and observability 24, 25 A dashboard and three symptom alerts others now rely on
4 Caching and scaling 16, 15 A cache design surviving a cold start, proven with a load test
5 Messaging and jobs 17, 36 A consumer with idempotency, DLQ and a lag alert in seconds

7 Reliability and incident response 20, 37 Runbooks for your service and one incident you commanded
8 Security 22 A threat model for one feature plus cross-tenant access tests
9 Migrations and compatibility 31, 32 A zero-downtime migration on a large table, with rollback
10 Containers, Kubernetes, cloud 26, 27, 28 Right-sized resources from real usage; deploys with no dropped requests

12 Design and judgment 40, 42, 43, 44 Two system designs, three ADRs, and an honest rubric self-score

A note on both plans: the "prove it" column is the real content. Reading a part takes two hours and produces a warm feeling of understanding that evaporates in a fortnight. Producing the artefact takes six hours and produces knowledge you still have in three years.

50.3 How to study this handbook

Every part of this book is designed to be studied in the same loop. Reading is only the first quarter of it.

flowchart LR
    R["Read a section"] --> B["Build the exercise"]
    B --> V["Break it at production volume"]
    V --> W["Write down what happened"]
    W --> T["Teach or explain it"]
    T --> R

Active recall beats re-reading. After finishing a section, close the book and write down the mechanism in your own words: how MVCC decides visibility, what a circuit breaker does in each state, what happens on a Kafka rebalance. Then check. The gap between what you thought you knew and what you could reproduce is the entire learning signal, and re-reading hides it.

Build while reading, not after. Every part has a practical exercise. Do it in a scratch repository with real PostgreSQL and Redis in Docker. Concepts you have only read stay abstract; concepts you have caused, broken and fixed become intuition. The specific moment that teaches you MVCC is the moment your own table triples in size during your own backfill.

Keep an incident diary. Every production problem you touch, at work or in your own projects, gets five lines: what happened, how you found out, what the cause was, what you did, and what you would build differently. Re-read it every quarter. After two years this document is worth more than any course, because it is calibrated to the systems you actually work on, and the patterns in it are yours.

Teach someone else. A fifteen-minute talk to your team on the last thing you learned will expose every soft spot in your understanding within the first five minutes of preparing it. Writing an internal document has the same effect. If you cannot explain it simply, you have memorised it rather than understood it.

Redo the exercises at production data volumes. This is the single most under-used piece of advice in the book. Almost every exercise behaves differently at 10 million rows than at 10 thousand: plans flip to sequential scans, sorts spill to disk, vacuum matters, connection pools saturate, exports run out of memory. Use generate_series to make the data. It takes ten minutes and changes what you learn.

Use Part 45 as self-tests, not as revision. Answer the interview questions out loud, from memory, before reading the answers, and preferably to another person who will ask "why?" twice. The questions are designed so that a memorised answer collapses on the first follow-up. When it collapses, you have found precisely the thing to go and learn.

Re-read the parts you are sure you already know. Every eighteen months, re-read Parts 3, 4, 11 and 13. You will find things that were invisible the first time because you lacked the experience to notice them. This is not a failure of the first reading; it is how depth works.

50.4 Reading list

The handbook is a map. These are the territories, with an honest line each on why and when.

Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Martin Kleppmann. The best book in our field. Read it after Stage 3, when you have felt replication lag and a partial failure yourself, or half of it will feel like abstract taxonomy. Then read it again a year later.

Database Internals, Alex Petrov. What a storage engine actually does: B-trees, LSM trees, WAL, consensus. Read it when Part 11 has made you curious rather than satisfied. Dense, precise, and it makes index behaviour obvious.

Site Reliability Engineering, Google. Read the chapters on SLOs, error budgets, alerting and postmortems; skim the rest. Best read when you are on call, because until then the incentives it describes feel theoretical.

Release It!, Michael Nygard. Stability patterns and antipatterns: circuit breakers, bulkheads, cascading failures, integration points. The most immediately actionable book on the list, and the one whose stories you will recognise from your own outages.

The Pragmatic Programmer, Hunt and Thomas. About craft and judgment rather than technology. Best read early and re-read every few years; the parts that matter change as you do.

Domain-Driven Design, Eric Evans. The strategic patterns — bounded contexts, ubiquitous language, context maps — are the valuable half and are in the back. Read those first. Dense; take it slowly.

Implementing Domain-Driven Design, Vaughn Vernon. The practical companion, with code. Read it when you are about to design a real aggregate boundary, not before; out of context it reads as ceremony.

Clean Architecture, Robert C. Martin. Useful for the dependency-rule idea and for thinking about boundaries. Read it critically: the principles are sound, the prescriptions are stronger than the evidence for them, and layers cost something.

Kafka: The Definitive Guide, Narkhede, Shapira and Palino. Read it when you actually run Kafka. The chapters on producers, consumers, delivery semantics and operations are the ones that matter; the rest can wait until you need it.

50.4.1 Documentation worth reading end to end

Documentation usually beats books for accuracy and loses on narrative. These specific sections are worth reading straight through, not just searching.

PostgreSQL documentation. Chapter 13 (Concurrency Control) — read every word, twice. Chapter 11 (Indexes). Chapter 14 (Performance Tips), including "Using EXPLAIN". Chapter 25 (Routine Database Maintenance Tasks), especially the vacuum sections. Chapter 5.12 (Table Partitioning). Chapter 30 (Write-Ahead Logging) and Chapter 27 (High Availability, Load Balancing and Replication) when you start operating it. These are perhaps 150 pages and they will make you better at your job than any five blog posts.

Node.js documentation. The guides "The Node.js Event Loop, Timers, and process.nextTick", "Don't Block the Event Loop", and "Backpressuring in Streams". Then the API reference for stream, worker_threads, perf_hooks and diagnostics_channel. The event-loop guide in particular is short and explains more production behaviour than its length suggests.

NestJS documentation. Read Overview and Fundamentals end to end, once, properly: modules, providers, injection scopes, lifecycle events, custom providers. Then Techniques (configuration, database, caching, queues, task scheduling, health checks) as you need them, and Microservices only when you are actually building one. Most NestJS confusion is dependency-injection confusion, and it is all in Fundamentals.

Redis documentation. The data-types pages with their command references, then "Redis persistence", "Key eviction", "Redis pipelining" and "Distributed locks with Redis", which is refreshingly honest about the limits of the pattern it describes.

Kubernetes documentation. Concepts: Pods, Deployments, Services, Configuration, Resource management, and Pod lifecycle including probes and termination. Then "Best practices for pod disruption". Skip the tutorials that build clusters by hand unless you will operate the control plane.

AWS Well-Architected Framework. The Reliability and Operational Excellence pillars are worth reading end to end even if you are not on AWS; they are a good checklist in disguise. The Cost Optimization pillar is worth it once you own a bill. Read the Security pillar's identity and detection sections.

50.5 Closing words

You have reached the end of a long book. Here is what I would say to you if we were sitting down after a project together.

The thing that compounds over a career is not the tools. In my time I have watched teams move from Perl to Ruby to Node to Go, from bare metal to VMs to containers to serverless and part of the way back, from SOAP to REST to GraphQL to gRPC and back to REST. Every one of those transitions was described as fundamental by the people selling it. Almost none of it changed what actually makes a backend engineer good.

What compounds is the fundamentals in Parts 1 to 4, and the habits in Part 43. Understanding how a process uses memory, how a scheduler works, what a network round trip costs and what TCP does and does not promise you — that knowledge was true in 1998, it is true today, and it will explain whatever runtime you are using in 2035. Every framework is a set of opinions about those primitives. When you know the primitives, learning a framework takes a week. When you do not, you can use one for five years and still be surprised by it.

The second thing that compounds is the questions. Can it time out. Can it duplicate. Can it arrive late or out of order. Can it partially succeed. What is the blast radius. Who owns this data. How would we know it broke. How do we undo it. Those questions do not care which language you write in. They are the difference between systems that survive their worst day and systems that discover their design flaws in front of customers. They are, more than anything else, what people mean when they say someone is senior.

The third thing, and the one that quietly determines careers, is being the person who can be trusted with production. Not the fastest coder or the one with the most opinions. The person who, when something important and unclear needs to be done, gets handed it — because they will find out what is actually true, they will say what they do not know, they will not make it worse at 03:00, they will tell you what happened afterwards, and they will finish it. That reputation takes years to build and about one bad decision made dishonestly to lose. It is also, in my experience, the single largest determinant of what work you get offered and what your career looks like at forty.

And now permission, which I mean sincerely: you do not need to know everything. Nobody does. I have been doing this for a long time and there are large areas of this book where I would need a day and a good colleague before I would trust my own opinion. Every engineer you admire is quietly ignorant of things you would find surprising. The people who look like they know everything are usually just confident in a narrow area and careful about where they speak.

What matters is not the size of what you know; it is being honest about its edges. "I don't know, let me find out" is a senior sentence. So is "I was wrong about this, here is what I learned". The engineers who cannot say either of those are the dangerous ones, because their systems fail in ways nobody predicted and nobody was allowed to question.

So: pick the next thing on the map. Build it, break it, operate it, write down what happened. Fix a class of problem rather than an instance. Leave the codebase and the people around you better than you found them. Take the pager, because that is where the real feedback lives. And be patient with yourself, because this takes years, and the years are the point.

Good luck. Go and build something that stays up.

Senior Checklist — Part 50

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I know which stage of the roadmap I am actually in, judged by what I can demonstrate rather than what I have read
  • I have identified the three parts whose prerequisites I skipped, and scheduled them
  • I do the practical exercises at production data volumes, not at development volumes
  • I keep an incident diary and re-read it quarterly
  • I test myself with Part 45's questions out loud before reading any answer
  • I have taught at least one topic from this book to another person
  • I have a written plan with dates for the next six months, and an artefact to produce each month
  • I re-read Parts 3, 4, 11 and 13 periodically, expecting to find new things
  • I have read at least the PostgreSQL concurrency-control chapter and the Node event-loop guide end to end
  • I can name what I do not know, out loud, without embarrassment

Part 50 — Key Takeaways

  • The fundamentals outlive every tool: processes, memory, the event loop, TCP, HTTP and the relational model explain whatever framework you use next.
  • The senior question set is the transferable skill — can it time out, duplicate, arrive late, arrive out of order, partially succeed; what is the blast radius; who owns the truth; how do we undo it.
  • The simplest design that meets a stated numeric requirement wins; every added component is a permanent tax on operations, onboarding and 03:00 debugging.
  • The database is where mistakes become permanent, so spend disproportionate effort on the schema, the indexes, the transaction boundaries and the migration path.
  • A timeout is not a failure, it is unknown; from that single fact follow idempotency keys, reconciliation, and the reason retries need thought.
  • "Done" means running in production, alerted on a business signal, deployable, rollback-safe, debuggable by a stranger and owned by a named rotation.
  • Measure before you optimise, and fix the class of problem rather than the instance; almost every slow system is one query, one lock, one missing index or one serialised loop.
  • Write decisions down when you make them, with the alternatives and the trigger that would make you revisit; the reader is a stranger in two years and it is probably you.
  • Mitigate before you diagnose, communicate on a fixed schedule, stay blameless, and make the postmortem actions someone's actual job.
  • Learn by building, breaking and operating at real data volumes; reading produces recognition, and only production produces judgment.
  • Your personal throughput caps your value, but the people you make better do not — which is why reviewing, writing, mentoring and deleting code are the job, not overhead.
  • You do not need to know everything; being trusted with production comes from being honest about the edges of what you know and finishing what you start.

Part 65 — More System Designs I

This Part continues the system-design case studies of Part 40, using the exact same method and twenty-section template. If you have not read Part 40, read its section 40.0 first: it defines the nine-move method (clarify, estimate, define APIs, model data, draw the high-level design, deep-dive the hot spots, address cross-cutting concerns, state tradeoffs, offer alternatives), the twenty-section template, and the default environment (NestJS on Kubernetes, PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka or SQS, S3, CloudFront). Everything here assumes that method; we do not repeat it.

The four systems in this Part are classics that probe different skills: a web crawler (politeness, deduplication, a distributed frontier), a distributed key-value store (partitioning, consistent hashing, replication, quorum — the heart of distributed systems), a unique ID generator (Snowflake IDs, clock skew, UUIDv7, sequences at scale), and a ticket and seat booking system (holds, expiring reservations, hot-event contention, payment coupling). Part 66 continues with four more. Read each as a worked example of the method, then produce your own designs the same way.

65.1 Web Crawler

65.1.1 Requirements

A web crawler systematically downloads web pages, extracts their content and links, and follows those links to discover more pages, feeding a search index, a dataset, or a monitoring system. The users are internal: a search team that wants the web indexed, a data team that wants a corpus, an operations team that wants to detect changes. The crawler must be a good citizen of the web — polite to the sites it visits — and it must scale to billions of pages without re-downloading the same page endlessly or getting trapped.

Imagine a diligent librarian cataloguing an infinite library by starting at a few books, reading each, noting the references it cites, and visiting those next, keeping a card for every book already catalogued so none is read twice, and never pulling so many books from one shelf at once that the shelf collapses. The librarian is the crawler; the references are links; the cards are the seen-set (deduplication); not overwhelming a shelf is politeness.

65.1.2 Functional requirements

  1. Start from a set of seed URLs and discover new URLs by following links.
  2. Download each page's content and store it (or pass it to a processing pipeline).
  3. Extract links from each page and enqueue the new ones for crawling.
  4. Never crawl the same URL twice (deduplication), within a refresh window.
  5. Respect politeness: obey robots.txt, limit the rate per domain, honor crawl-delay.
  6. Prioritize URLs (freshness, importance) rather than pure FIFO.
  7. Re-crawl pages periodically to detect changes (configurable per-page freshness).
  8. Avoid traps: infinite URL spaces, redirect loops, enormous pages.

65.1.3 Non-functional requirements

Property Target Why
Throughput 1,000 pages/second sustained (target scale) To cover a large web in reasonable time
Politeness Never exceed a per-domain rate (e.g. 1 request/second/domain default) Being blocked or harming a site is unacceptable
Deduplication A URL is crawled at most once per refresh window Re-crawling wastes the entire budget
Durability A crawled page and the frontier survive crashes Losing progress means re-crawling billions of pages
Scalability Scale fetchers horizontally One machine cannot crawl the web
Freshness Important pages re-crawled within their window A stale index is a poor one

65.1.4 Constraints

  • Must respect robots.txt and site rate limits absolutely; being a bad citizen gets the crawler's IPs banned and is reputationally and legally risky.
  • Budget for storage of billions of pages (object storage, S3) and for the frontier and seen-set.
  • The web is adversarial: spider traps, infinite calendars, malicious pages; the crawler must not be trapped or crashed by them.
  • Distributed by necessity; must coordinate deduplication and politeness across many fetcher machines.

65.1.5 Capacity estimation

Quantity Assumption Calculation Result
Pages to crawl Target corpus given 10 billion
Crawl rate Sustained given 1,000 pages/second
Time for one full pass 10B / 1,000 10,000,000 s about 116 days
Average page size HTML plus headers given about 100 KB
Storage for one pass 10B x 100 KB 1 PB raw (compressed ~200-300 TB)
Seen-set size 10B URLs x ~20 B (hash) about 200 GB (fits a Bloom filter + store)
Links per page average outlinks given about 50
Frontier growth each page yields ~50 links, most seen frontier of billions of URLs
Bandwidth 1,000 pages/s x 100 KB 100 MB/s = about 800 Mbps inbound

The numbers say: deduplication must be memory-efficient at 10B URLs (a Bloom filter, Part 1, in front of an exact store), the frontier is itself a big-data problem (billions of URLs, must be durable and prioritized), storage is object storage (S3), and politeness must be coordinated across fetchers so one domain is never hammered by many machines at once.

65.1.6 API design

The crawler is mostly internal; its "API" is operational and the component interfaces.

Operation Interface Notes
Add seeds POST /seeds { urls[] } Bootstrap the frontier
Enqueue URL internal: frontier.add(url, priority) From link extraction
Fetch next internal: frontier.next(domain-aware) Respects politeness
Mark seen internal: seen.add(urlHash) Bloom filter + store
Store page internal: store.put(url, content) To S3 + metadata
Get stats GET /stats Pages/s, frontier size, error rates
Pause/resume domain POST /domains/{d}/pause Operational control

65.1.7 Data model

erDiagram
    URL_FRONTIER ||--o{ FETCH_ATTEMPT : has
    PAGE ||--o{ EXTRACTED_LINK : yields
    URL_FRONTIER {
        text url_hash PK
        text url
        int priority
        timestamptz next_crawl_at
        text status
    }
    PAGE {
        text url_hash PK
        text url
        text s3_key
        bytea content_hash
        timestamptz crawled_at
        int http_status
    }
    DOMAIN_POLICY {
        text domain PK
        int crawl_delay_ms
        timestamptz next_allowed_at
        boolean blocked
    }

The frontier (URLs to crawl, prioritized, with next-crawl time), the seen-set (a Bloom filter in Redis for fast "probably seen" checks, backed by an exact store to resolve false positives), pages (content in S3, metadata in a store), and domain policy (per-domain crawl delay and next-allowed time for politeness). Content is addressed by content_hash so identical content fetched via different URLs is deduplicated at the content level too.

65.1.8 High-level architecture

flowchart LR
    SEED["Seed URLs"] --> FR["Frontier (prioritized queue)"]
    FR --> SCH["Scheduler (politeness-aware)"]
    SCH --> FET["Fetcher workers (distributed)"]
    FET --> ROB["robots.txt cache"]
    FET --> S3["Page store (S3)"]
    FET --> EXT["Link + content extractor"]
    EXT --> DEDUP["Dedup (Bloom filter + store)"]
    DEDUP --> FR
    FET --> DP["Domain policy (rate/delay)"]
    SCH --> DP

Flow: the scheduler pulls from the frontier, choosing URLs whose domain is allowed to be crawled now (politeness), and hands them to fetcher workers. Fetchers check robots.txt (cached), download the page, store it in S3, and pass it to the extractor, which finds links, deduplicates them against the Bloom filter and store, and enqueues the new ones back into the frontier. Domain policy enforces per-domain rate limits across all fetchers.

65.1.9 Component design

Component Responsibility Scaling
Frontier Durable, prioritized store of URLs to crawl, with next-crawl times Partitioned by domain hash
Scheduler Pick URLs whose domain is politeness-eligible now; prioritize Coordinates via domain policy in Redis
Fetcher workers Download pages, obey robots.txt, handle timeouts/traps Horizontal, stateless
Extractor Parse content, extract links, compute content hash Horizontal, per page
Dedup Bloom filter (fast probable-seen) + exact store (resolve false positives) Bloom in Redis, store partitioned
Domain policy Per-domain crawl delay, next-allowed time, block list Redis, shared across fetchers

The deduplication design is the interesting part. A Bloom filter (Part 1) in Redis gives a fast, memory-efficient "probably seen" check for 10B URLs in a few GB; a positive is confirmed against an exact store (to resolve the Bloom filter's false positives, which would otherwise skip a genuinely new URL). URL normalization (lowercasing host, removing fragments and tracking params, sorting query params) happens before hashing, so the same page via different URL spellings is one entry.

65.1.10 Database / store design

The frontier and seen-set are partitioned by domain hash so each partition owns a set of domains, which also localizes politeness (one partition's scheduler controls one domain's rate). Pages go to S3 (object storage, cheap at petabyte scale), with metadata in a partitioned store. The frontier is prioritized: a priority queue per partition ordered by crawl priority and next_crawl_at, so important and due pages are crawled first. Content-level dedup uses content_hash so mirror sites and duplicate content do not consume the budget.

65.1.11 Caching

Layer What TTL Why
robots.txt cache Per-domain crawl rules 24 h Avoid re-fetching robots.txt per URL
DNS cache Hostname to IP TTL-respecting Avoid a DNS lookup per request
Bloom filter (Redis) Seen URLs (probable) long Fast dedup without hitting the store
Domain policy (Redis) Next-allowed time per domain short Politeness coordination across fetchers

65.1.12 Messaging

The frontier itself is effectively a durable queue; new URLs from extraction are enqueued (Kafka or a partitioned queue, Part 17), keyed by domain so one domain's URLs land in one partition (politeness locality). Fetch results flow to the extractor via a queue. Re-crawl scheduling re-enqueues a page at its next_crawl_at. At-least-once delivery is fine because dedup makes re-processing idempotent.

65.1.13 Scaling

flowchart TB
    S1["1x: 1,000 pages/s"] --> S1a["Fetchers scaled to bandwidth, frontier partitioned by domain"]
    S1 --> S1b["Bloom filter in Redis, pages in S3"]
    S10["10x: 10,000 pages/s"] --> S10a["More fetcher nodes across regions, sharded frontier"]
    S10 --> S10b["Sharded Bloom filter, per-shard domain policy"]
    S100["100x"] --> S100a["Multi-region crawl, distributed frontier coordination"]
    S100 --> S100b["Content-defined dedup at scale, tiered storage"]
    S1 --> S10 --> S100

Fetchers scale horizontally (they are stateless); the frontier and seen-set scale by partitioning on domain hash; S3 scales for storage. The coordination challenge at scale is politeness: all fetchers for a domain must share its rate limit, which the domain-partitioned design and shared domain policy in Redis handle. Bandwidth, not CPU, is often the limit, so fetchers are placed for network throughput.

65.1.14 Security and safety

  • Politeness and robots.txt: absolute — obey robots.txt, per-domain rate limits, and crawl-delay, or get banned and cause harm.
  • Traps: cap URL depth and per-domain page counts, detect redirect loops, cap page size (reject enormous pages), and detect infinite URL spaces (calendars), so a trap does not consume the budget or crash a fetcher.
  • Malicious content: fetchers parse untrusted HTML; parse defensively (timeouts, size limits) so a malicious page cannot hang or crash a worker.
  • SSRF / scope: restrict the crawl to intended domains/schemes; never let a link drive the fetcher to internal addresses.
  • Legal/ethical: respect terms, identify the crawler via User-Agent, provide an opt-out.

65.1.15 Failure scenarios

Failure Detection Impact Mitigation Effect
Fetcher crash Health check, lease expiry In-flight URLs stalled URLs leased with timeout; re-enqueued on lease expiry None (re-crawled)
Spider trap (infinite URLs) Per-domain page-count spike Budget wasted on one domain Depth/count caps, trap detection Bounded
Bloom filter false positive Rare, by design A new URL skipped Exact store confirms; tune filter size Negligible
robots.txt change (now disallowed) Periodic re-fetch Crawling disallowed paths Re-fetch robots.txt per TTL; stop on disallow Compliant
One domain overwhelmed Domain error rate, complaints Harm, risk of ban Per-domain rate limit enforced across fetchers Prevented
Frontier store down Errors Crawling stalls Durable, replicated frontier; resume on recovery Pause, no loss
Enormous page Size at fetch Memory blowup Stream and cap page size Rejected cleanly

65.1.16 Observability

Metrics: pages/second, frontier size, per-domain request rate (to prove politeness), error rates by type (timeout, 4xx, 5xx, trap), dedup hit rate, re-crawl freshness, bandwidth. Alerts: per-domain rate exceeding the limit (politeness violation), frontier growth stalling (coverage problem), error-rate spikes. Dashboards: coverage (pages crawled vs target), freshness (pages overdue for re-crawl), politeness (per-domain rates).

65.1.17 Deployment

Fetchers and extractors as horizontally-scaled stateless deployments (Part 27); the frontier and seen-set on partitioned durable stores; Redis for Bloom filter and domain policy; S3 for pages. Crawl scope and rate limits from config. Rollout with canaries so a bad parser change does not corrupt the corpus. Per-domain pause as an operational control.

65.1.18 Cost considerations

The dominant costs are storage (petabytes of pages in S3; compression and tiering to cheaper storage classes matter) and bandwidth (ingress for crawling). Compute (fetchers, extractors) is secondary and can use spot instances. The seen-set and frontier stores are modest by comparison. Cost is controlled by crawling selectively (prioritize, do not re-crawl needlessly — the dedup and freshness logic directly controls the bill) and by tiered storage for old pages.

65.1.19 Tradeoffs

  • Bloom filter dedup (memory-efficient, tiny false-positive rate that rarely skips a URL) over an exact in-memory set (exact but needs ~200 GB RAM): we accept a negligible miss rate for huge memory savings.
  • Politeness over throughput: we cap per-domain rate even when we could crawl faster, because being banned or harming sites is unacceptable; throughput comes from breadth (many domains) not depth (hammering one).
  • At-least-once processing with idempotent dedup over exactly-once: simpler and the dedup makes reprocessing harmless.
  • Object storage (S3) for pages over a database: cheap at petabyte scale, at the cost of not querying page content in the store (that is the index's job).

65.1.20 Alternative architectures

Managed crawl + serverless: Lambda-based fetchers triggered from an SQS frontier, pages to S3, dedup in DynamoDB. Scales elastically and needs no fetcher fleet to manage; loses some control over politeness coordination and can cost more at sustained high throughput.

Single-machine crawler: for crawling one site or a small set (thousands to millions of pages), a single well-behaved process with an in-memory frontier and a local seen-set is far simpler and entirely adequate. This is what most "crawler" needs actually are, and the distributed design above is justified only at web scale. Build the simple version first.

65.2 Distributed Key-Value Store

65.2.1 Requirements

A distributed key-value store holds key -> value pairs across many machines, surviving machine failures, serving reads and writes at scale with low latency, and staying available even when some nodes or network links fail. This is the canonical distributed-systems design (the shape of Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak). The users are other services that need a fast, highly-available store for data that does not need relational queries. The design probes the deepest distributed-systems ideas: partitioning, replication, consistency, and the CAP tradeoff (Part 42).

Imagine a chain of identical lockers spread across many buildings. Each item (value) goes in a locker chosen by a formula from its tag (key), and a copy is placed in two nearby buildings too (replication), so if one building closes you still get your item. When you store or fetch, you can insist that a majority of the buildings confirm (strong consistency, slower) or accept one building's word (fast, maybe slightly stale). The buildings are nodes; the formula is consistent hashing; the copies are replicas; the majority rule is quorum.

65.2.2 Functional requirements

  1. put(key, value) stores a value; get(key) retrieves it; delete(key) removes it.
  2. Data is distributed across many nodes (partitioning).
  3. Data is replicated so the loss of a node does not lose data.
  4. The system stays available for reads and writes during node failures and network partitions (tunable).
  5. Tunable consistency: callers choose how many replicas must respond (quorum).
  6. Nodes can be added and removed with minimal data movement (elastic).
  7. Eventually, all replicas converge to the same value (anti-entropy, read repair).

65.2.3 Non-functional requirements

Property Target Why
Read/write latency p99 single-digit to low-tens of ms A fast store for other services
Availability Very high (survive node/AZ loss, stay writable) The reason to build this over a single database
Durability No data loss on single-node (or N-1 replica) failure Replication guarantees this
Scalability Linear with nodes added Add capacity by adding nodes
Consistency Tunable per operation (quorum) Trade consistency for availability/latency per need

65.2.4 Constraints

  • Distributed by definition; must handle node failure, network partitions and clock skew.
  • No single point of failure; masterless (every node equal) for availability.
  • Rebalancing when nodes join/leave must move minimal data (consistent hashing).
  • The CAP tradeoff (Part 42) is fundamental: during a partition, choose availability or consistency, tunable per operation.

65.2.5 Capacity estimation

Quantity Assumption Calculation Result
Keys Target given 10 billion
Value size average given 1 KB
Raw data 10B x 1 KB 10 TB
Replication factor 3 copies 10 TB x 3 30 TB stored
Nodes per-node capacity ~2 TB usable 30 TB / 2 TB about 15-20 nodes
Read/write rate Target given 100,000 ops/second
Per-node ops 100k / 15 about 7,000 ops/s/node
