The numbers say: partition 10B keys across ~15-20 nodes with 3x replication, each node handling a slice of keys and ~7,000 ops/s, and rebalancing must be cheap when the node count changes. These are the forces that make consistent hashing and quorum the right tools.

65.2.6 API design

Operation Signature Consistency option
Put put(key, value, W) W = replicas that must ack the write
Get get(key, R) R = replicas that must respond to the read
Delete delete(key, W) A delete is a write of a tombstone

The caller chooses W (write quorum) and R (read quorum). With R + W > N (replication factor), a read is guaranteed to see the latest write (strong consistency); with lower values, you get lower latency and higher availability but possible staleness. This per-operation tunability is the practical expression of the CAP tradeoff.

65.2.7 Data model

Just keys and values. The system's structure is in the placement:

key -> hash(key) -> position on the hash ring -> the N nodes clockwise own it

Each key's value is stored on N nodes (the "preference list"), e.g. N=3:
  key "user:42" -> hashes to ring position P -> stored on nodes A, B, C (next 3 clockwise)

Each stored value carries a version (vector clock or timestamp) to resolve conflicts.

There are no tables or joins; the data model is deliberately minimal. The sophistication is in where each key lives (consistent hashing) and how conflicting versions are reconciled (versioning).

65.2.8 High-level architecture

flowchart LR
    C["Client / service"] --> CO["Coordinator node (any node)"]
    CO --> RING["Consistent hash ring"]
    RING --> N1["Node A (replica)"]
    RING --> N2["Node B (replica)"]
    RING --> N3["Node C (replica)"]
    CO --> QUORUM["Quorum logic (R/W)"]
    N1 --> AE["Anti-entropy / read repair"]
    N2 --> AE
    N3 --> AE
    HH["Hinted handoff store"] --> N1

Any node can act as the coordinator for a request: it hashes the key to find the N replica nodes (the preference list), sends the read/write to them, waits for R or W acknowledgements (quorum), and returns. Replicas converge via read repair (fix stale replicas noticed during a read) and anti-entropy (background comparison and repair). When a replica is temporarily down, a hinted handoff stores the write on another node to be delivered when the replica recovers.

65.2.9 Component design

Component Responsibility
Consistent hashing ring Map keys to nodes; minimize movement when nodes change
Coordinator Route a request to the N replicas, enforce R/W quorum
Replica store Hold the data for its key ranges, with versions
Versioning (vector clocks / timestamps) Detect and resolve conflicting concurrent writes
Read repair Fix stale replicas detected during a read
Anti-entropy (Merkle trees) Background sync of divergent replicas
Hinted handoff Hold writes for a down replica, deliver on recovery
Gossip Nodes share membership and health (no central coordinator)

65.2.10 Deep dive: consistent hashing, replication, quorum

Consistent hashing (Part 42) places nodes and keys on a ring (hash space). A key is owned by the N nodes clockwise from its position. When a node is added or removed, only the keys between it and its neighbor move — about 1/N of the data — instead of rehashing everything (which naive modulo hashing would require). Virtual nodes (each physical node occupies many ring positions) spread load evenly and avoid hotspots.

Replication: each key is stored on N nodes (the preference list). This gives durability (lose a node, N-1 copies remain) and availability (read from any live replica).

Quorum: a write waits for W acknowledgements, a read for R responses. Choosing R + W > N guarantees a read sees the latest write (the read and write quorums overlap by at least one node). W=N, R=1 favors read speed; W=1, R=N favors write speed; W=R=quorum (⌈(N+1)/2⌉) balances. Lower R/W trade consistency for availability and latency — the CAP tradeoff, per operation.

N=3 replicas. Quorum = 2.
  Write with W=2: ack when 2 of 3 replicas confirm (survives 1 down, fast-ish)
  Read with R=2:  read 2 of 3, take the newest version (read repair fixes the third)
  R(2) + W(2) = 4 > N(3) -> a read always overlaps the latest write -> strong consistency
  Lower to R=1/W=1: faster, more available, but a read may miss the latest write (eventual)

Conflict resolution: concurrent writes to different replicas can diverge. Versioning (vector clocks, or last-write-wins by timestamp with its risks) detects conflicts; the system either resolves them (last-write-wins) or returns both versions for the application to reconcile. This is the price of high availability: during a partition, both sides may accept writes, and they must be reconciled later.

65.2.11 Caching

The store itself is the fast layer, so a separate cache is less common than in a database system; nodes keep hot data in memory. Clients may cache the ring topology to route directly to the right nodes (saving a coordinator hop).

65.2.12 Messaging

Gossip protocol for membership and failure detection (nodes periodically exchange state, so the cluster learns of joins, leaves and failures without a central coordinator). Hinted handoff and anti-entropy use background transfers between nodes. There is no external message broker; the coordination is peer-to-peer.

65.2.13 Scaling

flowchart TB
    S1["1x: ~20 nodes, 100k ops/s"] --> S1a["Consistent hashing, N=3, quorum reads/writes"]
    S10["10x: ~200 nodes, 1M ops/s"] --> S10a["More virtual nodes, multi-AZ replicas"]
    S10 --> S10b["Tune R/W per workload, read repair + anti-entropy"]
    S100["100x: multi-region"] --> S100a["Cross-region replication, locality-aware quorum"]
    S100 --> S100b["Conflict resolution across regions (eventual)"]
    S1 --> S10 --> S100

Adding nodes moves only ~1/N of the data (consistent hashing), so scaling is near-linear and low-disruption. Virtual nodes keep load even. Multi-region adds cross-region replication and the hard problem of conflict resolution across regions, typically eventual consistency with the application reconciling conflicts.

65.2.14 Security

Authentication and authorization at the client-to-coordinator boundary (which services may access which keyspaces), encryption in transit between nodes and from clients, and encryption at rest. Within the cluster, nodes trust each other, so the cluster network must be isolated. Multi-tenant keyspaces need isolation so one tenant cannot read another's keys.

65.2.15 Failure scenarios

Failure Detection Impact Mitigation Effect
Single node down Gossip failure detection That node's replicas unavailable N-1 replicas serve; hinted handoff holds its writes None (quorum still met)
Network partition Nodes unreachable across the split Split brain risk Tunable: favor availability (both sides write, reconcile later) or consistency (minority side refuses) Per CAP choice
Concurrent conflicting writes Diverging versions Which value wins? Vector clocks detect; resolve (LWW or app reconcile) Possible lost update under LWW
Replica permanently lost Health, capacity Under-replicated keys Re-replicate to a new node; anti-entropy Restored durability
Clock skew (last-write-wins) Monitoring Wrong write "wins" by bad timestamp Prefer vector clocks; sync clocks (NTP); be wary of LWW Possible lost write
Hot key Per-key load One replica set overloaded More virtual nodes; client cache; split hot key Mitigated
Rebalancing storm (node flapping) Topology churn Excess data movement Dampen membership changes; hysteresis Stable

65.2.16 Observability

Metrics: per-node ops/s and latency, quorum success/failure rate, replica lag and divergence, hinted-handoff queue size, anti-entropy repair volume, ring balance (per-node load), failure-detector state. Alerts: under-replicated keys, quorum failures, growing hinted-handoff backlog (a replica down too long), ring imbalance. Dashboards: cluster health, per-node load, consistency (divergence/repair rates).

65.2.17 Deployment

Nodes as a stateful cluster (StatefulSet on Kubernetes, or dedicated hosts) across multiple availability zones so an AZ loss does not lose quorum. Careful rolling upgrades (one node at a time, respecting quorum). Topology (replication factor, virtual nodes) as config. Adding/removing nodes is an operational procedure that triggers controlled rebalancing.

65.2.18 Cost considerations

Dominated by the storage and compute for N copies of the data across nodes (3x replication triples storage) and cross-AZ/cross-region network traffic for replication and quorum (cross-AZ data transfer is a real cost driver). Higher replication and stronger quorum cost more (more copies, more cross-node traffic). The cost is justified only when the availability and scale genuinely require a distributed store over a replicated single database.

65.2.19 Tradeoffs

  • Availability vs consistency (CAP): the core tradeoff, made tunable per operation via R/W quorums; during a partition you cannot have both, so you choose per operation.
  • Consistent hashing (minimal data movement on topology change) over modulo hashing (rehashes everything): essential for elastic scaling.
  • Eventual consistency with conflict resolution over strong consistency everywhere: buys availability and latency at the cost of possible stale reads and reconciliation complexity.
  • Masterless (no single point of failure, any node coordinates) over a primary/replica design: higher availability at the cost of conflict-resolution complexity.
  • Last-write-wins vs vector clocks: LWW is simple but can silently lose writes under clock skew; vector clocks are correct but more complex.

65.2.20 Alternative architectures

Use an existing distributed store (DynamoDB, Cassandra, Part 62): the honest default — these systems embody exactly this design, battle-tested; building your own is justified only by a very specific need, because a correct distributed KV store is extremely hard to get right (conflict resolution and partition handling are subtle). This is the strong recommendation: understand the design (to use these well and to interview), but use a proven implementation unless you have a compelling reason not to.

A replicated single database (PostgreSQL with replicas, Part 14): if your scale fits one primary plus replicas and you need transactions and queries, this is simpler and gives you more (relational power, strong consistency) than a KV store. Many systems that reach for a distributed KV store would be better served by PostgreSQL plus caching — the Part 62 lesson applies.

Strongly-consistent distributed store (a consensus-based system using Raft/Paxos, like etcd or Spanner-style): when you need strong consistency across nodes rather than tunable eventual consistency, a consensus protocol provides it, at the cost of lower availability during partitions and higher latency. The right choice depends on whether the workload needs availability (Dynamo-style) or strong consistency (consensus-style) during a partition.

65.3 Unique ID Generator

65.3.1 Requirements

A unique ID generator produces unique identifiers for records across a distributed system — order ids, message ids, event ids — at high throughput, with no coordination bottleneck, and ideally roughly time-ordered (so ids sort by creation time). The users are every service that creates records. The design probes distributed-systems fundamentals in a compact form: how do many machines generate globally unique ids without a central coordinator becoming a bottleneck or single point of failure, and what tradeoffs (sortability, size, predictability, clock dependence) does each approach make.

Imagine many ticket counters across a country, each needing to issue unique ticket numbers without phoning a head office for every ticket. If each counter has a unique counter-number baked into every ticket it prints, plus the time and a local sequence, every ticket is globally unique with no phone call. The counters are machines; the baked-in counter-number is the machine id; the time plus sequence makes each counter's tickets unique and roughly time-ordered. That is the Snowflake idea.

65.3.2 Functional requirements

  1. Generate globally unique ids with no duplicates, ever.
  2. High throughput: thousands to millions of ids per second across the system.
  3. No central coordination on the hot path (no bottleneck, no single point of failure).
  4. Roughly time-ordered (sortable by creation time) — valuable for database locality and debugging.
  5. Fit a reasonable size (ideally a 64-bit integer, or a compact string).
  6. Optionally, not trivially guessable/enumerable (do not leak volume or allow enumeration).

65.3.3 Non-functional requirements

Property Target Why
Uniqueness Absolute (zero collisions) A duplicate id corrupts data
Throughput Millions/second system-wide Every record creation needs one
Latency Microseconds (local generation) On the write hot path
Availability No single point of failure Cannot stop creating records
Sortability Roughly time-ordered DB index locality, debugging
Size 64-bit int or compact string Storage and index efficiency

65.3.4 Constraints

  • Must work across many machines without per-id coordination.
  • Clock-based approaches depend on time; clock skew and backward jumps are a real hazard.
  • 64-bit integer is the ideal size (efficient as a primary key); UUID (128-bit) is larger but needs no coordination at all.
  • Sortable ids improve database index locality (Part 12) but can leak ordering/volume information.

65.3.5 Capacity estimation

Quantity Assumption Calculation Result
ID generation rate System-wide peak given 1,000,000 ids/second
Bits needed for uniqueness/sec log2(1M) ~20 bits of per-second capacity
Snowflake layout (64 bits) timestamp + machine + sequence 41 + 10 + 12 see below
Timestamp range (41 bits, ms) 2^41 ms ~69 years
Machines (10 bits) 2^10 1,024 machines
Sequence per ms per machine (12 bits) 2^12 4,096 ids/ms/machine = 4M/s/machine

A 64-bit Snowflake id comfortably provides millions of ids per second across a thousand machines for decades. These numbers are what make the Snowflake layout work.

65.3.6 API design

Operation Signature Notes
Generate nextId(): bigint Local, microseconds, no network on the hot path
(Snowflake) configure machine id assigned at startup From config/coordination service

Generation is a local call, not a network request, which is the whole point — no round trip per id.

65.3.7 Data model

Snowflake-style 64-bit ID layout:

 | 1 bit | 41 bits timestamp (ms since epoch) | 10 bits machine id | 12 bits sequence |
   sign    ~69 years of milliseconds             1,024 machines      4,096 per ms

Example: id = (timestamp_ms << 22) | (machine_id << 12) | sequence
  - timestamp first -> ids sort roughly by time
  - machine_id -> uniqueness across machines (no coordination per id)
  - sequence -> uniqueness within a machine within one millisecond

The layout encodes time (for sortability), machine (for cross-machine uniqueness without coordination), and a per-millisecond sequence (for within-machine, within-ms uniqueness). No two machines share a machine id, so no two ids collide.

65.3.8 High-level architecture

flowchart LR
    APP["Service instance"] --> GEN["Local ID generator (Snowflake)"]
    GEN --> CLK["System clock (ms)"]
    GEN --> MID["Assigned machine id"]
    GEN --> SEQ["Per-ms sequence counter"]
    COORD["Machine-id assignment (startup only)"] -.-> MID

Each service instance generates ids locally from its clock, its assigned machine id, and an in-memory per-millisecond sequence. The only coordination is assigning a unique machine id at startup (from a coordination service like ZooKeeper/etcd, or from config/infrastructure), which happens once, not per id. The hot path is purely local arithmetic.

65.3.9 Component design and the approaches

Approach How Pros Cons
Snowflake-style timestamp + machine id + sequence, 64-bit Sortable, no per-id coordination, compact Clock-dependent (skew/backward jumps), needs machine-id assignment
UUIDv4 128-bit random Zero coordination, unguessable Not sortable, 128-bit (index locality worse), larger
UUIDv7 128-bit, time-ordered prefix + random Sortable (like Snowflake) and zero coordination 128-bit (larger than Snowflake's 64)
Database sequence DB auto-increment / sequence Simple, sortable, no collisions The database is a coordination point; hard across shards; enumerable
Ticket server / batched ranges A service hands out ranges of ids No per-id DB hit (batch), sortable A service to run; a range is lost if a holder dies

UUIDv7 deserves emphasis: it is a modern standard that combines UUID's zero-coordination property with time-ordering (a timestamp prefix plus randomness), giving the sortability of Snowflake without needing machine-id assignment, at the cost of 128 bits versus Snowflake's 64. For many systems today, UUIDv7 is the simplest good default — sortable, unique with no coordination, and widely supported.

65.3.10 Deep dive: clock skew and database sequences at scale

Clock skew and backward jumps are Snowflake's main hazard. The timestamp component assumes a monotonic clock; if the machine's clock jumps backward (NTP correction, VM pause), the generator could produce an id with an earlier timestamp than a previous one, risking a duplicate within the same ms/sequence space. Defenses: detect a backward jump and either wait until the clock catches up, or refuse to generate until time advances, and use the per-ms sequence to absorb many ids within one millisecond. A generator must never silently produce a smaller timestamp than one it already used.

Database sequences at scale: a single database auto-increment is simple and sortable but makes the database a coordination point and a bottleneck, and does not work cleanly across shards (two shards' sequences collide). Scaling options: give each shard a different sequence offset/step (shard 1: 1, 3, 5...; shard 2: 2, 4, 6...), or use a ticket server that hands out ranges so each instance gets a block of ids and only talks to the server once per block (amortizing the coordination). But sequences are enumerable (an id reveals roughly how many were created and lets an attacker guess neighbors), which is why public-facing ids often avoid raw sequences.

65.3.11 Caching

Not applicable in the usual sense; the per-ms sequence counter is in-memory per instance. A ticket-server approach caches a pre-fetched range of ids locally so most generations need no network.

65.3.12 Messaging

Not applicable on the hot path (generation is local). Machine-id assignment at startup uses a coordination service (ZooKeeper/etcd) or infrastructure-provided unique values (pod ordinal, instance metadata).

65.3.13 Scaling

flowchart TB
    S1["1x: thousands/s"] --> S1a["Snowflake or UUIDv7, local generation"]
    S10["10x: more instances"] --> S10a["More machine ids (within the 10-bit space)"]
    S100["100x: millions/s, many regions"] --> S100a["Larger machine-id space or UUIDv7 (no id assignment)"]
    S1 --> S10 --> S100

Because generation is local and coordination-free (except startup), it scales trivially by adding instances — each with its own machine id (Snowflake) or no coordination at all (UUIDv7/v4). The only scaling limit for Snowflake is the machine-id bit space (1,024 with 10 bits); more machines need more bits or UUIDv7.

65.3.14 Security

If ids must not be guessable or enumerable (exposing ids publicly), avoid raw sequences (enumerable) and consider UUIDv4 (random, unguessable) or encrypting/obfuscating a Snowflake id for external use while keeping the sortable form internally. A sortable id leaks creation order and volume, which may be sensitive (a competitor can estimate your order volume from id gaps), so public ids are often random or obfuscated even when internal ids are sortable.

65.3.15 Failure scenarios

Failure Detection Impact Mitigation Effect
Clock jumps backward (Snowflake) Timestamp < last used Risk of duplicate id Wait for clock to catch up, or refuse to generate until time advances Brief pause, no duplicate
Two machines share a machine id Collision monitoring Duplicate ids Strict unique machine-id assignment (coordination service) Prevented
Sequence exhausted in one ms Sequence overflow Cannot issue more this ms Wait until next ms (4,096/ms is usually ample) Microsecond wait
Ticket server down (range approach) Generation errors Instances run out of their range Pre-fetch next range early; fall back to another approach Degraded, not stopped
DB sequence bottleneck (sequence approach) Latency on create Slow record creation Batch ranges, per-shard offsets, or switch approach Mitigated
ID space exhaustion (41-bit timestamp) ~69 years out Eventually Plan epoch/layout; far-future problem None near-term

65.3.16 Observability

Metrics: id generation rate, per-ms sequence usage (near-exhaustion warning), clock-skew/backward-jump events (critical alert for Snowflake), machine-id assignment conflicts, ticket-range consumption rate. Alerts: any backward-clock event, any machine-id collision, sequence saturation. These are small but critical signals — a clock problem or id collision is a data-integrity emergency.

65.3.17 Deployment

Snowflake needs a reliable machine-id assignment at startup (from a coordination service or infrastructure-unique value like a pod ordinal), and reliable time sync (NTP) with backward-jump handling. UUIDv7/v4 need neither, which is why they are operationally simpler. Ensure the id approach is consistent across all services that must not collide.

65.3.18 Cost considerations

Negligible compute (local arithmetic). The real cost consideration is indirect: id size and sortability affect database index size and locality (Part 12) — a 64-bit sortable Snowflake id gives better index locality (sequential inserts) than a 128-bit random UUIDv4 (random inserts scatter across the index, hurting cache locality and causing page splits). This is why UUIDv7 (sortable) is preferred over UUIDv4 for primary keys: it keeps the index-locality benefit while needing no coordination.

65.3.19 Tradeoffs

  • Snowflake (64-bit, sortable, coordination-free hot path) vs UUIDv7 (128-bit, sortable, no coordination at all): Snowflake is more compact but needs machine-id assignment and is clock-sensitive; UUIDv7 is larger but operationally simpler. Both are sortable.
  • Sortable ids (index locality, debuggability) vs random ids (unguessable, no ordering leak): sortable helps the database and operators but leaks creation order/volume; choose by whether ids are public.
  • UUIDv7 over UUIDv4 for primary keys: sortability gives far better index locality (sequential inserts) than random UUIDv4, at the same size.
  • Database sequence (simple) vs distributed generator (scalable): sequences are simplest but bottleneck and do not shard; use them until scale or sharding forces a distributed approach.

65.3.20 Alternative architectures

Just use UUIDv7 (or the database's native sortable UUID support): for the vast majority of systems, UUIDv7 is the right default — unique with zero coordination, time-ordered for index locality, widely supported, no clock-skew handling or machine-id assignment to operate. Build the fancy Snowflake generator only when the 64-bit size genuinely matters (huge tables where the extra 8 bytes per row across billions of rows is significant). This is the pragmatic recommendation: understand Snowflake (for interviews and the rare case), default to UUIDv7.

Database auto-increment: for a single-database system at moderate scale, the database's own sequence is the simplest correct choice — no generator to build. Reach for distributed generation only when you shard or outgrow the single database's coordination.

Ticket server with batched ranges: a central service hands out id ranges to instances, which generate locally from their range. A middle ground that avoids per-id coordination while keeping ids compact and sortable, at the cost of running the service and losing a range if a holder dies.

65.4 Ticket and Seat Booking System

65.4.1 Requirements

A ticket and seat booking system lets users browse available seats for an event, hold one or more seats while they pay, and confirm the booking — without ever selling the same seat twice, even under intense contention when thousands of people rush for a popular event the moment tickets go on sale. The users are ticket buyers, and the business is event organizers. This design is the sharpest test of concurrency control under contention: the hard part is not scale in general but the hot moment when a popular event sells out and everyone wants the same few good seats at once.

Imagine a theatre box office on the morning tickets for a sold-out show go on sale. A crowd rushes the counter, all wanting seat A1. The clerk must give A1 to exactly one person, briefly reserve it while they find their wallet, release it if they do not pay in time, and never, ever hand the same seat to two people. The counter is the booking service; the brief reservation is the seat hold; the time limit is the hold expiry; "never two people" is the concurrency control that this whole design exists to guarantee.

65.4.2 Functional requirements

  1. Browse events and see which seats are available, held, or booked.
  2. Hold one or more seats for a short, fixed time while the user pays.
  3. Confirm the booking by paying within the hold window; the seats become booked.
  4. Release held seats automatically when the hold expires (the user did not pay).
  5. Never sell the same seat twice (the absolute invariant).
  6. Handle intense contention on popular events (thousands competing for the same seats).
  7. Handle payment coupling: the seat is only truly sold when payment succeeds.

65.4.3 Non-functional requirements

Property Target Why
Correctness A seat is sold at most once, always Double-selling is a serious business failure
Hold latency p99 low (hundreds of ms) Users expect an instant "seat held"
Contention handling Thousands competing for one event without collapse The on-sale moment is the whole challenge
Availability High during on-sale spikes The spike is exactly when the business needs it up
Hold expiry accuracy Holds release promptly (seconds after expiry) Expired holds must free seats for others
Consistency Strong for seat state (no double-sell) This is a correctness, not a performance, property

65.4.4 Constraints

  • The no-double-sell invariant is non-negotiable and requires strong consistency on seat state — this is a case where you cannot trade consistency for availability on the seat itself (contrast the KV store, 65.2).
  • Extreme contention is concentrated: a popular event's best seats are a hot row/key that thousands hit simultaneously (the hot-row problem, Part 13).
  • Payment is external, slow and can fail; the seat must be held during payment and released or confirmed based on the outcome.
  • Spikes are massive and brief (the on-sale instant), so the system must absorb a thundering herd without over-provisioning for the quiet rest of the time.

65.4.5 Capacity estimation

Quantity Assumption Calculation Result
Popular event seats A large venue given 50,000 seats
Users rushing at on-sale Demand far exceeds supply given 500,000 users in the first minutes
Peak requests Browsing + hold attempts 100,000+ requests/second at on-sale
Hold window Time to pay given 10 minutes
Contention on best seats Everyone wants the front rows thousands hitting the same ~100 seats
Payment time External provider given seconds to a minute

The numbers say: the system must handle a 100,000 rps spike concentrated on a tiny set of hot seats, with strong consistency so none is double-sold, holds that expire reliably, and a queue to tame the thundering herd. The contention, not the total scale, is the design driver.

65.4.6 API design

Method Path Request Response Status Idempotent Notes
GET /events/{id}/seats seat map with states 200 Yes Available/held/booked
POST /events/{id}/holds { seatIds[] } + Idempotency-Key { holdId, expiresAt } 201, 409 (taken), 429 Yes (idempotency key) Creates a hold
POST /holds/{holdId}/confirm { paymentToken } + Idempotency-Key booking 200, 409, 410 (expired) Yes Pay and confirm
DELETE /holds/{holdId} 204 Yes Release early
GET /holds/{holdId} hold status 200, 404, 410 Yes Check before confirm

Idempotency keys (Part 18) are essential: users on flaky mobile connections retry the hold and confirm requests, and a retry must not create a second hold or a double charge.

65.4.7 Data model

erDiagram
    EVENT ||--o{ SEAT : has
    SEAT ||--o| HOLD : currently_held_by
    SEAT ||--o| BOOKING : sold_as
    HOLD ||--o| BOOKING : becomes
    EVENT { uuid id PK, text name, timestamptz starts_at }
    SEAT {
        uuid id PK
        uuid event_id FK
        text label
        text status
        uuid hold_id
        timestamptz hold_expires_at
    }
    HOLD {
        uuid id PK
        uuid user_id
        timestamptz expires_at
        text status
    }
    BOOKING {
        uuid id PK
        uuid hold_id FK
        uuid user_id
        text payment_id
        timestamptz confirmed_at
    }
CREATE TABLE seats (
  id               uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  event_id         uuid NOT NULL,
  label            text NOT NULL,
  status           text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'available'
                   CHECK (status IN ('available','held','booked')),
  hold_id          uuid,
  hold_expires_at  timestamptz,
  version          integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,          -- optimistic locking
  UNIQUE (event_id, label)
);
-- Serves the expiry sweeper; partial index stays small
CREATE INDEX seats_hold_expiry_idx ON seats (hold_expires_at) WHERE status = 'held';

The seats table is the source of truth, and a seat's status plus version is where the no-double-sell guarantee lives.

65.4.8 High-level architecture

flowchart LR
    U["User"] --> WR["Waiting room / queue (for hot events)"]
    WR --> API["Booking API"]
    API --> SEATSVC["Seat service (hold/confirm)"]
    SEATSVC --> PG["PostgreSQL (seats, source of truth)"]
    SEATSVC --> RED["Redis (seat-state cache, hold locks)"]
    API --> PAY["Payment service (external)"]
    SWEEP["Hold-expiry sweeper"] --> PG
    SWEEP --> RED

For a hot event, users first pass through a waiting room / virtual queue that admits them to the booking API at a controlled rate, taming the thundering herd. The seat service performs holds and confirms against PostgreSQL (the source of truth for seat state) with strong concurrency control, caching the seat map in Redis for browsing. Payment is external; the hold spans the payment. A sweeper releases expired holds.

65.4.9 Component design

Component Responsibility
Waiting room / queue Admit users to the on-sale at a controlled rate (thundering-herd control)
Seat service Hold and confirm seats with strong concurrency control (no double-sell)
Seat state store PostgreSQL: the authoritative seat status with locking/versioning
Seat map cache Redis: the seat map for browsing (eventually consistent is fine for browsing)
Payment integration Charge during the hold; confirm or release based on outcome
Hold-expiry sweeper Release holds past their expiry, freeing seats

65.4.10 Deep dive: the no-double-sell concurrency control

This is the heart of the design. Holding a seat must be atomic and exclusive: among thousands trying to hold seat A1, exactly one succeeds. The robust approach is a conditional update in PostgreSQL that only succeeds if the seat is currently available (Part 13 on locking and the hot-row problem):

-- Atomic hold: only succeeds if the seat is still available.
-- If two requests race, only one updates a row (0 rows updated = lost the race -> 409).
UPDATE seats
   SET status = 'held', hold_id = $1, hold_expires_at = now() + interval '10 minutes',
       version = version + 1
 WHERE id = $2 AND status = 'available';
-- rows affected = 1 -> you got the seat; = 0 -> someone else did -> return 409

The WHERE status = 'available' makes the update conditional and atomic: PostgreSQL serializes the row update, so exactly one of the racing transactions finds the seat available and claims it; the rest update zero rows and are told the seat is taken. This is optimistic concurrency on the seat row and is the core guarantee. For multiple seats in one hold, do them in one transaction (all-or-nothing) with consistent lock ordering to avoid deadlocks (Part 13).

Confirming turns a valid (unexpired) hold into a booking, coupled with payment:

-- Confirm only if the hold is still valid (not expired, still held by this hold).
UPDATE seats SET status = 'booked'
 WHERE hold_id = $1 AND status = 'held' AND hold_expires_at > now();
-- then record the booking with the payment id, in the same transaction

Payment coupling is the subtle part: the seat is held, then payment is attempted (external, slow, fallible), then the seat is confirmed or released. The flow must handle payment success after hold expiry (rare race: hold expired and seat was resold — the payment must be refunded and the user told) and payment failure (release the hold). Idempotency keys ensure a retried confirm does not double-charge. The invariant throughout: a seat moves available -> held -> booked only via atomic conditional updates, so it is never booked twice.

65.4.11 Caching

The seat map for browsing is cached in Redis (eventually consistent is fine — a user seeing a seat as available that was just held will simply fail the atomic hold and get a 409, which is correct). The hold/confirm operations go to PostgreSQL, not the cache, because they need strong consistency. This split — cache the browse, verify at the write — is the Part 16 pattern: the hot read path is cached, the correctness-critical write path hits the source of truth.

65.4.12 Messaging

A hold expiry can be scheduled (a delayed message or a sweeper). Booking confirmations and cancellations emit events (outbox, Part 19) for downstream (email, inventory, analytics). The waiting room admits users by releasing queue tokens at a controlled rate.

65.4.13 Scaling

flowchart TB
    S1["1x: normal events"] --> S1a["Direct API, atomic seat updates in PG"]
    S10["10x: popular events"] --> S10a["Waiting room/queue tames the on-sale spike"]
    S10 --> S10b["Seat map cached, API autoscaled"]
    S100["100x: mega events (festival on-sale)"] --> S100a["Strict virtual queue admitting at controlled rate"]
    S100 --> S100b["Partition by event, hot-event isolation"]
    S1 --> S10 --> S100

The challenge is the concentrated spike, not steady throughput. The waiting room/queue is the key scaling tool: rather than let 500,000 users hit the booking API at once, admit them at a rate the system can handle, so the atomic seat updates never face more concurrency than PostgreSQL can serialize comfortably. Partitioning by event isolates a hot event so it does not affect others. The seat updates themselves are fast; the queue prevents them from being swamped.

65.4.14 Security

Prevent scalping and bots: rate-limit per user, require authentication, CAPTCHA or bot detection at the waiting room, limit seats per user per event. Prevent hold abuse (holding seats to deny others without buying) via per-user hold limits and the expiry. Ensure authorization (a user can only confirm their own hold). Protect against payment fraud (Part 23). The waiting room itself must be fair and resistant to queue-jumping.

65.4.15 Failure scenarios

Failure Detection Impact Mitigation Effect
Two users race for one seat Normal contention Only one can win Atomic conditional update; loser gets 409 Correct: one seat, one buyer
Hold expires before payment Sweeper Seat released, user pays late Confirm checks expiry; if seat resold, refund and apologize Rare, handled
Payment succeeds after hold expired Payment callback vs seat state User paid but seat gone Refund automatically, notify user Rare race, contained
Payment fails Provider response Hold wasted Release hold immediately, free the seat Seat freed promptly
Thundering herd at on-sale Traffic spike API/DB overload Waiting room admits at controlled rate Smoothed
Sweeper down Expiry lag alert Expired holds not released Redundant sweeper; confirm also checks expiry Degraded, self-healing
Duplicate hold/confirm (retry) Idempotency key Double hold/charge risk Idempotency keys dedupe None
DB hot row on the best seats Lock contention on A1 Serialization queue on one row Queue admits slowly; contention is on a fast update Bounded

65.4.16 Observability

Metrics: hold success/failure (409) rate, confirm success rate, hold-to-confirm conversion, hold expiry rate, payment success/failure, waiting-room queue depth and admit rate, seat-update latency and contention, double-sell count (must always be zero — alert immediately on any). Alerts: any double-sell (critical), sweeper lag (holds not releasing), payment-after-expiry races, queue overload. Dashboards: on-sale health (admit rate, holds/s, conversions), inventory (available/held/booked per event).

65.4.17 Deployment

Autoscaled stateless booking API; PostgreSQL (the source of truth) with enough capacity for the serialized seat updates; Redis for the seat-map cache and queue; a redundant sweeper (CronJob plus confirm-time expiry check as backup). The waiting room is deployed ahead of popular on-sales and tuned for the expected demand. Load-test the on-sale path specifically, because the spike is the whole risk.

65.4.18 Cost considerations

The system is quiet most of the time and spikes hard at on-sale, so autoscaling and the waiting room (which smooths the spike) control cost — you do not provision permanently for the peak. PostgreSQL must handle the serialized seat updates during the spike (the hot-row throughput), which is modest per update but concentrated. The waiting room lets you serve a huge demand spike with far less infrastructure than handling it all at once would require, which is its cost benefit as well as its correctness benefit.

65.4.19 Tradeoffs

  • Strong consistency on seat state (no double-sell) over availability: here, unlike the KV store (65.2), correctness wins absolutely — a seat's state must be strongly consistent, so we accept that seat updates serialize on the hot row.
  • Waiting room/queue (controlled admission) over letting everyone in: smooths the thundering herd and protects correctness, at the cost of users waiting in a queue (which, done well, is a better experience than errors).
  • Optimistic conditional update (atomic, no explicit lock held across the hold) over pessimistic row locks held for the whole payment: we do not hold a database lock during the slow external payment (that would be disastrous for throughput); instead the seat is marked held and the lock is released, with expiry handling the abandonment.
  • Cache the browse, verify at the write: eventually-consistent seat map for browsing (fast, scalable) with strongly-consistent holds (correct), accepting that a browsed-available seat may fail the hold (a correct 409).

65.4.20 Alternative architectures

Redis-based holds with atomic operations: hold seats via atomic Redis operations (a SET NX lock per seat with a TTL that is the hold expiry), with PostgreSQL as the durable record on confirm. Redis's atomic ops and native TTL make holds and expiry fast and simple, handling huge contention in memory; the tradeoff is Redis is not the durable source of truth, so you reconcile to PostgreSQL on confirm and handle Redis failures carefully. This is a common real approach for extreme-contention on-sales.

Pessimistic locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE): lock the seat row during the hold. Simple and correct for low contention, but holding locks under the on-sale thundering herd causes severe lock contention and does not scale to the spike; the optimistic conditional update is preferred for high contention. Pessimistic locking is fine for normal events and simpler to reason about.

Partitioned/sharded by event with per-event capacity: for a platform with many simultaneous on-sales, partition by event so each hot event is isolated on its own capacity and cannot starve others. Combined with the waiting room, this is how large ticketing platforms handle many big on-sales at once.

65.5 Closing: what these four designs teach

The four systems in this Part each stress a different core skill, and together they round out the distributed-systems toolkit that Part 40 began. The web crawler is about taming an unbounded, adversarial space with politeness, deduplication and a prioritized frontier — the discipline of being a good citizen while covering enormous ground. The distributed key-value store is the heart of distributed systems: partitioning by consistent hashing, replication, and the quorum knob that makes the CAP tradeoff tunable per operation — the design behind every NoSQL store in Part 62. The unique ID generator shows that even a tiny component is a distributed-systems problem, with real tradeoffs between coordination, sortability, size and clock dependence, and a pragmatic modern default in UUIDv7. The ticket booking system is the sharpest concurrency problem in the book: an absolute no-double-sell invariant under a concentrated thundering herd, solved with atomic conditional updates and a waiting room rather than by trading away correctness.

Read across them, the recurring senior lessons are clear. Contention and coordination, not raw throughput, are usually the hard part — the booking system's spike on a few seats and the KV store's quorum coordination are the real challenges, not the gross request count. The CAP tradeoff is a per-system choice: the KV store makes it tunable and often favors availability, while the booking system refuses to trade consistency on a seat because double-selling is unacceptable, and naming which invariant cannot be relaxed is the key design decision. The database's atomic operations and constraints are your best concurrency control, as the conditional seat update shows. And the "when not to build" alternative is always present: use a proven distributed KV store rather than writing your own, default to UUIDv7 rather than a bespoke Snowflake, crawl one site with a single simple process rather than a distributed fleet — build the complex version only when a specific requirement genuinely demands it.

Senior Checklist — Part 65

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can design a web crawler with politeness, deduplication (Bloom filter + store) and a prioritized, durable frontier
  • I can explain consistent hashing, replication, and how R/W quorums make consistency tunable (R + W > N)
  • I can reason about conflict resolution (vector clocks vs last-write-wins) and partition behavior in a distributed KV store
  • I can compare Snowflake, UUIDv4, UUIDv7 and database sequences and handle clock skew
  • I can guarantee no double-sell with an atomic conditional update and handle hold expiry and payment coupling
  • I can use a waiting room/queue to tame a thundering herd without trading away correctness
  • For each system I can name the alternative that avoids building it and when to prefer it

Part 65 — Key Takeaways

  • A web crawler is a politeness and deduplication problem as much as a throughput one: obey robots.txt and per-domain rate limits absolutely, dedup with a Bloom filter backed by an exact store, and keep a durable, prioritized, domain-partitioned frontier.
  • Consistent hashing places keys on a ring so adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the data; virtual nodes keep load even — this is what makes a distributed store elastic.
  • Replication plus quorum (R/W) makes consistency tunable per operation: R + W > N guarantees a read sees the latest write (strong), lower values trade consistency for availability and latency — the CAP tradeoff made operational.
  • High availability under partitions means accepting conflicting writes and reconciling them (vector clocks, read repair, anti-entropy, hinted handoff); last-write-wins is simple but can silently lose writes under clock skew.
  • A correct distributed KV store is extremely hard; use a proven one (DynamoDB, Cassandra) or even just PostgreSQL plus caching unless a specific requirement forces you to build one.
  • A unique ID generator is a distributed-systems problem: Snowflake gives compact, sortable, coordination-free ids but depends on the clock and machine-id assignment; UUIDv7 is the pragmatic modern default — sortable, zero coordination, at 128 bits.
  • Sortable ids (Snowflake, UUIDv7) give far better database index locality than random UUIDv4; handle clock backward-jumps in any time-based generator, and avoid raw sequences for public ids (they are enumerable).
  • The ticket-booking no-double-sell invariant is guaranteed by an atomic conditional update (WHERE status = 'available'), where exactly one racing transaction claims the seat and the rest get a correct 409 — the database's atomic row update is the concurrency control.
  • A waiting room/virtual queue tames the on-sale thundering herd by admitting users at a controlled rate, protecting both correctness and cost without permanently provisioning for the peak.
  • Across all four: contention and coordination are the hard part, not raw throughput; name the invariant that cannot be relaxed (a seat sold once) to decide where strong consistency is mandatory; and always consider the alternative that avoids building the complex system at all.

Part 66 — More System Designs II

This Part continues the system-design case studies, using the same method and twenty-section template as Part 40 and Part 65. If you have not read section 40.0, read it first for the nine-move method and the template. The four systems here each probe a distinct skill: a leaderboard and top-K system (Redis sorted sets, approximate top-K, sharded leaderboards), collaborative document editing (operational transform versus CRDTs, presence, offline sync), proximity search for nearby drivers and restaurants (geohash, quadtrees, PostGIS, high-rate location updates), and ad-click and metrics aggregation (high-volume ingestion, exactly-once counting, windowed aggregation, reconciliation). Together with Parts 40 and 65, these complete a broad library of worked designs.

66.1 Leaderboard and Top-K

66.1.1 Requirements

A leaderboard ranks users by a score — game scores, points, sales, engagement — and answers "what is the top N?", "what rank is this user?", and "who is near this user's rank?", updating in real time as scores change. The users are players (seeing their rank), the product (showing leaderboards), and sometimes analytics (top-K items by some metric). The design probes ranking at scale: how to maintain and query rankings efficiently when scores change constantly and the user base is huge, and when exact ranking becomes too expensive, how to approximate the top-K.

Imagine a scoreboard at a stadium that must instantly reflect every point scored and, on demand, show the top ten, your position, and the players just above and below you — for millions of competitors. Recomputing the whole ranking on every point would be impossible; the scoreboard keeps players in sorted order as scores change so any ranking question is answered by looking at a position in the sorted list. That sorted-order structure is what a Redis sorted set provides.

66.1.2 Functional requirements

  1. Update a user's score (set or increment) in real time.
  2. Get the top N users by score.
  3. Get a specific user's rank and score.
  4. Get the users ranked near a given user (the window around their rank).
  5. Support time-scoped leaderboards (all-time, this week, today).
  6. Scale to millions of users and frequent score updates.
  7. (Top-K variant) Find the top-K items from a high-volume stream (most-viewed products) approximately when exact is too costly.

66.1.3 Non-functional requirements

Property Target Why
Update latency p99 low (single-digit ms) Scores change constantly, in real time
Rank query latency p99 low (single-digit ms) Users check their rank frequently
Scale Millions of users, thousands of updates/second Popular games/apps
Freshness Rank reflects a score change within ~1s "Real-time" leaderboard
Accuracy Exact where feasible; approximate top-K acceptable for streams Exact ranking is costly at extreme scale

66.1.4 Constraints

  • Ranking must be fast for both updates and queries; recomputing a full sort per query is infeasible at millions of users.
  • Score updates are frequent and must not lose updates.
  • Exact top-K over a high-volume stream (billions of events) is expensive in memory; approximation (count-min sketch) trades a little accuracy for huge savings.
  • Time-scoped leaderboards (weekly) need expiry/reset without disrupting the all-time board.

66.1.5 Capacity estimation

Quantity Assumption Calculation Result
Users on a leaderboard Popular game given 10 million
Score updates Peak given 10,000/second
Rank queries Peak given 50,000/second
Redis sorted set memory ~70-100 B per member 10M x ~80 B about 800 MB per leaderboard
Top-K stream (approximate) high-volume product views given 1,000,000 events/second
Count-min sketch memory fixed, independent of item count a few MB (vs tracking every item)

The numbers say: a Redis sorted set holds 10M-user leaderboards in under a GB with O(log n) updates and rank queries, handling the update/query rates easily; but exact top-K over a 1M-event/second stream of many distinct items needs approximation (count-min sketch) to stay in a few MB rather than tracking counts for every item.

66.1.6 API design

Method Path Request Response Notes
POST /leaderboards/{id}/scores { userId, score } or { userId, delta } updated rank Set or increment
GET /leaderboards/{id}/top?n=10 top N users Top-N
GET /leaderboards/{id}/users/{userId} { rank, score } User's rank
GET /leaderboards/{id}/users/{userId}/neighbors?window=5 users around the user's rank Window around user

66.1.7 Data model

Redis sorted set (ZSET) per leaderboard:
  key: "leaderboard:game42:weekly"
  members: userIds, scores: their score
  ZADD leaderboard:game42:weekly 1500 user:7     -- set/update a score (O(log n))
  ZINCRBY leaderboard:game42:weekly 50 user:7     -- increment a score
  ZREVRANGE leaderboard:game42:weekly 0 9 WITHSCORES  -- top 10 (O(log n + k))
  ZREVRANK leaderboard:game42:weekly user:7       -- a user's rank (O(log n))
  ZREVRANGE ... around the user's rank            -- neighbors

Durable source of truth in PostgreSQL (scores table) for recovery:
  scores(leaderboard_id, user_id, score, updated_at)  -- rebuild the ZSET from this

The Redis sorted set is the fast ranking structure; PostgreSQL holds the durable scores so the sorted set can be rebuilt if Redis is lost (Redis is a cache/index here, not the sole source of truth for anything that matters, per Part 16).

66.1.8 High-level architecture

flowchart LR
    U["Client"] --> API["Leaderboard API"]
    API --> RZ["Redis sorted sets (ranking)"]
    API --> PG["PostgreSQL (durable scores)"]
    STREAM["High-volume event stream"] --> CMS["Count-min sketch (approx top-K)"]
    API --> CMS
    REBUILD["Rebuild job"] --> PG
    REBUILD --> RZ

Score updates go to both Redis (for instant ranking) and PostgreSQL (for durability), and rank queries hit Redis. For approximate top-K over a high-volume stream, a count-min sketch counts items in fixed memory. A rebuild job can reconstruct the Redis sorted sets from PostgreSQL after a Redis loss.

66.1.9 Component design

Component Responsibility
Leaderboard API Handle score updates and rank queries
Redis sorted sets Maintain sorted ranking; answer top-N, rank, neighbors fast
PostgreSQL scores Durable source of truth for scores; enables rebuild
Count-min sketch Approximate counts for top-K over high-volume streams in fixed memory
Rebuild job Reconstruct Redis sorted sets from PostgreSQL on recovery
Time-scope manager Create/reset/expire weekly/daily leaderboards

66.1.10 Deep dive: sorted sets, approximate top-K, sharding

Redis sorted sets are the core: they keep members ordered by score in a skip-list, so ZADD/ZINCRBY (update), ZREVRANK (rank), and ZREVRANGE (top-N and neighbors) are all O(log n) or O(log n + k). This gives exact, real-time ranking for millions of users in one data structure — the reason Redis is the standard leaderboard tool. Scores update instantly and any ranking question is a fast position lookup, not a re-sort.

Approximate top-K (count-min sketch): for the top-K-items-in-a-stream variant (most-viewed products over a billion-event stream), tracking an exact count per item needs memory proportional to the number of distinct items. A count-min sketch (Part 1) is a fixed-size probabilistic structure that estimates item counts using a few hash functions and counters, so it tracks approximate counts for any number of items in a few MB, over-estimating slightly but never under-estimating. Combined with a small heap of the current top-K, it answers "approximate top-K" in bounded memory. You accept small inaccuracy for enormous memory savings — the right trade when exact top-K is infeasible.

Sharded leaderboards: a single sorted set can become a bottleneck at extreme update rates or sizes. Sharding splits the leaderboard across multiple Redis instances (by user hash), with each shard maintaining a partial ranking; a global top-N merges the top-N from each shard (since the global top-N must be within each shard's top-N). Sharding adds the merge complexity but removes the single-instance limit. Most leaderboards never need this; a single sorted set handles millions of users.

66.1.11 Caching

The Redis sorted set is itself the fast layer. The top-N result (which changes as scores update but is read very frequently) can be cached with a short TTL (a second) so a flood of top-N reads does not recompute, trading a second of staleness for far fewer Redis calls.

66.1.12 Messaging

Score-generating events (a game result) can flow through a queue to the leaderboard updater for buffering and ordering. The high-volume stream for approximate top-K is consumed to update the count-min sketch.

66.1.13 Scaling

flowchart TB
    S1["1x: millions of users, one sorted set"] --> S1a["Redis ZSET, PG for durability"]
    S10["10x: higher update rate"] --> S10a["Cache top-N, buffer updates"]
    S100["100x: extreme scale"] --> S100a["Sharded leaderboards (merge top-N), approx top-K via sketch"]
    S1 --> S10 --> S100

A single Redis sorted set scales to millions of users and thousands of updates per second. Beyond that, cache the hot top-N, buffer updates, and if truly necessary shard the leaderboard across instances with a top-N merge. For stream top-K at extreme volume, the count-min sketch keeps memory bounded regardless of item count.

66.1.14 Security

Prevent score tampering: score updates must be authorized and validated server-side (never trust a client-submitted score without verification), and rate-limited to prevent flooding. For competitive leaderboards, anti-cheat validation of scores matters. Ensure a user can only see leaderboards they are entitled to.

66.1.15 Failure scenarios

Failure Detection Impact Mitigation Effect
Redis lost Connection errors Ranking unavailable Rebuild sorted sets from PostgreSQL scores Brief outage, no data loss
Lost score update Reconciliation Rank slightly off Durable write to PG; reconcile Redis against PG Corrected
Hot leaderboard (one huge game) Redis instance load Update/query latency Cache top-N; shard if needed Mitigated
Count-min over-estimate By design Top-K slightly off Acceptable approximation; exact for small sets Negligible
Score tampering Validation Fake rankings Server-side validation, anti-cheat, rate limits Prevented
Weekly reset race Reset job Updates during reset lost/misplaced Atomic reset (new key swap) Clean

66.1.16 Observability

Metrics: update and query rates and latency, sorted-set sizes, top-N cache hit rate, count-min sketch accuracy (compared periodically against exact for a sample), rebuild duration, Redis memory. Alerts: Redis memory nearing limits, update/query latency spikes, Redis/PG score divergence (reconciliation). Dashboards: leaderboard activity, rank-query performance.

66.1.17 Deployment

Redis (clustered if sharding) for the sorted sets; PostgreSQL for durable scores; the API autoscaled and stateless. Time-scoped leaderboards managed by a scheduler that atomically creates/resets keys. A rebuild job ready to reconstruct Redis from PostgreSQL after a failure.

66.1.18 Cost considerations

Redis memory is the main cost (sorted sets hold all members in memory — under a GB per 10M-user leaderboard, modest). PostgreSQL for durable scores is small. The count-min sketch's fixed small memory is the whole point for stream top-K — it avoids the huge memory of exact counting. Sharding adds instances only at extreme scale. Overall inexpensive for the capability.

66.1.19 Tradeoffs

  • Redis sorted set (in-memory, fast, exact) with PostgreSQL durability over PostgreSQL-only ranking (a query with ORDER BY score plus ROW_NUMBER is far slower at scale and loads the database): we keep the fast ranking in Redis and durability in PostgreSQL, accepting the dual write and rebuild path.
  • Approximate top-K (count-min sketch, bounded memory) vs exact counting (memory per distinct item): we accept slight over-estimation for enormous memory savings when the item count is huge.
  • Single sorted set (simple) vs sharded (scalable): stay single until scale forces sharding, because the top-N merge adds complexity; most leaderboards never need it.
  • Short-TTL cached top-N (fewer Redis calls) vs always-fresh: a second of staleness on the top-N for far less load.

66.1.20 Alternative architectures

PostgreSQL-only with an indexed score column and window functions (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC)): simple and durable with no Redis, and fine for small leaderboards or infrequent queries; it does not scale to millions of users with thousands of real-time updates and frequent rank queries, where the sorting load overwhelms the database. Use it for small or low-traffic leaderboards.

Managed real-time database (a service with built-in sorted/ranked structures): offloads operating Redis; viable when you prefer managed infrastructure, at the cost of less control and potential expense.

Precomputed periodic rankings: if real-time is not required (a daily leaderboard that updates once a day), compute the ranking in a batch job and serve the static result — far simpler, no sorted set needed. Match the design to the freshness requirement; not every leaderboard is real-time.

66.2 Collaborative Document Editing

66.2.1 Requirements

A collaborative document editing system lets multiple users edit the same document at the same time and see each other's changes in real time, with everyone's edits merging into a consistent result, showing who is present and where their cursor is (presence), and working even when a user goes briefly offline and reconnects. Think of a shared document editor. The users are people co-editing documents. This design probes the hardest problem in real-time collaboration: how to merge concurrent edits from multiple users into one consistent document without losing anyone's work or requiring locks.

Imagine several people editing the same physical page at once, each with a pen, all writing simultaneously in different (and sometimes the same) spots. Chaos — unless there is a magic rule by which, no matter the order their strokes land, everyone's page ends up identical and nobody's words are lost. That magic rule is the core of collaborative editing: a way to combine concurrent, conflicting edits so all copies converge to the same correct document. Operational transform and CRDTs are two such rules.

66.2.2 Functional requirements

  1. Multiple users edit the same document simultaneously.
  2. Each user sees others' edits in near real time.
  3. Concurrent edits merge into one consistent document (no lost edits, all copies converge).
  4. Presence: show who is in the document and their cursor/selection positions.
  5. Offline support: a user can edit offline and have changes merge on reconnect.
  6. Persist the document and its history (versions, undo).

66.2.3 Non-functional requirements

Property Target Why
Edit propagation latency Sub-second (feels real-time) Collaboration must feel live
Convergence All clients always converge to the same document The core correctness property
Concurrency Many simultaneous editors per document Real collaboration
Offline tolerance Edits merge correctly after reconnect Networks drop
Durability No committed edit is ever lost Users trust their work is saved

66.2.4 Constraints

  • Concurrent edits to the same region must merge deterministically to the same result on every client (convergence) — this is the central hard constraint.
  • Real-time means a persistent connection (WebSocket) per editor, with the scaling that implies (Part 40's chat system).
  • Offline edits can be arbitrarily stale on reconnect and must still merge correctly.
  • No locking: users edit freely and simultaneously, so the merge, not a lock, resolves conflicts.

66.2.5 Capacity estimation

Quantity Assumption Calculation Result
Concurrent editors per doc Typical collaboration given up to ~50 (usually far fewer)
Documents being edited Active given 100,000 concurrently
Edit operations per active editor ~a few/second typing thousands of ops/second total
WebSocket connections editors online hundreds of thousands
Document size typical given KBs to a few MB

The numbers say: the per-document concurrency is modest (tens of editors), so the hard problem is correctness of merging, not throughput; the scaling challenge is many persistent connections across many documents (like chat, Part 40), and routing all editors of one document to a coordination point.

66.2.6 API design

Mostly a real-time protocol over WebSocket, plus REST for document CRUD.

Operation Channel Notes
Open document REST GET /docs/{id} + WS subscribe Load current state, join the session
Send edit WS: op message A client's edit operation
Receive edits WS: broadcast op Others' transformed/merged operations
Presence WS: presence message Cursor/selection, join/leave
Save/version internal/periodic Persist state and history

66.2.7 Data model

Document: current content + a history of operations (for merge, undo, recovery).
  documents(id, content_snapshot, version, updated_at)
  operations(doc_id, seq, user_id, op, based_on_version, created_at)  -- the edit log

The merge model (one of):
  Operational Transform (OT): operations + a transform function that adjusts an
    incoming op against concurrent ops so positions stay correct.
  CRDT: each character/element has a unique, ordered identity so concurrent inserts/
    deletes merge deterministically regardless of order, without a central transform.

Presence (ephemeral, in Redis): who is in the doc, cursor positions (not persisted).

66.2.8 High-level architecture

flowchart LR
    E1["Editor A"] --> WS["WebSocket gateway"]
    E2["Editor B"] --> WS
    WS --> COORD["Doc coordinator (per document)"]
    COORD --> MERGE["Merge engine (OT or CRDT)"]
    COORD --> PRES["Presence (Redis)"]
    COORD --> PERSIST["Persistence (PostgreSQL: snapshots + op log)"]
    COORD --> WS

All editors of one document connect through a WebSocket gateway and are routed to that document's coordinator, which applies the merge model (OT or CRDT) to incoming operations, broadcasts the merged result to all editors so they converge, maintains presence in Redis, and persists snapshots and the operation log. Routing all editors of a document to one coordinator is key: concurrent edits are merged in one place (OT), or merged anywhere consistently (CRDT).

66.2.9 Component design

Component Responsibility
WebSocket gateway Hold editor connections, route by document
Document coordinator Own one document's session; apply and broadcast merged ops
Merge engine (OT or CRDT) Combine concurrent edits so all copies converge
Presence Track and broadcast who is editing and cursor positions (ephemeral)
Persistence Snapshot document state and store the op log for history/recovery
Offline sync Merge a reconnecting client's buffered edits against the current state

66.2.10 Deep dive: operational transform vs CRDTs, presence, offline

The core problem: two users concurrently edit the same region — A inserts "X" at position 5, B deletes position 3. B's delete shifts positions, so A's "at position 5" now means a different place. Naively applying both gives different results on different clients — divergence. The two solutions:

Operational Transform (OT): operations are transformed against concurrent operations before applying. When A's insert and B's delete happen concurrently, a transform function adjusts A's position to account for B's delete (and vice versa), so both clients, applying the transformed operations, reach the same document. OT requires a central coordinator to order and transform operations (or careful peer protocols), and the transform functions are famously tricky to get exactly right for all cases, but it is efficient (operations are small) and is used by major collaborative editors.

CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types): each element (character) gets a unique, globally-ordered identity, so an insert says "insert X between identity-7 and identity-9" rather than "at position 5". Because positions are stable identities, not shifting indices, concurrent operations merge deterministically in any order with no central transform — any two clients that have seen the same set of operations converge, regardless of order received. CRDTs are conceptually cleaner and support peer-to-peer and offline well, at the cost of metadata overhead (each element carries identity data), though modern CRDTs have reduced this substantially.

OT:   op positions are TRANSFORMED against concurrent ops -> needs ordering/coordination,
      small ops, tricky transform functions.
CRDT: elements have stable IDENTITIES -> merge in any order, no transform, no central
      coordinator needed, more per-element metadata.
Both guarantee convergence: all clients end with the same document.

Presence is separate and simpler: each client periodically sends its cursor/selection and online status; the coordinator broadcasts this to others. Presence is ephemeral (kept in Redis, not persisted) — it is fine to lose it on disconnect.

Offline sync: a client editing offline buffers its operations; on reconnect, it sends them and receives the operations it missed, and the merge model (OT transform or CRDT merge) reconciles them with the current state. CRDTs handle this especially naturally because operations merge regardless of order or delay. The convergence guarantee is what makes offline editing safe: no matter how stale the client, its edits merge without loss.

66.2.11 Caching

The current document state is kept in memory in the coordinator for the active session (fast application and broadcast of ops), with periodic snapshots to PostgreSQL. Presence is in Redis.

66.2.12 Messaging

Operations flow over WebSocket in real time. For scaling across coordinator instances, a pub/sub (Redis or a broker) propagates operations to all instances holding editors of the same document, or editors are routed so one document maps to one coordinator (simpler). Snapshots and the op log persist asynchronously.

66.2.13 Scaling

flowchart TB
    S1["1x: documents with tens of editors each"] --> S1a["Coordinator per doc, OT or CRDT, WS gateway"]
    S10["10x: many more documents/connections"] --> S10a["Shard documents across coordinators, Redis pub/sub"]
    S100["100x: massive concurrent editing"] --> S100a["CRDT for peer-friendly merge, edge presence, horizontal gateways"]
    S1 --> S10 --> S100

Scaling is the many-persistent-connections problem (like chat, Part 40): horizontal WebSocket gateways and routing documents to coordinators. Since per-document concurrency is modest, the work is spreading many documents across instances, not merging huge numbers of editors on one document. CRDTs ease scaling by removing the need for a single central transform point.

66.2.14 Security

Authorize who can view/edit each document; validate that operations come from an authorized editor. Prevent one user from corrupting the document via malformed operations (validate ops). Protect the op log and snapshots. Presence should not leak more than intended (who is viewing). For sensitive documents, encryption and access control (Part 23, Part 58).

66.2.15 Failure scenarios

Failure Detection Impact Mitigation Effect
Client disconnects mid-edit Connection drop Its buffered edits pending Offline buffer; merge on reconnect No loss
Coordinator crash Health check Active session lost Rebuild from last snapshot + op log; reconnect clients Brief interruption
Concurrent conflicting edits Normal Divergence risk OT transform / CRDT merge guarantees convergence Consistent result
Op lost in transit Sequence gap Divergence Op sequencing + resend; CRDT idempotent merge Recovered
Stale offline client reconnects Reconnect Many missed ops Merge buffered ops against current state Merged correctly
Op log corruption Validation History/recovery impaired Validate ops; snapshot regularly Bounded

66.2.16 Observability

Metrics: edit propagation latency, concurrent editors per document, convergence errors (divergence detected — should be zero, alert on any), WebSocket connection counts, reconnect/offline-merge rates, snapshot/op-log lag. Alerts: any divergence (critical correctness failure), propagation latency spikes, coordinator overload. Dashboards: active documents/editors, real-time latency, merge health.

66.2.17 Deployment

WebSocket gateways and coordinators as horizontally-scaled services; Redis for presence and pub/sub; PostgreSQL for snapshots and op logs. Careful rollout so a merge-engine change does not cause divergence (the highest-risk change — test convergence thoroughly). Sticky routing so a document's editors reach the same coordinator (or pub/sub across coordinators).

66.2.18 Cost considerations

Dominated by holding many persistent WebSocket connections (memory per connection) and the coordinators' in-memory document state, plus Redis for presence/pub-sub. CRDT metadata adds storage/bandwidth overhead per operation (a tradeoff versus OT's smaller ops). Overall driven by concurrent-connection scale, like chat, rather than by heavy computation.

66.2.19 Tradeoffs

  • OT (small ops, needs central coordination, tricky transforms) vs CRDT (no central transform, offline/peer-friendly, more metadata): OT is efficient and proven but complex to implement correctly; CRDTs are cleaner for offline and peer-to-peer at the cost of per-element overhead. The choice depends on whether you need peer-to-peer/offline-first (favor CRDT) or have a reliable central server and want minimal per-op overhead (OT is viable).
  • Central coordinator per document (simple merge) vs fully peer-to-peer (CRDT, no central point): central is simpler to operate; peer-to-peer (enabled by CRDTs) removes the central dependency at the cost of more client-side complexity.
  • Persist op log + snapshots (full history, recovery, undo) vs snapshots only (less storage): the op log enables history and robust recovery at storage cost.

66.2.20 Alternative architectures

Last-write-wins / lock-based editing: far simpler — lock the document (or a section) to one editor at a time, or just take the last save. This is adequate when true simultaneous editing of the same region is rare (most documents are edited by one person at a time), and avoids the entire OT/CRDT complexity. Build this first unless genuine real-time co-editing of the same regions is a core requirement; most "collaborative" needs are satisfied by section locking or presence-plus-last-write.

Use an existing collaborative-editing library/framework (a mature OT or CRDT library): implementing OT or CRDTs correctly from scratch is extremely hard (the transform/merge edge cases are a research-grade problem), so using a proven library is strongly preferred over building the merge engine yourself. Understand the models (to choose and use them well); do not reimplement them.

Managed real-time collaboration service: offloads the entire merge and connection problem to a provider; viable when you want collaboration without owning the hardest part, at the cost of dependency and expense.

66.3 Proximity Search (Nearby Drivers and Restaurants)

66.3.1 Requirements

A proximity search system answers "what is near this location?" — the nearby available drivers for a ride request, the restaurants within delivery range, the friends near you — efficiently, over data where locations change constantly (drivers move every few seconds) and queries are frequent. The users are riders needing a nearby driver, diners browsing nearby restaurants, and the matching systems that pair them. This design probes geospatial indexing: how to query "near a point" fast over millions of moving or static locations, when a naive "compute distance to every location" is far too slow.

Imagine needing the nearest taxi in a huge city. Checking the distance from you to every taxi in the city on every request would be hopeless. Instead, imagine the city divided into a grid of cells; you only need to check taxis in your cell and the adjacent ones, not the whole city. That spatial bucketing — only looking near where you are — is the essence of proximity search, and geohashes and quadtrees are two ways to do the bucketing.

66.3.2 Functional requirements

  1. Find entities (drivers, restaurants) within a radius of a point, or the nearest N.
  2. Handle frequently-changing locations (drivers update their position every few seconds).
  3. Filter by attributes (available drivers only; open restaurants that deliver here).
  4. Answer queries fast (riders expect instant matching).
  5. Scale to millions of entities and high query and update rates.

66.3.3 Non-functional requirements

Property Target Why
Query latency p99 low (tens of ms) Riders wait for a match
Update rate High (drivers update every ~4s) Positions change constantly
Query rate High (every ride request, every browse) Core to the product
Accuracy Close-enough nearest (slight approximation often fine) "Nearby" tolerates small imprecision
Scale Millions of entities, large metro areas City-scale services

66.3.4 Constraints

  • Naive distance-to-all is O(n) per query — infeasible at millions of entities; a spatial index is required.
  • Driver locations change every few seconds, so the index must support very high update rates, not just queries.
  • Queries filter by attributes (available, open, delivers-here), so the spatial search combines with attribute filtering.
  • "Nearby" tolerates slight approximation, which lets cheaper/faster approximate methods work.

66.3.5 Capacity estimation

Quantity Assumption Calculation Result
Drivers in a large metro Active given 100,000
Location updates every 4s per driver 100,000 / 4 25,000 updates/second
Proximity queries ride requests + browsing given 10,000/second
Restaurants (static) metro given 50,000
Index memory locations + ids modest (MBs)

The numbers say: updates (25,000/second) outnumber queries (10,000/second) for the moving-driver case, so the index must handle very frequent updates cheaply — this is what makes a simple in-memory geohash-bucketed index (fast updates) attractive over a heavier tree that is costly to update. Restaurants are static, so a PostGIS index (query-optimized) fits them.

66.3.6 API design

Method Path Request Response Notes
POST /locations { entityId, lat, lng } Update an entity's location (frequent)
GET /nearby ?lat&lng&radius&filter=available nearby entities, sorted by distance The proximity query
GET /nearest ?lat&lng&n=5&filter=... nearest N Nearest-N variant

66.3.7 Data model

Geohash approach (good for frequently-moving entities):
  A geohash encodes a lat/lng into a short string where a shared prefix = nearby.
  Bucket entities by geohash prefix (a grid cell). To query near a point, look at the
  point's cell and its 8 neighbors, then filter by exact distance.
  Store in Redis: GEOADD/GEOSEARCH use geohashes internally for exactly this.

PostGIS approach (good for static/queryable entities like restaurants):
  A PostgreSQL extension adding a geometry/geography type and spatial (GiST) indexes.
  restaurants(id, location geography(Point), is_open, delivers_radius_m, ...)
  CREATE INDEX ON restaurants USING gist (location);
  SELECT ... WHERE ST_DWithin(location, :point, :radius) ORDER BY location <-> :point;

Quadtree: a tree that recursively subdivides space into quadrants; dense areas get
  finer subdivision. Good for nearest-neighbor queries; costlier to update than geohash buckets.

66.3.8 High-level architecture

flowchart LR
    DRV["Drivers (frequent location updates)"] --> LOC["Location ingest"]
    LOC --> GEO["Redis geo index (moving entities)"]
    RIDER["Rider request"] --> QRY["Proximity query service"]
    QRY --> GEO
    QRY --> PG["PostGIS (static entities: restaurants)"]
    QRY --> FILTER["Attribute filter (available/open)"]

Frequently-moving entities (drivers) live in a Redis geo index (fast updates via GEOADD, fast radius queries via GEOSEARCH, built on geohashes). Static entities (restaurants) live in PostGIS (spatial index, rich queries, joined to attributes). The proximity query service queries the appropriate index, applies attribute filters, and returns results sorted by distance.

66.3.9 Component design

Component Responsibility
Location ingest Accept high-rate location updates, write to the geo index
Redis geo index Hold moving entities; fast update and radius query (geohash-based)
PostGIS Hold static entities with spatial index and attribute columns
Proximity query service Run the near/nearest query, filter by attributes, sort by distance
Attribute filter Combine spatial results with availability/open/range filters

66.3.10 Deep dive: geohash, quadtrees, PostGIS

Geohash encodes a latitude/longitude into a short string such that locations with a common prefix are geographically close (a longer shared prefix means closer). This turns "find nearby" into "find entities whose geohash shares a prefix" — a cheap string/bucket lookup. The trick for correctness: a point near a cell boundary has close neighbors in adjacent cells, so a proper query checks the point's cell and its 8 neighbors, then filters by exact distance. Geohash bucketing updates very cheaply (just move an entity to a new bucket), which suits frequently-moving drivers. Redis's geo commands (GEOADD, GEOSEARCH) implement exactly this — they store positions by geohash and do radius/box searches — making Redis a ready-made moving-entity geo index with fast updates and queries.

Quadtrees recursively subdivide space into four quadrants, subdividing dense areas more finely, giving efficient nearest-neighbor queries with good adaptivity to uneven density. They are powerful for queries but costlier to update than flat geohash buckets, so they suit relatively static data or query-heavy workloads more than the 25,000-updates/second driver case.
