PostGIS adds a spatial type and GiST spatial index to PostgreSQL, so you get exact, rich spatial queries (ST_DWithin for within-radius, <-> distance ordering for nearest) joined directly to attribute columns (is_open, delivers_radius) and relational data, all in one SQL query. This is ideal for static or less-frequently-updated entities (restaurants) where the query richness and the join to attributes matter, and it keeps everything in PostgreSQL (the "stay in PostgreSQL" theme of pgvector, Part 60, and TimescaleDB, Part 62). It is less suited to 25,000 updates/second of moving points, where Redis's lightweight geo index shines.

Choose the geo index by update rate and query needs:
  Frequently moving (drivers, 25k updates/s) -> Redis geo (geohash): cheap updates
  Static + rich queries + attribute joins (restaurants) -> PostGIS: query power, one DB
  Query-heavy, uneven density, less frequent updates -> quadtree: adaptive nearest-neighbor

66.3.11 Caching

Nearby-restaurant results for a location (static data) can be cached briefly, since restaurants do not move and open/close slowly. Driver proximity results are too volatile to cache (drivers move constantly), so they query the live geo index each time.

66.3.12 Messaging

High-rate location updates can flow through a queue to the ingest service to buffer bursts, though the Redis geo index is fast enough to take updates directly in many cases. Matching events (rider matched to driver) emit downstream.

66.3.13 Scaling

flowchart TB
    S1["1x: one metro"] --> S1a["Redis geo for drivers, PostGIS for restaurants"]
    S10["10x: many metros"] --> S10a["Partition geo index by region/city"]
    S100["100x: global"] --> S100a["Region-local geo indexes, route queries by location"]
    S1 --> S10 --> S100

Geospatial data partitions naturally by region/city: a query is always local to a location, so you shard the geo index by region and route each query to its region's index. This scales cleanly because proximity queries never need global data — a rider in one city never needs drivers in another. Redis geo handles the update rate per region; PostGIS handles restaurant queries per region.

66.3.14 Security

Location data is sensitive (it reveals where people are): restrict who can query whose location, do not expose precise locations beyond what is needed (a rider sees a driver's approximate position, not a precise track), rate-limit location queries to prevent scraping, and apply privacy/retention policies to location history (Part 22, Part 63). Authorization: a user can only query proximity for legitimate purposes (their own ride).

66.3.15 Failure scenarios

Failure Detection Impact Mitigation Effect
Redis geo index down Errors No driver proximity Fallback to PostGIS (slower) or cached last positions Degraded
Stale driver position Last-update timestamp Match a driver who moved Expire stale positions (TTL); recheck on match Mostly avoided
Boundary miss (geohash edge) Missing nearby result Nearest entity in adjacent cell missed Query the cell plus 8 neighbors Correct
Update flood Ingest overload Updates lag Buffer/queue updates; shard by region Smoothed
PostGIS query slow Latency Slow restaurant search Spatial index; cache results Mitigated
Hot region (city center) Load on one shard Latency in that region Finer partitioning of dense regions Balanced

66.3.16 Observability

Metrics: query latency (near/nearest), update rate and lag, index sizes, stale-position rate, cache hit rate (restaurants), per-region load. Alerts: query latency spikes, update lag (positions going stale), geo index unavailability, hot-region imbalance. Dashboards: proximity query performance, location freshness, per-region load.

66.3.17 Deployment

Redis (clustered, partitioned by region) for the moving-entity geo index; PostGIS (PostgreSQL with the extension) for static entities; the query service autoscaled and region-aware. Location ingest scaled for the update rate. Stale-position expiry via TTL on geo entries.

66.3.18 Cost considerations

Redis memory for the moving-entity index (modest — positions and ids) and PostgreSQL/PostGIS for static entities are the main stores; both are inexpensive at these data sizes. The cost scales with the update and query rates (compute for the query service) and with regions. Caching static results and partitioning by region keep it efficient.

66.3.19 Tradeoffs

  • Redis geo (cheap updates, geohash-based, in-memory) for moving entities vs PostGIS (rich queries, durable, one DB) for static entities: use each where its strength fits — Redis for the 25k-updates/second drivers, PostGIS for the query-rich, attribute-joined, slow-changing restaurants. This split matches the store to the update/query profile.
  • Geohash bucketing (cheap updates, approximate, boundary handling needed) vs quadtree (adaptive, good nearest-neighbor, costlier updates): geohash for high update rates, quadtree for query-heavy, less-frequently-updated data.
  • Approximate nearby (fast, slight imprecision) vs exact nearest (more work): "nearby" usually tolerates approximation, so cheaper approximate methods are fine; exact is reserved for when precision matters.
  • Region partitioning (scalable, queries are local) with the complexity of routing: proximity queries are naturally local, so region sharding scales cleanly, at the cost of routing and handling region boundaries.

66.3.20 Alternative architectures

PostGIS-only: use PostGIS for everything, including moving entities, accepting that 25,000 updates/second of point locations is heavier for a spatial index than for Redis geo. Viable at smaller scale or lower update rates, and simplest (one database, rich queries); it struggles at very high update rates, which is why Redis geo is paired with it for moving entities.

Redis geo-only: use Redis geo for everything, including restaurants, accepting that you lose PostGIS's rich spatial queries and attribute joins and must filter attributes separately. Viable when queries are simple radius searches; weaker when you need complex spatial queries or tight integration with relational attributes.

Specialized geospatial database / managed service: a dedicated spatial/location service can handle extreme scale and advanced queries; justified only when the Redis+PostGIS combination genuinely does not meet the scale or query needs, following the "do not add a store without a specific requirement" discipline (Part 62).

66.4 Ad-Click and Metrics Aggregation

66.4.1 Requirements

An ad-click (or metrics) aggregation system ingests a very high volume of events — ad clicks, impressions, page views, product views — and produces accurate aggregated counts and metrics (clicks per ad per hour, views per product per day), handling billions of events, counting correctly despite duplicates and retries, aggregating over time windows, and reconciling to catch any discrepancies. The users are advertisers (who are billed by clicks, so accuracy is money), analysts, and dashboards. This design probes high-volume ingestion and the hard problem of counting accurately at scale, where exactly-once counting matters because the counts are billed.

Imagine counting every person entering every store in a country, continuously, and billing each store by the count — so the count must be right, not approximately right, even though people stream in by the millions per second, some turnstiles double-report, and some reports arrive late. You cannot count each person by hand (volume), you must not double-count (billing accuracy), and you must handle late and duplicate reports. That is ad-click aggregation: massive ingest, exact counting despite duplicates, windowed aggregation, and reconciliation to catch errors.

66.4.2 Functional requirements

  1. Ingest a very high volume of events (clicks, impressions) reliably without loss.
  2. Aggregate events into counts/metrics over time windows (per ad per minute/hour/day).
  3. Count accurately despite duplicate events (retries, at-least-once delivery) — exactly-once semantics for the counts.
  4. Handle late-arriving events (an event delayed by network/offline device).
  5. Reconcile aggregates against raw events to catch and correct discrepancies.
  6. Serve aggregated results to dashboards and billing with low latency.

66.4.3 Non-functional requirements

Property Target Why
Ingest throughput Very high (millions of events/second) Ad/metrics scale
Count accuracy Exact for billed metrics (no over/under-count) Counts are money
No event loss Durable ingestion A lost click is lost revenue
Aggregation freshness Near real-time for dashboards; exact for billing (can lag) Different consumers, different needs
Reconciliation Aggregates provably match raw events Trust in the billed numbers

66.4.4 Constraints

  • Volume is enormous (millions of events/second), so ingestion must be a streaming/queue problem, not synchronous inserts.
  • At-least-once delivery (the reliable default, Part 17) means duplicates, but the counts must be exact — so deduplication/idempotency is essential for accuracy.
  • Events arrive out of order and late, so windowed aggregation needs watermarks and late-event handling (Part 63).
  • The counts are billed, so accuracy is a correctness requirement, not a nicety, and must be verifiable (reconciliation).

66.4.5 Capacity estimation

Quantity Assumption Calculation Result
Events/second Peak given 1,000,000/second
Event size small given about 200 B
Ingest bandwidth 1M x 200 B 200 MB/s
Events/day 1M x 86,400 about 86 billion/day
Raw storage/day 86B x 200 B (compressed less) tens of TB/day raw
Aggregates counts per ad per window tiny compared to raw

The numbers say: ingestion is a high-throughput streaming problem (Kafka, Part 17), raw events are huge (store in a columnar warehouse/lake, Part 63, or drop after aggregation), aggregates are small (the whole point of aggregating), and the system must count 86 billion events/day exactly despite duplicates — which forces careful deduplication and reconciliation.

66.4.6 API design

Operation Interface Notes
Ingest event POST /events or SDK -> queue High-volume, fire-and-forget to a durable queue
Get aggregate GET /metrics?adId&from&to&granularity Read precomputed aggregates
Reconciliation status GET /reconciliation Discrepancy reports

Ingestion returns fast (write to a durable queue and acknowledge); the heavy aggregation happens asynchronously.

66.4.7 Data model

Raw events (durable, high-volume): in Kafka (retained) and/or a columnar store/lake.
  event(event_id, ad_id, user_hash, type, event_time, received_time)
  event_id is a client/server-assigned unique id -> the key for deduplication.

Aggregates (small, served to dashboards/billing): pre-aggregated per ad per window.
  ad_metrics(ad_id, window_start, granularity, clicks, impressions)  -- in PostgreSQL

Dedup state: a store of seen event_ids per window (to count each event once),
  or idempotent aggregation keyed by event_id.

The event_id is the linchpin of exactly-once counting: every event carries a unique id, and the aggregation counts each id once, so duplicates (from at-least-once delivery) do not inflate the count.

66.4.8 High-level architecture

flowchart LR
    SRC["Clicks / impressions (huge volume)"] --> ING["Ingest -> Kafka (durable)"]
    ING --> STREAM["Stream processor (windowed aggregation + dedup)"]
    STREAM --> AGG["Aggregates (PostgreSQL: per ad per window)"]
    ING --> RAW["Raw events -> warehouse/lake"]
    RECON["Reconciliation job"] --> RAW
    RECON --> AGG
    AGG --> DASH["Dashboards / billing"]

Events are ingested into Kafka (durable, high-throughput buffer). A stream processor (Part 63) consumes them, deduplicates by event_id, aggregates into time windows, and writes small aggregates to PostgreSQL for serving. Raw events also land in a warehouse/lake. A reconciliation job periodically compares the aggregates against the raw events to catch and correct any discrepancy.

66.4.9 Component design

Component Responsibility
Ingest Accept events fast, write durably to Kafka, acknowledge
Kafka Durable, high-throughput, replayable event buffer
Stream processor Deduplicate by event_id, aggregate into windows, write aggregates
Aggregate store PostgreSQL: small per-ad-per-window counts for serving
Raw store Warehouse/lake: raw events for reconciliation and deep analysis
Reconciliation job Compare aggregates to raw counts; detect and fix discrepancies

66.4.10 Deep dive: exactly-once counting, windowing, reconciliation

Exactly-once counting is the heart. At-least-once delivery (Part 17) means the same click event can be delivered more than once (a producer retry, a consumer reprocessing after a crash). If you simply increment a counter per event, duplicates inflate the count — and since clicks are billed, that is over-billing. The defenses:

  • Deduplication by event_id: each event has a unique id; the aggregator tracks which ids it has counted (per window) and ignores repeats. This makes counting idempotent — re-processing an event does not double-count.
  • Idempotent aggregate updates with offset tracking: the stream processor records the last-processed Kafka offset together with the aggregate update in one atomic step, so reprocessing after a crash skips already-counted events (the pattern from Part 40's click consumer).

Either way, the count reflects each distinct event once, achieving exactly-once counting on top of at-least-once delivery — the practical way to get exact counts without the (often impossible) guarantee of exactly-once delivery.

Windowed aggregation (Part 63): events are aggregated into time windows (per minute, hour, day) by event time, with watermarks to decide when a window is complete and allowed lateness to incorporate late events. A click from a device that was briefly offline arrives late; within the allowed-lateness grace period it still lands in its correct window; beyond that, it is side-outputted for reconciliation rather than silently dropped — because a dropped click is lost revenue.

Reconciliation is the accuracy backstop (Part 63): periodically recompute the aggregates directly from the raw events (in the warehouse/lake) and compare against the served aggregates. Any mismatch — from a bug, a dropped event, a dedup miss — is detected and the aggregate corrected. Because the counts are billed, reconciliation is not optional: it is how you can stand behind the numbers. This is the lambda-style idea of a fast approximate/real-time path (the stream aggregates) backed by a slower exact path (reconciliation from raw events) that corrects it.

Exactly-once counting on at-least-once delivery:
  every event has a unique event_id -> count each id once (dedup) -> duplicates harmless
  + atomic (aggregate update, Kafka offset) -> crash reprocessing does not double-count
Windowing by event time + watermark + allowed lateness -> late clicks counted, not dropped
Reconciliation: recompute from raw events, compare to served aggregates, correct mismatches

66.4.11 Caching

Served aggregates are small and can be cached for dashboards (short TTL) since they update per window. The dedup state is effectively a cache/index of seen event ids within the active window.

66.4.12 Messaging

Kafka is central (Part 17): durable, high-throughput, replayable ingestion, partitioned (by ad id for aggregation locality, so one consumer sees all of an ad's events and can aggregate in memory before flushing). Replayability is key — if aggregation has a bug, you can reprocess from Kafka. At-least-once delivery with idempotent, deduplicating consumers is the contract.

66.4.13 Scaling

flowchart TB
    S1["1x: high volume"] --> S1a["Kafka ingest, stream processor, dedup + window"]
    S10["10x: millions/s"] --> S10a["More Kafka partitions + consumers, partition by ad id"]
    S100["100x: tens of billions/day"] --> S100a["Raw to lake, sampled real-time + exact reconciliation"]
    S1 --> S10 --> S100

Ingestion scales via Kafka partitions and consumer parallelism (partition by ad id for aggregation locality). Aggregates stay small regardless of event volume (the point of aggregating). At extreme scale, real-time dashboards may use sampling/approximation for speed while billing uses the exact reconciled counts — a fast-approximate plus slow-exact split.

66.4.14 Security

Prevent click fraud (fake clicks to inflate bills or drain competitors' budgets): bot detection, rate limiting, anomaly detection on click patterns, and validation — click fraud is a major real threat in ad systems. Protect PII in events (hash user identifiers, Part 63). Authorize who can read whose metrics. Ensure the billed counts cannot be tampered with.

66.4.15 Failure scenarios

Failure Detection Impact Mitigation Effect
Duplicate events (at-least-once) Normal Over-count, over-bill Dedup by event_id; idempotent aggregation Exact counts
Consumer crash mid-aggregation Offset lag Reprocessing Atomic (aggregate, offset); dedup No double-count
Late events Watermark Miss the window Allowed lateness; side output for very late; reconciliation Counted or reconciled
Dropped event Reconciliation mismatch Under-count, lost revenue Durable Kafka (no loss); reconciliation detects and corrects Caught and fixed
Aggregation bug Reconciliation mismatch Wrong counts Replay from Kafka with fixed code; reconcile Corrected
Click fraud Anomaly detection Inflated bills Fraud detection, rate limits, validation Mitigated
Ingest overload Kafka lag Delayed aggregation Kafka buffers; scale consumers Smoothed, not lost

66.4.16 Observability

Metrics: ingest rate, Kafka consumer lag, aggregation latency, dedup rate (duplicates caught), late-event rate, reconciliation discrepancies (should be ~zero; alert on any significant gap), fraud-detection signals. Alerts: reconciliation mismatch beyond tolerance (billing accuracy), consumer lag (aggregates falling behind), ingest loss (any event loss), fraud spikes. Dashboards: ingest/aggregation health, accuracy (reconciliation), fraud.

66.4.17 Deployment

High-throughput Kafka cluster; stream processor (Kafka Streams/Flink or custom consumers) scaled to the partition count; PostgreSQL for aggregates; a warehouse/lake for raw events; a scheduled reconciliation job. Replay capability (reprocess from Kafka) built in for fixing aggregation bugs. Fraud detection integrated at or near ingest.

66.4.18 Cost considerations

Dominated by the high-throughput ingestion (Kafka) and raw-event storage (tens of TB/day — store in cheap columnar lake storage, and retain raw events only as long as needed for reconciliation and analysis, Part 63). Aggregates are tiny and cheap. The cost is controlled by retention policy on raw events (the dominant storage cost) and by right-sizing the stream-processing fleet. Accuracy (dedup, reconciliation) costs some compute but is non-negotiable because the counts are billed.

66.4.19 Tradeoffs

  • Exactly-once counting via dedup + idempotent aggregation on at-least-once delivery over attempting exactly-once delivery (hard/impossible end to end): we get exact counts the practical way — unique event ids counted once — rather than chasing an exactly-once delivery guarantee.
  • Fast approximate real-time + slow exact reconciliation over a single exact real-time path: dashboards get near-real-time (possibly sampled) numbers quickly, while billing uses the exact reconciled counts, because real-time and exact are in tension at this volume.
  • Durable Kafka buffer (replayable, no loss) with the cost of running it over synchronous inserts (would never keep up and would lose events on failure): the durability and replay are worth the operational cost at this scale.
  • Retain raw events for reconciliation (storage cost) vs aggregate-and-drop (cheaper, no reconciliation): for billed counts, keeping raw events long enough to reconcile is worth the storage, because trust in the numbers requires it.

66.4.20 Alternative architectures

Approximate-only counting (count-min sketch, HyperLogLog for unique counts): for non-billed metrics where approximate counts suffice (rough dashboard trends), probabilistic structures count in tiny fixed memory with no exact-count machinery — far cheaper and simpler. Use this when accuracy is not billed; reserve the full exactly-once-plus-reconciliation design for metrics that are money.

Database-only aggregation: for moderate volume, insert events into PostgreSQL (partitioned by time, Part 14) and aggregate with SQL into summary tables (the Part 63 in-product analytics pattern). Simpler, no Kafka/stream processor; it does not scale to millions of events/second, but most "metrics" needs are far below that threshold — build this first unless the volume genuinely demands the streaming pipeline.

Managed analytics/streaming service: a managed ingestion-and-aggregation service offloads operating Kafka and stream processors; viable when you prefer managed infrastructure and accept its cost and constraints, especially for teams without a data-platform team.

66.5 Closing: what these four designs teach

The four systems in this Part each solve a distinct hard problem and reinforce patterns from across the book. The leaderboard shows that the right data structure — a Redis sorted set — turns an apparently expensive problem (ranking millions of users in real time) into fast, simple operations, and that when exact is too costly (top-K over a billion-event stream) a probabilistic structure (count-min sketch) trades a little accuracy for enormous savings. Collaborative editing is a correctness problem above all: concurrent edits must converge on every client, which operational transform and CRDTs achieve by two different rules, and which is hard enough that you use a proven library rather than building the merge engine yourself. Proximity search is about picking the right spatial index for the update/query profile — Redis geo for fast-moving drivers, PostGIS for query-rich static restaurants — and partitioning naturally by region because every query is local. Ad-click aggregation is about counting accurately at enormous scale: exactly-once counting on at-least-once delivery via unique event ids and idempotent aggregation, windowed by event time with late-event handling, and backed by reconciliation because the counts are billed.

Read across all three system-design Parts (40, 65, 66), the senior lessons compound. The right data structure or index often turns a hard problem easy — a sorted set for ranking, a geohash for proximity, a conditional update for no-double-sell. Accuracy versus cost is a recurring, deliberate trade: approximate top-K and sampled dashboards where approximation is fine, exact counting and reconciliation where the numbers are money. At-least-once delivery plus idempotent, deduplicating consumers is the standard reliable contract, appearing in the crawler, the metrics aggregator and the click stream. Reconciliation — comparing a derived result against the source of truth — is the backstop that catches silent errors wherever correctness matters. And every design carries a "when not to build" alternative: a PostgreSQL-only leaderboard for small scale, section-locking instead of CRDTs for most documents, PostGIS-only for modest location rates, database aggregation instead of a streaming pipeline for modest volumes. The simplest design that meets the requirement wins, and the method — clarify, estimate, model, design, deep-dive the hot spot, cover the cross-cutting concerns, state tradeoffs, offer alternatives — is what lets you produce the right design for any problem, not just recall these.

Senior Checklist — Part 66

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can build a real-time leaderboard with Redis sorted sets and know when to shard or approximate (count-min sketch)
  • I can explain operational transform vs CRDTs and why collaborative edits must converge on all clients
  • I can choose a geospatial index (geohash/Redis geo, PostGIS, quadtree) by update and query profile and partition by region
  • I can achieve exactly-once counting on at-least-once delivery via unique event ids and idempotent aggregation
  • I can window aggregates by event time with late-event handling and back them with reconciliation
  • For each system I can name the simpler alternative and when to prefer it
  • I can apply the full system-design method to a new problem, not just recall these designs

Part 66 — Key Takeaways

  • A Redis sorted set makes real-time ranking (update, rank, top-N, neighbors) fast and simple for millions of users; keep a durable copy in PostgreSQL for rebuild, and shard only at extreme scale.
  • When exact top-K over a huge stream is too costly, a count-min sketch counts approximately in fixed memory — trade slight over-estimation for enormous savings where exactness is not required.
  • Collaborative editing is a convergence problem: operational transform (transform ops against concurrent ops, needs coordination) and CRDTs (stable element identities, merge in any order, offline-friendly) both guarantee all clients converge; use a proven library rather than building the merge engine.
  • Choose a geospatial index by profile: Redis geo (geohash) for frequently-moving entities (cheap updates), PostGIS for query-rich static entities joined to attributes, quadtree for adaptive nearest-neighbor; partition by region because proximity queries are always local.
  • Exactly-once counting on at-least-once delivery is achieved by giving each event a unique id and counting it once (dedup) plus atomic aggregate-and-offset updates, not by chasing exactly-once delivery.
  • Aggregate by event time with watermarks and allowed lateness so late events (offline devices) are counted, not silently dropped, and side-output the very late for reconciliation.
  • Reconciliation — recomputing aggregates from raw events and comparing to the served counts — is the non-negotiable accuracy backstop whenever the numbers are billed or otherwise must be trusted.
  • The right data structure or index often turns a hard problem easy (sorted set, geohash, conditional update); choosing it is the core of the design.
  • Accuracy versus cost is a deliberate, recurring trade: approximate where it is acceptable (dashboards, non-billed top-K), exact with reconciliation where it is money (clicks, seats).
  • Every design has a simpler alternative that avoids building the complex system — PostgreSQL-only leaderboards, section-locking over CRDTs, PostGIS-only proximity, database aggregation over streaming — and the method of clarify-estimate-model-design-deep-dive-tradeoffs-alternatives is what lets you choose correctly for any new problem.

Part 67 — Low-Level Design and Machine Coding

The low-level design (LLD), or machine-coding, interview round is different from the system-design round (Parts 40, 65, 66). There you draw boxes, estimate capacity and reason about distributed systems; here you write actual, working, well-structured code for a single self-contained problem — a parking lot, an elevator, a rate limiter — usually in 60 to 90 minutes, and the interviewer judges the quality of your object modelling, your use of design patterns with reason, your extensibility, your naming, and whether it runs and is tested. It is the round where SOLID principles (Part 6) and design patterns stop being theory and become the thing you are scored on.

This Part teaches the LLD round: what it is and how it is scored, a repeatable method for solving any LLD problem, how to model objects well in TypeScript, how to think about concurrency in a Node context, and then eight fully worked problems — parking lot, Splitwise, elevator, movie ticket booking, rate limiter library, food-order state machine, in-memory key-value store with TTL and transactions, and logger/pub-sub — each with requirements, a class diagram, TypeScript code, tests, and the "interviewer twist" (the extension the interviewer springs on you to test whether your design is actually extensible). It builds directly on SOLID and design patterns (Part 6) and the algorithms of Parts 1 and 2.

67.1 What the LLD round is and how to approach it

67.1.1 What it is and how it is scored

Concept

The LLD/machine-coding round asks you to design and implement the classes and logic for a bounded problem — not a distributed system, but the object model and behavior of one component — producing code that compiles, runs, is reasonably tested, and could plausibly be the start of a real implementation. You are judged on how you decompose the problem into classes with clear responsibilities, how cleanly they interact, whether you apply patterns where they genuinely help (and can justify why), how easy your design is to extend, and the basic craft of naming, structure and tests.

Why does it exist?

System design tests whether you can architect; coding (algorithms, Parts 1-2) tests problem-solving; the LLD round tests the daily craft in between — can you take a fuzzy requirement and turn it into clean, extensible, correct object-oriented code under time pressure, the way you would when building a real feature. It reveals whether you actually apply SOLID and patterns in practice (not just define them), whether you write testable code, and whether your design survives a new requirement without a rewrite. It exists because this is most of what senior engineers actually do, and it is hard to fake.

How it is scored

Dimension What the interviewer looks for
Working code It compiles and runs; the core scenario works
Decomposition Classes with single, clear responsibilities (SRP, Part 6)
Extensibility New requirements fit without rewriting (OCP; the "twist" tests this)
Patterns with reason Patterns used where they help, and you can justify each (not pattern soup)
Naming and clarity Names reveal intent; code is readable
Tests Key behavior is tested; you think about edge cases
Communication You narrate your decisions and tradeoffs as you go

The two failure modes at the extremes: writing one giant procedural blob that "works" but is unstructured and unextensible (fails decomposition and the twist), and over-engineering with a dozen patterns and layers for a small problem (fails "patterns with reason" — pattern soup). The target is the middle: clean, well-named classes with the patterns the problem actually needs, tested, and ready to extend.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats the LLD round as a small version of real work and applies the same instincts: clarify the requirements first, model the core entities, define clean interfaces, pick patterns only where they earn their place, write the core logic, test it, and leave clear extension points. They narrate throughout — "I'm making this a strategy because the interviewer will likely want a different policy later" — because communication is scored and because it invites course-correction. They deliberately avoid both extremes (the procedural blob and the pattern soup), aiming for code a teammate could read and extend. They treat the interviewer's "twist" as the real test of their design: a good design absorbs the twist with a small, localized change; a bad one needs a rewrite.

Common mistakes

  • A giant procedural function that works but has no structure or extension points.
  • Pattern soup: applying many patterns to a small problem to look sophisticated.
  • No tests, or not thinking about edge cases.
  • Not clarifying requirements, then solving the wrong problem.
  • Silence — not narrating decisions, so the interviewer cannot follow the reasoning.

Interview questions

  1. What is the LLD/machine-coding round testing? The craft of turning a fuzzy requirement into clean, extensible, correct object-oriented code — decomposition, patterns-with-reason, naming, tests — the daily work of building features.
  2. What are the two extremes to avoid? A structureless procedural blob (unextensible) and over-engineered pattern soup (needless complexity); aim for clean classes with the patterns the problem actually needs.
  3. Why does the interviewer spring a "twist"? To test whether your design is genuinely extensible — a good design absorbs a new requirement with a small localized change; a poor one needs a rewrite.

Practical exercise

Take a small LLD prompt (a vending machine) and, without coding, list the core entities, their responsibilities, the one or two patterns you would use and why, and one likely interviewer twist and how your design would absorb it. Acceptance criteria: each class has a single clear responsibility, each pattern is justified, and the twist fits without a rewrite.

67.1.2 A repeatable method and object modelling in TypeScript

Concept

A repeatable method turns any LLD problem into a structured solution under time pressure: clarify requirements, identify entities, define interfaces, pick patterns, code the core, extend for the twist, test. Alongside it, good object modelling in TypeScript — classes versus interfaces, composition over inheritance, enums versus union types, immutability, and clear error types — is the raw material you shape with that method.

How it works — the method

The LLD method, in order (narrate each step aloud):
  1. Clarify requirements  -> ask about scope, edge cases, what is in/out; write them down
  2. Identify entities     -> the nouns become classes (ParkingLot, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket)
  3. Define interfaces      -> the behaviors, especially where variation is likely (pricing, allocation)
  4. Pick patterns          -> only where variation/extension is expected; justify each
  5. Code the core          -> the main happy-path scenario working, cleanly
  6. Extend for the twist   -> the interviewer's new requirement; show it fits
  7. Test                   -> key behaviors and edge cases

Each step maps to a scoring dimension. Clarifying stops you solving the wrong problem. Identifying entities is decomposition. Defining interfaces where variation is likely sets up extensibility (and the patterns). Picking patterns with justification is "patterns with reason". Coding the core proves it works. Extending for the twist proves extensibility. Testing proves correctness. Narrate each step so the interviewer follows your reasoning.

How it works — object modelling in TypeScript

The TypeScript modelling choices that make LLD code clean:

  • Classes vs interfaces: use an interface to define a contract (a PricingStrategy, a Repository) and class for things with state and behavior (a ParkingLot). Program to interfaces where variation is expected (Part 6, dependency inversion), so you can swap implementations.
  • Composition over inheritance: prefer composing behaviors (a ParkingLot has a PricingStrategy) over deep inheritance hierarchies, which are rigid and the classic LLD mistake. Inheritance for genuine "is-a"; composition for "has-a" and for pluggable behavior.
  • Enums vs union types: for a small fixed set of values, a TypeScript union of string literals (type Size = 'small' | 'medium' | 'large') is often cleaner than an enum and gives exhaustiveness checking (Part 69); use whichever the team prefers consistently.
  • Immutability: make value objects immutable (readonly fields) where it prevents bugs — a Money or a Ticket's core fields should not mutate unexpectedly.
  • Error types: define clear, specific error classes (SpotUnavailableError, InvalidTransitionError) rather than throwing generic Error, so callers can handle them and the code communicates what can go wrong.
// Modelling building blocks for LLD in TypeScript.
type VehicleSize = 'motorcycle' | 'car' | 'truck';   // union, exhaustiveness-checkable

interface PricingStrategy {                            // interface for a varying behavior
  price(durationMinutes: number, size: VehicleSize): number;
}

class SpotUnavailableError extends Error {}            // specific error type

class Money {                                           // immutable value object
  constructor(public readonly cents: number) {
    if (cents < 0) throw new Error('money cannot be negative');
  }
  add(other: Money): Money { return new Money(this.cents + other.cents); }  // returns new, not mutated
}

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior runs the method explicitly and narrates it, because the structure both produces better code and shows the interviewer a clear thought process. They model with composition over inheritance by default (deep inheritance is the most common LLD design smell), program to interfaces exactly where the problem will vary (which is where the interviewer's twist will land), and use immutability and specific error types to make the code robust and self-documenting. They resist over-abstraction: an interface or pattern is introduced only where variation is genuinely expected, not speculatively. The method and these modelling habits together let them produce clean, extensible code quickly and absorb the twist gracefully, which is exactly what the round rewards.

Common mistakes

  • Skipping requirement clarification and solving the wrong problem.
  • Deep inheritance hierarchies instead of composition (rigid, hard to extend).
  • Concrete dependencies everywhere instead of interfaces where variation is expected (hard to extend/test).
  • Generic Error throwing instead of specific error types.
  • Mutable value objects causing spooky bugs.
  • Abstracting speculatively (interfaces/patterns where no variation is expected).

Interview questions

  1. What is a repeatable method for an LLD problem? Clarify requirements, identify entities (classes), define interfaces where variation is likely, pick patterns with justification, code the core, extend for the twist, test — narrating each step.
  2. Why prefer composition over inheritance in LLD? Composition (has-a, pluggable behavior) is flexible and extensible; deep inheritance is rigid and the classic LLD smell. Use inheritance only for genuine is-a relationships.
  3. Where should you introduce interfaces and patterns? Exactly where the problem is expected to vary (pricing, allocation, strategy) — which is where the interviewer's twist lands — not speculatively everywhere.
  4. Why use specific error types over generic Error? They let callers handle specific failures and document what can go wrong, making the code more robust and readable.

Practical exercise

For the parking-lot problem, run the method's first four steps on paper: clarify three requirements, list the entities as classes with one-line responsibilities, identify the one or two behaviors that should be interfaces (because they will vary), and name the pattern you would use for each with a justification. Acceptance criteria: entities have single responsibilities, the varying behaviors are interfaces, and each pattern choice is justified by expected variation.

67.1.3 Concurrency in LLD answers, and why Node changes it

Concept

Many LLD problems (parking lot, booking, rate limiter) involve shared state that concurrent requests touch, so interviewers probe thread safety. The classic (Java/C++) answer is locks, synchronized blocks and atomic operations. In Node, the single-threaded event loop (Part 3, Part 70) changes the answer: your JavaScript runs one operation at a time with no preemption mid-function, so in-memory data races within a single process are largely a non-issue — but cross-process/cross-instance shared state (a real backend) still needs coordination.

How it works

In a classic threaded language, two threads can interleave mid-operation on shared state (read-modify-write races), so you protect shared state with locks or atomics. In Node, because a function runs to completion before any other JavaScript runs (Part 70), a synchronous read-modify-write on an in-memory structure cannot be interleaved by another request — so a simple in-memory counter or map needs no lock within one process. The subtlety: the moment you await (a database call, a network call), you yield, and another request can run in between, so state that spans an await can still race (a check-then-act across an await is not atomic). And the real backend runs many processes/instances, so shared state that must be consistent across them lives in a database or Redis, protected by the database's atomicity or a distributed lock — which is the Part 13 and Part 65 (seat booking) concurrency control.

Classic (threaded): shared in-memory state -> locks/atomics to prevent interleaving.
Node (single thread):
  - synchronous in-memory read-modify-write -> atomic within the process (no lock needed)
  - state spanning an `await` -> can race (yielded); use atomic ops or a lock
  - cross-process/instance shared state -> coordinate in DB/Redis (conditional update,
    distributed lock) exactly as in the seat-booking design (Part 65)

In the interview, state this clearly: "In Node, in-memory state within one process is safe for synchronous operations because of the event loop, so I will not add locks for that; for anything that spans an await or must be consistent across instances, I would use the database's atomicity or a distributed lock." This shows you understand concurrency and the runtime, which impresses more than reflexively adding locks everywhere.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior tailors the concurrency answer to Node rather than parroting the Java answer: no locks for synchronous in-memory state (the event loop serializes it), explicit care for state spanning an await (where yielding allows interleaving), and real coordination (database atomic operations, distributed locks) for cross-instance shared state, exactly as in the seat-booking design (Part 65). They point out that a real deployment runs many instances, so the LLD's in-memory structure would, in production, be a database or Redis with proper concurrency control. Showing this runtime-aware nuance — not "I'd synchronize everything" — demonstrates depth.

Interview questions

  1. How does Node's single-threaded model change the thread-safety answer in LLD? Synchronous in-memory read-modify-write is atomic within a process (the event loop serializes it), so no locks are needed there; but state spanning an await can race, and cross-instance shared state needs coordination in a database or Redis.
  2. When does in-memory state still race in Node? When a logical operation spans an await (a check-then-act across a yield point), because another request can run in between.
  3. How would the in-memory LLD structure work in a real multi-instance deployment? It would move to a database or Redis with atomic operations or a distributed lock for cross-instance consistency (the seat-booking pattern).

67.2 Worked problem: Parking Lot

67.2.1 Requirements

Design a parking lot: vehicles of different sizes park in appropriately-sized spots, the lot tracks availability, issues a ticket on entry, and charges a fee on exit based on duration. Clarify: multiple spot sizes (motorcycle, compact, large); a vehicle takes the smallest fitting spot (or a defined policy); ticket on entry, fee on exit; the lot reports availability. In/out of scope: we focus on allocation, ticketing and pricing; payment processing is stubbed.

67.2.2 Class diagram

classDiagram
    class ParkingLot {
        -levels: Level[]
        -pricing: PricingStrategy
        +parkVehicle(vehicle) Ticket
        +unpark(ticket) Money
        +availability() Map
    }
    class Level {
        -spots: Spot[]
        +findSpot(size) Spot
    }
    class Spot {
        -size: SpotSize
        -occupiedBy: Vehicle
        +canFit(vehicle) boolean
        +assign(vehicle)
        +release()
    }
    class Vehicle { <<interface>> +size() VehicleSize }
    class Ticket { +id +spot +entryTime }
    class PricingStrategy { <<interface>> +price(duration, size) Money }
    ParkingLot --> Level
    ParkingLot --> PricingStrategy
    Level --> Spot
    Spot --> Vehicle
    ParkingLot ..> Ticket

The design uses the strategy pattern for pricing (because the interviewer will likely want a different pricing policy — the twist) and keeps allocation behind a method so the allocation policy can also vary. Composition throughout (a lot has levels, a level has spots), no inheritance hierarchy of vehicles beyond a simple size.

67.2.3 Code

type VehicleSize = 'motorcycle' | 'car' | 'truck';
type SpotSize = 'small' | 'medium' | 'large';

const FITS: Record<VehicleSize, SpotSize[]> = {
  motorcycle: ['small', 'medium', 'large'],
  car: ['medium', 'large'],
  truck: ['large'],
};

interface PricingStrategy { price(durationMinutes: number, size: VehicleSize): Money; }

class Money { constructor(readonly cents: number) {} }

class SpotUnavailableError extends Error {}

class Spot {
  private occupiedBy: VehicleSize | null = null;
  constructor(readonly id: string, readonly size: SpotSize) {}
  canFit(v: VehicleSize): boolean { return this.occupiedBy === null && FITS[v].includes(this.size); }
  assign(v: VehicleSize) { this.occupiedBy = v; }
  release() { this.occupiedBy = null; }
  get free() { return this.occupiedBy === null; }
}

class Ticket {
  constructor(readonly id: string, readonly spot: Spot, readonly size: VehicleSize, readonly entryTime: number) {}
}

class ParkingLot {
  constructor(private readonly spots: Spot[], private readonly pricing: PricingStrategy) {}

  park(size: VehicleSize, now = Date.now()): Ticket {
    // smallest fitting free spot (allocation policy; could be its own strategy)
    const spot = this.spots
      .filter((s) => s.canFit(size))
      .sort((a, b) => sizeRank(a.size) - sizeRank(b.size))[0];
    if (!spot) throw new SpotUnavailableError(`no spot for ${size}`);
    spot.assign(size);
    return new Ticket(crypto.randomUUID(), spot, size, now);
  }

  unpark(ticket: Ticket, now = Date.now()): Money {
    const minutes = Math.ceil((now - ticket.entryTime) / 60000);
    const fee = this.pricing.price(minutes, ticket.size);
    ticket.spot.release();
    return fee;
  }

  availability(): Record<SpotSize, number> {
    const avail: Record<SpotSize, number> = { small: 0, medium: 0, large: 0 };
    for (const s of this.spots) if (s.free) avail[s.size]++;
    return avail;
  }
}

function sizeRank(s: SpotSize) { return { small: 0, medium: 1, large: 2 }[s]; }

// A concrete pricing strategy (hourly, by size) -- swappable for the twist.
class HourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy {
  constructor(private readonly ratePerHourCents: Record<VehicleSize, number>) {}
  price(minutes: number, size: VehicleSize): Money {
    const hours = Math.ceil(minutes / 60);
    return new Money(hours * this.ratePerHourCents[size]);
  }
}

67.2.4 Tests

// Using any test runner (Jest, Part 24). Key behaviors and edge cases.
const spots = [new Spot('a', 'small'), new Spot('b', 'medium'), new Spot('c', 'large')];
const lot = new ParkingLot(spots, new HourlyPricing({ motorcycle: 100, car: 200, truck: 400 }));

test('parks a car in the smallest fitting spot', () => {
  const t = lot.park('car');
  expect(t.spot.size).toBe('medium');            // not large; smallest that fits
});

test('throws when no spot fits', () => {
  lot.park('truck');                              // takes the only large spot
  expect(() => lot.park('truck')).toThrow(SpotUnavailableError);
});

test('charges by duration and size', () => {
  const t = lot.park('motorcycle', 0);
  const fee = lot.unpark(t, 90 * 60000);          // 90 min -> 2 hours
  expect(fee.cents).toBe(200);                     // 2 * 100
});

test('releases the spot on unpark', () => {
  const before = lot.availability().small;
  const t = lot.park('motorcycle');
  lot.unpark(t);
  expect(lot.availability().small).toBe(before);
});

67.2.5 Interviewer twist

"Now add tiered pricing: the first hour is free, and trucks pay double after 3 hours." Because pricing is a strategy behind an interface, you add a new PricingStrategy implementation (TieredPricing) and inject it — no change to ParkingLot, Spot or Ticket. If pricing had been hardcoded inside unpark, this twist would force editing core logic. This is exactly why the strategy pattern was chosen up front: the twist lands on the varying behavior you anticipated, and your design absorbs it with one new class. A second common twist — "support multiple entry/exit gates and reserved spots" — is absorbed by the allocation policy (make it a strategy too) and a reserved flag on Spot.

67.3 Worked problem: Splitwise

67.3.1 Requirements

Design an expense-sharing system: users in groups add expenses split among members (equally, by exact amounts, or by percentage), the system tracks who owes whom, and can simplify debts (minimize the number of transactions to settle). Clarify: split types (equal, exact, percentage); track balances; simplify debts; handle settlements. In scope: expenses, balances, debt simplification; out of scope: payment processing.

67.3.2 Class diagram

classDiagram
    class ExpenseService {
        -balances: BalanceSheet
        +addExpense(expense)
        +balancesFor(userId) Map
        +simplify() Transfer[]
    }
    class Expense {
        +paidBy: userId
        +amount: Money
        +split: SplitStrategy
    }
    class SplitStrategy { <<interface>> +shares(amount, participants) Map }
    class EqualSplit
    class ExactSplit
    class PercentageSplit
    class BalanceSheet {
        -owes: Map
        +apply(from, to, amount)
        +net(userId) number
    }
    ExpenseService --> BalanceSheet
    ExpenseService ..> Expense
    Expense --> SplitStrategy
    SplitStrategy <|.. EqualSplit
    SplitStrategy <|.. ExactSplit
    SplitStrategy <|.. PercentageSplit

The strategy pattern again for split types (the obvious variation point), and a BalanceSheet that tracks net balances. Debt simplification is a small algorithm on the net balances.

67.3.3 Code

interface SplitStrategy { shares(amountCents: number, participants: string[]): Record<string, number>; }

class EqualSplit implements SplitStrategy {
  shares(amount: number, participants: string[]) {
    const each = Math.floor(amount / participants.length);
    const rem = amount - each * participants.length;     // give the remainder to the first
    const out: Record<string, number> = {};
    participants.forEach((p, i) => (out[p] = each + (i === 0 ? rem : 0)));
    return out;
  }
}

class PercentageSplit implements SplitStrategy {
  constructor(private readonly pct: Record<string, number>) {}  // must sum to 100
  shares(amount: number, participants: string[]) {
    const out: Record<string, number> = {};
    for (const p of participants) out[p] = Math.round((amount * this.pct[p]) / 100);
    return out;
  }
}

class BalanceSheet {
  // net[user] > 0 means others owe this user; < 0 means this user owes.
  private net = new Map<string, number>();
  private add(user: string, delta: number) { this.net.set(user, (this.net.get(user) ?? 0) + delta); }

  applyExpense(paidBy: string, amount: number, shares: Record<string, number>) {
    this.add(paidBy, amount);                              // payer is owed the full amount
    for (const [user, share] of Object.entries(shares)) this.add(user, -share);  // each owes their share
  }

  net_(user: string) { return this.net.get(user) ?? 0; }
  entries() { return [...this.net.entries()]; }
}

interface Transfer { from: string; to: string; amountCents: number; }

class ExpenseService {
  private sheet = new BalanceSheet();

  addExpense(paidBy: string, amountCents: number, participants: string[], split: SplitStrategy) {
    this.sheet.applyExpense(paidBy, amountCents, split.shares(amountCents, participants));
  }

  // Simplify debts: greedily match biggest creditor with biggest debtor.
  simplify(): Transfer[] {
    const creditors = this.sheet.entries().filter(([, v]) => v > 0).map(([u, v]) => ({ u, v }));
    const debtors = this.sheet.entries().filter(([, v]) => v < 0).map(([u, v]) => ({ u, v: -v }));
    creditors.sort((a, b) => b.v - a.v); debtors.sort((a, b) => b.v - a.v);
    const transfers: Transfer[] = [];
    let i = 0, j = 0;
    while (i < debtors.length && j < creditors.length) {
      const amount = Math.min(debtors[i].v, creditors[j].v);
      transfers.push({ from: debtors[i].u, to: creditors[j].u, amountCents: amount });
      debtors[i].v -= amount; creditors[j].v -= amount;
      if (debtors[i].v === 0) i++;
      if (creditors[j].v === 0) j++;
    }
    return transfers;
  }
}

67.3.4 Tests

test('equal split tracks balances', () => {
  const s = new ExpenseService();
  s.addExpense('alice', 3000, ['alice', 'bob', 'carol'], new EqualSplit());  // alice paid 30
  // alice is owed 30 minus her own 10 share; bob and carol each owe 10
  const t = s.simplify();
  const total = t.reduce((a, x) => a + x.amountCents, 0);
  expect(total).toBe(2000);                       // bob + carol owe 20 total to alice
});

test('simplify minimizes transfers', () => {
  const s = new ExpenseService();
  s.addExpense('alice', 3000, ['alice', 'bob', 'carol'], new EqualSplit());
  s.addExpense('bob', 3000, ['alice', 'bob', 'carol'], new EqualSplit());
  const t = s.simplify();
  // alice and bob each net to even on the second expense; carol owes both
  expect(t.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(2);
});

67.3.5 Interviewer twist

"Add support for different currencies, and for settling only part of a debt." Currencies are absorbed by making Money currency-aware (and converting, or keeping per-currency balance sheets) — a localized change to the value object and BalanceSheet. Partial settlement is a new operation on BalanceSheet (applyPayment(from, to, amount)) that adjusts the nets, which the simplify algorithm then reflects. Because splits are a strategy and balances are isolated in BalanceSheet, both twists are localized. A design that computed balances ad hoc inside expense handling would struggle; isolating the balance logic is what makes it extensible.

67.4 Worked problem: Elevator System

67.4.1 Requirements

Design an elevator system: one or more elevators serve floor requests, moving up/down, picking up and dropping off, with a scheduling policy deciding which elevator serves a request and the order of stops. Clarify: multiple elevators; external requests (a floor, a direction) and internal requests (a destination floor from inside); a scheduling strategy; door and movement states. In scope: request handling, scheduling, elevator state; out of scope: physical hardware control.

67.4.2 Class diagram

classDiagram
    class ElevatorSystem {
        -elevators: Elevator[]
        -scheduler: SchedulingStrategy
        +requestExternal(floor, direction)
        +requestInternal(elevatorId, floor)
        +step()
    }
    class Elevator {
        -currentFloor: int
        -direction: Direction
        -state: ElevatorState
        -targets: SortedSet
        +addTarget(floor)
        +step()
    }
    class SchedulingStrategy { <<interface>> +assign(elevators, request) Elevator }
    class NearestElevator
    ElevatorSystem --> Elevator
    ElevatorSystem --> SchedulingStrategy
    SchedulingStrategy <|.. NearestElevator

Scheduling is a strategy (the obvious variation and twist point); each elevator is a state machine (idle, moving up/down, doors open). Composition: the system has elevators and a scheduler.

67.4.3 Code

type Direction = 'up' | 'down' | 'idle';
type ElevatorState = 'idle' | 'moving' | 'doors_open';

interface SchedulingStrategy { assign(elevators: Elevator[], floor: number, dir: Direction): Elevator; }

class Elevator {
  currentFloor = 0;
  direction: Direction = 'idle';
  state: ElevatorState = 'idle';
  private targets = new Set<number>();
  constructor(readonly id: string) {}

  addTarget(floor: number) { this.targets.add(floor); this.updateDirection(); }

  private updateDirection() {
    if (this.targets.size === 0) { this.direction = 'idle'; this.state = 'idle'; return; }
    const next = this.nextTarget();
    this.direction = next > this.currentFloor ? 'up' : next < this.currentFloor ? 'down' : 'idle';
    this.state = this.direction === 'idle' ? 'doors_open' : 'moving';
  }

  private nextTarget(): number {
    // simplest: nearest target in the current direction, else nearest overall
    const arr = [...this.targets].sort((a, b) => Math.abs(a - this.currentFloor) - Math.abs(b - this.currentFloor));
    return arr[0];
  }

  step() {
    if (this.targets.size === 0) return;
    const next = this.nextTarget();
    if (this.currentFloor < next) this.currentFloor++;
    else if (this.currentFloor > next) this.currentFloor--;
    if (this.currentFloor === next) { this.targets.delete(next); this.state = 'doors_open'; }
    this.updateDirection();
  }

  distanceTo(floor: number) { return Math.abs(this.currentFloor - floor); }
}

class NearestElevator implements SchedulingStrategy {
  assign(elevators: Elevator[], floor: number): Elevator {
    return elevators.slice().sort((a, b) => a.distanceTo(floor) - b.distanceTo(floor))[0];
  }
}

class ElevatorSystem {
  constructor(private readonly elevators: Elevator[], private readonly scheduler: SchedulingStrategy) {}
  requestExternal(floor: number, dir: Direction) { this.scheduler.assign(this.elevators, floor, dir).addTarget(floor); }
  requestInternal(elevatorId: string, floor: number) {
    this.elevators.find((e) => e.id === elevatorId)?.addTarget(floor);
  }
  step() { for (const e of this.elevators) e.step(); }
}

67.4.4 Tests

test('assigns the nearest elevator and moves toward the target', () => {
  const a = new Elevator('a'); a.currentFloor = 0;
  const b = new Elevator('b'); b.currentFloor = 8;
  const sys = new ElevatorSystem([a, b], new NearestElevator());
  sys.requestExternal(2, 'up');                   // nearest is a (floor 0)
  sys.step(); sys.step();
  expect(a.currentFloor).toBe(2);                 // a moved up to floor 2
  expect(b.currentFloor).toBe(8);                 // b did not move
});

test('serves an internal request', () => {
  const a = new Elevator('a');
  const sys = new ElevatorSystem([a], new NearestElevator());
  sys.requestInternal('a', 5);
  for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) sys.step();
  expect(a.currentFloor).toBe(5);
});

67.4.5 Interviewer twist

"Change the scheduling to a SCAN/elevator algorithm (keep going in one direction serving all requests, then reverse) instead of nearest-first." Because scheduling is a strategy and the elevator's target selection is encapsulated, you add a new SchedulingStrategy and adjust the nextTarget policy (ideally also behind a strategy), without rewriting the system. A second twist — "add express elevators that only serve certain floors" — is absorbed by giving an elevator a set of serviceable floors and having the scheduler respect it. The state machine and the pluggable scheduler are what make these twists localized changes rather than rewrites.

67.5 Worked problem: Movie Ticket Booking (seat locking)

67.5.1 Requirements

Design a movie ticket booking system: shows have seats, users select and book seats, and the same seat is never booked twice — with a brief hold on selected seats while the user pays, releasing the hold on timeout. Clarify: shows, seats per show, seat states (available, held, booked), a hold timeout, no double-booking. This is the LLD cousin of the seat-booking system design (Part 65); here we focus on the object model and the locking logic rather than the distributed scale.

67.5.2 Class diagram

classDiagram
    class BookingService {
        -shows: Map
        +hold(showId, seatIds, userId) Hold
        +confirm(holdId) Booking
        +releaseExpired(now)
    }
    class Show {
        -seats: Map
        +seat(id) Seat
    }
    class Seat {
        -state: SeatState
        -holdId: string
        -holdExpiresAt: number
        +tryHold(holdId, expiresAt) boolean
        +confirm(holdId) boolean
        +release()
    }
    class Hold { +id +seatIds +userId +expiresAt }
    class Booking { +id +holdId +seatIds }
    BookingService --> Show
    Show --> Seat
    BookingService ..> Hold
    BookingService ..> Booking

The no-double-book invariant lives in Seat.tryHold, which is an atomic check-and-set: it only holds a seat that is currently available, returning false otherwise. This mirrors the conditional update from the system-design version (Part 65).

67.5.3 Code

type SeatState = 'available' | 'held' | 'booked';

class Seat {
  private state: SeatState = 'available';
  private holdId: string | null = null;
  private holdExpiresAt = 0;
  constructor(readonly id: string) {}

  // Atomic within the event loop: no await, so no interleaving (see 67.1.3).
  tryHold(holdId: string, expiresAt: number, now: number): boolean {
    if (this.state === 'available' || (this.state === 'held' && this.holdExpiresAt <= now)) {
      this.state = 'held'; this.holdId = holdId; this.holdExpiresAt = expiresAt;
      return true;
    }
    return false;                                   // already held (valid) or booked
  }

  confirm(holdId: string, now: number): boolean {
    if (this.state === 'held' && this.holdId === holdId && this.holdExpiresAt > now) {
      this.state = 'booked'; return true;
    }
    return false;                                    // hold expired or not this hold
  }

  releaseIfExpired(now: number) {
    if (this.state === 'held' && this.holdExpiresAt <= now) {
      this.state = 'available'; this.holdId = null;
    }
  }
  get stateValue() { return this.state; }
}

class Show {
  private seats = new Map<string, Seat>();
  constructor(readonly id: string, seatIds: string[]) { for (const s of seatIds) this.seats.set(s, new Seat(s)); }
  seat(id: string) { const s = this.seats.get(id); if (!s) throw new Error('no such seat'); return s; }
  allSeats() { return [...this.seats.values()]; }
}

interface Hold { id: string; showId: string; seatIds: string[]; userId: string; expiresAt: number; }
class HoldFailedError extends Error {}

class BookingService {
  private shows = new Map<string, Show>();
  private holds = new Map<string, Hold>();
  constructor(private readonly holdMs = 5 * 60000) {}

  addShow(show: Show) { this.shows.set(show.id, show); }

  hold(showId: string, seatIds: string[], userId: string, now = Date.now()): Hold {
    const show = this.shows.get(showId)!;
    const holdId = crypto.randomUUID();
    const expiresAt = now + this.holdMs;
    const held: string[] = [];
    for (const id of seatIds) {
      if (show.seat(id).tryHold(holdId, expiresAt, now)) held.push(id);
      else { held.forEach((h) => show.seat(h).releaseIfExpired(now)); throw new HoldFailedError(`seat ${id} unavailable`); }
    }
    const hold: Hold = { id: holdId, showId, seatIds, userId, expiresAt };
    this.holds.set(holdId, hold);
    return hold;
  }

  confirm(holdId: string, now = Date.now()) {
    const hold = this.holds.get(holdId);
    if (!hold) throw new Error('no such hold');
    const show = this.shows.get(hold.showId)!;
    for (const id of hold.seatIds) if (!show.seat(id).confirm(holdId, now)) throw new HoldFailedError('hold expired');
    this.holds.delete(holdId);
    return { id: crypto.randomUUID(), holdId, seatIds: hold.seatIds };
  }

  releaseExpired(now = Date.now()) { for (const show of this.shows.values()) for (const s of show.allSeats()) s.releaseIfExpired(now); }
}

67.5.4 Tests

test('two holds for the same seat: only one succeeds', () => {
  const svc = new BookingService();
  svc.addShow(new Show('s1', ['A1', 'A2']));
  svc.hold('s1', ['A1'], 'alice');
  expect(() => svc.hold('s1', ['A1'], 'bob')).toThrow(HoldFailedError);  // no double-book
});

test('hold expires and seat becomes available', () => {
  const svc = new BookingService(1000);
  svc.addShow(new Show('s1', ['A1']));
  svc.hold('s1', ['A1'], 'alice', 0);
  svc.releaseExpired(2000);                         // past expiry
  expect(() => svc.hold('s1', ['A1'], 'bob', 2000)).not.toThrow();  // now bob can hold
});

test('confirm fails after hold expires', () => {
  const svc = new BookingService(1000);
  svc.addShow(new Show('s1', ['A1']));
  const h = svc.hold('s1', ['A1'], 'alice', 0);
  expect(() => svc.confirm(h.id, 2000)).toThrow(HoldFailedError);
});

67.5.5 Interviewer twist

"Make this work across multiple server instances." This is where the Node single-process atomicity (67.1.3) breaks down: the in-memory Seat is per-instance, so two instances could each hold the same seat. The answer is to move the seat state and the atomic hold into a shared store — the conditional update in PostgreSQL (UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'available') or an atomic Redis operation — exactly the seat-booking system design (Part 65). Narrating this transition from the single-process LLD to the distributed design shows you understand both the LLD craft and how it maps to real multi-instance production, which is a strong signal. A second twist — "hold the best-available seats automatically for a party of N" — is a new allocation method over the same seat primitives.

67.6 Worked problem: Rate Limiter Library (pluggable strategies)

67.6.1 Requirements

Design a reusable rate limiter library with pluggable algorithms: a caller asks "is this request (for this key) allowed?" and the limiter answers yes/no based on a configurable strategy (token bucket, fixed window, sliding window). Clarify: per-key limits (per user, per IP), multiple algorithms, a clean interface so callers do not care which algorithm. This is the LLD of the rate limiter whose algorithms are in Part 2 and whose distributed version is in Part 40.

67.6.2 Class diagram

classDiagram
    class RateLimiter {
        -strategy: RateLimitStrategy
        +allow(key) boolean
    }
    class RateLimitStrategy { <<interface>> +allow(key, now) boolean }
    class TokenBucket
    class FixedWindow
    class SlidingWindowLog
    RateLimiter --> RateLimitStrategy
    RateLimitStrategy <|.. TokenBucket
    RateLimitStrategy <|.. FixedWindow
    RateLimitStrategy <|.. SlidingWindowLog

The whole point is the strategy pattern: the algorithm is pluggable behind one interface, so the caller and the library are independent of which algorithm is used — this is the design the problem is really testing.

67.6.3 Code

interface RateLimitStrategy { allow(key: string, now: number): boolean; }

// Token bucket: refill tokens over time, allow if a token is available.
class TokenBucket implements RateLimitStrategy {
  private buckets = new Map<string, { tokens: number; last: number }>();
  constructor(private readonly capacity: number, private readonly refillPerSec: number) {}
  allow(key: string, now: number): boolean {
    const b = this.buckets.get(key) ?? { tokens: this.capacity, last: now };
    const elapsed = (now - b.last) / 1000;
    b.tokens = Math.min(this.capacity, b.tokens + elapsed * this.refillPerSec);  // refill
    b.last = now;
    if (b.tokens >= 1) { b.tokens -= 1; this.buckets.set(key, b); return true; }
    this.buckets.set(key, b);
    return false;
  }
}

// Fixed window: a count per fixed time window.
class FixedWindow implements RateLimitStrategy {
  private windows = new Map<string, { windowStart: number; count: number }>();
  constructor(private readonly limit: number, private readonly windowMs: number) {}
  allow(key: string, now: number): boolean {
    const start = Math.floor(now / this.windowMs) * this.windowMs;
    const w = this.windows.get(key);
    if (!w || w.windowStart !== start) { this.windows.set(key, { windowStart: start, count: 1 }); return true; }
    if (w.count < this.limit) { w.count++; return true; }
    return false;                                    // over the limit for this window
  }
}

// Sliding window log: timestamps within the window; precise but more memory.
class SlidingWindowLog implements RateLimitStrategy {
  private log = new Map<string, number[]>();
  constructor(private readonly limit: number, private readonly windowMs: number) {}
  allow(key: string, now: number): boolean {
    const times = (this.log.get(key) ?? []).filter((t) => t > now - this.windowMs);  // drop old
    if (times.length < this.limit) { times.push(now); this.log.set(key, times); return true; }
    this.log.set(key, times);
    return false;
  }
}

class RateLimiter {
  constructor(private readonly strategy: RateLimitStrategy) {}
  allow(key: string, now = Date.now()): boolean { return this.strategy.allow(key, now); }
}

67.6.4 Tests

test('token bucket allows up to capacity then refills', () => {
  const rl = new RateLimiter(new TokenBucket(2, 1));     // capacity 2, 1/sec refill
  expect(rl.allow('u1', 0)).toBe(true);
  expect(rl.allow('u1', 0)).toBe(true);
  expect(rl.allow('u1', 0)).toBe(false);                 // bucket empty
  expect(rl.allow('u1', 1000)).toBe(true);               // 1s later, 1 token refilled
});

test('fixed window resets each window', () => {
  const rl = new RateLimiter(new FixedWindow(2, 1000));
  expect(rl.allow('u1', 0)).toBe(true);
  expect(rl.allow('u1', 500)).toBe(true);
  expect(rl.allow('u1', 600)).toBe(false);               // 3rd in the window
  expect(rl.allow('u1', 1100)).toBe(true);               // new window
});

test('different keys are independent', () => {
  const rl = new RateLimiter(new FixedWindow(1, 1000));
  expect(rl.allow('u1', 0)).toBe(true);
  expect(rl.allow('u2', 0)).toBe(true);                  // separate key, own limit
});

67.6.5 Interviewer twist

"Make it distributed, shared across instances, and add a sliding-window-counter algorithm." Distributed is the key transition: the in-memory maps are per-instance, so a shared limit needs the state in Redis with atomic operations (the Lua-script approach in Part 40's rate limiter). Because the algorithm is behind the RateLimitStrategy interface, you add a RedisTokenBucket implementation that keeps state in Redis — the RateLimiter and callers are unchanged. Adding the sliding-window-counter algorithm is just another strategy class. The strategy interface is exactly what makes both twists additive: a new implementation, no change to the core. This is the payoff of designing the variation point as an interface from the start.

67.7 Interlude: patterns across these problems

Notice the recurring move in all five problems so far: identify the one behavior the interviewer is most likely to want to vary (pricing, split type, scheduling, the rate-limit algorithm, the allocation policy) and put it behind an interface as a strategy, so the twist lands on a pluggable implementation rather than on core logic. The state-machine pattern recurs too (elevator states, seat states, and the order state machine in 67.8). The remaining three problems add two more patterns — the observer/pub-sub pattern and careful use of composition for transactional state — rounding out the toolkit. The lesson is not "memorize these designs" but "anticipate the variation point, model it as an interface, and the twist becomes a one-class change."

67.8 Worked problem: Food-Order State Machine with Notifications

67.8.1 Requirements

Design a food-delivery order lifecycle: an order moves through states (placed, confirmed, preparing, out-for-delivery, delivered, cancelled) with only valid transitions allowed, and interested parties (the customer, the restaurant, analytics) are notified on each transition. Clarify: the allowed transitions, who is notified, that illegal transitions are rejected. This combines the state pattern (valid transitions) and the observer pattern (notifications) — the two patterns the problem is testing.

67.8.2 Class diagram

classDiagram
    class Order {
        -state: OrderState
        -observers: OrderObserver[]
        +transitionTo(next)
        +subscribe(observer)
    }
    class OrderStateMachine { +canTransition(from, to) boolean }
    class OrderObserver { <<interface>> +onTransition(order, from, to) }
    class CustomerNotifier
    class RestaurantNotifier
    class AnalyticsRecorder
    Order --> OrderStateMachine
    Order --> OrderObserver
    OrderObserver <|.. CustomerNotifier
    OrderObserver <|.. RestaurantNotifier
    OrderObserver <|.. AnalyticsRecorder

The state machine centralizes the allowed transitions (a data-driven table, as in Part 69's order example), rejecting illegal ones; observers are notified on each valid transition, decoupling the order from who reacts to its changes.

67.8.3 Code

type OrderState = 'placed' | 'confirmed' | 'preparing' | 'out_for_delivery' | 'delivered' | 'cancelled';

const ALLOWED: Record<OrderState, OrderState[]> = {
  placed: ['confirmed', 'cancelled'],
  confirmed: ['preparing', 'cancelled'],
  preparing: ['out_for_delivery', 'cancelled'],
  out_for_delivery: ['delivered'],
  delivered: [],
  cancelled: [],
};

class InvalidTransitionError extends Error {}

interface OrderObserver { onTransition(orderId: string, from: OrderState, to: OrderState): void; }

class Order {
  private state: OrderState = 'placed';
  private observers: OrderObserver[] = [];
  constructor(readonly id: string) {}

  subscribe(o: OrderObserver) { this.observers.push(o); }

  transitionTo(next: OrderState) {
    if (!ALLOWED[this.state].includes(next)) {
      throw new InvalidTransitionError(`cannot go from ${this.state} to ${next}`);
    }
    const from = this.state;
    this.state = next;
    for (const o of this.observers) o.onTransition(this.id, from, next);  // notify (observer)
  }
  get current() { return this.state; }
}

class CustomerNotifier implements OrderObserver {
  onTransition(orderId: string, _from: OrderState, to: OrderState) {
    if (to === 'out_for_delivery' || to === 'delivered') {/* send customer notification */}
  }
}
class RestaurantNotifier implements OrderObserver {
  onTransition(orderId: string, _from: OrderState, to: OrderState) {
    if (to === 'confirmed') {/* tell the restaurant to start */}
  }
}
class AnalyticsRecorder implements OrderObserver {
  onTransition(orderId: string, from: OrderState, to: OrderState) {/* record the transition */}
}

67.8.4 Tests

test('allows valid transitions and rejects invalid ones', () => {
  const o = new Order('o1');
  o.transitionTo('confirmed');
  o.transitionTo('preparing');
  expect(o.current).toBe('preparing');
  expect(() => o.transitionTo('delivered')).toThrow(InvalidTransitionError);  // must go out_for_delivery first
});

test('notifies observers on transition', () => {
  const o = new Order('o1');
  const seen: string[] = [];
  o.subscribe({ onTransition: (_id, _f, to) => seen.push(to) });
  o.transitionTo('confirmed'); o.transitionTo('cancelled');  // confirmed allows cancelled
  expect(seen).toEqual(['confirmed', 'cancelled']);
});

test('cannot transition out of a terminal state', () => {
  const o = new Order('o1');
  o.transitionTo('cancelled');
  expect(() => o.transitionTo('confirmed')).toThrow(InvalidTransitionError);
});

67.8.5 Interviewer twist

"Add a new state (returned) and a new observer (a loyalty-points service that awards points on delivery), and make notifications asynchronous/retryable." The new state is a one-line change to the ALLOWED table (data-driven transitions, so no logic to rewrite). The new observer is a new class subscribed to the order — the observer pattern means the order does not change at all. Making notifications async/retryable is localized to how observers are invoked (dispatch to a queue, Part 20, instead of calling synchronously). All three twists are additive because the state transitions are data and the reactions are decoupled observers — the exact separation the two patterns provide.

67.9 Worked problem: In-Memory Key-Value Store with TTL and Transactions

67.9.1 Requirements

Design an in-memory key-value store supporting get, set, delete, per-key TTL (expiry), and simple transactions (begin, commit, rollback) so a group of operations applies atomically or not at all. Clarify: TTL per key with lazy/active expiry; transactions that can be committed or rolled back; nested or single-level transactions (we do single-level with a staging layer). This tests careful state management and atomicity in a bounded setting.

67.9.2 Class diagram

classDiagram
    class KVStore {
        -data: Map
        -tx: Transaction
        +get(key)
        +set(key, value, ttlMs)
        +delete(key)
        +begin()
        +commit()
        +rollback()
    }
    class Entry { +value +expiresAt }
    class Transaction { -staged: Map -deleted: Set }
    KVStore --> Entry
    KVStore --> Transaction

The store holds entries with optional expiry; a transaction stages changes (sets and deletes) that are applied to the main store on commit and discarded on rollback — composition of a staging layer over the base store gives atomicity.

67.9.3 Code

interface Entry { value: string; expiresAt: number | null; }

class KVStore {
  private data = new Map<string, Entry>();
  private staged: Map<string, Entry> | null = null;    // transaction staging (null = no tx)
  private deleted: Set<string> | null = null;

  get(key: string, now = Date.now()): string | null {
    // transaction reads see staged changes first
    if (this.staged) {
      if (this.deleted!.has(key)) return null;
      const s = this.staged.get(key);
      if (s) return this.live(s, now) ? s.value : null;
    }
    const e = this.data.get(key);
    if (!e) return null;
    if (!this.live(e, now)) { this.data.delete(key); return null; }  // lazy expiry on read
    return e.value;
  }

  set(key: string, value: string, ttlMs?: number, now = Date.now()) {
    const entry: Entry = { value, expiresAt: ttlMs ? now + ttlMs : null };
    if (this.staged) { this.staged.set(key, entry); this.deleted!.delete(key); }
    else this.data.set(key, entry);
  }

  delete(key: string) {
    if (this.staged) { this.staged.delete(key); this.deleted!.add(key); }
    else this.data.delete(key);
  }

  begin() { if (this.staged) throw new Error('transaction already open'); this.staged = new Map(); this.deleted = new Set(); }

  commit() {
    if (!this.staged) throw new Error('no transaction');
    for (const k of this.deleted!) this.data.delete(k);
    for (const [k, v] of this.staged) this.data.set(k, v);   // apply staged atomically
    this.staged = null; this.deleted = null;
  }

  rollback() {
    if (!this.staged) throw new Error('no transaction');
    this.staged = null; this.deleted = null;                  // discard staged changes
  }

  private live(e: Entry, now: number) { return e.expiresAt === null || e.expiresAt > now; }
}

67.9.4 Tests

test('set/get/delete with TTL expiry', () => {
  const kv = new KVStore();
  kv.set('a', '1', 1000, 0);
  expect(kv.get('a', 500)).toBe('1');
  expect(kv.get('a', 1500)).toBe(null);             // expired
});

test('transaction commit applies atomically', () => {
  const kv = new KVStore();
  kv.set('a', '1');
  kv.begin();
  kv.set('a', '2'); kv.set('b', '3');
  expect(kv.get('a')).toBe('2');                     // reads see staged
  kv.commit();
  expect(kv.get('a')).toBe('2'); expect(kv.get('b')).toBe('3');
});

test('transaction rollback discards changes', () => {
  const kv = new KVStore();
  kv.set('a', '1');
  kv.begin();
  kv.set('a', '99'); kv.delete('a');
  kv.rollback();
  expect(kv.get('a')).toBe('1');                     // unchanged after rollback
});

67.9.5 Interviewer twist

"Add active expiry (a background sweeper, not just lazy on read) and nested transactions." Active expiry is a periodic sweep over data removing expired entries (plus the lazy check already on read as a backstop) — a localized addition.
